question: A summer insect swarms an eastern U.S. forest by the billions, its black body carrying two brilliant red compound eyes above clear, orange-veined wings. Which insect wears this eerie red-eyed look?
answer: The periodical cicada
choices: The periodical cicada
The luna moth
The dog-day katydid
The box elder bug
context: The adult periodical cicada has two brilliant red compound eyes set in a black body with clear, orange-veined wings — the eerie look people remember when billions surface at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical_cicadas

question: A periodical cicada nymph clings to a tree root deep in the dark soil, quietly sucking sap. For a 17-year cicada, roughly how much of its whole life is spent hidden underground like this before it ever sees daylight?
answer: About 99.5 percent of it
choices: About 99.5 percent of it
About half of it
About a tenth of it
About a quarter of it
context: Periodical cicadas spend about 99.5% of their entire lives underground as nymphs, sucking sap from tree roots in the dark for 13 or 17 years before ever seeing daylight. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical_cicadas

question: After more than a decade in the dark, a whole generation of periodical cicadas erupts from the ground in one synchronized spring. What environmental signal tips them off that the moment has finally come?
answer: The soil 8 inches down warming to about 64 degrees F
choices: The soil 8 inches down warming to about 64 degrees F
The first full moon after the spring equinox
The scent of new tree blossoms overhead
A sudden spring rain soaking the ground
context: A whole generation surfaces together when the soil 8 inches (20 cm) down warms to about 64°F (17.9°C). Underground, the nymphs appear to 'count' the years by sensing seasonal changes in the tree's xylem sap — an internal calendar with no clock. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical_cicadas

question: A male periodical cicada is barely the size of a thumb, yet his song carries across a whole forest, one of the loudest calls any insect makes. His tymbals, ribbed membranes on his sides, buckle hundreds of times a second to make the clicks. What lets so tiny a body throw that sound so far?
answer: His hollow abdomen works as a resonating chamber that amplifies the clicks into a roar
choices: His hollow abdomen works as a resonating chamber that amplifies the clicks into a roar
His wing veins trap and re-release the sound like a second pair of drums
His stiffened outer shell rings like a bell each time a tymbal snaps
His crowd of neighbors all click in unison to stack the sound louder
context: Only male cicadas sing, using a tymbal — a stiff, ribbed membrane on each side of the hollow abdomen, snapped in and out by muscles so fast the clicks blur into a continuous song. The hollow abdomen acts as a resonating chamber, helping make a cicada chorus one of the loudest sounds in the insect world, around 100 decibels — often called the loudest male chorus on Earth. Source: https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/05/05/cicadas/

question: Periodical cicadas do not hide, sting, or flee. Their whole defense is to surface all at once at over 1.5 million per acre, a strategy scientists call 'predator satiation.' How does simply arriving in such staggering numbers keep the species going?
answer: Predators fill up long before the swarm runs out, so most cicadas survive to mate
choices: Predators fill up long before the swarm runs out, so most cicadas survive to mate
The dense swarm confuses hunting birds into striking each other instead
The crush of bodies buries and smothers most ground predators outright
The sheer noise of the chorus drives most predators out of the forest
context: They emerge at more than 1.5 million cicadas per acre (about 370 per square meter) — so many that predators simply cannot eat them all, and most survive to mate. Scientists call this 'predator satiation.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical_cicadas  (Legend.)

question: Of all the intervals a cicada could wait, the periodical broods land on 13 and 17 years, never 12, 15, or 18. Biologists like Stephen Jay Gould find it striking that both are prime. What survival edge is that oddly chosen interval thought to give the cicadas?
answer: A predator on its own 2-, 3-, or 4-year cycle can almost never peak in the same year the cicadas emerge
choices: A predator on its own 2-, 3-, or 4-year cycle can almost never peak in the same year the cicadas emerge
The long wait starves out any predator that had specialized in eating cicadas
Neighboring broods on different primes never surface together and compete for food
The gap outlasts the memory any single predator can pass to its young
context: This is a leading hypothesis, not proven fact: a prime, indivisible cycle makes it nearly impossible for any predator with a shorter life cycle to line up and feast every time. It was first formally proposed by entomologists Monte Lloyd and Henry Dybas in a 1966 paper and later popularized by evolutionary biologist Stephen Jay Gould in a 1977 essay. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical_cicadas  (Legend.)

question: A 17-year cicada waits seventeen years underground, then finally climbs into the sunlight to sing and mate. Once it emerges as an adult, how long does it actually get to live above ground before it dies?
answer: Only four to six weeks
choices: Only four to six weeks
A full summer, then winter below
About one year
A single day and night
context: After 13 or 17 years underground, the emerged adults live only four to six weeks — just long enough to sing, mate, and lay eggs — and then die, and the cycle begins again. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical_cicadas

question: This burrowing African mammal has a long pig-like snout, tall rabbit-like ears, and a heavy tail, and slurps up ants and termites all night long. What is it?
answer: The aardvark
choices: The aardvark
The giant anteater
The pangolin
The armadillo
context: Orycteropus afer, the aardvark, is a mash-up of borrowed parts: a pig-like snout, long donkey- or rabbit-like ears, a heavy kangaroo-like tail, and spade-clawed digging feet. A big one weighs 60-80 kg and stretches over 2 metres including the tail. Its name is Afrikaans for 'earth pig,' and it is also called the antbear or Cape anteater. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aardvark

question: The aardvark belongs to the African superorder Afrotheria. Which animals are its closest living relatives?
answer: Elephants and manatees
choices: Elephants and manatees
Pigs and warthogs
Anteaters and pangolins
Armadillos and sloths
context: Despite the anteater-with-a-pig-snout look, the aardvark belongs to the African superorder Afrotheria, alongside elephants, manatees (sea cows), and hyraxes. Its resemblance to South American anteaters is convergent evolution: the same ant-eating body plan arising independently in unrelated lineages, not shared ancestry. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aardvark

question: The aardvark's teeth are so strange that its entire order, Tubulidentata ('tube-teeth'), is named for them: each rootless, ever-growing tooth is a bundle of thousands of thin, upright, hexagonal tubes of dentine cemented together. What do these teeth completely lack?
answer: Enamel
choices: Enamel
Any nerves
A blood supply
A jaw socket
context: An aardvark tooth has no enamel at all; it is built from vasodentin, thin hexagonal tubes of dentine, and the largest tooth holds about 1,500 of them. Because the teeth are rootless, they never stop growing, wearing down at the top as they push up from below. This tube-tooth is what gives the order its name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aardvark  (Legend.)

question: A single aardvark can hoover up as many as 50,000 ants and termites in one night. What body part does it use to reach deep into a nest and pull them out?
answer: A sticky snakelike tongue up to 30 cm long
choices: A sticky snakelike tongue up to 30 cm long
A pair of long grasping front claws
A narrow retractable snout-tube
A row of fine comb-like teeth
context: The aardvark feeds by breaking into ant and termite nests with its powerful spade-clawed feet, then slurping up the insects with a long, thin, snakelike, sticky tongue up to 30 centimetres (12 inches) long, enough to reach as many as 50,000 insects in a single night's foraging. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aardvark

question: Biologists call the aardvark a keystone species of the African savanna. Which effect of its life earns that title?
answer: Its abandoned burrows shelter warthogs, hyenas, owls, and pythons
choices: Its abandoned burrows shelter warthogs, hyenas, owls, and pythons
Its constant digging aerates and fertilizes the whole grassland soil
It eats enough termites to keep whole mounds from overrunning the plain
Its tunnels channel rainwater into pools the herds drink from
context: An aardvark can dig a yard of tunnel in roughly five minutes, and its main burrow can run 13 metres (43 feet) long. Abandoned burrows become shelters for a whole cast of animals: warthogs, hyenas, mongooses, hares, owls, pythons, lizards, ant-eating chats, and African wild dogs. Many would die in wildfire season without an aardvark hole to hide in, which makes the aardvark a keystone species. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aardvark

question: The aardvark cucumber (Cucumis humifructus) is the only cucumber that ripens its melon-like fruit about a foot underground. A 2025 study watched seven mammal species approach the buried melons. What did only the aardvark manage?
answer: Locate and dig up the buried fruit, then spread its seeds in its dung
choices: Locate and dig up the buried fruit, then spread its seeds in its dung
Crack the tough rind open with its tube-teeth once it surfaced
Pollinate the hidden flower by brushing past it in the dark
Carry the whole melon back to line the floor of its burrow
context: The aardvark cucumber grows its fruit about a foot underground and is the only cucumber species with buried fruit. The aardvark digs it up for the moisture, then passes the undigested seeds in its dung, replanting them with fertilizer. A 2025 study of seven mammal species found the aardvark was the ONLY one able to locate and reach the buried melons, confirming the plant depends on it. Source: https://news.mongabay.com/short-article/2025/02/study-confirms-that-ant-eating-aardvarks-have-a-craving-for-buried-melons/  (Legend.)

question: A blue whale the length of three school buses rolls to the surface, and warm spray erupts from the very TOP of its head. It breathes there because a whale is not a fish at all - it is a mammal, and over evolution that opening on its head is really a relocated version of what body part?
answer: Its nostrils
choices: Its nostrils
Its gill slits
Its ear canals
Its throat pouch
context: Whales and dolphins are mammals, not fish: they breathe air with lungs and have no gills. Over evolution the nostrils migrated to the top of the head and became the blowhole, so the animal can breathe at the surface while the rest of the body stays underwater. Source: Wikipedia 'Blowhole (anatomy)'; Whale & Dolphin Conservation (us.whales.org).

question: You can tell a great baleen whale like the blue whale from a toothed whale like a dolphin just by the spray, because the two kinds don't have the same number of blowholes on top of the head. How many does a baleen whale have?
answer: Two
choices: Two
One
Four
None - it uses gills
context: Baleen whales (like the blue whale) have two blowholes; toothed whales (like dolphins) have just one. Neither has gills - both are air-breathing mammals. Source: Wikipedia 'Blowhole (anatomy)'; Whale & Dolphin Conservation (us.whales.org).

question: The African lungfish looks like an ordinary fish, but drop it in a sealed tank of water with no way to reach the surface and it will die - it drowns. What is strange about how this fish gets its oxygen?
answer: It has a true lung and gulps air
choices: It has a true lung and gulps air
It absorbs it through its scales
It filters it from mud, not water
It needs no oxygen at all
context: The African lungfish (Protopterus) has a true lung and gulps air at the surface. It breathes air the way we do, not through gills like other fish - so with no access to air, it drowns. Source: education.nationalgeographic.org 'West African lungfish'; Britannica 'lungfish'.

question: The betta, or Siamese fighting fish, thrives in warm, stagnant puddles where the water holds almost no oxygen and other fish would suffocate - and you'll see it swim up to gulp a mouthful of air. What lets it do that?
answer: A labyrinth organ that works like a lung
choices: A labyrinth organ that works like a lung
An extra set of high-efficiency gills
A swim bladder full of stored oxygen
A layer of oxygen-making algae on its skin
context: The betta has a labyrinth organ - a maze of folded, blood-rich tissue that works like a lung. That is why it gulps air at the surface and can survive warm, stagnant, low-oxygen water where other fish would suffocate. Source: Wikipedia 'Anabantoidei'; bettasource.com 'betta-labyrinth-organ'.

question: A whale can never fully fall asleep, or it would sink and drown. Unlike a land mammal, whose breathing runs on automatic, a whale must actively decide to open its blowhole for each breath. What does its brain do to solve this?
answer: It keeps half the brain awake at a time
choices: It keeps half the brain awake at a time
It shuts down and floats on reflex
It stores enough oxygen to sleep for hours
It breathes automatically like we do
context: A whale is a 'conscious breather' - it actively contracts muscles to open its blowhole for every breath. Because breathing is not automatic, it can never sleep fully; it keeps half its brain awake to remember to surface, or it would drown. Source: baleinesendirect.org (respiratory system); Scientific American 'How do whales and dolphins sleep without drowning?'

question: When an electric eel is trapped underwater with no way to reach the surface, it drowns - because its gills are barely developed and it grabs roughly 80% of its oxygen straight from the air. About how often does this fish have to come up for a breath?
answer: Every ten minutes or so
choices: Every ten minutes or so
Once a day
Only when the water warms up
Never - it uses its gills
context: The electric eel is an obligate air-breather: it must surface roughly every ten minutes, getting about 80% of its oxygen from air. Its gills are so poorly developed that trapped underwater with no air, it drowns. Source: Wikipedia 'Electric eel'; seriouslyfish.com 'Electrophorus electricus'.

question: A diving beetle slips beneath the pond and a bead of pure liquid SILVER seems to cling to its underside, glinting as it swims. That shimmer isn't metal - it's the beetle's survival gear. What is it?
answer: A trapped bubble of air held under its wing covers
choices: A trapped bubble of air held under its wing covers
A pocket of glowing bioluminescent slime
A polished shell that reflects like a mirror
A cloud of tiny gas-producing bacteria
context: When it dives, the diving beetle traps a shining silvery bubble of air beneath its hard wing covers (the elytra), held by water-repellent hairs. It carries its own scuba tank - the bubble looks like a bead of liquid silver underwater. Source: kqed.org 'Nature's scuba divers'; NC State (genent.cals.ncsu.edu).

question: The marine iguana of the Galapagos is the only lizard on Earth that feeds in the sea, diving on one lungful of air to graze on algae. But it is cold-blooded, and the cold ocean saps its body heat. What must it do the moment it climbs back out?
answer: Bake on the black rocks in the sun
choices: Bake on the black rocks in the sun
Shiver until its muscles rewarm
Eat a second time to make heat
Dive again to escape the wind
context: The marine iguana dives around 15 meters (about 50 feet) on a single breath to graze underwater algae. Because it is cold-blooded, the cold ocean drains its heat, so afterward it must haul out onto black rocks to bake in the sun before it can move well again. Source: gogalapagos.com; everywherewild.com. (legend-flavored wonder)

question: The diving-bell spider is the only spider on Earth that spends almost its whole life underwater - resting, hunting, mating, and laying eggs all beneath the surface. How does it keep a supply of air down there to breathe?
answer: It builds a silk dome and fills it with air from the surface
choices: It builds a silk dome and fills it with air from the surface
It grows temporary gills for the underwater months
It breathes dissolved oxygen straight through its legs
It surfaces for every single breath, all day long
context: The diving bell spider (Argyroneta aquatica) builds a dome of silk anchored to water plants and fills it with air carried down from the surface - a shimmering underwater 'diving bell' where it lives its whole life below the water. Source: Wikipedia 'Diving bell spider'; wildlifetrusts.org 'water spider'. (wonder-flagged legend)

question: When its pool dries to cracked mud, the African lungfish burrows down and curls back on itself with its head toward the opening, then oozes so much mucus that a hardened cocoon sets around its body. Months later, some have been dug up ALIVE after how long in this buried, dried-out sleep?
answer: Up to four years
choices: Up to four years
About one week
Roughly two months
A single day
context: Sealed in its mud cocoon, the lungfish can wait out drought for months - and some have been documented surviving dried, buried, and dormant for up to four years, then waking and swimming away when the rains return. This months-long dormancy is called aestivation. Source: oxsci.org; the-scientist.com 'Lungfish cocoons are alive, sort of'. (legend-tier wonder)

question: The diving beetle's silver bubble is more than a stored tank - scientists call it a 'physical gill.' As the beetle burns through the oxygen inside, the bubble keeps partly refilling on its own, letting the beetle stay down far longer than the tank alone should allow. Where does that fresh oxygen come from?
answer: It diffuses IN from the surrounding water
choices: It diffuses IN from the surrounding water
The beetle's body chemically makes more
It leaks up from mud stirred below
Sunlight splits it out of the water
context: The bubble is a 'physical gill': as the beetle uses up the oxygen, more oxygen diffuses in from the surrounding water to refill it, so the water itself keeps topping up the tank. Field Museum scientist Crystal Maier: 'The relatively large surface area of the bubble allows it to exchange oxygen with the surrounding water.' Source: kqed.org 'Nature's scuba divers'. (payoff rung)  (Legend.)

question: The diving beetle's self-refilling bubble-gill sounds like an endless air supply, but it always fails and the beetle has to pop up for a fresh one. One gas the water can't wash away builds up inside the bubble faster than the oxygen can be replaced. Which gas ends the dive?
answer: Nitrogen
choices: Nitrogen
Carbon dioxide
Helium
Hydrogen
context: The bubble-gill has a catch: over time nitrogen builds up and concentrates in the bubble while oxygen is spent faster than the water can refill it. Eventually the beetle must release the old bubble and surface for a fresh one. Source: kqed.org 'Nature's scuba divers'.

question: No mammal on Earth holds its breath deeper or longer than Cuvier's beaked whale. On a single lungful of air, one recorded dive lasted an astonishing 3 hours and 42 minutes - beating even the sperm whale and the elephant seal. Roughly how deep did another of its record dives reach?
answer: Nearly 3 kilometers down
choices: Nearly 3 kilometers down
About 300 meters down
Around 50 meters down
Just past 1 kilometer down
context: Cuvier's beaked whale holds the mammal record: one dive lasted 222 minutes (3 hours 42 minutes) on a single breath, and another reached 2,992 meters - nearly 3 km, about 9,800 feet - beating even the sperm whale and elephant seal. Source: sciencenews.org 'Cuvier's beaked whale longest record dive'; Wikipedia. (legend-tier record)

question: A sperm whale dives a kilometer down on one breath, yet its lungs are only about 3% of its body cavity and collapse near-empty under the pressure - so the breath keeping it alive can't be stored there. A clue sits in its flesh, which is nearly BLACK instead of red, stained by ten times the oxygen-binding protein packed into human tissue. Where does this whale actually stockpile the oxygen it dives on?
answer: Bound up inside its muscle
choices: Bound up inside its muscle
In an air sac behind the ribs
Dissolved through its blubber
In hollow, air-filled bones
context: The oxygen-binding protein is myoglobin - the same molecule that makes red meat red. Elite divers pack it into muscle roughly ten times denser than humans can, so about a third of the whale's whole-body oxygen store rides in muscle (with most of the rest in blood), and only a tiny fraction in the collapsing lungs. Mirceta et al. (2013, Science) found the trick: in deep divers the myoglobin molecule carries a strong positive electric charge on its surface, so the crowded copies repel each other like same-pole magnets instead of clumping and misfolding - a 'non-stick' charge that turns muscle itself into an oxygen tank, a molecular aqualung. Sources: Mirceta et al. 2013, Science (nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/130614-diving-mammal-myoglobin-oxygen-ocean-science); lung/oxygen-store fractions via uk.whales.org and orcaireland.org.

question: For a century, naturalists fought over which living fish is our own closest fishy cousin - the nearest relative of every land animal with a backbone. Two air-gulpers led the field: one survives droughts sealed in a mucus cocoon in the mud, the other a 'living fossil' rediscovered alive in 1938. Different genes kept naming different winners until whole genomes settled it. Which fish is the closest living relative of all land vertebrates?
answer: The lungfish
choices: The lungfish
The coelacanth
The bichir
The mudskipper
context: Whole-genome analysis put the question to rest: the lungfish, not the coelacanth, is the closest living relative of every land vertebrate - meaning our own deepest fishy cousin is the same air-gulping fish that survives droughts sealed in a mucus cocoon in the mud. The lungfish genome turned out to be a monster in its own right: the South American Lepidosiren paradoxa carries over 90 billion DNA base pairs, about thirty times the human genome and the largest of any animal yet sequenced, bloated by 'jumping genes' copying themselves. Sources: Amemiya et al. 2013, Nature 496:311 (nature.com/articles/nature12027) and Brinkmann/Takezaki nuclear-gene analyses; genome size via Schartl et al. 2024, Nature (uni-wuerzburg.de).  (Legend.)

question: Stretch a wandering albatross's wings tip to tip and you get the longest span of any bird alive today. Roughly how wide?
answer: About 11 to 12 feet
choices: About 11 to 12 feet
About 4 to 5 feet
About 20 to 22 feet
About 6 to 7 feet
context: The wandering albatross has the longest wingspan of any living bird, up to about 11-12 feet (3.5 m), with the largest ever recorded at 3.7 m (12.1 ft). Source: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution / National Geographic.

question: A wandering albatross can hang in the air for hours over the open ocean without a single flap. A special tendon in its shoulder makes this possible by doing what?
answer: Locking the wing open with no muscle effort
choices: Locking the wing open with no muscle effort
Pumping warm blood into the wingtips
Snapping the wing shut between gusts
Storing fat to burn during the glide
context: A tendon in the albatross's shoulder mechanically locks the wing open in the extended position, so no muscle effort is needed to hold it out and the bird can glide for hours. Source: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, 'New Research Unlocks Clues About the Iconic Flight of the Wandering Albatross.'

question: A wandering albatross almost never flaps, yet it crosses whole oceans without tiring, using the wind as its only fuel. What does it physically do to steal that energy from the wind?
answer: Climbs into the fast upper air, then dives into the slow surface air
choices: Climbs into the fast upper air, then dives into the slow surface air
Beats its wings hard only on the downwind stretches
Rides warm columns of air spiraling up off the sea
Coasts down the sloping face of each swell like a hill
context: Wind moves faster higher up and slower right at the sea surface. The albatross repeatedly climbs into the faster upper air and dives back into the slower air near the waves, harvesting energy from that difference over and over. This technique is called dynamic soaring. Source: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution; National Geographic, 'Albatross's Effortless Flight Decoded.'

question: A wandering albatross gulps down seawater as it feeds, yet the salt never poisons it. A gland tucked above its eyes handles the overload by doing what?
answer: Dripping concentrated brine out its nostrils
choices: Dripping concentrated brine out its nostrils
Storing the salt in hollow leg bones
Sweating it out through the feet
Coughing up salt crystals in a pellet
context: A special salt gland above the eyes concentrates the excess salt into a briny solution that drips out through the bird's tube-shaped nostrils and down its beak. Albatrosses belong to a group called 'tubenoses' named for exactly these tube-like nostrils. Source: Audubon, 'How Do Seabirds Drink Salt Water?'; Cordell Bank National Marine Sanctuary (NOAA).

question: A foraging wandering albatross can cover a staggering distance in a single day, then keep it up for days on end, all while burning almost no energy. Roughly how far in one day?
answer: About 950 km
choices: About 950 km
About 120 km
About 300 km
About 60 km
context: A foraging wandering albatross can cover roughly 950 km (about 590 miles) in a single day, averaging around 40 km/h, and sustain it for days while spending almost no energy thanks to dynamic soaring. Source: British Antarctic Survey tracking data; WHOI research.

question: One tracked wandering albatross made a complete loop around Antarctica without ever touching land. How long did the whole circuit take?
answer: Just 46 days
choices: Just 46 days
Just over a year
Nearly 200 days
About one week
context: A GPS-tracked wandering albatross circumnavigated Antarctica in just 46 days, covering about 11,600 km without landing. Source: British Antarctic Survey GPS-logger study (2013-2021).  (Legend.)

question: A Laysan albatross named Wisdom, wearing biologists' ankle band #Z333, still returns to the same Pacific atoll to raise chicks. What record does Wisdom hold?
answer: Oldest known wild bird in the world
choices: Oldest known wild bird in the world
Longest single migration ever tracked
Largest clutch ever laid by a seabird
Fastest bird over open water
context: Wisdom, banded with red ankle band #Z333 by biologist Chandler Robbins in 1956, is at least 74 years old, making her the oldest known wild bird in the world. She has hatched an estimated 30+ chicks. Source: USGS / Wikipedia (Wisdom the albatross); Smithsonian Magazine.  (Legend.)

question: A wandering albatross pair splits up for months, each roaming thousands of miles of empty ocean alone. When the two finally reunite at the nest, what do they do?
answer: Perform an elaborate greeting dance
choices: Perform an elaborate greeting dance
Fight to win back the nest site
Feed each other regurgitated squid
Rebuild the nest from scratch
context: Albatrosses mate for life, and a reunited pair performs an elaborate greeting dance: sky-pointing, wing-spreading, and loud clucking calls. Source: KQED Science, 'Love Is an Albatross'; Marine Ornithology (courtship behaviour of the wandering albatross).

question: A wandering albatross lays a single egg, and its chick sits in the nest waiting to grow flight feathers far longer than the chicks of most birds. About how long does the chick wait before its first flight?
answer: Around 278 days
choices: Around 278 days
Around 60 days
Around 120 days
Around 400 days
context: The wandering albatross has the longest incubation of any bird (about 78 days), and its single fluffy chick then sits in the nest for around 278 days, nearly nine months, before it can fly. Because raising one chick takes so long, a pair breeds only every other year. Source: Birdfact; Animal Diversity Web (Diomedea exulans).

question: Wandering albatrosses are among the longest-lived of all birds, cruising the Southern Ocean decade after decade. Out in the wild, about how long can one live?
answer: 50 to 60 years or more
choices: 50 to 60 years or more
10 to 15 years
25 to 30 years
Over 100 years
context: The albatross can live 50 to 60 years or more in the wild, one of the longest-lived of all birds. Source: Cornell Lab / British Antarctic Survey; Audubon.

question: A wandering albatross finds scattered patches of squid and krill across hundreds of miles of open ocean where nothing is visible from the air. A 2008 GPS study cracked how: the bird zig-zags upwind toward its meal. What is it actually following?
answer: A chemical scent the sea releases where plankton are being grazed
choices: A chemical scent the sea releases where plankton are being grazed
The flash of sunlight glinting off shoals of fish near the surface
The low rumble that feeding whales send through the water
A drop in air pressure that marks where storms churn up prey
context: When krill graze on phytoplankton, the plankton release dimethyl sulfide (DMS) - the 'ocean' smell. The albatross catches this scent on the wind and works upwind in a zig-zag to the patchy prey. When Gabrielle Nevitt's team GPS-tagged 19 wandering albatrosses over the southern Indian Ocean, these upwind turning approaches accounted for 37% of daytime prey captures and 47% of nighttime captures - the first hard evidence that these seabirds smell their way to food across the open sea. Source: Nevitt, Losekoot & Weimerskirch 2008, 'Evidence for olfactory search in wandering albatross, Diomedea exulans,' PNAS 105(12); https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0709047105

question: For decades, 21-foot-wingspan fossil seabirds from Antarctica were filed as the largest albatrosses that ever lived, because their leg and foot bones matched an albatross so closely. A closer look at their jaws overturned that. What were the fossils really?
answer: A separate seabird lineage whose beaks bristled with tooth-like bony spikes
choices: A separate seabird lineage whose beaks bristled with tooth-like bony spikes
An early branch of the albatross family that later shrank down to modern sizes
A giant petrel cousin that lost the power of flight and dived for its food
A flightless diving bird convergent on penguins of the northern seas
context: The giant 'albatrosses' were pelagornithids - the 'bony-toothed' or pseudotooth birds, a lineage whose jaws bore tooth-like bony spikes. Convergent evolution had made their leg and foot bones nearly identical to an albatross, which is what fooled taxonomists. True fossil albatrosses were in fact modest: Aldiomedes angustirostris, from an almost-complete ~3-million-year-old Pliocene skull in New Zealand's Tangahoe Formation, reached only about 90% the size of today's smallest living albatross and had a slender, fish-eating beak. Sources: Berkeley News 2020, 'Antarctica yields oldest fossils of giant birds with 21-foot wingspans' (https://news.berkeley.edu/2020/10/27/antarctica-yields-oldest-fossils-of-giant-birds); Mayr & Tennyson 2019, Ibis (https://phys.org/news/2019-07-scientists-albatross-skull-pliocene-epoch.html)

question: An Antarctic seabird stands through the polar winter in -40C blizzards with winds over 100 mph, eating nothing, keeping one precious thing warm the whole time. Where does the male emperor penguin hold his single egg?
answer: Balanced on top of his feet under a belly flap
choices: Balanced on top of his feet under a belly flap
Tucked beneath one folded wing against his side
Buried in a shallow scrape of packed snow
Cradled in his beak against his chest
context: The male emperor penguin (Aptenodytes forsteri) balances the single egg on top of his feet under a warm belly flap, holding it at about 38C while the air outside drops to -40C or colder with winds over 100 mph. This is the 'all-in' end of parenting: everything poured into one egg. Source: Wikipedia, Emperor penguin; Australian Antarctic Program breeding cycle.  (Legend.)

question: A sea turtle hauls herself up a moonlit beach, digs a pit in the sand, and lays roughly a hundred eggs. After she buries the clutch, what does she do next?
answer: Drags herself back to the ocean and leaves forever
choices: Drags herself back to the ocean and leaves forever
Coils around the nest and guards it until they hatch
Fans cool water over the buried eggs each night
Carries the eggs one by one into a tidal pool
context: A female sea turtle digs a pit, lays roughly 80 to 120 eggs (up to about 200), buries them, and drags herself back to the ocean forever. The hatchlings dig themselves out weeks later and race to the sea with no parent present. This is the 'none' end of the spectrum. Source: NOAA Ocean Service, 'How do sea turtles hatch?'; FWC Sea Turtle FAQ.

question: A female giant Pacific octopus retreats into her den, hangs tens of thousands of tiny rice-grain eggs from the ceiling in strands, and settles in to guard them. For roughly six months, what does she do about eating?
answer: Nothing — she never eats, living on her own body fat
choices: Nothing — she never eats, living on her own body fat
Slips out briefly each night to snatch a passing crab
Nibbles the weakest eggs to fuel guarding the rest
Filters plankton from the water she blows over them
context: For roughly six months the mother giant Pacific octopus (Enteroctopus dofleini) never eats. She continuously blows water over her eggs and grooms off algae, living on her own body fat, and dies soon after the eggs hatch. The all-in extreme. Source: Wikipedia, Giant Pacific octopus.  (Legend.)

question: A female ocean sunfish drifts in open water and does the exact opposite of the guarding octopus: she gives her young zero care and instead bets on sheer numbers. In a single spawning, how many eggs can a Mola mola release?
answer: Up to about 300 million — more than any known vertebrate
choices: Up to about 300 million — more than any known vertebrate
A neat clutch of around 100, hidden in kelp
Roughly 10 thousand, glued to a floating log
Two large eggs she shelters under a fin
context: The female ocean sunfish (Mola mola) can release up to 300 million eggs at a time — more than any other known vertebrate — each only about 0.13 cm across, and gives no care at all. Nearly all are eaten; a few survive. This is the number-as-wonder because the contrast with the octopus makes it mean something. Source: Wikipedia, Ocean sunfish; Animal Diversity Web, Mola mola.  (Legend.)

question: A cichlid mother senses a predator and does something startling: her whole brood of tiny fry vanishes in an instant, darting to safety in a place no other fish keeps its young. Where do the fry hide?
answer: Back inside her own mouth
choices: Back inside her own mouth
Under a flat rock she guards
Inside an empty snail shell
Beneath a raft of algae
context: In many mouthbrooding cichlids the mother scoops her fertilized eggs into her mouth and holds them — and later the hatched fry — for up to about two weeks, not eating the whole time, letting them dart back into her mouth when danger threatens. Source: Wikipedia, Mouthbrooder; Natural History Museum.

question: The emperor penguin father fasts through the whole Antarctic winter with the egg on his feet, eating nothing for roughly 120 days. What does that fast cost his body by the time the female returns?
answer: He loses about 20 kg, dropping from around 38 down to 18
choices: He loses about 20 kg, dropping from around 38 down to 18
He loses about 5 kg but stays close to his full weight
He holds his weight steady by slowing his metabolism to near zero
He loses so much he can no longer walk to the sea afterward
context: The male emperor penguin fasts about 120 days total (roughly two months just incubating), eating nothing, and can lose around 20 kg — dropping from about 38 kg down to 18 kg. All-in investment measured in his own body. Source: Wikipedia, Emperor penguin.

question: When the female emperor penguin finally returns from the sea, she and the waiting male must pass the egg foot-to-foot in a frantic few seconds. If the egg slips loose and stays exposed for more than about two minutes, what happens to it?
answer: The embryo inside freezes and dies
choices: The embryo inside freezes and dies
The parents can no longer tell it apart from others
The shell cracks under the pressure of the wind
A skua swoops in and steals it away
context: When the female passes the egg to the male, they must complete the hand-off in seconds; if the egg is exposed to the polar air for more than about two minutes, the embryo freezes and dies. Source: penguinehub.com; Live Science, 'How Do Emperor Penguin Dads Stop Their Eggs From Freezing?'

question: Among cardinalfish, mouthbrooding falls to the FATHER — he cannot eat while a mass of eggs fills his jaws. Every two to three minutes he opens his mouth wide. Why?
answer: To churn and re-aerate the eggs with fresh water
choices: To churn and re-aerate the eggs with fresh water
To count and reposition any egg that slipped loose
To warn off rivals with a threatening gape
To swallow the weakest eggs and thin the brood
context: In cardinalfish it is the father who mouthbroods: he holds the egg mass and every two to three minutes opens his jaws to churn and re-aerate the eggs, unable to feed the whole time. Source: Underwater Photography Guide, Mouthbrooding Cardinalfish; Wikipedia, Mouthbrooder.

question: The sea turtle's 'make thousands, tend none' gamble sounds reckless until you see the odds it is built to survive. Of every 1,000 hatchlings that scramble from the sand toward the waves, about how many reach adulthood?
answer: Around 1
choices: Around 1
Around 100
Around 500
Around 900
context: Only about 1 in 1,000 sea turtle hatchlings survives to adulthood — the 'make thousands, tend none' bet works only because so many are laid. The number is the payoff: the stem builds the expectation the answer shatters. Source: Loggerhead Marinelife Center; SEE Turtles life cycle.

question: Biologists split parents into two camps: few-and-tended, pouring everything into a handful of young, versus many-and-abandoned, flooding the sea with eggs and walking away. The ocean sunfish sits at the many-and-abandoned extreme. Of these four other mothers, which one shares that same extreme with the sunfish?
answer: The sea turtle
choices: The sea turtle
The giant Pacific octopus
The cardinalfish father
The mouthbrooding cichlid
context: The two strategies are two answers to one problem, not a better and worse one: few-and-tended (the octopus, the penguin) versus many-and-abandoned (the sunfish, the sea turtle). Biologists call these r-selection versus K-selection. The choices name only the animals, so the player must actually know each mother's care strategy: the sea turtle buries her clutch and gives no care, sitting at the same many-and-abandoned extreme as the sunfish, while the octopus starves guarding her eggs, the cardinalfish father mouthbroods, and the cichlid shelters her fry in her mouth — all tenders. Source: Wikipedia, Ocean sunfish (r-selection); Animal Diversity Web, Mola mola; NOAA Ocean Service.

question: The giant Pacific octopus mother stops eating the moment she starts guarding her eggs and dies as they hatch. In a 1977 experiment, Jerome Wodinsky surgically removed a pair of organs behind her eyes from brooding females -- and the mothers abandoned the eggs, started eating, and lived months longer. What did that prove the starvation-and-death really is?
answer: A hormone-driven self-destruct program, not simple exhaustion
choices: A hormone-driven self-destruct program, not simple exhaustion
A slow starvation forced by guarding the eggs too closely
The ordinary old age of a creature at the end of its years
A poisoning caused by chemicals leaking from the egg strands
context: The pair of organs are the optic glands, behind the eyes. When Wodinsky removed both glands from brooding female Octopus hummelincki, the mothers abandoned their eggs, resumed feeding, gained weight, and lived roughly five to six months longer than normal -- proving the post-brooding shutdown is a hormonally programmed self-destruct, not exhaustion or old age. A 2022 study traced it further: after laying, the optic gland shifts cholesterol metabolism and floods the body with 7-dehydrocholesterol, the same molecule elevated in a human genetic disorder linked to self-injury. Source: Wodinsky, J. (1977), 'Hormonal Inhibition of Feeding and Death in Octopus,' Science 198(4320):948-951 (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.198.4320.948); Wang & Ragsdale (2022), 'Steroid hormones of the octopus self-destruct system,' Current Biology (sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982222006613).  (Legend.)

question: Through the Antarctic winter the emperor penguin father keeps his egg at body heat while the air outside sits near -40C. The egg is not just tucked under a flap -- it presses against one specific thing on him, and the fathers pack into tight huddles to defend it. What keeps the egg alive?
answer: A bare, blood-rich patch of belly skin held near body heat
choices: A bare, blood-rich patch of belly skin held near body heat
A thick cushion of down feathers wrapped over the shell
A pouch of stored fat the father presses against the shell
A layer of warm oil the father smears across the shell
context: That featherless, blood-rich patch of skin is the brood patch, kept at about 36-37C -- a gap of roughly 75-80C over the -40C air outside. The father cannot feed for the whole two-month incubation, so the birds huddle together, with temperatures deep in the center of a huddle reaching about 37C, and shuffle positions so each takes a turn out of the wind. Source: Gilbert et al. (2006), 'Body temperature changes induced by huddling in breeding male emperor penguins,' Am. J. Physiology (journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/ajpregu.00912.2005).

question: The electric eel of the Amazon can stun a horse, but its name is a lie: it's no true eel at all. Trace its family tree and this river monster turns out to be a knifefish, most closely related to which two familiar fish?
answer: Catfish and carp
choices: Catfish and carp
Moray and conger
Salmon and trout
Pike and perch
context: Despite the name, the electric eel (order Gymnotiformes) is a knifefish, far closer to catfish and carp than to true eels like the moray. A fun teach-before-test correction. Source: Wikipedia, Electric eel; Mongabay 2019.

question: Inside an electric eel, its shock organs look like living batteries: thousands of flat cells stacked and wired end to end down each side. The eel builds this power from the same cell type that, in most animals, only makes muscles twitch. What is one of these stacked cells called?
answer: An electrocyte
choices: An electrocyte
A motor end plate
A Sachs' organ cell
An ampulla of Lorenzini
context: Roughly 6,000 electrocytes sit end-to-end in a stack like batteries wired in series, with about 35 stacks in parallel down each side of the eel's long body. Source: Wikipedia, Electric eel.

question: For two centuries scientists thought there was just one electric eel. In 2019 a team led by Carlos David de Santana studied 107 specimens and split it into three species — then clocked Volta's electric eel firing the strongest bioelectric shock ever measured from any living animal. How high did that one jolt go?
answer: 860 volts
choices: 860 volts
700 volts
1,100 volts
2,400 volts
context: E. voltai was measured at 860 volts, beating the old 650-volt record — the strongest bioelectric shock ever recorded from any animal. One measurement from one fish: the strongest ever recorded, not a routine output. Source: de Santana et al. 2019, Nature Communications; Mongabay 2019.  (Legend.)

question: Kenneth Catania filmed a hunting electric eel do one thing to a struggling fish that at least doubled the strength of its shock. What was the eel doing?
answer: Curling head to tail around the prey
choices: Curling head to tail around the prey
Beating its tail against the prey
Swallowing the prey whole first
Rubbing its belly on the riverbed
context: By curling to bring its positive head and negative tail together around the prey, the eel concentrates the field and at least doubles the shock — an 'electric embrace' that runs the prey's muscles to exhaustion. Source: Catania 2015, Smithsonian.

question: In 1800, Alexander von Humboldt claimed he watched electric eels leap up out of an Amazon pool to shock a herd of horses — a tale mocked as tall for two hundred years. In 2016 Kenneth Catania filmed eels doing exactly this. Why does leaving the water and pressing against the target make the eel's attack far worse?
answer: The full jolt drives straight into the target instead of spreading through the water
choices: The full jolt drives straight into the target instead of spreading through the water
The air lets the eel build a bigger charge before firing
Wet skin insulates the eel so it feels nothing
Leaping lets the eel bite and shock at the same time
context: Underwater the current disperses and weakens; by leaping to press its chin against a threat, the eel drives the full jolt straight in. Catania's video confirmed Humboldt's long-doubted 1800 account of eels battling horses. Source: Catania 2016, PNAS; Science News.  (Legend.)

question: The electric eel is a knifefish, but it isn't the only fish that fights with electricity. The torpedo ray also stuns prey with a jolt, yet it stores its charge in a completely different place from the eel's long body. Where does the torpedo ray keep its two electric organs?
answer: Inside its broad pectoral 'wings'
choices: Inside its broad pectoral 'wings'
Coiled inside its whip-like tail
Behind its eyes in its skull
Lining the roof of its mouth
context: The torpedo ray makes its charge in two large kidney-shaped organs set inside its flat pectoral fins, each packed with hundreds to over a thousand electrocytes; the great torpedo (Torpedo nobiliana) can hit ~220 volts, enough to knock down a person. Source: Elasmo-research; Wikipedia, Electric organ (fish).

question: A shock from Volta's electric eel can top 500 volts — far above a household wall socket. So you'd expect it to push a monstrous current through anything it touches. Yet measure the current in a full eel discharge and it peaks near just 1 amp, a tenth of a wall outlet's. So what actually makes the eel's blast so dangerous?
answer: The high voltage drives current across a body in a rapid volley of pulses
choices: The high voltage drives current across a body in a rapid volley of pulses
It sustains one enormous unbroken current for several full seconds
It heats the surrounding water until the prey is scalded and stunned
It magnetizes the prey so later pulses strike with far more force
context: The eel's weapon is high VOLTAGE but low CURRENT: a full discharge peaks near ~1 ampere at ~500 volts, roughly 500 watts, yet only about a tenth the amperage of a household wall outlet (10-20 A). The danger is the high voltage driving that current across a body, delivered in bursts of up to ~500 pulses per second (500 Hz), each lasting only ~2 milliseconds. It's the voltage and the rapid volley, not a huge sustained current. Source: Wikipedia 'Electric eel' (~1 ampere at 500 V; up to 500 Hz; ~2 ms pulses) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_eel ; power/amperage comparison corroborated by Scientific American and a Fluke case study.

question: An electric eel, a torpedo ray, and an elephantnose fish all build power organs from ordinary muscle cells — yet their lineages split long before any of them could shock. A 2014 genome study found this organ was reinvented at least six separate times in fishes. What astonished the team about how those unrelated fish each built it?
answer: They all recruited the very same set of genes and developmental pathways
choices: They all recruited the very same set of genes and developmental pathways
They each borrowed the necessary genes from prey they had eaten
They independently invented six completely unrelated genetic recipes
They pooled their genes by interbreeding across the separate lineages
context: The myogenic electric organ is one of evolution's favorite reruns: a 2014 genomic study (Science, June 27, 2014; co-led by Jason Gallant, Michael Sussman and Harold Zakon, and including the first full electric-eel genome) found it evolved INDEPENDENTLY at least six separate times in fishes. Every time, unrelated lineages converted ordinary muscle cells into giant electricity-making electrocytes — and each reached for the SAME 'genetic toolbox,' recruiting the same set of genes and developmental pathways despite millions of years of separate evolution. Source: Gallant, Traeger et al. (2014), 'Genomic basis for the convergent evolution of electric organs,' Science 344(6191):1522 — https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1254432 ; https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2014/06/140626141652.htm

question: A low, wide, four-legged plant-eater lumbered across Late Cretaceous North America with its whole back plated in bony armor, its broad belly held close to the ground like a living tank. Which armored dinosaur was this?
answer: Ankylosaurus
choices: Ankylosaurus
Stegosaurus
Triceratops
Iguanodon
context: Ankylosaurus was the classic armored tank of the dinosaur world: low, broad, four-legged, and plated head to tail in bony armor as it grazed the Late Cretaceous of North America. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ankylosaurus' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankylosaurus).

question: Ankylosaurus was big for an armored dinosaur, stretching roughly 6 to 8 meters long. About how much did this squat, plated grazer weigh?
answer: As much as an elephant, 5 to 8 tonnes
choices: As much as an elephant, 5 to 8 tonnes
As much as a cow, under 1 tonne
As much as a blue whale, over 100 tonnes
As much as a house cat, a few kilograms
context: At 6 to 8 meters (20 to 26 feet) long and perhaps 5 to 8 tonnes, Ankylosaurus carried roughly an elephant's weight in body plus bony armor. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ankylosaurus' (6-8 m long, 4.8-8 t).

question: Ankylosaurus wore its armor as bony plates called osteoderms, set right into its skin from tiny knobs to big tiles over a foot long. One protection it had that almost no other dinosaur is known to have shared covered a surprising spot. Which part of Ankylosaurus was also armored?
answer: Its eyes, shielded by bony eyelids
choices: Its eyes, shielded by bony eyelids
Its throat, sheathed in bony scutes
Its snout tip, capped with a bony guard
Its cheeks, plated in bony tiles
context: Ankylosaurus had bony eyelids formed from the palpebral bones, plates of bone that could shield the eyes, a protection almost no other dinosaur is known to have had. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ankylosaurus' (palpebral bones over the eyes); AMNH.  (Legend.)

question: Ankylosaurus was a walking fortress of bony plates, yet one region of its body carried no armor at all, and a predator that could reach that spot had a real chance. Which part of Ankylosaurus went bare?
answer: Its belly
choices: Its belly
Its snout
Its feet
Its throat
context: Ankylosaurus was armored on top but bare underneath, so it hugged the ground to keep that soft belly away from a predator's jaws. Its species name magniventris means 'great belly.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Ankylosaurus' (magniventris = 'great belly'); AMNH.

question: Ankylosaurus carried a massive knob of bone at the tip of its tail, heavy enough to shatter bone when it swung. Its skeleton shows something unusual about the last seven tail vertebrae. What was it?
answer: Fused into a single stiff handle
choices: Fused into a single stiff handle
Hollowed out to lighten the swing
Studded with backward-pointing spikes
Split into two independent lobes
context: The last seven tail vertebrae fused into a stiff handle, with knobs of bony armor welded over the tip; one known club measured 60 cm long and 49 cm wide. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ankylosaurus' (tail club 60 cm long, 49 cm wide; last seven caudal vertebrae form the handle).  (Legend.)

question: Ankylosaurus had a wide skull ending in a broad, flat beak rather than a narrow, pointed snout. From that beak shape, how did this dinosaur most likely feed?
answer: By cropping low plants without picking favorites
choices: By cropping low plants without picking favorites
By stripping tall trees of their top branches
By digging up roots with its clawed feet
By ambushing and swallowing small animals
context: Its wide, low skull ended in a beak used to crop low-growing ferns and shrubs, feeding by non-selective low browsing rather than picking choice leaves. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ankylosaurus' (wide low skull, beak for non-selective low-browse cropping).

question: Inside an ankylosaur's snout, the nasal passage wasn't a straight tube but a crazy-straw of loops and twists, running about 2.5 feet folded inside the skull. Researchers modeling airflow found this coiled airway served a specific physiological job. What did all that looping accomplish?
answer: Recovering breath heat and cooling blood to the brain
choices: Recovering breath heat and cooling blood to the brain
Amplifying its calls into deep booming honks
Storing air for long underwater dives
Filtering out dust before it reached the lungs
context: In the relative Euoplocephalus the airway ran about 808 mm folded inside the snout and worked like a heat exchanger, recovering up to 84% of a breath's heat and cooling blood before it reached the small brain. Source: Bourke, Porter & Witmer (2018), 'Convoluted nasal passages function as efficient heat exchangers in ankylosaurs,' PLOS ONE.  (Legend.)

question: A famous claim says an ankylosaur could shatter a T. rex leg with its tail club. When Arbour and Snively modeled the actual impacts, they found the bone-breaking blow was not something every ankylosaur could deliver. Which animals actually had the force to break a predator bone?
answer: Only the biggest-clubbed adults, whose knobs cleared bone strength tenfold
choices: Only the biggest-clubbed adults, whose knobs cleared bone strength tenfold
Any adult, since the fused handle always multiplied the swing enough
Only the fastest swingers, whose whip-quick tails outran the bone limit
Only the oldest, whose brittle knobs cracked but still delivered the blow
context: In their finite-element study, Arbour and Snively found that only large knobs (wider than about 500 mm) generated bone-breaking force: roughly 364 to 718 MPa of impact stress, an order of magnitude past the ~64 to 84 MPa shear strength of cortical bone. Average knobs (48 to 101 MPa) and small knobs (29 to 56 MPa) fell short. So the leg-shattering feat was real, but it belonged to the biggest-clubbed adults, not to every ankylosaur. Source: Arbour & Snively 2009, PLOS ONE, 'Estimating Impact Forces of Tail Club Strikes by Ankylosaurid Dinosaurs' -- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2726940/

question: For an animal the size of an elephant, Ankylosaurus had almost comically tiny teeth, only millimeters tall, and jaws too weak to grind up the ferns it swallowed nearly whole. Its species name, magniventris, points to how it got nutrients from food it barely chewed. What did the work its teeth could not?
answer: Gut microbes fermenting the unchewed plants in a huge chambered belly
choices: Gut microbes fermenting the unchewed plants in a huge chambered belly
A gizzard of swallowed stones grinding the plants into paste
Acid strong enough to dissolve whole ferns before they reached the gut
A second row of hidden grinding teeth set deep in the throat
context: Adult Ankylosaurus teeth were only a few millimeters tall (juvenile teeth measured just 3.2 to 3.3 mm), and its jaws had low mechanical advantage, so it barely chewed. Its name magniventris means 'great belly,' and paleontologists infer it relied on hindgut fermentation in a huge, broad-ribbed gut, much like modern herbivorous lizards with enlarged, chambered colons: gut microbes, not teeth, broke down the tough unchewed plants. Source: Carpenter 2004 redescription and Arbour & Mallon 2017 (FACETS), via Wikipedia 'Ankylosaurus' -- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankylosaurus

question: The Burgess Shale of British Columbia has preserved Anomalocaris in enough detail that scientists can measure its whole body from head to tail fan. How long could this Cambrian hunter grow?
answer: Up to about a meter
choices: Up to about a meter
Up to about a centimeter
Up to about ten meters
Up to about thirty meters
context: At up to about 1 meter (100 cm) long, Anomalocaris was the largest predator of the Burgess Shale and a giant of its day. Most Cambrian animals were only a few centimeters, so it towered over its whole world. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale (burgess-shale.rom.on.ca/fossils/anomalocaris-canadensis/).

question: Anomalocaris had no fins. Sixteen structures ran in a row down each side of its body, from just behind the head all the way to the tail. What were these structures?
answer: Flexible flaps
choices: Flexible flaps
Beating gills
Suction discs
Jointed paddle-legs
context: Anomalocaris swam by rippling rows of flexible flaps down both sides of its body. One specimen shows sixteen lateral flaps whose overlapping, wave-like undulations pushed it through the open water, with a three-part tail fan for sharp turns while chasing prey. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale; Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomalocaris).

question: Anomalocaris seized prey with a pair of jointed limbs, each about fourteen segments long, that curled out from the front of its head and swept food toward its mouth. What lined the inner edge of these two front limbs?
answer: Rows of trident-like spikes
choices: Rows of trident-like spikes
A fringe of fine filtering hairs
A row of glowing light organs
Bands of sticky suction cups
context: In front of its mouth Anomalocaris had two spiny grasping arms (frontal appendages), jointed limbs of about fourteen segments each, lined with trident-like spikes it used to seize and hold prey and sweep it toward its mouth. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale (burgess-shale.rom.on.ca/fossils/anomalocaris-canadensis/).  (Legend.)

question: An Anomalocaris fed through a hard mouth unlike anything alive today: a circle of overlapping plates ringed with tooth-like points, which clamped shut to grip and crush its catch. What everyday object was this mouth shaped like?
answer: A pineapple slice
choices: A pineapple slice
A closed fist
A hinged beak
A drinking straw
context: Its mouth was a strange ring of hard overlapping plates, a circular 'oral cone' shaped like a pineapple slice and ringed with teeth-like points, which it clamped shut on prey to grip and crush it. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale; Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomalocaris).  (Legend.)

question: In 1892 Joseph Whiteaves found a single spiny limb of Anomalocaris and, with only that one fragment, mistook it for a curled tail. That blunder is preserved in the animal's name, which means what?
answer: Odd shrimp
choices: Odd shrimp
Ring mouth
Giant hunter
Spiny claw
context: The name 'Anomalocaris' means 'odd shrimp' (or 'abnormal shrimp'). In 1892 Joseph Whiteaves found only a detached grasping arm and thought it was the tail of a shrimp or lobster, so the whole animal ended up named after a single misread body part. Source: Wikipedia, Anomalocaris (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomalocaris); UC Berkeley Understanding Science (undsci.berkeley.edu/this-is-not-the-shrimp-youre-looking-for/).  (Legend.)

question: A rare fossil of an Anomalocaris eye from Australia let scientists count the lenses packed inside it, revealing vision as sharp as a modern dragonfly's, half a billion years ago. Roughly how many lenses did that single eye hold?
answer: About 16,000
choices: About 16,000
About 160
About 8
About 40
context: Anomalocaris had big compound eyes on stalks with astonishingly sharp vision: a fossil eye from the Emu Bay Shale of Australia holds at least 16,000 tiny lenses, rivaling a modern dragonfly and making it one of the keenest-sighted hunters of its time. Source: Paterson et al. 2011, 'Acute vision in the giant Cambrian predator Anomalocaris', Nature 480:237-240 (nature.com/articles/nature10689).  (Legend.)

question: Before 1985, Anomalocaris's parts were scattered across the fossil record under different names, each thought to be its own creature. The ring-shaped mouth, in particular, had been catalogued by Charles Walcott as an entirely different kind of animal. What had he classified that mouth as?
answer: A jellyfish
choices: A jellyfish
A sea urchin
A coiled worm
A snail shell
context: Anomalocaris's pieces were first mistaken for separate creatures: the grasping arm as a shrimp, the body as a sponge or sea cucumber (Laggania), and the ring-shaped mouth catalogued by Charles Walcott as a jellyfish, which he named Peytoia. Not until 1985 did Harry Whittington and Derek Briggs find the pieces joined and realize they were one animal. Source: Whittington & Briggs 1985; Wikipedia, Anomalocaris; UC Berkeley Understanding Science.  (Legend.)

question: For over a century Anomalocaris was pictured as the terror that pried open trilobites. In 2023, scientists built a digital model of its grasping arm and loaded it under stress: the thin gripping spines bent and snapped against mineralized armor. What did the test conclude those arms were actually built to catch?
answer: Soft-bodied prey
choices: Soft-bodied prey
Armored trilobites
Buried burrowers
Drifting plankton
context: The old reputation wasn't baseless: Cameron Nedin's 1999 paper pointed to real clues -- Cambrian trilobites with round and W-shaped healed bite wounds, and large fossil fecal pellets stuffed with crushed shell -- and proposed Anomalocaris rocked a trilobite back and forth in its mouth until the armor failed. But Bicknell et al. (2023, Proc. R. Soc. B 290:20230638) ran finite-element analysis on a 3D model of the frontal appendage and found the ventral gripping spines (endites) would suffer high stress and plastic deformation against a hard trilobite shell -- they would bend and break. Combined with the soft oral cone showing no wear from armored prey, the study concluded the grasping arms of Anomalocaris canadensis were built for soft-bodied prey, not shell-crushing. Whether some radiodonts still tackled hard prey remains debated. Source: Bicknell et al. 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10320336/ ; Nedin 1999, Geology 27:987-990.

question: Anomalocaris rippled through Cambrian seas on rows of soft swimming flaps down its flanks, and it already carried the stalked compound eyes that mark its cousins the arthropods. Yet one hallmark of every living arthropod, from crab to beetle, never appears anywhere on its body -- which is why it sits just outside them on the stem lineage. What did it never grow?
answer: Jointed trunk limbs
choices: Jointed trunk limbs
Sensory antennae
Grinding jaw plates
Paired book gills
context: Anomalocaris belongs to the extinct order Radiodonta, an early-diverging branch just outside the crown-group arthropods. It shows arthropod hallmarks such as stalked compound eyes and segmented frontal appendages, but lacks the defining feature of modern arthropods: jointed, two-branched (biramous) walking and swimming trunk limbs. Instead of legs, its trunk bore only soft, flexible swimming flaps with feathery setal blades (gills) above them. It likewise had no true sensory antennae, no chewing jaws (its disk-like oral cone was a soft suction mouth that couldn't bite hard), and no book gills. That has-it/lacks-it mix is exactly why paleontologists prize it as a snapshot of the arthropod body plan mid-assembly during the Cambrian explosion. Source: Wikipedia 'Anomalocaris' (Radiodonta lacking biramous trunk limbs; setal-blade gills; soft suction oral cone); Frontiers in Earth Science 2023 review, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/earth-science/articles/10.3389/feart.2023.1160285/full

question: In a Canadian forest in midwinter, dig under the leaf litter and you can find a small brown frog frozen so hard it clinks like an ice cube -- no heartbeat, no breathing -- yet come spring it thaws and hops away. Which frog pulls this off?
answer: The wood frog
choices: The wood frog
The bullfrog
The tree frog
The leopard frog
context: The wood frog (Lithobates sylvaticus, formerly Rana sylvatica) lets up to about two-thirds of the water in its body turn to ice each winter, then thaws out in spring and simply hops away. Source: NSF, 'Frozen Frogs Don't Croak'; Audubon, 'Frogs Freeze to Survive the Alaskan Winter'.  (Legend.)

question: The crocodile icefish, hauled from the freezing Antarctic sea, is the only backboned animal on Earth with no red blood cells and no hemoglobin at all. What does its blood look like instead?
answer: Clear and white
choices: Clear and white
Bright red
Deep blue
Dark green
context: The crocodile icefish (family Channichthyidae) is the only vertebrate with no red blood cells and no hemoglobin -- the pigment that makes blood red -- so its blood runs clear and translucent white. Source: Quanta Magazine, 'Icefish Study Adds Another Color to the Story of Blood'; The Blood Project.  (Legend.)

question: Antarctic notothenioid fish live in seawater near minus 1.9 C -- colder than the point where their blood should freeze solid. Special proteins in their bodies find every tiny ice crystal that sneaks in and do what to it?
answer: Grip it so it can't grow
choices: Grip it so it can't grow
Melt it into water
Push it out through the gills
Wrap it in fat
context: These antifreeze glycoproteins latch onto any tiny ice crystal that gets inside and stop it from growing, so ice can't spread through the fish. Source: PMC8851421, 'Antifreeze Proteins: A Tale of Evolution'; PNAS 94(8):3811 (DeVries lab).  (Legend.)

question: Before the wood frog freezes, ice would normally burst its cells from the inside. Its liver stops that by flooding the cells with huge amounts of one substance, so ice forms only in the gaps around them, never inside. What does it flood in?
answer: Glucose
choices: Glucose
Salt
Ethanol
Vinegar
context: The liver dumps huge amounts of glucose (blood sugar) into the cells; the sugar keeps the cells themselves from freezing while ice forms only in the safe spaces between them. Source: PubMed 8409827, 'Glucose concentration regulates freeze tolerance in the wood frog'; Audubon.

question: When a wood frog is fully frozen it isn't merely sluggish -- everything halts for months: no heartbeat, no breathing, no brain activity. Then warm spring soil arrives. Roughly how long does it take, once thawed, for the frog to be back to normal?
answer: About 10 hours
choices: About 10 hours
About 10 minutes
About 10 days
About 10 weeks
context: The heart and brain restart on their own after months of silence, and within about 10 hours the frog is back to normal. Source: Discover Wildlife, 'This strange animal survives winter by stopping its heart'; Blue Ridge Discovery Center, 'Frozen Frogs'.  (Legend.)

question: A round swelling on a goldenrod stem hides a fly larva that freezes on purpose all winter. In autumn it floods itself with glycerol; then, as the cold deepens, it brews a SECOND protectant to push its survival down to about minus 40 C. What is that second substance?
answer: Sorbitol
choices: Sorbitol
More glycerol
Seawater
Melted fat
context: The goldenrod gall fly larva (Eurosta solidaginis) adds sorbitol as a second cryoprotectant when it gets colder, surviving frozen down to about minus 40 C and thawing over and over all winter. Source: Storey Lab, 'Goldenrod gall fly'; JEB 221(15):jeb177956.

question: The Arctic ground squirrel takes the OPPOSITE path from the wood frog -- it refuses to turn to ice. In hibernation its body drops to about minus 2.9 C, below water's freezing point, yet its blood stays liquid. How does it keep from icing up?
answer: It clears out the specks ice would form around
choices: It clears out the specks ice would form around
It packs its blood with antifreeze proteins
It lowers its blood's freezing point with glycerol
It keeps its blood moving too fast to freeze
context: The squirrel 'supercools': it cleans out the tiny particles that ice would normally form around, so its blood stays liquid at minus 2.9 C -- the lowest body temperature ever measured in a mammal. Source: Scientific American, 'What the Supercool Arctic Ground Squirrel Teaches Us'; UAF Centennial (Brian Barnes research).  (Legend.)

question: The notothenioid binds ice crystals with a grip that evolution never engineered any release for. What strange lifelong price does the fish pay for carrying that antifreeze?
answer: The trapped ice never melts, even in summer-warm water
choices: The trapped ice never melts, even in summer-warm water
The trapped ice slowly crowds and starves its cells
The thin blood can no longer carry any oxygen
The eggs it lays will not survive open water
context: The proteins grip the ice so tightly that trapped crystals refuse to melt even when summer sea-water warms above their normal melting point, so the fish can carry damaging ice inside its body for its whole life. Source: Cziko et al., PNAS 111(40):14583 (2014), 'Antifreeze protein-induced superheating of ice inside Antarctic notothenioid fishes'.  (Legend.)

question: With no hemoglobin, each drop of the icefish’s blood carries very little oxygen. Evolution compensated by supersizing one organ far beyond a normal fish’s. Which organ did it enlarge?
answer: Its heart
choices: Its heart
Its liver
Its brain
Its stomach
context: The icefish grew an oversized heart that pumps four to five times more blood per body weight than a normal fish, plus up to about four times the blood volume and extra-wide vessels, so a large amount of thin, clear blood moves fast at low pressure. Source: Scientific American; Spacedaily.

question: The Antarctic notothenioid builds its ice-gripping antifreeze from a long, dull-repetitive protein backbone. Tracing the gene back, biologists found it was not invented from scratch but rebuilt from a gene the fish already carried for a completely different job. What was that borrowed gene originally for?
answer: A digestive enzyme that breaks down food in the gut
choices: A digestive enzyme that breaks down food in the gut
A tough structural protein that builds the scales
A sensor protein that detects water pressure
An oxygen-storing protein packed in the muscle
context: One of biology's clearest cases of a brand-new gene born from an old one. Chen, DeVries & Cheng (PNAS 94:3811, 1997) showed the antifreeze glycoprotein gene was assembled from a pancreatic trypsinogen gene -- a digestive-enzyme gene -- by keeping the old gene's front and back ends and copying a tiny nine-letter 'Thr-Ala-Ala' snippet over and over to grow the long ice-gripping backbone. They called it the first clear example of an old protein gene spawning an entirely new protein with a new function. The switch happened only about 5-14 million years ago, right when the Antarctic Ocean first froze. Source: Chen, DeVries & Cheng, 'Evolution of antifreeze glycoprotein gene from a trypsinogen gene in Antarctic notothenioid fish,' PNAS 94:3811 (1997) -- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC20523/

question: The crocodile icefish is the only vertebrate with no hemoglobin: its blood runs clear and carries barely a tenth of the oxygen a red-blooded fish carries, yet it lives right alongside red-blooded cousins in the same water. Biologists still argue over why it lost its red blood cells at all. Which explanation does the leading review defend?
answer: No measured benefit -- a mutation that stuck only because cold, predator-poor water relaxed selection
choices: No measured benefit -- a mutation that stuck only because cold, predator-poor water relaxed selection
Clear blood raised oxygen delivery in the thick, frigid Antarctic water
Thinner, cell-free blood cut the heart's pumping cost in the cold
Scrapping red cells freed up iron the fish reused in other tissues
context: A genuine, still-live scientific debate. Sidell & O'Brien's 2006 review argues there is no measured fitness advantage to being white-blooded: icefish live right alongside red-blooded cousins, and their clear blood carries only about 10 percent of the oxygen. The hemoglobin-loss mutation likely survived only because frigid, isolated, predator-poor Antarctic waters relaxed the pressure long enough for extreme compensations -- an enormous heart, huge blood volume, and scaleless skin that soaks oxygen straight from the water -- to evolve and keep the fish alive. Whether the loss was ever adaptive at all is still argued. Source: Sidell & O'Brien, 'When bad things happen to good fish: the loss of hemoglobin and myoglobin expression in Antarctic icefishes,' J. Exp. Biol. 209:1791 (2006) -- https://www.researchgate.net/publication/7129088

question: In loose dry sand, a small buried insect digs a smooth cone-shaped pit and waits at the bottom with only its wide jaws poking up. An ant that wanders over the rim slides down the crumbling walls straight into those jaws. Which insect is this?
answer: The antlion
choices: The antlion
The ambush bug
The dung beetle
The tiger beetle
context: The antlion larva (family Myrmeleontidae) buries its whole body at the bottom of the pit, leaving only its jaws exposed just below the surface. The sloped sand walls do the hunting: prey that touches the rim slides down into the waiting jaws. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antlion  (Legend.)

question: An ant that falls into an antlion's sand pit doesn't just get grabbed — as it scrambles up the crumbling wall trying to escape, the buried larva at the bottom does something to drag it back down. What does the antlion do?
answer: Flicks sand up at the ant to trigger tiny landslides
choices: Flicks sand up at the ant to trigger tiny landslides
Squirts a jet of sticky glue up the wall
Vibrates the whole pit like a drumhead
Whistles to summon other larvae
context: With violent jerks of its head the antlion showers the climbing ant with flung sand, setting off little avalanches that carry the ant back down into its jaws. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antlion  (Legend.)

question: The antlion larva's whole body is built to travel only ONE way — which is why, as it hunts for a spot to dig, it leaves squiggly winding doodle-trails in the sand. Which way can it move?
answer: Only backward
choices: Only backward
Only forward
Only sideways, like a crab
Only in tight circles
context: The antlion larva can only walk backward. Wandering backward in search of a spot to dig, it leaves squiggly winding trails in the sand — which is why in North America it's nicknamed the 'doodlebug'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antlion

question: After years as a fierce sand-throwing pit-digger, the antlion larva finally pupates and emerges as its winged adult form. What does the grown-up antlion look like?
answer: A delicate, long-winged flier often mistaken for a damselfly
choices: A delicate, long-winged flier often mistaken for a damselfly
A stout, furry night-flier like a small moth
A hard-shelled beetle with a horned head
A hovering, striped insect resembling a wasp
context: The adult antlion has long, lacewing-like wings and looks so unlike its larva that it's frequently mistaken for a damselfly or dragonfly — and it no longer eats ants. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antlion  (Legend.)

question: An antlion larva can hunt in its sand pit for years and never once leaves a single dropping. What is the strange reason it never poops?
answer: It has no anus at all
choices: It has no anus at all
Its food leaves no solid waste behind
It sheds its whole gut with each molt
It turns all its waste into silk
context: The larva has no anus and cannot expel waste; everything from years of hunting is stored inside its body and only released after it becomes an adult. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antlion  (Legend.)

question: About the size of a raven, Archaeopteryx lived roughly 150 million years ago and mixed traits no modern animal shares: a mouth of small teeth, clawed fingers, and a long bony tail, but also true feathers and a wishbone. What do scientists say a fossil like this is best understood as?
answer: A signpost of one group turning into another over deep time
choices: A signpost of one group turning into another over deep time
A hoax assembled from two different fossils
A giant insect that only looked like a bird
A creature with no living relatives at all
context: Birds ARE living dinosaurs, and Archaeopteryx sits on that road as a creature part dinosaur, part bird, preserved in the fine Solnhofen limestone of southern Germany. Source: UCMP Berkeley 'Archaeopteryx: An Early Bird'; National Geographic (2014); Britannica 'Archaeopteryx'.

question: One Archaeopteryx skeleton had its feathers so poorly preserved in the stone that its first describers filed it under the wrong animal entirely, missing that it was a bird at all. What did they initially catalog this fossil as?
answer: A small bipedal dinosaur (a Compsognathus)
choices: A small bipedal dinosaur (a Compsognathus)
A flying reptile (a pterosaur)
A fossil fish (a Leedsichthys)
An early crocodile (a Goniopholis)
context: A real-world demonstration of how close the two groups are: with the feathers barely showing, the bird was taken for a small bipedal dinosaur, a Compsognathus. Source: UCMP Berkeley 'Archaeopteryx: An Early Bird'.

question: Archaeopteryx already had feathers and a wishbone, yet it still kept its teeth, its clawed hands, and its long bony tail all at the same time. What does this patchwork of old and new parts tell scientists about the PACE of the change from dinosaur to bird?
answer: Evolution swapped one system at a time, not all at once
choices: Evolution swapped one system at a time, not all at once
The switch happened in a single dramatic generation
The tail shortened before any feathers grew
Each animal reshaped its own body as it grew
context: Because it mixes traits, the transition proceeded piecemeal: feathers and a wishbone arrived while teeth, clawed hands, and a bony tail were still hanging around. Source: NCBI/PMC5418581 'Mosaic evolution in an asymmetrically feathered troodontid'; Wikipedia 'Archaeopteryx'.

question: A famously well-preserved Archaeopteryx showed long feathers running from head to foot, even covering its legs 'like trousers.' Since feathers show up on a creature that was a poor flier at best, what do scientists now think feathers were originally FOR, before flight?
answer: Warmth or showing off
choices: Warmth or showing off
Rowing through shallow water
Grabbing and holding prey
Filtering food from mud
context: Paleontologist Oliver Rauhut: 'The only thing we can say with some certainty is that [feathers] did not primarily evolve for flight, as it was long believed.'
