The scientists summed up the sequence as 'First show off, then take-off.' Source: National Geographic (2014); ScienceDaily '140703091959' and 'First show off, then take-off' (2014).  (Legend.)

question: Modern birds anchor their big flight muscles to a deep keeled breastbone, but Archaeopteryx had only a flat sternum. Given that missing anchor, how did paleontologist Mark Norell describe what its flying was actually like?
answer: Maybe like a turkey if it really tried
choices: Maybe like a turkey if it really tried
A smooth soaring glide for miles
A hovering hummingbird beat
No airborne ability whatsoever
context: Without the keel, Archaeopteryx was 'probably not a strong flier.' Norell said it 'probably didn't fly like a bird at all, maybe like a turkey if it really tried.' Source: UCMP Berkeley; National Geographic (2014, Mark Norell quote); Wikipedia 'Archaeopteryx'.

question: On the forearm of a Velociraptor, a fast ground predator that never left the ground, scientists found six evenly spaced bumps along the bone. In living birds, that exact row of bumps marks where one specific structure is anchored to the arm. What do those bumps hold in place?
answer: The shafts of long wing feathers
choices: The shafts of long wing feathers
The tendons of a grasping claw
A row of protective bony scales
The muscles that fold the wing
context: Quill knobs on a ground-bound raptor show it wore feathers even though it never flew, so feathers came long before flight and weren't a bird-only trait. Source: Turner et al., 'Feather Quill Knobs in the Dinosaur Velociraptor,' Science 317:1721 (2007); EurekAlert 'Velociraptor had feathers'. LEGENDARY find.

question: Feathered, wishboned, and outwardly bird-like, Archaeopteryx should have rocketed to adult size in weeks the way hatchling birds do. But when scientists cut thin sections of its bone, they found dense, nearly blood-vessel-free tissue that lays down maddeningly slowly. What did that bone reveal about how this creature actually grew up?
answer: It took years, growing at the plodding pace of a cold-blooded dinosaur
choices: It took years, growing at the plodding pace of a cold-blooded dinosaur
It reached full size in weeks, exactly like a modern songbird chick
It stopped growing early and stayed a permanent juvenile its whole life
It grew in yearly spurts timed to the wet and dry seasons
context: Gregory Erickson and colleagues (2009, PLOS ONE) found Archaeopteryx bone is nearly avascular, parallel-fibered tissue, one of the slowest-growing bone types, the kind seen in cold-blooded reptiles and non-bird dinosaurs rather than the explosively fast bone of modern birds. By one estimate it took on the order of years, roughly 970 days, to reach adult size, growing about three times slower than living precocial birds. So even with feathers and a wishbone, its growth engine and metabolism were still that of a dinosaur, another way the transition was a mosaic: the appearance changed before the physiology did. Source: Erickson et al. 2009, PLOS ONE, 'Was Dinosaurian Physiology Inherited by Birds? Reconciling Slow Growth in Archaeopteryx' (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0007390, PMC2756958); AMNH 'Archaeopteryx Lacked Rapid Bone Growth' (https://www.amnh.org/explore/news-blogs/archaeopteryx-slow-bone-growth).

question: To settle whether Archaeopteryx truly flapped or merely glided, Dennis Voeten fired synchrotron X-rays through its wing bones and read the internal architecture, thin walls threaded with dense blood-vessel channels, and matched it against living birds. Its bones plotted right on top of one particular kind of flier. Which one?
answer: Pheasants, which burst into short powered flights to clear obstacles
choices: Pheasants, which burst into short powered flights to clear obstacles
Albatrosses, which lock their wings and soar for days without a flap
Hummingbirds, which hover in place on a blur of beating wings
Penguins, whose stiffened wings row them through open water
context: In 2018 Dennis Voeten and colleagues used propagation phase-contrast synchrotron X-ray microtomography at the European Synchrotron to image the interior of Archaeopteryx wing bones. The thin, densely vascularized walls matched living birds that actively flap, not gliders or soarers, so Archaeopteryx was an active flapping flier, but its bones plotted closest to birds like pheasants that fly in short bursts to clear obstacles or escape predators, not to long-distance soarers. The twist: the wing bones showed flight adaptations while the shoulder girdle did not, so it could not raise its wing fully above its back for the modern high-lift flight stroke. It flew, but not the way any bird flies today, the live edge of the how-did-it-fly debate. Source: Voeten et al. 2018, Nature Communications, 'Wing bone geometry reveals active flight in Archaeopteryx' (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-03296-8, PMC5849612); Sci-News summary (https://www.sci.news/paleontology/archaeopteryx-active-flyer-05814.html).

question: In the fine limestone of Solnhofen in Bavaria, quarrymen have pulled out a crow-sized creature from 150 million years ago that scientists call the single most famous 'halfway' fossil ever found. What did this animal wear that no reptile before it had grown?
answer: A full coat of true feathers
choices: A full coat of true feathers
A shell of bony plates
A crest of spines
A layer of thick fur
context: Archaeopteryx lived on a tropical archipelago of low islands that is now the Solnhofen region of southern Germany, in the Late Jurassic. It is one of the most famous 'transitional fossils' ever found. Source: UCMP Berkeley - Archaeopteryx: An Early Bird; Wikipedia - Archaeopteryx.

question: Archaeopteryx of Late Jurassic Germany looked so bird-like that it was crowned the 'Urvogel,' the primeval bird. Yet hidden inside that bird-like face was a holdover from its reptile ancestors. What lined its jaws?
answer: Rows of small sharp teeth
choices: Rows of small sharp teeth
A hard horny beak
A long sticky tongue
A pouch of stored seeds
context: Archaeopteryx had real feathers and wings like a bird, yet unlike any bird alive today its jaws were lined with small sharp teeth - a reptilian holdover. Source: UCMP Berkeley - Archaeopteryx: An Early Bird; Britannica - Archaeopteryx.

question: A modern bird's wing ends in a smooth feathered tip, but the wing of Archaeopteryx ended in something no living bird carries. What did each of its wings still bear at its tip?
answer: Three clawed fingers
choices: Three clawed fingers
A single curved spur
A webbed flap of skin
A pad of blunt scales
context: On each wing Archaeopteryx kept three clawed fingers that no living bird has - claws that could have grasped prey or gripped tree branches. Source: UCMP Berkeley - Archaeopteryx; Fossilicious species profile.

question: Its feathers-but-teeth, claws, and a bony tail made Archaeopteryx the textbook example of a creature caught mid-change. Which two great animal groups did this one fossil famously bridge?
answer: Meat-eating dinosaurs and birds
choices: Meat-eating dinosaurs and birds
Fish and amphibians
Reptiles and mammals
Insects and spiders
context: The mix made Archaeopteryx one of the most famous 'transitional fossils' ever found - evidence that birds descended from dinosaurs, sharing traits with meat-eating dromaeosaurs like the raptors. Source: Wikipedia - Archaeopteryx; UCMP Berkeley.

question: The Solnhofen limestone captured each feather of Archaeopteryx down to the vane. Looking at that fossil vane, scientists were startled by how much it already resembled what?
answer: The flight feather of a modern bird
choices: The flight feather of a modern bird
A soft tuft of down
A reptile's overlapping scale
A simple hairlike bristle
context: The limestone preserved the vane of a flight feather so clearly that it showed the shape of a modern flight feather already present 150 million years ago. Source: Wikipedia - Archaeopteryx (feathers); Natural History Museum dino-directory.

question: Flightless birds like ostriches grow symmetric feathers, with an equal width of vane on each side of the shaft; flying birds do not. When scientists checked an Archaeopteryx flight feather, which pattern did it match?
answer: Lopsided vanes, like a flying bird
choices: Lopsided vanes, like a flying bird
Even vanes, like an ostrich
A bare shaft with no vane
Twin shafts sharing one base
context: The Archaeopteryx flight feather had asymmetric vanes - narrow on one edge, wide on the other - the lopsided shape that in modern birds pushes air for lift, hinting the wing was built to fly, not just for show. Source: Feduccia & Tordoff, 'Feathers of Archaeopteryx: asymmetric vanes indicate aerodynamic function' (PubMed 17811125); NHM dino-directory.

question: Scientists still honestly argue whether Archaeopteryx truly flew or mostly glided, because its skeleton is missing a key part of a strong flier's engine room. What did its chest lack?
answer: A deep keeled breastbone
choices: A deep keeled breastbone
A wishbone of any kind
A rib cage entirely
A set of hollow bones
context: Archaeopteryx lacked the deep keeled breastbone that anchors a modern bird's powerful flight muscles, so at best it managed weak, flappy flight - whether it flew or glided is still honestly debated. Source: UCMP Berkeley - Archaeopteryx (flat sternum); Wikipedia - Archaeopteryx (flight).

question: Archaeopteryx has an oddly long upper-arm bone, which opens a gap between its wing feathers and its body where air would leak through and spoil lift. The 2025 Chicago specimen finally showed how the animal sealed that gap. What did paleontologists find running along its upper arm?
answer: A row of long tertial feathers
choices: A row of long tertial feathers
A flap of bare gliding skin
A second short pair of wings
A fringe of stiff tail plumes
context: The 14th Archaeopteryx skeleton, the 'Chicago specimen' at the Field Museum, was described in Nature in 2025 by Jingmai O'Connor and colleagues using UV light and CT scans. It preserved long tertial feathers on the upper arm for the first time in any Archaeopteryx. Because its humerus is unusually long, those tertials are exactly what fills the leak-prone gap between wing and body, letting the wing act as one continuous airfoil. Closely related feathered dinosaurs have wing feathers that stop at the elbow with no tertials, which is a big reason they could not fly and Archaeopteryx could. Source: https://www.sci.news/paleontology/chicago-archaeopteryx-13912.html ; https://www.fieldmuseum.org/about/press/uv-light-and-ct-scans-helped-scientists-unlock-hidden-details ; Nature 2025, s41586-025-08912-4.  (Legend.)

question: With its feathers and wings, Archaeopteryx looks built for the fast, richly vascularized growth of a modern bird, which fledges within weeks. So scientists thin-sectioned its bone and counted the microscopic growth rings to clock how fast it actually grew. Compared with a living bird its size, how did it grow?
answer: About three times slower
choices: About three times slower
About twice as fast
The same rate, but no yearly rings
Slower, but grown within one year
context: A 2009 study led by Gregory Erickson, with Mark Norell and others (PLOS ONE), thin-sectioned Archaeopteryx bone and found poorly vascularized, parallel-fibered 'reptilian-grade' tissue with growth lines (LAGs, annual rings) in the larger London and Solnhofen specimens. Those rings show it kept growing across the second and third years of life, pausing each year like a small non-avian dinosaur, at roughly three times slower than modern precocial birds of similar size (maximal rates of 1.87-2.2 g/day, about a third of the rate for extant precocial land birds). So despite its feathers and wings, its metabolism and growth were still dinosaur-like, not fully bird-like, which is why the plain 'twice as fast', 'same rate', and 'grown within one year' answers are all wrong. Source: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0007390 (Erickson et al., PLOS ONE, 2009); https://www.amnh.org/research/science-news/2009/archaeopteryx-lacked-rapid-bone-growth-the-hallmark-of-birds.

question: In the mangroves of Southeast Asia and northern Australia lives a slim, silvery fish, banded in black, that eats insects perched on leaves it can never reach. How does this little hunter bring down a bug sitting on a branch above the water?
answer: It spits a jet of water to knock the bug into the pond
choices: It spits a jet of water to knock the bug into the pond
It leaps and snatches the bug from the branch with its fins
It lures the bug down by wiggling like a floating seed
It waits for wind to shake the bug loose from the leaf
context: The archerfish (genus Toxotes) is one of the only animals that uses a projectile of water as a weapon, firing a precise jet from below the surface to knock insects off overhanging leaves and branches into the water, where it eats them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archerfish

question: An archerfish takes aim at a beetle two feet up on a leaf and fires. What does the very first shot usually do?
answer: Hits the beetle dead-on and knocks it into the water
choices: Hits the beetle dead-on and knocks it into the water
Falls short, so the fish circles for a better angle
Splashes wide, warning the beetle to fly off
Startles the beetle into dropping on its own
context: An adult archerfish almost always hits on the very first shot; a well-practiced fish can score a near-100% hit rate on insects up to about 65 cm (2 ft) away, and its jet can reach prey as far as 3 metres (about 10 feet) overhead. Source: https://elifesciences.org/reviewed-preprints/92909v1 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archerfish

question: An archerfish has no hands and no tool, yet it fires a tight jet of water like it came from a nozzle. Where does the archerfish build the barrel that shapes and launches its watery bullet?
answer: Inside its own mouth, pressing its tongue into a grooved roof
choices: Inside its own mouth, pressing its tongue into a grooved roof
In its throat, where a ring of muscle squeezes the water out
Between its lips, which purse into a tight round hole
In a pouch behind its gills that fills and then bursts
context: The archerfish presses its tongue up against a deep groove in the roof of its mouth, turning the groove into a narrow tube exactly like the barrel of a gun, then snaps its gill covers shut to blast water down the barrel. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archerfish

question: Light bends where air meets water, so an archerfish looking up at a bug on a leaf sees it shifted from where it really is, off by as much as 25 degrees. Faced with a target its own eyes place in the wrong spot, what does the archerfish do?
answer: Corrects for the bend and aims at the bug's true position
choices: Corrects for the bend and aims at the bug's true position
Aims straight at the image it sees and fires anyway
Rises to the surface so the water no longer distorts the view
Fires a spread of shots to cover every possible spot
context: The archerfish compensates for refraction, aiming at the insect's real location rather than the distorted position its eyes show it. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2982040/ ; https://elifesciences.org/reviewed-preprints/92909v1

question: An archerfish's mouth muscles are far too weak to fire the hard-hitting blast it lands on distant bugs; the punch is actually built in mid-air, after the water leaves its mouth. What clever trick makes the flying jet stronger than the fish that fired it?
answer: Water shot later races ahead and bunches the jet into one slug
choices: Water shot later races ahead and bunches the jet into one slug
The jet spins like a rifle bullet and drills through the air
A pocket of air behind the water pushes it faster as it flies
The jet freezes into a tiny bead that strikes like a pebble
context: LEGEND-level physics: water shot later travels faster than the water shot first, so the back of the jet catches the front mid-flight and bunches into one compact, hard-hitting slug, about six times more powerful than the fish's mouth muscles alone, the same physics as a drop-on-demand inkjet printer. Source: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0047867 (Vailati et al. 2012, PLOS ONE)

question: In Stefan Schuster's experiment, some archerfish sat out the whole training with not a single practice shot, yet the moment they were finally given a turn they nailed fast-flying targets almost as well as the trained experts. Where did their sharp aim come from?
answer: Copying the aim of trained fish purely by observation
choices: Copying the aim of trained fish purely by observation
A burst of instinct that switched on the first time they went hungry
A knack for the skill they were simply hatched already knowing
A chemical cue in the tank water that carried the trick between fish
context: LEGEND-level cognition: in Schuster's 2006 study, archerfish that never fired during training suddenly shot almost as well as the experts once given a turn, learning to hit fast-flying targets purely by observing other fish. Source: https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(06)01013-X (Schuster, Current Biology 2006)

question: A slender, graceful seabird patrols the coast: a black cap pulled over its crown, white cheeks, and a deeply forked 'swallow' tail. What color are the Arctic tern's bill and feet?
answer: Blood-red
choices: Blood-red
Bright yellow
Slate-gray
Jet-black
context: The Arctic tern has a blood-red beak and blood-red feet, set against a black crown, white cheeks, and a deeply forked tail. Source: Wikipedia, Arctic tern.

question: The Arctic tern breeds near the North Pole and winters near the South Pole, a small seabird whose life stretches across the whole planet. For which record does this bird stand ahead of every other animal on Earth?
answer: The longest migration of any animal
choices: The longest migration of any animal
The fastest level flight of any bird
The most non-stop days aloft of any seabird
The highest-altitude migration of any bird
context: Egevang et al.'s 2010 tracking study was titled 'Tracking of Arctic terns reveals longest animal migration' — pole to pole, Arctic breeding grounds to Antarctica and back, every single year. Source: Egevang et al. 2010, PNAS.  (Legend.)

question: The Arctic tern spends the northern part of its year breeding near the North Pole, then crosses the entire globe to spend the rest of the year near the South Pole. What does chasing the sun this way give it that likely no other creature gets?
answer: Two summers and more daylight than any animal alive
choices: Two summers and more daylight than any animal alive
A warm climate but very little food
A shorter journey than flying straight south
Fewer predators at both ends
context: Because it lives in perpetual summer at both poles, the Arctic tern sees two summers a year and very likely more daylight than any other animal on Earth. Source: Wikipedia, Arctic tern; discoverwildlife.com. LEGEND.

question: When scientists tracked the Arctic tern, they found it does not fly straight south at all — its route curves down the Atlantic in a great zigzagging S-shaped loop. So how far does one bird actually travel in a single year?
answer: About 70,900 km (~44,000 miles)
choices: About 70,900 km (~44,000 miles)
About 12,000 km (~7,500 miles)
About 250,000 km (~155,000 miles)
About 5,000 km (~3,000 miles)
context: Because it loops rather than flying a straight line, the true round trip averages about 70,900 km a year (range 59,500–81,600 km). Source: Egevang et al. 2010, PNAS.

question: Arctic terns often live 30 years or more, and every year of that long life the bird flies its full pole-to-pole loop. Add up one bird's whole lifetime of flying — about 2.4 million km — and what famous distance does it match?
answer: Roughly three round trips to the Moon and back
choices: Roughly three round trips to the Moon and back
Roughly one trip around the Earth
Roughly a trip to the Sun
Roughly a trip to the nearest star
context: Over a life of 30-plus years the bird flies roughly 2.4 million km — the equivalent of about three return journeys to the Moon. Source: Egevang et al. 2010, PNAS; National Geographic. LEGEND.

question: The Arctic tern does not beat straight across the ocean; it rides the prevailing winds in a huge S-shaped loop that spirals down through the South Atlantic and back up through the North Atlantic. Which way does its loop actually turn at each end?
answer: Counterclockwise around the South Atlantic, clockwise around the North Atlantic
choices: Counterclockwise around the South Atlantic, clockwise around the North Atlantic
Clockwise around the South Atlantic, counterclockwise around the North Atlantic
Clockwise around both the South and North Atlantic
Counterclockwise around both the South and North Atlantic
context: The tern's sigmoidal route runs counterclockwise around the South Atlantic gyre and clockwise around the North Atlantic gyre, riding each ocean's prevailing winds rather than fighting a straight-line crossing. Source: Egevang et al. 2010, PNAS.

question: To measure the Arctic tern's journey, scientists needed a tracking tag that a 100-gram bird could carry pole to pole without being burdened. How heavy were the geolocators they fitted to the birds?
answer: Just 1.4 grams
choices: Just 1.4 grams
About 20 grams
About 100 grams
About half a gram
context: The team fitted 1.4-gram geolocators to 11 birds (10 from Greenland, 1 from Iceland) — light enough not to burden a bird that weighs only about 100 grams. Source: Egevang et al. 2010, PNAS; National Geographic.

question: In 1987 a farmer near Plaza Huincul in Argentina found a huge object jutting from his land and, sure of what it was, phoned the local museum to report it. What did farmer Guillermo Heredia think he had found?
answer: A petrified log
choices: A petrified log
A meteorite
A whale skull
A buried statue
context: The 'log' was a gigantic bone of Argentinosaurus, one of the largest land animals ever known. His call to the museum began the discovery. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentinosaurus  (Legend.)

question: Argentinosaurus stretched perhaps 30 to 35 meters from nose to tail-tip, and its estimated weight of 65 to 80 tons was so enormous that scientists reach for a herd of a single familiar animal to picture it. Its weight was compared to how many of what?
answer: A dozen elephants
choices: A dozen elephants
A hundred horses
Fifty cattle
A thousand dogs
context: At 65 to 80 tons, Argentinosaurus weighed more than a dozen African elephants and stretched nearly the length of a basketball court. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentinosaurus

question: Argentinosaurus is among the largest animals ever to walk the Earth, famous for a length of 30 to 35 meters. How did paleontologists arrive at that figure?
answer: They scaled up its whole body from a handful of its own bones
choices: They scaled up its whole body from a handful of its own bones
They scaled it up from a close relative's complete skeleton
They measured the stride length in a fossil trackway
They compared it to the largest living whale
context: Argentinosaurus is known from only a handful of bones, about seven back vertebrae, some ribs, a shinbone and a hip bone, so its 30-35 m length and 70-plus-ton weight are reconstructed by scaling up the whole animal from those few fragments, not measured from a complete skeleton. Honest paleontology flags the uncertainty. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentinosaurus  (Legend.)

question: An adult sauropod could stretch some thirty meters from nose to tail, yet every one began life inside a shell a person could cradle in two hands. From hatchling to full grown, a giant like this multiplied its length by roughly what factor?
answer: About 100 times longer
choices: About 100 times longer
About 5 times longer
About 20 times longer
About 1,000 times longer
context: A sauropod hatched from an egg only about the size of a cantaloupe to a basketball, then grew perhaps 100 times longer to reach adult size, an explosive growth spurt over decades. Source: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-sauropod-dinosaurs-became-the-biggest-land-animals-again-and-again/  (Legend.)

question: Argentinosaurus hauled 65 to 80 tons on four legs. Its giant back bones and neck bones hid a feature that surprised paleontologists who sectioned them. Cut one of those bones open, and what would you find inside?
answer: Air-filled chambers
choices: Air-filled chambers
Solid marrow cores
Coiled cartilage bundles
Dense mineral crystals
context: Argentinosaurus's bones were internally lightened by a complex pattern of air-filled chambers, the same pneumatic trick modern birds use, letting the giant carry 70-plus tons without a crushingly heavy skeleton. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentinosaurus

question: To learn how a 65-to-80-ton titanosaur got around, Bill Sellers and colleagues built a digital muscle-and-bone model of Argentinosaurus and let a computer hunt for its most efficient gait across every setting. No matter how the software searched, the giant's motion topped out at one thing. What was the fastest way this body could ever move?
answer: A slow walk of about 2 meters per second
choices: A slow walk of about 2 meters per second
A heavy pounding trot between trees
A brief charging run over short distances
A rocking gallop on all four legs
context: Sellers and colleagues (2013) ran forward-dynamic simulations of an 83-tonne Argentinosaurus in their GaitSym software, using a genetic algorithm to find the most efficient gait. The optimizer could only ever produce a slow walk, top speed roughly 2 m/s (about 5 mph), and never a run or gallop; the authors concluded that an 83-tonne body is 'approaching a functional limit' for a land animal. Source: Sellers et al. 2013, PLOS ONE, 'March of the Titans: The Locomotor Capabilities of Sauropod Dinosaurs' (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0078733).

question: Whether Argentinosaurus or its rival Patagotitan holds the crown as the largest dinosaur ever found is still argued by paleontologists, and the answer keeps flipping between the two. What decides which titan comes out on top?
answer: Which set of back bones the estimate is measured from
choices: Which set of back bones the estimate is measured from
Which one left the greater number of fossil eggs
Which was discovered and formally named first
Which came from the more complete adult skeleton
context: In 2017 Carballido and colleagues argued that Patagotitan (about 37 m, roughly 69 tonnes) edged out Argentinosaurus by about 10 percent, using the cross-sectional area of its front back-vertebrae. In 2019 Gregory Paul countered that Argentinosaurus was still larger because its dorsal (back-bone) column was considerably longer, and several later analyses again favor Argentinosaurus as the biggest known titanosaur. Which one ranks first genuinely flips depending on which bones you measure. Source: Wikipedia 'Argentinosaurus' and 'Patagotitan', citing Carballido et al. 2017 and Paul 2019 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentinosaurus); SV-POW analysis (https://svpow.com/2017/08/09/dont-believe-the-hype-patagotitan-was-not-bigger-than-argentinosaurus/).

question: A small, spiky lizard of the South African hills is cornered by a hungry mongoose out on open rock. With nowhere to run, the armadillo girdled lizard does something startling with its OWN body to turn itself into a spiny, unbitable ball. What does it do?
answer: It grabs its own tail in its mouth and curls into a ring
choices: It grabs its own tail in its mouth and curls into a ring
It puffs up with air until it is too wide to swallow
It sheds its tail and skitters off on the stump
It flattens against the rock and plays dead
context: Frightened, the armadillo girdled lizard (Ouroborus cataphractus) bites its own tail and curls into a spiky loop, so its hard armored back and spined tail face outward and its soft belly is hidden inside the ring. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armadillo_girdled_lizard

question: When the armadillo girdled lizard bites its own tail and curls into a tight ring, its armored back and spined tail bristle outward on every side. The whole point of the maneuver is to hide one body part where a predator's teeth simply cannot reach it. Which part does the curled loop lock away in its center?
answer: Its soft, unarmored belly
choices: Its soft, unarmored belly
Its delicate ear openings
Its still-growing new tail tip
Its store of body fat for the dry season
context: When the armadillo girdled lizard curls into its tail-in-mouth ring, the hard armored back and spined tail face outward while the soft, vulnerable belly is hidden inside the loop - the one part predator teeth could pierce is tucked safely in the center. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armadillo_girdled_lizard

question: Pick up an armadillo girdled lizard and it feels less like a soft little reptile and more like something rigid and hard-cased, its back and tail so stiffly protected that a predator's teeth skid right off. What is this natural covering most like?
answer: The riveted plate armor of a knight
choices: The riveted plate armor of a knight
The fused bony dome of a tortoise shell
The overlapping plates of a pangolin
The bristling quills of a porcupine
context: Rows of thick, squarish, spiny keeled scales cover the lizard's back and tail like plate armor. That armor, plus the ball-curling, is why it is named after the armadillo. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armadillo_girdled_lizard

question: The armadillo girdled lizard of South Africa produces just one or two young each year, and the way they enter the world is rare among lizards - and rarer still, the mother may even stay and tend to them afterward. How do her young arrive?
answer: The female gives birth to live, wriggling babies
choices: The female gives birth to live, wriggling babies
The eggs are carried inside the mother's mouth
A single huge egg is buried and guarded for months
The young hatch from eggs glued under a rock ledge
context: Unlike most lizards, the armadillo girdled lizard does not lay eggs - the female gives birth to live young, usually just one or two at a time, after a gestation of about six to eight months. She is also one of the few lizards that may care for her offspring after birth. Source: https://www.sanbi.org/animal-of-the-week/armadillo-girdled-lizard/

question: Picture a lizard, and you probably picture a loner basking by itself. The armadillo girdled lizard flips that expectation completely with how it spends its life in the South African rocks - a social habit almost no other lizard keeps. What does its living arrangement look like?
answer: Colonies of 30 to 60 packed into one crevice
choices: Colonies of 30 to 60 packed into one crevice
A bonded pair that defends one crevice for life
A mother alone with her single yearly hatchling
Rival males each guarding a separate sun-rock
context: Instead of living alone like most lizards, the armadillo girdled lizard lives in social groups packed into rock cracks - colonies of up to 30 to 60 individuals of all ages sharing the same crevice, which is highly unusual for a reptile. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armadillo_girdled_lizard

question: A slow, tank-like African mammal is covered head-to-tail in overlapping hard plates, and those plates are made of keratin -- the very same stuff as your fingernails. Which animal is it?
answer: the pangolin
choices: the pangolin
the porcupine
the badger
the wombat
context: The pangolin is the only mammal covered head-to-tail in scales, and the scales are keratin -- the same protein as your fingernails and hair. Source: ZSL Pangolins (zsl.org); National Geographic Kids pangolin facts.

question: A jackal charges a tortoise on open ground. The tortoise doesn't run for cover -- it just pulls its head, legs and tail out of sight and waits. How can it defend itself with no cover anywhere near?
answer: it carries its fortress on its back
choices: it carries its fortress on its back
it plays dead until the jackal leaves
it puffs up too big to bite
it squirts a foul warning spray
context: A tortoise defends itself by drawing its head, legs and tail inside the shell -- a fortress it carries everywhere, so it never needs a burrow or rock. Source: Mesker Park Zoo Turtle Facts (PDF); allturtles.com Turtle Anatomy 101.

question: A lion bats and paws at a scaly African mammal but can't get one claw under a single scale to pry it open. That behavior is exactly what the Malay word 'pengguling' -- the root of 'pangolin' -- describes. What does 'pengguling' mean?
answer: one who rolls up
choices: one who rolls up
one who digs deep
one who climbs high
one who walks by night
context: 'Pengguling' means 'one who rolls up' -- the pangolin folds into an armored keratin ball a predator can't pry open. Source: Harvard Museum of Natural History, 'Pangolins: What's in a Name?'; Pangolin -- Wikipedia.

question: A hermit crab moves house by crawling out of one borrowed shell into a bigger one. A turtle can NEVER do this -- it can never leave its shell. Why not?
answer: the shell is its own fused ribs and spine
choices: the shell is its own fused ribs and spine
the shell is glued on by tough skin
the shell regrows too slowly to shed
the shell is welded shut by muscle
context: A turtle's shell is not a house it borrows -- it is the turtle's own ribcage and backbone, fused and flattened into the dome, so it can never crawl out. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'A turtle's shell has a lot in common with your ribs'; Turtle shell -- Wikipedia.

question: Most armadillos, when danger comes, sprint away or dig frantically. Just one kind can instead snap shut into a perfect sealed ball, its head-plate and tail-plate locking the seam. Which one?
answer: the three-banded armadillo
choices: the three-banded armadillo
the nine-banded armadillo
the giant armadillo
the pink fairy armadillo
context: The three-banded armadillo (genus Tolypeutes) is the only armadillo that curls into a complete sealed ball, its head-plate and tail-plate interlocking to lock the seam shut. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo, La Plata three-banded armadillo; Brazilian three-banded armadillo -- Wikipedia.

question: A pangolin's order is Pholidota, Greek for 'clad in scales.' Beyond rolling into a ball, those sharp overlapping scales do one more thing when the pangolin flexes its body. What?
answer: they work as slashing blades
choices: they work as slashing blades
they rattle out a warning
they lock its limbs in place
they soak up a snake's venom
context: The order Pholidota means 'clad in scales'; the sharp overlapping scales double as blades a pangolin can slash with by flexing its body. Source: Pangolin -- Wikipedia (order Pholidota).

question: Cornered on a bare South African rock, the armadillo girdled lizard grabs its own tail in its jaws and curls up. What does a predator now face instead of a soft belly?
answer: a spiny ring of sharp scales
choices: a spiny ring of sharp scales
a cloud of foul spray
a lashing whip of a tail
a mouthful of loose skin
context: The armadillo girdled lizard bites its own tail and curls into a spiny ring -- an 'ouroboros' -- so a predator meets a wall of sharp scales instead of its soft belly. Source: IFLScience, 'Armadillo Girdled Lizards Turn Themselves Into An Ouroboros'; Armadillo girdled lizard -- Wikipedia; SANBI.  (Legend.)

question: The glyptodon was an extinct armadillo relative as big as a Volkswagen Beetle, weighing up to two tons, its back plated in hundreds of bony osteoderms. What shape did that back armor take?
answer: a single solid dome
choices: a single solid dome
a row of bristling spikes
a set of sliding bands
a coat of thick fur
context: Glyptodon was a car-sized armadillo relative whose back carried a domed shell of hundreds of fused bony plates (osteoderms) -- unlike the sliding bands of living armadillos or the spiked tail-club of its relative Doedicurus. Source: Britannica, 'Glyptodon'; Live Science, 'Volkswagen-Size Armored Mammal Is Armadillo Ancestor'; Glyptodont -- Wikipedia.

question: Because a turtle's shell IS its ribcage, one bone sits in a place found in no other backboned animal on Earth -- ours sit outside the ribs. Which bone sits INSIDE the turtle's ribs?
answer: its shoulder blades
choices: its shoulder blades
its hip bones
its collarbone
its breastbone
context: In every other backboned animal the shoulder blades sit outside the ribs; because a turtle's shell is its fused ribcage, its shoulder blades sit inside it. Source: Turtle shell -- Wikipedia; Nature Communications, 'The endoskeletal origin of the turtle carapace.'

question: A 220-million-year-old fossil turtle, Odontochelys, still had teeth and only broadened, half-grown ribs where a modern turtle's domed back-shell would be -- yet its underside was already sheathed in a complete, fully-formed bony sheet. Paleontologists say the fossil settles a long argument over the order the two halves of the shell evolved. Which half came first?
answer: the belly plate, before the back shell
choices: the belly plate, before the back shell
the neck bones, before the leg bones
the horny beak, before the true teeth
the tail club, before the domed back
context: Odontochelys semitestacea means 'toothed turtle with a half-shell.' Described in Nature in 2008 (Li, Wu, Rieppel & Wang), it had a fully ossified plastron (belly plate) but only broadened ribs and no finished carapace on top -- the exact layout of a modern turtle embryo caught mid-development. That resolved the long debate: the plastron evolved before the carapace. Odontochelys also still had teeth in its jaws, which every living turtle has since traded for a horny beak. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odontochelys ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turtle_shell ('The fossil showed that the plastron evolved before the carapace').

question: Deep in the rainforest, a colony of army ants never digs a burrow or builds a mound. When the marching stops for the night, hundreds of thousands of workers hook leg to leg and become the shelter itself, walling in the queen and young. What do biologists call this temporary ant-built structure?
answer: A bivouac
choices: A bivouac
A formicary
A carton nest
A royal cell
context: Army ants have no fixed nest. The workers grip each other with hooked feet to form a temporary living nest, called a bivouac, that shelters the queen and brood inside. Source: Discover Magazine, 'How Army Ants Build City-Like Nests Using Their Own Bodies' / Nature Communications s41467-022-28773-z.

question: Steering a raid of Eciton burchellii is done by workers that are blind or nearly so. With no useful eyes to guide two hundred thousand ants across the forest floor, what does the swarm rely on to hold its shape and direction?
answer: Touch and chemical scent trails
choices: Touch and chemical scent trails
Wind direction on their antennae
Vibrations from a lead drummer ant
Magnetic sense in their antennae
context: Army ant workers are blind or nearly blind. They run the entire raid by touch and by pheromone trails they lay down with their own bodies. Source: The Conversation, 'Bridges, highways, scaffolds...' / Britannica, 'Eciton army ant'.

question: When an army ant column reaches a gap it cannot detour around, the raid does not stop or slow. Within seconds a structure appears across the gap, and the column pours straight over it. What have these ants made?
answer: A living bridge of their own bodies
choices: A living bridge of their own bodies
A rope of dried saliva
A raft of floating leaves
A tunnel dug under the gap
context: Army ants build living bridges from their own bodies, hooking together with tarsal claws so nestmates can cross rough ground without slowing. Source: Powell & Franks, PNAS 'Army ants dynamically adjust living bridges' (2015) / AntWiki, 'The Ants Chapter 16'.

question: Scott Powell and Nigel Franks laid planks drilled with holes of many sizes across an army ant trail and watched the traffic. The workers didn't avoid the holes. Instead, each ant did something at a hole that let prey-laden nestmates sprint home at full speed. What did each ant do at a hole?
answer: Plugged a hole its body exactly fit
choices: Plugged a hole its body exactly fit
Dropped a pebble to fill it
Spun a silk patch across it
Widened it into a shortcut
context: Each ant selected a hole matching its own body size and flattened into it, filling potholes with living bodies so the column ran home at full speed. Source: Powell & Franks study, via ScienceBlogs 'Army ants plug potholes with their own bodies' (2009). (legend)

question: The bivouac of an army ant colony is nothing but living bodies clinging together, yet the ants do not just huddle passively. As the outside air heats and cools through the day, they keep the core steady near 28.5 degrees Celsius. How do the workers manage this in a nest made only of themselves?
answer: Opening and closing air passages through the mass
choices: Opening and closing air passages through the mass
Fanning their wings to move air
Carrying the queen to cooler ground
Sealing the whole cluster shut at dawn
context: Even a nest made only of ants is thermoregulated: the colony opens and closes air passages to hold the core near 28.5 degrees C while outside temperatures swing. Source: Franks, 'Thermoregulation in army ant bivouacs' (1989), Physiological Entomology.

question: Imagine a millipede as long as a grown man is tall, and then some, scuttling across a Carboniferous forest floor 326 million years ago, more than 100 million years before the first dinosaurs. That was Arthropleura. Just how long did the biggest ones grow?
answer: About 2.7 metres, over 8 feet
choices: About 2.7 metres, over 8 feet
About 40 centimetres, ankle height
About 1 metre, knee height
About 6 metres, bus length
context: Arthropleura is the largest land invertebrate ever known to have lived. The biggest reached about 2.6 to 2.7 metres (over 8 feet) long, roughly the length of a small car, and weighed around 50 kilograms. Source: University of Cambridge, 'Millipedes as big as cars once roamed England'; Natural History Museum (2021).  (Legend.)

question: A giant adult Arthropleura had more than 30 armoured body segments running down its 2-metre-plus length. Counting the legs on any single one of those segments reveals the signature that marks it as a millipede relative. What did each segment carry?
answer: Two pairs of walking legs
choices: Two pairs of walking legs
A single pair of legs
One clawed grasping leg
No legs, just armour
context: Two pairs of legs per body segment is the millipede signature (centipedes carry one pair per segment). A big adult had roughly 28 to 32 segments, leaving it scuttling on dozens of legs. Source: Wikipedia 'Arthropleura' (body structure).

question: In January 2018 a block of sandstone cracked off a cliff and split open on the beach at Howick Bay in Northumberland, England. A former PhD student spotted giant Arthropleura remains inside, the find that finally pinned down its true monster size. But the 75-centimetre object was not what it first looked like. What had actually hardened in that rock over 300 million years?
answer: A shed skin the animal had outgrown
choices: A shed skin the animal had outgrown
A crushed complete skeleton
A fossilised clutch of eggs
A footprint pressed into mud
context: Dr Neil Davies called it 'a complete fluke of a discovery.' The fossil was a moulted piece of exoskeleton, about 75 cm long, that had filled with sand and hardened. Most Arthropleura fossils are these cast-off skins, not carcasses. Source: University of Cambridge giantmillipede story; Britannica 'Arthropleura'.

question: An 8-foot armoured Arthropleura sounds like the nightmare predator of the coal forests, yet it had no venom fangs and no grabbing claws. Scientists now picture this giant living a very different life than its size suggests. How did it actually feed?
answer: Munching rotting logs, leaf litter, and seeds
choices: Munching rotting logs, leaf litter, and seeds
Ambushing amphibians in the shallows
Sucking sap from giant tree ferns
Filtering plankton from swamp water
context: Arthropleura is now thought to be a detritivore, eating rotting wood, leaf litter, and nuts and seeds like modern millipedes, not a hunter. Source: Natural History Museum (2021); Wikipedia 'Arthropleura' (diet).

question: Textbooks long explained the Carboniferous giants like Arthropleura and the huge dragonfly Meganeura with a single cause: the ancient air was extra rich in oxygen, letting bodies balloon. Studying the fossils, Dr Neil Davies argued that oxygen 'cannot be the only explanation.' What did he point to instead?
answer: A rich, high-nutrient diet in the ancient forests
choices: A rich, high-nutrient diet in the ancient forests
A far weaker pull of ancient gravity
Warmer seas driving faster growth
A total absence of any predators
context: Scientists long credited high Carboniferous oxygen for insect and millipede gigantism, but Davies noted oxygen alone cannot explain it, pointing to the nutrient-rich food available in those forests. Source: University of Cambridge giantmillipede story (Dr Neil Davies quote).

question: An assassin bug (family Reduviidae) doesn't chew its prey. It drives a curved needle-like beak into a captured insect, pumps in saliva that turns the victim's insides to soup, and then does WHAT with that soup?
answer: Sucks it out through the beak like a milkshake
choices: Sucks it out through the beak like a milkshake
Spits it back out to attract more prey
Stores it in a pouch to feed its young
Lets it drip onto the ground as a scent trail
context: The saliva carries paralytic toxins and digestive enzymes that liquefy the victim's tissues OUTSIDE the body (called extraoral digestion); the bug then drinks the liquefied insides up through the same beak, the rostrum. The saliva is potent enough to dissolve prey much larger than the bug itself. Source: Reduviidae - Wikipedia; Britannica 'Assassin bug'.

question: The nymph of the assassin bug Acanthaspis petax drains ants dry, then does something ghoulish with the empty husks: it glues them, with sticky threads from its own belly, into a walking pile it carries. Where does that pile of dead ants ride?
answer: Stacked on its own back as a disguise
choices: Stacked on its own back as a disguise
Wedged inside its hollow beak
Buried in a hidden pantry underground
Strung along a silk line behind it
context: The nymph secretes sticky threads from special abdominal hairs and cements the drained ant carcasses into a heap on its back that can hold roughly a dozen or more bodies - a mound of its own victims worn as camouflage. Source: Acanthaspis petax - Wikipedia; Newsweek 'Assassin Bug Stacks Its Victims on Its Back'. (Legend-status wonder.)

question: Scientists wondered whether the Acanthaspis petax nymph's backpack of dead ants really protects it, or whether its movement was what saved it. So they offered jumping spiders both bare nymphs and corpse-wearing ones - even DEAD, preserved bugs. What did the test reveal?
answer: Spiders attacked bare nymphs about ten times more often
choices: Spiders attacked bare nymphs about ten times more often
Spiders ignored both kinds of nymph entirely
Spiders preferred the corpse-wearing nymphs
The backpack only helped while the nymph was moving
context: Jackson & Pollard (2007, Journal of Zoology) found jumping spiders struck bare nymphs about ten times as often as backpack-wearing ones - and because the effect held even for dead, motionless bugs, the disguise ITSELF fools the spider's vision, not any movement. Source: Jackson & Pollard 2007, 'Bugs with backpacks deter vision-guided predation by jumping spiders'; summarized National Geographic. (Legend-status wonder.)

question: The feather-legged assassin bug (Ptilocnemus lemur) of Australia hunts fierce jack jumper ants bigger than itself. A gland on its body oozes an intoxicating secretion, and it waves a feathery hind leg. Why offer the ant that leg?
answer: The ant grabs and tastes it, and the bug twists to stab its neck
choices: The ant grabs and tastes it, and the bug twists to stab its neck
The leg squirts glue that pins the ant in place
The leg snaps off to distract the ant while the bug flees
The ant carries the leg home, poisoning its whole colony
context: Entomologists nicknamed it the 'fatal attraction' strategy: the trichome gland's secretion lures the ant into grabbing and tasting the feathery leg, whereupon the bug twists around and drives its beak into a soft spot at the ant's neck joint - the ant is drawn in by the very leg that leads it to its death. Source: Ptilocnemus lemur - Wikipedia; myrmician 'Ptilocnemus lemur: the ant assassin'. (Legend-status wonder.)

question: The atlas moth of Asia is one of the biggest moths alive, its wings so broad that people who spot one often mistake it for a bird. Held open, how wide can an atlas moth's wings span?
answer: Nearly a foot across
choices: Nearly a foot across
About the width of a coin
Roughly a hand-span, tip to tail
Barely wider than a thumbnail
context: An atlas moth's wingspan reaches about 25-30 cm - up to nearly a foot across - and by wing surface area it has more total wing than almost any insect on Earth. Source: Natural History Museum, London - Spotlight: the atlas moth.

question: When a hungry bird closes in on a resting atlas moth, the moth flaps and writhes so the curved, patterned tips of its forewings suddenly rear up and jerk toward the attacker, which flees. The pattern on those wingtips mimics the head of which dangerous animal?
answer: A cobra
choices: A cobra
A great owl
A scorpion
A wolf spider
context: The atlas moth's forewing tips are patterned to resemble a cobra's head; by flapping so the two 'snake heads' rear up, the moth scares off predators. Its Cantonese name even translates to 'snake's head moth.' Source: Natural History Museum, London; California Academy of Sciences - Atlas Moth. (Legend/defense wonder.)

question: An adult atlas moth lives only about one or two weeks and spends that whole life doing nothing but searching for a mate. Why does it die so fast, no matter how safe it stays?
answer: It has no working mouth and can never eat
choices: It has no working mouth and can never eat
It burns out its wings within days of flying
Its blood freezes the first cold night
It cannot see well enough to find food
context: The adult atlas moth has only a tiny, useless proboscis - it can never eat, and survives just a week or two on fat it stored as a caterpillar, existing only to mate and lay eggs. Source: Wikipedia - Attacus atlas; HowStuffWorks - The Atlas Moth Is a Behe-moth.  (Legend.)

question: A female atlas moth barely moves after hatching - she clings near her old cocoon and releases a faint chemical scent into the night air. A male can find her from kilometers away across dark forest. What lets him track that scent from so far?
answer: Huge feathery antennae that catch her scent
choices: Huge feathery antennae that catch her scent
Large eyes that see her glowing in the dark
A long tongue that tastes her on the breeze
Sharp ears tuned to the beat of her wings
context: The male atlas moth has enormous, feathery antennae that detect a female's pheromones from kilometers away and home in on her. The female is larger and stays put near her cocoon, releasing scent, while the smaller male does the flying. Source: Animal Diversity Web / Wikipedia - Attacus atlas.

question: A small pink salamander drifts through the canals of Mexico City, and behind its head a frilly feathery 'crown' sticks out into the water. What is that six-branched crown doing for it?
answer: Pulling oxygen straight from the water
choices: Pulling oxygen straight from the water
Sensing electric fields from prey
Storing fat for the dry season
Warning rivals to keep away
context: The axolotl's showy 'crown' is a set of six branched external gills; oxygen passes straight from the water into the blood flowing through them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axolotl

question: An axolotl seems to smile up at you from its tank, mouth curved in a cheerful little grin. What is actually behind that permanent 'happy' face?
answer: Just the upturned shape of its mouth
choices: Just the upturned shape of its mouth
A puff of air held in its cheeks
A ring of muscle it flexes to greet you
Rows of tiny teeth showing through
context: The pale-pink, black-eyed axolotl isn't feeling anything by its grin — the smile is simply the fixed upturned shape of its face. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axolotl

question: An axolotl looks like it never grew up: feathery gills, a soft larval body, a tadpole-like tail fin it never sheds. Yet it is not a helpless juvenile. What can this eternal-baby body still do?
answer: Breed and lay eggs while still in its larval form
choices: Breed and lay eggs while still in its larval form
Feed only on milk-like fluid from its mother
Survive on land for months between water spells
Change its sex once each breeding season
context: Staying a larva forever is called neoteny (or paedomorphosis): the axolotl keeps its feathery gills and larval body yet becomes sexually mature and breeds, never transforming into a land salamander. Legend among biologists as the classic case. Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2019.00237/full

question: An axolotl loses a whole back leg to a hungry tankmate. Weeks later the stump is gone and something has taken its place. What has happened to that leg?
answer: A complete new leg has grown back
choices: A complete new leg has grown back
A stiff scarred nub has sealed the wound
The gills nearby have enlarged to compensate
A cartilage flap now covers the gap
context: An axolotl regrows a lost limb whole — bone, muscle, nerve, blood vessels, even the tiny pigment patterns — over and over, with no scar. A biology legend. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/health/article/axolotl-regrow-limbs-retinoic-acid-human-medicine

question: Millions of axolotls swim in labs and home aquariums around the world. Yet out in nature the wild axolotl is critically endangered. Where does the last wild population cling on?
answer: The canals of Lake Xochimilco
choices: The canals of Lake Xochimilco
A hot spring in the Sierra Madre
The mouth of the Rio Grande
A flooded quarry near Veracruz
context: Pollution and sewage crashed the wild population 99% between 1998 and 2014; perhaps 50 to 1,000 axolotls survive, only in the canals of Lake Xochimilco — an animal nearly extinct in nature yet everywhere in captivity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axolotl

question: The axolotl doesn't stop at legs. A lab tracks one that has had part of an internal organ removed, and watches it rebuild the missing piece. Which organ can it repair this way?
answer: Parts of its heart
choices: Parts of its heart
Its stomach lining
One of its gills' roots
A cracked rib
context: Beyond limbs, the axolotl can regrow its tail, jaw, parts of its heart, sections of its spinal cord, and even portions of its brain — which is why labs from Vienna to Boston keep colonies. A biology legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axolotl

question: When you cut yourself, the wound seals fast with tough collagen that hardens into a scar. An axolotl's wound does something different first — after clearing the debris, what mode does it switch back into?
answer: Embryo-style growth
choices: Embryo-style growth
Rapid collagen sealing
A slow dormant standstill
Hard shell-like plating
context: Instead of scarring, the axolotl's wound pauses, clears the debris, and reverts to embryo-style growth — so it rebuilds the part perfectly with no scar. A biology legend. Source: https://siliconcanals.com/sc-c-axolotls-can-regrow-entire-limbs-parts-of-their-heart-sections-of-their-spinal-cord-and-even-portions-of-their-brain-and-they-do-it-without-forming-scar-tissue-which-is-why-labs-from-vienna-to-bo/

question: When a human body receives a transplanted organ from another person, the immune system usually attacks the newcomer as foreign. Graft a piece of another axolotl's brain or an eye onto an axolotl and what happens instead?
answer: The alien organ settles in and works normally
choices: The alien organ settles in and works normally
The graft is walled off in a hard capsule
The host absorbs it within a few days
The tissue survives but never connects up
context: An axolotl's immune system doesn't reject transplants the way ours does; scientists have grafted eyes and pieces of another axolotl's brain onto one and had the foreign organs work normally. A biology legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axolotl

question: The axolotl seems locked into its baby form forever. But scientists found a chemical switch that forces it to finally grow up. Dose it with thyroid hormone and what does the animal become?
answer: A land-crawling salamander with no gills
choices: A land-crawling salamander with no gills
A giant twice its normal size
A blind, cave-dwelling drifter
A hard-shelled bottom-crawler
context: Given thyroid hormone, the axolotl loses its gills, its tail fin shrinks, and it crawls onto land looking almost exactly like its cousin the tiger salamander. A biology legend. Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2019.00237/full

question: In a 1968 Science paper, researchers grafted a second whole head onto an axolotl. The odd part was not that the graft survived — axolotls accept transplants. It was what the extra head did on its own. What did the grafted head do?
answer: Snapped at and fed on passing prey by itself
choices: Snapped at and fed on passing prey by itself
Slowly shrank until it was reabsorbed
Fused its brain into the original head
Grew a third head budding from its base
context: In the 1968 experiment ('Transplantation of Axolotl Heads,' Science) the grafted second head not only survived without rejection but grew and behaved like a normal head — snapping at and feeding on prey independently of the host. A biology legend. Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.162.3852.460 (Science, 1968, 'Transplantation of Axolotl Heads')

question: Amputate an axolotl limb and it normally regrows perfectly. But researchers first wiped out one type of immune cell, the macrophages, from the animal before cutting. This time the leg never came back. What formed at the stump instead?
answer: A permanent scar of tough collagen
choices: A permanent scar of tough collagen
A cluster of the missing macrophages
A shrunken half-limb missing its foot
A blister that reopened the wound
context: This 2013 experiment (Godwin, Pinto & Rosenthal) pinned regeneration on the immune system: with macrophages depleted before amputation, the stump healed like a mammal wound, capping itself in thick mature type-I collagen instead of forming a blastema. The macrophages fully returned within about two weeks, but by then the window had closed and no limb grew. Their early inflammatory signals are the switch between scar-free regrowth and scarring. Source: Godwin, Pinto & Rosenthal, "Macrophages are required for adult salamander limb regeneration," PNAS 2013 (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1300290110).

question: When the axolotl genome was sequenced in 2018, it broke a record as the largest ever assembled and hid a genuine shock: one gene long thought essential to build every other vertebrate simply was not there. Which gene had gone missing?
answer: Pax3, with a cousin gene covering its job
choices: Pax3, with a cousin gene covering its job
Sox2, replaced by an ancient viral insert
Hox13, the limb-tip patterning master
Myf5, the muscle-founder switch gene
context: At about 32 gigabases, over ten times the human genome and roughly 19 Gb of repetitive junk-like DNA, the axolotl genome needed a purpose-built assembler (MARVEL). The find that stunned developmental biologists: Pax3, considered indispensable in all other vertebrates, is absent, and its close relative Pax7 has taken over its role. Mutating Pax7 in axolotls reproduces the very defects mice suffer when they lose Pax3. Source: Nowoshilow et al., "The axolotl genome and the evolution of key tissue formation regulators," Nature 2018 (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature25458).

question: A wide-eyed, nocturnal lemur found only on Madagascar, and the largest nocturnal primate on Earth:
answer: the aye-aye
choices: the aye-aye
the slow loris
the tarsier
the sugar glider
context: The aye-aye (Daubentonia madagascariensis) runs about 15 inches of body with a bushy tail even longer than that, weighing roughly 4-6 pounds. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye

question: The aye-aye is the only primate that finds food by percussive foraging: it taps a tree trunk up to eight times a second and listens hard. What is it actually sensing under the bark?
answer: a hollow echo where a grub tunnel runs
choices: a hollow echo where a grub tunnel runs
sap rising through the trunk
the scent of insect eggs
the tree's own heartbeat
context: Tap-scanning fills between 5 and 41 percent of the aye-aye's foraging time; it listens for the hollow echo that betrays a grub tunnel hidden under the bark. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye

question: As the aye-aye taps a branch, tall ridges inside its oversized bat-like ears go to work on the faint echo coming back from under the bark. What do those inner ridges do to that echo?
answer: focus and funnel it toward the eardrum
choices: focus and funnel it toward the eardrum
split it into two delayed signals
cancel out its own tapping noise
amplify only the highest frequencies
context: The ridges work like a lens, funneling the faint echo of the aye-aye's own taps and the movement of larvae under the bark, so it can pinpoint prey it cannot see. Source: https://factanimal.com/aye-aye/

question: Once the aye-aye hears the hollow of a grub tunnel, it gnaws through the bark with front teeth that do something no other primate's teeth do. What is strange about those incisors?
answer: they never stop growing for its whole life
choices: they never stop growing for its whole life
they are coated in venom
they glow to lure insects
they fall out and regrow yearly
context: These rodent-like, ever-growing incisors are unique among primates and are the reason early naturalists mistook the aye-aye for a rodent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye

question: The aye-aye taps wood, listens for a grub, chisels a hole, then fishes the larva out with a thin finger. On other continents an entirely different creature does this exact job with its beak. Why did a primate evolve to fill that role on Madagascar?
answer: the island has no woodpeckers
choices: the island has no woodpeckers
its grub prey burrow too deep for any beak
Madagascar's birds are all fruit-eaters
the island's woodpeckers went extinct long ago
context: Madagascar has no woodpeckers, so the aye-aye evolved to fill that empty niche, doing with a wiry middle finger the exact job a woodpecker's beak does elsewhere. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye  (Legend.)

question: The aye-aye's wiry middle finger hooks larvae out of winding grub tunnels deep inside the wood. Its knuckle carries a joint found in no other primate hand. Which joint is it?
answer: a ball-and-socket joint
choices: a ball-and-socket joint
a fused rigid joint
a double-hinged joint
a sliding cartilage pad
context: The ball-and-socket knuckle joint is the only one of its kind in a primate hand, letting the middle finger rotate freely as it hooks a grub. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye

question: In 2019 researchers solved a puzzle about the aye-aye: its real fingers are so specialized for fishing grubs out of bark that they can't do one everyday job -- grip a branch to hold on. Yet it climbs just fine. How does it manage?
answer: a whole extra thumb of bone and cartilage grew just for gripping
choices: a whole extra thumb of bone and cartilage grew just for gripping
its long claws hook over the branch and lock in place
its long bushy tail coils around the branch like a fifth limb
its hind feet grip while its hands stay free to work
context: NC State researchers Adam Hartstone-Rose and Edwin Dickinson found the aye-aye has a hidden sixth digit, a 'pseudothumb' with its own fingerprint. Hartstone-Rose: 'It has both a bone and cartilaginous extension and three distinct muscles that move it.' Source: https://news.ncsu.edu/2019/10/aye-aye-extra-finger/  (Legend.)

question: A near-hairless wild pig roams the Indonesian island of Sulawesi. Local people named it the pig-deer because the male's strange tusks reminded them of a deer's antlers. Which animal is this?
answer: the babirusa
choices: the babirusa
the warthog
the Malayan tapir
the collared peccary
context: 'Babirusa' comes straight from Indonesian 'babi rusa' — literally 'pig-deer.' It is a wild pig of Sulawesi and a few nearby islands (the Togian, Sula, and Buru islands), and its near-hairless grey body only adds to the odd look. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babirusa

question: The male babirusa's upper canine teeth do something no other pig on Earth does with its teeth. Where do those canines end up?
answer: piercing up through the skin on top of its snout
choices: piercing up through the skin on top of its snout
jutting sideways past its fleshy cheeks
curving down below its lower jaw
fusing into a single bony ridge along its back
context: The male's upper canines don't exit the mouth at all — they grow straight UP, pushing through the skin on top of the snout, then curve backward over the face toward the forehead. It is one of the strangest sets of teeth in the animal kingdom. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babirusa  (Legend.)

question: The male babirusa is famous for its bizarre upcurving tusks. But most people picture only two of them, when in fact the male carries four tusks in all. What is the second pair?
answer: a lower pair of canines that also curve upward
choices: a lower pair of canines that also curve upward
a hidden pair rooted deep in the throat
a spare pair that only grow in old age
a pair of flat grinding tusks at the back
context: The male has FOUR tusks: the famous upper pair that pierces the snout, plus a lower pair of canines that also sweep upward. In dominance fights the lower tusks work as offensive weapons while the snout-tusks act more like defensive guards. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babirusa

question: The male babirusa's upper tusks never stop growing. On an old male that never wears his down, the endless tusk can, in rare cases, do something grim to the babirusa. What?
answer: it curls round and grows into the animal's own skull
choices: it curls round and grows into the animal's own skull
it snaps off and blinds one of its eyes
it locks the animal's jaw permanently shut
it splits the tip of the snout clean in two
context: Because the tusks never stop growing, an unworn one can, in rare cases, keep arcing until it curls round and penetrates the animal's own skull — a creature that literally grows its teeth through its face and, occasionally, back into its own head. Source: https://blogs.ucl.ac.uk/museums/2016/08/12/specimen-of-the-week-252-the-babirusa-skull/  (Legend.)

question: In the deep ocean twilight, a small fish only about 15 cm long hangs motionless with a bizarre feature: the whole top of its head is a transparent, fluid-filled dome you can see straight through, like a windshield over its skull. What is this fish called?
answer: The barreleye
choices: The barreleye
The blobfish
The anglerfish
The viperfish
context: The barreleye (Macropinna microstoma) has a see-through dome covering the top of its skull. Despite its otherworldly, alien-looking head, it is only about 15 cm (6 inches) long. Source: MBARI animal page (mbari.org/animal/barreleye-fish); Robison & Reisenbichler 2008, Copeia.  (Legend.)

question: Look inside the barreleye's clear glass-like dome and you find two glowing green tubes — its real eyes. Instead of looking forward like yours, in their resting position these tubular eyes point in one surprising direction. Where do they aim?
answer: Straight up through the transparent skull
choices: Straight up through the transparent skull
Straight down toward the seafloor
Out to the left and right sides
Backward toward its own tail
context: The tubular green eyes point straight UP through the see-through skull to spot prey silhouetted against the faint light drifting down from far above. Source: MBARI news; Robison & Reisenbichler 2008.  (Legend.)

question: On the front of the barreleye's 'face' sit two dark spots exactly where a fish's eyes would normally be — so the first divers to see one were fooled. But the barreleye's real eyes are the green tubes tucked up inside its dome. So what are the two dark spots on its face actually?
answer: Nostrils — smell organs
choices: Nostrils — smell organs
A second pair of backup eyes
Light-producing lures
Openings to its gills
context: The two dark spots that look like eyes are actually nares — the fish's nostrils, its smell organs. The real eyes are the green tubes hidden inside the transparent dome. Source: MBARI animal page; Wikipedia (Macropinna).

question: The barreleye's tubular eyes normally aim straight up, so for years scientists were stumped by one puzzle: how could a fish that only looks upward ever guide food into its own tiny mouth below? In 2008, MBARI revealed the trick. What can those eyes do?
answer: Rotate forward inside the dome to follow food down
choices: Rotate forward inside the dome to follow food down
Detach and float free to chase prey
Shoot a beam of light onto the mouth
Grow a third eye near the jaw
context: MBARI solved the decades-old paradox in 2008: the tubular eyes can rotate forward inside the transparent dome, swiveling like binoculars to follow prey down to the mouth. Source: Robison & Reisenbichler 2008, Copeia 2008(4):780-784; MBARI news.  (Legend.)

question: MBARI's scientists found that a barreleye can't just swivel its eyes forward on their own — the eyes reach the forward-pointing position only in tandem with a specific move of the fish's whole body. What must the barreleye do for its eyes to swing forward?
answer: Roll its whole body from horizontal to vertical
choices: Roll its whole body from horizontal to vertical
Beat its tail hard three times
Drift into a shaft of brighter light
Press its snout against the prey
context: Robison and Reisenbichler watched a live specimen rotate its tubular eyes from pointing up to pointing forward as it tipped its body from horizontal to vertical to feed — the eyes turn as the whole fish rolls upright, so the eye rotation is coupled to the body's roll rather than happening on its own. Source: ScienceDaily 2009; Robison & Reisenbichler 2008.

question: The barreleye lives in the ocean's 'twilight zone,' roughly 600 to 800 meters down, where sunlight fades toward total darkness. To survive there it barely swims at all — instead it hangs almost perfectly still in the water. How does it hold its position so precisely?
answer: With large flat fins making tiny adjustments
choices: With large flat fins making tiny adjustments
By anchoring to rocks with a sticky foot
By filling a float sac with gas
By clinging to passing jellyfish
context: The barreleye hovers almost motionless around 600-800 meters (2,000-2,600 feet) down, using large flat fins to hold position with tiny, precise adjustments. Source: MBARI animal page; ScienceDaily 2009.

question: Researchers think the barreleye is a thief. It hovers beneath a siphonophore — a colonial drifter trailing stinging tentacles over 10 meters long — and picks off small animals already snared there. Its stomach even held jelly fragments. But those tentacles sting; what lets the barreleye raid them safely?
answer: The clear dome shields its eyes from the stinging cells
choices: The clear dome shields its eyes from the stinging cells
A slime coat that neutralizes the venom
It only strikes when the siphonophore sleeps
Thick scales armor-plate its whole body
context: Researchers think the barreleye hovers beneath a siphonophore and picks off small animals already trapped in its stinging tentacles; the transparent dome is thought to shield its delicate eyes from the stinging cells. Captured specimens had jelly fragments in their stomachs. Source: MBARI news; ScienceDaily 2009; Robison & Reisenbichler 2008.

question: W. M. Chapman described the barreleye in 1939, yet for 65 years every drawing of it left the top of the head blank — no artist had ever seen the transparent dome intact until MBARI filmed a live one in 2004. Why did those decades of net-caught specimens never show the dome?
answer: The fragile dome collapsed or tore off as nets hauled the fish up
choices: The fragile dome collapsed or tore off as nets hauled the fish up
The dome turns cloudy and opaque the moment the fish dies
The dome dissolves in the preservative used to store specimens
The dome retracts inside the skull whenever the fish is startled
context: Described in 1939 by W. M. Chapman, the barreleye was known only from net-caught specimens whose fragile transparent dome arrived collapsed or torn away — so old drawings left it out entirely. MBARI's ROVs captured the first footage of a living barreleye with its dome intact in 2004, 65 years later. Source: Wikipedia (Macropinna); MBARI news; Robison & Reisenbichler 2008.  (Legend.)

question: A small green lizard in a Central American stream rears up onto its two back legs and sprints straight across the open water without sinking, earning it a nickname from a famous Bible scene. What is that nickname?
answer: the Jesus Christ lizard
choices: the Jesus Christ lizard
the water dragon
the mangrove skater
the pond skimmer
context: The basilisk (genus Basiliscus) of Central and South American rainforest streams dashes across the surface of a pond or stream on its hind legs without sinking, so it looks like it is running on top of the water — hence the 'Jesus Christ lizard' nickname. Source: National Geographic — Green basilisk lizard.  (Legend.)

question: A basilisk lizard is basking on a branch high over a rainforest stream when a snake slides up the trunk toward it. There is no branch to leap to and no room to run. What does the cornered basilisk do to escape the snake?
answer: drops straight down out of the tree into the water
choices: drops straight down out of the tree into the water
clamps flat and motionless against the bark
wedges itself into a hollow in the trunk
spreads its ribs into a gliding flap
context: A startled basilisk bolts for the nearest water — and it will even drop straight down out of a tree into the water below to flee, then sprint or swim away, leaving a land predator stranded. Source: Wikipedia — Common basilisk; National Geographic — Green basilisk lizard.

question: A young basilisk can sprint clear across a stream on the surface, dashing 10 to 20 meters (33-66 ft) over open water. A full-grown adult, several times heavier, tries the very same crossing. How far does the heavy adult get before it sinks?
answer: only a few meters
choices: only a few meters
the same 10 to 20 meters
roughly 50 meters
the full width — an adult never sinks
context: Only the light young pull it off well: juvenile basilisks can sprint 10 to 20 m (33-66 ft) across open water, while heavy adults manage only a few meters before their weight breaks them through the surface and they sink. Source: Wikipedia — Common basilisk; Biology Insights.

question: A basilisk fleeing across a pond has to keep each foot from breaking through before the next one lands, slapping the surface so fast that no foot ever sinks in. How many times per second does a sprinting basilisk's feet hit the water?
answer: up to about 20 times
choices: up to about 20 times
about 3 times
about 100 times
about 500 times
context: A basilisk running on water takes up to 20 footsteps per second, slapping so fast that each foot pushes off before the water can close over it. Source: Biology Insights — How Basilisk Lizard Feet Enable Running on Water; National Geographic.

question: Scientists calculated whether a human could ever run across a lake the way a basilisk sprints across a pond. It comes down to leg power: to slap the water fast enough to hold up our own weight, how much more muscle would a person need than they actually have?
answer: about 15 times as much
choices: about 15 times as much
about twice as much
about a tenth more
no more than they already have
context: Glasheen and McMahon calculated that to hold up our weight a human would have to slap the water faster than 30 m/s, needing roughly 15 times the muscle power a person actually has — so no human can do it. Source: Glasheen & McMahon 1996, Nature 380:340-342, as summarized in water-running scaling literature.  (Legend.)

question: A shark the length of a bus glides toward a diver off the Scottish coast, mouth hanging wide open. The diver holds still. What does this second-largest fish in the sea actually do to a person in the water?
answer: Nothing at all -- it is a harmless giant
choices: Nothing at all -- it is a harmless giant
Delivers a crushing, bone-breaking bite
Wraps and squeezes prey like a python
Stings with venom-tipped fin spurs
context: The basking shark (Cetorhinus maximus) is completely harmless to people; despite its huge size and gaping mouth it is a gentle, non-aggressive giant. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basking_shark

question: The basking shark can grow past 33 feet and weigh several tons -- the second-biggest fish alive after the whale shark. With a mouth that huge, what does this monster actually feed on?
answer: Tiny drifting plankton
choices: Tiny drifting plankton
Seals hauled out on rocks
Schools of tuna and mackerel
Other sharks its own size
context: For all its size, the basking shark eats nothing but tiny plankton -- straining out copepods and other minute animals from the seawater. Source: https://www.marlin.ac.uk/species/detail/1438

question: A single 5-metre basking shark strains up to 500 tons of seawater an hour to sieve out its plankton. The whale shark and megamouth both work their throats to pump and gulp water across the filter. How does the basking shark drive all that water through its gills?
answer: It simply swims forward with its mouth open
choices: It simply swims forward with its mouth open
It gulps and spits water like a bellows
It suctions prey in with a piston throat
It fans water inward with its huge pectoral fins
context: The basking shark is a passive ram filter-feeder: unlike the megamouth and whale sharks it does no pumping or sucking, relying only on the water it forces through its gills just by swimming forward at about 2 knots. A single 5-metre shark can filter up to 500 tons of seawater an hour this way. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basking_shark

question: As the basking shark cruises with its cavernous mouth open, seawater pours in but the tiny copepods stay behind and the water flows on out through the gills. What catches the food?
answer: Dark, bristle-like gill rakers
choices: Dark, bristle-like gill rakers
A sticky mucus net in the throat
Rows of small hooked teeth
A muscular grinding gizzard
