context: The basking shark strains plankton with dark, comb-like gill rakers on its gill arches; they catch the food while the water passes on through the gills. Its actual teeth are tiny (5-6 mm), useless for feeding. Source: https://asknature.org/strategy/specialized-gills-filter-plankton/

question: In 1977 the Japanese trawler Zuiyo-maru hauled up a rotting carcass off New Zealand: a small head on a 1.5-metre neck with four flippers. The crew measured it as a plesiosaur before dumping it. What did tissue tests later reveal it to be?
answer: A decayed basking shark
choices: A decayed basking shark
A true surviving plesiosaur
A giant deep-sea squid
An unknown long-necked seal
context: A rotting basking shark loses its lower jaw, gills and fins first, leaving a 'head' on a long 'neck' -- so decayed ones repeatedly get mistaken for plesiosaurs (a 'pseudo-plesiosaur'). Amino-acid tests on saved Zuiyo-maru tissue showed it was a dead basking shark. Legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zuiyo-maru_carcass

question: For decades naturalists thought the basking shark passed the lean winter by sinking to the seabed and hibernating, its filter idle. David Sims recalculated the true energetic cost of ram-filtering and found the animal actually lives on a knife-edge. What did his numbers reveal it does instead?
answer: Keeps feeding on any patch dense enough, and just abandons thin water
choices: Keeps feeding on any patch dense enough, and just abandons thin water
Buries itself deep in the seafloor sediment until the spring bloom returns
Switches to hunting and gulping small schooling fish once copepods thin out
Drops its whole metabolism near zero and coasts along on stored liver oil
context: Sims's threshold-foraging work put a real energy budget on the giant filter. Pushing that cavernous mouth through the water creates enormous drag, so filtering only pays off above a plankton density of roughly 0.5 grams per cubic metre; below that the shark burns more energy than it gains and stops feeding, moving on to hunt richer water. Because that break-even threshold is lower than anyone expected, the shark never needs to hibernate -- it can profit on plankton year-round wherever the water is thick enough. Source: Sims 1999 & Sims et al. 2003, 'Threshold foraging behaviour of basking sharks on zooplankton: life on an energetic knife-edge?' (PMC1690094); CORDIS/Nature, 'UK study disproves basking shark hibernation myth.'

question: Off County Clare, Ireland, drones filmed something no one had recorded for this species: up to two dozen mature basking sharks slowly wheeling nose-to-tail, gently rolling belly-up and brushing fin to body as they turned. What were the sharks doing in that stacked, doughnut-shaped ring?
answer: Courting -- each sizing up many possible mates at once
choices: Courting -- each sizing up many possible mates at once
Herding a drifting plankton swarm into one richer patch
Settling a dominance order by jostling for the ring's centre
Basking in the sun-warmed surface before a long deep dive
context: David Sims and colleagues assembled underwater and aerial footage from 2016 to 2021 to describe this 'torus': groups of 6 to 23 mature sharks, equal males and females, circling in a ring 17 to 39 metres across and stacked in layers down to about 16 metres deep, with gentle fin-to-body touching and belly-rolling. Sims called it a slow-motion speed-dating event, where each shark can assess many potential partners at once -- the first courtship behaviour ever documented for the basking shark. Source: Sims et al., Journal of Fish Biology, 2022, 'Circles in the sea' (PubMed 36073958; PMC9826005); phys.org, 'Mysterious circling behavior of basking sharks explained.'

question: A bald eagle pins a fish under its talons, then leans down to feed. What is the shape of the beak it tears the flesh with?
answer: A downward-curving hook
choices: A downward-curving hook
A flat sieve like a comb
A slim hollow straw
A hard chisel point
context: A raptor's hooked upper bill lets it tear flesh from prey the talons hold pinned — the shape follows a meat-eater's diet. Source: raptor.umn.edu/about-us/news/what-makes-raptor-part-1-hooked-beaks

question: A woodpecker reaches insects that tunnel deep under the bark of a tree. What is its bill shaped like to get at them?
answer: A hard, straight chisel
choices: A hard, straight chisel
A curved tearing hook
A flat scooping spoon
A stretchy fishing net
context: A woodpecker's straight, hard bill works like a chisel, drilling into wood to reach insects hidden under bark. Source: calacademy.org/explore-science/woodpecker-inspiration

question: A hummingbird hovers at a deep, tube-shaped flower to drink the nectar pooled at the bottom. What is its bill shaped like to reach in?
answer: A slender needle
choices: A slender needle
A broad flat spoon
A hooked tearing blade
A blunt cracking wedge
context: A hummingbird's slender, needle-like bill is built to reach down inside deep tube-shaped flowers for nectar. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword-billed_hummingbird

question: A brown pelican's throat pouch looks like a floppy afterthought — yet in one plunge-dive it scoops up more water and fish than the whole bird weighs. About how much does that pouch hold?
answer: About 3 gallons
choices: About 3 gallons
About 1 gallon
About 6 gallons
About a half gallon
context: The pelican's gular pouch can hold about 3 gallons (11 liters) of water and fish, then drains the water out before the bird swallows the catch. Source: seaworld.org/animals/facts/birds/brown-pelican/

question: A roseate spoonbill wades a shallow lagoon, holding its flat bill a little open and sweeping it steadily side to side, then snaps it shut on a passing shrimp. Which sense tells the bird the exact moment to snap?
answer: Touch
choices: Touch
Sight
Smell
Hearing
context: The spoonbill holds its flat bill slightly open and sweeps it through mud, snapping shut the instant it feels a shrimp or small fish — it hunts by touch, not by sight. Source: nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/news/bold-bizarre-and-brilliant-8-fascinating-facts-about-roseate-spoonbill

question: A flamingo feeds with its head turned upside-down, dragging its bill backward through the water. Comb-like ridges strain tiny brine shrimp and algae from the water — and something in that food does what to the bird?
answer: Turns its feathers pink
choices: Turns its feathers pink
Makes it grow taller
Sharpens its eyesight
Curls its long neck
context: Comb-like ridges called lamellae strain out brine shrimp and algae; pigments in that food are what turn a flamingo pink. Source: nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/news/why-are-flamingos-pink-and-other-flamingo-facts

question: A stubby finch feeds only on tightly sealed conifer cones, working a seed out from between two shut scales — something a finch with an ordinary straight bill cannot do. What lets its bill pry a scale open?
answer: Bill tips that cross past each other for leverage
choices: Bill tips that cross past each other for leverage
A hooked upper bill for tearing
A comb of ridges lining the bill
A pouch under the lower bill
context: The crossbill's upper and lower bill tips cross past each other; jammed between two cone scales, the crossed tips give the leverage to pry a scale apart, and the tongue lifts out the seed. Legend-flagged as one of the ladder's vivid handles. Source: allaboutbirds.org/news/craig-benkmans-40-year-fascination-with-crossbills-and-conifers/

question: On one spruce tree, two crossbill species feed side by side and never compete for the same cones. What single trait sorts each species onto its own cones?
answer: The size of its bill
choices: The size of its bill
The color of its feathers
The time of day it feeds
The height it perches at
context: The small-billed white-winged crossbill works tiny spruce and tamarack cones, while the heavier-billed red crossbill breaks into big pine cones — bill size sorts the birds onto different cones on the same tree. Source: allaboutbirds.org/news/craig-benkmans-40-year-fascination-with-crossbills-and-conifers/

question: On one small island chain, a set of closely related finches carry wildly different bill shapes, from heavy and blunt to fine and pointed. What single thing does each bill's shape track?
answer: The food that bird eats
choices: The food that bird eats
The color of its mate
The island's rainfall
The song it sings
context: Give one island a dozen foods and evolution carves a dozen bills — Darwin's finches are closely related species whose bills scale from nut-cracker to insect-tweezer, with only about six genes explaining nearly half the variation in beak size. Source: news.ucsc.edu/2023/10/darwin-finches/

question: A falcon's hooked bill carries an extra notch on its upper edge — the tomial tooth — that hawks and eagles lack. The falcon fits a prey's neck into that notch and bites. What does the bite do?
answer: Severs the spinal cord for a fast kill
choices: Severs the spinal cord for a fast kill
Crushes the prey's skull
Punctures a lung to slow it
Snaps a wing so it cannot flee
context: The tomial tooth lets a falcon sever a prey's spinal cord for a quick kill — a feature hawks and eagles do not have. Source: birdsandblooms.com/birding/bird-species/birds-of-prey/falcon-vs-hawk/

question: The sword-billed hummingbird carries a bill 8 to 12 cm long — the only bird whose bill is longer than the rest of its body. It is so long the bird cannot use it for one everyday grooming job, and must do that job with its feet instead. Which job?
answer: Preening its feathers
choices: Preening its feathers
Scratching an itchy head
Wiping mud off its face
Fluffing its throat patch
context: The sword-billed hummingbird's bill is too long to preen with, so the bird scratches and cleans itself using its feet. Legend-flagged as a vivid handle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword-billed_hummingbird

question: Glenn Tattersall filmed a toucan to test a hunch about its oversized bill. Besides handling fruit, what hidden second job did his study reveal the bill does?
answer: Dumps body heat like a radiator
choices: Dumps body heat like a radiator
Stores fat for the dry season
Amplifies the bird's call
Filters mud from its water
context: Tattersall's infrared study found the toucan pumps blood into its bill to dump body heat, making it one of the largest thermal 'windows' in the animal kingdom — rivaling an elephant's ears. Legend-flagged. Source: science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1175553

question: A drought hit Daphne Major in 1977, and by the next year about 85% of the medium ground finches were dead — but the die-off was not random. Peter and Rosemary Grant found the survivors shared one trait of the beak. Which beak did the drought favor?
answer: The biggest, strongest beaks
choices: The biggest, strongest beaks
The smallest, lightest beaks
The most sharply hooked beaks
The most brightly colored beaks
context: The drought left mostly large, tough Tribulus seeds; birds with the biggest, strongest beaks could crack them and survived, so the survivors shared that one trait — natural selection acting in a single dry year. Legend-flagged. Source: knowledge.carolina.com/discipline/life-science/biology/evolution-of-the-galapagos-finch/

question: On Daphne Major the 1977 drought had favored the biggest beaks. When a second harsh drought hit in 2004, a bigger rival species had arrived and was hogging the large seeds. This time the medium ground finches that survived carried the opposite beak. Which one?
answer: The smallest beaks, better on the seeds left over
choices: The smallest beaks, better on the seeds left over
The biggest beaks, same as the 1977 winners
The longest beaks, for probing cactus flowers
The most hooked beaks, for tearing tough husks
context: Same island, same species as the famous 1977 result -- but the OPPOSITE winner. A population of the much larger LARGE ground finch had colonized Daphne Major and monopolized the big, hard seeds, so during the 2004-2005 drought the medium ground finches with SMALLER beaks (better at the small seeds left over) survived and the big-beaked ones died. This is a textbook case of 'character displacement' caught in real time, and selection against the large-beak type was fierce (selection coefficient s = 0.59). Lamichhaney and colleagues later traced the shift to the HMGA2 gene: birds carrying two copies of the small-beak variant (HMGA2*S) survived far better. Source: Lamichhaney et al. 2016, 'A beak size locus in Darwin's finches facilitated character displacement during a drought,' Science, Apr 22 2016 (PubMed 27102486; Princeton/Uppsala/ScienceDaily coverage), corroborated across multiple outlets.  (Legend.)

question: A crossbill's bill is not just crossed but handed: each bird's lower tip bends fixed to the left or the right for life, so it can only work a cone from one side. Craig Benkman found red crossbills split almost exactly 50/50 between the two. What keeps that even balance?
answer: Whichever type is rarer finds more untouched cones, so it thrives
choices: Whichever type is rarer finds more untouched cones, so it thrives
Chicks copy the crossing direction of the parent that feeds them
The crossing direction flips to match each new cone crop
Left and right tips wear down at exactly the same rate
context: A crossbill's crossed tip is 'handed' -- it crosses either to the left ('sinistral') or the right ('dextral'), fixed for life, forcing the bird to attack cones from one direction. Lefties and righties literally walk around a cone in opposite directions and pry from opposite sides. Craig Benkman found red crossbills occur in a roughly 1:1 ratio and argued it is held there by negative frequency-dependent selection: whichever morph is rarer has more un-worked cones available, so it does better, which pulls the ratio back toward even. (White-winged crossbills are skewed ~3:1 toward right-crossing.) Source: Craig Benkman's work and Springer, 'Are the ratios of bill crossing morphs in crossbills the result of frequency-dependent selection?' (Evolutionary Ecology); Scottish Wildlife Trust, Montana Public Radio, Bootstrap Analysis coverage, corroborated across sources.  (Legend.)

question: A flat-tailed North American rodent fells whole trees with its front teeth and dams a stream into a pond. Look at those two upper front teeth and you notice something odd for teeth: what color are they?
answer: Bright orange
choices: Bright orange
Pale white
Jet black
Dull gray
context: A beaver's incisors are famously orange because the outer enamel is packed with iron instead of the ordinary magnesium in most animal teeth. The iron makes them harder and more acid-resistant, so they resist decay without brushing. Source: https://scienceinsights.org/why-are-beaver-teeth-orange-its-iron-in-the-enamel/

question: A beaver spends its life gnawing through hard tree trunks, yet its teeth never wear down to nubs. How does it keep chewing wood for a lifetime?

choices: Its teeth never stop growing
It grows a fresh set each spring
It swaps to back molars for wood

context: A beaver's incisors grow continuously, so it must gnaw constantly to wear them down. New tooth forms at the root as fast as the tip wears away, keeping a chisel edge for life. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/blog/beaver-teeth-everything-you-need-to-know/

question: At the pond's edge sits a dome of mud and sticks where a beaver family lives. A fox prowls the bank but cannot get in. Where did the builders put the front door so predators can't follow?
answer: Underwater, entered by diving
choices: Underwater, entered by diving
On the roof, reached by climbing
Behind a wall of thorns
Facing away, hidden in reeds
context: A beaver builds its lodge with an entrance underwater, so a fox or wolf cannot follow it inside. The dam floods a safe moat around the home, and the family enters by diving. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/articles/ecosystem-engineers-how-beavers-build-wetlands-that-help-fight-climate-change/

question: A beaver's iron-hard enamel sits only on the FRONT face of each incisor; the softer dentin behind wears away faster with every bite. What does that lopsided wear do to the tooth as the beaver gnaws?
answer: Grinds it into a fresh chisel edge
choices: Grinds it into a fresh chisel edge
Splits it down the middle
Curls the tip back into the mouth
Dulls it into a flat stub
context: Because the hard iron enamel wears slower than the soft dentin behind it, every bite grinds the tooth back into a sharp chisel edge. The beaver's teeth sharpen themselves. Source: https://scienceinsights.org/why-are-beaver-teeth-orange-its-iron-in-the-enamel/

question: A beaver dives and swims through murky pond water with its eyes wide open, yet it sees clearly and its eyes stay unhurt. What piece of built-in gear lets it do that?
answer: A see-through third eyelid
choices: A see-through third eyelid
A ring of tiny scales
An oily protective film
A pair of bony eye-shields
context: A beaver has a transparent third eyelid that slides across each eye like built-in swim goggles, letting it see clearly underwater while keeping the water out. Source: https://forthriverstrust.org/mammals-week-anatomy-of-a-beaver/

question: A beaver swims across the pond, then a shadow overhead spooks it. In a flash it brings its broad flat tail down hard on the water with a loud CRACK. Besides steering as a rudder, what is that slap for?
answer: Warning the colony of danger
choices: Warning the colony of danger
Stunning fish to eat
Splashing mud onto the dam
Cooling itself in summer heat
context: A beaver's flat scaly tail is a Swiss-army tool: a rudder for steering while swimming, and an alarm. When danger appears, the beaver slaps it hard on the water with a loud crack to warn the whole colony. Source: https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/castoreum/

question: A beaver clamps a leafy branch in its front teeth and dives to stash it in an underwater larder, staying under for many minutes. How does it swim with its mouth full without water pouring down its throat?
answer: Its lips close behind the front teeth
choices: Its lips close behind the front teeth
It blocks its throat with its tongue
It swims with the branch held in a paw
It keeps the branch pinched above water
context: Before diving, a beaver seals itself shut: valve-like muscles clamp the nostrils and ears closed, and its lips close BEHIND the front teeth, so it can carry a branch underwater without swallowing water. It can stay under for about 15 minutes. Source: https://beaversinengland.com/beaver-biology/beaver-biology-2/

question: Deep in Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park lies a beaver dam so enormous that a scientist scanning satellite images spotted it from space in 2007. Stretched end to end, how long is the largest beaver dam on Earth?
answer: About 800 meters, eight football fields

About 80 meters, one football field
About 8 kilometers across a valley
About 8 meters, a garden hedge
context: The largest known beaver dam stretches about 800 meters, the length of eight football fields, hidden in Wood Buffalo National Park. It was so big it showed up on satellite imagery in 2007. Source: https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/nt/woodbuffalo/nature/beaver_gallery  (Legend.)

question: A shaggy, black, cat-sized mammal prowls the rainforest canopy of South and Southeast Asia, and the strangest thing about it hits your nose before your eyes: it reeks of hot buttered popcorn. Its keepers nicknamed it the 'bearcat,' though it's really a relative of the civets. What is this popcorn-smelling tree-dweller?
answer: The binturong
choices: The binturong
The red panda
The kinkajou
The fossa
context: The binturong (Arctictis binturong) is a viverrid — a relative of the civets — not a bear and not a cat, despite its 'bearcat' nickname. Its genus name Arctictis is Greek for 'bear-weasel.' It really does smell strongly of hot buttered popcorn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binturong ; https://today.duke.edu/2016/04/popcorn-scented-binturong

question: Chemists expected the binturong scent to be some exotic new civet compound. Instead, the 2016 Duke study found a molecule people had smelled in their own kitchens for ages — the identical aroma compound floating off a familiar food. Which food shares the binturong's signature molecule?
answer: Popcorn and cooked jasmine rice
choices: Popcorn and cooked jasmine rice
Fresh-cut cucumber and melon rind
Ripe banana and pear skin
Roasted coffee and dark chocolate
context: The compound is 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline (2-AP) — the very same molecule that makes popcorn and cooked jasmine rice smell the way they do. Greene et al. (2016) found it in every binturong urine sample they tested. Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27056047/ ; https://today.duke.edu/2016/04/popcorn-scented-binturong

question: Here was the puzzle for the Duke researchers: in popcorn, that buttery-smelling molecule forms only under high cooking heat, when sugars and amino acids react. Lead scientist Christine Drea asked how a binturong makes a cooking smell without ever cooking. What is their leading answer for where the compound comes from?
answer: Bacteria living on the animal's skin, fur, or gut make it as the urine passes
choices: Bacteria living on the animal's skin, fur, or gut make it as the urine passes
A special heat-producing gland warms the urine to 'cook' it
The animal eats fermenting fruit that already contains it
Its liver synthesizes the finished molecule directly
context: In popcorn, 2-AP forms through the Maillard reaction — sugars and amino acids reacting under high heat. A binturong never gets that hot, so Christine Drea asked, 'How does this animal make a cooking smell, but without cooking?' The team believes microbes on the binturong's skin, fur, or gut produce the compound as the urine passes. Source: https://today.duke.edu/2016/04/popcorn-scented-binturong

question: High in the canopy, a binturong walks headfirst straight DOWN a tree trunk without slipping, claws gripping the whole way — a descent that sends most climbing mammals sliding. What lets the binturong pull it off?
answer: Its hind ankles rotate a full 180 degrees to keep the claws hooked
choices: Its hind ankles rotate a full 180 degrees to keep the claws hooked
Suction pads on the soles of its feet grip the bark
It descends by hanging from its tail and letting go in stages
Backward-curving spines along its belly catch the trunk
context: The binturong can rotate its hind ankles a full 180 degrees, so its claws stay hooked into the bark even while it climbs down a trunk head-first — a trick most tree mammals can't manage. It also has a fully prehensile tail it uses as a fifth limb to anchor and balance in the trees. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/animals/binturong/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binturong

question: A blanket octopus never dens in a reef crevice and never crawls the seafloor. Where does this octopus spend its entire life?
answer: Drifting in the open blue ocean, far above any bottom
choices: Drifting in the open blue ocean, far above any bottom
Clinging to floating rafts of drifting seaweed at the surface
Riding on the backs of large drifting jellyfish
Hovering in the warm water just above deep-sea vents
context: The blanket octopus is pelagic — it lives in the open ocean far from any reef or seafloor, drifting through tropical and subtropical waters from the surface down to about 250 meters. Most octopuses are bottom-dwellers, which makes this open-water lifestyle unusual. Source: https://octonation.com/octopedia/blanket-octopus/

question: A tuna closes in on a female blanket octopus. She has no shell, no reef, and no bottom to flee toward — just sheets of webbing strung between her arms. She uses that webbing to save herself. What does she do with it?
answer: Snaps it open like a giant iridescent cape to look enormous and terrifying
choices: Snaps it open like a giant iridescent cape to look enormous and terrifying
Wraps herself into a tight armored ball
Catches the current with it to outrun the tuna
Scoops the tuna into it like a net and eats it
context: The female unfurls a huge iridescent 'blanket' — sheets of webbing strung between her arms — and spreads it so she suddenly looks enormous and scary, ballooning out to intimidate tuna, sailfish and even sharks. Source: https://octonation.com/fun-facts-about-the-female-blanket-octopus/

question: The blanket octopus can safely touch the Portuguese man o' war, a drifting siphonophore whose sting can kill. Rather than just avoiding it, the octopus rips pieces off the man o' war — and does what with them?
answer: Holds the stinging tentacles in its arms as venomous whips
choices: Holds the stinging tentacles in its arms as venomous whips
Eats them to absorb the venom into its own skin
Weaves them into its blanket for extra color
Uses them as bait to lure fish closer
context: Legendary. The blanket octopus tears pieces off the man o' war's deadly tentacles and holds them in its arms like whips, using the stolen stingers as weapons to attack prey and fend off predators. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanket_octopus

question: A female blanket octopus can stretch to about 2 meters — roughly the height of a doorway. The male of the very same species is one of the tiniest in the whole animal kingdom. What everyday object is the male about the size of?
answer: A walnut
choices: A walnut
A grape
A paperclip
A thumbtack
context: Legendary. The blanket octopus shows one of the most extreme size gaps in the animal kingdom: the female can reach about 2 meters (6.6 ft), while the male is only about 2.4 cm — roughly the size of a walnut. Source: https://www.iflscience.com/the-blanket-octopus-has-the-most-extreme-sexual-dimorphism-in-the-animal-kingdom-80008

question: The tiny male blanket octopus fills one specialized arm, the hectocotylus, with sperm. When it is time to mate with the giant female, what does he do with that arm?
answer: He detaches it and hands the whole arm over to her
choices: He detaches it and hands the whole arm over to her
He wraps it around her mantle and holds on for days
He uses it to fight off rival males nearby
He plants it on the seafloor for her to find later
context: Legendary. The tiny male mates by handing over a whole detachable arm — the hectocotylus — which he packs with sperm and gives to the female; the male almost certainly dies shortly after. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanket_octopus

question: For centuries the walnut-sized male blanket octopus was known only from dead specimens hauled up in trawl nets and plankton samples. When did scientists finally observe a living adult male for the first time?
answer: In 2002, off Australia's Great Barrier Reef
choices: In 2002, off Australia's Great Barrier Reef
In 1902, in a European aquarium
In the 1850s, during a deep-sea dredging voyage
In the 1970s, from a research submarine
context: The dwarf male was such a puzzle that no living one was seen until 2002, when Mark Norman and colleagues found the world's first live adult male off Australia's Great Barrier Reef, calling it 'the world's most sexually size-dimorphic large animal.' Source: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00288330.2002.9517126

question: In the 1820s, naturalists cutting open female blanket octopuses and argonauts kept finding a strange squirming thread inside. Georges Cuvier named it Hectocotylus octopodis and filed it as a brand-new animal. What did that thread actually turn out to be, once Kolliker and Muller studied whole dwarf males decades later?
answer: The dwarf male's own detachable arm, left behind after mating
choices: The dwarf male's own detachable arm, left behind after mating
A parasitic ribbon-worm that feeds on octopus eggs
A coiled string of the female's own unfertilized eggs
A stinging thread stripped from a Portuguese man o' war
context: One of biology's great mistaken-identity blunders. Cuvier described the severed hectocotylus as its own parasitic worm species. In the 1840s Albert von Kolliker (examining both argonaut and blanket-octopus specimens) and Heinrich Muller -- who found whole dwarf males whose enlarged arm dropped off when touched -- proved the "worm" was really the male's own detached mating arm. Source: OctoNation, "How Male Argonauts Taught Scientists About Octopus Sex"; Wikipedia "Hectocotylus"; Della Chiaje/Cuvier historical record.  (Legend.)

question: Blanket octopuses tear stinging tentacles loose from the Portuguese man o' war and brandish them as living weapons -- but only the tiny males and smallest immature females are ever found holding one, never an octopus longer than about 7 centimeters. Why does the borrowed stinger drop out of the arsenal once a blanket octopus grows past that size?
answer: A bigger octopus's larger suckers can't grip the narrow stinger without tearing it
choices: A bigger octopus's larger suckers can't grip the narrow stinger without tearing it
Larger octopuses lose their immunity to the man o' war's venom as they mature
The stinger's venom breaks down too fast to be useful on a slow-moving adult
Bigger octopuses can no longer swim close enough to a man o' war to harvest one
context: Individuals longer than about 7 cm have never been seen carrying the tentacles -- their larger suckers likely can't grip the narrow stingers without injury. The borrowed weapon gives the small males a "size refuge," which researchers propose may itself have pushed females to grow enormous while males stayed miniature. Source: Norman, Paul, Finn & Tregenza 2002, "First encounter with a live male blanket octopus," NZ J. Marine & Freshwater Research 36:733-736; citing Jones 1963 and Thomas 1977.

question: The internet's 'saddest fish in the world' is a blobfish photographed in a boat, its face a sagging, melted droop. But that gooey blob is a fish yanked out of its world. Down at its home a kilometre deep, a living blobfish actually looks like:
answer: a normal blunt-headed pink fish with big black eyes
choices: a normal blunt-headed pink fish with big black eyes
a translucent jelly with glowing blue veins
a spiny grey lump bristling with venom quills
a flat ribbon of skin with no eyes at all
context: The famous melted-face look only appears at the surface: built for crushing deep-sea pressure, the blobfish's body relaxes and collapses in our thin air 'much like a washed-up jellyfish.' At depth it is an ordinary-looking pink fish with feathery fins. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'The blobfish: a bloated guide to the world's ugliest animal' (sciencefocus.com).  (Legend.)

question: A blobfish is caught in a trawl net a kilometre down and hauled to a boat deck. On the surface its body sags into the famous gooey droop. Which change up here turned a firm fish into slop?
answer: the crushing squeeze its body needed suddenly vanished
choices: the crushing squeeze its body needed suddenly vanished
the sunlight burned and blistered its skin
the warm surface water boiled its blood
the thin surface air poisoned its gills
context: At home the blobfish lives where water presses on it 60 to 120 times harder than air presses on us at the surface. A body engineered against that crushing squeeze simply falls apart once the pressure is gone. Source: Wikipedia, Psychrolutes marcidus (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychrolutes_marcidus).

question: A blobfish has almost no muscle and barely any bone; chasing prey would burn energy the food-poor deep can't spare. So how does it manage to feed at all?
answer: it gulps whatever edible scraps drift right past its mouth
choices: it gulps whatever edible scraps drift right past its mouth
it filters mud through long comb-like teeth
it lures prey with a glowing lure on its head
it scrapes algae off rocks with a rasping tongue
context: Strong bones and big muscles cost energy the food-poor deep can't spare, so the blobfish hovers nearly motionless and swallows small crustaceans, sea snails, and drifting scraps, 'whatever passes right in front of them.' As one expert put it, 'Being lazy is a survival strategy.' Source: BBC Science Focus (sciencefocus.com); Australian Museum, fathead / Mr Blobby page.

question: In 2013 a comedy contest to win conservation attention for un-cute endangered animals crowned the blobfish 'World's Ugliest Animal.' The mournful photo everyone shares is one real museum specimen, nicknamed 'Mr Blobby.' What made his face droop even sadder than a fresh blobfish?
answer: preserving him in alcohol tightened his skin and shrank his nose
choices: preserving him in alcohol tightened his skin and shrank his nose
years drying out in a display jar cracked and slackened his face
the trawl net's crushing haul mangled his features on the way up
a rare skin disease had melted his features before capture
context: 'Mr Blobby' (specimen AMS I.42771-001) was netted by trawl on the 2003 NORFANZ expedition on the Norfolk Ridge northwest of New Zealand. Preserving him in alcohol tightened his skin and shrank his nose, exaggerating the sad droopy look, and a tiny parasitic copepod was found clinging to his mouth. Source: Australian Museum, 'Blobfish (aka Mr Blobby)' (australian.museum); Wikipedia, Ugly Animal Preservation Society.  (Legend.)

question: A tiny sea slug called the blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) spends its whole life adrift at the ocean surface. How does it ride there?
answer: Belly-up, floating upside down
choices: Belly-up, floating upside down
Clinging to a rock with one foot
Buried in the sandy seabed
Riding on a sea turtle's shell
context: The blue dragon floats upside down at the very surface, belly toward the sky, drifting at the mercy of the wind and currents with almost no power to swim on its own. Source: https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/fact-file/fact-file-blue-dragon-glaucus-atlanticus/  (Legend.)

question: The blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) is only about 3 centimeters long, smaller than a grape. How badly can this tiny slug sting a swimmer?
answer: Worse than the Portuguese man o' war it ate
choices: Worse than the Portuguese man o' war it ate
About the same as a mild mosquito bite
Not at all — it has no sting of its own
Only a faint tingle you'd barely notice
context: Despite being smaller than a grape, the blue dragon can sting a human worse than the man o' war did, causing nausea, pain, and vomiting. It concentrates the venom it steals, so the thief becomes deadlier than its victim. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucus_atlanticus  (Legend.)

question: The blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) feeds on the Portuguese man o' war and swallows its stinging cells whole, without setting them off. What becomes of those swallowed stingers inside the slug?
answer: The strongest ones are moved into its own body
choices: The strongest ones are moved into its own body
They pass through and are excreted intact
They dissolve harmlessly in its gut acid
They are packed into eggs to arm its young
context: The blue dragon swallows the man o' war's stinging cells (nematocysts) undigested and moves the STRONGEST ones into its own body — a trick called kleptocnidy, meaning 'stolen stingers.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucus_atlanticus  (Legend.)

question: The blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) drifts at the ocean surface, exposed to hunters both above the water and below it. How is its small body colored?
answer: Blue on one side, silver-grey on the other
choices: Blue on one side, silver-grey on the other
Bright red all over as a poison warning
See-through so light passes through it
A dull sandy brown, top and bottom alike
context: Its camouflage is counter-shaded in REVERSE: the side pointing up to the sky is brilliant blue to hide against the sea from above, and the side pointing down into the water is silver-grey to hide against the bright surface from below. Because the blue dragon floats upside down, this puts the blue on its belly. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucus_atlanticus  (Legend.)

question: The blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) can barely swim, yet it never sinks from the surface. What keeps this little slug afloat?
answer: An air bubble it holds in its stomach
choices: An air bubble it holds in its stomach
Oil-filled fins that spread like a raft
A jelly float grown on its back
Beating thousands of tiny leg-paddles
context: The blue dragon stays afloat by swallowing and holding an air bubble in its stomach — a gas-filled sac in its belly acts like a built-in life-jacket, helped by the surface tension of the water. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucus_atlanticus  (Legend.)

question: A blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) lies washed up dead and drying on the sand. A curious child reaches for the pretty blue shape. Why should they keep their hands off?
answer: Its stingers still fire on contact days after death
choices: Its stingers still fire on contact days after death
Its drying body puffs out a cloud of toxic spores
Its skin turns acidic and burns whatever touches it
Its blue pigment soaks in and poisons through the skin
context: The blue dragon's venom stays active even after the slug is DEAD — a washed-up blue dragon on the beach can still sting you, because the borrowed stinging cells fire on contact. Source: https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/fact-file/fact-file-blue-dragon-glaucus-atlanticus/  (Legend.)

question: The blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) swallows loaded man o' war stinging cells without setting them off, but a few always fire inside it. Beyond storing the survivors, how does its gut keep the fired ones from harming it?
answer: Mucus quiets the stingers, and tough chitin plates in the gut soak up the ones that fire
choices: Mucus quiets the stingers, and tough chitin plates in the gut soak up the ones that fire
Heat from its stomach denatures the stingers and makes them fall limp before they fire
It fires each stinger into a sealed water sac that then vents harmlessly to the open sea
It starves itself for days so the loaded stingers slowly discharge on their own instead
context: The disarming is a two-part trick. First, the slug's mucus suppresses nematocyst discharge (in the related aeolid Aeolidia papillosa, mucus cut prey-stinger firing by roughly 60% below control). Second, a tough chitin cuticle plus granular-chitin discs called 'spindles' line the gut and act like biological sandbags, absorbing any stinger that still goes off. So swallowing a man o' war whole is not luck: it chemically quiets the weapons, then physically shields its own insides from the ones that fire anyway. Source: PMC review 'Acquisition and Use of Nematocysts by Cnidarian Predators' (PMC2783962), citing Aeolidia papillosa mucus-suppression and buccal chitin 'spindle' data.

question: For years the blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) was cast as a man o' war specialist that killed with its borrowed stings. A 2025 aquarium study of its feeding overturned that story. How did the slug actually catch live fish?
answer: It grabbed and pinned them with its long front cerata, then bit down near the gills
choices: It grabbed and pinned them with its long front cerata, then bit down near the gills
It stunned the passing fish with a sudden burst of its stored stinging cells
It lured small fish in under its belly using its bright glowing blue underside
It snared them in sticky mucus threads it spun out from its muscular foot
context: Reared in aquaria, Glaucus atlanticus used its enlarged front cerata like ARMS, pinning live whitebait (Japanese anchovy) between them and biting near the gills. Histology found a well-developed muscle-fiber layer at the base of these front cerata, which are built longer than the rest 'like an arm,' giving the grip needed to seize fast prey. It fed as a generalist on several cnidarians plus fish, not as a man o' war specialist, and the stolen stingers were NOT observed doing the killing: capture was by physical grip and biting. The frilly cerata, long thought to be purely a defensive sting-battery, turned out to be grasping limbs too. Source: Yamamoto et al. 2025, Ecology, 'Blue angels have devil hands: Predatory behavior using cerata in Glaucus atlanticus' (PMC11912302 / doi:10.1002/ecy.70062).  (Legend.)

question: A small octopus is hunting along an Australian tide pool, its skin a drab, mottled grey-brown that blends into the rocks. Then something disturbs it, and in a third of a second its skin erupts with dozens of glowing electric-blue rings. What is this sudden flash of rings?
answer: A warning display that says 'do not touch'
choices: A warning display that says 'do not touch'
A net it spreads to trap passing fish
A trail of light that lures prey closer
A glow it uses to see in dark water
context: The blue rings are aposematic — a 'do not touch' signal. When resting, the blue-ringed octopus (Hapalochlaena) is a drab grey-to-yellowish brown that camouflages into the rocks; the famous rings stay hidden until it is threatened. Source: Australian Geographic, 'Fact File: Blue-ringed octopus'; Natural History Museum (London).

question: The blue-ringed octopus would rather scare you off than fight you. Its glowing rings are pure bluff and warning — so what is the ONE thing that actually makes this tiny octopus bite a human?

context: The rings are a warning, not an attack — the octopus flashes rather than fights, and only bites if it is grabbed or stepped on. Source: Natural History Museum (London), 'The blue-ringed octopus: small, vibrant and exceptionally deadly'.

question: You could hold a blue-ringed octopus in one hand — including its arms it is only about the size of a golf ball. Yet a single one of these tiny animals carries enough venom to do WHAT? (LEGEND)

Dissolve a crab's shell in seconds
Stun every fish in a small tide pool
Glow brightly enough to read by
context: The blue-ringed octopus is only about 12-20 cm including its arms, yet one carries enough venom to kill over 20 adults within minutes. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blue-ringed octopus'.  (Legend.)

question: The blue-ringed octopus is an ambush hunter of small crabs and shrimp. It doesn't crush its prey — instead it uses one hard body part to punch through a crab's tough shell and inject venom. What is that tool?

question: The venom of the blue-ringed octopus isn't some one-of-a-kind cephalopod poison. It is tetrodotoxin — the very same toxin found in one notorious fish that Japanese chefs must be licensed to prepare. Which fish shares this exact poison? (LEGEND)
answer: The pufferfish
choices: The pufferfish
The stonefish
The lionfish
The electric eel
context: The venom is tetrodotoxin (TTX), the same poison found in pufferfish (and in some poison dart frogs and newts). The blue-ringed octopus was the first animal known to use tetrodotoxin as a venom. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blue-ringed octopus'; Science (1978).  (Legend.)

question: A person bitten by a blue-ringed octopus can make a full recovery — their own body slowly breaks the tetrodotoxin down over about a day. But the venom shuts down one thing that cannot wait even a few minutes. What must a rescuer do for the victim in the meantime? (LEGEND)
answer: Breathe for them with a ventilator
choices: Breathe for them with a ventilator
Warm them with heated blankets
Feed them fluids and sugar
Keep the wound above the heart
context: The venom paralyzes the breathing muscles; a victim is kept alive by artificial respiration / a ventilator until the body clears the toxin on its own. Survive the first 24 hours on breathing support and recovery is usually complete. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blue-ringed octopus'; Snopes citing Aquarium of the Pacific.  (Legend.)

question: Here is the twist about the blue-ringed octopus's deadly tetrodotoxin: the octopus doesn't manufacture it at all — the poison is made somewhere else entirely. Where does this toxin actually come from? (LEGEND)
answer: Symbiotic bacteria in its salivary gland
choices: Symbiotic bacteria in its salivary gland
Prey it swallows and stores unchanged
Bacteria in the seawater it filters
A dose it inherits pre-loaded from its mother
context: The octopus does not make the tetrodotoxin itself — symbiotic bacteria living in its posterior salivary gland manufacture the toxin for it. Source: Marine Biology (Springer); Wikipedia, 'Blue-ringed octopus'.  (Legend.)

question: The blue-ringed octopus doesn't rely on a single all-purpose poison. Researchers have found it stores its venom as two distinct kinds in separate glands, each doing a different job. Besides subduing prey, what is the second job this two-venom system handles?
answer: Fighting off predators, separate from the prey venom
choices: Fighting off predators, separate from the prey venom
Digesting the crab once it is dead
Sealing the wound the beak makes
Coloring the warning rings blue
context: The blue-ringed octopus carries two different venoms in separate glands — one to subdue prey and a second used in defense against predators. Source: Great Barrier Reef Foundation, 'Blue-Ringed Octopus Facts'.

question: The blue-ringed octopus can flash roughly 60 electric-blue rings across its skin in a THIRD of a second — faster than most animals can shift color at all. How does it pull off a flash this fast?
answer: Muscle-controlled skin pouches snap open over inert mirror cells
choices: Muscle-controlled skin pouches snap open over inert mirror cells
The mirror cells suddenly light up with a glow of their own
A rippling wave of blue pigment floods across the skin
The rings rise up on the skin as tiny inflating bumps
context: The blue iridophores are physiologically inert mirrors tucked into muscle-controlled skin pouches that snap open to reveal the flash, while surrounding brown cells darken for contrast — flashing 50-60 rings in about a third of a second. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology 215(21):3752, Mäthger et al.

question: A blue-ringed octopus carries tetrodotoxin, a poison that kills by jamming the sodium channels its nerves and muscles run on. So why doesn't it paralyze itself? Researchers sequenced the gene for its own sodium channel and found the answer written into the protein.
answer: Three swapped amino acids reshape the docking site so the toxin slips off
choices: Three swapped amino acids reshape the docking site so the toxin slips off
A thick mucus layer sheathes its nerves and soaks up the toxin first
It walls the toxin off in glands its own nerves never make contact with
Its blood runs a carrier protein that ferries the toxin safely away
context: Geffeney et al. (2019) sequenced the Greater Blue-ringed Octopus sodium-channel gene HlNaV1 and found three amino-acid substitutions in the tetrodotoxin-binding site that lower the channel's affinity for the toxin. The striking part is that pufferfish, newts and salamanders, and TTX-resistant snakes independently evolved the SAME kinds of substitutions to survive the SAME poison. That is convergent evolution at its clearest: unrelated animals, facing the identical problem of not killing themselves with their own weapon, arrived at the identical molecular fix. Source: Geffeney, Williams, Rosenthal, et al., 'Convergent and parallel evolution in a voltage-gated sodium channel underlies TTX-resistance in the Greater Blue-ringed Octopus: Hapalochlaena lunulata,' Toxicon (2019), https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10148497 ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31550451/

question: A male blue-lined octopus is a fraction of the female's size, and she readily cannibalizes suitors. In 2025, scientists filmed how the male mates for 40 minutes and more without being eaten. What is his trick?
answer: He bites her aorta at the back of her head and stops her breathing
choices: He bites her aorta at the back of her head and stops her breathing
He mates at arm's length, reaching in with a single specialized arm
He darts in, deposits sperm, and flees before she can turn on him
He mimics a female's coloring to slip past her guard unnoticed
context: Chung et al. (2025, Current Biology) documented the blue-lined octopus (Hapalochlaena fasciata) as the first known animal to weaponize venom for mating. The much smaller male bites the far larger female exactly over the aorta at the back of her head and injects tetrodotoxin; her breathing slows and stops after about eight minutes and her body goes pale, immobilizing her for the 40 to 75 minutes of mating so she cannot cannibalize him. It is a targeted, non-lethal dose delivered to precisely the right spot: she recovers fully afterward, resumes eating, and lays eggs days later. Source: Chung et al., Current Biology (March 2025), reported by Smithsonian Magazine https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/these-male-octopuses-use-venom-to-subdue-female-mates-and-avoid-being-eaten-after-sex-180986208/ and CNN https://www.cnn.com/2025/03/13/science/blue-lined-octopus-venom-mating-scli-intl

question: A full-grown African elephant weighs about three tons. Astonishingly, one single body part of a blue whale weighs about as much as that whole elephant all on its own. Which part?

question: A blue whale heart preserved at the Royal Ontario Museum stands about six and a half feet tall counting the aorta and weighs nearly 400 pounds — the biggest of any animal that ever lived. Museum staff joked it was large enough to do WHAT?

question: People love to picture a child crawling through a blue whale's main artery, the aorta. The truth is far more modest. About how wide across is this biggest blood vessel of any animal?

question: A blue whale doesn't sip krill politely. To feed, it charges straight into a swarm, throws its mouth wide open, and takes in a single enormous gulp. How much does that one gulp bring in?

A volume about equal to its own head and throat
A slow steady stream it sips for minutes
About a bathtub's worth at a time

Source: Goldbogen lab / Stanford; Journal of Experimental Biology 214:131 'Mechanics, hydrodynamics and energetics of blue whale lunge feeding'; Mongabay 'Swallowing swimming pools'.  (Legend.)

question: Krill are shrimp-like creatures barely the size of your finger. The biggest blue whales, feeding on nothing else, can pack away an astonishing amount of them in a single day. About how much?

Around half a ton

question: A blue whale's calls carry for hundreds of miles through the ocean, yet a person floating right beside one might never hear them. Why do these calls escape human ears entirely?

question: A human baby might gain a few ounces a day. A nursing blue whale calf, fed on its mother's rich milk, grows so fast that its DAILY weight gain is closer to what a person might gain in a whole year. About how much does it add each day?
answer: About 200 pounds

About 5 pounds
About 40 pounds
About 1,000 pounds

question: The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived, so its giant body plan must be ancient — or so it seems. When Slater, Goldbogen and Pyenson traced whale fossils across more than 30 million years, what did the record actually reveal about how this size arose?
answer: It leapt from about 10 m to 30 m only in the last few million years, on several branches at once
choices: It leapt from about 10 m to 30 m only in the last few million years, on several branches at once
It crept upward at a slow, steady pace across the whole thirty-million-year span
It was already near today’s length in the earliest baleen whales and simply held there
It shrank down from far larger ancestors and has been getting smaller ever since
context: For most of whale history the biggest baleen whales were only about 10 m long. The jump to today's ~30 m happened rapidly and independently on several branches of the family tree around 4.5 million years ago, when the first ice ages began concentrating krill into dense patches through wind-driven coastal upwelling — suddenly it paid to be a colossal filter feeder. The blue whale is the biggest animal ever, yet its body plan is evolutionarily recent and was reinvented more than once. Source: Slater, Goldbogen & Pyenson, 'Independent evolution of baleen whale gigantism linked to Plio-Pleistocene ocean dynamics,' Proceedings of the Royal Society B 284:20170546 (2017); Smithsonian Institution news release (2017).

question: A blue whale gulps a swimming-pool of water and must strain out the krill through hundreds of fringed baleen plates. The obvious picture is water pushing straight through the fringe like a kitchen sieve — but flow-tank studies showed that picture is wrong. How does the water actually move through the rack?
answer: It flows lengthwise along the inside of the plates, sweeping krill to the back of the mouth
choices: It flows lengthwise along the inside of the plates, sweeping krill to the back of the mouth
It is forced head-on through the fringe, which clogs and must be cleared between gulps
It is spat back out the same way it came in, leaving the krill stuck to the outer fringe
It is pumped through tiny pores in every plate the way a sponge draws water inward
context: This is cross-flow filtration. Instead of dead-end straining, where water pushes straight through and quickly clogs the fringe, the water slides sideways along the inner face of the baleen rack, carrying trapped krill backward to gather at the rear of the mouth for swallowing while keeping the ~0.5–2 mm bristles clear. Flow-tank experiments (first on bowhead baleen) overturned the intuitive sieve model. Source: Werth et al., 'Baleen Hydrodynamics and Morphology of Cross-Flow Filtration in Balaenid Whale Suspension Feeding,' PLOS ONE (2016) (PMC4769178); Frontiers in Marine Science, 'Dynamic filtration in baleen whales' (2024).

question: A giant sea worm buries almost its whole body in the seabed, leaving only its head poking out. Five antennae stick up from the sand. What are those antennae doing for the buried bobbit worm?
answer: Acting as tripwires that a passing fish brushes
choices: Acting as tripwires that a passing fish brushes
Filtering plankton from the passing current
Soaking up sunlight to warm its buried body
Waving to attract a mate across the sand
context: The bobbit worm buries nearly its entire body and leaves only its head exposed, waiting motionless. When a fish brushes one of the five antennae, the worm strikes. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'What is a bobbit worm?' — https://www.sciencefocus.com/nature/what-is-a-bobbit-worm  (Legend.)

question: A bobbit worm can hide almost its entire body underground with only its jaws exposed. Stretched out, the longest one ever recorded was closer in length to which of these?
answer: A grown man lying down, nearly 10 feet
choices: A grown man lying down, nearly 10 feet
A dinner fork, about 8 inches
A garden snake, about 2 feet
A school bus, about 40 feet
context: The longest bobbit worm ever recorded measured 299 cm — nearly 10 feet — though its body averages only about 25 mm (one inch) wide, making it one of the longest worms in the ocean. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eunice aphroditois' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eunice_aphroditois  (Legend.)

question: When a fish brushes the bobbit worm's antennae, the worm strikes in milliseconds and yanks the prey down into the sand. What can its jaws sometimes do to a fish in that single strike?
answer: Slice it clean in two
choices: Slice it clean in two
Crush its skull in one bite
Tear off a chunk and let the rest flee
Pin it against the sand and swallow it whole
context: The strike is so fast the fish gets only milliseconds to flee. The worm's razor-sharp jaws can sometimes slice the prey clean in two before dragging it down into the sand. Those jaws are paired mandibles and larger serrated, hooked maxillae that snap shut like scissors. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'What is a bobbit worm?' — https://www.sciencefocus.com/nature/what-is-a-bobbit-worm  (Legend.)

question: A bobbit worm can subdue and slowly eat animals far bigger than itself, dragging them down into its burrow. After its jaws grab the prey, what does the worm do to keep such a large meal from struggling?
answer: Injects a toxin that stuns or kills it
choices: Injects a toxin that stuns or kills it
Squeezes it until it stops moving
Drowns it by holding it under the sand
Waits days for it to tire itself out
context: After grabbing prey, the bobbit worm injects a toxin that stuns or kills it, letting the worm subdue and digest animals far larger than itself, which it drags underground to eat. Source: ScienceInsights, 'What Is a Bobbit Worm? The Ferocious Ambush Predator' — https://scienceinsights.org/what-is-a-bobbit-worm-the-ferocious-ambush-predator/

question: At the Blue Reef Aquarium in Newquay, coral was being shredded overnight and fish kept vanishing, yet baited traps came up empty for weeks. When staff finally took the reef apart rock by rock, what had been living hidden in the tank?
answer: A 1.2-metre bobbit worm named 'Barry'
choices: A 1.2-metre bobbit worm named 'Barry'
An escaped moray eel from a nearby tank
A cluster of hungry crown-of-thorns starfish
A venomous stonefish buried in the gravel
context: Staff noticed coral being shredded overnight and fish vanishing, and baited traps came up empty for weeks. The culprit was a 1.2-metre bobbit worm the staff named 'Barry'. To catch him they dismantled the reef display rock by rock; when cornered, the worm bit clean through a 20-pound fishing line before they pulled him out. Source: BBC Science Focus + The Misfits Pair archive — https://themisfitspair.com/2009/04/01/barry-the-giant-sea-worm-discovered-by-aquarium-staff-after-mysterious-attacks-on-coral-reef/  (Legend.)

question: 'Barry' the bobbit worm was never bought by the Blue Reef Aquarium and no one saw him arrive. How did this monster worm actually get into the tank where he grew for years?
answer: He hitchhiked in as a tiny juvenile inside 'live rock'
choices: He hitchhiked in as a tiny juvenile inside 'live rock'
He crawled up a drainpipe from the sea outside
He was slipped in as a prank by a departing worker
He hatched from eggs stuck to a new fish's fins
context: Barry had hitchhiked in as a tiny juvenile hidden inside a piece of 'live rock' the aquarium had bought, then grew undetected in the tank, possibly for years — one reason a bobbit worm can go unseen for so long is that it recoils and vanishes down its burrow whenever a bright light hits it. Source: BBC Science Focus + The Misfits Pair archive — https://themisfitspair.com/2009/04/01/barry-the-giant-sea-worm-discovered-by-aquarium-staff-after-mysterious-attacks-on-coral-reef/  (Legend.)

question: Bobbit worms are soft and boneless, so their bodies almost never fossilize. Yet in 20-million-year-old Taiwanese rock, scientists found 319 fossils of these ancient ambush predators. Since no worm was preserved, what got fossilized instead?
answer: The L-shaped burrow the worm hunted from
choices: The L-shaped burrow the worm hunted from
A cast of the worm’s serrated jaws
The mucus coating its whole body
A tangle of shed skins and molts
context: This is one of the rare cases where a predator's BEHAVIOR fossilized rather than its body. Yu-Yen Pan and colleagues named the trace fossil Pennichnus formosae from ~20-million-year-old Miocene rock (Taliao Formation) in northeast Taiwan — L-shaped burrows up to 2 m long and only 2–3 cm wide, the buried lair of an ancient bobbit-type worm. Near the top of each burrow, X-ray scans show an abrupt spike in iron: chemical residue of the worm's mucus, which fed sulfate-reducing bacteria that built iron-sulfide minerals as the worm rebuilt and reinforced its lair after each violent strike. Repeated dragging of prey down the funnel left distinctive 'feather-like' collapse structures at the mouth. (A jaw cast would seem a fair guess — bobbit-worm jaws DO survive elsewhere as fossils called scolecodonts — but here it was the burrow, not the animal, that was preserved.) Source: Pan et al., Scientific Reports 11:1174 (2021), via PMC7820589 and Nature s41598-020-79311-0.

question: A buried bobbit worm hits a passing fish faster than almost any other invertebrate can move. Its jaws sit at the front of a soft, boneless body with no arm or claw to throw them forward. So how does the worm launch its jaws at the prey?
answer: It turns its throat inside-out, hurling the jaws forward
choices: It turns its throat inside-out, hurling the jaws forward
It coils and snaps a muscular tail like a whip
It fires the jaws on a jet of pressurized water
It rams its whole burrow upward against the fish
context: The strike is powered by pharynx eversion: the worm turns its muscular throat inside-out, flinging the jaw apparatus — interlocking mandibles plus serrated maxillae — forward like a spring-loaded gin trap, then retracts the whole thing to drag prey underground. Having no hard skeleton, the worm holds its long shape with a hydrostatic (fluid-pressure) skeleton — the same pressurized-fluid trick that powers the launch. The record wild specimen measured 299 cm (about 9.8 ft) yet was only ~25.5 mm wide, making it the longest known polychaete; despite the fearsome hunting it also scavenges algae and dead matter and lives only about 3–5 years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eunice_aphroditois, with strike-eversion mechanics corroborated by ScienceInsights and BiologyInsights secondary summaries.

question: The female bolas spider builds no web to trap prey. Instead she dangles a single silk thread tipped with one sticky glue ball and swings it at flying moths in the dark. What is she copying with that swing?
answer: A cowboy's bolas, a weighted throwing rope
choices: A cowboy's bolas, a weighted throwing rope
A frog's tongue, flicked and retracted
A spider's usual flat orb web
A bat's wide-mouthed mid-air scoop
context: The spider swings her single glue-tipped line like a bolas — a South American throwing weapon of weights on cords — to snag moths right out of the air, which is how the spider got its name. Source: https://spiderbytes.org/2015/03/17/bolas-spiders-masters-of-deception/  (Legend.)

question: Swinging a glue ball only works if a moth flies within reach. Rather than wait for one to blunder past, the bolas spider actively draws male moths in from far across the dark. How does it pull them in?
answer: It releases a chemical that mimics a female moth's perfume
choices: It releases a chemical that mimics a female moth's perfume
It glows a soft blue-green light moths drift toward
It plays a high buzz matching a female moth's wingbeat
It heats its body so moths mistake it for a warm flower
context: The spider gives off a chemical that mimics the sex pheromone of a FEMALE moth, so male moths trace the fake scent trail straight to the swinging glue ball. Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00380049  (Legend.)

question: By day the bolas spider can't hunt, so it curls up motionless on a silk mat on a leaf and disguises itself as something no hungry bird would ever want to eat. What does it pretend to be?
answer: A fresh bird dropping
choices: A fresh bird dropping
A drop of morning dew
A curled dead leaf
A clump of pale fungus
context: Motionless on its silk mat, the bulbous, waxy-white spider looks exactly like a fresh bird dropping, so predators pass it by. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastophora_hutchinsoni

question: Watch one Mastophora hutchinsoni all night and something odd shows up: the moths stuck to its glue ball before 11 p.m. and the ones caught after 11 p.m. belong to two different species. What does the spider do at 11 p.m. to cause the switch?
answer: It changes the exact scent it fakes, matching a second moth species
choices: It changes the exact scent it fakes, matching a second moth species
It swings the ball faster to snag the bigger moths flying late
It creeps to a fresh leaf where the later moths gather
It brightens the glue ball so the later moths can see it
context: Mastophora hutchinsoni fakes one moth species' pheromone early in the evening, then switches to a completely different species' scent after 11 p.m., matching whichever moths are flying at that hour — so the species stuck to its glue ball changes as the night goes on. Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00049-002-8332-2  (Legend.)

question: Grab a bombardier beetle, a small ground beetle, and it fights back in a way that startles the attacker into dropping it: from the tip of its abdomen it launches a defense with a loud popping BANG. What is that defense?
answer: A jet of boiling-hot chemical spray
choices: A jet of boiling-hot chemical spray
A cloud of sticky silk threads
A blinding flash of green light
A blast of foul-smelling gas only
context: When seized, the bombardier beetle fires a caustic spray from the rear of its abdomen with an audible pop. The spray is genuinely scalding, not just smelly. Source: Natural History Museum, London -- 'Bombardier beetles and their caustic chemical cannon' (nhm.ac.uk).

question: The bombardier beetle's spray is not just an unpleasant smell -- it comes out hot enough to scald whatever it touches. How hot is the jet as it leaves the beetle?
answer: Close to 100 C, the boiling point of water
choices: Close to 100 C, the boiling point of water
Around body temperature, about 37 C
A little above freezing, near 5 C
Hot enough to melt metal, over 1,000 C
context: The jet shoots out at close to 100 C (212 F) -- the boiling point of water -- so it scalds the mouth or feet of an attacker. Source: Wikipedia 'Bombardier beetle' citing Aneshansley & Eisner, 'Biochemistry at 100 C'; Natural History Museum, London.

question: A bombardier beetle carries the makings of a scalding weapon inside its own body without ever cooking itself. It manages this by keeping two chemicals -- hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinone -- in a particular arrangement until the instant it fires. What arrangement keeps the beetle safe?
answer: The two chemicals are stored in separate sacs, apart
choices: The two chemicals are stored in separate sacs, apart
The two chemicals are frozen solid until needed
A thick layer of fat soaks up all the heat
The chemicals are diluted with water until harmless
context: The beetle stores hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinone in separate little reservoirs, safely apart, and only lets them meet at the instant of firing. Source: Natural History Museum, London; Wikipedia 'Bombardier beetle'.

question: When a cornered bombardier beetle finally combines its two chemicals in the reinforced chamber at the back of its abdomen, enzymes there make the reaction violent enough to reach boiling point and explode outward. Which enzymes trigger that explosive reaction?
answer: Catalase and peroxidase
choices: Catalase and peroxidase
Pepsin and trypsin
Amylase and lipase
Luciferase and rennin
context: The reaction chamber is lined with catalase and peroxidase; when the stored chemicals meet these enzymes the reaction is fast and hot enough to boil and blast outward. Source: Wikipedia 'Bombardier beetle'; Chemistry Steps, 'The Chemistry Behind Bombardier Beetle's Spray'.

question: The bombardier beetle's scalding jet does not pour out in one steady stream. High-speed photography revealed it fires in a rapid machine-gun burst -- about 70 blasts too fast for the eye to separate. Roughly how fast is that pulsing?
answer: About 500 pulses per second
choices: About 500 pulses per second
About 5 pulses per second
About 20 pulses per minute
One long pulse lasting five seconds
context: The spray fires as a biological pulse jet -- roughly 70 pulses at about 500 per second. The rapid pulsing also protects the beetle: each tiny explosion is released before the next, so the reinforced chamber never overloads. Source: Wikipedia 'Bombardier beetle' citing Dean, Aneshansley, Edgerton & Eisner, 'Defensive spray of the bombardier beetle: a biological pulse jet,' Science (1990).

question: A toad flicks out its tongue and swallows a bombardier beetle whole. Deep in the toad's stomach the beetle fires its spray -- and in one experiment 43% of the toads then did something surprising more than an hour later. What did those toads do?
answer: Vomited the beetle back up alive
choices: Vomited the beetle back up alive
Grew immune and ate more beetles
Fell asleep for the rest of the day
Changed color from the beetle's dye
context: Toads that swallowed bombardier beetles heard a faint 'bu' or 'vu' pop from inside their own stomach, and 43% vomited the beetle back up -- sometimes over 90 minutes later. Beetles spent 12 to 107 minutes inside, scuttled off covered in slime, and nearly all survived; one lived at least 562 more days. Source: Sugiura & Sato, 'Successful escape of bombardier beetles from predator digestive systems,' Biology Letters (2018).  (Legend.)

question: A male satin bowerbird spends weeks weaving two neat parallel walls of twigs on the forest floor, decorating the ground between them, and returns to the same spot to work it season after season. What is this twig structure actually for?
answer: A stage for courting females
choices: A stage for courting females
A nest for the pair's eggs
A shelter from rain and heat
A store for hoarded food
context: The bower is NOT a nest. The male builds it purely as a stage to court females; the female builds a separate, plain saucer-like nest of sticks in a tree fork up to 30-35 meters high and raises the young entirely alone. Source: Australian Museum, Satin Bowerbird.

question: A satin bowerbird will fly kilometers to raid gardens and even swipe a rival's loot, all to gather objects of one single color that matches his own glossy plumage and dark violet eyes. Which color does he hoard?
answer: Blue
choices: Blue
Red
Yellow
White
context: The satin bowerbird is obsessed with blue, decorating his bower with blue clothes pegs, drinking straws, bottle tops and blue parrot feathers, stealing objects from as far as 12 kilometers away because blue matches his own glossy blue-black plumage and violet-blue iris. Source: Australian Museum, Satin Bowerbird; Coffs Botanic Garden 'Bower Power'.  (Legend.)

question: A female satin bowerbird tours several rival males' bowers, watches each strut and quiver his wings, and picks the one that impresses her. After she mates, who does the work of building the nest and raising the chicks?
answer: The female, entirely on her own
choices: The female, entirely on her own
The mated pair, together at the bower
The winning male, at his bower
A group of nearby males
context: The male builds the bower purely as a courtship stage; the female builds a separate, plain saucer-like nest of sticks in a tree fork up to 30-35 meters high and raises the young entirely alone. Female bowerbirds are the judges who inspect several rival bowers before choosing. Source: Australian Museum, Satin Bowerbird; Coffs Botanic Garden 'Bower Power'.

question: A male satin bowerbird chews berries into a purple pulp mixed with spit, then daubs it along the inner walls of his bower. To spread the paint he grips a tool in his beak and works it back and forth. What does he hold as a paintbrush?
answer: A wad of bark
choices: A wad of bark
A soft green leaf
A tuft of moss
A blue feather
context: The male satin bowerbird builds two parallel walls of sticks (an 'avenue' bower), then paints the inner walls with a mixture of chewed berry pulp, vegetable matter and saliva, holding a wad of bark in his beak as a paintbrush. Source: Australian Museum, Satin Bowerbird; Coffs Botanic Garden 'Bower Power'.  (Legend.)

question: A young male satin bowerbird looks olive-green like a female for years, practicing at scrappy trial bowers, before he finally turns the glossy blue-black of an adult courter. About how long does that transformation take?
answer: Seven years
choices: Seven years
A single season
Two years
Twenty years
context: A male satin bowerbird takes a full seven years to develop his adult glossy blue-black plumage; until then young males look olive-green like females and practice building and displaying at temporary bowers. Source: Australian Museum, Satin Bowerbird; Coffs Botanic Garden 'Bower Power'.

question: A male great bowerbird lays out his stones and bones in a careful size order -- tiniest where the female will stand, largest at the far end. When she peers down the avenue, this arrangement warps what she sees. What illusion does the gradient create?
answer: He appears larger against the shrunken court
choices: He appears larger against the shrunken court
The court glitters as if wet with dew
His feathers seem a brighter blue
The avenue looks longer than it is
context: The great bowerbird arranges stones and objects in a size gradient (smallest near the avenue where the female stands, largest at the far edge), creating a forced-perspective illusion that makes the courtyard look smaller and uniform, so the displaying male appears relatively larger to the watching female. Source: National Geographic, 'Male bowerbirds create forced perspective illusions'; Endler et al., Current Biology (2010).  (Legend.)

question: The golden bowerbird builds not walls but twin maypole towers of sticks, the tallest bowers any bird makes -- and each is inherited, rebuilt on the same spot generation after generation. How old is the oldest known bower of theirs?
answer: Over forty years old
choices: Over forty years old
About one year old
Over a hundred years old
Exactly ten years old
context: Golden bowerbirds build the tallest bower structures known, twin maypole towers that are inherited and rebuilt across generations, with the oldest recorded bowers over 40 years old and more than 2 meters tall. Source: Nature.org 'Kleptomaniac Love Architects'.

question: A sea creature drifts in warm Australian shallows, but instead of the usual round dome it has a clear, cube-shaped bell with four flat sides and a bundle of trailing tentacles at each corner. What is it called?
answer: The box jellyfish
choices: The box jellyfish
The moon jellyfish
The sea gooseberry
The Portuguese man o' war
context: The box jellyfish is named for its body: a see-through, cube-shaped bell with four flat sides, unlike the round dome of an ordinary jellyfish. A cluster of tentacles trails from each of the four corners. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish

question: Most jellyfish are helpless drifters, carried wherever the current takes them. The box jellyfish is different: it powers itself through the water. How fast can it go, and how sharply can it turn?
answer: About 1.5 metres per second, whipping a 180-degree turn in a few beats of its bell
choices: About 1.5 metres per second, whipping a 180-degree turn in a few beats of its bell
About 1.5 metres per second, but it can only ever swim in a straight line
So slowly it can't beat the current, so it still just drifts like other jellyfish
Fast in bursts, but only backwards, tentacles first
context: A box jellyfish does not just drift like most jellyfish; it actively swims, reaching about 1.5 metres per second and rapidly turning up to 180 degrees in just a few contractions of its bell. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish  (Legend.)

question: Around the bell of Chironex fleckeri sit four little sensory pods, and every one of them carries a set of eyes. Add them all up, and how many eyes does this brainless jellyfish have?
answer: 24 eyes
choices: 24 eyes
8 eyes
12 eyes
48 eyes
context: Chironex fleckeri has 24 eyes clustered on four sensory pods called rhopalia, six eyes each. Astonishingly, it has NO brain to see with, just a ring of nerves around its bell. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish; https://aussieanimals.com/profiles/box-jellyfish-chironex-fleckeri/  (Legend.)

question: The box jellyfish has no brain at all, just a ring of nerves around its bell. Yet some of its two dozen eyes are not simple light patches. What kind of eyes are a few of them?
answer: True camera eyes with real lenses, corneas, and retinas that form an image
choices: True camera eyes with real lenses, corneas, and retinas that form an image
Bare pits that can only tell light from dark
Compound eyes, thousands of tiny units like a fly's
Mirror eyes that reflect light instead of focusing it
context: Some of the box jellyfish's 24 eyes have real lenses, corneas, and retinas, true camera-type eyes that can form an image, which is astonishing for an animal with no brain to process the picture. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish  (Legend.)

question: A box jellyfish tentacle is lined with hundreds of thousands of microscopic coiled harpoons. What actually makes one of these stinging cells fire and shoot its barb?
answer: Sensing the chemicals on skin, not touch alone
choices: Sensing the chemicals on skin, not touch alone
Any touch at all, driftwood or skin
A change in water temperature nearby
The shadow of prey passing overhead
context: A box jellyfish tentacle is lined with hundreds of thousands of stinging capsules called nematocysts, microscopic coiled harpoons that fire not from touch alone but when they sense the chemicals on skin, so they don't waste on driftwood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4379534/

question: Chironex fleckeri is among the most venomous animals alive, and it is the sting Australian swimmers fear most of all. What can a serious sting do to a person?
answer: Stop the heart, killing untreated victims within two to five minutes
choices: Stop the heart, killing untreated victims within two to five minutes
Cause hours of full-body paralysis while the victim stays conscious
Blind a victim, though it is almost never fatal
Only a painful welt, dangerous just to small children
context: Chironex fleckeri is among the most venomous animals alive; a serious sting can cause the heart to stop, and untreated victims have died within two to five minutes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chironex_fleckeri; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7285912/

question: A box jellyfish's clear bell tumbles and tilts every which way as it swims. Inside each sensory pod, a heavy crystal weight hangs down on a flexible stalk. What job does that dangling weight do?
answer: Pulled straight down by gravity, it keeps the eyes aimed up-and-down however the bell rolls
choices: Pulled straight down by gravity, it keeps the eyes aimed up-and-down however the bell rolls
It stores light like a battery so the eyes can still work in the dark
It adds ballast so the jellyfish can sink to the bottom to hunt
It grinds against the nerve ring to signal when prey drifts near
context: In each rhopalium a heavy crystal weight called a statolith acts like a tiny plumb bob, hanging on a flexible stalk so the eyes stay pointed up-and-down no matter how the jellyfish's bell tumbles or tilts. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish

question: Lift the bony flap on the side of a fish's head and you find neat stacks of soft, feathery red tissue tucked underneath. Underwater, this is the organ the fish uses to do what?
answer: Breathe
choices: Breathe
Taste its food
Steer while swimming
Sense water pressure
context: Those red feathery stacks are the gills - a fish's underwater lungs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_gill

question: A fish's gills, tucked under the flap on each side of its head, are a vivid red - not pink or grey but a deep blood-red. What makes them that color?
answer: Blood packed right at the surface
choices: Blood packed right at the surface
A red waxy coating that repels water
Red pigment cells for camouflage
Iron-rich slime the fish secretes
context: Each filament is crammed with tiny capillaries where blood picks up oxygen - the red you see IS the blood lying just under a wafer-thin surface. Source: https://australian.museum/learn/animals/fishes/fish-dissections/
