question: A goldfish resting quietly in a bowl isn't swimming, yet the bony covers over its gills keep fluttering open and shut, open and shut. What is that steady flutter doing?
answer: Pumping a fresh flow of water across its gills
choices: Pumping a fresh flow of water across its gills
Cooling its blood in warm water
Shaking loose bits of trapped food
Signaling to other fish nearby
context: By opening its mouth and flaring the gill cover (buccal pumping), a resting fish drives water over its gills without swimming a stroke - which is why the covers visibly flutter. Source: https://poseidonsweb.com/how-fish-breathe-ram-ventilation-buccal-pumping/

question: A fish's water enters the mouth and exits under the gill cover, always flowing one way and never washing back. A land animal, by contrast, pulls each breath in and pushes it back out the same opening. What single advantage does the fish's one-way flow give its gills?
answer: They never bathe in water already drained of oxygen
choices: They never bathe in water already drained of oxygen
They pull oxygen across twice as fast per breath
They never touch water colder than the fish's blood
They filter out the salt before oxygen crosses
context: Lungs are a dead end - fresh and used air share one pipe, so some stale air always lingers. A fish's flow runs straight through, so its gills always face water it has not yet stripped of oxygen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_gill

question: A fish faces a problem a land animal never does: the very stuff it breathes from holds far less oxygen than air does. Compared to the same volume of air, how much less oxygen does water actually hold?
answer: Around thirty times less
choices: Around thirty times less
Around a hundred times less
Around five times less
About half as much
context: Air packs roughly 30 times more oxygen per unit volume than water - which is why a fish must pass an enormous amount of water over its gills just to get by. Source: http://www.howfishbehave.ca/pdf/oxygen.pdf

question: Pull the gills from a fast-cruising tuna and then from a sluggish bottom-dweller of the same size, and one set is unmistakably richer - a denser thicket of comb-like red filaments crowding every arch. Whose gills are the more developed, and why?
answer: The tuna's - a relentless swimmer needs far more surface to feed its muscles
choices: The tuna's - a relentless swimmer needs far more surface to feed its muscles
The bottom-dweller's - lying still, it must hoard every scrap of oxygen
Neither - gill development is fixed at birth and identical in both
The tuna's - fast water flow scours its filaments larger over time
context: Bony fish carry four pairs of gill arches lined with comb-like filaments, and the more active the swimmer, the more developed those combs become - a hard-driving tuna packs far denser filaments than a fish that rests on the bottom. Source: https://australian.museum/learn/animals/fishes/fish-dissections/

question: Freshwater is famously oxygen-poor - a single litre carries only about 8 cubic centimetres of oxygen, against roughly 210 in the same litre of air. To grab enough from such thin pickings, what must a fish's gills have above all?
answer: Enormous surface area
choices: Enormous surface area
A powerful pumping muscle
A way to warm the water first
Thick protective walls
context: With water holding only about a twenty-sixth of air's oxygen, gills solve it with sheer area - vast thin surfaces so more oxygen can cross into the blood at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_gill

question: Inside a single lamella, a fish's blood is driven the OPPOSITE way to the water flowing over the outside - the two run against each other along the whole plate. This one design choice is why a fish can strip far more oxygen from water than it otherwise could. How does running them against each other manage that?
answer: The blood always meets water still richer in oxygen than itself
choices: The blood always meets water still richer in oxygen than itself
The two flows cancel out and let oxygen settle at a steady midpoint
The oxygen is squeezed across faster by the blood's higher pressure
The blood loads fastest right where it enters and then coasts
context: This is countercurrent exchange: because blood and water run opposite ways, the blood never catches up to water it has already emptied - it always faces water a little richer than itself, so oxygen keeps crossing along the whole lamella instead of stopping halfway. Source: https://fishbio.com/an-efficient-exchange/

question: If a fish's blood and the passing water flowed side by side in the SAME direction, they'd soon settle to the same oxygen level and the fish could pull out only about half. By running them in OPPOSITE directions instead, how much of the water's oxygen can a fish actually strip away?
answer: Around 80 to 90 percent
choices: Around 80 to 90 percent
Around 55 percent
Around 30 percent
Around 100 percent
context: Same-direction flow equalizes at roughly 50 percent; countercurrent flow, running blood against water, lets a fish harvest about 80 to 90 percent of the oxygen present - the payoff of the whole design. Source: https://fishbio.com/an-efficient-exchange/

question: A tuna is such a relentless swimmer that it can no longer work its gill covers fast enough to pump water at speed. Its solution is drastic: it swims with its mouth gaping to force water through - and this locks it into a rule it can never break. What is that rule?
answer: It must keep swimming forever or it suffocates
choices: It must keep swimming forever or it suffocates
It can only breathe in warm surface water
It must return to shallow water each night
It can never swim faster than its own gill-pumping
context: This is ram ventilation - the tuna rams water through its gills by moving forward, so if it ever stops swimming, the flow stops and it drowns. Great white, mako, salmon, and whale sharks live under the same sentence. Source: https://poseidonsweb.com/how-fish-breathe-ram-ventilation-buccal-pumping/  (Legend.)

question: Most sharks must swim their whole lives to keep water moving over their gills. But a nurse shark lies motionless on the sea floor for hours at a stretch. With its mouth sometimes buried in sand, how does it keep breathing without moving?
answer: It pumps water in through small holes behind its eyes
choices: It pumps water in through small holes behind its eyes
It absorbs oxygen straight through its skin
It surfaces every few minutes to gulp air
It slows its heart until it barely needs oxygen
context: The nurse shark uses cheek muscles to pump water over its gills (buccal pumping), and when its mouth is buried it draws water through spiracles - small openings behind the eyes - a trick that lets it rest where ram-ventilating sharks never could. Source: https://theliquidearth.org/2025/09/meet-the-buccal-pumpers-sharks-that-mastered-the-art-of-staying-still/  (Legend.)

question: A frog begins life as a tadpole breathing through gills, then grows lungs and climbs out of the water for good. The axolotl and the mudpuppy break that whole script - they spend their entire lives underwater. How do they pull that off?
answer: Keep feathery external gills their whole lives
choices: Keep feathery external gills their whole lives
Grow a second set of lungs as adults
Breathe only through their moist skin
Return to the egg stage each winter
context: The axolotl and mudpuppy never trade gills for lungs - they keep the feathery external gills sprouting from the head for life, staying underwater forever. This holding-onto-youth is called neoteny. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axolotl  (Legend.)

question: A tuna drowns if it STOPS swimming. The African lungfish faces the mirror danger: drop it into a tank of perfectly clean, fully oxygenated water and hold it below, and it drowns anyway. Its gills alone cannot save it. Why must this fish reach the surface to survive?
answer: Its gills have shrunk so far it must gulp air into a true lung or suffocate
choices: Its gills have shrunk so far it must gulp air into a true lung or suffocate
Its gills only work while the fish is drifting slowly downward through water
Its gills seal shut in cool water and reopen only in the warm surface layer
Its gills strip salt from water and starve without the surface film of minerals
context: The African lungfish (genus Protopterus) is an 'obligate air-breather.' Its gills have reduced so far that they can no longer pull enough oxygen from water; nearly all of an adult's oxygen uptake happens across a true paired lung, while the shrunken gills mostly dump carbon dioxide. Cut off from the surface, it suffocates even in fully oxygenated water. In the dry season it goes further, burrowing into mud and sealing itself in a mucus cocoon (estivation): its gill lamellae actually collapse and it survives for months breathing air alone at a drastically lowered metabolic rate. It is a living snapshot of the evolutionary crossover from breathing water to breathing air - the mirror of the ram-ventilating tuna, which drowns if it stops swimming, while the lungfish drowns if it can't reach the top. Source: WebSearch corroborated across lungfish.info 'How Lungfish Breathe Air,' ScienceDirect 'Lungfish - an overview,' and PubMed 25499100 (Signal molecule changes in the gills and lungs of Protopterus annectens during aestivation).  (Legend.)

question: The red feathery gill grabs oxygen - but tucked among that same tissue sit special cells busy with a second job that has nothing to do with breathing. A shark in the sea and a trout in a river both carry them, each tuned to its own water. What quiet task are these cells performing?
answer: Holding the blood at the right saltiness against the water outside
choices: Holding the blood at the right saltiness against the water outside
Sensing the water temperature so the fish knows when to spawn
Storing spare oxygen for moments the fish holds still and rests
Regrowing filaments worn thin by the endless rush of water
context: The fish gill is not just a lung-underwater - it is also the animal's kidney and its acid-base buffer. Beyond gas exchange, it is the dominant site where a fish dumps its nitrogen waste (as ammonia) and controls its blood salt and pH. The work is done by mitochondrion-packed cells wedged among the respiratory tissue, historically called 'chloride cells' and now 'ionocytes.' In seawater - saltier than the fish's blood - these cells actively pump excess salt OUT; a freshwater fish, flooded by dilute water, runs the very same cells in reverse to pull scarce ions IN. So the same organ that captures oxygen is quietly excreting waste and holding the fish's internal chemistry steady. Source: Wikipedia 'Fish gill' corroborated by Evans, Piermarini & Choe (2005), 'The Multifunctional Fish Gill,' Physiological Reviews 85:97-177.

question: Justin Schmidt didn't just score the bullet ant's sting a 4 and move on. In his 2016 book, he reached for a searing image of exactly what that pain feels like. How did he describe it?
answer: Like walking over flaming charcoal with a nail in your heel
choices: Like walking over flaming charcoal with a nail in your heel
Like a lit blowtorch held against bare skin
Like a hot iron rod driven through the wrist
Like acid poured into an open wound
context: Schmidt called it 'pure, intense, brilliant pain... like walking over flaming charcoal with a three-inch nail embedded in your heel' in The Sting of the Wild (2016). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schmidt_sting_pain_index  (Legend.)

question: A single bullet ant sting brings waves of burning, throbbing agony long after the ant is gone. Venezuelans gave it a blunt nickname stating exactly how long the ordeal lasts. What do they call it?
answer: The 24-hour ant
choices: The 24-hour ant
The three-day ant
The one-hour ant
The all-week ant
context: The pain can continue unabated for up to a full day, which is why Venezuelans call it 'hormiga veinticuatro,' the 24-hour ant. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraponera_clavata  (Legend.)

question: To pass into manhood, boys of the Satere-Mawe people of Brazil must slide a hand into a woven glove for about ten minutes, then repeat the ordeal some twenty times over their youth. What is packed inside that glove?
answer: Dozens of live bullet ants
choices: Dozens of live bullet ants
Glowing embers
Stinging nettles
Venomous spiders
context: The Satere-Mawe first sedate the ants in an herbal solution, then weave them into a glove of cashew-palm leaves with the stingers turned inward toward the wearer's hand. Source: https://whyevolutionistrue.com/2014/08/06/the-worst-pain-known-to-humans-the-bullet-ant-gloves-of-brazil/  (Legend.)

question: The bullet ant's agony isn't from acid or swelling. A single peptide in the venom, poneratoxin, hijacks the electrical system inside your nerves. What does it do to make the pain so relentless?
answer: Jams the sodium channels that carry nerve signals
choices: Jams the sodium channels that carry nerve signals
Dissolves the fatty sheath around each nerve
Floods the muscles with excess calcium
Starves the nerve endings of oxygen
context: Poneratoxin locks up the voltage-gated sodium channels nerves use to fire, scrambling the signals they send each other. There are no recorded human deaths from the sting, and the toxin fully clears the body within about a day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraponera_clavata

question: A long, ringed, soft-bodied animal squirms through tropical soil, looking exactly like a giant earthworm or a burrowing snake - yet it is neither. It has no legs at all, and it is really an amphibian, a close relative of frogs. What is this legless creature?
answer: A caecilian, a legless amphibian
choices: A caecilian, a legless amphibian
A slow-worm, a legless lizard
A blindworm, a burrowing snake
An amphiuma, an eel-like salamander
context: Caecilians (order Gymnophiona) are the least-known group of amphibians - true amphibians like frogs and salamanders, but with no legs and a long, segmented, worm-like body. They are not worms and not snakes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caecilian

question: A caecilian - the legless burrowing amphibian - spends its whole life hidden underground, so most people have never seen one. Its 220-plus species thrive across warm, wet tropics on several continents, yet one large continent, though plenty tropical and wet, has never had a single native caecilian. Which continent is caecilian-free?
answer: Australia
choices: Australia
Africa
South America
southern Asia
context: There are over 220 caecilian species across 10 families, found in the tropics of South and Central America, Africa, southern Asia and the Seychelles - but never in Australia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caecilian

question: A caecilian hunts through pitch-dark soil almost blind, yet it still tracks down prey. Between each eye and nostril sits a small organ found in no other animal with a backbone, which it pushes out and pulls back as it burrows. What is this one-of-a-kind organ?
answer: A chemical-sensing tentacle
choices: A chemical-sensing tentacle
A pair of infrared pit organs
A pair of heat-tasting tongues
A set of pressure-sensing whiskers
context: The tentacle sits in a groove between eye and nostril, can be pushed out and pulled back, and connects to the animal's smell system - a sensory organ unique among all vertebrates that lets a nearly blind caecilian hunt underground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caecilian

question: A mother Boulengerula taitanus caecilian rests coiled as her newly-hatched babies swarm over her body, scraping at her with a special set of baby teeth found only in the young. What are those baby teeth FOR?
answer: Peeling and eating her skin
choices: Peeling and eating her skin
Gripping her as she carries them
Combing parasites from her sides
Draining milk from a belly pore
context: Alexander Kupfer and his team first documented this skin-feeding (dermatophagy) in Boulengerula taitanus. The babies scrape off the fatty skin about every three days - the time a new layer takes to regrow - and can grow up to 10 times their own weight in a single week. It is a form of maternal care, not cruelty. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04403  (Legend.)

question: In 2020 researchers reported that the ringed caecilian, Siphonops annulatus, shares a trait otherwise famous in snakes - and if confirmed it would be the OLDEST known land vertebrate to have it, older even than snakes themselves. Which trait?
answer: An oral venom system
choices: An oral venom system
A regrowing set of fangs
A glow-in-the-dark bite
A paralyzing tail spine
context: Researchers found tiny glands at the base of the teeth that release fluid when the caecilian bites, carrying phospholipase A2 - an enzyme bees, wasps and snakes use to inflict a burning, tissue-dissolving sting. This reported finding is still under study, but if confirmed it may make caecilians the oldest land vertebrate with an oral venom system - older even than venomous snakes. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7385905/

question: The one-humped dromedary owns the hot Arabian and African deserts. Its shaggier cousin, the Bactrian, thrives instead in the Gobi, where a single year swings through a punishing temperature range. How wide a span does the Bactrian endure?
answer: From about -20 F up to 120 F
choices: From about -20 F up to 120 F
A steady 60 F year-round
From freezing up to about 80 F
From about 40 F up to 140 F
context: The two-humped Bactrian is the cold-desert camel, handling the Gobi's brutal swing from roughly -20 F up to 120 F, while the one-humped dromedary rules the hot deserts. Source: San Diego Zoo, Camel; Britannica, Camel.

question: A camel plods across open dunes without sinking, where a horse's narrow hooves would punch straight down into the loose sand. What keeps the camel on top?
answer: Broad two-toed feet
choices: Broad two-toed feet
Tiny hardened hooves
A single padded toe
Long curved climbing claws
context: Each broad, two-toed foot spreads and flattens under the camel's weight, then contracts when lifted, working like a natural snowshoe that keeps it from sinking into loose sand. Source: San Diego Zoo, Camel.

question: Everyone 'knows' a camel's hump is a built-in water tank for crossing the desert. That popular picture is wrong. What is actually packed inside the hump?
answer: Fat, a concentrated energy reserve
choices: Fat, a concentrated energy reserve
Water stored for the journey
A spongy sac of blood
Coiled muscle for climbing
context: The hump is a concentrated fat reserve the camel burns when food is scarce. Keeping the fat in one hump rather than spread under the skin also lets the rest of the body shed heat more easily. Source: WWF, What do camels store in their humps?

question: A camel finds a hungry-looking cactus bristling with six-inch needles and simply eats it, spines and all, without a scratch inside its mouth. What handles the needles as they go down?
answer: Cone-shaped mouth spikes that steer each needle point-first down
choices: Cone-shaped mouth spikes that steer each needle point-first down
A thick saliva coating that dissolves the spines before swallowing
Molars that snap each needle off cleanly at its base
A second set of lips that strips the spines away first
context: Cone-shaped keratin papillae line the camel's mouth and rotate the spines so they slide straight down the throat point-first; a vet described them as feeling almost like plastic. Source: National Geographic, Arabian Camels Eat Cacti With Hardened Mouth Structures.

question: A camel arrives at a trough dangerously dehydrated and drinks nonstop for about ten minutes without lifting its head. How much water can it take on in that single session?
answer: Over 100 liters
choices: Over 100 liters
About 10 liters
Under 2 liters
Around 30 liters
context: A dehydrated camel can gulp well over 100 liters in about ten minutes; the San Diego Zoo cites up to 145 liters (32 gallons) in a single drink, replacing about a third of its body weight almost at once. Source: San Diego Zoo, Camel.

question: Sweating dumps heat but spends precious water, so through the blazing day a camel does something with its own physiology that most mammals never risk. What does it do?
answer: Lets its body temperature climb by day and cool at night
choices: Lets its body temperature climb by day and cool at night
Slows its heartbeat to a near-standstill until dusk
Shunts blood away from its skin to trap heat inside
Shuts down its kidneys to hoard every last drop
context: Rather than sweating, a camel lets its core temperature swing widely, cooling to about 34-35 C overnight and coasting up to 41-42 C by day. Storing the heat in its own body instead of evaporating water to shed it saves enormous amounts of water. Source: Schmidt-Nielsen, 1956, Body Temperature of the Camel and Its Relation to Water Economy.

question: A South American grazer plods through a savanna near a river, chomping grass — four feet long, and as heavy as a grown man, roughly the size of a big dog. Every animal in its family group is a rodent, and this is the biggest kind of rodent alive anywhere on Earth. What is it?
answer: The capybara
choices: The capybara
The beaver
The porcupine
The muskrat
context: The capybara (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris) is the largest living rodent — over four feet long and typically 35–66 kg (77–146 lb), about the mass of a grown man. The heaviest wild one on record was a 91 kg (201 lb) female from Brazil. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capybara

question: A capybara spends every waking hour grinding tough, gritty grass between its big front teeth. That constant scraping wears the enamel away fast — enough to file an ordinary tooth down to a useless stub. Yet an old capybara bites just as well as a young one. What trick of a rodent's front teeth beats the wear?
answer: The teeth never stop growing
choices: The teeth never stop growing
New adult teeth replace the worn ones each year
A hard enamel cap makes them wear-proof
Saliva slowly rebuilds the worn edges
context: Like all rodents, the capybara's front incisors grow continuously throughout its life, replacing exactly what constant grass-grinding wears away. That is the defining rodent trait — the word 'rodent' comes from Latin for 'to gnaw.' Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/things-you-might-not-know-about-capybaras.html

question: A capybara can lower itself into a pond until nearly its whole body is gone beneath the surface, yet stay fully alert to a jaguar creeping along the bank — the same way a hippo lurks. What feature of a capybara's head makes this possible?
answer: Its eyes, ears, and nostrils all sit high on top of the head
choices: Its eyes, ears, and nostrils all sit high on top of the head
A long snorkel-like snout it lifts above the surface
A wide flat skull that keeps the whole face above water
Nostrils that pinch shut while raised eye sockets watch
context: A capybara's eyes, ears, and nostrils are all set high on the top of its head, so it can float with almost its whole body submerged and still see, hear, and breathe — the same layout a hippopotamus uses. It can even sleep in the water with just its nose poking out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capybara  (Legend.)

question: Grass is so hard to digest that much of the protein and B vitamins a capybara's gut bacteria produce would slip away unabsorbed. To reclaim that lost nutrition, a capybara does something each morning that startles people who watch it. What does it do?
answer: It re-eats its own soft morning droppings
choices: It re-eats its own soft morning droppings
It licks mineral-rich mud from the riverbank
It chews the cud back up like a cow
It eats the droppings of the young in its group
context: The capybara is a hindgut fermenter: an enlarged cecum and colon full of bacteria break down grass cellulose its stomach cannot. Because the nutrients those bacteria make would otherwise be lost, it re-eats its soft morning droppings (coprophagy), passing the food through twice to absorb the protein and B vitamins — the same trick rabbits use. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capybara ; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00264639  (Legend.)

question: A glossy black flightless bird taller than a grown man stalks the rainforests of northern Queensland and New Guinea, its bare neck painted electric blue and topped by a tall horny helmet. Name this giant of the forest floor.
answer: The cassowary
choices: The cassowary
The greater rhea
The secretary bird
The shoebill stork
context: The southern cassowary stands up to about 2 metres (6 feet) tall, with glossy black feathers, bright blue skin on the head and fore-neck, red on the rear neck, and a tall greyish 'casque' helmet. Source: Australian Museum, Southern Cassowary.

question: Zookeepers who work with big flightless birds hand the cassowary one title above the ostrich, the emu, and the rhea. What reputation has this rainforest bird earned?
answer: The world's most dangerous bird
choices: The world's most dangerous bird
The world's fastest bird
The world's heaviest bird
The world's loudest bird
context: The cassowary is widely called the world's most dangerous bird. A 2019 death in Florida (its 75-year-old owner) was the first human fatality attributed to a cassowary in 93 years. Source: Guinness World Records, 'Why the cassowary is the world's most dangerous bird'.  (Legend.)

question: A cornered cassowary does not flee; it leaps and drives both feet forward at whatever threatens it. On the inner toe of each foot rides the weapon that has earned it its deadly name. What is it?
answer: A dagger-like claw up to five inches long
choices: A dagger-like claw up to five inches long
A ring of backward-facing barbs
A gripping talon like an eagle's
A blunt spur it uses to trip
context: The inner toe on each foot ends in a dagger-like claw up to about 12 cm (5 inches) long. A threatened cassowary leaps and kicks, and the claw can slash open internal organs. Source: Wikipedia, Cassowary / Southern cassowary.  (Legend.)

question: A baby cassowary trotting behind its father looks nothing like the black adult; for its first months a bold pattern hides it against the dark forest floor. Field guides say the chick most resembles what?
answer: A watermelon
choices: A watermelon
A newborn fawn
A ring-tailed lemur
A rolled-up pangolin
context: Cassowary chicks hatch striped like watermelons — brown-and-cream banded down the back and thighs for camouflage — and lose the stripes at about 3 to 6 months, turning plain brown. Source: Birdfact, 'Baby Cassowaries' / San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance factsheet.

question: Deep in dense foliage a cassowary makes a sound felt more than heard: a booming note near 32 hertz, right at the floor of human hearing. Researchers think the bird uses so deep a pitch to do one thing a higher call could not. What?
answer: Carry far through thick rainforest foliage
choices: Carry far through thick rainforest foliage
Startle predators into freezing
Echo off the ground to map the forest
Mimic the calls of other animals
context: Cassowaries produce some of the lowest-frequency sounds known in any bird — deep booming notes reaching about 32 Hz — thought to carry through dense foliage where higher-pitched calls fade. The casque may act as a receiver/amplifier for these calls, though its exact function is still debated. Source: Researchgate, 'Low-Frequency Vocalizations by Cassowaries' / Rainforest Trust, 'Seven Things'.

question: A chameleon sits perfectly still, spots an insect a good distance off, and strikes without moving its body. Its weapon shoots out, hits the bug, and reels back in about the time it takes to blink. What launches to make the catch?
answer: Its tongue, flung out past twice its body length
choices: Its tongue, flung out past twice its body length
A jet of sticky venom sprayed from its jaw
A whip of its coiled, grabbing tail
A puff of glue blown from its throat
context: A chameleon's tongue rockets out about 2.5 times its own body length and slams into an insect in roughly 20 milliseconds, a fraction of a blink. Source: Brown University, 2016 (Christopher Anderson study of Rhampholeon spinosus); Wikipedia, Chameleon.

question: A resting chameleon can keep watch on a hawk overhead and a beetle behind it at the very same moment, because of one bizarre thing its two eyes can do that yours cannot. What is it?
answer: Each eye swivels on its own, aiming in a different direction
choices: Each eye swivels on its own, aiming in a different direction
Both eyes glow to spot warm-blooded prey in the dark
The eyes see straight through leaves and thin bark
The eyes flatten to give a single wide panorama
context: A chameleon's two eyes swivel independently inside cone-shaped turrets, letting it watch two directions at once and scan almost a full 360-degree circle without turning its head; its brain analyzes two separate images. Source: Wikipedia, Chameleon; AskNature 'Eyes Give 360-degree Vision'.

question: For most of the time a chameleon's two eyes roam apart, aimed in different directions. But the instant it spots a bug worth catching, the eyes do something sudden together. What happens right before the strike?
answer: Both eyes snap forward onto the same target to judge distance
choices: Both eyes snap forward onto the same target to judge distance
Both eyes squeeze shut to protect against the recoil
The eyes flash a bright color to freeze the prey
The eyes retract deep into the skull for safety
context: When a chameleon locks on, both eyes fix forward on the same target for depth perception precise to within a few millimeters, because once the tongue fires there is no chance to correct its aim. Source: animalsaroundtheglobe.com; AskNature 'Eyes Give 360-degree Vision'.

question: Most people think a chameleon turns colors to blend into leaves and vanish. Biologists say that is mostly wrong. What is a chameleon's color change really for, more than hiding?
answer: Broadcasting its mood and controlling its temperature
choices: Broadcasting its mood and controlling its temperature
Poisoning any predator that bites its bright skin
Confusing prey so insects freeze in place
Marking a trail so it can find its way home
context: Chameleons change color mainly to signal mood and intentions and to warm up or cool down, not chiefly to camouflage; a calm chameleon and an angry, showing-off one are literally different colors. Source: Wikipedia, Chameleon; Nature Communications ncomms7368 (Teyssier et al. 2015).

question: Of the roughly 200 chameleon species on Earth, about half of them live in only one place and turn up nowhere else in the wild. Where is this one island home to so many of them?
answer: Madagascar
choices: Madagascar
The Galapagos Islands
New Zealand
Borneo
context: About half of all roughly 200 described chameleon species live only on Madagascar, found nowhere else on Earth. Source: Wikipedia, Chameleon ('200 species described as of June 2015'; about half restricted to Madagascar).

question: A male Jackson's chameleon wears three forward-pointing horns on its face, and when two males meet on a branch they use them in a very direct way. What do the rival males do with those horns?
answer: Lock them together and try to shove each other off the branch
choices: Lock them together and try to shove each other off the branch
Rub them to make a buzzing sound that scares off hawks
Dig them into bark to pry out hidden grubs
Flash them bright red to attract nearby females
context: Male Jackson's chameleons wear three forward-pointing horns reminiscent of a tiny Triceratops, and rival males lock horns and try to push each other off a branch. Source: Wikipedia, 'Jackson's chameleon'.

question: On Madagascar scientists found a chameleon so tiny its whole body is just over half an inch long and it can perch on the tip of your finger. Which size record might this nano-chameleon hold?
answer: It may be the smallest reptile on Earth
choices: It may be the smallest reptile on Earth
It is the smallest chameleon but not the smallest reptile
It is the smallest reptile that lays eggs
It is the smallest land animal with a backbone
context: The nano-chameleon Brookesia nana from Madagascar has a body just over half an inch long (male body 13.5 mm, total ~22 mm) and may be the smallest reptile on Earth. Source: Mongabay 2021; Wikipedia 'Brookesia nana'; discovered by Frank Glaw's team.  (Legend.)

question: Stretch a chameleon's skin one way and it flashes blue; let it relax and it glows yellow and red, the very same skin, no waiting and no pigment injected. How does one patch of skin flip colors on demand?
answer: Structural color from a grid of tiny crystals
choices: Structural color from a grid of tiny crystals
Pigment released from color glands under the skin
Reflected heat glowing out through the scales
Dye absorbed from the leaves it eats
context: Chameleon skin holds a grid of guanine nanocrystals; tightening or loosening the grid changes which wavelengths reflect, blue when packed tight, yellows and reds when spread apart, a structural color, not pigment. Source: Teyssier et al., Nature Communications 2015 (ncomms7368); phys.org 2015.  (Legend.)

question: When a chameleon's tongue slams onto an insect, the very tip does the holding, and it grips harder the faster the tongue yanks back, so the lizard can reel in prey heavier than seems possible. What coats that tongue tip?
answer: A super-sticky slime about 400 times thicker than human spit
choices: A super-sticky slime about 400 times thicker than human spit
Rows of tiny backward-curved hooks like a cat's tongue
A ring of muscle that clamps shut like a fist
A patch of static charge that pulls the bug in
context: The tongue tip is coated in mucus about 400 times more viscous than human saliva, and it grips harder the faster the tongue snaps back, letting the chameleon reel in surprisingly heavy prey. Source: Nature Physics, Fabian Brau/Pascal Damman (U. Mons), 2016; National Geographic 'Chameleons' Secret Hunting Weapon: Super-Sticky Mucus'.

question: Scientists measured the power packed into a chameleon's tongue launch, per kilogram of muscle, and ranked it against every backboned animal. Only one kind of creature beats it. Which animals out-power the chameleon's tongue?
answer: Salamanders
choices: Salamanders
Cheetahs
Hummingbirds
Rattlesnakes
context: A chameleon's tongue produces about 14,000 watts per kilogram of muscle, the highest per-kg power of any reptile, bird, or mammal, and second among all vertebrates only to salamanders. Source: Brown University, 2016, Christopher Anderson (14,040 W/kg).

question: A chameleon still snatches prey at a body temperature of 3.5 C, when nearby lizards are frozen too stiff to move, and its tongue launch barely weakens in that cold. That cold-proof shot reveals how the tongue truly fires. What powers it?
answer: A slow muscle first loads coiled collagen sheaths that then recoil like a bow
choices: A slow muscle first loads coiled collagen sheaths that then recoil like a bow
A fast muscle contracts hard enough to fling the whole tongue like a whip
Blood pumped in under high pressure swells the tongue and shoots it out
A burst of air suction behind the tongue snaps it out at the target
context: The tongue is a spring, not a muscle flung by brute force. An 'accelerator' muscle contracts slowly and stretches a sleeve of at least ~10 collagen sheaths wrapped around a stiff tongue-bone spur (the entoglossal process); the loaded sheaths then slide off the bone's rounded tip and recoil all at once, releasing stored elastic energy for accelerations up to ~500 m/s squared. The giveaway that it is elastic and not direct muscle: in veiled chameleons tested from 15 to 35 C, projection power fell only ~10-19% per 10 C, while muscle-powered RETRACTION fell 42-63% per 10 C, letting the animal keep feeding down to a body temperature of 3.5 C. Source: de Groot & van Leeuwen 2004, Proc. R. Soc. B (https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rspb.2003.2637); Anderson & Deban 2010, PNAS 107:5495 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2851764/).

question: Humans gauge distance by comparing the slightly different views from two eyes. A chameleon can nail the range to a bug with a single eye, no second view to compare. How does one eye measure how far the prey sits?
answer: It focuses that eye and reads the focus setting as the distance
choices: It focuses that eye and reads the focus setting as the distance
It clocks how fast the bug drifts across the eye as the head sways
It swings both turret eyes forward to lock on an instant before striking
It matches the bug against a remembered size to estimate range
context: This deepens the older 'both eyes snap forward to triangulate' picture. A chameleon judges depth by monocular corneal accommodation: it focuses one eye and reads the focal setting as a distance. Its eye pairs a negative (concave) lens behind a strongly positive (convex) cornea, enlarging the retinal image so tiny focus changes are readable, and it can shift focus about 60 diopters per second with an amplitude near 45 diopters, faster and more precise than any other reptile. This makes the chameleon the only vertebrate that can judge depth with a single eye. Source: Harkness 1977, Nature 267:346 (https://www.nature.com/articles/267346a0); Ott, Schaeffel & Kirmse 1998, J. Comp. Physiol. A (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s003590050182).

question: Everyone crowns the flea the great insect high-jumper, but a 6-millimeter bug clears 70 centimeters straight up -- more than twice a flea's height. Which insect actually holds the record?
answer: The froghopper (spittlebug)
choices: The froghopper (spittlebug)
The click beetle
The desert locust
The mole cricket
context: The froghopper (Philaenus spumarius) leaps about 70 cm straight up -- roughly 100 to 140 times its own body length, more than twice as high as a flea, making it the true insect jump champion. It gets the name spittlebug because its young hide in blobs of froth on plant stems. Source: Nature (Burrows 2003, 'Froghopper insects leap to new heights', 424:509) via NPR 2003-08-01.  (Legend.)

question: A froghopper is only about 6 millimeters long, yet it is the insect high-jump champion. Measured against the length of its own body, roughly how high does one of its leaps reach?
answer: Over 100 times its body length
choices: Over 100 times its body length
About 5 times its body length
About 15 times its body length
About 40 times its body length
context: The froghopper leaps roughly 100 to 140 times its own body length. Scaled to a six-foot human, that would be like clearing a stack of tall buildings. Source: Nature (Burrows 2003, 424:509).

question: A froghopper's jumping legs are barely half its body length and make up only 2 percent of its whole mass, far too little muscle to fling the insect that high. So where does the launch power actually come from?
answer: Springs built into its body that muscle slowly loads and then releases
choices: Springs built into its body that muscle slowly loads and then releases
A rapid drumbeat of many small muscle twitches
Air forced out through breathing pores as a jet
A running start that builds momentum before liftoff
context: The legs are only about half the body length and just 2% of body mass, so the power cannot come from the leg muscles firing directly -- it is stored in springs first. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology 209:4607 (Burrows).

question: To fire its jump, a froghopper first slowly tenses big muscles to bend internal springs, hooks both hind legs in a cocked position with microscopic Velcro-like teeth, then trips the hold. What can you hear as it launches -- if anything?
answer: An audible click
choices: An audible click
A faint buzz
A sharp snap of the legs
A high whine
context: The froghopper locks its cocked legs with microscopic teeth (microtrichia) and fires with an audible click as the latch releases. Source: BMC Biology 6:41 (Burrows, Shaw & Sutton 2008).  (Legend.)

question: A froghopper's jump spring is a bow-shaped arch of stiff cuticle coated in a rubbery protein. Shine ultraviolet light on a fresh froghopper and that protein betrays exactly where the spring sits. What does the UV light reveal?
answer: A bright blue glow along the spring
choices: A bright blue glow along the spring
A red heat shimmer around the legs
A green shadow under the wings
A crackling spark at the joints
context: The spring material is resilin, a rubber-like protein that fluoresces bright blue under UV light; the glow traces the bow-shaped cuticle arch whose snap-back recoil -- not muscle -- powers the leap. Source: BMC Biology 6:41 (Burrows, Shaw & Sutton 2008).

question: In its thousandth-of-a-second launch, a froghopper hits an acceleration so violent it briefly feels hundreds of times the force of gravity. A fighter pilot blacks out near 9. Roughly what force does the froghopper endure?
answer: Around 400 to 550 times gravity
choices: Around 400 to 550 times gravity
Around 20 times gravity
Around 90 times gravity
Around 200 times gravity
context: The froghopper accelerates at about 5,400 m/s2, briefly experiencing roughly 400 to 550 g (versus 2 to 3 g for a human), reaching take-off speed in under a thousandth of a second. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology 209:4607 (Burrows).  (Legend.)

question: A grasshopper builds its jump by clenching a huge thigh muscle, but instead of firing straight away, half that energy is banked by bending two curved braces of hard cuticle layered with resilin. Where on the leg sit these bent, energy-storing braces?
answer: At the knee
choices: At the knee
At the ankle
Along the foot
At the hip
context: The grasshopper/locust bends two curved braces at the knee called semi-lunar processes -- composites of hard cuticle and resilin -- banking about half the extensor muscle's energy before release. Source: J. Exp. Biol. 215:3501 (Burrows).

question: A kangaroo does the opposite of a catapult jumper: rather than storing energy for one big blast, its enormous leg tendons act like pogo-stick springs on every bound. Because of them, something surprising happens to the animal as it speeds up. What?
answer: Its hopping gets more efficient the faster it goes
choices: Its hopping gets more efficient the faster it goes
Its hopping burns far more energy at speed
It must switch to a four-legged gallop
It quickly overheats and has to stop
context: Dawson and Taylor (1973) found a kangaroo's oxygen use barely rises with speed; at 6 m/s, elastic tendon recoil can save a red kangaroo up to about 70% of its energy. Source: Nature 246:313 (Dawson & Taylor 1973).  (Legend.)

question: When a kangaroo moves slowly it plants its thick tail on the ground with each step. Scientists put walking kangaroos on a force platform to measure what that planted tail actually contributes. Compared with the animal's other limbs, how much forward push does the tail supply?
answer: As much as the front and hind legs combined
choices: As much as the front and hind legs combined
Almost none -- it only steadies the body
A little, about a tenth of the legs' effort
Only enough to lift the tail's own weight
context: O'Connor and colleagues (2014) found the tail supplies as much forward propulsion as the front and hind legs combined -- doing as much work as a human leg does when walking. Source: Biology Letters 10:20140381.  (Legend.)

question: Why do a flea and a froghopper need a spring at all, when a kangaroo just powers its hops with muscle? The answer is a hard limit built into muscle itself. What can't muscle do that forces tiny jumpers to store energy first?
answer: Contract fast enough to deliver the power in a single instant
choices: Contract fast enough to deliver the power in a single instant
Stay contracted long enough to hold a pose
Work at all in a cold-blooded body
Push and pull in the same motion
context: Muscle contracts too slowly to deliver power fast enough for a tiny launch, so small animals slowly load a spring and trip a latch to release the energy in an instant -- called latch-mediated spring actuation (LaMSA). Source: J. Exp. Biol. 226:jeb246070 review.

question: A trap-jaw ant can slam its spring-loaded jaws down onto the ground and fling its whole body into the air. Researchers pitted these ants against pit-digging antlion larvae, then glued some ants jaws shut to test whether the jump is a genuine escape tool or just a quirk. What did gluing the jaws do?
answer: Cut their escape rate to a quarter
choices: Cut their escape rate to a quarter
Left their escape rate unchanged
Made them slightly faster on foot
Turned the jump into a courting dance
context: The trap-jaw ant Odontomachus latches its mandibles open under spring tension, then releases them in one of the fastest movements in the animal kingdom -- fast enough that slamming the jaws against the ground hurls the ant clear of danger. Larabee and Suarez staged encounters with pit-digging antlions, predators that ambush ants sliding into their sand pits. Ants with working jaws escaped 60 to 79 percent of the time; ants whose mandibles were glued shut escaped only 26 percent -- making the jaw-jump roughly 2.3 to 4.7 times more likely to save the ant. The ants use two launch styles: a steep vertical 'escape jump' (take-off angle around 76 degrees) to flee the pit, and a low 'bouncer defense' jump (around 27 degrees) that knocks the ant backward off an attacker. Source: Larabee & Suarez 2015, 'Mandible-Powered Escape Jumps in Trap-Jaw Ants Increase Survival Rates during Predator-Prey Encounters', PLOS ONE 10(5):e0124871 -- https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0124871 ; Patek et al. 2006, PNAS on ballistic jaw propulsion -- https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0604290103

question: On the open plains of Africa, one slender, small-headed spotted cat can out-accelerate a sports car off the line, going from a standstill to over 110 km/h (70 mph) in just over three seconds. Which land animal is it?
answer: The cheetah
choices: The cheetah
The lion
The leopard
The African wild dog
context: The cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) is the fastest land animal, hitting more than 110 km/h in just over three seconds -- out-accelerating many sports cars from a standstill. Source: Cheetah Conservation Fund, cheetah.org/learn/about-cheetahs/  (Legend.)

question: Field researchers can pick one wild cheetah out from another on sight, no ear-tags or collars needed -- each cat carries its own built-in ID, the way a person's fingerprint is theirs alone. Which markings do the researchers read?
answer: The pattern of spots on its body and the rings on its tail
choices: The pattern of spots on its body and the rings on its tail
The exact shade of gold in its coat
The number of whiskers on each side of its face
The curl and length of its tail
context: A cheetah's spots cover nearly its whole body, and -- like a human fingerprint -- the spot pattern and the ring pattern of its tail are unique to each individual. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo, nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/news/why-do-cheetahs-have-spots-and-other-cheetah-facts

question: A cheetah mother needs to gather her cubs, scattered and hidden in the tall grass of the savanna. Unlike a lion, she cannot roar to summon them. What surprising sound does she make instead to call the cubs in?
answer: A birdlike chirp
choices: A birdlike chirp
A wolflike howl
A drawn-out yowl
A rumbling bellow
context: Unlike other big cats, the cheetah cannot roar; instead it chirps like a bird, purrs, growls, hisses and stutters, and a mother uses birdlike chirps to call her cubs. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo, nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/news/why-do-cheetahs-have-spots-and-other-cheetah-facts

question: Most cats keep their claws sheathed and razor-sharp for gripping prey, sliding them out only to strike. A sprinting cheetah does the opposite -- its claws are blunt and stay half-out like a dog's. What job are those exposed claws doing as it runs?
answer: Biting into the ground for traction like a sprinter's track spikes
choices: Biting into the ground for traction like a sprinter's track spikes
Slashing at prey with every stride to wound it early
Sharpening themselves against the dirt as it runs
Sensing vibrations in the ground from fleeing prey
context: The cheetah's claws are blunt and only semi-retractable, staying partly out like a dog's -- they bite into the ground like a sprinter's track spikes for traction, and ridges on the hard paw pads grip like tire tread. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo; SeaWorld, seaworld.org/animals/all-about/cheetah/characteristics/

question: Two black stripes run from the inner corner of each cheetah's eye straight down its face. Out on the glaring open plains, what do these 'tear marks' do for a hunting cheetah?
answer: Absorb the sun's glare so it can keep prey in sharp focus
choices: Absorb the sun's glare so it can keep prey in sharp focus
Warn rival cheetahs to keep off its territory
Channel rain and sweat away from its eyes
Signal its mood to cubs following behind it
context: The black 'tear marks' work like the eye-black athletes wear or the crosshairs of a scope -- they absorb sun glare bouncing off the cheeks so the cat can keep prey in sharp focus across the bright open plains. Source: Cheetah Conservation Fund; iere.org/why-do-cheetahs-have-black-tears/

question: A cheetah at full gallop looks like it's flying -- twice in every single bound all four feet leave the ground at once, and its hind legs swing impossibly far forward, past its front paws. Which part of its body makes that enormous reach possible?
answer: Its unusually flexible spine, coiling and uncoiling each stride
choices: Its unusually flexible spine, coiling and uncoiling each stride
Its extra-long back legs
Its wide, deep ribcage
Its loosely jointed shoulders
context: The cheetah's flexible spine flexes and extends like a spring with every stride, throwing the hind legs far forward; at full gallop it lifts all four feet off the ground twice per stride -- once stretched full-out and once with legs tucked under. Source: Cheetah Conservation Fund; SeaWorld, seaworld.org/animals/all-about/cheetah/adaptations/  (Legend.)

question: At a dead sprint, a fleeing gazelle can jink sideways in an instant -- a turn that would send most chasing animals tumbling head over heels. A cheetah swings one long body part side to side to shift its balance and stay glued to the turn. What is it steering with?
answer: Its long tail, working as a counterweight and rudder
choices: Its long tail, working as a counterweight and rudder
Its outstretched forelegs, leaning into the bend
Its whiskers, sensing the shift in air
Its ears, flattening to cut wind resistance
context: The cheetah's long tail works as a counterweight and rudder: it swings side to side to shift the cat's balance so it can make hairpin turns at speed that would send other animals tumbling; the flattened, ringed tuft at the tip acts like the rudder. Source: Cheetah Conservation Fund; SeaWorld, seaworld.org/animals/all-about/cheetah/adaptations/  (Legend.)

question: An all-out cheetah sprint burns oxygen at a furious rate, and the cat has to shove huge volumes of air into its chest with every second of the chase. Which feature of its head and airway is built to gulp down that air fast enough to feed the run?
answer: Enlarged nostrils opening into air-filled sinuses
choices: Enlarged nostrils opening into air-filled sinuses
A long muzzle packed with extra scent receptors
A wide mouth it pants through to cool the blood
A flexible windpipe that coils to store spare air
context: To feed the sprint, the cheetah gulps air through enlarged nostrils and air-filled sinuses; its breathing leaps from about 60 breaths a minute at rest to around 150 during a chase, fed by an oversized heart, lungs, liver and large arteries. Source: SeaWorld, seaworld.org/animals/all-about/cheetah/adaptations/

question: A cheetah is the fastest thing on land, yet it can hold that top speed for only a matter of seconds -- if it hasn't caught its prey in roughly 30 seconds, it has to break off and let the animal go. What forces the world's fastest sprinter to quit so fast?
answer: Lactic acid floods its muscles and it runs out of energy
choices: Lactic acid floods its muscles and it runs out of energy
Its heart cannot pump fast enough to stay conscious
Its blunt claws wear down and lose their grip
Its spine cramps and locks from the constant flexing
context: A cheetah can only hold its top speed for a matter of seconds -- prey must be caught within roughly 30 seconds -- because the anaerobic sprint floods its muscles with lactic acid and it simply runs out of energy. Source: Cheetah Conservation Fund; National Geographic. This is the real limit -- see the busted-overheating myth for the fuller story.  (Legend.)

question: When researchers fitted five wild Botswana cheetahs with GPS-and-motion collars, the cats logged a blistering top speed of 93 km/h -- yet most of their hunts were run at only moderate speed. What did the collars show actually decided most successful hunts?
answer: Grip and sharp maneuvering, with muscle power for braking and turning
choices: Grip and sharp maneuvering, with muscle power for braking and turning
Sheer top-end speed reached in a dead-straight sprint line
Hunting in coordinated pairs to trap and corner the prey
Ambushing from cover instead of chasing at all in open ground
context: A GPS-and-motion-collar study of five wild cheetahs in Botswana recorded a top speed of 25.9 m/s (58 mph / 93 km/h), but found most hunts were run at only moderate speed -- success came from grip, sharp maneuvering and muscle power for braking and turning, not from raw top speed. Source: Wilson et al., 'Locomotion dynamics of hunting in wild cheetahs,' Nature 2013, nature.com/articles/nature12295  (Legend.)

question: Ice-age North America had its own long-legged, spotted sprinter, Miracinonyx, so cheetah-like that it was long filed as an American cousin of the African cheetah. Then DNA and skeleton work overturned that family tree. What did the new evidence reveal about this vanished cat?
answer: It was a close cousin of the cougar that only looks cheetah-like through convergent evolution
choices: It was a close cousin of the cougar that only looks cheetah-like through convergent evolution
It was the direct ancestor of the African cheetah before the cats crossed into Asia
It was a giant relative of the lion that had lost its mane over generations
It was a big cat unrelated to any feline alive today, a lineage all its own
context: Miracinonyx trumani, the 'American cheetah,' died out at the end of the last ice age. Genetic and skeletal analyses now place it as a close relative of the cougar (Puma), not the true cheetah -- the two lineages arrived at the same lean, fast-pursuit body independently, a textbook case of convergent evolution. Unlike the African cheetah, Miracinonyx kept retractable claws and could rotate its forelimbs to grapple prey, and recent elbow-joint studies suggest it hunted in a way with no living analogue. It also anchors the famous 'ghost predator' idea: the pronghorn, still the fastest runner in the Americas, is far faster than any predator alive today, and its speed was long explained as an escape from Miracinonyx -- yet a 2026 analysis argues pronghorns were already fast BEFORE Miracinonyx appeared, so the coevolution story is now contested. Source: Sci.News, 'Miracinonyx trumani' (cougar-relative, convergence) https://www.sci.news/paleontology/miracinonyx-trumani-11656.html ; Royal Society Biology Letters 2022 elbow morphology https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsbl.2022.0483 ; Hardy & Kort, Quaternary International (pronghorn isotopes, anachronism doubt) https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1040618222002658 ; Wikipedia, Miracinonyx https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miracinonyx  (Legend.)

question: Graft a patch of skin between two unrelated lions, and each cat's body flags the stranger's tissue as foreign and sloughs it off within days. Surgeons ran the same experiment on fourteen unrelated cheetahs from across the population -- and every single graft healed in and stayed, an outcome otherwise seen only between identical twins. What is it about cheetahs, and not other big cats, that produces this result?
answer: A recent population bottleneck left every cheetah so genetically uniform its immune system reads any other as itself
choices: A recent population bottleneck left every cheetah so genetically uniform its immune system reads any other as itself
A cheetah heals wounds so fast that grafted skin bonds before the immune system can react
Cheetahs alone among cats never mount an immune attack on transplanted living tissue
The tested cats had all descended from a single famous zoo pair a few years earlier
context: In a landmark 1985 study, Stephen O'Brien and colleagues performed 14 reciprocal skin grafts between unrelated cheetahs, and all 14 were accepted -- an outcome normally seen only between identical twins. The cats are so uniform at their MHC genes (the 'self ID' the immune system checks) that one cheetah's tissue does not register as foreign. Surveying 200-plus genetic loci, the team traced this to a severe population bottleneck in the species' recent past; modern estimates put cheetah genetic diversity at roughly 0.1-4% of a typical mammal's. The uniformity persists in wild-born cats, ruling out mere captive inbreeding. Source: O'Brien et al. 1985, 'Genetic Basis for Species Vulnerability in the Cheetah,' Science 227:1428 (14 accepted reciprocal skin grafts, MHC monomorphism, 200+ loci) https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.2983425 ; Cheetah Conservation Fund summary https://cheetah.org/resource-library/genetic-basis-for-species-vulnerability-in-the-cheetah/

question: A little beetle you might flip off a log has a horrifying trick: when something bites it, it fires a scalding chemical spray out its tail. Which beetle does this?
answer: The bombardier beetle
choices: The bombardier beetle
The stag beetle
The dung beetle
The click beetle
context: The bombardier beetle (subfamily Brachininae) is named for its artillery-like blast: it keeps two harmless chemicals stored apart inside its body and mixes them with enzymes in a hardened reaction chamber only when attacked. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardier_beetle  (Legend.)

question: A striped animal ambling through the yard lifts its tail, stamps its front feet, and hisses at a dog. What is it warning the dog it will do next?
answer: Fire a reeking musk that sears the eyes and nose
choices: Fire a reeking musk that sears the eyes and nose
Bite with venom-filled fangs
Release a cloud of stinging spores
Puff up to twice its size
context: A skunk (family Mephitidae) warns before it sprays, stamping its feet, raising its tail, and hissing to give a predator a chance to back off. Its musk is made of sulfur compounds called thiols, which sear a predator's eyes and nose. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/science/Why-Do-Skunks-Spray ; https://www.dvm360.com/view/skunk-spray-toxicosis-odiferous-tale

question: The bombardier beetle stores TWO harmless liquids in separate tanks inside its body, safely apart until the instant it is attacked. What are the two chemicals it keeps ready to combine?
answer: Hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide
choices: Hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide
Vinegar and baking soda
Formic acid and alcohol
Venom and saliva
context: Kept apart, hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide are harmless; only when the beetle mixes them with enzymes in its reaction chamber do they react. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardier_beetle  (Legend.)

question: When the bombardier beetle is bitten, it dumps its two stored chemicals together with enzymes into a hardened chamber. What violent thing happens to the fluid in that instant?
answer: It flash-heats to near boiling and blasts out
choices: It flash-heats to near boiling and blasts out
It freezes solid into a plug
It glows and blinds the attacker
It turns to a harmless foam
context: The mixing reaction is violently exothermic: it flash-heats the fluid to near 100C (boiling water) and fires the scalding spray out the tail at whatever bit it. Source: https://www.chemistrysteps.com/the-chemistry-behind-bombardier-beetles-spray/  (Legend.)

question: A skunk's musk is famous for its reeking stink, but the startling part is how precisely it lands the spray on a threat several feet away. How does a skunk aim its shot so well?
answer: Each musk gland ends in its own nozzle it can point
choices: Each musk gland ends in its own nozzle it can point
It sprays a wide cloud and hopes to hit
It waits until the threat is pressed against its tail
Wind currents steer the droplets to the target
context: The skunk fires musk from two glands under its tail, each with its own aimable nipple, accurate to about 3 meters (with the smell then carried on the wind up to 1.5 km). Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/skunk

question: A shark clamps down on a hagfish, and in a fraction of a second the water around its mouth becomes nearly a liter of choking slime that clogs its gills. What did the hagfish release to make that slime explode into being?
answer: Tiny packets of coiled protein threads and mucus
choices: Tiny packets of coiled protein threads and mucus
A cloud of black ink
A jet of venom
Bubbles of air from its skin
context: A grabbed hagfish releases tiny thread-and-mucus packets that explode on contact with seawater into about a liter of choking slime in a fraction of a second. One liter is 99.996% seawater; the rest is tens of thousands of silk-like protein threads plus mucin. Sources: https://www.nature.com/articles/srep00131 ; https://sites.chapman.edu/fudge/project/biophysics-of-hagfish-slime/  (Legend.)

question: Firing near-boiling fluid so close to its own body should cook a bombardier beetle from the inside. As the pressure spikes inside its reaction chamber, what keeps its own organs safe?
answer: The pressure slams shut the valves to its storage tanks
choices: The pressure slams shut the valves to its storage tanks
A thick layer of fat insulates the chamber
It cools the fluid down just before firing
It only fires while facing away from itself
context: Inside the reaction chamber the vapor pressure spikes so hard it slams shut the valves from the storage chambers, protecting the beetle's own organs, then vents the blast outward. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3565695/  (Legend.)

question: Cornered by a predator, some sea cucumbers do something almost unbelievable to escape. What does the desperate animal do?
answer: Rips open its own rear and flings its guts at the attacker
choices: Rips open its own rear and flings its guts at the attacker
Splits in two and both halves crawl away
Inflates until the predator cannot swallow it
Sheds its skin and leaves it behind as a decoy
context: A cornered sea cucumber can eviscerate: it contracts so hard its cloaca tears open and it ejects its own toxic, holothurin-coated guts at the predator, then regrows the lost organs over days to weeks. Source: https://www.iflscience.com/sea-cucumbers-kill-predators-by-firing-sticky-organs-out-their-butts-68395  (Legend.)

question: A ladybug's bright red-and-black is not decoration; it is a billboard. Poke one and it oozes bitter yellow fluid to make you spit it out. What is that fluid?
answer: Its own blood, bled on purpose when poked
choices: Its own blood, bled on purpose when poked
Venom squeezed from a gland in its leg
Saliva welling up from its mouth
An oil sweated out through its shell
context: A cornered ladybug reflex-bleeds, oozing bitter yellow fluid from the leg joint nearest the poke, laced with the alkaloid coccinelline. Its red-and-black colors advertise that it tastes foul. Source: https://www.colorado.edu/asmagazine/2020/07/21/ladybugs-bright-colors-advertise-toxic-chemical-defenses

question: High-speed film of a firing bombardier beetle revealed its spray is no steady jet. Thomas Eisner's team found it fires in rapid machine-gun bursts. Roughly how fast are those pulses?
answer: About 500 pulses per second
choices: About 500 pulses per second
About 5 pulses per second
About 50 pulses per second
About 5,000 pulses per second
context: High-speed film by Thomas Eisner's team showed the spray comes out in machine-gun pulses at roughly 500 pulses per second (Aneshansley & Eisner, Science, 1990). Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.2349480  (Legend.)

question: The whip scorpion sprays the most concentrated acid of any animal from the base of its tail, and the shock is what it is: the very same acid found in a common kitchen bottle. Which acid is it?
answer: The acid that makes vinegar sour
choices: The acid that makes vinegar sour
The acid that makes lemons sour
The acid that curdles sour milk
The acid that makes apples tart
context: The whip scorpion, or vinegaroon (genus Mastigoproctus), sprays acetic acid, the acid in vinegar, from a pore at the base of its whip-like tail; the concentration reaches about 84%, the highest concentration of acetic acid known in nature. The long tail is a sensory feeler, not a stinger. Sources: https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN890 ; https://a-z-animals.com/animals/vinegaroon/  (Legend.)

question: Skeptics long argued the bombardier beetle's scalding, aimed spray was too intricate to have evolved by degrees. Biologists answered with Metrius contractus, the most primitive bombardier beetle alive -- its glands hold the same hot quinone chemistry, yet it cannot shoot a jet. What does this living halfway-beetle do with its chemicals instead?
answer: Oozes a bubbling froth that clings over its own body
choices: Oozes a bubbling froth that clings over its own body
Squirts a thin stream a full body-length behind itself
Leaks the fluid slowly from pores along its own back
Saves the mix until it can land one carefully aimed shot
context: Metrius contractus (subfamily Paussinae) is the crucial living intermediate that answers the old 'irreducibly complex' objection to the bombardier beetle. Where advanced Brachininae fire a pulsed, steerable jet, Metrius has the same two-chamber gland and hot quinone chemistry but only oozes a bubbling froth that spreads over its own body -- the ancestral 'foam' stage that preceded the explosive spray. The full graded pathway (quinones already made to harden the shell, then stored as a deterrent, then catalase making it hotter and foamier, then aimed pulsed fire) shows the weapon could build up in useful steps. Source: Eisner et al. 2000, PNAS, 'Spray mechanism of the most primitive bombardier beetle (Metrius contractus)' (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10729276/); Wikipedia 'Bombardier beetle' on the incremental-pathway rebuttal.  (Legend.)

question: Some sea cucumbers fire sticky white threads out the rear at an attacker; the threads shoot out and stretch to about twenty times their length in a heartbeat, then snare the predator in cords it cannot pull free. The odd part is how thin soft threads turn into unbreakable ones. How do they suddenly become tough and inescapable?
answer: A trigger protein locks their collagen rigid on contact
choices: A trigger protein locks their collagen rigid on contact
Tiny muscles inside the threads clench them all tight
Backward barbs along the threads catch and knot in skin
Seawater dries their sticky coating into a hard glaze
context: These are Cuvierian tubules, distinct from the sea cucumber's better-known trick of ejecting its guts. They work through 'mutable collagenous tissue,' the same catch-connective tissue that lets echinoderms go instantly stiff or floppy. During ejection the collagen wall is deliberately soft and low-resistance, so a tubule can elongate roughly twentyfold in seconds; then, on contact with the attacker, a stiffening protein called tensilin cross-links the collagen so the now-adhesive threads become tough and inextensible -- trapping the predator with no muscle doing the work. Source: Demeuldre, Flammang et al. 2017, Journal of Experimental Biology, 'Mechanical adaptability of sea cucumber Cuvierian tubules involves a mutable collagenous tissue' (https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/220/11/2108/17941).

question: A diver spots what looks like a matched pair of tiny, brilliantly colored spiral fir trees poking straight out of a living coral head. But it isn't two little plants growing side by side. What are the twin spirals really?
answer: The two feathery crowns of a single worm hidden in the coral
choices: The two feathery crowns of a single worm hidden in the coral
A colony of tiny coral polyps stacked in a spiral
A pair of small sea anemones sharing one rock
Two baby starfish curled up to feed
context: The Christmas tree worm (Spirobranchus giganteus) lives head-down inside a tube bored into the living coral, with only its two spiral crowns showing. The 'trees' are not two animals but the twin crowns of one worm. Source: NOAA, oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/xmas-tree.html.

question: A Christmas tree worm's colorful spiral crowns sit out in the open on the reef, where a hungry fish could snap them off in an instant. The moment a shadow slides over it or the water stirs, what does the worm do?
answer: Yanks its whole crown down into its burrow in a blink
choices: Yanks its whole crown down into its burrow in a blink
Puffs the crown up bigger to look dangerous
Squirts a cloud of ink and drifts away
Flashes a warning color and holds its ground
context: The worm is so sensitive it retracts at the slightest touch or a passing shadow, then re-emerges very slowly about a minute later to test the water. Sources: MarineBio; NOAA.

question: The feathery, hair-fringed spiral branches (called radioles) on a Christmas tree worm work like a net, catching drifting plankton and sweeping it to the worm's mouth to eat. But those same branches do a second, completely different job at the same time. What is it?
answer: They pull oxygen out of the seawater, working like gills
choices: They pull oxygen out of the seawater, working like gills
They soak up sunlight to make sugars like a plant
They inject venom into anything that brushes past
They glow to lure prey closer in the dark
context: The radioles do double duty: catching food AND absorbing oxygen from the water like gills, so the worm eats and breathes with the very same feathery crown. Sources: NOAA; Wikipedia (Spirobranchus giganteus).

question: When a Christmas tree worm snaps its crown down into the coral, it doesn't just hide in an open hole — it seals the tube shut behind itself. What does it use to cork the entrance?
answer: A trapdoor lid made from one of its own modified branches
choices: A trapdoor lid made from one of its own modified branches
A blob of sticky mucus it spits over the opening
A borrowed empty snail shell wedged in the gap
A flap of the coral it pinches closed like a mouth
context: After retracting, the worm plugs its tube with an operculum — a modified radiole (one of its crown branches) reshaped into a trapdoor lid that seals the hole while the worm hides. Sources: Wikipedia (Spirobranchus giganteus); MarineBio.

question: A Christmas tree worm fires its crown down into the coral before anything actually touches it — a mere shadow sliding overhead is enough to trigger the retreat. For that to work, the crown itself has to sense the intruder. Built right into the feathery spiral branches are what?
answer: Rows of real compound eyes that catch the passing shadow
choices: Rows of real compound eyes that catch the passing shadow
Clusters of taste buds that sample chemicals in the water
Coils of stinging cells like those a jellyfish fires
Tufts of fine hairs that feel the shifting current
context: Serpulid worms like Spirobranchus evolved compound eyes built into the radioles — the feathery feeding branches — and in the S. giganteus complex each eye packs an estimated 600 to 1,000 tiny lenses. Their visual pigment peaks near 464 nm, the blue of downwelling reef light, so the eyes work as a silhouette-detecting 'burglar alarm': they catch the shadow of an approaching object and fire the withdrawal reflex before the worm is ever touched. Source: Bok, Porter & Nilsson, 'Radiolar Eyes of Serpulid Worms,' The Biological Bulletin 233(1), 2017.

question: A worm permanently cemented onto a living coral head sounds like a freeloader. But marine biologists genuinely disagree about the relationship, and careful reef studies point in opposite directions. What does some of the evidence suggest these worms sometimes do for their host coral?
answer: Shield it from crown-of-thorns starfish that would eat it
choices: Shield it from crown-of-thorns starfish that would eat it
Feed it sugars the way algae inside the coral do
Cement its loose rubble together after a storm breaks it
Ferry its spawning larvae out to colonize fresh reef
context: Whether these worms help or harm their host is a real, unsettled debate. A landmark Great Barrier Reef study (DeVantier, Reichelt & Bradbury, Marine Ecology Progress Series 32:307-310, 1986) found the worms may protect Porites coral from crown-of-thorns starfish: in 5 of 7 colonies, living coral tissue was significantly associated with the worms near the feeding fronts, hinting at a coevolved mutualism. But later work off Curacao (van der Schoot & Hoeksema, 2019) found the opposite is often true — the worm's scraping operculum injured the coral in roughly 21 to 62 percent of cases, worst when turf algae grew on the lid. No verdict: the relationship appears to swing between help and harm depending on the reef.  (Legend.)

question: In the wet cloud forests of Colombia and Ecuador lives a tiny bird, chestnut-brown with a scarlet-red cap, that courts females with a clear violin-like tone. But he never opens his beak to make it. What part of his body does he sing with instead?
answer: His wings
choices: His wings
His tail
His feet
His chest
context: The male club-winged manakin (Machaeropterus deliciosus) is the only bird known to sing with its wings rather than its voice. He rubs two specially thickened wing feathers together behind his back to produce a pure, violin-like tone. Source: All About Birds / Cornell Lab, 'Singing With His Wings'; Bostwick et al., PMC2842718 ('Resonating feathers produce courtship song').  (Legend.)

question: The male club-winged manakin makes his violin-like tone the way a cricket chirps: by dragging one body part across another, over a hundred times a second. For a cricket it is one leg scraped over a wing. But for the manakin, one wing feather scrapes over its neighbor like a bow over a string. What is special about that neighbor feather, the one being scraped?
answer: It is ridged like a tiny washboard
choices: It is ridged like a tiny washboard
It is coated in slippery oil
It is hollow like a flute tube
It is tipped with a hard claw
context: One of the manakin's wing feathers has a shaft bumpy with a row of ridges, like a tiny washboard; a stiff neighboring feather scrapes across those bumps the way a bow crosses a violin string, and each bump adds a click that blurs into a pure tone. This rub-to-sing method is called stridulation — the same trick a cricket uses — but only the manakin does it among birds. Source: All About Birds / Cornell Lab, 'Singing With His Wings'; AskNature, 'Resonating feathers produce courtship song'; Bostwick et al., PMC2842718.  (Legend.)

question: The male club-winged manakin knocks his wing feathers together so hard to make his tone that his wing bones had to be rebuilt to take the pounding. The female never makes a sound. When scientists looked at her skeleton, they expected ordinary wing bones. What did they actually find in the silent female's wings?
answer: The same dense, solid wing bone the male has
choices: The same dense, solid wing bone the male has
Ordinary thin-walled hollow bones, unlike his
Wing bones fused into a single stiff rod
An extra air sac threaded through the bone
context: The male's wing bone (the ulna) is filled in and mineralized to nearly three times the volume of a normal bird's — solid, not hollow — so it survives being knocked together over and over. The surprise is that females carry the same dense, heavy wing bone even though only males make the sound: a rare case where a mating display reshaped the WHOLE species' skeleton, making every bird — male or female — a slightly worse flier. Source: Bostwick, Riccio & Humphries, PMC3440988 ('Massive, solidified bone in the wing of a volant courting bird'); Wikipedia, 'Club-winged manakin' (solid wing bones present in females).  (Legend.)

question: A hulking crab hauls itself up a coconut palm on a Pacific island — heavier than a housecat, with a leg-span that can stretch nearly a meter tip to tip. What record does the coconut crab hold?
answer: The largest land arthropod on Earth
choices: The largest land arthropod on Earth
The fastest-running crab on Earth
The only crab that lives in freshwater
The most venomous crab on Earth
context: The coconut crab (Birgus latro) is the biggest land arthropod alive: it can span more than 3 feet (over 0.9 m, some reports near a meter) from leg-tip to leg-tip and weigh up to about 9 pounds (4.1 kg). Source: Wikipedia, Coconut crab (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coconut_crab).

question: A coconut is so tough a person usually needs a tool to open one. Yet on tropical islands one animal will spend hours doing it with nothing but its own body. Which animal cracks open whole coconuts?
answer: The coconut crab
choices: The coconut crab
The giant fruit bat
The green sea turtle
The monitor lizard
context: A coconut crab can climb a coconut palm and, over hours, husk and crack open a whole coconut with its claws — a nut a person would normally need tools to open. Charles Darwin described this behavior on the Keeling Islands. Sources: Darwin, The Voyage of the Beagle, Ch. 20 (standardebooks.org); Natural History Museum (nhm.ac.uk).

question: Island residents call the coconut crab the "robber crab." What earned it that nickname?
answer: It hauls off pots, silverware, and shiny objects
choices: It hauls off pots, silverware, and shiny objects
It steals eggs from other crabs' burrows
It waits to snatch food from sleeping birds
It digs up buried seeds people have planted
context: The nickname 'robber crab' comes from its habit of carrying off anything it can grab — pots, silverware, shiny objects. Its claws can lift objects up to about 29 kg (64 lb). Sources: Wikipedia, Coconut crab (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coconut_crab); GreaterGood (greatergood.com/blogs/news/cs-robber-crabs-bio).

question: Cracking a coconut can take a coconut crab hours of patient work. But this giant is a hunter and scavenger too, and on Christmas Island it can deal with a live red crab startlingly fast. How fast?
answer: In seconds
choices: In seconds
In a full day
Over a week
Across a month
context: Coconut crabs are broad scavengers and hunters, not just nut-crackers: they eat carrion, and on Christmas Island can tear apart a live red crab in seconds — far faster than the hours a coconut takes. Source: Science News (sciencenews.org/article/coconut-crab-pinches-lion-eats-dumpster-diver).

question: Scientists led by Shin-ichiro Oka clamped a force gauge into the claws of 29 wild coconut crabs to measure their squeeze. The strongest crushed down harder than what?
