question: The platypus and the echidna lay eggs, which almost sounds like they belong with the reptiles. Yet scientists are certain they are true mammals. Once her egg hatches, what does a monotreme mother do that settles the matter?
answer: Feeds her young on milk
choices: Feeds her young on milk
Guards a nest of dozens of eggs
Swallows the eggshell for calcium
Carries the hatchling on her back
context: Making milk is the defining mammal trait. Monotremes have no nipples, so the milk oozes out through patches of skin and the hatchling laps it up. Source: Australian Museum 'What is a monotreme?'; Australian Platypus Conservancy.

question: A female seahorse swims up to a male, but instead of him giving her anything, SHE deposits her eggs into a special pouch on HIS belly. From there the male does something that no male of almost any other animal can do. What happens next?
answer: The male gives birth to the babies
choices: The male gives birth to the babies
The male eats the eggs to hide them
The female returns to guard the pouch
Both parents abandon the eggs at once
context: In seahorses (genus Hippocampus) the female deposits her eggs into a pouch on the male's belly, and he carries them, feeds them through a network of blood vessels, and gives live birth himself. This is real male pregnancy, not a metaphor. Source: University of Sydney 'Pregnant male seahorses support growing babies by forming placenta'; Project Seahorse.  (Legend.)

question: When a male seahorse gives birth, it is no gentle release: his pouch contracts in strong waves for hours, and the tiny young shoot out in bursts. From a single father in one birth, roughly how many babies can emerge?
answer: Up to about 2,000
choices: Up to about 2,000
About 3 or 4
Exactly 12
Around 50
context: A single male seahorse can release up to about 2,000 young at once, shooting them out of his brood pouch in bursts over hours of labour. Source: University of Sydney; Biology Insights 'How Many Babies Do Seahorses Give Birth To?'.  (Legend.)

question: Pythons and boa constrictors look alike and are often confused, yet they bring their young into the world in different ways. A python lays a clutch of eggs and coils around it. When a female boa constrictor's young are ready, what does she do?
answer: Gives birth to live snakelets
choices: Gives birth to live snakelets
Guards a hidden clutch until it hatches
Carries her young inside her throat
Coils around a warmed nest for weeks
context: Boa constrictors are live-bearers. A female carries her young inside for about four to five months, then gives birth to a wriggling litter of ten to sixty-five live snakelets. Source: A-Z Animals 'Snakes That Give Birth to Live Young'; Study.com 'Boa Constrictor vs. Python'.

question: The common European adder, Vipera berus, bears live young instead of laying eggs. That single ability lets it hold a record no other snake on Earth can match. What is that record?
answer: It lives farther north than any other snake
choices: It lives farther north than any other snake
It is the largest snake in Europe
It survives longer without food than any snake
It gives birth to the most young at once
context: By bearing live young and basking to warm them, Vipera berus reaches all the way up to 69 degrees North, inside the Arctic Circle, farther north than any other snake alive. Source: Wiley/Evolution, Lynch 2009; NCBI PMC8415537.

question: A beachcomber finds a tough, leathery pouch washed up on the sand, dark and dried out, with four curly 'horns' curling from its corners. Sharks and skates leave these behind. People who find them gave them a name straight out of a fairy tale. What is a case like this called?
answer: A mermaid's purse
choices: A mermaid's purse
A dragon's tooth
A siren's shell
A kraken's egg
context: Some sharks and skates lay eggs instead of bearing live young, sealing each embryo in a tough leathery case with four curly horns. Beachcombers who find them washed ashore call them a 'mermaid's purse.' Source: UF/IFAS Extension 'Mermaid's Purse'; Wikipedia 'Egg case (Chondrichthyes)'.

question: Inside a sand tiger shark mother, up to 50 tiny embryos begin to grow at once. When the biggest one becomes the first to grow teeth, what does it do to its siblings?
answer: Devours all its smaller siblings
choices: Devours all its smaller siblings
Pushes them out to be born early
Shares its food to keep them alive
Splits off to form a twin
context: In the sand tiger shark (Carcharias taurus), the largest embryo, first to grow teeth, turns cannibal and eats its smaller siblings, so only one pup survives in each of the mother's two wombs, born about 3 feet long. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History 'Sand Tiger Shark'.  (Legend.)

question: A frog stays chained to its pond because its naked jelly eggs dry out in the open. Then the first reptiles evolved an egg sealed inside a shell with four inner membranes, carrying its own supply within. That one invention branched into three great groups of backboned animals alive today. Which three?
answer: Reptiles, birds, and mammals
choices: Reptiles, birds, and mammals
Reptiles, birds, and sharks
Reptiles, mammals, and lungfish
Birds, mammals, and salamanders
context: The amniotic egg, with its shell plus four membranes (amnion, chorion, yolk sac, and allantois), was one of the greatest inventions in the history of life. By carrying its own sealed supply, it gave rise to all reptiles, birds, and mammals, freeing backboned animals from the ponds that trap frogs. Source: Cleveland Museum of Natural History 'The Amniotic Egg'; Lumen Learning 'Amniotes'; Wikipedia 'Amniote'.

question: A 248-million-year-old Chaohusaurus, one of the first fish-shaped ocean reptiles, was found fossilized mid-birth: one pup still sealed in the body cavity, a second half-out through the pelvis, a third already lying beneath the mother. Modern fully-marine reptiles deliver tail-first so the newborn's head stays inside until the last second and cannot drown. But every skull in this fossil pointed the same way, and that single detail told scientists live birth in this line began on land, not at sea. Which way were the pups emerging?
answer: Head-first
choices: Head-first
Tail-first
Belly-up
Curled nose-to-tail
context: Head-first delivery is the land-vertebrate pattern; the tail-first trick evolved later, in fully aquatic ichthyosaurs, to keep a newborn from drowning during a long birth. Because this early Chaohusaurus (specimen AGM I-1) still birthed head-first, Motani and colleagues argued these sea reptiles inherited live birth from land-dwelling ancestors rather than evolving it in the ocean. The fossil captured three offspring at once: one still enclosed in the body cavity, one exiting the pelvic girdle, and one already born and lying beneath the mother; all skulls pointed caudally, toward the tail, the head-first signature. Source: Motani et al. 2014, 'Terrestrial Origin of Viviparity in Mesozoic Marine Reptiles Indicated by Early Triassic Embryonic Fossils,' PLOS ONE 9(2):e88640. https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0088640

question: An American alligator's egg holds no sex chromosomes, so whether it hatches male or female is set weeks later by the temperature of the nest alone. Biologists incubated clutches across a full range of warmth and mapped which eggs became which sex. What did the temperatures actually produce?
answer: Cool and hot nests both gave females; males came only from the middle
choices: Cool and hot nests both gave females; males came only from the middle
Cool and hot nests both gave males; females came only from the middle
Cool nests gave males and hot nests gave females, in a clean split
Cool nests gave females and hot nests gave males, in a clean split
context: This is 'temperature-dependent sex determination,' and the alligator follows the counterintuitive Pattern II: females emerge at both the cool and the hot extremes, while males appear only in a narrow middle band, roughly 90.5 to 92.3 F (32.5 to 33.5 C); below about 88.7 F (31.5 C) or above about 94.1 F (34.5 C), all females. In the wild this maps onto habitat, so warmer nests built up on levees tend to produce males while cooler wet-marsh nests produce females. It is also why a warming climate can skew whole populations toward one sex. Sources: Wikipedia 'American alligator' and 'Temperature-dependent sex determination.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperature-dependent_sex_determination

question: In the murky rivers of Africa swims a blunt-headed catfish with no dorsal fin and three pairs of whiskery barbels. Grab one and it drops you flat — a full-grown adult knocked off their feet with no bite, no sting, no ink cloud in the water. What is this fish's built-in weapon?
answer: A powerful electric shock
choices: A powerful electric shock
A mouthful of venomous fangs
A cloud of blinding ink
A row of poisonous spines
context: The electric catfish (Malapterurus electricus) can deliver a jolt measured up to about 350 volts in a half-meter fish, and higher in big adults — enough to knock a grown person back. It grows up to about 1.2 meters (4 feet) and 20 kg (44 lb). Source: Wikipedia, Electric catfish; Animal Diversity Web, Malapterurus electricus.

question: The electric catfish spends the day hidden away, then emerges into the dark for only about four or five hours after sunset to hunt. Firing bursts of shocks to paralyze its prey in the blackness, how big a meal can this fish take down?
answer: Prey up to half its own size
choices: Prey up to half its own size
Only tiny insects and worms
Prey no bigger than its barbels
Just algae scraped off rocks
context: The catfish hunts in the dark: it has tiny eyes and comes out for about 4 to 5 hours after sunset, firing bursts of shocks to paralyze fish, frogs, and other prey — and it can swallow prey up to half its own size. Source: Animal Diversity Web, Malapterurus electricus.

question: In almost every electric fish, the shock-making organ sits packed in the TAIL. The electric catfish breaks that rule. Where is ITS electric organ?
answer: Spread as a jelly-like sheet under most of its skin
choices: Spread as a jelly-like sheet under most of its skin
Spread as a jelly-like sheet across its blunt head
Spread as a jelly-like sheet along its lower belly
Spread as a jelly-like sheet around its whiskery barbels
context: In most electric fish the electric organ sits in the tail, but the electric catfish's organ wraps almost its whole body, forming a jelly-like layer just under the skin over the trunk — so the shock radiates from all around the fish. Source: Animal Diversity Web, Malapterurus electricus; Wikipedia, Electric catfish.

question: The electric catfish wasn't born with a battery inside it. Its shock-producing organ — a sheet of millions of stacked flat cells called electroplaques — evolved out of an ordinary part of its body. Which part?
answer: Its muscle
choices: Its muscle
Its liver
Its gills
Its skin scales
context: Its electric organ evolved out of ordinary body muscle, turning millions of stacked flat cells called electroplaques into a shock-producing sheet (derived from anterior body musculature). Source: Wikipedia, Electric catfish; en-academic.com electric catfish entry.

question: Egypt's very first pharaoh united the two lands around 3100 BC, and his famous Narmer Palette is carved with his royal name — spelled with just two picture-signs, an animal and a chisel. Which creature is that first sign, making the founder-king literally '_____-Chisel'?
answer: A catfish
choices: A catfish
A crocodile
A heron
A hippopotamus
context: Egypt's first pharaoh, Narmer (around 3100 BC), was named after a catfish: his name is written with two signs, 'n'r' (catfish) and 'mr' (chisel) — so the first king of a united Egypt was literally 'Catfish-Chisel,' and the catfish appears on his famous Narmer Palette. Egyptians recorded the electric catfish this early — carving it into tomb walls at Saqqara, including the Mastaba of Ti, more than 4,000 years ago — long before anyone understood electricity. Source: Wikipedia, Narmer Palette; National Geographic, 'Egypt's first pharaohs loved catfish — and worshipped them.'  (Legend.)

question: The electric catfish's shock organ is built from millions of separate shock-cells, yet they all fire in the same instant to hit prey with one clean jolt. What keeps that swarm of cells perfectly in step?
answer: A single giant nerve cell commands them all
choices: A single giant nerve cell commands them all
A tiny pacemaker crystal in its skull
A ring of muscle that squeezes them together
A chemical signal released into its blood
context: All those millions of shock-cells are wired to fire together by a single giant nerve cell — one neuron in the spinal cord commands the whole electric organ, which is why scientists prize this fish for studying nerves. Source: Animal Diversity Web, Malapterurus electricus; Springer, electromotor system of Malapterurus electricus.

question: A long, snake-shaped fish glides through the muddy rivers of South America. It is famous for the jolt it delivers, and its very name calls it a kind of sea creature it isn't even related to. So what IS the electric eel, really?
answer: A knifefish
choices: A knifefish
A true eel
A catfish
A lamprey
context: Despite its name, the electric eel is not a true eel at all. It belongs to the order Gymnotiformes, the knifefishes, and is more closely related to the banded knifefish than to the marine eels (order Anguilliformes) it superficially resembles. Source: Wikipedia, Electric eel (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_eel).

question: An electric eel spends its life underwater, yet a keeper who blocked one from reaching the top of the tank could actually kill it. Every couple of minutes the eel does something no goldfish ever needs to do. What must it do to stay alive?
answer: Surface to gulp air
choices: Surface to gulp air
Rest on the bottom
Shed its slime coat
Empty its stomach
context: The electric eel is an obligate air-breather: it must rise to the surface and gulp air through its mouth roughly every two minutes, and can drown if kept from reaching the top. Source: Wikipedia, Electric eel (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_eel).

question: An electric eel keeps its heart, stomach, and other vital organs crammed into the front fifth of its body, sealed away from the danger behind them. What fills the entire long tail-end - about 80% of the eel?
answer: Its electric organs
choices: Its electric organs
A long, coiled gut
Fat for buoyancy
Egg sacs
context: The electric organs make up about 80% of the electric eel's long body. Its vital organs are packed into just the front ~20% and sequestered from the electricity the animal generates in the rest of its length. Source: Wikipedia, Electric eel (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_eel).

question: An electric eel's shock doesn't come from one big generator. Inside its body sit about 6,000 tiny cells called electrocytes running down its length, and the eel can fire them all at once for one huge jolt. Which everyday power source works on the very same trick the eel uses to build its voltage?
answer: Batteries stacked in a flashlight
choices: Batteries stacked in a flashlight
A single big capacitor
The coils in an electromagnet
A spinning generator
context: An electric eel's jolt comes from roughly 6,000 electrocytes wired end-to-end in series, exactly like the batteries stacked in a flashlight, so their individually tiny voltages add up into one enormous discharge. Source: Wikipedia, Electric eel; Science ABC (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_eel).

question: The electric eel hunts at night in water so dark and muddy that its eyes are almost useless, yet it still homes in on fish hidden in the murk. Besides the high-voltage blast it saves for the kill, it runs a second, gentler electric setting all the time. How does the eel find its way and its prey in the blackness?
answer: It reads faint electric fields it makes
choices: It reads faint electric fields it makes
It follows scent trails in the water
It listens for the prey's heartbeat
It feels for warmth given off by prey
context: The electric eel has two electrical modes from one organ system: a weak, constant low-voltage pulse from Sachs' organ that works like radar (electrolocation), letting it navigate murky water and detect hidden prey, plus a separate high-voltage blast to stun. Source: Catania, The Astonishing Behavior of Electric Eels (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6646469/).

question: Kenneth Catania at Vanderbilt was lifting electric eels with a metal-rimmed net when a cornered eel did something no textbook had described. Instead of shocking down into the water, it rose up and pressed its chin against the metal. What was the eel doing?
answer: Leaping out to shock the threat directly
choices: Leaping out to shock the threat directly
Trying to climb over the rim
Biting to test the net
Playing dead against the metal
context: Kenneth Catania discovered by accident that a cornered electric eel will leap out of the water and press its chin against a threat to deliver its shock through the air. Source: Vanderbilt News, Electric eels make leaping attacks (https://news.vanderbilt.edu/2016/06/06/electric-eels-make-leaping-attacks/).  (Legend.)

question: When a cornered electric eel rises out of the water and presses its chin against an attacker, it is climbing higher and higher up the target as it goes. Kenneth Catania measured the jolt at each height. What happens to the shock the higher the eel climbs?
answer: It grows stronger
choices: It grows stronger
It stays the same
It briefly cuts out
It scatters harmlessly
context: Underwater the eel's current dissipates in every direction, but when it rises out of the water the circuit is forced through the target and back. The higher the electric eel climbs, the greater the voltage and current delivered. Source: Vanderbilt News; AIP Inside Science (https://news.vanderbilt.edu/2016/06/06/electric-eels-make-leaping-attacks/).  (Legend.)

question: An electric eel cannot see the fish frozen in the mud in front of it. So it fires a rapid doublet of two high-voltage pulses, and instantly the hidden prey twitches and gives itself away. Kenneth Catania showed the pulses do this by remotely triggering something inside the prey. What do they trigger?
answer: The prey's own muscles
choices: The prey's own muscles
The prey's sense of smell
A rush of prey blood
The prey's swim bladder
context: To find prey it cannot see, an electric eel fires two high-voltage pulses about 2 milliseconds apart. This remotely fires the hidden prey's own muscles, making it twitch and reveal its location. Catania described it as the eel asking 'are you alive?' and the prey being unable not to answer. Source: Catania (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6646469/).  (Legend.)

question: In 1800 Alexander von Humboldt described electric eels leaping to attack a herd of about 30 horses driven into a pool, with two horses stunned and drowned. For roughly 200 years scientists dismissed the story. What finally happened to Humboldt's tale?
answer: Catania's leaping study proved it true
choices: Catania's leaping study proved it true
New records proved it exaggerated
It was traced to a mistranslation
No eel was ever found there again
context: Humboldt's account of eels battling horses was mocked as 'tommyrot' for two centuries, until Kenneth Catania's discovery that electric eels leap to shock threats above the water showed the story was plausible after all. Source: PNAS, Leaping eels electrify threats (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1604009113).  (Legend.)

question: For 250 years the electric eel was thought to be a single species. In 2019 C. David de Santana's team split it into three, and one newcomer, Electrophorus voltai, set a record for every living thing on Earth. What did it register?
answer: The highest voltage of any animal
choices: The highest voltage of any animal
The longest body of any fish
The oldest known lifespan
The deepest freshwater range
context: In 2019 de Santana's team split the electric eel into three species. One of them, Electrophorus voltai, discharged 860 volts, the highest voltage ever measured from any living animal. Its record jolt is thought to be an adaptation to the poorly conducting clear highland water it lives in. Source: Cornell Chronicle; Nature Communications 2019 (https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2019/09/scientists-shocked-discover-two-new-species-electric-eel).  (Legend.)

question: A big catfish thrashes too hard for the electric eel to pin down with a single blast. So the eel bends its whole body into a tight horseshoe, folding head toward tail with the struggling fish trapped in the curve between them. Kenneth Catania measured what this pose does to the jolt. Why does curling up help?
answer: It brings the eel's two poles close, doubling the shock
choices: It brings the eel's two poles close, doubling the shock
It shields the eel's soft belly from the prey's spines
It lets the eel breathe air while its head stays down
It hides the eel's shape from other hunting eels
context: The positive pole of the eel's electric field sits in its head and the negative pole in its tail. By curling into a horseshoe, the eel sandwiches struggling prey between the two poles, and Catania's instrumented dead-fish 'chew toy' recorded that this more than DOUBLES the voltage driven into the victim. The doubled field fires the prey's muscles in repeated ~100 Hz volleys until they seize up in total fatigue and paralysis - Catania likened the effect to dosing the prey with the paralytic drug curare. This is a second body maneuver, distinct from the leap-and-chin-press. Source: news.vanderbilt.edu/2015/10/28 (Catania, Current Biology 2015); coverage in Scientific American and Christian Science Monitor.  (Legend.)

question: Growing an electric organ is a fantastically complex feat, yet electric fishes around the world have built one from ordinary muscle at least six separate times. Darwin himself puzzled over how unrelated animals could independently assemble the very same intricate organ. When scientists finally sequenced the electric eel's genome to find out, what did they discover the six lineages had done?
answer: Reused nearly the same set of genes each separate time
choices: Reused nearly the same set of genes each separate time
Each invented a completely different genetic toolkit
Copied the working genes from the fish they hunted
Inherited the organ from one shared ancient ancestor
context: The myogenic electric organ has evolved independently at least six times across unrelated fish lineages, a puzzle of the kind Darwin flagged: how could nature build the same complex organ over and over in animals that never shared it? A 2014 study that sequenced the electric eel genome (Gallant, Zakon, Sussman et al.) found the answer written in the genes - every lineage reached for essentially the SAME 'genetic toolbox,' recruiting the same genes and developmental pathways to convert plain muscle into an electric organ each time. It is convergent evolution captured at the level of the DNA. Source: science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1254432 (Gallant et al. 2014, Science); phys.org/news/2014-06-truth-electric-fish.html.  (Legend.)

question: A shark glides over a flat sandy seabed where a flounder lies completely buried — invisible, motionless, giving off no smell the shark can follow. Yet the shark suddenly wheels and digs the fish straight out. What did it home in on?
answer: The faint electricity leaking from the flounder's beating heart and twitching muscles
choices: The faint electricity leaking from the flounder's beating heart and twitching muscles
The warmth of the flounder's body radiating up through the sand
A trail of scent molecules drifting from the buried fish
The tiny grains of sand shifting as the fish breathed
context: Every heartbeat and muscle twitch of a living animal leaks a faint electric field into the seawater around it. Sharks and rays read that field directly, so a fish that hides from eyes, nose, and ears still 'glows' electrically. Adrianus Kalmijn proved this by burying battery-powered electrodes in sand: sharks dug up the wires and ignored a dead fish nearby, homing on the electric field, not sight or smell. LEGEND. Source: Kalmijn, 'The Discovery of the Shark's Electric Sense', American Scientist.

question: High-speed cameras caught a shark doing something that looks reckless in the very last split-second before its jaws close on a thrashing meal. What does it do?
answer: It snaps its eyes shut and finishes the strike blind
choices: It snaps its eyes shut and finishes the strike blind
It rolls completely upside down
It stops swimming and drifts in
It flares its gills wide open
context: In the final second before biting, a shark often closes its eyes to protect them from a thrashing meal — a protective reflex filmed by high-speed cameras. With its vision shut off, it steers the last strike purely by the electric sense of its ampullae. LEGEND. Source: americanscientist.org, 'The Discovery of the Shark's Electric Sense'.

question: A platypus dives to hunt on a dark riverbed and does something startling: it seals its eyes, its ears, AND its nostrils tightly shut for the whole dive. With every one of those senses switched off, what does it hunt with instead?
answer: Roughly 40,000 electroreceptors spread across its rubbery bill
choices: Roughly 40,000 electroreceptors spread across its rubbery bill
A long sticky tongue that tastes prey in the water
Whiskers that feel currents stirred by moving prey
Echoing clicks it bounces off the riverbed
context: The platypus hunts underwater completely 'blind' — eyes, ears, and nostrils all sealed shut — steering entirely by about 40,000 electroreceptors scattered over its rubbery bill that pick up the electric muscle-signals of hidden prey. Source: Pettigrew, 'Electroreception in monotremes', Journal of Experimental Biology 202:1447 (1999); Australian Platypus Conservancy.  (Legend.)

question: A hunting platypus carries two separate senses on its bill: one for electric fields, one — the 'push-rod' sensors — for pressure. A single shrimp tail-flick trips both, and from that one flick, in total darkness, the platypus pins down exactly how far off the shrimp is. How do two senses give it a distance?
answer: The electric signal outruns the slower pressure wave, and the platypus times the gap between them
choices: The electric signal outruns the slower pressure wave, and the platypus times the gap between them
A close shrimp trips both senses, while a distant one trips only the electric sensors
The electric signal comes in stronger for close prey and weaker for far prey
The push-rod sensors near the tip fire for close prey, those near the base for far prey
context: Electricity races through water faster than a pressure wave travels. So a shrimp's tail-flick reaches the platypus's electric sensors a split-second before its pressure sensors. The platypus reads that tiny time gap to judge distance — triangulating a shrimp in total darkness. LEGEND. Source: Pettigrew et al. 1998; Pettigrew 1999, Journal of Experimental Biology.

question: The elephantnose and the knifefish hunt in muddy, pitch-dark river water where a shark's trick of feeling for the electricity that prey leak would turn up almost nothing worth eating. What do these fish do instead to find a meal they cannot see?
answer: They make their own weak electric field and feel how nearby objects distort it
choices: They make their own weak electric field and feel how nearby objects distort it
They store up a charge and stun small prey with a jolt
They light up glowing patches to lure prey close in the dark
They stir up the mud and snap at whatever swims out
context: 'Weakly electric' fish generate their own weak electric field with an electric organ in the tail, then feel how nearby objects bend that field — a living electric-field radar — to navigate and hunt where there is nothing to see. Source: Wikipedia, Peters's elephantnose fish; Electric organ (anatomy); New England Aquarium.

question: Two knifefish swim close and their self-made electric fields happen to land at nearly the same frequency, so neither fish can read its own signal cleanly anymore. Within milliseconds, both are sensing sharply again. What did they do?
answer: Each nudged its own discharge frequency away from the other's
choices: Each nudged its own discharge frequency away from the other's
Each fired one strong pulse to swamp the other's signal
One fish went silent and coasted until the other swam off
Both matched to one shared frequency and pulsed in unison
context: When two knifefish overlap at nearly the same frequency, their fields interfere. Each fish then shifts its own discharge frequency away from the other — a reflex scientists named the 'jamming avoidance response' — so each keeps its private radar channel clear. Source: Neuroethology: Jamming Avoidance Response in Electric Fish, nelson.beckman.illinois.edu.

question: In 2013 Clarke and colleagues found the first electric sense ever shown in an insect: a bumblebee, they reported, can pick up the faint static charge a flower carries. Through what part of its body does the bee detect that charge?
answer: Its body hairs, which bend in the presence of the charge
choices: Its body hairs, which bend in the presence of the charge
Its antennae, which taste the charge chemically
Its compound eyes, which see the charge as a glow
Its wings, which vibrate faster near a charge
context: Clarke, Whitney, Sutton and Robert reported in Science (2013) that bumblebees sense the weak static electric charge a flower carries — the first electroreception ever shown in an insect — detected through their body hairs, which bend in the charge's presence. LEGEND. Source: Clarke et al., 'Detection and Learning of Floral Electric Fields by Bumblebees', Science (Apr 5, 2013).

question: A shark's ampullae are plumbed with a clear jelly that carries the electric signal inward. When physicists finally measured how well that jelly moves electric charge, they got a result no one expected from ordinary animal goo. What was so startling about it?
answer: It conducts protons better than almost any material on Earth, rivaling engineered fuel-cell polymer
choices: It conducts protons better than almost any material on Earth, rivaling engineered fuel-cell polymer
It conducts electrons swiftly yet blocks protons entirely, unlike any known biological tissue
It insulates so completely that the signal must instead creep along the walls of the pore
It shuttles charge only in one direction, acting like a living diode that bars any reverse flow
context: The jelly filling the ampullae of Lorenzini is about 97% water, yet Josberger et al. (2016) measured its proton conductivity at only ~40 times below Nafion, the best synthetic proton-conducting polymer humans have engineered for fuel cells - making it the most proton-conductive biological material ever found. The conduction comes from a polyglycan, keratan sulfate, donating protons into the watery gel. So the shark's electric antenna is wired with a natural super-conductor of protons. Source: Josberger, Hassanzadeh, Deng, Sohn, Rego, Amemiya & Rolandi (2016), 'Proton conductivity in ampullae of Lorenzini jelly', Science Advances 2:e1600112, https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.1600112 ; UW News https://www.washington.edu/news/2016/05/13/proton-conducting-material-found-in-jelly-that-fills-organs-of-sharks-skates-and-rays/

question: A shark and a skate build their electric sense from the very same starter cell, which fires using one shared calcium channel. Yet a shark uses its sense to hunt prey, while a skate uses its to find a mate. What single difference splits one sense into two?
answer: A different second channel in each: one drives sharp repeated spikes, the other soft graded ripples
choices: A different second channel in each: one drives sharp repeated spikes, the other soft graded ripples
A different body of water in each: one hunts in salt, the other only ever in fresh
A different number of pores in each: one carries thousands, the other barely a dozen
A different nerve in each: one wires straight to the jaw, the other to the swimming muscles
context: Bellono, Leitch & Julius (2018) found that shark and skate electrosensory cells both start a signal with the same low-threshold voltage-gated calcium channel, CaV1.3 - but they amplify it differently. Sharks add voltage-gated potassium channels that let the cell fire big, repetitive voltage spikes, dumping neurotransmitter at near-maximum: perfect for catching a prey twitch. Skates instead use a calcium-activated potassium channel that produces small, finely graded oscillations, better for reading the steady field of another skate. Same starter channel, a different second 'amplifier' channel - predator-tuning versus social-tuning. Source: Bellono, Leitch & Julius (2018), 'Molecular tuning of electroreception in sharks and skates', Nature 558:122-126, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-018-0160-9 ; Harvard MCB summary https://www.mcb.harvard.edu/department/news/investigating-sharks-skates-sense-electric-fields/

question: One bull of this species, shot in Angola, stood about 13 feet at the shoulder and weighed over 10 tonnes. Which living land animal is the largest of all?
answer: The African elephant
choices: The African elephant
The white rhinoceros
The hippopotamus
The giraffe
context: A record African bush elephant bull from Angola stood roughly 13 feet at the shoulder and weighed an estimated 10 or more tonnes; the mounted specimen, nicknamed 'Henry,' still stands in the Smithsonian. It is the largest land animal alive today. Source: Guinness World Records, 'Largest land mammal'; IFLScience, 'Henry the Fenykovi Elephant.'

question: On a blistering afternoon, when just fanning its ears no longer keeps it cool, an elephant reaches its trunk to the riverbank and coats its skin and the backs of its ears with something. What does it plaster on to beat the heat and block the sun?
answer: Sticky mud
choices: Sticky mud
Dry leaves
Loose feathers
Tree bark
context: When ear-flapping isn't enough, an elephant sprays water, flings wet river-sand, or plasters sticky mud onto its skin and the backs of its ears to cool down and shield itself from the sun. Source: AskNature, 'Large Ears Aid Cooling'; Shenton Safaris, 'Cooling down.'

question: An elephant can uproot a whole tree with its trunk, then coil that same trunk gently around one blade of grass. What lets a single limb do both jobs?
answer: It contains no bone at all, only muscle
choices: It contains no bone at all, only muscle
It is jointed like a finger
It is filled with air sacs
It has a flexible cartilage rod inside
context: An elephant's trunk is a 'muscular hydrostat' like your tongue or an octopus arm, containing no bone at all, only muscle, long counted at around 40,000 muscle units. Source: Cleveland Zoological Society, 'Truth or Tail: 40,000 muscles.'

question: On a hot day an elephant's huge flat ears fan back and forth almost nonstop, even when the rest of the animal stands still. Beyond stirring a breeze, what is all that flapping actually accomplishing?
answer: Cooling the blood before it returns to the body
choices: Cooling the blood before it returns to the body
Sensing distant thunder
Storing water for later
Warning rivals with the flapping sound
context: The ears work as living radiators: blood vessels near the surface let flapping fan the blood cool. The returning blood can be 3 to 5 degrees C cooler, and an elephant can cool its whole blood supply this way in about 20 minutes. Source: Kariega Game Reserve; AskNature, 'Large Ears Aid Cooling.'

question: A guide points at a distant elephant and says she can tell it is African, not Asian, just from the very end of its trunk. What is she looking at?
answer: The tip has two finger-like lips, not one
choices: The tip has two finger-like lips, not one
The tip is bright pink, not gray
The tip splits into three prongs
The tip has a small tuft of hair
context: An African elephant's trunk ends in TWO finger-like tips, or lips; an Asian elephant's ends in only ONE, a quick field way to tell the two species apart. Source: A-Z Animals, 'Exploring the Fascinating World of Elephant Trunks.'

question: An elephant's tusks keep growing about 6 to 7 inches every year for the animal's entire life, and the longest ever recorded topped 11 feet. What kind of body part is a tusk, really?
answer: An overgrown incisor tooth
choices: An overgrown incisor tooth
A curved horn of keratin
An extended jawbone
A hardened nasal bone
context: Tusks are overgrown incisor teeth that never stop growing, adding roughly 6 to 7 inches a year; the longest on record exceeded 11 feet. Source: Britannica, 'Tusk (anatomy)'; Inverdoorn, 'Elephant Tusks: 10 Facts.'

question: With no bone and no joints anywhere inside it, an elephant's trunk can shove over a small tree, then turn around and do something so delicate it stuns the keepers watching. What is that delicate feat?
answer: Picking up a single blade of grass
choices: Picking up a single blade of grass
Untying a knotted length of rope
Threading a strap through a buckle
Balancing a pebble on its very tip
context: With no bone or joints, the same trunk that uproots a tree can curl around a single blade of grass; the tip's hair-thin muscle bundles give it that fingertip precision. Source: Science/AAAS, 'Elephant trunk's stunning microscopic musculature may explain its dexterity.'

question: When a drought strikes and the nearest water is gone, an elephant family survives or starves on one thing: whether their leader remembers where water still flows, from a route walked only once. Who leads the herd?
answer: The oldest female, the matriarch
choices: The oldest female, the matriarch
The largest tusked bull
A pair of scout males
The youngest breeding female
context: Herds are led by a matriarch, the oldest female, whose memory of distant water can save the family. In Amboseli's severe 2009 drought, families led by older matriarchs lost far fewer calves than those with younger leaders. Source: Live Science, 'In Elephant Society, Matriarchs Lead'; Amboseli Trust for Elephants.

question: Elephants do not sip through the trunk like a straw. They pull several liters of water up inside it, then curl it into the mouth and pour. When researchers measured that intake, how fast was the water rushing up the trunk?
answer: Up to about 330 miles per hour
choices: Up to about 330 miles per hour
About 15 miles per hour
About 60 miles per hour
About 900 miles per hour
context: A study clocked the suction inside the trunk at up to 330 miles per hour, far faster than anyone expected for an animal drinking. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Elephant Trunks Can Suck Water at 330 Miles Per Hour.'

question: In 1984 Katy Payne stood in a zoo elephant house and felt a strange throbbing in the air, though she heard nothing. She had stumbled onto how elephants talk to one another across miles. What was carrying their message?
answer: Infrasound rumbles too low for human ears
choices: Infrasound rumbles too low for human ears
Ultrasonic squeaks too high to hear
Puffs of scent on the wind
Flashes of light from their eyes
context: Elephants communicate in infrasound, rumbles around 14 to 35 Hz, below the roughly 20 Hz floor of human hearing. Katy Payne discovered it in 1984 when she felt the throbbing in the air; the calls carry for miles. Source: academic.oup.com/BioScience, 'A throbbing in the air'; Psychology Today.

question: When an elephant herd comes upon the body of a dead elephant, they do something field researchers have watched them repeat again and again. What do they do at the body?
answer: Gather quietly and touch it with their trunks
choices: Gather quietly and touch it with their trunks
Trumpet loudly and charge past it
Bury it under piles of branches
Ignore it and move on at once
context: Elephants behave as if they mourn: they gather quietly, touch the body with their trunks, and return to the bones for years. Field tests found they lingered far longer over elephant skulls and ivory than over other species' bones, even the bones of strangers. This is described as observed behavior, not proven human-style grief. Source: Londolozi Blog; Biology Letters field study, summarized at Forbes.  (Legend.)

question: Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell noticed elephants at Mushara sometimes freeze and go still as statues even when the source is far off. Her buried-speaker experiments at the waterhole revealed the surprising body part they were 'listening' with. What was it?
answer: Their feet, sensing vibrations in the ground
choices: Their feet, sensing vibrations in the ground
Their trunk tip, feeling shifts in air pressure
Their broad ears, catching faint distant echoes
Their long tusks, picking up tremors in the earth
context: Elephant rumbles also travel through the ground as seismic waves, and elephants can 'listen' with their feet. O'Connell-Rodwell's buried-speaker experiments at Mushara showed an underground alarm call made a herd close ranks and freeze. Source: Science/AAAS, 'Talking Through the Ground'; KQED, 'How Elephants Listen With Their Feet.'  (Legend.)

question: Elephants have huge bodies and trillions of cells, yet almost never get cancer. Vincent Lynch found the trick: a broken, long-dead gene their ancestors reactivated, which now rushes into a failing cell and forces it to self-destruct. What is this revived gene called?
answer: A reawakened "zombie" gene, LIF6
choices: A reawakened "zombie" gene, LIF6
An always-active repair enzyme
A newly evolved stress hormone
A gene borrowed from a virus
context: The answer is Peto's Paradox: bigger, longer-lived bodies have more cells and more chances for cancer, yet elephants get it less than humans. LIF6 was a dead pseudogene, a broken copy of the leukemia inhibitory factor gene, that the elephant lineage switched back on. When DNA is damaged, the tumor-suppressor TP53 flips LIF6 on; the LIF6 protein travels to the cell's mitochondria and triggers apoptosis, killing the damaged cell before it can become a tumor. Strikingly, this TP53-to-LIF6 switch evolved at the very same time elephant ancestors grew to giant size, so the anti-cancer gene came online as they got big. (Elephants also carry about 20 copies of TP53, versus one in humans.) Source: Lynch et al., Cell Reports 2018, PubMed 30110634; 'Solving Peto's Paradox,' PMC6369797.

question: An elephant seems to stand on five toes, but John Hutchinson's CT scans found a sixth prop hidden in the fatty heel pad, so long overlooked that museum staff used to slice it off and throw it away. What is that hidden sixth structure?
answer: A giant sesamoid bone, a false sixth toe
choices: A giant sesamoid bone, a false sixth toe
A true toe built for bearing weight
A wedge of stiffened heel cartilage
A fused knot of foot tendons
context: It is a giant sesamoid bone, called a prepollex in the front foot and a prehallux in the hind, that projects downward like a stiletto heel, spearing the fat pad and propping the foot up so the elephant effectively walks on tiptoe. It was missed for centuries because it starts as cartilage and only turns to bone late in adult life, and preparators routinely cut it off. Hutchinson's team at the Royal Veterinary College confirmed it with CT scanning; the structure appears to have evolved as early elephants grew larger, roughly 40 million years ago. Source: Hutchinson et al., Science 2011, 'From Flat Foot to Fat Foot' (doi:10.1126/science.1211437); phys.org 2011-12.

question: In pitch-black muddy African rivers where eyes are almost useless, the elephantnose fish still swims straight to buried prey and dodges obstacles. It generates a weak field around its whole body and 'sees' by feeling how nearby objects bend that field. What kind of field is it?
answer: An electric field
choices: An electric field
A magnetic field
A sound field
A heat field
context: This sense is called active electrolocation: an organ near the fish's tail puts out a weak electric field, and receptors all over the skin feel how objects distort it, letting the fish 'see' shape and distance in total darkness. Source: ScienceDaily / University of Bonn, von der Emde group (2016), https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/06/160624100245.htm

question: The elephantnose fish looks like it has a little trunk drooping from its face, which earned it its name. But that dangling 'trunk' is not a nose at all. What is it really?
answer: A mobile chin that sweeps the riverbed
choices: A mobile chin that sweeps the riverbed
An extra-long upper lip
A fleshy antenna on its forehead
A breathing tube to the surface
context: The 'trunk' is a movable chin extension called the schnauzenorgan. The fish sweeps it over the mud like a metal detector, hunting for buried insect larvae by feel. Source: Nature News, 'Seeing through the chin' (2007), quoting Gerhard von der Emde, https://www.nature.com/news/2007/070820/full/news070820-10.html

question: A juicy insect larva lies buried in the mud, invisible, right beside a pebble of the very same size and shape. Without ever seeing either one, the elephantnose fish tells the living larva from the dead stone. What difference does it feel between them?
answer: The larva stores charge like a tiny capacitor
choices: The larva stores charge like a tiny capacitor
The larva sits a little warmer than the stone
The larva leaks a faint smell the stone lacks
The larva hums at a pitch the stone cannot
context: Living tissue — animals, plants, larvae — stores electric charge like a tiny capacitor, while stones and mud only resist current. The fish feels that difference, so it knows a buried larva is alive without seeing it. Source: von der Emde, 'Active electrolocation of objects in weakly electric fish,' J. Experimental Biology 202:1205 (1999), https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/202/10/1205/

question: The elephantnose fish carries one of the biggest brains relative to its body of any fish, and that brain is astonishingly power-hungry — it burns a far larger share of the animal's oxygen than any other backboned animal ever measured, human brains included. About what share of its oxygen does its brain consume?
answer: Around 60 percent
choices: Around 60 percent
Around 5 percent
Around 20 percent
Around 95 percent
context: Its brain burns roughly 60% of the fish's oxygen — about three times the share of any other vertebrate measured, needed to process the flood of electrical information from its whole-body electric sense. Source: Nilsson, 'Brain and body oxygen requirements of Gnathonemus petersii,' J. Experimental Biology 199:603 (1996), https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9318319/  (Legend.)

question: When several elephantnose fish gather, each one can suddenly sense objects far beyond its own short sensing range — as if its reach tripled. How does simply being in a group extend one fish's range this way?
answer: It reads its neighbors' pulses too
choices: It reads its neighbors' pulses too
It swims in tight, fast circles to scan more water
It stirs up mud to feel the current
Its own pulses grow stronger near other fish
context: Each fish can read the pulses its neighbors emit, so a group acts like a shared radar network — tripling how far each fish can effectively sense. Researcher Nathaniel Sawtell says these electric images are 'beamed to nearby fish at the speed of light.' Source: Phys.org / Columbia (2024), Sawtell & Pedraja on collective sensing, https://phys.org/news/2024-03-scientists-uncover-evidence-electric-elephantnose.amp

question: Waddling across the Antarctic sea ice stands the largest and tallest penguin alive, about 4 feet tall and up to 100 pounds. Which one?
answer: The emperor penguin
choices: The emperor penguin
The gentoo penguin
The Adelie penguin
The little blue penguin
context: The emperor penguin stands roughly 1.15 m (about 4 feet) and weighs up to about 45 kg (100 lb) — bigger than any other living penguin. Source: Britannica, https://www.britannica.com/animal/emperor-penguin

question: The emperor penguin is a bird, but it will never fly a single inch. Where on Earth does this flightless bird live?
answer: Only in Antarctica
choices: Only in Antarctica
Only in the Arctic
Across northern Canada
On tropical island beaches
context: Emperor penguins are flightless birds found only in Antarctica, and remarkably they breed during the coldest, darkest months of the Antarctic winter — when no other bird raises its young. Source: British Antarctic Survey, https://www.bas.ac.uk/about/antarctica/wildlife/penguins/emperor-penguin/

question: A mother emperor penguin lays her single egg, then leaves for weeks of feeding at sea. She hands the egg to the father — who keeps it off the killing ice by holding it exactly where?
answer: Balanced on the tops of his feet
choices: Balanced on the tops of his feet
Cradled inside his folded wings
Buried in a scrape of packed snow
Carried in his long beak
context: The father balances the egg on the tops of his feet and covers it with a warm fold of belly skin called the brood pouch. Source: British Antarctic Survey, https://www.bas.ac.uk/about/antarctica/wildlife/penguins/emperor-penguin/

question: With the mother gone to sea, the father emperor penguin stands over his egg through the polar winter — and for those roughly 65 to 75 days of incubation, how much does he eat?
answer: Nothing at all
choices: Nothing at all
A few small fish a week
Krill scooped from the snow
Whatever the mother brings back
context: The male incubates the egg on his feet for about 65 to 75 days without eating anything at all, surviving entirely on stored fat through the polar winter. Considered a legendary feat of endurance. Source: British Antarctic Survey, https://www.bas.ac.uk/about/antarctica/wildlife/penguins/emperor-penguin/

question: Across the whole breeding cycle the father emperor penguin starts the winter near 38 kg. By the time the mother returns, roughly what has happened to his body?
answer: He has lost about 20 kg, dropping to around 18 kg
choices: He has lost about 20 kg, dropping to around 18 kg
He has gained weight from eating snow
He stays almost exactly the same weight
He roughly doubles in size to insulate
context: Across the whole breeding cycle the fasting father goes roughly 120 days without food and can lose about 20 kg, dropping from around 38 kg down to 18 kg. A legendary feat of endurance. Source: Wikipedia, Emperor penguin, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_penguin

question: Thousands of father emperor penguins survive the -40 winter pressed shoulder to shoulder in one packed mass. They don't just stand still — what do the birds constantly do?
answer: Shuffle in slow waves so everyone rotates through the middle
choices: Shuffle in slow waves so everyone rotates through the middle
Huddle tighter as the wind rises
Shrink the pack into a smaller circle
Lean inward together against the wind
context: The fathers pack into a huddle of over 4,000 males; the birds constantly shuffle in slow waves every 30 to 60 seconds so no one is stuck on the freezing edge for long. Source: Audubon (reporting Zitterbart et al., PLoS ONE), https://www.audubon.org/news/not-so-black-and-white-research-reveals-intricacies-penguin-huddles  (Legend.)

question: Outside the emperor penguin huddle the Antarctic air sits near -40 degrees C. Deep inside the packed mass of bodies, researchers recorded temperatures climbing all the way up to what?
answer: About 37.5 degrees C, near human body heat
choices: About 37.5 degrees C, near human body heat
Just above freezing, around 2 degrees C
About -10 degrees C, only a little warmer
Around 15 degrees C, like a cool room
context: Inside the packed huddle it gets so warm that recorded temperatures reach up to about 37.5 degrees C — near human body heat — even while the outside air is around -40 degrees C. Source: Audubon (Zitterbart huddle research), https://www.audubon.org/news/not-so-black-and-white-research-reveals-intricacies-penguin-huddles  (Legend.)

question: An emperor penguin egg is deadly fragile in the Antarctic cold — touch the ice and it can freeze in seconds. Sometimes a chick hatches before the mother is back with food, yet the starving father still manages to feed it for a few days. How?
answer: With 'crop milk' produced in his throat
choices: With 'crop milk' produced in his throat
With regurgitated fish from his stomach
With fat scraped from his own belly
With melted snow warmed in his beak
context: If the chick hatches before the mother returns, the father feeds it 'crop milk' — a protein-rich, curd-like substance made in his throat — but he can only produce it for about 3 to 7 days. Source: Penguins International, https://www.penguinsinternational.org/how-do-penguins-feed-their-chicks/  (Legend.)

question: Emperor penguins dive deeper than any other bird on Earth. Out of more than 137,000 recorded dives, only 12 ever passed 500 m deep — and researchers found something startling about those 12. What was it?
answer: Every one was made by the same single penguin
choices: Every one was made by the same single penguin
They all happened during the same storm
They were all made by chicks, not adults
None of them caught any prey
context: The deepest reliably measured dive was 564 m (1,850 ft), and out of over 137,000 recorded dives, all 12 that passed 500 m were made by the same single penguin. Considered a legendary record. Source: Guinness World Records, https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/deepest-dive-by-a-bird

question: On its deepest dives an emperor penguin stays under so long that it must ration every scrap of oxygen. To do it, the bird throttles the one organ that spends the most. During an 18-minute dive, researchers clocked its heart slowing to a low of what?
answer: Just 3 beats per minute, one beat every 15 seconds
choices: Just 3 beats per minute, one beat every 15 seconds
Around 6 beats per minute, one beat every 10 seconds
About 14 beats per minute, one beat every 4 seconds
Roughly 20 beats per minute, one beat every 3 seconds
context: A resting emperor penguin's heart runs near 73 bpm and climbs to about 175 bpm just before a dive. But once a dive passes the roughly 5.6-minute aerobic limit, the heart drops into extreme bradycardia, averaging a minimum near 14 bpm. In one 18-minute dive it fell to just 3 bpm and held near 6 bpm for over 5 minutes; about 10% of long dives dropped to 5 bpm or lower. Slowing the heart to near-stopped meters out the bird's limited oxygen so it lasts the whole dive. Source: Meir, Stockard, Williams, Ponganis & Kooyman (2008), 'Heart rate regulation and extreme bradycardia in diving emperor penguins,' Journal of Experimental Biology 211(8):1169 -- https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/211/8/1169/18165/

question: A modern emperor penguin stands about 1.2 m and is the biggest penguin alive today. But dig into the 34-million-year-old rock of Seymour Island off Antarctica and you meet Palaeeudyptes klekowskii, whose bones tell you it was what?
answer: A giant penguin near 2 m tall and about 115 kg
choices: A giant penguin near 2 m tall and about 115 kg
A flying seabird the size of a modern albatross
A tiny penguin no larger than a pigeon
A seal-like mammal only distantly related to birds
context: Palaeeudyptes klekowskii -- the 'Mega Penguin' -- came from the Late Eocene La Meseta Formation on Seymour Island, Antarctica, dated to about 34-37 million years ago. A 2014 study by Carolina Acosta Hospitaleche, working from the most complete Eocene penguin skeleton yet found, estimated it stood up to 2 metres (6.6 ft) and weighed as much as 115 kg -- nearly twice a modern emperor's mass and the tallest, heaviest penguin then known to science. Giant penguins once ruled the same Antarctic coasts where emperors breed today. Source: Acosta Hospitaleche (2014), Geobios 47(3), on Palaeeudyptes klekowskii; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palaeeudyptes_klekowskii

question: A wandering albatross skims the Southern Ocean on the widest wings of any bird alive today. Held straight out, tip to tip, how far do they stretch?
answer: About 3.5 metres, wide enough to span a car
choices: About 3.5 metres, wide enough to span a car
About 1 metre, the length of your arm
About 8 metres, longer than a school bus
About 30 centimetres, like a pigeon's
context: The wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans) has the largest wingspan of any living bird, up to about 3.5 m (11.5 ft); the largest reliably measured reached about 3.7 m. Source: https://biologydictionary.net/wandering-albatross/

question: The common swift feeds, mates, and even sleeps without touching down. After leaving the nest, how long can a young swift stay airborne before it lands again?
answer: About 10 months without landing once
choices: About 10 months without landing once
About 10 minutes between perches
About 10 hours, then it must roost
About 10 days over open water
context: The common swift (Apus apus) can stay aloft for about 10 months straight — eating flying insects, mating, and sleeping on the wing — the longest continuous flight known for any bird. Source: https://www.sci.news/biology/common-swifts-stay-ten-months-air-04324.html

question: One small seabird chases summer from the top of the world to the bottom and back every year, making the longest migration of any animal on Earth. Which bird?
answer: The Arctic tern
choices: The Arctic tern
The wandering albatross
The common swift
The bar-tailed godwit
context: The Arctic tern (Sterna paradisaea) migrates pole to pole and back, averaging about 70,900 km a year; some tracked birds cover over 80,000 km. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_tern

question: A wandering albatross can hang in the air for hours, even days, without a single wingbeat. What in its shoulder lets it hold those huge wings open using no muscle effort at all?
answer: A tendon that locks the outstretched wing in place
choices: A tendon that locks the outstretched wing in place
A pocket of warm air that floats it like a balloon
A ring of stiff feathers that props the wing open
A lightweight hollow bone that never tires
context: A shoulder tendon locks the wandering albatross's outstretched wing open with zero muscle effort, so it can glide for hours or days without flapping. Source: https://www.whoi.edu/press-room/news-release/new-research-unlocks-clues-about-the-iconic-flight-of-the-wandering-albatross/

question: The Arctic tern breeds in the far north, then flies to the opposite end of the planet and back — every single year of its life. That endless polar commute wins it a record no other creature alive can match. Which one?
answer: It sees more sunlight in a year than any animal on Earth
choices: It sees more sunlight in a year than any animal on Earth
It dives deeper chasing fish than any other seabird
It goes the longest of any animal without sleep
It survives the coldest temperatures of any bird
context: By chasing summer from Arctic to Antarctic and back, the Arctic tern spends roughly two-thirds of its life in continuous day and sees more sunlight in a year than any other creature. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_tern

question: A five-month-old bar-tailed godwit left Alaska and flew for 11 days and 1 hour straight — no food, no water, no rest — before touching down. Where did that record nonstop flight finally end?
answer: Tasmania, about 13,560 km away
choices: Tasmania, about 13,560 km away
Hawaii, about halfway across the Pacific
Antarctica, at the edge of the ice
Japan, along the Asian coast
context: Juvenile bar-tailed godwit '234684' flew nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania, about 13,560 km, in 11 days and 1 hour (departed October 13, 2022) — the longest nonstop flight ever recorded for a bird. Source: https://www.usgs.gov/centers/alaska-science-center/news/juvenile-bar-tailed-godwit-b6-sets-world-record

question: On a single feeding trip a wandering albatross may cover 10,000 to 15,000 km in under three weeks, riding the wind the whole way. Some go so far they do what?
answer: Circle the entire Southern Ocean around the bottom of the world
choices: Circle the entire Southern Ocean around the bottom of the world
Cross the equator into the northern hemisphere
Follow the same fishing boat for months
Land on Antarctica to rest between legs
context: A wandering albatross can cover 10,000–15,000 km in 10–20 days, sometimes over 500 km a day, and some circle the entire Southern Ocean. Source: https://www.quarkexpeditions.com/blog/wildlife-guide-wandering-albatross-facts

question: The wandering albatross barely flaps, yet crosses oceans. In 'dynamic soaring' it climbs into the wind up the face of a wave, then wheels and dives downwind across the trough. Where does the free energy come from?
answer: The wind moves slower near the water and faster higher up
choices: The wind moves slower near the water and faster higher up
The warm water heats the air into a rising thermal
Each wave gives its wings a push as it passes
Its heavy body drops faster than gravity alone
context: In dynamic soaring the albatross steals speed from the wind gradient — slow air near the surface, fast air above — gaining energy across the wave without flapping. Source: https://www.whoi.edu/press-room/news-release/new-research-unlocks-clues-about-the-iconic-flight-of-the-wandering-albatross/

question: A frigatebird can sleep on the wing with just half its brain at a time. Scientists found that the waking half is always tied to one particular eye. Which eye stays open?
answer: The one facing the direction it is turning, to watch its path
choices: The one facing the direction it is turning, to watch its path
The one facing the sun, to hold a steady heading
The one facing down, to spot fish on the water
The one facing the wind, to feel the gusts coming
context: When a frigatebird circles on a rising air current, the brain half linked to the eye facing the turn stays awake to watch its path while the other half sleeps. Source: https://www.mpg.de/10673637/frigatebirds-sleep

question: Before its nonstop trans-Pacific flight, the bar-tailed godwit rebuilds its own body — shrinking its liver, kidneys, and gut, absorbing up to a quarter of them. Why sacrifice working organs before the biggest trip of its life?
answer: To make room for fat and enlarge its heart and flight muscles
choices: To make room for fat and enlarge its heart and flight muscles
To become light enough to be lifted by tailwinds alone
To stop needing food or water for the whole journey
To pack extra water into the space they leave behind
context: The godwit shrinks its liver, kidneys, and gut to make room for fat and to grow its heart and breast muscles for the flight — because 'guts don't fly.' Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/ecology-and-evolution/articles/10.3389/fevo.2021.685764/full

question: Niels Rattenborg's team taped tiny brainwave recorders to nesting frigatebirds, which flew off for up to 10 days. The recordings caught them sleeping in mid-air at sunset — but the amount stunned the team. How much sleep a day?
answer: About 42 minutes, a fraction of what they get on land
choices: About 42 minutes, a fraction of what they get on land
A full 8 hours, the same as on the nest
Almost none — under a single minute
Exactly half a day, one brain-half at a time
context: Rattenborg's recorders showed frigatebirds slept in flight as the sun set, but only about 42 minutes a day — far less than on land. Source: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/08/160803111738.htm

question: The albatross, the swift, the frigatebird, and the godwit each cross enormous distances, yet a plain flapping bird would drop from the sky trying the same trip. What runs a flapping flier out of gas that these four dodge?
answer: The fuel cost of constant flapping
choices: The fuel cost of constant flapping
The danger of landing on open water
The need to navigate by the stars
The weight of carrying their own food
context: All these long-haul fliers solved the same problem — covering huge distances without the fuel cost of constant flapping — with wind-riding tricks: the albatross steals energy from wind over waves, the swift and frigatebird ride rising air, the godwit rides tailwinds after loading up on fat. Source: https://www.whoi.edu/press-room/news-release/new-research-unlocks-clues-about-the-iconic-flight-of-the-wandering-albatross/

question: Textbooks say the albatross soars by stealing energy from the wind gradient — slower air near the waves, faster air higher up. When Gottfried Sachs reconstructed real GPS flight tracks in 2013, the gradient turned out to matter almost nothing. So where did his data say the free energy actually comes from?
answer: The upper turn of each loop, where the bird wheels from heading upwind to heading downwind
choices: The upper turn of each loop, where the bird wheels from heading upwind to heading downwind
The warm air rising off the sun-heated ocean, giving steady lift the way it lifts a soaring hawk
The wind gradient after all, just harvested lower down in the calmer air of the wave troughs
The push of the following swells, whose moving crests shove the gliding bird forward from behind
context: For decades the free energy in dynamic soaring was pinned on the wind gradient. Sachs and colleagues reconstructed real flight cycles from GPS and inertial sensors and argued the gradient's contribution is 'insignificant' — most of the energy is grabbed in the sharp upper curve of each loop, as the bird pivots from into-the-wind to downwind. It is still a live debate over WHERE in the cycle the gain happens. Those reconstructed loops stayed within just 0–15 m of the sea, lasted about 10 seconds each, and swung the bird's airspeed up to nearly 30 m/s (about 108 km/h) — all without a wingbeat. Source: Sachs et al., 'Experimental verification of dynamic soaring in albatrosses,' Journal of Experimental Biology 216:4222 (2013).  (Legend.)

question: A great frigatebird can stay over open ocean for two months without landing — and it has no choice, because its feathers are not waterproof and a splashdown at sea would soak it and drown it. So how does it climb thousands of metres to rest and glide without ever touching down?
answer: It flies straight into towering cumulus clouds and rides their updrafts nearly 4,000 m up
choices: It flies straight into towering cumulus clouds and rides their updrafts nearly 4,000 m up
It beats its wings in a fast steep spiral until the thin high air finally levels it off
It waits on a floating log or turtle until a rising sea breeze lifts it back aloft
It skims low over the waves and lets each crest bounce it a little higher each time
context: Unlike most seabirds, a frigatebird cannot float — its plumage soaks through — so the open ocean gives it nowhere to land. Henri Weimerskirch's team satellite-tagged frigatebirds near Madagascar (Science, 1 July 2016) and found they deliberately fly INTO cumulus clouds to ride the updrafts to nearly 4,000 m — into freezing air — then glide long distances back down without flapping. Individuals stayed aloft for up to about two months, covering more than 400 km a day; young birds can remain almost continuously airborne for over a year. Source: Weimerskirch et al., Science 353 (2016).

question: An octopus opening a jar in an aquarium tank keeps a whole ocean of pumping going inside it. How many hearts does an octopus have beating in its body?
answer: Three
choices: Three
One
Six
Two
context: Two branchial hearts pump blood through the gills to pick up oxygen; a third systemic heart then drives that oxygen-rich blood around the rest of the body. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Ten Wild Facts About Octopuses'.

question: An octopus settles onto a coral reef and folds its arms over a rock. If you could see the blood moving through its body right now, what color would it be?
answer: Blue
choices: Blue
Bright red
Green
Clear
context: Octopus blood is blue because it carries oxygen with hemocyanin, a copper-based protein, instead of iron-based hemoglobin; the copper turns blue when it meets oxygen the way our iron turns red. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Ten Wild Facts About Octopuses'.

question: One animal is the tallest alive, with a two-metre neck, and its heart must fight gravity harder than almost any creature's just to pump blood all the way up to its own brain. Which animal is it?
answer: The giraffe
choices: The giraffe
The elephant
The camel
The ostrich
context: A giraffe's heart pumps blood at roughly double a human's pressure to drive it up the two-metre neck against gravity. Source: Novartis, 'Giraffes have high blood pressure. Why don't they drop dead?'; Giraffe Conservation Foundation.

question: A living fossil with a hard domed shell and a long spiked tail, its blood is harvested by medicine to keep vaccines free of contamination. What creature is this?
answer: The horseshoe crab
choices: The horseshoe crab
The hermit crab
The sea scorpion
The trilobite
context: A substance in horseshoe-crab blood clots instantly around bacterial contamination, catching it in vaccines and drugs. Source: AssayGenie, 'Horseshoe Crab Blood and Endotoxin Testing'; Natural History Museum, 'Horseshoe crab blood: the miracle vaccine ingredient'.

question: An octopus has three hearts, and two of them are set aside for just one job: loading fresh oxygen onto the blood at the gills. Why does that loading job need its own dedicated pair of hearts?
answer: It takes a high pressure of its own
choices: It takes a high pressure of its own
It has to be kept ice-cold
It only happens while the octopus sleeps
It uses a different colored blood
context: The octopus must hold different blood pressures at the same time: high pressure at the gills to load oxygen, and a separate push from the systemic heart to send that blood to the body — so the gill-loading job gets its own dedicated pair of hearts. Source: Smithsonian Magazine; This Amazing World comparative physiology summaries.

question: Octopus blood is blue, not red, because of the metal it uses to grab oxygen. Human blood turns red from iron. Which metal ferries oxygen in an octopus and turns its blood blue?
answer: Copper
choices: Copper
Gold
Zinc
Silver
context: The octopus carries oxygen with hemocyanin, a copper-based protein; copper turns blue with oxygen the way iron-based hemoglobin turns our blood red. The horseshoe crab has blue blood for the exact same reason. Source: Smithsonian Magazine octopus article.

question: Octopuses can jet through open water in a burst, but they almost always prefer to crawl slowly across the sea floor instead. What happens inside the octopus that makes jetting so exhausting?
answer: Its main heart stops beating
choices: Its main heart stops beating
Blood pools uselessly in its arms
Its gills can't reload oxygen fast enough
Its blue pigment can't hold enough oxygen
context: The systemic (main) heart actually stops beating when the octopus jets through open water, which exhausts it, so octopuses usually prefer to crawl. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Ten Wild Facts About Octopuses'.

question: A giraffe must drive blood straight up a two-metre neck to reach its brain, fighting gravity the whole way. Compared with a human, how strong is the giraffe's blood pressure?
answer: About double a human's
choices: About double a human's
About the same as a human's
About half a human's
Almost none at all
context: A giraffe's blood pressure reaches roughly 280/180 to 300/180 mmHg, about double a human's, to force blood up the long neck. Source: Novartis, 'Giraffes have high blood pressure. Why don't they drop dead?'; Giraffe Conservation Foundation.

question: A giraffe bends its long neck down to a waterhole to drink, and for a moment its head is far below its heart. Blood surges toward the brain and should black it out. What in the giraffe's body stops that surge from reaching its skull?
answer: One-way valves in its neck veins
choices: One-way valves in its neck veins
A muscular ring inside its aorta
A valve at the exit of its heart
A clamp of muscle at the base of the skull
context: Valves in the neck veins block blood from rushing back into the skull, so the giraffe does not pass out from the sudden pressure surge when it lowers its head to drink. Source: Novartis, 'Giraffes have high blood pressure...'; Hemodynamics and Drinking in the Giraffe, PMC12012874.

question: Horseshoe-crab blood is one of the most valuable liquids on Earth because of what it does the moment bacteria contaminate a vaccine or drug. How does it catch that contamination?
answer: It clots into a gel around it
choices: It clots into a gel around it
It changes color to flag the batch
It binds the toxin so it can be filtered out
It triggers immune cells to swarm it
context: A substance in horseshoe-crab blood clots instantly around bacterial contamination, catching it in vaccines and drugs; the blood is worth roughly $60,000 a gallon. Source: AssayGenie; Natural History Museum, 'Horseshoe crab blood: the miracle vaccine ingredient'.

question: The Antarctic icefish carries no oxygen pigment, so it must move a huge volume of thin, watery blood to survive — and running its oversized heart drains an astonishing share of the fish's whole energy budget. Roughly what fraction does that pumping cost the icefish?
answer: About 22%
choices: About 22%
About 5%
About 8%
About 50%
context: The icefish's enormous heart pumps about five times more blood than a normal fish and burns roughly 22% of the fish's energy budget (versus about 5% in ordinary fish) just to move that thin, pigment-free blood, helped by cold, oxygen-rich Antarctic water. Source: Wikipedia, 'Channichthyidae'; Scientific American icefish article.

question: An earthworm has no single chambered heart at all. Instead of one pump, a set of muscular tubes wraps around its gut and squeezes rhythmically to push its blood along. How many of these pumping 'hearts' does an earthworm have?
answer: Five pairs
choices: Five pairs
A single pair
Twelve pairs
One large one
context: The earthworm has no single heart; it uses five pairs of pulsing 'aortic arches' (often called pseudohearts) that squeeze rhythmically to push blood around its closed circulatory system. Source: Sciencing, 'How Many Hearts Does An Earthworm Have?'; CK-12, 'What is unique about an earthworm's heart?'.

question: The Antarctic icefish is the only vertebrate whose blood carries no hemoglobin, and biologists once assumed it had simply switched off making the protein in the cold. Reading its genome overturned that: the explanation was more final than a switched-off gene. What had actually happened to the icefish's hemoglobin?
answer: The gene itself is physically deleted
choices: The gene itself is physically deleted
The gene is silenced but still intact
The protein misfolds and is destroyed
A cold-triggered mutation stalls it
context: In 15 of the 16 crocodile-icefish species the beta-globin gene is entirely gone and the alpha-globin gene is partly deleted — the DNA is missing, not merely switched off. The loss of myoglobin, the oxygen-store protein in muscle, happened separately and independently at least four times, so 6 of the 16 species also lack myoglobin in the heart. To move oxygen dissolved straight in watery plasma, icefish evolved blood volumes up to four times a red-blooded fish's, unusually wide capillaries, and a cardiac output about five times greater — yet their blood still carries under 20% the oxygen of their hemoglobin-bearing relatives. Source: Sidell & O'Brien, 'When bad things happen to good fish: the loss of hemoglobin and myoglobin expression in Antarctic icefishes,' Journal of Experimental Biology 209:1791 (2006); Wikipedia 'Crocodile icefish' (gene-deletion, 4x blood volume, 5x cardiac output).

question: Horseshoe-crab blood is drawn by medicine because a single kind of blood cell, the amebocyte, jams the sample into a gel the instant it meets bacterial contamination. Granules inside that cell hold one named protein that the alarm cascade converts into the clot. Which protein is it?
answer: Coagulogen
choices: Coagulogen
Hemocyanin
Fibrinogen
Thrombin
context: The crab's blood cells, called amebocytes, are packed with granules of a protein named coagulogen. When they touch bacterial endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide, LPS), a clotting-factor cascade fires and converts the coagulogen into a gel clot — this is the LAL (Limulus amebocyte lysate) test. It carries an ethical cost: bleeding is estimated to kill roughly 22-30% of the returned crabs. A synthetic drop-in replacement, recombinant Factor C (rFC), was recognized by the US Pharmacopeia (chapter <86>) in May 2025, offering a path to stop bleeding wild crabs. Source: Wikipedia 'Limulus amebocyte lysate' (amebocytes, coagulogen granules, LPS-triggered cascade; 22%/30% mortality from a 2009 Massachusetts study; recombinant Factor C and USP <86> official May 2025).

question: You are driving a country road at night when two coins of greenish-gold light flare in your headlights at the edge of the woods, then vanish as a deer turns its head. That glow comes from a layer built into the deer's eye that your own eyes lack. What is that layer?
answer: A mirror-like sheet behind the retina that bounces light back through it
choices: A mirror-like sheet behind the retina that bounces light back through it
A clear oily film spread across the front of the eyeball
A ring of tiny muscles that widens the pupil in the dark
A dense mat of blood vessels that feeds the retina from behind
context: That mirror is the tapetum lucidum, Latin for 'bright tapestry.' It sits behind the retina and reflects light that the photoreceptors missed on the way in, sending it back through them so the eye gets a second chance to catch each scrap of light. Humans and most other primates have none, so our eyes don't shine. Source: Britannica, 'tapetum lucidum'; Wikipedia, 'Tapetum lucidum.'

question: A cat's eyes blaze back at you from a dark room, but yours photograph as ordinary red 'red-eye' in a flash. The cat has a mirror behind its retina that throws light back out; you do not. So where does the plain red glow in a human flash photo actually come from?
answer: Blood in the retina at the back of the eye lighting up in the flash
choices: Blood in the retina at the back of the eye lighting up in the flash
The camera's own flash bulb reflected off the wet cornea
The colored iris reflecting the camera's light straight back
A film of tears scattering the flash across the front of the eye
context: Because humans and most primates lack a tapetum lucidum entirely, a flash reaches the back of the eye and lights up the blood-rich retina, and the camera catches that red. A cat's mirror, by contrast, retro-reflects the light straight back, so its eyes shine instead of going red. Source: Institute for Environmental Research and Education, 'What animals have a tapetum?'; Wikipedia, 'Tapetum lucidum.'

question: A house cat can pick out a moving mouse in near-darkness that would leave you blind, yet it cannot tell a red toy from a green one the way you can. The retina makes a trade to pull this off. What is a cat's retina packed with?
answer: Rod cells, six to eight times as many as a human eye holds
choices: Rod cells, six to eight times as many as a human eye holds
Cone cells, packed far more densely than a human's
Extra lenses layered inside to magnify what little light there is
A second, deeper retina that switches on only after dark
