a thick cushion of fat sealed beneath the bone
context: Each osteoderm was roughly 2.5 cm thick and built like an engineered sandwich panel: two dense outer layers of compact bone enclosing a porous inner lattice about 66% pore space, with struts only ~0.25 mm thick. That layout lets the plate soak up impact energy and stop a crack before it splits the whole plate (no catastrophic failure) -- exactly the property engineers copy for lightweight bio-inspired armor. Source: 'Analyzing nature's protective design: the glyptodont body armor,' J. Mech. Behav. Biomed. Mater. (2018), sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1751616118301656; corroborated via biomimetic-armor review literature and Glyptodon histology sources.

question: For 150 years no one knew if the car-sized glyptodon was an armadillo cousin, a turtle relative, or something odder. In 2016 scientists cracked a giant club-tailed glyptodont's mitochondrial genome and got a jolt: it sat deep INSIDE the living armadillos. Tracing the mass back down that branch to its small burrowing ancestor gave a second shock. By what factor had this lineage's body mass grown?
answer: more than 300-fold, to around two tonnes
choices: roughly 10-fold, to about 60 kilograms
roughly 50-fold, to about 300 kilograms
more than 300-fold, to around two tonnes
nearly 1,000-fold, to over five tonnes
context: Delsuc, Poinar and colleagues sequenced the complete mitochondrial genome of Doedicurus, a giant club-tailed glyptodont. It nests deep inside the living armadillos, making glyptodonts the subfamily Glyptodontinae within family Chlamyphoridae, having split from other armadillos about 35 million years ago. The kicker: the last common ancestor of glyptodonts and modern armadillos weighed only about 6 kg, yet Pleistocene glyptodonts reached roughly 2,000 kg -- a more than 300-fold increase in body mass over that lineage. Source: Delsuc, Poinar et al., Current Biology 26(4):R155-R156 (2016), corroborated via Sci-News and ScienceDaily (2016/02/160222134051.htm).

question: Japanese fishermen who hauled up a strange pale deep-sea shark named it 'tenguzame' after a long-nosed, red-faced goblin of their folklore. English speakers translated the name directly, giving this fish what everyday name?
answer: goblin shark
choices: goblin shark
vampire squid
ghost catfish
demon stingray
context: 'Tenguzame' (天狗鮫) honors the tengu, a red-faced long-nosed goblin of Japanese folklore; 'goblin shark' is a direct translation. Source: Wikipedia 'Goblin shark' (etymology); Florida Museum of Natural History profile.

question: A young goblin shark looks ghostly white, and the color deepens as it ages. But even the adult's strange pinkish tint is no trick of the light or paint. What actually makes this shark pink?
answer: red blood vessels showing through its thin, pale skin
choices: red blood vessels showing through its thin, pale skin
a diet of pink shrimp staining its body
glowing pigment cells that ward off rivals
a coating of pink algae from the seafloor
context: The goblin shark's skin is so thin and pale that the red blood vessels underneath show right through it, giving a real pink hue that deepens with age. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History profile; Wikipedia 'Goblin shark'.

question: The goblin shark hunts in pitch-black water hundreds of meters down, where eyes are nearly useless. Its long, flat, blade-like snout is studded with jelly-filled sensors called ampullae of Lorenzini. What do those sensors let the shark find in the dark?
answer: the faint electric fields given off by hidden animals
choices: the faint electric fields given off by hidden animals
the warmth radiating from a prey animal's body
the chemical scent trail left by wounded fish
the pressure waves of a distant tail beat
context: Ampullae of Lorenzini are jelly-filled electroreceptors; the goblin shark's blade snout sweeps them through the dark deep sea to detect the weak electric fields of buried or hidden prey. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History profile; Wikipedia 'Goblin shark'.

question: The goblin shark is weak-muscled and flabby, yet it hangs almost motionless in deep water, drifting toward prey until its jaws fire. One enormous organ, up to about a quarter of its whole body weight, keeps it nearly weightless. Which organ is it?
answer: its huge oil-filled liver
choices: its huge oil-filled liver
its air-filled swim bladder
its water-logged spongy skeleton
its oversized fatty brain
context: The goblin shark's oil-filled liver can reach about a quarter of its body weight; the light oil makes it nearly neutrally buoyant, so this slow ambush predator can hover in the dark and drift toward prey. Sharks have no swim bladder. Source: Wikipedia 'Goblin shark'; Smithsonian Ocean.

question: When a goblin shark catches prey, its whole mouth catapults forward out of its face, then snaps back flush against the head. High-speed NHK footage of two wild sharks feeding, analyzed by Nakaya's team in 2016, clocked this launch at up to 3.1 meters per second. What record does that strike hold?
answer: the fastest jaw of any shark
choices: the fastest jaw of any shark
the deepest recorded shark strike
the widest gape of any deep-sea fish
the longest teeth of any predatory shark
context: At up to 3.1 m/s, the goblin shark's jaw protrusion is the fastest of any shark and the fastest jaw-protrusion speed ever recorded for a fish. LEGEND. Source: Nakaya et al. 2016, Scientific Reports 'Slingshot feeding of the goblin shark'; Hokkaido University press release.

question: The goblin shark's slingshot jaws launch forward a distance equal to about 9% of its whole body length, catapulted by a double set of elastic ligaments at the jaw joints. Compared with a normal shark's, how much more protrusible are they?
answer: 2 to 9 times more protrusible
choices: 2 to 9 times more protrusible
only slightly, by about a tenth
exactly the same, just faster
less protrusible but far stronger
context: The jaws shoot out 8.6-9.4% of the shark's body length, and are 2.1 to 9.5 times more protrusible than a normal shark's, sprung by a double set of elastic ligaments at the jaw joints. Source: Nakaya et al. 2016, Scientific Reports; Wikipedia 'Goblin shark' (jaw protrusion figures).

question: The goblin shark is a living fossil: the only survivor of a whole shark family, the Mitsukurinidae, whose lineage reaches back roughly 125 million years to the age of the dinosaurs. When scientists first studied it, what did they mistake it for?
answer: a long-extinct fossil shark, Scapanorhynchus
choices: a long-extinct fossil shark, Scapanorhynchus
a young great white that had lost its color
a hybrid of a sawfish and a deep-sea eel
an ordinary sand tiger shark with a deformity
context: The goblin shark is the sole living member of Mitsukurinidae, a lineage ~125 million years old; early scientists confused it with the extinct fossil shark Scapanorhynchus. LEGEND. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History; Wikipedia 'Goblin shark'.

question: A goblin shark fires its whole mouth out of its face like a slingshot, so scientists expected it to work like other fast-mouthed fish: yank the jaws open to create a vacuum and pull the prey in. But Nakaya's 2016 high-speed study found the opposite. The shark keeps its gill slits open and only projects the jaws AFTER the gape is fully open. What kind of feeder does that make it?
answer: a ram feeder that overtakes prey by rushing its mouth over it
choices: a ram feeder that overtakes prey by rushing its mouth over it
a suction feeder that draws prey in on an inward vacuum
a filter feeder that strains drifting plankton from the water
a bite-and-shake feeder that tears loose chunks of flesh
context: The giveaway is timing and plumbing. A suction feeder snaps its gape open first to build a vacuum and would clamp its gill slits shut to hold that low pressure. The goblin shark does neither: it fully opens its gape, keeps the gill slits open the whole time (so water flows out, not in), and only THEN catapults the jaws. Nakaya's team measured the pressure inside the mouth staying positive, pushing water outward rather than sucking prey inward. So the fastest jaws of any shark are not a vacuum gun at all; they are a ram — the mouth lunges out and swallows the prey by overtaking it. The elastic launch is stored in stretched cartilage and ligament: the basihyal (tongue-support) cartilage is hauled back and down and the palatonasal ligament stretches to its maximum around 279 ms into the strike, then that tension snaps the jaws forward. Source: Nakaya et al. 2016, 'Slingshot feeding of the goblin shark Mitsukurina owstoni', Scientific Reports (PMC PMC4901258, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4901258/).

question: A goblin shark impales soft, slippery grenadiers and squid on its long, straight, lengthwise-grooved front fangs. But near the corners of its jaws sits a second, completely different set of teeth built for a different job. What are those rear teeth shaped to do?
answer: crush hard-shelled prey like crabs
choices: crush hard-shelled prey like crabs
impale even larger slippery fish
filter tiny plankton from the water
grip the seafloor while resting
context: One shark, two toolkits. The front (anterior) teeth are long, narrow, nearly straight fangs, finely grooved lengthwise, made to punch through and hold soft, slick deep-sea prey like grenadiers (rattail fish) and squid. But the posterior teeth near the jaw corners are small and flattened for crushing hard, shelled prey like crabs and other crustaceans. A single goblin shark can carry roughly 35-53 upper and 31-62 lower tooth rows across those two jobs. Source: Wikipedia 'Goblin shark' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goblin_shark); diet corroborated by Yano et al.'s stomach-content survey of 121 specimens from Tokyo Submarine Canyon.

question: The Goliath birdeater of the South American rainforest is the heaviest spider on Earth, with a body the size of a clenched fist. Pick up a full-grown one and it weighs about as much as what?
answer: A young puppy
choices: A young puppy
A single grape
A pair of scissors
A garden snail
context: Theraphosa blondi tops out around 175 grams (6 oz) — the greatest mass of any spider. The giant huntsman spider has longer legs, but the Goliath wins on sheer bulk and body size. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goliath_birdeater

question: Prowling the rainforest floor after dark, this giant South American spider is a patient ambush hunter. Despite the myth baked into its name, what does the Goliath birdeater most often drag back to its burrow?
answer: Earthworms and toads
choices: Earthworms and toads
Hummingbird chicks
Roosting bats
Wandering scorpions
context: On the forest floor it takes earthworms, insects, frogs, toads, lizards, and even small snakes and rodents — there are essentially no records of it regularly hunting birds. The 'birdeater' name came from Maria Sibylla Merian's 1705 engraving of a Suriname tarantula attacking a hummingbird; one famous picture stuck the myth to the whole species. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/invertebrates/facts/goliath-birdeater

question: Corner a Goliath birdeater and its inch-long fangs are almost the last thing it reaches for. Instead the spider swivels around, scrapes its hind legs across its own belly, and aims something at your eyes and face. What does it launch?
answer: A cloud of tiny barbed itching hairs
choices: A cloud of tiny barbed itching hairs
A jet of stinging venom
A sticky net of silk
A spray of foul musk
context: The hairs are urticating setae — microscopic, harpoon-shaped barbs the spider flicks off its abdomen. They lodge in an attacker's eyes and skin and itch fiercely, a far better first defense than a bite whose venom is only mild to humans. Source: https://www.aaas.org/news/weird-wonderful-creatures-goliath-birdeater

question: Alone in the Guyana rainforest at night, Harvard entomologist Piotr Naskrecki turned to find a puppy-sized Goliath birdeater right behind him. It was making a loud noise almost no other spider on Earth can produce. What was making it?
answer: Its hard-tipped feet clicking on the ground
choices: Its hard-tipped feet clicking on the ground
Its fangs snapping open and shut
Wind rattling through its leg hairs
Air hissing from its breathing holes
context: The Goliath birdeater is essentially the only spider that makes noise as it walks: its feet carry hardened tips and claws that tap the forest floor — Naskrecki described the clicking as 'not unlike a horse's hooves.' (It can also hiss loudly by rubbing leg bristles together — stridulation — but the walking-click is what gave it away that night.) Source: https://thesmallermajority.com/2014/10/08/the-sound-of-little-hooves-in-the-night/  (Legend.)

question: A frog from the rushing rainforest rivers of Cameroon holds the title of biggest frog on Earth. How big does the goliath frog get?
answer: About the size and weight of a house cat
choices: About the size and weight of a house cat
About the size of a mouse
About the size of a large dog
About the size of a horse
context: The goliath frog (Conraua goliath) can reach about 13 inches (34 cm) long and weigh up to 7.3 pounds (about 3.3 kg) -- roughly the size and weight of a house cat. It lives in southwestern Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea. Source: Wikipedia, Goliath frog; Britannica.

question: The male goliath frog can't croak like other frogs -- it lacks the vocal sac that lets frogs boom out a call. So how does a male attract a mate?
answer: He opens his mouth and whistles
choices: He opens his mouth and whistles
He drums the water with his hind legs
He flashes a bright throat pouch
He builds a tower of stones
context: Despite being the largest frog on Earth, the goliath frog has no vocal sac and cannot make a loud croak. To attract a mate, the male opens his mouth and makes a whistling sound. Source: Animal Diversity Web; Wikipedia.

question: In 2019 scientists watched goliath frogs do something never before documented in any African frog or toad. Along the riverbank, what were the giant frogs doing?
answer: Dragging rocks to wall off little ponds as nests for their eggs
choices: Dragging rocks to wall off little ponds as nests for their eggs
Carrying their tadpoles around on their backs
Spinning ropes of slime between the reeds
Digging deep burrows to sleep through the dry season
context: In 2019 scientists discovered the goliath frog builds nests: it clears little ponds along the riverbank and shoves rocks around the edge to wall them off, then a parent guards the eggs. It was the first nest-building ever documented in an African frog or toad. Source: Schaefer et al. 2019, Journal of Natural History; Mongabay.  (Legend.)

question: No frog on Earth grows as huge as the goliath frog, and biologists have puzzled over what pushed one species to swell so far past all its relatives. Which explanation do the scientists who study it favor?
answer: Hauling the heavy stones it needs to build its nests
choices: Hauling the heavy stones it needs to build its nests
A diet of unusually large river crabs and fish
Being a leftover giant from a cooler ancient climate
Growing big armor to survive its riverbank predators
context: To build its nests the goliath frog drags rocks weighing more than half its own body weight -- up to about 2 kg (over 4 pounds). Scientists think this heavy lifting is so demanding it may have driven the species to become the biggest frog on Earth. Source: Schaefer et al. 2019, Journal of Natural History; Mongabay.  (Legend.)

question: Watch a wild gray wolf pack cross the snow and you are not looking at a gang of unrelated fighters that teamed up. Almost always, what IS a wolf pack?
answer: A family: two parents and their pups from the last few years
choices: A family: two parents and their pups from the last few years
A crew of the strongest wolves drawn from many litters
A truce between two neighboring packs sharing a hunt
A group of females who drove off all the adult males
context: A wild pack is a breeding pair (the mother and father) plus their offspring from recent years, living and hunting together. Source: International Wolf Center, wolf.org/wolf-info/just-for-kids/wolf-families/.

question: Alone on the open tundra, a gray wolf tips its head back and lets loose a long howl. About how far can that single sound travel across the flat, treeless ground before it fades?
answer: About 10 miles
choices: About 10 miles
About half a mile
About 100 miles
About 30 feet
context: A wolf howl carries roughly 10 miles (16 km) across open tundra, and about 6 miles through forest where trees muffle it. Source: Britannica, 'Why Do Wolves Howl?'; coolwoodwildlifepark.com.

question: A gray wolf pack scatters across miles of forest, then a storm rolls in and the light dies. One wolf throws back its head and howls, and the others answer. Besides finding each other in the storm, what else does that howling do?
answer: Warns rival packs to keep off the pack's territory
choices: Warns rival packs to keep off the pack's territory
Frightens prey into freezing so it is easier to catch
Mimics an elk call to lure curious prey closer
Echoes off hills so the pack can map the terrain
context: Wolves howl to assemble the pack before and after a hunt, to relocate one another during a storm, and to warn neighboring packs to stay off their territory. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo; Wolf Conservation Center, 'Wolves and Howling'.

question: A gray wolf is no cheetah — it can't win a short sprint against a healthy deer. Yet a single wolf tracking prey can cover an astonishing distance in one day by trotting steadily for hours. Roughly how far?
answer: More than 50 miles in a single day
choices: More than 50 miles in a single day
About 3 miles in a single day
About 200 miles in a single day
Less than 1 mile in a single day
context: Wolves are endurance hunters, trotting at about 5 mph for hours and covering more than 50 miles in a day while tracking prey — one wolf chased a caribou for 5 miles, another a deer for 12. Source: Wolf Conservation Center, 'How Fast Do Wolves Run?'; Wikipedia, 'Hunting behavior of gray wolves'.

question: A gray wolf pack approaches a herd of elk. Rather than charging straight into the crowd, they work to do one specific thing first. What is the wolves' opening move?
answer: Split a single animal off from the rest of the herd
choices: Split a single animal off from the rest of the herd
Surround the whole herd so nothing can escape
Stampede the herd toward a cliff edge
Attack the largest and strongest bull head-on
context: Wolves try to cut one animal away from the group; if a prey animal stands its ground they often leave it and look for one that runs. Most hunts of large hoofed prey actually fail, so wolves test many animals to find a weak or slow one. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hunting behavior of gray wolves'.

question: For decades people spoke of the 'alpha wolf' — the animal that supposedly clawed its way to the top of the pack. Biologist L. David Mech, who popularized that idea in a 1970 book, later corrected himself about wild packs. In a real wild pack, who are the wolves everyone follows?
answer: Simply the parents — the breeding pair
choices: Simply the parents — the breeding pair
The oldest, most experienced wolf, kin or not
The single best hunter, who leads the chase
The mother alone, while the father ranges apart
context: The 'alpha' idea came from watching captive strangers thrown together, not wild families. Mech popularized it in 1970, then published a 1999 correction in the Canadian Journal of Zoology: in the wild the 'leaders' are just the parents. Source: Mech (1999); Scientific American, 'Is the Alpha Wolf Idea a Myth?'.  (Legend.)

question: When a gray wolf pack's hunters return to the den, the pups are too young to have joined the chase and need feeding. How do the returning adults get meat to the waiting pups?
answer: They regurgitate swallowed meat for the pups to eat
choices: They regurgitate swallowed meat for the pups to eat
They drag the whole carcass back to the den mouth
They lead the pups out to feed at the kill site
They store meat in cheek pouches and spit it out
context: Every wolf in the pack helps raise the pups: babysitters guard them while hunters are away, and returning hunters bring up swallowed meat, regurgitating it for the pups to eat. Source: International Wolf Center; Frontiers for Young Minds, 'It Takes A Pack To Raise A Pup'.

question: In 1995, gray wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park after about 70 years gone. Scientists watched the elk change not just their numbers but WHERE they dared to graze — and that shift set off a chain of change. As elk stopped lingering in exposed streamside valleys, what began to happen along the rivers?
answer: Browsed-down aspen and willow started growing tall again
choices: Browsed-down aspen and willow started growing tall again
The rivers dried up as plants drank the water
Elk vanished entirely from the whole park
Grass replaced every tree along the banks
context: With elk no longer lingering in open valleys, over-browsed willow and aspen recovered; taller willows let beavers return to build dams — a chain scientists call a trophic cascade. Researchers caution the effect is real but partly overstated, since drought, bears, and human hunting also thinned the elk. Source: Ripple & Beschta (2012), 'Trophic cascades in Yellowstone'; MeatEater Conservation.  (Legend.)

question: A great white shark that loses a front tooth in a struggle is back to a full bite within a day or two. Where does the replacement tooth come from?
answer: It rolls forward from a spare row waiting behind
choices: It rolls forward from a spare row waiting behind
It regrows slowly from the empty gum socket
It hardens from soft cartilage in the jaw
A neighboring tooth widens to close the gap
context: A great white's teeth are arranged in rows like a conveyor belt: when a front tooth is lost, one from the row behind rolls forward into the working position, sometimes in as little as 24 to 48 hours. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark; smartscience.blog/sharks-teeth-rows-anatomy.

question: A great white carries about 300 teeth at once, stacked in up to seven rows. Yet only a small fraction are ever doing the biting at any moment. Why?
answer: Most sit in reserve behind the front row until they roll forward
choices: Most sit in reserve behind the front row until they roll forward
Most stay flattened against the jaw until a big meal
Most are still buried and only erupt in old age
Most are too blunt to use and act as ballast
context: Of roughly 300 teeth in up to seven rows, most sit in reserve behind the working front row and are never used to bite until they roll forward to replace a lost tooth. Source: nationalgeographic.com/animals/fish/facts/great-white-shark; americanoceans.org/facts/how-many-rows-of-teeth-do-sharks-have.

question: A great white's upper and lower teeth do different jobs on a struggling seal. The broad upper teeth carry serrated, saw-toothed edges. What are the narrower lower teeth built to do?
answer: Grip and hold the catch in place
choices: Grip and hold the catch in place
Crush shell and bone to powder
Comb food particles from the water
Inject a paralyzing venom
context: The upper teeth are broad triangles with serrated edges built for shearing flesh, while the lower teeth are narrower and more pointed for gripping and holding the catch in place. Source: elasmo-research.org/education/white_shark/teeth.htm; americanoceans.org/facts/shark-teeth-facts.

question: Fossil shark teeth are among the most common fossils a beachcomber can find, far more common than fossil bones. What about a shark's life explains why its teeth litter the seabed?
answer: It sheds and replaces teeth endlessly, tens of thousands in a lifetime
choices: It sheds and replaces teeth endlessly, tens of thousands in a lifetime
Its teeth are made of near-indestructible diamond-hard enamel
It deliberately spits worn teeth onto known spawning grounds
It grows a fresh full set every single year like antlers
context: Because a shark never stops shedding and replacing teeth, it can go through tens of thousands of teeth across its lifetime, one reason fossil shark teeth are so common. Source: nhm.ac.uk/discover/what-can-shark-teeth-tell-us.html; americanoceans.org/facts/shark-teeth-facts.

question: The great white's electric sense, the ampullae of Lorenzini, is among the most sensitive electroreception known in any animal. How faint an electric field can it still pick up?
answer: Around five billionths of a volt per centimetre
choices: Around five billionths of a volt per centimetre
Around five thousandths of a volt per centimetre
Around five volts per centimetre
Around five hundred volts per centimetre
context: The ampullae of Lorenzini can detect electric fields as tiny as about five nanovolts per centimetre (five billionths of a volt), among the most sensitive electroreception known in any animal. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ampullae_of_Lorenzini; marinebiodiversity.ca/sharks-sixth-sense-how-electric-fields-guide-these-ocean-predators.

question: A great white can pick a wounded seal out from a healthy one even in murky water, well before it can see the animal clearly. What about the injured seal gives it away from a distance?
answer: Its leaking electrolytes make an electric field up to three times stronger
choices: Its leaking electrolytes make an electric field up to three times stronger
Its blood turns the surrounding water faintly magnetic
Its panicked heartbeat sends out a low sound only sharks hear
Its torn skin glows under the shark's ultraviolet vision
context: A wounded animal leaks charged electrolytes into the water, creating an electric field up to three times stronger than an uninjured one, so to a great white's electric sense an injured seal or fish effectively lights up. Source: elasmo-research.org/education/white_shark/electroreception.htm.

question: Most fish are cold-blooded, running at the temperature of the sea around them. A great white is not: a net of blood vessels called the rete mirabile, Latin for 'wonderful net,' does something unusual with the heat its muscles make. What does the net do with that heat?
answer: It traps the body's own heat instead of losing it at the gills
choices: It traps the body's own heat instead of losing it at the gills
It pumps the heat out fast to keep the brain from overheating
It converts the heat into a faint electric charge
It stores the heat in fatty deposits for the winter
context: Unlike most fish, the great white is partly warm-blooded (regional endothermy): a countercurrent network of blood vessels called the rete mirabile, Latin for 'wonderful net,' traps its own body heat instead of losing it at the gills. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark; biologyinsights.com/are-great-white-sharks-warm-blooded.

question: Researchers slipped temperature probes into great whites swimming in cold seas of about 13 to 16 degrees Celsius. The readings inside the sharks were startling next to that chilly water. What did the probes show?
answer: Stomach temperatures near 25 to 27 degrees Celsius
choices: Stomach temperatures near 25 to 27 degrees Celsius
Stomach temperatures matching the water almost exactly
Stomach temperatures below freezing, kept liquid by salts
Temperatures that swung wildly with every burst of speed
context: The rete mirabile keeps a great white's swimming muscles, brain, and eyes several degrees warmer than the sea; one study measured stomach temperatures of 24.7 to 26.8 degrees Celsius in water of only about 12.9 to 16.1 degrees. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark.

question: The great white's warm-blooded trick is not unique to it, but shared with a whole family of fast ocean hunters, the mackerel sharks. Which pair are its warm-bodied relatives?
answer: The shortfin mako and the salmon shark
choices: The shortfin mako and the salmon shark
The whale shark and the basking shark
The tiger shark and the bull shark
The hammerhead and the nurse shark
context: The warm-blooded trait is a family trait shared by all the mackerel sharks (family Lamnidae), including the great white's fast cousins the shortfin mako and the salmon shark. Source: sharks4kids.com/post/2019/01/31/endothermic-sharks; biologyinsights.com/are-great-white-sharks-warm-blooded.

question: At Seal Island in False Bay, South Africa, a great white waits in the dark water far below a swimming seal, then rockets straight up so hard it can launch its entire body clear of the surface. Researchers gave this vertical strike a nickname. What did they call it?
answer: The 'Polaris' breach
choices: The 'Polaris' breach
The 'Torpedo' roll
The 'Kraken' rise
The 'Thunder' lunge
context: At Seal Island, great whites hunt by lurking below and rocketing straight up at a seal, an ambush so violent the shark often launches its whole body clear of the surface. Researchers named this vertical strike the 'Polaris' breach, after the submarine-launched missile. Source: elasmo-research.org/education/white_shark/predation.htm; sharkdivingmosselbay.co.za/seal-island.  (Legend.)

question: The great white's ambush from below works partly because of its two-tone coloring, dark on top and white underneath. Against the bright ocean surface, how does that pale belly help the shark?
answer: It blends with the bright surface so the seal never sees it coming
choices: It blends with the bright surface so the seal never sees it coming
It reflects sunlight to dazzle and blind the seal
It flashes a warning that scatters a fleeing shoal
It mimics the pale belly of a harmless fish
context: The breach works because of countershading: the shark's dark grey back hides it against the sea floor while its white belly blends with the bright surface, so a seal never sees the attacker rising from below at over 40 km/h. Source: southafrica.net; ultimate-animals.com/predatory-strategies-of-great-white-sharks-at-seal-island.

question: Watching great whites breach on seals at Seal Island year after year, researchers tracked how often the attack actually landed. For such a feared hunter, the number is humbling, and young Cape fur seals often get away. About how often does a breach attack succeed?
answer: Only about half the time, near 47 percent
choices: Only about half the time, near 47 percent
Almost always, near 95 percent
Rarely, near 5 percent
Every single time once launched
context: Long-term study at Seal Island found the success rate of a breach attack is only about 47 percent, so young Cape fur seals frequently escape. Source: sharkdivingmosselbay.co.za/seal-island; sharkresearch.earth.miami.edu.

question: Zoos and aquariums keep sharks of many kinds, but a great white almost always dies within days. Only the Monterey Bay Aquarium has ever shown one for long, and even its record run ended when the young shark was released. How long did that record last?
answer: About 198 days
choices: About 198 days
About 5 years
About 20 years
About 3 days
context: No aquarium can keep a great white for long. The Monterey Bay Aquarium is the only one ever to display one successfully, and its record was 198 days in 2004 to 2005 before the young shark was released back into the wild. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monterey_Bay_Aquarium; pbs.org/wnet/nature/oceans-in-glass.

question: A great white cannot survive long in even the largest tank. Part of the reason is how it breathes, unlike a goldfish resting on the bottom of a bowl. What must a great white do to get oxygen?
answer: Keep swimming constantly to push water over its gills
choices: Keep swimming constantly to push water over its gills
Surface regularly to gulp air like a whale
Pump its cheeks to draw water while resting
Absorb oxygen through its skin when still
context: Great whites fail in tanks because they must swim constantly to push water over their gills to breathe, and they roam such distances that in a tank they injure themselves swimming into walls and often refuse to eat. Source: a-z-animals.com/animals/great-white-shark/facts; thejakartapost.com/life/2019/07/06.

question: Tagging revealed that California's great whites vanish each year on a long journey out to a barren stretch of open mid-Pacific between Baja and Hawaii, where they linger for months. Scientists gave that mysterious spot a nickname. What did they call it?
answer: The 'White Shark Cafe'
choices: The 'White Shark Cafe'
The 'Blue Desert'
The 'Shark Graveyard'
The 'Midnight Reef'
context: California's great whites make an epic open-ocean migration to a barren patch of the mid-Pacific between Baja and Hawaii that scientists nicknamed the 'White Shark Cafe,' where they linger for months before returning. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark; sharkstewards.org/sharktober.

question: Great whites were once thought to live only a few decades, but a 2014 study that counted growth bands like tree rings pushed that figure far higher. How long can a great white actually live?
answer: Over 70 years
choices: Over 70 years
About 15 years
About 200 years
About 500 years
context: Great whites are among the longest-lived cartilaginous fish: a 2014 age study estimated they can reach over 70 years old, far older than scientists once believed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark; fisheries.noaa.gov/species/white-shark.

question: A famous female great white nicknamed 'Deep Blue,' filmed off Guadalupe Island and thought to be about 50 years old, is one of the biggest ever caught on camera. Roughly how long is she?
answer: About 6 metres, some 20 feet
choices: About 6 metres, some 20 feet
About 3 metres, some 10 feet
About 12 metres, some 40 feet
About 1 metre, some 3 feet
context: 'Deep Blue,' filmed off Guadalupe Island and thought to be roughly 6 m (20 ft) long and about 50 years old, is one of the biggest great whites ever caught on camera. Source: surfertoday.com/environment/who-is-the-deep-blue-shark.  (Legend.)

question: Its teeth look like shrunken versions of the giant megalodon's, so people long assumed the great white was that monster's dwindled descendant. But fossils of a transitional shark from Peru, with teeth caught mid-way through growing their serrations, point to a very different ancestor. What did the great white actually evolve from?
answer: A broad-toothed mako shark, not megalodon
choices: A broad-toothed mako shark, not megalodon
A shrunken, cold-water line of megalodon
An early hammerhead that lost its head-wings
A deep-sea goblin shark that moved to the surface
context: The great white (Carcharodon carcharias) descends not from megalodon but from a lineage of broad-toothed mako sharks (Cosmopolitodus/Carcharodon hastalis). The transitional Carcharodon hubbelli, described by Dana Ehret from Peru's Pisco Formation (about 6.5 million years old), preserves teeth mid-way through developing serrations. Megalodon sits in a separate family (Otodontidae, genus Otodus), and the tooth resemblance is now read as convergent evolution, not close kinship. One paleontologist quipped that fewer people believe the megatooth sharks are related to great whites than believe the Earth is flat. Source: Smithsonian Ocean, 'Shark Teeth Tell Great White Shark Evolution Story'; Florida Museum of Natural History (Ehret et al. 2012, Palaeontology); Wikipedia 'Great white shark' and 'Carcharodon hubbelli'.

question: Sand tiger sharks are infamous for womb cannibalism: the first embryo to develop eats its unborn siblings until a single survivor is born. Great white pups grow up in the same dark uterus over roughly a year, yet several are born together, large and strong. How do they feed in there without turning on each other?
answer: They eat unfertilised eggs, not their siblings
choices: They eat unfertilised eggs, not their siblings
They devour the weakest of their siblings
A cord ferries the mother's blood into each pup
They absorb nutrients straight through their skin
context: Great white embryos feed by oophagy, swallowing dozens of unfertilised nutrient eggs (one study counted 50 to 70 egg capsules per uterus) and drinking a lipid-rich 'uterine milk' the mother secretes, a process called lipid histotrophy documented at over 79 litres in one female. Because separate nutrient eggs are on offer, several embryos coexist and are born large and robust after roughly 12 months of gestation, rather than devouring their siblings the way sand tiger pups famously do. Source: Sato et al., 'How great white sharks nourish their embryos... lipid histotrophy in lamnoid shark reproduction' (PMC5051657, ncbi.nlm.nih.gov); Wikipedia 'Great white shark'.

question: A giant fish haunts the black, near-freezing Arctic deep, reaching 21 feet long and over 2,200 pounds and cruising water barely above the freezing point. What is this cold-and-dark giant?
answer: Greenland shark
choices: Greenland shark
Bull shark
Reef manta ray
Blue marlin
context: The Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus) reaches about 6.4 m (21 ft) and over 1,000 kg (2,200+ lb), living in water from -1.1C to 7.4C at depths of 100 to 1,200 m. Source: Wikipedia 'Greenland shark' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland_shark).

question: Almost every wild Greenland shark carries a glowing pinkish-white parasitic copepod, Ommatokoita elongata, permanently anchored to one very specific spot on its body, where it feeds for years. Where does this parasite live?
answer: on the cornea of each eye
choices: on the cornea of each eye
in the gill slits
inside the nostrils
on the tip of the snout
context: The ~30 mm copepod anchors to the cornea of each eye and, as it feeds, scars and clouds it, leaving the shark nearly blind. Source: Wikipedia 'Ommatokoita' and 'Greenland shark'; Ocean Action Hub (oceanactionhub.org/greenland-shark-eye-parasite/).  (Legend.)

question: The eye parasite leaves the Greenland shark nearly blind, yet this barely hurts its hunting in the pitch-black Arctic deep, where eyes are nearly useless anyway. What does the shark rely on instead to find prey it cannot see?
answer: a powerful sense of smell
choices: a powerful sense of smell
echolocation clicks
a lateral heat-sensing pit
bioluminescent lures
context: In the lightless deep the shark hunts by smell, aided by electroreceptive pores on its snout to detect prey it cannot see. Source: Wikipedia 'Greenland shark'; Institute for Environmental Research and Education (iere.org/why-do-greenland-sharks-have-parasites-in-their-eyes/).

question: Greenland shark flesh is laced with high levels of urea and trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO). These chemicals keep the shark from freezing in near-0C water, but they also do something to any animal that eats the raw flesh. What?
answer: it acts as a poison
choices: it acts as a poison
it turns the blood to jelly
it triggers a deep sleep
it corrodes the stomach lining
context: The urea and TMAO act like antifreeze in near-freezing water but make the raw meat poisonous; sled dogs that eat it can become unable to stand. Source: Wikipedia 'Greenland shark'.

question: The Greenland shark is a deep-sea scavenger that will swallow almost anything that sinks to the seafloor. Which of these has actually been recovered from inside their stomachs?
answer: moose, horse, reindeer, and even polar bears
choices: moose, horse, reindeer, and even polar bears
musk oxen, walrus tusks, and caribou hides
beluga skulls, seal pups, and arctic fox pelts
sled dogs, harp seals, and narwhal ribs
context: Remains of moose, horse, reindeer, and even polar bears (thought to have died of other causes and then been scavenged) have been recovered from Greenland shark stomachs, showing this deep-sea giant will eat almost anything that sinks. Source: Wikipedia 'Greenland shark' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland_shark).

question: The Greenland shark is the slowest fish in the sea for its size, creeping along at about a foot per second, under 1 mph. Yet scientists keep finding seal remains in its stomach. How does the sluggish shark catch a fast seal?
answer: it creeps up on seals asleep in the water
choices: it creeps up on seals asleep in the water
it stampedes them into a wall of ice
it spits a jet of water to stun them
it waits at breathing holes to ambush them
context: Scientists think the shark sneaks up on seals dozing in the water, where they sleep to hide from polar bears, only to be caught by the silent, creeping shark. Source: Watanabe et al. 2012, J. Exp. Marine Biology and Ecology; NBC News (nbcnews.com/id/wbna47952603); Live Science.  (Legend.)

question: A Greenland shark loads its tissues with urea to keep from freezing, but urea has a nasty side effect: on its own it creeps between proteins and pries them apart, unfolding them into useless tangles. The shark survives only because a second molecule, TMAO, is always there. What does TMAO do?
answer: it holds the proteins folded and also braces them against the crushing deep-sea pressure
choices: it holds the proteins folded and also braces them against the crushing deep-sea pressure
it drives the leftover urea back out through the gills and into the surrounding seawater
it hardens into microscopic crystals that seal each protein away from the roaming urea
it seeps into the skin so that predators taste the bitter poison and spit the shark back out
context: The shark's flesh is a two-molecule pressure-armor system. Urea alone accumulates at a protein's surface and unfolds it, but TMAO (trimethylamine N-oxide) counteracts both urea's damage and the protein-crushing effect of deep-sea hydrostatic pressure, so TMAO concentration rises with depth. PNAS 2024 work shows TMAO physically strips urea out of the water shell around proteins. The same toxin that makes the raw meat deadly to humans is what keeps the shark's own proteins from unfolding in the freezing, high-pressure deep. Source: 'Trimethylamine-N-oxide depletes urea in a peptide solvation shell,' PNAS 2024 (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2317825121); Yancey et al., 'Unusual organic osmolytes in deep-sea animals.'

question: Scientists dated these sharks using a Cold-War signature: 1950s-60s atomic bomb tests dumped a spike of carbon-14 into the ocean. When they read the eye-lens cores, that bomb-pulse spike appeared in one group of sharks but was missing from the rest, and that split cracked the puzzle. Which sharks carried the atomic mark?
answer: only the smallest sharks, meaning the giant ones were already alive before the tests
choices: only the smallest sharks, meaning the giant ones were already alive before the tests
only the largest sharks, meaning they had been feeding most recently near the surface
every shark alike, since the carbon spread evenly through the whole ocean at once
only the female sharks, since a mother passes the carbon to her pups during pregnancy
context: The 2016 Nielsen study dated 28 female sharks (81-502 cm). Only the smallest sharks (about 220 cm or under) carried the bomb-pulse spike of carbon-14, proving those individuals were born after roughly 1960, while the big ones predated the atomic age entirely. This calibration pegged sexual maturity at about 156 plus or minus 22 years and the largest 5-meter shark at roughly 392 plus or minus 120 years old. Source: Nielsen et al. 2016, Science 353:702 (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aaf1703); ScienceDaily 2016-08-11.  (Legend.)

question: A crab tumbles in the surf and a gull hammers at it with its beak, yet the crab shrugs it off unhurt - and it has no bone anywhere inside its body. What is the crab wearing that both shields it and gives its muscles something to pull against from the outside?
answer: An exoskeleton
choices: An exoskeleton
A carapace scale
A cartilage frame
A keratin plate
context: Arthropods (insects, crustaceans, arachnids) build their skeleton outward as a rigid shell of chitin. It protects the soft body and anchors the muscles, doing from the outside the job your bones do from the inside. Source: Britannica, Arthropod - Form and Function; EBSCO Exoskeletons research starter.

question: A young crab's shell is hard and rigid, and here is the catch that comes with wearing your skeleton on the outside: once that shell hardens, it cannot stretch a millimeter. So how does an arthropod locked inside an unstretchable suit of armor manage to get any bigger at all?
answer: It sheds the whole shell and swells into a new, larger one before it hardens
choices: It sheds the whole shell and swells into a new, larger one before it hardens
It slowly dissolves the shell from the inside and reabsorbs it
It grows extra shell around the seams to widen the fit
It stays the same size and simply lives longer instead
context: This shedding is called molting, or ecdysis. Because a hardened exoskeleton cannot be enlarged, the animal grows a new soft skeleton underneath, climbs out of the old one, and puffs up to a bigger size before the new shell sets. Source: Britannica, Ecdysis; EBSCO Exoskeletons ('Once formed and hardened, an exoskeleton cannot be enlarged').

question: For thirteen or seventeen years a periodical cicada nymph waits in the dark underground, then climbs a tree at night and hauls itself out of its old skeleton. In the first hours after it emerges, before its shell hardens and its true colors come in, what does this freshly born cicada look like?
answer: Soft and ghostly pale - often white or light green
choices: Soft and ghostly pale - often white or light green
Deep brown, the same color as the shell it just left behind
Bright red as a warning to predators
Translucent like clear glass, showing its organs
context: A freshly emerged cicada is soft and pale - often white or light green - which earns it the nickname 'ghost cicada' until its body hardens, its wings expand, and its true colors come in within a few hours. Source: a-z-animals.com cicada crawl-out article; spiderzoon.com cicada-nymph.  (Legend.)

question: After a cicada crawls out of its old skeleton, the discarded brown shell stays hooked to the bark, a hollow, perfect copy of the insect down to the empty leg-tips - a ghost of the animal that left it. Biologists don't just call it a 'shell'; they have a real name for this cast-off exoskeleton. What is it?
answer: An exuvia
choices: An exuvia
A pupa
A chrysalis
A nymph
context: The empty molted skeleton is an exuvia (plural exuviae). It is the complete discarded exoskeleton, hollow but still shaped like the insect, including the hollow legs. Source: arhfoundation.org 'What Are the Shells Cast Off From Cicada Larva Called?'; MSU Extension Cicada Exuviae newsletter.

question: A garden spider loses a leg to a bird's beak. It is not stuck that way: at its next molt, a new leg appears. What is unusual about how that new leg first comes back?
answer: It emerges smaller and paler, then catches up to full size across later molts
choices: It emerges smaller and paler, then catches up to full size across later molts
It comes back full-sized and fully colored right away
It grows back longer than the leg it replaced
It grows back a different color than the rest of its legs
context: A spider can regenerate a lost leg at a molt. The new leg first emerges thinner, shorter, and paler than the original, then grows toward full size over the next two to four molts. Source: academicpath.org 'Can Spiders Regrow Legs'; pestwhisperer.com Spider Molting; NCBI PMC12211592.

question: A young lobster's shell, like every arthropod's, cannot expand as its body grows, so the only way to get bigger is to keep shedding it and building a new one. In just its first five to seven years of life, roughly how many times does a lobster shed its shell?
answer: About 25 times
choices: About 25 times
About 3 times
About 100 times
About once a year, so 5 to 7 times
context: A lobster grows by molting again and again - shedding its shell around 25 times in the first 5 to 7 years - because the hard shell simply cannot stretch with the body. Source: NOAA Fisheries 'Fun Facts About Luscious Lobsters'; lobsteranywhere.com Lobster Molt.

question: A lobster wriggles out of its old shell and lies beside it, its new shell so thin it's like wet paper. Then it does something startling with the empty shell it just crawled out of. What does the freshly molted lobster do?
answer: Eats its own discarded shell
choices: Eats its own discarded shell
Buries the old shell to hide from predators
Carries the old shell on its back as armor
Leaves at once to find calcium-rich prey
context: After molting, a lobster often devours its own recently vacated shell. The old shell is rich in calcium, which the lobster reuses to harden its new, paper-thin shell faster. Source: lobsteranywhere.com Lobster Molt; parl.ns.ca American Lobster Life Cycle ('devouring their own recently vacated shells').

question: A Mexican salamander called the axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) is a favorite of biology labs for one astonishing trick: if it loses a whole leg to a predator, over the next forty to fifty days that leg comes back complete with bone, muscle, nerves, and blood vessels. What is most remarkable about how the new leg finishes?
answer: It grows back perfectly, with no scar at all
choices: It grows back perfectly, with no scar at all
It grows back a slightly different color
It grows back smaller and thinner
It grows back covered in protective scales
context: The axolotl regrows an entire limb — bone, muscle, nerves and blood vessels — flawlessly and scar-free in roughly 40 to 50 days. Scar-free healing is exactly what makes it so precious to researchers. Source: Biology Insights (biologyinsights.com); MDI Biological Laboratory (mdibl.org).  (Legend.)

question: Many lizards can snap off their own tail to escape a grabbing predator and then grow a replacement — but scientists who X-rayed the new tail found it is a fake. The original tail is built on a backbone of many small linked vertebrae. What actually forms the skeleton of the regrown one?
answer: A single unsegmented tube of cartilage
choices: A single unsegmented tube of cartilage
A branching frame of cartilage rods
A chain of tiny cartilage beads
A fresh row of small new vertebrae
context: The replacement tail is not a true tail: instead of a jointed backbone of small vertebrae, its skeleton is one unsegmented tube of cartilage, with no bone at all. Dropping the tail to escape is called autotomy. Source: USC Stem Cell (stemcell.keck.usc.edu/perfect-lizard-tail/); ASU News.

question: A deer sheds and regrows a complete set of antlers every single year — and no other mammal grows bone anywhere near as fast. In the biggest species, wapiti (elk), how much length can an antler pack on in a single day at peak growth?
answer: About 27 millimeters — roughly an inch
choices: About 27 millimeters — roughly an inch
About 3 millimeters — a pencil-tip's width
About 1 millimeter — barely visible
About 100 millimeters — a whole hand's width
context: Antler is the fastest-growing bone known in any mammal, elongating up to ~2 cm a day in big species, with wapiti hitting ~27 mm/day. A brand-new full set regrows annually. Source: NCBI PMC10733395; Alaska Dept. of Fish & Game.  (Legend.)

question: When threatened, a sea cucumber does something that sounds impossible to survive: it violently blasts a portion of its own internal organs — including its guts — out through its rear end. This startles or entangles the attacker. What happens to the sea cucumber afterward?
answer: It regrows the lost organs over a few weeks
choices: It regrows the lost organs over a few weeks
It survives but can never feed again
It seals the wound and lives as an empty shell
It dies within hours from the loss
context: This defensive organ-dumping is called evisceration. Having startled or tangled a predator, the sea cucumber simply regrows the expelled organs over a few weeks. Source: Wikipedia: Evisceration (autotomy); PBS NOVA.  (Legend.)

question: A regrown lizard tail may look fine, but its skeleton is one solid tube of cartilage rather than a chain of jointed vertebrae — so it behaves differently from the original. Compared with the tail it replaced, the new one is:
answer: Far less flexible along its whole length
choices: Far less flexible along its whole length
Far more flexible and whip-like
Exactly as bendy as before
Able to grip branches like a hand
context: One solid cartilage tube can't bend at joints the way a segmented backbone can, so the replacement is far less flexible. The lizard trades a perfect tail for a good-enough spare. Source: ASU News — 'Researchers discover regenerated lizard tails are different from originals'.

question: While a deer's antlers lengthen, they are not bare bone: they are sheathed in velvet, a fuzzy living skin so packed with nerves and blood vessels that a growing antler is one of the fastest-building tissues alive. Then, every year, the old hardened antlers simply drop off and the whole cycle starts again. What bodily change sets off that annual fall?
answer: A drop in the deer's testosterone
choices: A drop in the deer's testosterone
A sudden rise in body temperature
The first heavy snowfall of winter
A shortage of calcium in the blood
context: Velvet is the nerve- and blood-vessel-rich skin that feeds fast-growing antler bone. The annual cycle restarts when a drop in testosterone makes the old antlers fall off. Source: Alaska Dept. of Fish & Game; onX Hunt.

question: Most starfish can regrow a lost arm, but they usually need part of the central disc to rebuild the whole body. Starfish of the genus Linckia break that rule: a single severed arm, with no central disc at all, can slowly rebuild an entire new animal. The lopsided shape it takes while doing so earned these starfish their nickname. What is it?
answer: A comet
choices: A comet
A pinwheel
A five-pointed disc
A curled shell
context: A lone Linckia arm can regrow a new disc and little arms, so it looks like a comet: a bright growing 'head' with the original arm fading behind like a tail — hence 'comet stars'. Source: Wikipedia: Starfish regeneration.  (Legend.)

question: The planarian, a small flatworm, is the reigning champion of regeneration: cut into pieces lengthwise or crosswise, each separate fragment does something remarkable. What does each fragment do?
answer: Regrows into a complete worm, whole new head and all
choices: Regrows into a complete worm, whole new head and all
Heals over into a lifeless lump of tissue
Grows back only the tail end, never a head
Fuses back together into the original worm
context: Cut a planarian into pieces and each piece regrows into a complete worm, including a brand-new head and brain. Source: Wikipedia: Planarian; Max-Planck-Gesellschaft (mpg.de).  (Legend.)

question: The axolotl does not stop at legs. Scientists prize it — and study it hoping one day to heal human patients — because it can regrow tissues that most animals lose forever. Beyond limbs and tail, what else can an axolotl rebuild?
answer: Parts of its heart, jaws, brain, and spinal cord
choices: Parts of its heart, jaws, brain, and spinal cord
Its lungs, kidneys, and gills
Its shell, teeth, and claws
Its scales, fins, and whiskers
context: The axolotl can regrow its tail, parts of its heart, its jaws, and even portions of its brain and spinal cord — which is why labs study it for possible human spinal-injury repair. Source: MDI Biological Laboratory (mdibl.org); Biology Insights.

question: A planarian can rebuild an entire worm from a tiny scrap of itself — because a huge share of its cells are neoblasts, adult stem cells able to become any body part. Researchers proved neoblasts are the secret with a brutal test: blast a worm with radiation to destroy them, and it loses all power to regenerate and dies. What single step restores that power?
answer: Transplanting one neoblast back into the worm
choices: Transplanting one neoblast back into the worm
Feeding it a rich diet for several weeks
Placing it in warmer, cleaner water
Cutting it again to trigger a fresh response
context: Up to 20% or more of a planarian's cells are neoblasts. Radiation wipes them out and the worm dies; transplanting a single neoblast back restores regeneration. Source: Wikipedia: Planarian; Whitehead Institute (wi.mit.edu).

question: In the 1960s, fishermen tried to destroy destructive crown-of-thorns starfish by hauling them up, chopping them into pieces, and throwing the pieces back into the sea. Because of how these animals regenerate, what may their effort have actually accomplished?
answer: It may have multiplied the starfish instead of killing them
choices: It may have multiplied the starfish instead of killing them
It poisoned the reef with rotting starfish
It drove the starfish into deeper water only
It had no effect on the starfish at all
context: Since some starfish regrow whole animals from pieces, chopping them up and returning them to the water may have accidentally multiplied the crown-of-thorns rather than killing them. Source: Wikipedia: Starfish regeneration.  (Legend.)

question: Planarians were once called 'immortal under the edge of a knife.' Modern labs pushed that reputation to its limit, hunting for the smallest scrap that could still rebuild a whole worm. How tiny a fragment of the animal proved to be enough?
answer: About 1/279th of the worm
choices: About 1/279th of the worm
About one-tenth of the worm
About one-half of the worm
About one-thousandth of the worm
context: A fragment as small as 1/279th of a planarian can still rebuild a complete new animal — hence 'immortal under the edge of a knife.' Source: Wikipedia: Planarian.  (Legend.)

question: A planarian's regenerating fragment is steered by an internal chemical called the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway. In the lab, scientists deliberately disrupt that chemistry in a cut fragment as it regrows. What startling animal grows where an ordinary tail should have formed?
answer: A second head — a two-headed worm
choices: A second head — a two-headed worm
No head at all, just a blunt stump
A body twice its normal length
A second, separate worm splitting off
context: Disrupting the Wnt/beta-catenin signal (or applying an electric field) makes a fragment grow a head where a tail should be — a two-headed planarian. Source: IFLScience; Whitehead Institute (wi.mit.edu).  (Legend.)

question: The axolotl regrows a whole limb by first building a blastema — a ball of progenitor cells that swells at the wound stump around five to seven days after amputation and rebuilds cartilage, muscle, and nerve. But adult salamanders of most other species can't pull off this trick. What is unusual about the axolotl's whole life that biologists tie to its lifelong regenerative power?
answer: It never fully grows up, keeping feathery gills and a larval body for life
choices: It never fully grows up, keeping feathery gills and a larval body for life
It swaps to breathing air and crawls onto land as it matures
It sheds and completely regrows its skin every few weeks
It slows its heartbeat to a near halt while a limb rebuilds
context: The axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) is neotenic, or paedomorphic: it never undergoes the metamorphosis that turns other salamanders into land animals, staying in a larval-like aquatic form with external feathery gills for life. That retained embryonic-like state is tied to its exceptional regenerative power. The blastema begins forming about 5–7 days after amputation, reaches an initial 1–2 mm, and peaks in cell proliferation around 14–21 days; its multipotent cells rebuild cartilage, muscle, and connective tissue while retaining positional memory. Source: Grokipedia 'Blastema' (timeline: 5–7 day onset, 1–2 mm, 14–21 day peak proliferation) and Grokipedia 'Axolotl' (neoteny).

question: A deer's velvet antler is the fastest-growing tissue any mammal makes, driven so hard by growth-factor genes that its gene-expression fingerprint reads closer to a bone tumor than to normal bone. Yet deer almost never get cancer — zoo records put their rate around five times lower than other mammals. Which built-in trio does the most to keep the racing antler from turning malignant?
answer: Beefed-up tumor-suppressor genes, mass cell suicide, and the yearly casting of the whole antler
choices: Beefed-up tumor-suppressor genes, mass cell suicide, and the yearly casting of the whole antler
A chilled antler core, a hard blood cutoff at full size, and a mineral shell that seals the tip
An immune sheath that devours mutant cells, an acidic core, and a scab coat over the beam
A frozen store of stem cells, a walled-off growth zone, and a nightly pause in cell division
context: A fast-growing antler's gene-expression profile correlates more strongly with osteosarcoma, bone cancer (r = 0.67–0.78), than with normal bone (r = 0.33–0.47). Three proto-oncogenes (FOS, FAM83A, REL) are under positive selection in deer and cancer-promoting growth-factor genes (FGF19, FGF21, PDGFD) run hot. Deer restrain this with tumor-suppressor genes under positive selection — the p53-regulator PML shows the strongest selection signal of all — plus massive apoptosis (up to ~64% of cells in the inner antler layer are programmed to die) and the annual casting of the hardened antler, which physically discards any rogue cells. Zoo records show deer get cancer roughly 5x less often than other mammals. Source: PMC10733395 'Deer antlers: the fastest growing tissue with least cancer occurrence'; genetics corroborated by Science 2019 (doi:10.1126/science.aav6335).  (Legend.)

question: Half a mile down in the black Pacific, a slim two-foot eel drifts near an empty stomach when a shrimp swims past. It has only tiny teeth and cannot chase fast prey through the dark. What lets this deep-sea eel snatch a meal from the emptiness in a single instant?
answer: Its whole head swells open like a soap bubble into a pouch bigger than its body
choices: Its whole head swells open like a soap bubble into a pouch bigger than its body
It fires a jet of venom that stuns the passing shrimp
It wraps its long tail around the prey and crushes it
It buries itself in the seafloor mud to ambush from below
context: The pelican eel (Eurypharynx pelecanoides) is famous for a mouth that balloons open into a huge pelican-like pouch, scooping up prey much larger than its own body in the empty deep. Source: Nautilus Live (nautiluslive.org/video/2018/09/20/gulper-eel-balloons-its-massive-jaws).  (Legend.)

question: The pelican eel's gaping pouch looks built to gulp down big fish whole. But look inside and you find only tiny teeth. In truth, what does this monster-mouthed eel of the deep mostly eat?
answer: Small crustaceans it nets from the drifting water
choices: Small crustaceans it nets from the drifting water
Other eels nearly as long as itself
Squid it drags down from shallower water
Chunks of whale carcass fallen to the seafloor
context: Despite its monstrous gape and tiny teeth, the pelican eel mostly eats small crustaceans -- the huge mouth is an all-purpose net for whatever rare meal drifts by, not a tool for swallowing big fish. Source: Wikipedia: Pelican eel (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelican_eel).

question: In the pitch dark where the pelican eel lives, its body tapers into a long, whip-thin tail that trails far behind the rest of the animal. Right at the very tip of that tail sits one special structure. What is it?
answer: A glowing organ that flashes pink and red
choices: A glowing organ that flashes pink and red
A cluster of taste buds that smells prey in the water
A whip-like flap it lashes to stir up drifting food
A dense knot of nerves that senses nearby movement
context: The eel's whip-thin tail is tipped with a bioluminescent organ that shines pink and gives off occasional bright red flashes -- a lure it may wave to draw prey toward its open mouth. Source: Wikipedia: Pelican eel (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelican_eel).  (Legend.)

question: Most fish keep themselves from sinking with a gas-filled float inside their body, topping it up as they rise and dive. The pelican eel, drifting between 500 and 3,000 meters down, has no such float at all. How does its body stay buoyant instead?
answer: Jelly-filled spaces around its backbone hold it up
choices: Jelly-filled spaces around its backbone hold it up
Large gulps of swallowed air trapped in its gut
Broad oily fins that spread its weight across the water
Constant slow swimming that keeps it from sinking
context: The pelican eel has no swim bladder; instead of the gas-filled float most fish use, its body relies on gelatinous, jelly-filled spaces around the backbone to stay buoyant -- a cheap, low-energy body plan for a place where food is scarce. Source: Wikipedia: Pelican eel (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelican_eel).

question: The hairy frog of Cameroon, nicknamed the 'horror frog,' looks defenseless until a predator grabs it. Then it does something no other animal is known to do to defend itself. What?
answer: It deliberately snaps the bones in its own toes and shoves the sharp ends out through its skin as claws
choices: It deliberately snaps the bones in its own toes and shoves the sharp ends out through its skin as claws
It inflates its whole body until the attacker cannot get its jaws around it
It squirts a jet of foul sticky slime from glands along its spine
It sheds its entire tail, which keeps twitching to distract the predator
context: This is why it earned the nicknames 'horror frog' and 'Wolverine frog.' At rest there are no claws to see at all; the frog literally wounds itself to arm itself when threatened. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_frog; Blackburn, Hanken & Jenkins 2008, 'Concealed weapons: erectile claws in African frogs,' Biology Letters.  (Legend.)

question: A cat's claw and a bird's talon both have a hard outer sheath over the bone inside. The hairy frog's newly-made claws are strange because of what they are made of. What ARE those claws?
answer: Bare bone, just the frog's own sharpened toe-bones with no covering at all
choices: Bare bone, just the frog's own sharpened toe-bones with no covering at all
A cluster of stiffened hairs matted together with dried slime
Curved spurs of thick keratin like a rooster grows on its leg
Hollow quills that snap off in the wound and grow back later
context: Unlike a cat's or a bird's claw, the hairy frog's claws have no hard outer sheath. They are simply the frog's own toe-bones, sharpened and punched out raw through the skin of the foot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_frog; Blackburn et al. 2008, Biology Letters.

question: The male hairy frog grows what looks like a coat of 'hair' along his flanks and thighs in the breeding season, made of thin fringes of skin. But it is not hair at all. What are those fringes actually for?
answer: Soaking up extra oxygen from the water so he can stay under longer
choices: Soaking up extra oxygen from the water so he can stay under longer
Trapping a warm layer of air to survive cold mountain streams
Sensing ripples in the water to detect an approaching predator
Attracting females by shimmering in the light like a lure
context: The 'hair' is really fringes of thin skin flaps (dermal papillae) packed with tiny blood vessels, working like external gills. The male grows them so he can breathe underwater for long stretches while standing guard over the clutch of eggs. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_frog; iere.org/what-is-the-hairy-frog-and-why-is-it-hairy.

question: Scientists have watched the hairy frog drive its bone-claws OUT through its skin and filmed exactly how it happens. But there is one part of the whole trick they still cannot explain. What is it?
answer: How the claw ever goes back in once the danger has passed
choices: How the claw ever goes back in once the danger has passed
Which of the toes fire their claws first when the frog is grabbed
How the frog avoids bleeding to death from the self-inflicted wound
Why only the males, and never the females, can grow the claws
context: The extension is well documented, but researchers can only hypothesize that the claw slides back passively as the torn skin heals. That 'retract-and-heal' half of the story is still unconfirmed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_frog, which states the retraction mechanism 'is not known' and is only hypothesized.

question: For years Hallucigenia was reconstructed upside down, standing on stiff spines as if they were its legs. Around 1991, drilling into better fossils exposed something hidden beneath the rock that overturned the picture. What had been concealed there?
answer: A row of soft clawed walking legs
choices: A row of soft clawed walking legs
A fringe of feeding tentacles
A set of gripping suckers
A line of breathing gills
context: Flipped right-side up, Hallucigenia walked on soft clawed legs while the roughly seven pairs of stiff spines stood up along its back as protection. Researchers found the second row of walking legs by drilling out rock that had hidden it. Source: PalaeontologyOnline.com; fossilguy.com (Ramskold and Hou).  (Legend.)

question: For decades scientists thought a dark blob at one end of Hallucigenia was its head. In 2015 a new study revealed what that blob actually was. What did the 'head' turn out to be?
answer: Decay fluids squeezed out of the body
choices: Decay fluids squeezed out of the body
A cluster of unhatched eggs
A bundle of grasping tentacles
A hard shell it retreated into
context: The blob was decay fluid or gut contents that had oozed from the body during fossilization; the real head was at the opposite end. So scientists had the animal not only upside down but back-to-front. Under an electron microscope the true head showed a simple face with a pair of eyes and a ring of plates around a mouth lined with tiny needle-like teeth. Source: Smith and Caron 2015, Nature; PalaeontologyOnline.com; ROM.  (Legend.)

question: Once Hallucigenia was read correctly, its clawed feet gave away its family tree: each claw is built from three cones stacked one inside another. That same nested-cone claw structure is found in which living animals?
answer: Velvet worms
choices: Velvet worms
Sea urchins
Horseshoe crabs
Tardigrades
context: The nested-cone claws match those of today's velvet worms (onychophorans), soft caterpillar-like animals. Hallucigenia sits near the base of the lineage that also led to insects, spiders, and crustaceans. It remains the classic textbook lesson in how hard the strangest Cambrian fossils are to read. Source: Smith and Caron 2015, Nature; ROM; Wikipedia.

question: A shark cruises the reef with its head flattened sideways into a wide, flat bar, an eye riding each far tip. Which shark is unmistakable from that silhouette alone?
answer: Hammerhead shark
choices: Hammerhead shark
Tiger shark
Nurse shark
Lemon shark
context: That flattened head has a real name: the cephalofoil, Greek for 'head-wing.' It is not a random shape but a sensory wing that spreads the shark's detectors far apart across its width. Source: Cape May Whale Watch & Research Center, 'The Hydrodynamic Head Of Hammerhead Sharks.'

question: Among the hammerheads, one species is the outright giant, averaging about 15 feet and reaching up near 20 feet long. Which hammerhead is the biggest of the family?
answer: Great hammerhead
choices: Great hammerhead
Scalloped hammerhead
Bonnethead
Winghead shark
context: The great hammerhead (Sphyrna mokarran) tops the family at roughly 4.6 m on average, with the largest reaching around 6.1 m. Source: Wikipedia, 'Great hammerhead'; Florida Museum Discover Fishes.

question: A hammerhead swings its wide head in slow arcs low over bare sand, then suddenly stops and digs a stingray out of a spot where nothing was showing. What was the flat head sensing under the sand?
answer: The faint electric fields of the buried ray
choices: The faint electric fields of the buried ray
The warmth rising off the buried ray
The ray's shadow cast on the sand
Vibrations from the ray's flicking tail
context: The underside of the hammer is studded with ampullae of Lorenzini, jelly-filled pores that sense the tiny electric fields of living animals. The wide head spreads them into a broad array, so the shark sweeps the seafloor like a wide-beam metal detector, feeling for prey it cannot see. Source: Reef Check, 'Why Do Hammerheads Have Hammer Heads'; Elasmo Research, 'Sandy Plains: Great Hammerhead Shark.'

question: Michelle McComb swept lights all around caught hammerheads and recorded their eyes' electrical response to each flash. She found the hammerhead has one thing no normal shark can claim. What did those tests reveal?
answer: A nearly 360-degree field of view
choices: A nearly 360-degree field of view
A pair of long-range zoom eyes
Eyes that glow to light the seabed
A blind spot it herds prey into
context: An eye on each tip gives the shark a full view up and down its own body at once, plus a stereo view straight behind it. McComb recorded the eyes' electrical response to light swept around the animal to prove the wraparound coverage. Source: Live Science, 'Hammerhead Sharks See 360 Degrees in Stereo'; McComb et al., Journal of Experimental Biology 2009.  (Legend.)

question: A hammerhead's two nostrils sit not up front but out at the very tips of its wide head, an odd place to put a nose. Kajiura's team found this wide spacing hands the shark a trick a plain-headed shark cannot do. What does the wide-set nose let it work out?
answer: Which direction a smell is coming from
choices: Which direction a smell is coming from
How far off the food still is
How big the hidden prey must be
Whether the prey is alive or dead
context: It literally smells in stereo: a scent reaches one tip-mounted nostril a split second before the other, and that tiny time gap tells it which way to turn. The scalloped hammerhead's whole brain is built around this wide nose, with its smell-processing region taking up about 7% of brain mass, roughly double the ~3% in other shark families. Source: Smithsonian Ocean, 'Do Sharks Smell in Stereo'; Kajiura research, Current Biology 2010.

question: A great hammerhead attacks a stingray by first slamming it against the seabed with a blow from above. Before it bites chunks from the ray's wings, it does something no other shark does. What is its next move?
answer: Pinning the ray flat with its own head
choices: Pinning the ray flat with its own head
Wrapping the ray up in its long tail
Spinning hard to tear the ray loose
Swallowing the ray whole in one gulp
context: The head is both sensor and sledgehammer: it knocks the ray down, pins it with the flat of the hammer, then pivots to feed. The great hammerhead even eats rays whole, venomous tail-spine and all; one caught off Florida had 96 stingray spines lodged in and around its mouth and was barely bothered. Source: Wikipedia, 'Great hammerhead,' citing Strong et al. Bahamas field observations.  (Legend.)

question: Scalloped hammerheads hunt alone through the night, so it stuns divers off Cocos Island that by day hundreds of them mass into a slow-circling wall you can swim among. Where does this daytime crowd reliably gather?
answer: Over an underwater mountain
choices: Over an underwater mountain
Inside a coral lagoon
Along a deep-sea trench
Around a sunken shipwreck
context: These underwater mountains are called seamounts. The most famous gathering is at the Alcyone seamount off Cocos Island, Costa Rica, where from June to September divers see schools of hundreds. Cocos, the Galapagos, and Malpelo form a route divers call the 'Hammerhead Triangle.' Source: PLOS One, Cocos Island scalloped hammerhead study; Diveplanit, 'The Hammerhead Triangle.'

question: The great hammerhead's head spans only about a quarter of its body length, but one small relative wears a cephalofoil so extreme it stretches nearly half the animal's entire length. Which shark has the widest head in the family?
answer: The winghead shark
choices: The winghead shark
The bonnethead
The smalleye hammerhead
The scoophead
context: The winghead (Eusphyra blochii) has the most extreme cephalofoil of all, about 40-50% of its body length, versus roughly 23-27% for the great hammerhead. The wider the head, the farther apart its sensors and the wider its sensory sweep. Source: Aussie Animals, 'Winghead Shark'; Wikipedia, 'Great hammerhead.'

question: Scalloped hammerheads are warm-water sharks, yet they dive past 800 metres into water near freezing to hunt, and their swimming muscle somehow stays warm the whole way down. A shark cannot warm its blood, and the gills bleed heat straight into the sea. Mark Royer tagged them and filmed one at 1,044 metres to see the trick. What does the shark do on the way down?
answer: It clamps its gill slits shut the entire dive
choices: It clamps its gill slits shut the entire dive
It shunts warm blood inward away from the skin
It shivers its swimming muscles to make heat
It rides down inside a pocket of warmer water
context: The gills are where a fish's warm blood meets the sea across a thin membrane, so in 5C water at depth they would strip the shark's body heat away in minutes. By clamping the gill slits shut and holding its breath -- about 17 minutes per dive, with only ~4 minutes spent hunting on the bottom before it races back up to breathe -- the scalloped hammerhead seals off that heat leak, and tagged muscle temperature stays warm all the way down, cooling only as it nears the surface and opens its gills again. Source: Royer et al., 'Breath holding as a thermoregulation strategy in the deep-diving scalloped hammerhead shark,' Science (2023), DOI 10.1126/science.add4445, https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.add4445 ; ScienceDaily 2023-05-11 https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2023/05/230511164453.htm  (Legend.)

question: A bonnethead at an Omaha zoo had been netted as a pup and kept three years with no male shark anywhere near her, then one day she gave birth to a healthy pup. Keepers were stunned. How was the pup made?
answer: Her egg grew into a pup with no sperm at all
choices: Her egg grew into a pup with no sperm at all
She had stored a male's sperm for those three years
A second female in the tank had fertilised her eggs
A shred of her own body tissue budded into a pup
context: Stored sperm was the obvious suspect -- some sharks bank it for months -- but the pup's DNA held only its mother's genetic material, ruling that out and marking the first genetically confirmed virgin birth (parthenogenesis) in any shark. The mechanism is automictic parthenogenesis: the unfertilised egg fuses with a sister cell (a polar body) from its own meiosis instead of a sperm, so the pup is homozygous, essentially a half-clone of the mother. Source: Chapman, Shivji et al., 'Virgin birth in a hammerhead shark,' Biology Letters 3(4):425-427 (2007), DOI 10.1098/rsbl.2007.0189, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2390672/

question: On the Tasmanian seafloor lives a tiny fish that is a hopeless swimmer — drop it into open water and it barely gets anywhere. Yet it covers the bottom just fine, going where it needs to go. How does the handfish get around?
answer: It walks step by step on hand-like fins
choices: It walks step by step on hand-like fins
It jets backward by squirting water
It undulates along the sand like an eel
It rides the current wherever it flows
context: The handfish is a poor swimmer that mostly crawls, a slow, sedentary bottom-dweller. It plants its splayed pectoral fins on the sand and pushes itself forward step by step. Those fins are so hand-shaped that the family name comes from the Latin 'bracchium', meaning 'arm'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handfish  (Legend.)
