question: An invasive Northern Pacific seastar creeps toward a spotted handfish's egg mass. The tiny mother won't flee. She wedges her body between the predator and her eggs and drives it off with a specific move. How does she shove the seastar off course?
answer: She wipes it away with her tail
choices: She wipes it away with her tail
She stabs it with venomous fin spines
She squirts ink to blind it
She bites through its arm
context: A mother spotted handfish defends her eggs from the invasive Northern Pacific seastar by wedging herself between the predator and the eggs and wiping it with her tail to shove it off course. Source: https://handfish.org.au/spawning-behaviour-of-spotted-handfish/

question: Bomb a reef of ordinary fish and it slowly refills; bomb a reef of handfish and it stays empty almost forever. Marine biologists trace this fragility to one quirk of how handfish come into the world. What is it?
answer: Its young hatch as tiny walkers that never drift out
choices: Its young hatch as tiny walkers that never drift out
Its larvae drift far but survive only on their birth reef
Its females spawn just one clutch in an entire lifetime
Its eggs need a warm current no other reef can supply
context: Handfish have no free-swimming larval stage: the eggs hatch directly into fully-formed miniature adults that drop onto the sand and start walking. Because no larvae drift on the current, a wiped-out reef gets no settlers from anywhere else — the very trait that makes it wondrous also makes it fragile. Handfish also spawn every year, and hatchlings can settle wherever they drop, so the other explanations do not hold. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handfish

question: Deep in the Amazon canopy weaves a massive slate-gray and black eagle, its white belly bright against the leaves, crowned with a double crest of feathers it can raise straight up on its head. Which rainforest raptor is this?
answer: The harpy eagle
choices: The harpy eagle
The bald eagle
The peregrine falcon
The snowy owl
context: The harpy eagle (Harpia harpyja) is a huge rainforest eagle of Central and South America -- slate-black above, white below, with a distinctive double crest it can raise on its head. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle.

question: The harpy eagle carries the largest talons of any living eagle. Its curved rear talon reaches nearly 5 inches -- so long it matches, almost exactly in length, the front claw of one particular animal. Whose claw does that hind talon match?
answer: A grizzly bear's front claw
choices: A grizzly bear's front claw
A house cat's front claw
A jaguar's front claw
A river otter's front claw
context: A female harpy eagle's rear (hind) talon reaches about 12.3 cm -- nearly 5 inches -- roughly the length of a grizzly bear's front claw, the largest talon of any living eagle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle; Audubon '10 Fun Facts About the Harpy Eagle'.  (Legend.)

question: A wild howler monkey clings to a branch high in the canopy when a harpy eagle drops on it. Yet in one Panama study, monkeys were not the harpy's main meal at all -- a single kind of prey made up a startling 79% of everything it ate. What was on the menu most?
answer: Sloths
choices: Sloths
Snakes
Fish
Deer
context: In one study, sloths made up 79% of the harpy eagle's prey. It plucks sloths and monkeys straight off the branches, and a female can grab prey nearly her own weight and fly off without ever landing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle.

question: The harpy eagle hunts by day, yet it carries a ring of feathers around its face that it can raise flat like a shallow dish -- a feature you would normally expect only on a night-hunting owl. What does raising that feather disc do for the eagle?
answer: Funnels faint sounds to its ears
choices: Funnels faint sounds to its ears
Shades its eyes from midday glare
Signals a warning to its mate
Sheds a rainforest downpour
context: Like an owl, the harpy eagle has a facial disc of feathers it can raise to funnel sound to its ears -- rare among diurnal (daytime) raptors -- helping it hear hidden prey before it sees them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle; Los Angeles Zoo.

question: Most eagles raise a chick every year or two. The harpy eagle is far rarer at it -- so much rarer that losing even one breeding pair can set a whole area back for years. How often does a harpy pair actually raise a chick?
answer: Just one chick every 2-3 years
choices: Just one chick every 2-3 years
A brood of six every spring
Several chicks every year
A new chick every single month
context: A harpy eagle pair raises just one chick every 2-3 years -- one of the slowest reproduction rates of any eagle -- which is why the species is so vulnerable to habitat loss. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle; Audubon.

question: In the open ocean's twilight zone there is no rock or weed to hide behind, so a small fish called the hatchetfish stays invisible from below with a trick that sounds backwards. What does it do to keep a predator looking up from seeing its dark shape?
answer: Shines rows of lights along its belly
choices: Shines rows of lights along its belly
Squirts a cloud of black ink
Buries itself in the sandy bottom
Turns its skin bright coral red
context: This is called counter-illumination. Rows of light organs (photophores) along the hatchetfish's belly glow pale blue and shine downward, matching the faint sunlight from above so a predator looking up sees only background light and no dark silhouette. In the open ocean the best way to vanish isn't to be dark — it's to make your own light. Sources: https://twilightzone.whoi.edu/explore-the-otz/creature-features/hatchetfish/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_hatchetfish  (Legend.)

question: Face-on in the twilight zone, a silvery fish shrinks until it is almost impossible to see, then swings sideways and flashes into a broad silver flank. What about its body pulls off that near-vanishing act?
answer: Its body is a thin blade, flattened side-to-side
choices: Its body is a thin blade, flattened side-to-side
Its scales fold flat like closing shutters
Its skin turns clear as glass on cue
It hollows out a see-through gap down its middle
context: The body is a thin silver blade, so compressed side-to-side that seen edge-on it is nearly two-dimensional and almost vanishes, slipping through the water 'with barely a trace.' That hatchet-blade shape is what gives the fish its name. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_hatchetfish ; https://twilightzone.whoi.edu/explore-the-otz/creature-features/hatchetfish/

question: A hatchetfish's eyes are nothing like the ordinary round domes most fish carry on the sides of their heads — their strange form is a big clue to how it makes a living in the dim twilight zone. What shape are they?
answer: Tube-shaped, pointing straight up
choices: Tube-shaped, pointing straight up
Flat, like a pair of coins
Ringed with glowing dots
Split into dozens of tiny lenses
context: The hatchetfish has huge tube-shaped eyes that point straight up, so it stares at the dim glow above and spots prey by their dark silhouettes drifting overhead — hunting for shadows against the light, the very same weakness its own glowing belly hides from below. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_hatchetfish

question: Each night the hatchetfish rides a daily elevator up toward the surface to feed, then sinks back into the dark by dawn. Its pale-blue belly lights glow the whole way. What does it do with them on that journey?
answer: Turns them up and down like a dimmer switch
choices: Turns them up and down like a dimmer switch
Flashes them in a fast warning pattern
Swaps their color from blue to green
Pulses them in time with its heartbeat
context: The hatchetfish rides a daily vertical migration, rising at night to feed on copepods, ostracods, and fish larvae and sinking back down by dawn. It turns its pale-blue belly lights up or down like a dimmer switch to track the changing brightness of the water, so it keeps erasing its own shadow the whole way. Being able to regulate that intensity gives it an edge over other twilight-zone fish using the same camouflage. Source: https://twilightzone.whoi.edu/explore-the-otz/creature-features/hatchetfish/

question: Down deep, a hunter sweeps a living searchlight through the black water. The hatchetfish's skin is packed with tiny crystals arranged in long parallel bundles. When that beam sweeps across it, what does the beam become?
answer: A soft, diffuse blur
choices: A soft, diffuse blur
A bright pinpoint glint
A mirror of the hunter's own beam
A ring of rainbow colors
context: The hatchetfish's skin doesn't just mirror light — it is packed with organized guanine crystals arranged in long parallel bundles that scatter light softly in every direction, so a predator's bioluminescent searchlight gets a diffuse blur instead of a bright flash. Penn physicist Alison Sweeney: 'nature is generally quite a bit more sophisticated in how it has evolved to manipulate light.' Source: https://www.futurity.org/hatchetfish-oceans-light-camouflage-1468942-2/

question: A penguin stands barefoot on Antarctic ice all day and its feet never freeze to the surface. The secret is that its feet are deliberately kept:
answer: just above freezing, cold and cheap
choices: just above freezing, cold and cheap
as warm as its chest and belly
completely numb and bloodless
warmed by a layer of fat in the sole
context: Warm arteries running down into a penguin's legs are bundled right against the cold veins coming back up, so the outgoing blood hands its heat to the returning blood before it reaches the feet. Feet kept just above freezing lose almost no heat and don't melt into the ice. Source: Britannica Blog, 'Penguin Feet: Avoiding Frostbite in the Antarctic'; CoolAntarctica.

question: In a penguin's leg the arteries carrying warm blood DOWN are bundled tight against the veins carrying cold blood back UP. Why run them side by side in opposite directions?
answer: the warm blood hands its heat to the returning blood, recycling it
choices: the warm blood hands its heat to the returning blood, recycling it
the veins keep the arteries from freezing solid
it lets the leg pump blood without a heartbeat
it warms the cold blood so the feet stay toasty
context: This is countercurrent heat exchange: warm blood flowing out runs against cold blood flowing in, and heat leaks across from one to the other, so it is recycled back into the body instead of being flushed out to the freezing feet. Herons and ducks stand for hours in near-freezing water using the same leg bundles. Source: Britannica Blog, 'Penguin Feet'; Biology Insights, 'How Do Penguins Stay Warm'.

question: A great white shark hunts fast and hard in cold seas where other fish turn sluggish. It manages this because, unlike most fish, it can keep its body:
answer: 6 to 10 degrees C warmer than the water
choices: 6 to 10 degrees C warmer than the water
exactly matched to the water temperature
cooled well below the water to save energy
dry inside a sealed body cavity
context: A great white and its lamnid cousins hold their swimming muscles 6.5 to 10 degrees C above the surrounding sea, so their muscles stay powerful in cold water where a cold-blooded fish would go slow. Source: Oceans Research, 'Are sharks warm-blooded?'; GGCWiki, 'Adaptations for selective thermoregulation in large predatory fish'.

question: Tuna and the great white shark keep their swimming muscles warm in cold seas. Warm blood leaving the muscle is routed to run right alongside the cold blood coming in, handing over its heat before it can escape out the gills. Anatomists named this dense blood-vessel net with a Latin phrase meaning:
answer: wonderful net
choices: wonderful net
muscle furnace
warm heart
deep coil
context: The structure is the rete mirabile, Latin for 'wonderful net': warm blood leaving the muscle runs against cold blood coming in and hands its heat back, so the warmth is recycled rather than flushed out the gills. Source: American Scientist, 'How Tunas and Lamnid Sharks Swim'; Wikipedia, 'Rete mirabile'.

question: A swordfish carries a heater organ built from a modified eye muscle that warms its eyes and brain 10 to 15 degrees C above the cold sea. What advantage does a warm-eyed swordfish gain over a cold-eyed fish?
answer: it detects rapid motion far better and spots darting prey
choices: it detects rapid motion far better and spots darting prey
it can see colors invisible to warm-blooded animals
its eyes glow to lure prey in the dark
it never needs to blink while hunting
context: A heated retina responds faster, so the swordfish catches quick-flitting prey a cold-eyed fish would miss. Source: Fritsches, Brill & Warrant, 'Warm Eyes Provide Superior Vision in Swordfishes', Current Biology 2005; Science AAAS, 'Hot Eyes for Cold Fish'. (Legend-tier wonder.)

question: A reindeer breathes air at 40 below zero, yet the air reaching its lungs is warmed to body temperature. Scroll-like bones inside its nose, wrapped in warm blood vessels, don't just heat the incoming breath; on the way out they also:
answer: reclaim the heat and moisture from the outgoing air
choices: reclaim the heat and moisture from the outgoing air
filter frozen dust from the airway
pump extra oxygen into the blood
seal the nostrils shut against the wind
context: The nasal scroll-bones warm every incoming breath from -40 C up to about +38 C, then recover the heat and moisture back out of the exhaled air, so almost nothing is wasted. Source: Blix et al., 'Nasal heat exchange in the reindeer', PubMed 3992062; ScienceDaily, 'The magical reindeer nose'.

question: Tunas and lamnid sharks are not close cousins, yet each evolved the same warm-blood-against-cold-blood muscle plumbing on its own, roughly 40 to 60 million years apart. A biologist looking at penguins, reindeer and these fish all landing on the identical trick would label it an example of:
answer: convergent evolution
choices: convergent evolution
genetic drift
sexual selection
adaptive radiation
context: Convergent evolution is when unrelated lineages independently arrive at the same solution; keeping warm blood next to cold blood is such a good idea that evolution stumbled onto it separately in fish, birds and mammals. Genetic drift is random allele change, sexual selection is mate-driven, and adaptive radiation is one lineage fanning into many niches. Source: American Scientist, 'How Tunas and Lamnid Sharks Swim: An Evolutionary Convergence'.

question: A whale swimming hard builds up dangerous muscle heat, but its flippers and tail flukes are bare-skinned and thin, meeting the cold sea with no blubber over them. When the whale starts to overheat, what does it do with those bare flukes?
answer: floods them with warm blood so heat pours into the water
choices: floods them with warm blood so heat pours into the water
clamps their blood vessels shut to hold warmth in
shivers them fast to burn off the extra energy
tucks them tight against the body to shed heat
context: The flippers and flukes are 'thermal windows.' Instead of routing blood through the vein bundles that normally recycle warmth, the overheating whale sends extra blood straight out to the bare skin, so the heat radiates into the sea. The very same countercurrent plumbing that saves heat can run in reverse to dump it. Source: Georgia Dolphin Ecology Program, 'Chill Out, Hot Stuff!'; SeaWorld, 'Baleen Whales - Adaptations'.

question: In a fish's gills the same opposite-directions trick grabs OXYGEN instead of heat: water flows over the gills one way while blood flows the other. Because the blood always meets fresher, more oxygen-rich water, it can strip out about:
answer: 90% of the oxygen in the water
choices: 90% of the oxygen in the water
30% of the oxygen in the water
half the oxygen, then the rest at the tail
only what the fish can gulp at the surface
context: If blood and water flowed the SAME way they would quickly reach a stalemate; flowing opposite, the blood keeps meeting richer water and pulls out up to ~90% of its oxygen. Source: FishBIO, 'An efficient exchange: countercurrent oxygen exchange in fish'; AskNature, 'Gills Exchange Oxygen Efficiently'.

question: A tuna or a mako shark warms only patches -- the swimming muscle, the eyes, the brain -- while the heart pumps cold blood like any other fish. In 2015 the opah, a round silver fish of the deep sea, broke that pattern. Heating itself by endlessly flapping its wing-like pectoral fins and trapping that warmth with fat-wrapped vessel nets in its gills, the opah turned out to be:
answer: warm right through, heart and all
choices: warm right through, heart and all
warm only along its spine
cold except for its glowing eyes
warm only after a fast burst of swimming
context: The opah (Lampris guttatus) is the first fish shown to be whole-body endothermic -- warm all over, heart included, not just in isolated muscle, eye or brain patches like tuna and sharks. It makes heat by constantly flapping its wing-like pectoral fins, then holds that heat in with counter-current vessel nets (retia) sitting right inside its gills -- the one place warm blood would normally dump all its heat straight into the sea. Those gill retia are wrapped in a fat layer with less than half the thermal conductivity of ordinary tissue, insulating the exchanger and letting the opah stay roughly 5 degrees C warmer than the cold water it hunts in. Source: Wegner, N.C., Snodgrass, O.E., Dewar, H. & Hyde, J.R. (2015) 'Whole-body endothermy in a mesopelagic fish, the opah, Lampris guttatus', Science 348(6236):786-790 (DOI 10.1126/science.aaa8902); National Geographic, 'Meet the Comical Opah, the Only Truly Warm-Blooded Fish'.

question: A gill's opposite-directions vessel net simply grabs oxygen out of the passing water. A deep-sea fish's swim bladder uses the very same net wired for a far harder job: pumping pure oxygen INTO the bladder even though the gas already packed inside pushes back with brutal force. The trick that lets it beat that pressure is that the outgoing vein leaks its oxygen back onto the incoming artery, so that:
answer: each loop stacks onto the last, compounding the load
choices: each loop stacks onto the last, compounding the load
a molecular pump spends ATP to force gas across
the sluggish blood simply gives the gas more soak time
a vast folded surface lets more gas cross at once
context: The gill rete is a simple countercurrent EXCHANGER -- it just recovers heat or oxygen as two bloodstreams pass in opposite directions. The swim-bladder rete does something far stronger: it is a countercurrent MULTIPLIER. Oxygen unloaded on the outgoing venous side back-diffuses across onto the incoming artery, where it reloads onto hemoglobin; because that returned gas is added on top of what the artery already carries, each pass compounds the concentration, and the small single-step difference stacks up over and over along the long parallel capillaries. It is driven by the Root effect -- lactic acid from the gas gland acidifies the blood and forces its hemoglobin to dump oxygen -- and this compounding is what lets deep-sea fish secrete oxygen into the bladder against pressures up to about 380 atmospheres, starting from a partial pressure near 0.2 atmospheres in the water. No ATP pump, no extra surface, no slowed flow does this: it is pure recompounding geometry. Source: Wikipedia 'Rete mirabile' (rete pumps O2 from a partial pressure near 0.2 atm into a bladder at hundreds of atmospheres; Root effect drives back-diffusion so arterial O2 compounds until it exceeds bladder pressure); Pelster, PMC10209234 'The rete mirabile: a possible control site for swimbladder function'; PLOS One 2012, 'O2-Filled Swimbladder Employs Monocarboxylate Transporters ... Lactate-Induced Root Effect Hemoglobin'.

question: Of all the strange fossils left in the seas 270 million years ago, Helicoprion left the strangest signature of all: a single tight spiral, wound like a coiled clock spring. What was that spiral made of?
answer: A whorl of saw-like teeth
choices: A whorl of saw-like teeth
A ring of armored bone plates
A coiled shell like a nautilus
A band of overlapping scales
context: Helicoprion means 'spiral saw' in Greek (helikos = spiral, prion = saw) -- a perfect name for a coil of teeth arranged like the blade of a circular saw. It swam the Permian seas roughly 290 to 270 million years ago, long before the first dinosaurs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helicoprion

question: For over a century the buzzsaw spiral was the ONLY part of Helicoprion anyone ever dug up, so nobody could tell where on the body it belonged -- until a 2013 CT scan of a fossil finally settled it. Where did the tooth-spiral actually sit?
answer: Coiled inside its lower jaw
choices: Coiled inside its lower jaw
Curling off the tip of its snout
Standing up along its back fin
Trailing behind it on its tail
context: Scientists led by Leif Tapanila CT-scanned a fossil and found the whorl sat in the lower jaw. Tapanila said the teeth 'fit in the back of the mouth, right next to the back joint of the jaw.' Before that, guesses had stuck the spiral everywhere -- off the snout like an elephant's trunk, on the tail, on the back fin, even poking out of the throat. Source: https://phys.org/news/2013-02-helicoprion-scientists-mysteries-ancient-shark.html  (Legend.)

question: Helicoprion stayed a mystery for more than a hundred years for one simple reason: paleontologists almost never found any part of it EXCEPT that tooth-spiral. What made the rest of its body vanish before it could fossilize?
answer: Its skeleton was cartilage, which rots away
choices: Its skeleton was cartilage, which rots away
Deep-sea scavengers stripped every carcass
Its bones were too small to leave a trace
Acidic Permian mud dissolved the buried bone
context: Like sharks and their relatives, Helicoprion had a skeleton made of cartilage rather than bone. Cartilage rots away instead of fossilizing, so the hard tooth-whorl was almost the only piece that ever survived -- which is exactly why nobody could figure out where it went for so long. Source: https://phys.org/news/2013-02-helicoprion-scientists-mysteries-ancient-shark.html

question: Helicoprion's tooth-spiral was a complete record of every single tooth the animal ever grew -- it never shed one in its life. New teeth kept sprouting at the front of the jaw, so where did all the old teeth end up?
answer: Curled inward into the center of the coil
choices: Curled inward into the center of the coil
Fused into one solid slicing ridge
Dissolved and reabsorbed into the jaw
Ground flat against the toothless upper jaw
context: Instead of falling out the way most teeth do, each old tooth stayed anchored and rolled inward toward the middle of the coil as fresh teeth grew at the working front. That is why the whorl coils tighter and tighter toward its center -- the innermost teeth are the ones the animal grew as a baby. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helicoprion  (Legend.)

question: With a mouth full of saw-like teeth, Helicoprion was assumed for decades to be a shark. But when the 2013 scan finally revealed its skull anatomy, it turned out to be a much closer cousin of which living group instead?
answer: The ratfishes and chimaeras
choices: The ratfishes and chimaeras
The rays and skates
The lampreys and hagfish
The coelacanths
context: Only the teeth were shark-like; as Tapanila put it, 'everything else is Holocephalan' -- the group that includes today's ratfishes and chimaeras. When it closed its jaw, the whorl rolled backward in a slicing motion; Tapanila said 'the analogy to a circular saw is almost perfect,' and it likely sawed through soft prey like squid. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/buzzsaw-jaw-helicoprion-was-a-freaky-ratfish

question: The 2015 study 'Eating with a saw for a jaw' found Helicoprion's spiral was no single uniform slicer -- different stretches of the coil did different jobs as the lower jaw swept closed. Which task fell to the FRONT teeth of the whorl?
answer: Hooking and dragging prey inward
choices: Hooking and dragging prey inward
Grinding shells into fragments
Filtering plankton from seawater
Anchoring the jaw to the skull
context: Ramsay and colleagues (Journal of Morphology, 2015) modeled the whorl as a multi-tool: as the lower jaw rotated shut the anterior teeth hooked and dragged prey inward, the middle teeth pierced and cut, and the rear teeth near the jaw joint sheared and shoved the food deeper toward the throat -- the tooth paths traced arcs like curved slashing swords. The animal likely fed by opening and closing the jaw in a repeating sawing cycle that caught, cut, and swallowed in one motion. Source: Ramsay et al. 2015, Journal of Morphology 276:47-64, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25181366/

question: North America's biggest salamander lurks under flat rocks in cold Appalachian streams: a flat-headed, two-foot giant whose baggy skin hangs in ruffled, layered folds down each side. Backwoods locals gave it a whole zoo of nicknames. Which one did they actually pin on it?
answer: Lasagna lizard
choices: Lasagna lizard
Bristle toad
Mud minnow
River newt
context: The hellbender (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis) earned a whole pile of folk names: 'lasagna lizard' for its ruffled, layered skin folds, plus 'snot otter' for its slimy skin, 'devil dog,' 'mud devil,' and 'Allegheny alligator.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellbender

question: A hellbender barely uses its lungs - it pulls almost all its oxygen straight out of the stream, right through its skin. Plenty of stream animals boost skin-breathing in different ways. What is the hellbender's trick?
answer: It hangs in loose, baggy wrinkles and side-folds
choices: It hangs in loose, baggy wrinkles and side-folds
It is packed with dense capillary beds just under the surface
It secretes a thin mucus film that traps dissolved oxygen
It is riddled with microscopic pores like a sponge
context: Those loose folds hugely increase the skin's surface area, so more oxygen can soak in from the water. The ruffled look is exactly why one folk name is 'lasagna lizard.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellbender

question: On a still day, a hellbender lying under its rock will suddenly start rocking its whole body back and forth and rippling its baggy side-folds. Why does it bother making all that motion?
answer: To sweep fresh oxygen-rich water past its skin
choices: To sweep fresh oxygen-rich water past its skin
To warn rival hellbenders off its rock
To force stale water out of its lungs
To signal a mate hiding nearby
context: By swishing fresh water past its folds, the hellbender keeps the oxygen coming even when the water goes still - the skin can only soak up what actually flows past it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellbender

question: A rainforest giant nearly seven inches long, the male Hercules beetle carries two enormous horns that close on a rival like a giant pincer — a smaller one and a much larger one. Which part of his body does the larger horn sprout from?
answer: His back, above the wing-covers
choices: His back, above the wing-covers
His head, between the eyes
His jaws, like a beetle's mandibles
The underside of his belly
context: Most of that seven-inch record length is horn, not body. A male grows a smaller horn jutting up from his head and a much larger one arching down from his back (the pronotum); the two meet like a giant pincer. Only males grow them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hercules_beetle  (Legend.)

question: Two male Hercules beetles clamp horns on a branch, fighting for a mate. Once a beetle catches his rival in the pincer, how does he win?
answer: He pries the rival loose and hurls him off the branch
choices: He pries the rival loose and hurls him off the branch
He crushes the rival's shell until it cracks
He squeezes until the rival stops struggling
He drags the rival down into the leaf litter
context: Each beetle tries to catch the other between its upward head-horn and its downward back-horn, then pry and throw him off the branch. The horn works as a lever: muscles in the thorax rotate the head to drive the long horn upward and lift the enemy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hercules_beetle

question: A Hercules beetle's wing-covers are olive-green or yellow one hour and near-black the next, though the beetle itself is unchanged. What flips its color?
answer: Rising humidity in the air around it
choices: Rising humidity in the air around it
The beetle growing older
A fresh meal of tree sap
A flash of a threat display
context: The elytra (wing-covers) shift with the weather: olive-green or yellow when the air is dry, darkening toward black as the humidity rises around the beetle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hercules_beetle

question: Before it ever grows a horn, a Hercules beetle spends up to two years as a fat, C-shaped white grub tunneling through rotting wood. How does that grub compare to the adult it becomes?
answer: It grows heavier than the adult beetle
choices: It grows heavier than the adult beetle
It is far smaller than the adult
It has tiny working horns already
It is see-through with no color
context: A Hercules beetle larva can reach about 4.5 inches (11 cm) long and weigh over 100 grams, heavier than the horned adult it becomes. The giant adult is the short chapter: after years underground it lives only about three to six months, sipping sap and fruit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hercules_beetle

question: A two-and-a-half-tonne grey giant wallows in an African river all day, then hauls out at dusk to mow the grass on the bank. Despite eating nothing but plants, it kills more people across Africa each year than lions or sharks do. Which animal is this?
answer: The hippopotamus
choices: The hippopotamus
The Cape buffalo
The white rhinoceros
The Nile crocodile
context: Hippos (Hippopotamus amphibius) kill an estimated 500 or more people a year in Africa — deadlier to humans than lions or sharks — yet they are grazers that eat only grass. Their danger comes from aggression and sheer bulk, not from hunting. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/hippopotamus

question: A hippo lives its whole life in rivers and lakes, yet a big bull crossing a deep pool never paddles at the surface the way other huge mammals do. How does it actually get across the deep water?
answer: It walks along the bottom, pushing off the riverbed
choices: It walks along the bottom, pushing off the riverbed
It floats high and dog-paddles across the top
It rolls sideways and lets the current carry it
It beats its stubby tail to scull forward
context: A hippo is too dense to float, so it can't truly swim. It walks and pushes off the riverbed in a slow-motion underwater gallop, toes barely touching the bottom. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/hippopotamus

question: For a century naturalists filed the hippo alongside pigs, going by the shape of its molar teeth. Then blood-protein and DNA evidence in the 1900s pointed to a completely different group of living relatives — one nobody had expected. What animals turned out to be the hippo's closest living relatives?
answer: Whales and dolphins
choices: Whales and dolphins
Pigs and warthogs
Rhinos and tapirs
Elephants and manatees
context: Until 1909 hippos were grouped with pigs based on their molars, but blood-protein and DNA evidence proved their closest living relatives are the cetaceans — whales, dolphins, and porpoises. The two lines are thought to have split from a shared water-loving ancestor around 55 million years ago. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippopotamus

question: When a hippo throws its head back and gapes its jaws to nearly 150 degrees — almost a straight line — it isn't yawning from boredom; it's a threat display. That wide-open mouth reveals its most fearsome weapons. What are they?
answer: Tusk-like canines that never stop growing
choices: Tusk-like canines that never stop growing
Rows of razor-edged shearing molars
A pair of horns rooted in the jaw
Backward-curving fangs full of venom
context: Inside the gaping mouth are tusk-like canine teeth that keep growing throughout life, reaching about 50 cm (20 inches) long. They stay sharp by grinding against the lower incisors as the hippo chews. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippopotamus

question: A crow-sized bird of the Amazon and Orinoco swamps has a spiky reddish crest, a bare blue face, and glaring red eyes, and it spends its days munching leaves in the riverside trees. Which bird is it?
answer: The hoatzin
choices: The hoatzin
The scarlet macaw
The great egret
The horned screamer
context: The hoatzin (Opisthocomus hoazin) is about 65 cm long but weighs only around 700 grams, with an unfeathered blue face, maroon eyes, and a spiky rufous crest. It lives in the swamps and riverside forests of the Amazon and Orinoco basins and eats mostly leaves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoatzin

question: A newly hatched hoatzin, still bald and clumsy in its nest over the Amazon water, has something on each wing that no adult bird alive keeps — a tool it uses to scramble and grip through the branches. What does the chick have?
answer: Two working claws on each wing
choices: Two working claws on each wing
A second, hidden set of eyelids
A hooked egg-tooth on each wing
A sticky pad under each wingtip
context: Hoatzin chicks are born with two functional claws on each wing and use them to clamber through branches over the water. They are the only living birds with working wing-claws, a trait they lose as adults. Source: https://www.aip.org/inside-science/the-baby-birds-that-use-wing-claws-to-climb-through-the-amazon  (Legend.)

question: A snake glides toward a hoatzin nest hung on a branch above the river, and the bald, flightless chick is cornered with nowhere to run. What does the chick do to survive?
answer: It flings itself off the branch and escapes underwater
choices: It flings itself off the branch and escapes underwater
It plays dead and lies limp in the nest
It shrieks without pause to summon both parents
It presses flat against the bark and holds still
context: When a predator threatens the nest, a hoatzin chick drops from the branch into the water below and swims to safety underwater — in tanks the chicks swim by moving both wings together in a breast-stroke-like motion — before later climbing back up to the nest. Source: https://www.aip.org/inside-science/the-baby-birds-that-use-wing-claws-to-climb-through-the-amazon  (Legend.)

question: The hoatzin eats mostly leaves and, alone among birds, breaks them down by fermenting them with bacteria in a huge crop — the same slow process that works in a cow's stomach. Among the people who share the Amazon with it, this leaf-eater has earned a blunt nickname. What do the locals call it?
answer: The 'stinkbird'
choices: The 'stinkbird'
The 'river ghost'
The 'leaf dragon'
The 'thunder crow'
context: The hoatzin is the only bird known to digest its leafy diet by foregut fermentation, with bacteria in an enlarged crop breaking down the leaves much as in a cow. The fermenting leaves give it a disagreeable, manure-like smell, earning it the nickname 'stinkbird'; because it smells so bad, locals only hunt it for food in times of dire need. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoatzin  (Legend.)

question: Corner a North American hognose snake and, when its threats fail, it puts on a shocking show: it writhes, convulses, flips belly-up, gapes its mouth, and lets its tongue loll out — then goes limp and still. What is the harmless snake pretending to be?
answer: Freshly dead and rotting
choices: Freshly dead and rotting
A venomous coral snake
A tangled clump of roots
A much larger snake
context: The hognose snake (genus Heterodon) is famous for this theatrical death-feign — belly-up, mouth agape, tongue lolling out. It is one of the animal kingdom's most committed fake-death acts. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_hognose_snake

question: A hognose snake lies belly-up in the grass, 'dead' — tongue lolling, mouth gaping. You gently flip it right-side up onto its belly to check. The instant its feet-less body settles upright, what does the hognose do?
answer: Immediately rolls straight back onto its back
choices: Immediately rolls straight back onto its back
Bolts away at full speed
Bites the hand that touched it
Freezes stiff as a stick
context: The act is so committed that a hognose insists on being 'dead': turn it belly-down and it flops right back over, as if a corpse could only possibly be lying on its back. Source: https://animals.howstuffworks.com/snakes/hognose-snake.htm

question: A hognose snake isn't just lying still to look dead — it goes further to smell and look convincingly like a rotting corpse. Beyond flipping belly-up with a lolling tongue, what extra grisly step does it add to sell the death?
answer: Smears foul musk and bleeds from its mouth
choices: Smears foul musk and bleeds from its mouth
Sheds its skin in one fast piece
Puffs its whole body up like a balloon
Rattles the dry tip of its tail
context: The hognose smears foul-smelling musk from its cloaca and can even rupture blood vessels to bleed from its mouth and cloaca — making the 'corpse' look and smell genuinely rotten to a predator. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_hognose_snake

question: The hognose snake gets its name from an upturned, hardened scale at the very tip of its nose. In sandy soil, the snake puts this odd snout to work like a tool. What does it do with it?
answer: Shovels toads out of the sand
choices: Shovels toads out of the sand
Cracks open bird eggs
Scrapes bark off logs
Combs seeds from grass
context: The upturned, keeled rostral scale at the tip of the snout works like a little shovel, letting the hognose dig burrowing toads out of sandy soil. Source: https://srelherp.uga.edu/snakes/eastern-hognose-snake/

question: The eastern hognose snake is a toad specialist, but toads have two defenses: they gulp air to balloon up too big to swallow, and their skin oozes powerful poison. The hognose beats the poison with enlarged adrenal glands. How does it defeat the balloon trick?
answer: Enlarged rear teeth puncture and deflate the toad
choices: Enlarged rear teeth puncture and deflate the toad
It swallows the puffed toad whole anyway
It waits days for the toad to shrink
It squeezes the toad in tight coils
context: A puffed-up toad is meant to be un-swallowable, but the hognose has enlarged rear teeth that puncture and deflate it. Enlarged adrenal glands pump out hormones to counter the toad's skin toxins, and mild rear-fang venom helps subdue it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_hognose_snake

question: About the size of a small dog and weighing only 9 to 16 kilograms, this stocky black-and-white African weasel-relative holds the Guinness World Record as the 'most fearless animal' for standing its ground against lions instead of running. Name it.
answer: The honey badger
choices: The honey badger
The wolverine
The Tasmanian devil
The African civet
context: The honey badger (Mellivora capensis) is the largest land mustelid in Africa yet weighs only about 9 to 16 kg. Its reputation for standing up to far larger predators earned the Guinness listing. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey_badger ; https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/honey-badger-guide  (Legend.)

question: The ground of the African dry season bakes rock-hard in the sun, yet a honey badger fleeing or chasing prey can vanish underground almost on the spot. Roughly how long does it take one to dig a fresh burrow into that hard-packed earth?
answer: About 10 minutes
choices: About 10 minutes
About half a day
About three days
About two weeks
context: Honey badgers are among the animal kingdom's best diggers and can tunnel a burrow into hard, sun-baked ground in about 10 minutes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey_badger

question: A honey badger raids a wild beehive for larvae and honey and stays there tearing it open while hundreds of bees sting it, barely reacting. What is its hide actually like, that lets it endure the stings, porcupine quills, and even a machete blow in a fight?
answer: Skin about 6 millimeters thick and rubbery
choices: Skin about 6 millimeters thick and rubbery
A thin skin backed by a dense pad of fat
A hide sheathed in overlapping keratin plates
A hide coated in a thick protective mucus
context: The skin on a honey badger's neck is roughly 6 mm (a quarter inch) thick and tough and rubbery enough to shrug off bee stings, quills, and machete cuts. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey_badger

question: Researchers Colleen and Keith Begg in the Kalahari watched a puff adder bite a honey badger in the face. The badger collapsed and lay as if dead for about two hours. What happened next?
answer: It woke, got up, and returned to finish eating the snake that bit it
choices: It woke, got up, and returned to finish eating the snake that bit it
It was carried off by a jackal before it could recover
It stayed down and did not survive the venom
Its mate dragged it into a burrow to sleep off the bite
context: Documented by Begg & Begg in National Geographic's 'Snake Killers: Honey Badgers of the Kalahari.' The badger passed out for about two hours, then recovered and finished its meal; full recovery came within about five hours. A legendary but observed event. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=chtdRCrZKuw

question: Cobra venom paralyzes prey by targeting a muscle receptor, but on a honey badger the same venom has little effect. Pigs and hedgehogs independently evolved almost the identical defense. What protects the honey badger?
answer: A charged amino acid swapped into the receptor's toxin-binding site
choices: A charged amino acid swapped into the receptor's toxin-binding site
The muscle receptor is missing from its cells entirely
It grows extra receptors so the venom spreads too thin to work
Its receptors only change shape after the venom binds, shaking it loose
context: Drabeck et al. (2015), 'Why the honey badger don't care,' found a positively charged amino acid substituted into the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor's binding site, so the venom can't attach. Pigs and hedgehogs arrived at almost the same solution separately. Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25796346/

question: A honeybee colony runs like a single city of tens of thousands. Nearly all the bees are sterile females who do every job -- foraging, building, nursing, guarding. What is the name for these worker-bee females who run the whole hive?
answer: Workers
choices: Workers
Drones
Queens
Nymphs
context: A colony is overwhelmingly sterile female workers; a small hive holds about 20,000 bees, a large one can top 100,000, with one queen and a few hundred male drones. Source: https://www.mdbka.com/bee-information/ ; https://canr.udel.edu/maarec/honey-bee-biology/the-colony-and-its-organization/

question: A honeybee finds a rich patch of flowers and flies home. Back on the comb, in the crowded dark, she runs a tight figure-eight over and over: a straight dash down the middle, a fast shudder of her whole body, then a loop back to start again, while her hivemates crowd close to read her. What is this famous move called?
answer: The waggle dance
choices: The waggle dance
The swarm call
The scent trail
The nectar hum
context: The returning forager traces a figure-eight on the vertical comb, running a straight line while shaking her abdomen, then looping back to repeat it -- a symbolic message to her hivemates. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance  (Legend.)

question: When a honeybee does her waggle dance on the vertical comb, the straight middle run points at an angle. That angle is not random -- it is a code for one specific piece of information the other bees need before they fly out. What does the angle of the run tell them?
answer: Which direction to fly, measured from the sun
choices: Which direction to fly, measured from the sun
How many bees to send out
How sweet the nectar is
Which flower species to seek
context: The angle of the waggle run relative to straight-up equals the angle to the flowers relative to the sun: waggle straight up means fly toward the sun; a run 45 degrees left means fly 45 degrees left of the sun. Source: https://www.planetbee.org/post/the-waggle-dance-bees-high-tech-navigation-system ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance  (Legend.)

question: A honeybee's waggle run encodes direction in its angle. But a dancer varies one other thing too -- sometimes a brief, snappy shudder, sometimes one drawn out far longer. What does the LENGTH of the waggle run encode?
answer: The distance to the flowers
choices: The distance to the flowers
The wind speed outside
The number of open blooms
The time of day to leave
context: The longer she waggles, the farther the food: a short waggle means the flowers are close, a long one means a longer flight. Direction lives in the angle, distance in the duration. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance  (Legend.)

question: A honeybee's waggle dance points the way to flowers using the sun's angle. Yet she dances deep inside the hive, on a vertical comb, in total darkness -- she cannot see the sky at all. So what does she use in place of the sun to set the angle of her run?
answer: Gravity, treating straight-up as 'toward the sun'
choices: Gravity, treating straight-up as 'toward the sun'
The Earth's magnetic field
The warmth radiating from the hive entrance
The scent drifting in from outside
context: In the dark she substitutes 'straight up' for 'toward the sun,' using gravity as her compass since she cannot see the sky -- an abstract translation from sun-angle to gravity-angle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance  (Legend.)

question: In 1927 Karl von Frisch claimed the honeybee's dance was a true symbolic language, and fellow scientists scoffed -- surely an insect could not tell another insect anything in code. To settle it, he ran a test that would win him a Nobel Prize: he read a dance, then watched where the recruits went. What did the watching bees do that proved him right?
answer: Flew straight to a spot none of them had ever visited
choices: Flew straight to a spot none of them had ever visited
Circled the hive at random until they stumbled on food
Simply followed the dancer back out to the same patch
Waited for a scent trail before leaving the comb
context: Von Frisch proved the dance is a symbolic language: recruits who only watched the dance flew directly to a food source they had never been to, guided solely by the coded angle and duration. He shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen. His 1927 claim of an insect 'language' was widely dismissed at first. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1973/frisch/facts/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_von_Frisch  (Legend.)

question: A queen honeybee and an ordinary worker hatch from eggs so alike you cannot tell them apart. Yet one becomes an egg-laying queen and the other a sterile laborer. The whole difference comes down to what a chosen larva is fed. What is fed to the larva destined to be queen?
answer: Royal jelly
choices: Royal jelly
Extra pollen
Crushed drones
Fermented nectar
context: A queen is made, not born: the chosen larva is fed royal jelly throughout development, while workers are cut off from it after three days. The royal-jelly larva grows into a queen. Source: https://extension.psu.edu/an-introduction-to-queen-honey-bee-development ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_jelly  (Legend.)

question: A prime honeybee queen has one overwhelming job, and she does it at a staggering pace -- each pale egg about half the size of a grain of rice, laid one after another all day long. In a single day, her total output of eggs actually outweighs her own body. About how many does she lay per day?
answer: About 2,000
choices: About 2,000
About 50
About 200
About 40,000
context: In her prime a queen lays about 2,000 eggs a day -- more than her own body weight in eggs daily, each egg about half the size of a grain of rice. Source: https://www.mdbka.com/bee-information/

question: A honeybee needs wax to build her comb, and she does not gather it -- she manufactures it inside her own body. Tiny pale flakes ooze from eight glands on the underside of her abdomen, and she chews and shapes them. But this only works if one condition is met inside the hive. What must the hive be?
answer: Warm, around 95 F
choices: Warm, around 95 F
Humid and misty
Packed with fresh pollen
Crowded shoulder to shoulder
context: Eight glands on the underside of a worker's abdomen secrete flakes of wax, which she chews and shapes -- but the hive must be warm (around 95 F / 35 C) for wax to form. Source: https://www.honeyflow.com/blogs/beekeeping-basics/how-do-bees-make-beeswax ; https://www.buddhabeeapiary.com/blog/honey-bee-wax-comb

question: Honeybee wax is enormously expensive to make: a colony eats about eight pounds of honey to produce a single pound of wax. Given that steep cost, a worker packs her precious wax into storage cells of one particular shape, repeated across the whole comb. What shape is a honeycomb cell?
answer: A hexagon
choices: A hexagon
A circle
A triangle
A square
context: Bees build hexagonal cells because the hexagon stores the most honey using the least wax and is one of the strongest shapes for the material -- and wax is costly, about 8 pounds of honey eaten per 1 pound of wax made. Source: https://www.sciencefriday.com/educational-resources/why-do-bees-build-hexagonal-honeycomb-cells/ ; https://www.vegasbees.com/post/honeybee-feats-of-strength-making-one-pound-of-beeswax

question: When a honeybee stings an animal to defend her hive, it is a one-way trip -- she will not survive it. A wasp can sting again and again and fly off unharmed, but the honeybee dies within minutes of a single sting. What is it about her sting that kills her?
answer: The stinger tears free, ripping out part of her body
choices: The stinger tears free, ripping out part of her body
Her wings lock and she cannot fly
Her venom turns inward and poisons her
She goes permanently blind
context: The honeybee's stinger is barbed like a fishhook, so it lodges in the victim's flesh; when she pulls away it tears free along with part of her abdomen and venom sac -- fatal self-sacrifice for the colony. A wasp's smooth stinger slides out cleanly, so it can sting repeatedly and survive. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/Do-Bees-Die-After-Stinging ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bee_sting  (Legend.)

question: A honeybee flies over a meadow that looks, to us, like a scatter of plain-colored flowers. To her it is lit with glowing bull's-eyes and lines pointing straight into each bloom, guiding her to the nectar. She sees these hidden 'landing strips' because her eyes pick up a band of light ours cannot. What light is that?
answer: Ultraviolet
choices: Ultraviolet
Infrared
X-rays
Radio waves
context: Bees see ultraviolet light invisible to humans; their receptors are tuned to ultraviolet, blue, and green. Flowers like buttercups, sunflowers, and pansies reveal UV 'nectar guides' -- landing strips and bull's-eyes -- only under UV light. Source: https://apiaryproject.com/blog/honey-bee-vision-uv-compound-eyes-how-bees-see ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nectar_guide

question: A drone honeybee hatches from an egg the queen never fertilized -- his whole body built from her genes alone, just 16 chromosomes where his sisters carry 32. Because that single unfertilized egg had only one parent behind it, one kind of blood relative that every worker and queen possesses is, for a drone, flatly impossible. Which relative can a drone never have?
answer: A father
choices: A father
A brother
A daughter
A grandfather
context: This is haplodiploidy: in honeybees a fertilized egg becomes a female, an unfertilized egg becomes a male. So a drone develops from an egg with no sperm at all -- he is haploid, carrying only his mother's 16 chromosomes, and has literally no father. Yet he still has a maternal grandfather, because his mother hatched from a fertilized egg with two parents. He can also father daughters: every one of his roughly 10 million sperm is a genetic clone of his single genome. The 'no father, but a grandfather' family tree even traces out a Fibonacci sequence of ancestors -- 1, 1, 2, 3, 5. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_(bee) -- drones haploid (16 chromosomes), arrhenotokous parthenogenesis, no father, maternal grandfather, Fibonacci ancestry, ~10M clonal sperm; haplodiploidy corroborated by multiple bee-genetics sources.

question: For years scientists genuinely fought over whether the waggle dance MEANS anything -- Adrian Wenner insisted bees just sniff out food by smell and the dancing is noise. In 1989 Axel Michelsen ended the argument with one device: a small dancer of brass and beeswax, its razor-blade wing buzzing near 280 times a second, sent onto the comb. What did this thing do that settled it?
answer: Recruited real bees to a target spot only it had named
choices: Recruited real bees to a target spot only it had named
Released the exact floral scent the foragers were tracking
Out-danced the live bees until they abandoned their own runs
Proved the smell trail worked even with the dance removed
context: This was a real scientific fight, not a settled story. Von Frisch had claimed in the 1940s that the dance was a symbolic code; in 1967 Adrian Wenner mounted a serious challenge -- bees, he argued, find food by following floral and hive odors, and the dance carries no information. To test it, Axel Michelsen's team built a mechanical robot bee out of brass and beeswax, with a razor-blade wing that buzzed at about 280 cycles per second (Hz). Programmed to perform specific waggle dances, the robot successfully steered real recruits to a chosen spot in the field, proving the dance itself -- not smell -- carries the location. James Gould's manipulated-dance experiments pointed the same way. Source: link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10739-005-0552-1 (The Bee Battles: von Frisch, Wenner and the dance-language controversy); Michelsen robot-bee corroborated via link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00166696 and the ACP Social Insects summary -- 280 Hz brass-and-beeswax robot recruited real bees to a target.

question: In a honeypot ant colony deep under the desert, a few special workers are fed nectar by their sisters again and again, far past a normal meal. What happens to the body of one of these gorged ants?
answer: Its abdomen swells into a round, translucent globe the size of a grape, full of honey
choices: Its abdomen swells into a round, translucent globe the size of a grape, full of honey
It grows a second pair of wings and flies off to start a new colony
It sprouts a hard armored shell to guard the nest entrance
It turns bright red to warn birds that it tastes bitter
context: These gorged workers are called repletes. Fed liquid nectar until their crop stretches, a replete becomes a living storage jar for the whole colony. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeypot_ant

question: A honeypot ant replete has been fed so much nectar that its grape-sized belly is far too heavy to carry — it can no longer walk. Where does it spend the coming months?
answer: Hanging motionless upside down from the ceiling of the underground nest
choices: Hanging motionless upside down from the ceiling of the underground nest
Buried in a sealed mud cell at the very bottom of the nest
Floating in a shallow pool the workers dig near the entrance
Riding on the backs of ordinary workers who carry it from room to room
context: Too swollen to move, repletes hang from the nest roof — a wall of living honey jars overhead — sometimes for months. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myrmecocystus_mexicanus

question: During a long desert drought, a hungry honeypot ant approaches one of the swollen repletes hanging from the ceiling and strokes its antennae. What does the replete do in response?
answer: Regurgitates a drop of stored liquid from its crop into the hungry ant's mouth
choices: Regurgitates a drop of stored liquid from its crop into the hungry ant's mouth
Splits open along its belly so the colony can scoop the honey out
Releases a scent that calls other workers to come and share
Drops from the ceiling and rolls toward the nest entrance
context: Nestmates 'milk' the repletes this way, and the whole colony drinks from these living jars through droughts and winter famines. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeypot_ant

question: In the Australian desert the Arrernte people call a swollen honeypot ant 'Yarumpa,' and traditionally the women and children go digging for them. What are they after when they carefully unearth the repletes?
answer: To eat the swollen amber abdomens as a sweet — a rare source of sugar in the desert
choices: To eat the swollen amber abdomens as a sweet — a rare source of sugar in the desert
To collect the ants as bait for catching desert lizards
To grind the whole ants into a paste that keeps flies away
To move the colony to a wetter patch of ground before the dry season
context: Aboriginal Australians dig up the repletes of Camponotus inflatus and eat the honey-filled abdomens, a natural candy in a land with little sugar. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camponotus_inflatus

question: The pinkish-brown, cinnamon-fawn bird of Europe and Asia struts along the ground, then throws up a tall crest tipped with black that opens like a fan when it lands or takes alarm. Which bird is it?
answer: The hoopoe
choices: The hoopoe
The bee-eater
The nightjar
The waxwing
context: The hoopoe (Upupa epops) is unmistakable: cinnamon-fawn body, black-and-white barred wings, and a fan-like crest tipped with black that pops up in alarm, courtship, or on landing, then folds sleekly flat while the bird forages. In flight it bounds along like a giant butterfly, its broad wings half-closing at the end of each beat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_hoopoe

question: A hoopoe mother crouches in a cramped hole-nest with her eggs, unable to flee a predator or a creeping tide of parasites. During breeding, her preen gland switches from ordinary oil to a thick brown brew she paints over her feathers and eggs. What is startling about this breeding-season brew?
answer: It reeks of rotting meat
choices: It reeks of rotting meat
It glows faintly in the dark
It hardens into a shell
It tastes bitter to the tongue
context: During nesting, the female hoopoe's uropygial (preen) gland switches to a thick brown liquid that smells of rotting meat, and she paints it over her feathers and eggs to repel predators and parasites. The stink comes largely from dimethyl sulfide, and the secretion is actually made by symbiotic Enterococcus bacteria living in her gland that also produce antibacterial chemicals shielding the eggs from harmful microbes. Sources: https://www.audubon.org/news/the-hoopoe-emissary-kings-secreter-stink ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2842625/

question: A hoopoe mother smears foul secretion to guard the nest, but her chicks come armed too. From about six days old, when an intruder looms at the hole, a hoopoe chick hisses like a snake and jabs upward with its bill. What is its second, grosser weapon?
answer: Squirt streams of liquid feces
choices: Squirt streams of liquid feces
Flash a bright warning patch
Puff up to twice its size
Play dead until it leaves
context: From about six days old, hoopoe chicks add a second gross weapon to the mother's stink: they turn their tails toward an intruder and squirt streams of liquid feces at it while hissing snake-like and jabbing upward with the bill. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_hoopoe

question: Wading through the shallows on ancient walking legs, hard brown domed shell like an upturned bowl and a long spike for a tail, the horseshoe crab wears a name that lies: it is no crab at all. Its closest living relatives are:
answer: spiders and scorpions
choices: spiders and scorpions
clams and oysters
true crabs and lobsters
jellyfish and corals
context: The horseshoe crab is a chelicerate, sharing a lineage with arachnids rather than crustaceans — which is why it is nicknamed the 'sea spider.' Source: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life (digitalatlasofancientlife.org); Defenders of Wildlife.

question: The horseshoe crab has crawled the shallows so long that its body has barely changed in about 450 million years — surviving all five of Earth's great mass extinctions. It was already an old animal, walking the seafloor, before the first dinosaurs ever appeared. About how big is that head start over the dinosaurs?
answer: more than 200 million years
choices: more than 200 million years
about 20 thousand years
about 5 million years
more than 2 billion years
context: Horseshoe crabs are 'living fossils' — their form has barely changed in about 450 million years, meaning they walked the shallows more than 200 million years before the first dinosaurs and survived all five great mass extinctions. Source: Defenders of Wildlife.

question: A wave dumps a horseshoe crab onto its back, legs kicking uselessly at the sky — a deadly spot, since it can dry out or be picked off. It has no stinger and no venom, yet the long spiky tail (the telson) is what saves it. How?
answer: stabs it into the sand and levers itself over
choices: stabs it into the sand and levers itself over
grips a rock to haul itself upright
spins in circles to dig a righting pit
pushes off a neighboring crab's shell
context: Contrary to popular belief, the telson is neither a stinger nor poisonous; the crab jabs it into the ground and uses it as a lever to flip right-side-up when stranded on its back, and to steer while swimming. Source: South Carolina DNR; Maryland DNR.

question: When a horseshoe crab is wounded and its blood meets the air, it wells up not red but a startling BLUE. What does its blood use to carry oxygen - the reason for that color?
answer: a copper-based protein
choices: a copper-based protein
iron-rich hemoglobin
dissolved chlorophyll
liquid silver droplets
context: Instead of iron-based red hemoglobin, horseshoe crab blood uses a copper-based protein called hemocyanin to carry oxygen; the copper turns the blood blue when it meets air. Source: The Horseshoe Crab (horseshoecrab.org); Britannica.  (Legend.)

question: Before a vaccine or an injectable medicine can be trusted, drug makers dose a sample with a fluid drawn from an animal — and if bacterial toxins are present, that fluid clots into a warning gel. That toxin-trapping fluid comes from the blue blood of the:
answer: horseshoe crab
choices: horseshoe crab
electric eel
sea cucumber
giant clam
context: Cells in horseshoe crab blood called amebocytes instantly clot into a gel when they touch bacterial toxins, trapping the germs. This 'LAL' test checks that injectable medicines and vaccines, including COVID-19 vaccines, are free of contamination. Source: The Horseshoe Crab (horseshoecrab.org); NCBI LAL technology review.  (Legend.)

question: Look closely at a horseshoe crab and you find eyes almost everywhere — two big compound eyes on top, small simple eyes, a pair underneath near the mouth, and light sensors on the tail. Add them all up and this animal has how many eyes?
answer: ten
choices: ten
two
five
twenty
context: A horseshoe crab has ten eyes scattered over its body — two large compound eyes (each with about 1,000 light-sensing units), several simple eyes, two on its underside near the mouth, and light sensors on its tail. Source: Florida FWC; Maryland DNR.

question: On spring high tides near the full and new moon each May, thousands of horseshoe crabs bury millions of green eggs on Delaware Bay's beaches. A threatened shorebird times a 9,000-mile Arctic migration to arrive and gorge on those eggs. In two weeks of feasting, the red knot does what to its own body?
answer: nearly doubles its body weight
choices: nearly doubles its body weight
grows an extra set of wings
turns its feathers bright green
sheds its entire skeleton
context: The fat-rich horseshoe crab eggs let the threatened red knot, mid-migration to its Arctic breeding grounds, nearly double its body weight in about two weeks — fuel it needs to finish the flight. Each female crab buries clusters of about 3,000–5,000 eggs. Source: Delaware DNREC; New Jersey DEP.

question: A hummingbird works a flowerbed, threading from bloom to bloom with a control in the air that no other bird can match at a flower. What flight feat sets the hummingbird apart from every other bird family?
answer: Truly hover in place and fly backward
choices: Truly hover in place and fly backward
Glide for hours without a single wingbeat
Dive faster than any other bird
Sleep in the air while still flying
context: The hummingbird is the only bird family that can truly hover and even fly backward (and briefly upside down) — no other bird can. Source: Audubon, 'Hummingbird Flight Is Like Nothing Else in the Bird World.'  (Legend.)

question: A hummingbird hangs motionless at a flower, its wings a gray blur you can hear but barely see. That blur is what the bird is named for. About how fast are those wings actually beating in ordinary hovering?
answer: About 50 times every second
choices: About 50 times every second
About 5 times every second
About twice every second
About once every second
context: In ordinary hovering a hummingbird beats its wings roughly 50 times a second — the blur that makes the humming sound it's named for. Source: BBC Science Focus; Science World, 'Flight of the Hummingbird.'

question: Every other bird gets its lift only on the DOWNstroke; the upbeat is dead, wasted time. A hovering hummingbird cheats this — its wing pushes air down on the way FORWARD and again on the way BACK, tracing a shape in the air. What figure does the wingtip trace to make lift on both halves of the beat?
answer: A flat figure-8
choices: A flat figure-8
A tight vertical circle
A straight up-and-down line
A wide sideways oval
context: The hummingbird's wingtip traces a flat figure-8, and the wing rotates at the shoulder so both the forward and the backward stroke tilt to push air down — unlike the down-only stroke of every other bird. Source: BBC Science Focus; AskNature hummingbird hover strategy.

question: Holding a body dead-still in the air takes enormous power, so a hummingbird is built almost entirely around its flight engine. Compared with an ordinary bird, whose breast muscles are a modest slice of its weight, how much of a hummingbird is breast muscle?
answer: Almost a third of its body weight
choices: Almost a third of its body weight
About a tenth of its body weight
Barely a twentieth of its body weight
Roughly two-thirds of its body weight
context: A hummingbird's breast (pectoral) flight muscles make up almost a third of its body weight — twice the muscle fraction of an ordinary bird. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'Super pecs and 1,200 heartbeats per minute.'

question: Most birds barely bother with the upstroke — it makes almost no lift. A hummingbird is different: it drives a big upstroke muscle, the supracoracoideus, so the lifting UPbeat pulls real weight. About how much of a hovering hummingbird's total lift comes from that upstroke?
answer: About a quarter of its lift
choices: About a quarter of its lift
Almost none of its lift
About half of its lift
Nearly all of its lift
context: Unlike other birds, a hummingbird's big upstroke muscle (the supracoracoideus) makes the lifting upbeat supply about a quarter of its total lift — the rest of the bird world barely uses the upstroke at all. Source: BBC Science Focus; Tough Little Birds, 'hummingbird flight.'

question: To hold itself frozen in the air at a flower, a hovering hummingbird runs its engine at a rate that would kill almost anything else. A human heart beats about 80 times a minute. How fast does the hummingbird's heart hammer while it hovers?
answer: Around 1,200 beats a minute
choices: Around 1,200 beats a minute
Around 200 beats a minute
Around 500 beats a minute
Around 90 beats a minute
context: A hovering hummingbird's heart beats around 1,200 times a minute — versus about 80 in a human. Source: BBC Science Focus; AnimalCorner hummingbird anatomy.  (Legend.)

question: Hovering burns so much fuel that a hummingbird can't store enough to last the night, so each night, to keep from freezing before dawn, it lets its whole body go cold and lets its racing heart slow far down. That daytime heart pounds around 1,200 beats a minute. About how far down does it drop during this nightly shutdown?
answer: To as few as ~50 beats a minute
choices: To as few as ~50 beats a minute
To around 90 beats a minute
To around 130 beats a minute
To around 180 beats a minute
context: Hovering costs so much that a hummingbird cannot survive the night on its reserves, so it drops into torpor — heart falling from ~1,200 beats a minute to as few as ~50, body going cold until dawn. Source: forumscience.com; JEB, 'Flight Thermogenesis and Energy Conservation in Hovering Hummingbirds.'  (Legend.)

question: A small creature hovers at a flowerbed on a summer afternoon, wings beating so fast — about 85 times a second — that they blur into a hum, and its long tongue probes each bloom for nectar. Passersby swear a tiny hummingbird has strayed into the garden. But it is no bird at all. What kind of animal is it?
answer: A moth
choices: A moth
A bee
A hoverfly
A bat
context: The hummingbird hawkmoth (Sphingidae) hovers at flowers exactly like a hummingbird, beating its wings about 85 times a second — faster than a hummingbird's ~50 — so people mistake the insect for a tiny bird. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology jeb230920; A-Z Animals.

question: Hummingbirds and hawkmoths hang still at a flower and sip nectar with the very same flat figure-8 wingstroke — yet the two lineages are only distantly related and each worked it out on its own. Across the whole animal kingdom, how many separate times has true hovering flight been invented this way?
answer: Only about four times
choices: Only about four times
Hundreds of times
In nearly every flying group
Just once, then inherited
context: True hovering evolved independently only about four times in nectar feeders — hummingbirds, some bats, hoverflies, and hawkmoths — a classic case of convergent evolution onto the same figure-8 solution. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology jeb230920; PBS Nature.

question: A hoverfly hangs dead-still in the summer air, striped bold black-and-yellow like a wasp, yet this two-winged fly has no sting at all — only the colors. Why do those borrowed stripes keep the harmless hoverfly alive?
answer: Predators burned once by wasps avoid anything striped like one
choices: Predators burned once by wasps avoid anything striped like one
The stripes reflect sunlight and hide its outline in the glare
The pattern startles a bird into flinching just long enough
Wasps recognize the stripes and defend it as one of their own
context: The hoverfly wears the black-and-yellow stripes of a wasp or bee as pure bluff — Batesian mimicry — despite having no sting at all; predators that have learned to avoid stinging wasps leave the lookalike alone. Source: RHS, 'Hoverflies: Identification & Control'; Wikipedia, 'Hoverfly.'

question: A dragonfly can hang and dart with rare precision because, unlike a hummingbird's two wings, it has four — and it can steer each one on its own. It saves flapping power with a specific timing trick between its front and back pairs. What does the dragonfly do with them to cut the energy cost of hovering?
answer: Beats the front and back wings out of phase
choices: Beats the front and back wings out of phase
Beats all four wings in perfect unison
Holds the back wings still and beats only the front
Folds the front wings and glides on the back
context: A dragonfly hovers with four independently controlled wings; when its front and back wings beat out of phase (crossing near mid-stroke) it saves flapping power, letting it hang and dart precisely. Source: Royal Society Interface, Usherwood & Lehmann; Royal Society Open Science rsos.202275.

question: A kestrel appears to hover over a field, its body hanging pinned in one spot as it scans the grass for voles below. Unlike a hummingbird, it isn't truly beating its wings in still air to stay put. How does the kestrel actually hold its place?
answer: It faces into a headwind and flaps just enough to cancel it
choices: It faces into a headwind and flaps just enough to cancel it
It hangs on a warm updraft rising off the sunlit field
It locks its wings and glides in a tight circle
It grips the air with specially slotted feathers
context: The kestrel 'wind-hovers' by facing into a headwind and flapping just fast enough to cancel it — not truly beating in still air — which is why its old English name is the 'windhover.' Source: Birdfact, 'Kestrel Hovering'; Opposite View Wildlife.  (Legend.)

question: For 180 years textbooks said a hummingbird pumps nectar up its grooved tongue by capillary action, the way a paper towel wicks water. High-speed film of the tongue actually hitting nectar killed that idea. What is the tongue really doing when its tips touch the nectar?
answer: Its flattened grooves spring open and suck up a column of nectar
choices: Its flattened grooves spring open and suck up a column of nectar
Its outer surface wicks a thin film upward by capillary action
Its muscular walls squeeze in a slow wave to push nectar back
Its hollow core draws nectar up like a straw under suction
context: A 2015 study (Alejandro Rico-Guevara, Tai-Hsi Fan, Margaret Rubega, Proc. R. Soc. B) high-speed-filmed 18 species and falsified 180 years of capillary-action textbook claims. The tongue is squeezed flat as it extends; the instant its grooved tips touch nectar, the collapsed grooves spring back open, and that elastic re-expansion actively sucks up a column of nectar an order of magnitude faster than capillarity could. It works as an elastic micropump, not a paper towel, which is what lets a hummingbird lick a flower up to ~20 times a second. Source: Rico-Guevara, Fan & Rubega, 'Hummingbird tongues are elastic micropumps,' Proc. R. Soc. B 2015 (royalsocietypublishing.org; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26290074).

question: Every one of the ~360 living hummingbird species lives only in the Americas, so the family looks purely New World. Then paleontologist Gerald Mayr described 32-million-year-old hovering, nectar-feeding hummingbirds from a fossil site far outside that range. Which region turned up those oldest known hummingbird fossils?
answer: Southern Germany
choices: Southern Germany
Southern Ecuador
Southern Mexico
Southern Brazil
context: In 2004 Gerald Mayr described Eurotrochilus, a stem-group hummingbird already built for hovering and nectar-feeding, from ~32-million-year-old (early Oligocene, Rupelian) specimens at the Wiesloch-Frauenweiler clay pit in southern Germany, with more later found in France and Poland. So hummingbirds hovered over Old World flowers 30+ million years ago, then vanished from that hemisphere entirely, leaving every living species in the Americas. The family that seems quintessentially American left its oldest fossils in Europe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurotrochilus (Mayr, 2004); corroborated en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hummingbird.

question: A tiny bird of Cuba, locally called the zunzuncito, is the smallest bird alive on Earth -- a male weighs less than a penny. What is it?
answer: The bee hummingbird
choices: The bee hummingbird
The pygmy owl
The golden-crowned kinglet
The zebra finch
context: The bee hummingbird (Mellisuga helenae) averages about 5.5 cm (2 inches) long and under 2 grams -- lighter than a penny -- making it not only the smallest bird but the smallest warm-blooded animal on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bee_hummingbird

question: Other birds can hang in the air only by facing into a stiff wind, and every one of them can travel in just one direction: forward. A hummingbird needs no wind to hold its spot -- and it can do something no other bird on Earth can. What can it do that they cannot?
answer: Fly backward
choices: Fly backward
Sleep in flight
Breathe underwater
Glide for miles
context: A hummingbird is the only bird that can truly hover in place and fly backward. Other birds can hang briefly in a headwind, but only the hummingbird can reverse in mid-air. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/birds/facts-about-hummingbirds

question: Most birds only get lift on the downstroke, pushing air down. A hummingbird can hover because it sweeps its wings in a special path that makes lift on BOTH the forward and the return stroke. What shape does the wingtip trace?
answer: A figure-eight
choices: A figure-eight
A tight circle
A straight up-and-down line
A rising spiral
context: By sweeping its wings in a figure-eight, a hummingbird generates lift on both the forward stroke and the backstroke -- unlike other birds, which only get lift pushing down. This is what lets it hover and reverse. Source: https://news.oregonstate.edu/news/research-shows-hummingbird-flight-evolutionary-marvel

question: A hummingbird's tiny body runs so hot that it burns fuel almost as fast as it takes it in -- it must sip nectar every 10 to 15 minutes or starve. About how much of its OWN body weight in sugar does it eat in a single day?
answer: About half
choices: About half
About a tenth
About a fiftieth
About a thousandth
context: A hummingbird eats roughly half its own body weight in sugar every day and must feed every 10 to 15 minutes -- it would starve overnight if it simply slept. Source: https://birdwatchingbuzz.com/hummingbird-heart-rate/

question: To power a body that hovers and burns fuel this fast, a hummingbird's heart races far beyond anything a human could survive. Roughly how many times can it beat in a single minute?
answer: Over 1,200
choices: Over 1,200
Around 300
Around 70
Around 12
context: A hummingbird's heart can beat over 1,200 times a minute (rates up to about 1,260 bpm have been recorded), and it breathes roughly 250 times a minute even at rest. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/blog/10-incredible-hummingbird-facts/

question: A bee hummingbird builds a cup nest only about an inch across and lays two of the tiniest eggs of any bird. What everyday object is each egg about the size of?
answer: A coffee bean
choices: A coffee bean
A chicken egg
A golf ball
A grape
context: A bee hummingbird lays two eggs, each about the size of a coffee bean, in a cup nest only about 2.5 cm (1 inch) across. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bee_hummingbird

question: A hummingbird holds so little fuel that just sleeping through a cold night would starve it. Instead it enters a nightly near-shutdown, dropping its heart rate from over a thousand beats a minute to as few as forty. What is this survival state called?
answer: Torpor
choices: Torpor
Hibernation
Molting
Migration
context: In torpor a hummingbird's heart rate can fall from over 1,000 to as few as ~40-50 beats a minute, cutting energy use by about 95 percent -- letting it survive cold nights on its tiny fuel reserves. Source: https://www.science.org/content/article/survive-frigid-nights-hummingbirds-cool-themselves-record-low-temperatures
