question: Before it crosses the Gulf of Mexico, a ruby-throated hummingbird spends weeks gorging so heavily that it changes its own body dramatically for the 18-to-22-hour nonstop flight. What does it do to fuel the trip?
answer: Nearly doubles its body weight in fat
choices: Nearly doubles its body weight in fat
Grows a second set of flight feathers
Enlarges its heart permanently
Hollows out its bones for lightness
context: A ruby-throated hummingbird crosses the Gulf of Mexico in a single nonstop flight of up to 500 miles, flying alone for 18 to 22 hours -- nearly doubling its body weight in fat beforehand to fuel the trip. Source: https://www.reconnectwithnature.org/news-events/the-buzz/5-things-about-hummingbirds

question: For its backstroke to make lift, a hummingbird has to flip its whole wing upside down between strokes. It manages this by twisting the wing at one joint through nearly 180 degrees -- the arm bone itself rotating. Which joint does the twisting?
answer: The shoulder
choices: The shoulder
The wrist
The elbow
The knuckle
context: To flip its wing over for the lift-generating backstroke, a hummingbird rotates its wing at the shoulder nearly 180 degrees -- the humerus itself twists. Source: https://www.threads.com/@museumofscience/post/DORoQMhiO9l/

question: The diving peregrine falcon is often called the fastest animal on Earth, and relative to its own size it covers about 200 of its body lengths every second. In his courtship dive, a male Anna's hummingbird sets the highest length-relative speed known in any vertebrate. How many of his own body lengths does he cover each second?
context: During his courtship dive, a male Anna's hummingbird covers 385 times its own body length every second -- the highest length-relative speed known in any vertebrate, beating even the diving peregrine falcon (about 200 body lengths per second). Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/annas-hummingbird-outflies-falcons-and-fighter-pilots  (Legend.)

question: A fighter pilot in a hard turn blacks out somewhere around 9 g -- nine times the pull of gravity. A male Anna's hummingbird yanks out of its steep courtship dive so violently that its tiny body takes a sudden jolt of g-force too. Roughly how many g's does the bird pull in that pull-up?
answer: Nearly 10 g
choices: Nearly 10 g
About 3 g
About 30 g
About 100 g
context: Pulling out of its courtship dive, an Anna's hummingbird endures nearly 10 times the force of gravity -- more than a fighter pilot endures before blacking out. Source: https://www.sciencenews.org/article/hummingbird-pulls-top-gun-stunts

question: Every other flying vertebrate that lives on nectar still stores fuel the ordinary way. But hummingbirds burn the sugar they just drank almost directly, and researchers traced this to a single change deep in their ancestry, dated to when hovering first evolved. What was that change?
answer: Their ancestor lost a muscle enzyme gene
choices: Their ancestor lost a muscle enzyme gene
Their ancestor gained a second sugar-storing organ
Their ancestor doubled its fat-making capacity
Their ancestor evolved a faster-emptying stomach
context: Osipova and colleagues found that FBP2 (fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 2), a gluconeogenic muscle enzyme, was inactivated in the common ancestor of all living hummingbirds about 48-30 million years ago -- exactly the window when hovering flight and nectar-feeding evolved. When they knocked FBP2 out of bird cells, glycolysis rose and the cells built more mitochondria and respired harder, running more efficiently. So a gene LOSS, not a gain, helped unlock hovering flight. Source: Osipova et al. 2023, Science 379:185, "Loss of a gluconeogenic muscle enzyme contributed to adaptive metabolic traits in hummingbirds."

question: All ~360 hummingbird species alive today live only in the Americas, so scientists long assumed the nectar-hovering lineage arose there. Then Gerald Mayr reexamined tiny long-billed skeletons that had sat misidentified in a museum drawer for years. Dated to ~30 million years ago, the bird he named Eurotrochilus upended that assumption. How?
answer: It lived in Europe, far from the Americas
choices: It lived in Europe, far from the Americas
It chased insects instead of sipping nectar
It could not hover despite a slender bill
It outweighed a present-day carrion crow
context: Mayr described Eurotrochilus in 2004 from Early Oligocene deposits (~28-34 million years ago); more fossils later turned up in Germany, France, and Poland. It already had the diagnostic long nectar bill (~15.5-20 mm, about 2.5x its skull length) and hovering wing structure -- so the nectar-hovering lineage evolved in the Old World and only later vanished there, leaving today's hummingbirds solely in the Americas. The genus name means "unexpected European version of a hummingbird." Source: Mayr 2004; Wikipedia "Eurotrochilus"; Science, "Ancient Hummingbirds Were European."

question: A whale-watcher off New England spots a 40-ton whale with knobbly, bump-covered skin on its head and, sticking out from its sides, the longest limbs of any animal on Earth — pale wings nearly 5 meters long. Which whale is it?
answer: The humpback whale
choices: The humpback whale
The blue whale
The sperm whale
The narwhal
context: The humpback (Megaptera novaeangliae) has the longest flippers of any whale — up to about a third of its whole body, nearly 5 meters (16 feet), the longest limbs of any animal on Earth. Source: https://gentlegiants.is/news/2025/08/03/the-pectoral-fins-of-a-humpback-whale-nature-s-marvels-of-movement-and-communication/

question: Run a hand over a humpback whale's head and you feel rows of round bumps, each about the size of a golf ball. Look closely at one bump and you find something surprising growing out of it:
answer: a single hair, thought to sense the water
choices: a single hair, thought to sense the water
a tiny suction cup for grip
a glowing spot to lure prey
a venomous spine for defense
context: Each knobbly bump on a humpback's head is a tubercle, about golf-ball sized, with one hair sprouting from it — thought to help the whale sense the water flowing around it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: Whale-watchers adore the humpback whale because of what a 40-ton, 17-meter animal does at the surface: it hammers its huge flippers and tail down with cracking booms, and then it does something no crowd forgets:
answer: hurls its whole body out of the water in a leap
choices: hurls its whole body out of the water in a leap
spins on its back for hours like an otter
walks along the seabed on its flippers
builds a floating nest of seaweed
context: Humpbacks slap their flippers and tails against the surface, and breach — hurling their whole bodies out of the water — which is why whale-watchers love them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: The humpback whale's scientific name is Megaptera novaeangliae. The 'novaeangliae' part marks it as a New Englander, from where it was first named — but the 'Megaptera' part honors the single most enormous part of the humpback's body. Which feature does that name celebrate?
answer: its enormous flippers
choices: its enormous flippers
its wide fluked tail
its arched, humped back
its fan-shaped blowhole spray
context: 'Mega-ptera' is Greek for 'giant wing' — the humpback was named for its enormous flippers, the longest limbs of any animal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: A humpback whale is a bus-length animal — up to 17 meters and 40 tons. You would expect it to turn like an oil tanker. Instead, thanks to its giant flippers, it turns like a dolphin: it can spin around inside its own body length, and even do one thing most big whales cannot:
answer: swim backward
choices: swim backward
hold its breath for a whole day
sleep with its whole brain at once
drink seawater safely
context: The humpback's oversized flippers let a 40-ton, 17-meter animal turn inside its own body length like a dolphin, and even swim backward. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: On the winter breeding grounds, humpback whales fill the water with long, eerie song. But the singers are not the whole population — who among the humpbacks actually sings?
answer: only the males
choices: only the males
only the mothers with calves
only the oldest whales
the whole pod together
context: Only male humpbacks sing, and only on the winter breeding grounds — the song is thought to be a mating display, not a message carrying a specific meaning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: A humpback whale's song is not just random moaning. Scientists found it is built like music, with small parts joining into larger ones: 'units' join into phrases, phrases build into themes, and ordered themes make the whole song. And a male will do what with that finished song?
answer: repeat it over and over for hours
choices: repeat it over and over for hours
sing it once, then never again
teach it only to his own calf
trade it for a different male's song
context: A single humpback song runs several minutes, and a male can sing it on repeat for hours — Hawaiian recordings caught sessions lasting up to seven hours. The musical structure was first described by Payne and McVay. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale  (Legend.)

question: When a group of humpback whales finds a school of fish, they hunt with a trap made of air. Diving below the school, the whales blow a rising spiral of bubbles — a curtain the fish will not cross — that herds the school into a tight ball. Then the whole group does what?
answer: lunges up through the middle with mouths open
choices: lunges up through the middle with mouths open
waits for the bubbles to stun the fish
drives the ball toward a second waiting pod
dives deep and lets the fish scatter
context: In bubble-net feeding, humpbacks blow a spiraling curtain of bubbles the fish won't cross, herding them into a ball, then all lunge up through the center with mouths open. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubble-net_feeding  (Legend.)

question: Bubble-net feeding is not something humpback whales are simply born knowing — it is learned and passed from whale to whale, so only some populations do it. In one refinement, a single 'caller' whale contributes something that makes the group strike together:
answer: a trumpeting feeding call that signals everyone to lunge at once
choices: a trumpeting feeding call that signals everyone to lunge at once
a burst of clicks that stuns the fish
a slap of its tail to start the dive
a wall of bubbles twice as tall as the others
context: Bubble-net feeding is learned and culturally transmitted, so only some populations do it; one 'caller' whale even trumpets a feeding call to signal the group to lunge at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubble-net_feeding

question: Here is the strangest thing about humpback whale song: across an entire population, the males don't each invent their own tune. Instead, what do all the males of a population sing — and how does it change?
answer: the same song, and when it changes they all switch together
choices: the same song, and when it changes they all switch together
a new song every night, chosen at random
their mother's song, kept unchanged for life
a fixed song that never changes over generations
context: Every male in a population sings the same song, and when the tune changes the whole population adopts the new version together — a shared culture whales learn from one another. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9428538/  (Legend.)

question: A new hit song among humpback whales spreads like a fashion trend across the ocean. A fresh tune starts near eastern Australia and travels whale-to-whale through New Caledonia, Tonga, the Cook Islands and French Polynesia. Researchers tracked one such song moving in a striking way:
answer: eastward for 14,000 km, all the way to Ecuador
choices: eastward for 14,000 km, all the way to Ecuador
in a loop back to where it began within a season
only among whales that had met face to face
faster than the whales themselves could migrate
context: New humpback songs sweep eastward across the Pacific, tracked whale-to-whale from eastern Australia across 14,000 km all the way to Ecuador — a cultural wave moving through a whole ocean. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9428538/  (Legend.)

question: Engineers copying the humpback whale bolted a row of bumps onto the leading edge of a flipper-shaped wing, then raced it against a smooth one in a wind tunnel. The bumps split the oncoming flow and funnel it into the grooves between them — a trick designers now borrow for turbine blades and fans. What did the bumps buy?
answer: it kept its grip on the flow far past the angle where the smooth wing stalled out
choices: it kept its grip on the flow far past the angle where the smooth wing stalled out
it shed a trailing plume of warm water that the smooth wing could never produce
it hummed a deep note that herded nearby fish straight into the path of the wing
it sprouted a fresh row of bumps to replace any that wore smooth over time
context: The humpback's leading-edge flipper bumps, called tubercles, are a stall-delaying wing device, not decoration. In a landmark 2004 Physics of Fluids study, Miklosovic, Murray, Howle and Fish tested two polycarbonate scale-model flippers — one smooth, one bumped — in a wind tunnel and found the tubercled model delayed the stall angle by about 40% while also increasing lift and cutting drag past stall. The rows of bumps split the incoming water and funnel it into the valleys between them, keeping flow attached at steep angles of attack so a 40-ton whale can bank into tight turns without its flipper stalling like a wing. This 'tubercle effect' has since been applied to wind-turbine blades, fans and airplane wings. Source: Miklosovic, Murray, Howle & Fish (2004), Physics of Fluids, 'Leading-edge tubercles delay stall on humpback whale flippers'; corroborated by Fish & Battle (1995), J. Morphology 225:51-60 (PubMed 7650744) and ScienceDaily 2004-05-12.

question: A humpback whale lunges into a bait ball and takes in a mouthful of water as big as its whole body. Inside the flexible joint between the two halves of its lower jaw sits a grape-sized organ found in 2012, present in no other creature on Earth. What does that never-before-seen organ do?
answer: it feels the jaw swing wide and the throat balloon out, timing the whole lunge
choices: it feels the jaw swing wide and the throat balloon out, timing the whole lunge
it stores a reserve of oxygen that feeds the brain through a long, deep dive
it strains the ocean salt back out of the seawater the whale gulps down
it shapes the deep booming notes the male threads all through his long song
context: Rorqual whales, including the humpback, carry a sensory organ that nothing else on Earth has, discovered only in 2012. Pyenson and colleagues, reporting in Nature, found a grape-sized organ embedded in the fibrous joint between the two unfused halves of the lower jaw. Packed with mechanoreceptors — nerve endings and papillae in a gel-like matrix derived from an ancestral tooth socket — it senses jaw rotation and throat-pouch expansion in real time and feeds that to the brain to choreograph the split-second timing of a lunge: when to open, how far the pouch has filled, and when to clamp shut. Source: Pyenson et al. (2012), Nature 485:498, 'Discovery of a sensory organ that coordinates lunge feeding in rorqual whales' (PubMed 22622577); Smithsonian Insider 2012.

question: Swim back to the age of dinosaurs and you would meet the ichthyosaur cutting through the sea: a smooth body like a dolphin or a tuna, a triangular fin on its back, flippers, and a crescent tail. But one thing set it apart from every fish around it. What was it?
answer: It had to surface to breathe air
choices: It had to surface to breathe air
It had gills like the fish it hunted
It never left the deep water
It laid its eggs on the seafloor
context: The ichthyosaur was a reptile, not a fish. It breathed air, so it rose to the surface the way a dolphin does today -- yet dolphins would not appear for another 200 million years. Source: Simple English Wikipedia, Ichthyosaur.

question: The ichthyosaur carried colossal eyes -- in the biggest kinds, nearly the size of a dinner plate. Where did such enormous eyes let it hunt?
answer: Hunting in the black depths of the deep ocean
choices: Hunting in the black depths of the deep ocean
Watching the shore for its egg-laying beach
Spotting prey across the bright open surface
Reading the color of coral in the reef
context: Enormous eyes gather as much light as possible, letting the ichthyosaur hunt where almost no light reaches -- the deep ocean, or the surface at night. Source: Kiddle, Temnodontosaurus facts for kids.

question: Scientists measured the eye of the giant ichthyosaur Temnodontosaurus platyodon at roughly 25 centimeters -- about 9.8 inches -- across, the largest eye known in any animal ever. Which living creature's eye does that rival?
answer: The colossal squid
choices: The colossal squid
The blue whale
The great white shark
The saltwater crocodile
context: At about 25 cm across, the ichthyosaur's eye matches the colossal squid's -- among the very largest eyes nature has produced. Source: Wikipedia, Temnodontosaurus. (Legend-tier wonder.)

question: Land reptiles like turtles and lizards crawl ashore and bury a clutch of eggs. But fossils reveal that the ichthyosaur, marooned far out at sea, handled its young a completely different way. What did the fossils show?
answer: It gave birth to live young in the open water
choices: It gave birth to live young in the open water
It carried its eggs in its mouth until they hatched
It glued its eggs to floating driftwood
It returned to the same beach its ancestors used
context: Some ichthyosaur fossils preserve a mother caught mid-birth, a baby half-emerged from her body -- proof these sea reptiles bore live young rather than laying eggs on land. Source: Live Science, Oldest Fossil of Reptile Live Birth Found. (Legend-tier wonder.)

question: In China, paleontologists split open a fossil of a mother Chaohusaurus, an early ichthyosaur, and found three young preserved with her -- one already born, one still inside, and one caught halfway out. That halfway pup was emerging HEAD-first, not the tail-first way of dolphins and whales. To scientists, that head-first exit was a clue about one thing. What did it tell them?
answer: Ichthyosaurs inherited live birth from land-living ancestors
choices: Ichthyosaurs inherited live birth from land-living ancestors
Ichthyosaurs had only recently returned to land
The mother was the last of an egg-laying line
The pup had turned the wrong way and drowned
context: Head-first birth points to land ancestors that already bore live young, rather than the trait being invented for sea life. Later ichthyosaurs are found giving birth tail-first, like dolphins. Source: NPR, Fossil Shows Triassic-Era Sea Creature Gave Birth.

question: The ichthyosaur, the tuna, the dolphin, and the lamnid shark come from four completely unrelated branches of the animal kingdom -- yet all four converged on the very same torpedo body, wide crescent tail and stiff fins. What single problem drove such distant lineages to the identical shape?
answer: The need to swim fast for long distances in open water
choices: The need to swim fast for long distances in open water
The need to hide their color against the seafloor
The need to survive freezing polar temperatures
The need to crush hard-shelled prey with strong jaws
context: The ichthyosaur (reptile), dolphin (mammal), tuna (bony fish), and lamnid shark (shark) are four separate lineages that all evolved the same streamlined 'thunniform' shape -- the optimal body for fast, sustained swimming in open water. Source: NCBI PMC, Skeletal convergence in thunniform sharks, ichthyosaurs, whales, and tunas.

question: A stunning Stenopterygius ichthyosaur fossil kept traces of its actual skin -- and its coloring followed a pattern you still see on sharks and dolphins today: dark on the back, pale on the belly. What job did that two-tone scheme do?
answer: Camouflage from predators looking down or up
choices: Camouflage from predators looking down or up
Warned rivals off its hunting territory
Attracted mates during the breeding season
Soaked up sunlight to warm its blood
context: Dark-above, light-below coloring -- called countershading -- hides an animal against the dark depths from above and the bright surface from below. The same fossil also preserved a layer of blubber. Source: NC State News, Soft Tissue Shows Jurassic Ichthyosaur Was Warm-Blooded. (Legend-tier preservation.)

question: In 1811 on the crumbling cliffs of Lyme Regis in Dorset, a poor family of fossil-hunters pried loose the first complete ichthyosaur skeleton ever to reach London's scientists -- a 17-foot creature. The person who dug out most of that skeleton was a surprise. Who did the digging?
answer: A twelve-year-old local girl
choices: A twelve-year-old local girl
A twelve-year-old apprentice boy
A young village schoolteacher
A young dockside fisherman
context: Mary Anning's brother Joseph spotted the skull in 1811 when Mary was just twelve; she dug out the rest of the 17-foot skeleton months later, on the Dorset cliffs. Source: Wikipedia, Mary Anning. (Legend of paleontology.)

question: When Mary Anning's dolphin-shaped sea-reptile skeleton first came out of the Dorset cliff in November 1811, no one had a name for such a creature. Reporting the strange find, the local newspaper called it something familiar but wrong. What did they call it?
answer: A crocodile
choices: A crocodile
A whale
A sea serpent
A giant fish
context: The November 1811 paper labeled it a 'crocodile' -- science had no name yet for this air-breathing, dolphin-shaped sea reptile. Source: Wikipedia, Mary Anning.

question: The giant ichthyosaur Temnodontosaurus stretched about 9 meters -- 30 feet -- and ruled its seas as a top predator. One fossil's stomach revealed just how far its menu went. What surprising prey did it contain?
answer: Other, younger ichthyosaurs
choices: Other, younger ichthyosaurs
A large sea turtle
Its own shed teeth
Chunks of driftwood
context: One Temnodontosaurus preserved three juvenile ichthyosaurs and many cephalopod hooks in its gut -- this top predator ate its own kind. Source: Wikipedia, Temnodontosaurus.

question: In 2021, workers draining a reservoir at Rutland Water uncovered the biggest and most complete ichthyosaur skeleton ever found in Britain -- nicknamed the 'Rutland Sea Dragon.' Just how big was this Jurassic giant?
answer: About 10 meters long, the length of a bus
choices: About 10 meters long, the length of a bus
About 6 meters long, the length of a rowboat
About 14 meters long, the length of two buses
About 8 meters long, the length of a large van
context: The Rutland Sea Dragon runs about 10 meters (33 feet) with a skull weighing roughly a tonne -- the largest and most complete ichthyosaur fossil ever found in Britain. Source: Natural History Museum, Britain's largest ever ichthyosaur discovered in Rutland Water.

question: Early fossil collectors kept finding ichthyosaur tails with a sharp downward bend near the tip. Certain it was damage from being crushed in the rock, they snapped the bones straight to tidy the specimens up. Then the flawless Holzmaden fossils, with body outlines intact, revealed the bend was no accident. What were the collectors destroying?
answer: The bony support for the tail fin's lower lobe
choices: The bony support for the tail fin's lower lobe
A store of insulating blubber under the skin
The last ribs protecting a swallowed meal
A row of spines that ran along the back
context: An advanced ichthyosaur's crescent tail is mostly soft tissue, but the backbone stiffens the lower lobe: the tail vertebrae bend sharply downward and run inside it. Before the exquisitely preserved Holzmaden (Germany) Stenopterygius specimens showed the true two-lobed tail with its body outline intact, collectors read that downward kink as post-mortem breakage and routinely straightened the tails to 'fix' them, wiping out the real anatomy. Source: Capeia 'The Evolutionary History of Ichthyosaurs' 2017 (https://beta.capeia.com/paleobiology/2017/09/25/the-evolutionary-history-of-ichthyosaurs); PeerJ Solnhofen ichthyosaur soft-tissue paper (https://peerj.com/articles/13173/).

question: Across the African savanna, a herd stays in contact over miles using rumbles pitched too low for a human ear to catch — mostly 14 to 35 Hz, below our hearing floor. Which animal is calling?
answer: The African elephant
choices: The African elephant
The spotted hyena
The plains zebra
The African wild dog
context: Elephants call to each other in infrasound — rumbles mostly 14–35 Hz, below the ~20 Hz human hearing floor — that roll across the savanna for miles. Source: OUP BioScience, 'A throbbing in the air' (academic.oup.com/bioscience/article/49/5/353/227165); loveelephants.org/elephant-infrasound.

question: An elephant's rumble also shakes the ground, and a distant elephant can pick up that far-off call even when no sound ever reaches it through the air. By what studied pathway does the vibration reach its inner ear?
answer: Up through its feet and leg bones
choices: Up through its feet and leg bones
In through its wide flapping ears
Along its trunk to the nasal cavity
Through the fatty pad behind its eyes
context: Seismic vibrations travel up through the feet and leg bones to the inner ear (bone conduction), bypassing the eardrum — so an elephant can pick up a distant rumble it never heard through the air. Source: KQED, 'How Elephants Listen ... With Their Feet' (kqed.org/science/1926248); O'Connell-Rodwell, 'Keeping an Ear to the Ground,' Physiology 2007 (journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physiol.00008.2007).

question: A field elephant catching a faint tremor in the ground freezes, leans forward, and lifts one foot with the toe pointed down. As it presses back down, what does the foot do to read the vibration better?
answer: Spreads to widen its contact with the ground
choices: Spreads to widen its contact with the ground
Curls its edges up to form a hollow cup
Taps out a quick reply against the soil
Rolls onto its outer rim to muffle its weight
context: When picking up a distant seismic signal, elephants freeze, lean forward, lift a foot and point the toe down, then press their feet into the ground — spreading the foot to expand its contact area by up to about 20% to feel the vibration better. The vibration is caught by Pacinian corpuscles, pressure-sensing receptors packed around the edges of the foot. Source: KQED, 'How Elephants Listen ... With Their Feet' (kqed.org/science/1926248).

question: In the open ocean, one animal sings the lowest, farthest-carrying calls of any creature on Earth — fundamental pitches down around 10 to 40 Hz that may reach another singer across an entire ocean basin. Which is it?
answer: The blue whale
choices: The blue whale
The bottlenose dolphin
The humpback whale
The harbor seal
context: Blue and fin whales sing the lowest, farthest-traveling calls of any animal — fundamentals around 10–40 Hz — among the loudest natural sounds in the sea (up to ~188 dB underwater), potentially detectable by other whales across an entire ocean basin. Source: Wikipedia 'Whale vocalization'; Frontiers in Marine Science, 'Source Level of Antarctic Blue and Fin Whale Sounds' (frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fmars.2021.792651).

question: The Namib Desert golden mole has no working eyes at all, yet it 'sand-swims' through the dunes and dips its head against the sand to locate clusters of termites under grassy mounds. What sense guides this blind hunter to its prey?
answer: Reading vibrations in the ground
choices: Reading vibrations in the ground
Sniffing scent trails on the breeze
Sensing the warmth of the mounds
Tasting salts left in the sand
context: The Namib Desert golden mole is blind and 'sand-swims' through dunes, dipping its head to read seismic vibrations — finding termite prey clustered under grassy mounds purely by feeling ground vibrations, with no eyes to guide it. Source: Wikipedia 'Seismic communication'; Narins et al., 'Seismic sensitivity in the Desert Golden Mole' (researchgate.net/publication/11290943).

question: Giraffes were long thought to be nearly silent. Then researchers combed through 947 hours of night recordings from zoos and found the animals had been doing something in the dark that the keepers themselves had never noticed. What were the giraffes doing?
answer: Humming to each other in low tones
choices: Humming to each other in low tones
Grinding their teeth in slow rhythm
Whistling sharply through their nostrils
Stamping a beat with their front hooves
context: 947 hours of zoo recordings turned up 65 low, sustained hums averaging about 92 Hz — a nocturnal sound the zookeepers themselves had never noticed. Source: Baotic, Stoeger et al., 'Nocturnal humming vocalizations,' BMC Research Notes (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4565008); PBS NOVA (pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/giraffes-hum-to-each-other).

question: The blue whale already owns the lowest voice on Earth, yet across the Northeast Pacific its song fell about 31% in pitch between 1963 and 2008, and 7 of 10 song types worldwide are all sliding downward together. McDonald, Hildebrand and Mesnick argue the cause is counterintuitive. What is their leading explanation?
answer: As whaling ends and mates crowd closer, males no longer need a loud high call to carry far
choices: As whaling ends and mates crowd closer, males no longer need a loud high call to carry far
Ship-engine noise now masks the high notes, forcing whales to sing far lower to be heard
Warming, less salty water carries low pitches better, so the songs sank to match it
Older surviving males dominate the choruses, and their aging voices simply drop with age
context: The blue whale's song is not only the deepest on the planet, it is getting deeper: the best-documented Northeast Pacific song type dropped about 31% in tonal frequency between 1963 and 2008, and 7 of the world's 10 blue-whale song types are shifting downward. The leading (and still debated) idea from Mark McDonald, John Hildebrand and Sarah Mesnick is that as populations recover from whaling, potential mates are closer, so males no longer need to sing loud-and-high to be heard far away and can afford to drop the pitch. Crucially, the trend is worldwide and steady, which argues AGAINST human ocean noise as the cause. Source: McDonald, Hildebrand & Mesnick 2009, 'Worldwide decline in tonal frequencies of blue whale songs', Endangered Species Research; Scripps Institution of Oceanography news release, https://scripps.ucsd.edu/news/pitch-blue-whale-songs-declining-around-world-scientists-discover  (Legend.)

question: The blind Namib golden mole reads faint ground tremors to find termites, and the trick is one grotesquely swollen ear bone. Of 117 mammals measured its middle-ear malleus is the heaviest for body size — about 18 mg, near a human ear-bone in a mouse-sized skull. How does that dead weight let it feel the ground?
answer: The heavy bone lags behind the moving skull, and that slip drives the inner ear
choices: The heavy bone lags behind the moving skull, and that slip drives the inner ear
The bone rings like a struck bell, amplifying each tremor into a lasting tone
The bone seals the ear canal, so only ground-borne shakes ever reach the nerve
The bone stores the vibration as heat, which the mole senses as a warm pulse
context: Golden moles have the greatest ossicular mass relative to body size of 117 mammal species measured: the Namib golden mole's malleus weighs around 18 mg, closer to a human's (28 mg) or a cat's than to a similarly sized mouse's (0.28 mg). Matthew Mason proposed the mechanism is 'inertial bone conduction' — when a seismic wave shakes the skull, the heavy malleus lags behind, and that relative motion drives the inner ear, a model predicting a 30–60 dB boost in low-frequency sensitivity. The blind mole uses it to home in on wind-shaken clumps of dune grass and the termites beneath. Source: Mason, 'Bone conduction and seismic sensitivity in golden moles (Chrysochloridae)' and 'Middle ear dynamics... Cape golden mole' (J. Exp. Biol. 2006); summarized via Wikipedia 'Golden mole' and the Afrotheria Specialist Group, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_mole

question: A honeybee colony's female workers are all sterile — they never breed. So who exactly are these thousands of workers to the queen who laid them?
answer: Her own daughters
choices: Her own daughters
Unrelated hired help
Her older sisters
Bees from other hives
context: Every worker in the hive is the queen's own daughter, hatched from her eggs, yet they forage, nurse, and build the comb instead of breeding. A colony is essentially one giant family serving one mother. Source: Animal Diversity Web, Apis mellifera account.

question: A honeybee colony is almost entirely female — one queen and her sterile daughters. The colony's only males are a few thousand seasonal bees. What is the drones' one and only job?
answer: To mate with a queen
choices: To mate with a queen
To guard the hive entrance
To fan the comb cool
To scout for flowers
context: Drones are the hive's only males — a seasonal few thousand whose sole role is to mate with a queen. They do no work inside the hive at all. Source: Animal Diversity Web, Apis mellifera account; 'Reproductive Senescence in Drones of the Honey Bee' (PMC6358831).

question: A honeybee queen doesn't leave sex to chance — she decides it egg by egg. She leaves some of her eggs unfertilized. What hatches from one of those?
answer: A male drone
choices: A male drone
A second queen
A sterile worker
Nothing — it fails
context: This system is called haplodiploidy: fertilized eggs become female, unfertilized eggs become male drones, so the queen controls the sex of each egg. Source: Animal Diversity Web, Apis mellifera account.

question: A leafcutter-ant colony (Atta) can grow to roughly five million workers, and every one of them is the sterile daughter of a single mother. To keep a colony that size going, how long can that one Atta queen live?
answer: Over a decade
choices: Over a decade
A single summer
About three years
Just a few months
context: One Atta queen — mother to up to five million sterile workers — can live over ten years, laying the eggs for the entire colony that whole time. Source: Britannica, 'Leafcutter ant'; San Diego Zoo Global Atta cephalotes fact sheet.

question: Leafcutter ants (Atta) work like a single superorganism: workers come in graded sizes, each size locked to its own job. The huge-jawed 'majors' guard the nest, but the tiniest workers, the 'minims,' spend their whole lives farming something in the deep chambers. What are the minims farming down there?
answer: A garden of fungus
choices: A garden of fungus
A herd of aphids
A store of seeds
A brood of larvae
context: Leafcutter minims tend the colony's fungus garden — the ants cut leaves not to eat them but to feed a fungus they farm and then eat. The graded worker sizes doing fixed jobs are why the colony functions like one body, a 'superorganism.' Source: Britannica, 'Leafcutter ant'; Holldobler & Wilson, 'The Leafcutter Ants: Civilization by Instinct'.

question: Army ants (Eciton) build no permanent nest at all. When night falls, the colony still has to shelter its queen and larvae in an overnight camp called a bivouac. How do they build the walls of that camp?
answer: They link their own bodies together
choices: They link their own bodies together
They pile up chewed leaves
They dig a fresh burrow each dusk
They wall it with hardened saliva
context: Each night an Eciton colony hooks together with leg-claws into a hanging living wall — the bivouac — sheltering the queen and larvae inside their own bodies. Legend among naturalists for its strangeness. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eciton burchellii'; Britannica, 'Eciton army ant'.

question: An Eciton army-ant soldier is so specialized as a living weapon that it depends entirely on the ordinary workers for one basic need. What can a soldier no longer do for itself?
answer: Feed itself
choices: Feed itself
Groom its own body
Follow the scent trail
Right itself when flipped
context: An Eciton soldier's oversized sickle jaws are built purely for combat and can't handle food, so ordinary workers must feed the soldiers by mouth. Source: Britannica, 'Eciton army ant'; Bug of the Week, 'Rapacious raiders: Army ants, Eciton spp.'

question: A mature Macrotermes termite queen barely resembles the workers around her: her abdomen swells so enormously (a change called physogastry) that she becomes a pale egg-laying engine, unable to move on her own. Roughly how many eggs a day can she pump out?
answer: About 30,000
choices: About 30,000
About 300
About 3,000
About 300,000
context: In Macrotermes the queen's swollen abdomen can reach about 11 cm (4.3 in) long, and she lays roughly 30,000 eggs a day for years. A near-legendary figure among social insects. Source: Britannica, 'Termite: Natural history'; ScienceDirect S0022191025000782.

question: Why would a female bee or ant give up breeding entirely to raise her sisters? One leading hypothesis points to a quirk of haplodiploidy: because of how sex is decided, two full sisters share a surprising fraction of their genes. On average, about what fraction?
answer: About three-quarters
choices: About three-quarters
About one-half
About one-quarter
About one-third
context: Under haplodiploidy, full sisters share on average about 75% of their genes — more than the 50% a mother shares with her own young. This is a leading idea (W.D. Hamilton's) for why workers raise sisters, not settled fact. Source: Wikipedia, 'Evolution of eusociality'.

question: The naked mole-rat (Heterocephalus glaber) runs an insect-style society under the East African savanna — one breeding queen, dozens of sterile diggers. For a rodent, it holds one more astonishing record: how long can a naked mole-rat live?
answer: About 30 years
choices: About 30 years
About 3 years
About 8 years
About 15 years
context: Naked mole-rats are the longest-living rodents known — individuals have reached about 30 years in captivity, roughly ten times a house mouse's lifespan. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, 'Naked mole-rat'; UT Health San Antonio, 'Longest-lived naked mole rat in captivity dies after 30 years'.

question: When a naked mole-rat queen dies, the colony has no heir waiting — several females may fight to the death for the throne. The winner then changes physically as she takes over breeding. What part of the new queen's body actually grows?
answer: Her backbone lengthens
choices: Her backbone lengthens
Her teeth fall out
Her fur grows back
Her eyes enlarge
context: After a fatal succession fight, the new naked mole-rat queen's lumbar vertebrae grow about 32% longer, lengthening her spine to carry more young. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, 'Naked mole-rat'; PMC2864304.  (Legend.)

question: The naked mole-rat lives in packed, stuffy burrows where oxygen runs desperately low, and it can survive total oxygen loss for about 18 minutes unharmed. Its trick: when the ordinary sugar-burning pathway seizes up without oxygen, its cells flood the blood with a different sugar and burn that anaerobically instead. Which sugar?
answer: Fructose
choices: Fructose
Glucose
Galactose
Ribose
context: When oxygen vanishes, normal glucose metabolism jams at an oxygen-dependent step and most mammals' brain cells die within minutes. The naked mole-rat dodges this by switching to fructose and running it through a fructose-driven pathway that plants and a few other organisms use — bypassing the blocked step entirely. It can endure roughly 18 minutes of total anoxia with no apparent injury, and survive at least 5 hours in extreme low-oxygen conditions that would kill a human. Source: Park, Lewin et al., 'Fructose-driven glycolysis supports anoxia resistance in the naked mole-rat,' Science 2017 (356:6335; PMC6661067); 18-minute anoxia figure via Max Delbrueck Center reporting.

question: For decades the textbook answer for why worker bees and ants abandon breeding was haplodiploidy: sisters share three-quarters of their genes. But termites are eusocial and NOT haplodiploid, which cracked that story. Jacobus Boomsma's replacement idea says every origin of these sterile-worker societies traces to an ancestral queen whose mating had which feature?
answer: She mated with a single male for her whole life
choices: She mated with a single male for her whole life
She mated with many males and stored their sperm
She mated with several of her own brothers
She took a fresh mate every breeding season
context: Boomsma's 'monogamy hypothesis' (2007) argues that eusociality could only take its first step in lineages whose ancestral mother mated with just one male for life. Under strict lifetime monogamy, a female is exactly as related to her full siblings as to her own offspring — so staying home to raise siblings costs her nothing genetically. Boomsma showed all eight independent origins of eusociality in the Hymenoptera trace to a monogamous ancestor, and this has largely displaced the older three-quarters haplodiploidy story as the explanation for the initial evolutionary step. Source: Boomsma, 'Lifetime monogamy and the evolution of eusociality,' Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 2009 (PMC2781870). The haplodiploidy link itself was separately challenged by Nowak, Tarnita & Wilson, Nature 2010.

question: One of the largest deer that ever lived stood about 2 m (6 ft 7 in) at the shoulder and weighed up to 700 kg -- over 1,500 lb. What living animal was the extinct Irish elk about the size of?
answer: An Alaskan moose
choices: An Alaskan moose
A white-tailed deer
A wild boar
A red fox
context: The Irish elk (Megaloceros giganteus) was one of the largest deer that ever lived -- about 2 m at the shoulder and up to 700 kg, matching a modern Alaskan moose. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_elk ; smithsonianmag.com/smithsonian-institution/irish-elk-biggest-antlers-ever-180977706

question: Its name is doubly misleading. The Irish elk was not actually an elk -- DNA shows its closest living relative is another kind of deer. Which one?
answer: The fallow deer
choices: The fallow deer
The reindeer
The roe deer
The mule deer
context: Despite the name, the Irish elk was a giant deer, not an elk. DNA evidence settled that its nearest living relative is the fallow deer. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_elk ; sciencenews.org/article/dna-pegs-irish-elks-nearest-relatives

question: The male Irish elk grew the largest antlers of any animal known -- a single spread so wide it matched something everyday in scale. Tip to tip, how wide did that rack get?
answer: As long as a family car
choices: As long as a family car
As wide as a doorway
As long as a canoe
As tall as a person
context: A male Irish elk carried the largest antlers of any animal ever known -- up to about 3.6 m (12 ft) tip to tip, and 4.26 m (14 ft) in the largest recorded specimen: as wide as a family car is long. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_elk ; iflscience.com/enormous-extinct-deer-had-even-more-enormous-antlers-but-we-dont-know-why-72818  (Legend.)

question: Each spring the male Irish elk faced the same enormous task with his car-wide, ~40 kg rack. What happened to those antlers over the course of the year?
answer: Grew the whole rack anew and dropped it
choices: Grew the whole rack anew and dropped it
Kept the same rack for life
Only added a few new points each year
Grew it larger without ever shedding
context: Each spring the stag started from bare stubs and rebuilt the entire car-wide, ~40 kg (88 lb) rack, then shed it and did it all again the next year. Sources: smithsonianmag.com/smithsonian-institution/irish-elk-biggest-antlers-ever-180977706 ; nhm.ac.uk/discover/irish-elk-giant-deer.html  (Legend.)

question: Antlers that huge sound like weapons, but the giant rack of the Irish elk stag was built mostly for one thing when rival males met. What was the main purpose of those enormous palms?
answer: Showing off to win mates
choices: Showing off to win mates
Digging for buried roots
Sweeping snow off grazing
Scaring away wolf packs
context: The giant antlers were mainly for display, an extreme case of sexual selection. Rivals interlocked the lower parts of their antlers to push and shove for the right to mate -- but the huge flat palms were chiefly a show. Sources: smithsonianmag.com/smithsonian-institution/irish-elk-biggest-antlers-ever-180977706 ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_elk

question: Rebuilding that entire antler rack each spring demanded a huge surge of calcium and phosphate. Models suggest where the Irish elk stag pulled most of those minerals from to grow one season of antler.
answer: From the calcium in his own bones
choices: From the calcium in his own bones
From salt licks he swallowed
From mineral-rich spring grass
From bark stripped off trees
context: Models suggest up to 80% of the calcium a stag could draw came from its own skeleton -- about twice the mineral drain a moose faces. A stag that couldn't refill from good grazing risked osteoporosis, brittle bones. Source: markwitton-com.blogspot.com/2020/11/megaloceros-giganteus-behind-antlers.html

question: For years people blamed the Irish elk's giant antlers for its extinction. Stephen Jay Gould reopened the question in 1974. What does the evidence now point to as the real cause?
answer: Changing climate and vanishing habitat
choices: Changing climate and vanishing habitat
The sheer weight of its antlers
A disease carried by early cattle
Competition from the moose
context: Gould's 1974 essay showed the antlers scaled as expected for the deer's size (allometry) and were a display advantage, not a fatal handicap. As Ice Age forests and mineral-rich plants disappeared, the deer couldn't get enough food to rebuild bone and antler each year; human hunting may have delivered the final blow to already-stressed herds. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_elk ; daily.jstor.org/the-cartoonishly-giant-antlers-of-the-irish-elk ; nhm.ac.uk/discover/irish-elk-giant-deer.html

question: The mineral drain of regrowing the rack was only half the stag's springtime burden. Modeling the Irish elk's yearly antler growth against a modern moose's, biologists found the giant deer paid a far steeper cost of one other kind. What did that antler growth demand so much more of?
answer: Energy -- about three-quarters of what all his fat and muscle reserves took
choices: Energy -- about three-quarters of what all his fat and muscle reserves took
Sleep -- roughly double the daily rest a resting moose needed each night
Water -- nearly triple a moose's daily intake drawn straight from marsh pools
Salt -- far more than any mineral lick on the open steppe could ever supply
context: Antlers cost minerals AND raw energy. Moen, Pastor & Cohen's (1999) simulation estimated that growing the Irish elk's rack demanded roughly 75% as much energy as the stag needed to lay down all his summer fat and protein reserves combined -- versus only about 50% in a living moose. So the giant deer paid a proportionally far steeper springtime energy tax than any deer alive today, a hidden cost on top of the calcium and phosphorus it pulled from its own skeleton. Source: Moen, Pastor & Cohen (1999), 'Antler growth and extinction of Irish elk' (experts.umn.edu publication summary; WebSearch corroboration).

question: The classic story says the Irish elk's monstrous antlers doomed the STAGS. A 2008 model challenged that: antler mass is evolutionarily cheap to shrink, so male losses barely dent a herd. It pointed instead to a different group crushed by the shortening Ice-Age growing season. Who took the real hit?
answer: The females, whose output of fast-growing young could fall by half
choices: The females, whose output of fast-growing young could fall by half
The calves, whose first-winter survival dropped as the cold set in
The eldest bulls, whose worn teeth failed on the coarser tundra grass
The wanderers, whose long migrations no longer reached green pasture
context: O'Driscoll Worman & Kimbrell (2008, Oikos 117:1397) modeled the extinction and argued the 'giant antlers doomed the stags' story is largely wrong -- antler size is evolutionarily flexible, and losing big-antlered males barely dents population growth. Their model instead squeezed the FEMALES: as the Pleistocene growing season shortened, the heavy cost of gestating and rearing fast-running precocial young could have cut female reproductive output by up to about 50%, so stressed mothers, not stressed big-antlered bulls, most plausibly drove the collapse. This remains a live scientific debate, not a settled verdict. Source: O'Driscoll Worman & Kimbrell (2008), 'Getting to the hart of the matter: did antlers truly cause the extinction of the Irish elk?', Oikos 117:1397-1405 (Wiley; ResearchGate abstract).

question: A squid needs no fins or tail to shoot through the sea. It draws water into its muscular mantle, then blasts it out through a narrow, steerable tube — rocketing itself off in the opposite direction. What is this way of swimming called?
answer: Jet propulsion
choices: Jet propulsion
Wave gliding
Fin paddling
Tail whipping
context: The squid works exactly like a rocket ship: fluid fired hard one way pushes the body the other way. The tube it fires through is called the funnel, or siphon. Source: https://www.sciencefriday.com/educational-resources/jet-setting-cephalopods/

question: A clam that swims: it opens its two shells to suck in water, then slams them shut to blast the water out the back, hopping clumsily away from an attacking starfish. Which shelled animal is this?
answer: A scallop
choices: A scallop
A barnacle
A limpet
An oyster
context: Most clams and oysters are cemented down or buried, but a scallop can clap its shells to jet across the seafloor in awkward hops — one of very few swimming bivalves. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/scallop-bivalve  (Legend.)

question: Every jet swimmer in the sea — squid, octopus, jellyfish, scallop — obeys the same rule of physics: shove water hard in one direction, and an equal push sends you the other way. Which law of motion is this?
answer: Newton's third law
choices: Newton's third law
Newton's first law
The law of gravity
The law of buoyancy
context: Newton's third law says every action has an equal and opposite reaction. It's why a fired jet of water becomes forward motion for the animal — no legs, fins, or tail required. Source: https://www.sciencefriday.com/educational-resources/jet-setting-cephalopods/

question: A squid steers with one flexible part: aim it forward and the squid shoots backward, swivel it sideways and the squid turns. A single nozzle does all the steering. What is this tube called?
answer: The funnel
choices: The funnel
The mantle
The gill
The fin
context: The funnel (also called the siphon) is a bendy nozzle. By pointing it, a squid controls both direction and turns — steering and thrust from one organ. Source: https://www.sciencefriday.com/educational-resources/jet-setting-cephalopods/

question: An octopus usually crawls along the seafloor on its arms. But when a predator closes in and it needs to vanish fast, it changes tactics entirely. What does the octopus do to escape?
answer: Fires a jet of water and shoots backward
choices: Fires a jet of water and shoots backward
Freezes and plays dead
Digs straight down into the sand
Curls into a tight armored ball
context: The octopus blasts water from its funnel for a burst of speed, and can even squirt a cloud of ink through the same funnel to cover its getaway. Source: https://biologyinsights.com/how-does-the-octopus-move-from-crawling-to-jet-propulsion/

question: The neon flying squid does something no swimmer should: it jets so hard at the surface that it launches clear out of the water. Once airborne it spreads its fins and arms into little wings and glides. Roughly how far can it travel through the air?
answer: About 30 meters
choices: About 30 meters
About 30 centimeters
About 3 meters
About 300 meters
context: That's the length of a swimming pool, crossed entirely in the air. Spreading its fins and arms for lift, the squid truly 'flies' as an escape — though it risks being snatched by seabirds up there. Source: https://www.calacademy.org/explore-science/the-flying-squid  (Legend.)

question: A jellyfish swims by squeezing its bell to push out a ring of water, then coasts between squeezes instead of pulsing constantly. For the amount of energy it spends per distance traveled, where does the jellyfish rank among all swimming animals?
answer: The most efficient swimmer of any animal
choices: The most efficient swimmer of any animal
Roughly tied with a tuna
The least efficient large swimmer
Average for a soft-bodied animal
context: Measured by cost of transport — energy burned per distance — no swimming creature yet measured beats the jellyfish. The trick is coasting between pulses instead of paddling nonstop. Source: https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1306983110  (Legend.)

question: The nautilus jets backward through its funnel like other cephalopods, but it has a second trick its cousins lack. It also adjusts gas and water inside the sealed chambers of its coiled shell. What does controlling that gas let the nautilus do?
answer: Control its buoyancy, rising and sinking
choices: Control its buoyancy, rising and sinking
Grow a new shell chamber overnight
Glow to lure in prey
Sting attackers with venom
context: By tuning the gas-to-water ratio in its shell chambers, the nautilus hovers, rises, or sinks — jetting and ballast in one animal, like a submarine that also rockets. Source: https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/species/chambered-nautilus/science

question: Only one insect is known to swim by jet propulsion — and it does it in a truly bizarre way. The dragonfly nymph, its underwater larval stage, sucks water into its rear and blasts it back out to shoot forward. Where does this water go in and out?
answer: Its rectum, where it also breathes
choices: Its rectum, where it also breathes
Its mouth, spat out its gills
A pair of belly pores
Hollow tubes in its legs
context: The nymph breathes through gills lining its rectum. Firing that same water out the anus jets it forward to catch prey or flee — the only insect known to swim this way. Source: https://www.iflscience.com/dragonfly-babies-breathe-through-their-butts-but-thats-not-all-76934  (Legend.)

question: When a jellyfish's bell springs back to shape after a squeeze, the recoiling water forms a spinning ring — a vortex — that shoves the animal forward with no muscle effort at all, like a rubber band snapping back. What does the jellyfish gain from this free push?
answer: It travels about 30% farther each cycle
choices: It travels about 30% farther each cycle
It roughly doubles the water it moves per squeeze
It cuts its muscle energy nearly in half
It adds a second full-power muscle stroke
context: The passive suction of the vortex ring is a second, free stroke — motion the jellyfish never paid muscle energy for. That recycled push is why it out-coasts every other swimmer measured. Source: https://phys.org/news/2013-10-reveals-jellyfish-efficient-swimmers-video.html  (Legend.)

question: A squid fires its escape jet by contracting its whole mantle at once, driven by a single fiber so enormous — up to a millimeter thick — that scientists could thread electrodes right inside it. That freak of size made this squid part the tool for one of biology's biggest breakthroughs. What did probing it finally let researchers work out?
answer: How an electrical signal races down a cell
choices: How an electrical signal races down a cell
How a muscle converts its sugar into motion
How the lens bends light onto the retina
How the blood ferries oxygen to the tissues
context: The squid's lightning escape reflex runs on the giant axon — the fattest nerve fiber in the animal kingdom, up to about 1 mm across (hundreds of times thicker than an ordinary nerve) and conducting at roughly 25 m/s so the entire mantle clenches almost in one instant for a single hard blast. That freakish thickness let Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley slide electrodes inside a working nerve and measure exactly how an impulse fires — work that won the 1963 Nobel Prize and founded modern neuroscience. The animal's jet-propulsion escape is literally what made that discovery possible. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squid_giant_axon; conduction velocity ~25 m/s corroborated at sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/squid-giant-axon.

question: Jet propulsion is one of the oldest ways an animal ever swam. Four cephalopod dynasties all rocketed through the sea by squirting water out a funnel-shaped tube, but only one was already doing it in the Cambrian and Ordovician seas, more than 450 million years ago — long before fish came to rule. Which came first?
answer: The shelled nautiloids
choices: The shelled nautiloids
The coiled ammonites
The ten-armed belemnites
The hovering cuttlefish
context: All four are cephalopods that swim by jetting water through a funnel, but they did not arrive together. The shelled nautiloids came first: they were already jetting through a funnel-like 'hyponome' in the Late Cambrian and diversifying through the Ordovician, well over 450 million years ago — long before fish dominated the seas. The other three inherited the same water-jet design far later: the coiled ammonites appeared in the Early Devonian (~410 million years ago), and the bullet-shaped belemnites and the hovering cuttlefish are Mesozoic-and-later coleoids, closer cousins of modern squid. The squid's rocket has a half-billion-year backstory, and the nautiloids started it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautiloid (hyponome jet, Late Cambrian origin, Ordovician diversification); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonoidea (ammonoids first appear in the Early Devonian).

question: A gleaming metallic blue-green wasp barely 22 mm long attacks a cockroach several times its own size. But instead of killing its giant prey outright, the emerald jewel wasp does something far stranger to the roach:
answer: turns it into an obedient living zombie
choices: turns it into an obedient living zombie
spins it into a tight silk cocoon
freezes it solid inside a wax cell
splits it in half with its jaws
context: The emerald jewel wasp (Ampulex compressa) hunts cockroaches far bigger than itself. Rather than killing the roach, it turns it into a living, obedient zombie that later walks to its own grave under its own power. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_cockroach_wasp  (Legend.)

question: The emerald jewel wasp needs its cockroach alive but perfectly still for the tricky work ahead. Its first sting jabs the nerve-cluster in the roach's front legs, buying a couple of minutes of stillness. Why does it need the roach frozen for exactly those minutes?
answer: to line up a second, precise sting
choices: to line up a second, precise sting
to lay all of its eggs at once
to drag it underground straight away
to drink from the roach's back
context: The wasp stings the cockroach twice. The first sting hits the front-leg nerve-cluster and paralyzes the front legs for a couple of minutes, just long enough to hold the roach still for the real strike that follows. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_cockroach_wasp  (Legend.)

question: With the roach held still, the emerald jewel wasp drives its second sting into a shocking target and injects venom there. Afterward the roach can still walk, right itself, even swim, yet it has lost all urge to flee danger. Where did that second sting go?
answer: straight into the roach's brain
choices: straight into the roach's brain
into the roach's wing muscles
into the roach's egg sac
into the roach's rear leg joint
context: The second sting goes directly into the cockroach's brain. The venom switches off the roach's escape reflex: it can still walk, right itself, and swim, but it has completely lost the urge to run away from danger. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_cockroach_wasp  (Legend.)

question: Its venom delivered, the emerald jewel wasp now needs to move its docile cockroach to the burrow. How does the wasp get it there?
answer: it pulls the roach along by an antenna
choices: it pulls the roach along by an antenna
it rides on the roach's back and taps
it rolls the roach ahead like a ball
it flies while gripping the roach's wings
context: The wasp grabs what is left of an antenna and leads the docile roach on a walk to its burrow, pulling it along exactly like a dog on a leash. The roach walks under its own power to its own tomb. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_cockroach_wasp  (Legend.)

question: Inside the sealed burrow the emerald jewel wasp glues a tiny egg to the underside of the still-living cockroach. About three days later the egg hatches, and the newborn larva does something the paralyzed roach never resists:
answer: it chews inside and eats the roach alive
choices: it chews inside and eats the roach alive
it carries the roach up to the surface
it molts and flies away at once
it stings a fresh cockroach itself
context: The egg hatches in about three days. The newborn larva chews a hole into the still-living roach and burrows inside, eating the roach's organs from within while the roach stays alive and never fights back. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_cockroach_wasp  (Legend.)

question: A moss-green, owl-faced parrot the size of a small cat waddles across the New Zealand forest floor at night. What can this bird, alone among the world's parrots, NOT do?
answer: Fly
choices: Fly
See in the dark
Nest in trees
Make any sound
context: The kakapo (Strigops habroptilus) is the only flightless parrot on Earth. Its wings are too small and its feathers too soft to lift it, so it walks the forest floor and hauls itself up trees with beak and strong legs instead. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C4%81k%C4%81p%C5%8D

question: The kakapo evolved in a New Zealand with no ground mammals to flee, so it never took to the air. Among all the world's parrots, which record does this grounded bird hold?
answer: The world's heaviest parrot
choices: The world's heaviest parrot
The world's fastest parrot
The world's rarest parrot
The world's smallest parrot
context: A male kakapo averages about 2 kg (4.4 lb), some 400 g heavier than the flighted hyacinth macaw, the largest parrot that still takes to the air. Grounded life in a predator-free land let it grow bulky. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C4%81k%C4%81p%C5%8D

question: On a still New Zealand night, a low pulse below 100 Hz throbs across the hills every second or two — a sound more felt in the chest than heard. To broadcast this deep mating call, a male kakapo inflates what part of his body like a balloon?
answer: An air sac in his chest
choices: An air sac in his chest
His hollow leg bones
The pouch beneath his beak
The webbing of his feet
context: The male kakapo pumps up a stretchy air sac in his chest and releases a 'boom' below 100 Hz, so low it carries as a felt vibration. He repeats it every one to two seconds through the night. Source: https://www.doc.govt.nz/nature/native-animals/birds/birds-a-z/kakapo/behaviour/

question: Before he booms all night, a male kakapo scoops out a shallow bowl in the dirt and lies down inside it. What does lying in this dug bowl do for his call?
answer: Amplifies it so it carries up to a kilometre
choices: Amplifies it so it carries up to a kilometre
Cools his body during the long hours of effort
Steadies its low pitch so females hear it clearly
Shields his soft feathers from the night rain
context: The dug bowl acts like a natural amplifier, bouncing the low boom out across the hills — up to a kilometre on a calm night, several kilometres in the wind. Legendary among New Zealand naturalists. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C4%81k%C4%81p%C5%8D

question: For millions of years one instinct kept the kakapo safe on New Zealand's predator-free forest floor — the very instinct that doomed it once cats and stoats arrived. What does a startled kakapo do?
answer: Freezes and trusts its camouflage
choices: Freezes and trusts its camouflage
Flees down a burrow
Screams to warn the flock
Plays dead and stops breathing
context: Freezing and relying on its mottled green feathers worked against sight-hunting hawks, but introduced cats and stoats hunt by smell — and a motionless bird is simply an easy meal. The kakapo's own strong, sweet, musty odour betrays exactly where the frozen bird hides. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C4%81k%C4%81p%C5%8D

question: A kakapo may sit out two, three, even four years without breeding, the whole population waiting together. Then one forest tree bears a bumper crop of fruit and the birds suddenly breed as one. Which tree's rare heavy fruiting are they waiting for?
answer: The rimu tree
choices: The rimu tree
The rata tree
The kauri tree
The manuka tree
context: Kakapo breed only in 'mast' years, when the rimu fruits heavily — an event that comes just once every few years. The birds hold off until the forest can feast, so seasons can be years apart. Source: https://www.nzbirdsonline.org.nz/species/kakapo

question: A tiny hopping rodent bounds across the Mojave and Sonoran deserts, and here is the astonishing part: it can live its entire life and never once drink a drop of water. What is it?
answer: The kangaroo rat
choices: The kangaroo rat
The desert cottontail
The antelope ground squirrel
The kit fox
context: The kangaroo rat (genus Dipodomys) of the American Southwest is famous for going its whole life without drinking. It survives on the water hidden inside dry seeds, wrung out by an extraordinary body. Source: trendingamerican.com; Open University OpenLearn (Schmidt-Nielsen desert-animal physiology).  (Legend.)

question: The kangaroo rat never sips from a puddle, yet it never dies of thirst. Where does nearly all of its water actually come from?
answer: Water its body makes while burning dry seeds for energy
choices: Water its body makes while burning dry seeds for energy
Dew it licks off cactus spines at dawn
Moisture stored in a special second stomach
Blood it drinks from insects it catches
context: When any animal burns food for energy through respiration, the chemistry releases water as a by-product — 'metabolic water.' The kangaroo rat lives almost entirely on this internal water made from the dry seeds it eats, drinking none from outside. Source: Open University OpenLearn; rockdoveblog.wordpress.com.  (Legend.)

question: Its scientific name Dipodomys means "two-foot mouse" — it bounds along on two long hind legs like a miniature kangaroo. When a kangaroo rat flees across open sand, what does it use its extra-long tail for?
answer: A counterbalance for sharp mid-air turns
choices: A counterbalance for sharp mid-air turns
A whip to lash at pursuing snakes
A prop to stand upright and scan for danger
A store of fat to survive lean seasons
context: A kangaroo rat's tail is longer than its whole body, and it acts as a counterbalance — letting the animal make sharp, sudden turns in mid-leap without tumbling. Source: a-z-animals.com; desertmuseum.org.

question: A sidewinder rattlesnake lunges at a desert kangaroo rat from inches away. Too slow to leap fully clear, the rat twists in the air. What does it do to the snake before the fangs land?
answer: Drop-kicks it away with both hind feet
choices: Drop-kicks it away with both hind feet
Sprays a cloud of scent to blind it
Bites down hard on the snake behind its head
Freezes flat so the strike passes over
context: Researchers filming these encounters found kangaroo rats that couldn't fully dodge would twist mid-air and drop-kick the snake 'ninja-style' with their powerful hind feet, flinging it away before venom could be injected — then land back on their feet. Source: news.mongabay.com; sciencedaily.com (Rulon Clark, SDSU, 2019).  (Legend.)

question: A big Australian animal carries its newborn in a pouch and gets everywhere on two enormous hind legs, its heavy tail swung out straight behind it as a counterweight. What is it?
answer: A kangaroo
choices: A kangaroo
A wombat
A capybara
An anteater
context: The red kangaroo is a marsupial that travels by hopping, using its thick tail as a counterweight to stay balanced through every bound. Source: Discover Wildlife, How and why kangaroos hop (discoverwildlife.com).

question: A red kangaroo fleeing a threat across the open outback stretches into leaps so long that a single bound can carry it more than 8 metres. About how fast can that sprint get?
answer: Roughly 70 km/h
choices: Roughly 70 km/h
Roughly 20 km/h
Roughly 130 km/h
Roughly 200 km/h
context: A sprinting red kangaroo can reach about 70 km/h and leap as high as 3 metres, clearing single bounds of over 8 metres. Source: A-Z Animals, How High and Far Can a Kangaroo Jump (a-z-animals.com).  (Legend.)

question: A kangaroo speeds up across the plain to outrun a threat. Yet a fast kangaroo and a slow one hop at nearly the same rhythm. So how does a hopping kangaroo actually go faster?
answer: It takes longer leaps
choices: It takes longer leaps
It leans further forward to gain ground
It drops onto all fours to run
It pushes harder with its tail
context: Instead of hopping faster, a kangaroo lengthens each leap. Because the hopping rhythm barely changes, going faster costs it almost no extra energy. Source: trishansoz.com; Discover Wildlife.

question: A kangaroo grazing too slowly to hop plants its thick tail on the ground and swings its hind feet forward between steps. During that slow walk, how much forward push does the tail alone provide?
answer: As much as all four limbs combined
choices: As much as all four limbs combined
Only a light steadying touch
About half what one hind leg gives
None -- it just balances
context: In this slow five-legged gait, scientists call it pentapedal walking, a kangaroo's tail provides as much forward push as its four limbs combined, doing about as much work as a human leg does in a stride. Source: O'Connor et al. 2014, Biology Letters; Science News.  (Legend.)

question: A kangaroo's tail seems too floppy to work like a leg, yet it can push and prop with it. What packed inside the tail lets it act like a limb?
answer: More than 20 highly jointed vertebrae
choices: More than 20 highly jointed vertebrae
A second set of hip muscles
A stiff internal rod of cartilage
A pad of springy fat
context: A kangaroo's tail contains over 20 jointed vertebrae, while each leg has only a few long bones, so the tail bends and grips like a segmented limb. Source: O'Connor et al. 2014, Biology Letters, via Asian Scientist.

question: A newborn kangaroo, blind and hairless and no bigger than a jellybean, somehow gets from the birth canal to its mother's pouch within minutes. How does this tiny joey make the journey?
answer: It crawls unaided up through her fur
choices: It crawls unaided up through her fur
She lifts it in her paws to the pouch
She carries it there in her mouth
It is born already inside the pouch
context: Weighing under 2 grams, the newborn joey drags itself up through its mother's fur to the pouch in about three minutes, swimming with its forelimbs, with no help from her. Source: trishansoz.com; interestinganimals.net.

question: Dawson and Taylor tested hopping red kangaroos in 1973 and found something that stunned them: past a certain speed, a faster kangaroo does something surprising with its oxygen. What?
answer: It burns LESS oxygen the faster it goes
choices: It burns LESS oxygen the faster it goes
It burns oxygen at a steady flat rate
Its oxygen use suddenly doubles
It stops breathing between hops
context: Past a threshold speed, hopping gets cheaper: the kangaroo's giant tendons store each landing's energy and snap back to launch the next hop, doing more of the work as speed rises. Source: Dawson & Taylor 1973, cited in eLife 96437.

question: A female red kangaroo already nursing a joey can hold a second, spare embryo frozen at the 70-100 cell stage, pausing it for up to 11 months until the pouch is free. What keeps that backup embryo on hold?
answer: The suckling of the pouch joey
choices: The suckling of the pouch joey
The mother's body temperature
A seasonal drop in daylight
The pouch joey's heartbeat
context: The suckling joey sends a hormonal signal that freezes the spare embryo; if the pouch joey dies, that signal stops and the paused embryo immediately starts growing. This pausing is called embryonic diapause. Source: PubMed 7014870; a-z-animals.com.

question: High above the tree line in the snowy Southern Alps of New Zealand's South Island lives an olive-green bird that nests in the cold above 1,600 meters, where you'd never expect its kind. What kind of bird is the kea?
answer: The world's only true alpine parrot
choices: The world's only true alpine parrot
A high-altitude eagle
A snow-dwelling penguin
A mountain-nesting owl
context: The kea (Nestor notabilis) is the only true alpine parrot on Earth, breeding above 1,600 m in New Zealand's Southern Alps. Ornithologist John Gould first described it in 1856; 'notabilis' means 'noteworthy,' and it earned the nickname 'the clown of the mountains.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kea

question: Tourists who park at New Zealand ski fields come back to find the rubber trim and wiper blades pried off their cars and their backpacks unzipped and shredded. The culprit is the kea, an alpine parrot. Why does it do all this wrecking?
answer: Out of sheer investigative play and curiosity
choices: Out of sheer investigative play and curiosity
To build a nest from the scraps
To defend its territory from rivals
To find insects hidden in the rubber
context: Kea are notorious mountain vandals, dismantling skis and snowboards and flying off with unguarded clothing purely to investigate and play. One kea at Fiordland National Park famously made off with a tourist's passport, and keas have even been documented dragging traffic cones into roadways. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kea

question: Bruce, a kea whose entire upper beak had been broken off since he was a chick, couldn't preen his feathers the normal way. Keepers watched him invent an astonishing workaround no parrot had ever been seen to do. What did Bruce teach himself to do?
answer: Wedge a pebble against his lower beak and use it as a comb
choices: Wedge a pebble against his lower beak and use it as a comb
Roll in dust to strip the dirt from his feathers
Ask other keas to preen him in return
Dip his feathers in water to clean them
context: Bruce held a small pebble between his tongue and lower beak and used it to comb his feathers. Scientists judged it deliberate: in over 90% of the times he picked up a pebble he then preened, he consistently chose pebbles of a particular size, and no other kea in his enclosure did it. Source: https://www.auckland.ac.nz/en/news/2021/09/10/disabled-kea-uses-tools-for-self-care.html  (Legend.)

question: Six kea learned that a black token always won food and an orange one never did; watching a hand pull a hidden token from jars, they reliably bet on the jar holding more black. This made kea only the second kind of animal, after great apes, ever shown to reason about raw odds. How long ago did the kea line split from the ape line that shares this rare mind?
answer: About 312 million years ago
choices: About 312 million years ago
About 25 million years ago
About 6 million years ago
About 65 million years ago
context: In a 2020 experiment, kea named Blofeld, Bruce, Loki, Neo, Plankton, and Taz bet on the jar with the higher proportion of winning tokens, making kea only the second kind of animal, after the great apes, ever shown to grasp probability by statistical inference. Birds and humans last shared an ancestor about 312 million years ago, so this reasoning evolved independently in a parrot brain. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-14695-1  (Legend.)

question: A king cobra can stretch to about 18 feet, the longest of any venomous snake alive. Laid out straight, that record length is closest to what everyday object?
answer: A full-grown giraffe standing tall
choices: A full-grown giraffe standing tall
A stretch limousine parked at the curb
A city bus at a bus stop
A one-story house from ground to roof
context: The king cobra (Ophiophagus hannah) is the longest venomous snake in the world, reaching about 18 feet, roughly the height of a tall adult giraffe. A stretch limo, city bus, and house are all considerably longer or taller. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/king-cobra

question: A cornered king cobra does something almost no other snake can: it lifts the front part of its body straight up and keeps sliding forward at whoever threatens it. How high can it rear?
answer: Enough to look a standing adult in the eye
choices: Enough to look a standing adult in the eye
Just a few inches, like a striking rattlesnake
Barely off the ground, coiled to spring
Onto its tail-tip, balanced fully upright
context: A threatened king cobra can raise up to a third of its body off the ground and still move forward, tall enough to meet a grown person eye to eye. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/king-cobra

question: A king cobra hunts down other snakes, and it will take on even the deadliest ones. Which of these venomous snakes does it hunt, kill, and swallow whole?
answer: The banded krait
choices: The banded krait
The Malabar pit viper
The green vine snake
The Russell's viper
context: Its genus name Ophiophagus means 'snake-eater.' The king cobra feeds mainly on other snakes and regularly hunts venomous species, including banded kraits, Indian cobras, and even other king cobras. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_cobra

question: A king cobra will swallow prey most snakes would never dare, gulping down victims longer than its own body. Which of these snakes will it overpower and swallow whole?
answer: A big reticulated python
choices: A big reticulated python
A thick emerald tree boa
A long Asian rat snake
A striped Indian racer
context: The king cobra will hunt and swallow other snakes, including big reticulated pythons, Indian cobras, and banded kraits, and it will even eat other king cobras. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_cobra

question: A single king cobra bite injects up to two-tenths of a fluid ounce of neurotoxin. That one dose carries enough venom to kill roughly what?
answer: A full-grown elephant
choices: A full-grown elephant
A single large dog
A small flock of chickens
One grown man, barely
context: The neurotoxin in one bite is enough to kill 20 people, or even an elephant. It attacks the nervous system, and without treatment a person can die in as little as 30 minutes. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/king-cobra

question: Almost every snake abandons its eggs the moment they are laid, but the female king cobra does something no other snake does: she stays. What does she guard for weeks until they hatch?
answer: A mounded nest of dry leaves
choices: A mounded nest of dry leaves
A burrow dug into damp clay
A raft of woven floating reeds
