question: The desert sidewinder rattlesnake crosses loose, scorching sand a strange way — its head already points where it's going while its body seems to roll diagonally across the dune. Why does it throw its body into sideways loops instead of just slithering ahead?
answer: Only two short segments touch the burning sand at a time; the rest is lifted into the air
choices: Only two short segments touch the burning sand at a time; the rest is lifted into the air
The looping motion lets it move much faster than an ordinary slither
It needs to keep its rattle raised and shaking as a warning the whole time
The loops let it change direction instantly without turning its head
context: The sidewinder rattlesnake (Crotalus cerastes) throws loops of its body sideways so that at any instant only two short segments press on the ground — the rest is held in the air, minimizing contact with the burning loose sand. Sources: Britannica, Sidewinder — https://www.britannica.com/animal/sidewinder ; Jayne, What Defines Different Modes of Snake Locomotion (ICB 2020) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7391877/

question: A sidewinder leaves a broken trail across a dune — a row of separate marks, each one curved into the shape of a letter J. A tracker who has never seen the snake can still read off exactly which way it was heading. What tells the direction?
answer: Each J-shaped mark hooks toward the way the snake was traveling
choices: Each J-shaped mark hooks toward the way the snake was traveling
The open mouth of each J faces the way the snake was traveling
The deeper end of each print shows where the heavier head pressed down
A faint drag-line links the prints and trails off behind the snake
context: A sidewinder's trail is a row of separate, disconnected J-shaped marks, and each hook points the way the snake was traveling — so even the empty tracks reveal its heading. (The prints stay disconnected because only two parts of the body touch down at a time, but it's the hook of the J that gives away the direction.) Sources: Wikipedia, Crotalus cerastes — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crotalus_cerastes ; Britannica — https://www.britannica.com/animal/sidewinder

question: A snake meets a smooth vertical pole — nothing to grip, no bumps to catch, and a plain slither just slides straight back down. It still hauls itself to the top. What does its body do to beat the smooth pole?
answer: Jams into tight bends to wedge still, pushes the front up, then drags the rest after
choices: Jams into tight bends to wedge still, pushes the front up, then drags the rest after
Rips its belly skin forward in waves and suctions itself flat to the metal
Whips into fast S-curves and rides the ripples straight upward
Splays its ribs into a wide ribbon and shimmies up on the flat
context: This is concertina locomotion, used to climb smooth poles or thread narrow tunnels: the snake bunches into tight bends to anchor itself, extends the front, re-anchors, and drags the back up — folding and unfolding like a squeezebox. There's nothing to push sideways against on a smooth pole, so this wedge-and-haul grip is the only way up — which is why it's slow and tiring, the snake keeping a firm anchor with part of its body the entire climb. Sources: Jayne, What Defines Different Modes of Snake Locomotion (ICB 2020) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7391877/ ; Wikipedia, Concertina movement — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concertina_movement

question: The horned rattlesnake lies almost buried in desert sand, waiting for prey, with two little raised scales jutting up above its eyes like tiny horns. Those 'horns' aren't weapons — what do they actually do for the snake?
answer: Fold down to shade the eyes and keep sand from drifting over them
choices: Fold down to shade the eyes and keep sand from drifting over them
Detect the body heat of approaching prey in the dark
Rattle together to add to its warning sound
Help it dig down into the loose sand to hide
context: The sidewinder is also called the 'horned rattlesnake' for its raised supraocular scales — little horns above each eye. They fold down to shade the eyes or keep sand from drifting over them while the snake lies almost buried, waiting in the desert. Source: Wikipedia, Crotalus cerastes — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crotalus_cerastes

question: A legless creature slides through the grass, and two details stop you cold: it blinks its eyes right at you, and there's a small ear-hole on the side of its head. You reach for 'snake' — but a true snake can do neither of those things. So what are you really looking at?
answer: A legless lizard, such as a glass lizard
choices: A legless lizard, such as a glass lizard
A burrowing skink whose legs have shrunk to tiny stubs
A caecilian, a limbless burrowing amphibian
An eel that has crawled up out of the water
context: A 'snake' that can blink or has a visible ear-hole is really a legless lizard, like a glass lizard (Ophisaurus). Snakes have no eyelids — their eyes are sealed under a clear scale, the brille — and no external ears, so neither trait belongs to a true snake. Legless lizards also carry most of their length in the tail, and many can drop that tail to escape a predator, which no snake can do. Source: Mental Floss, 5 Slithering Differences Between Snakes and Legless Lizards — https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/85553/5-slithering-differences-between-snakes-and-legless-lizards

question: Every legless gait leans on one trick of the belly scales, the scutes: they let the snake's underside slide easily in one direction but bite and catch in another, so a push turns into travel instead of a wasted wiggle. Which way do the scute edges slide most freely?
answer: Forward — they slip ahead but catch when dragged back or sideways
choices: Forward — they slip ahead but catch when dragged back or sideways
Backward — they slip behind but catch when pushed ahead
Sideways — they slip across but catch along the body's length
Every way equally — the scutes have no preferred direction at all
context: A snake's belly scales grip better in one direction than the other — like the treads on a tire. Friction is low sliding forward but high sliding backward or sideways: the trailing edges catch on tiny bumps to push while the leading edges slip forward almost freely. That one-way grip is what turns a wriggle into forward travel. Sources: Snakes move their scales to increase friction (Marvi & Hu); The Mechanics of Slithering Locomotion, PNAS — https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0812533106

question: The paradise flying snake of Southeast Asia has no wings, yet it can sail from one treetop to the next. Instead of gliding on outstretched limbs, what does it do with its own body to catch the air?
answer: Splays its ribs to flatten into a wide, hollowed ribbon
choices: Splays its ribs to flatten into a wide, hollowed ribbon
Inflates its lungs to balloon out and drift on the breeze
Spins rapidly like a falling maple seed to slow its drop
Sheds a flap of loose belly skin that opens like a parachute
context: The paradise flying snake (Chrysopelea paradisi) has no wings — it splays its ribs to flatten its whole body from a round cross-section into a wide, concave ribbon, a hollowed airfoil. Then it keeps sending S-waves down its body as it glides between trees: the same slither, only with the ground removed. Sources: Wikipedia, Chrysopelea paradisi — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysopelea_paradisi ; Virginia Tech News (Socha, 2020) — https://news.vt.edu/articles/2020/06/eng-flying-snakes-2020-study.html  (Legend.)

question: For nearly a century biologists sorted every legless slither into exactly four modes and thought the list was complete. Then in 2021, studying invasive brown tree snakes on Guam, researchers filmed one climbing a smooth 'snake-proof' baffle a brand-new way. How did it climb?
answer: Wrapping into a single loop around the pole and shifting bends to inch up
choices: Wrapping into a single loop around the pole and shifting bends to inch up
Gripping with a sticky pad newly found on the tip of its tail
Leaping upward in short hops off its coiled lower body
Rippling its belly skin to suction itself to the metal
context: This is 'lasso locomotion,' the surprising fifth mode discovered in 2021. The brown tree snake (Boiga irregularis) wraps its body into a single loop — a lasso — around a pole, then shifts tiny bends inside that loop upward to inch up a cylinder it otherwise couldn't climb. It was caught on camera because invasive brown tree snakes, accidentally brought to Guam around 1950, had wiped out most of the island's forest birds, and researchers filming snake-proof baffles on nest-box poles saw the snakes lasso straight up them. Bruce Jayne said the snake advances 'by shifting the location of each bend.' Source: Colorado State University / Warner College (Savidge, Jayne, Seibert; Current Biology 2021) — https://warnercnr.source.colostate.edu/scientists-discover-bizarre-new-mode-of-snake-locomotion/  (Legend.)

question: The belly scutes were long thought to be fixed hardware — rough one way, smooth the other, and that was that. But filming corn snakes revealed the grip is muscle-adjustable in real time: a snake that is awake and gripping hard has roughly DOUBLE the friction of a limp, unconscious one. What are its belly muscles actually doing to earn that extra bite?
answer: Tilting each belly scale up on edge to dig its rear rim into the ground
choices: Tilting each belly scale up on edge to dig its rear rim into the ground
Sweating a sticky film from glands between the scales to glue itself down
Inflating the whole underside with air to press more scale area onto the ground
Curling the scale tips into tiny hooks that latch onto grit and roots
context: Marvi, Hu and colleagues showed corn snakes contract their belly muscles to lift and tilt the ventral scales, raising each scale's angle of attack against the ground — a conscious, actively-scaling snake roughly doubles its friction coefficient over an unconscious one whose scales lie flat. This is the deeper mechanism under the scute-anisotropy rung: the grip is not fixed hardware but muscle-tuned moment to moment, letting one section anchor while another slides. Engineers copied it into 'Scalybot,' whose individually-servoed belly scales climbed foam inclines up to 45 degrees, matching a real corn snake. Source: Marvi, Hu et al. 2016, 'Snakes move their scales to increase friction' (Biotribology) — https://hu.gatech.edu/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/Hu16SnakeTribo.pdf ; corroborated by newatlas.com Scalybot coverage and researchgate.net/publication/267491606.

question: A python embryo starts building tiny hindlimbs — buds, even a scrap of leg skeleton — then quits partway, leaving only the little pelvic spurs an adult python keeps. The limb gene SHH still exists in snakes; what broke is the switch that should turn it on in the limb bud. That the program only stalls, never erasing, is the evidence behind a startling fossil claim. What do the fossils suggest happened to snake legs over deep time?
answer: Legs were lost, then partly regrown, then lost again — more than once
choices: Legs were lost, then partly regrown, then lost again — more than once
Legs shrank once, steadily and for good, as early snakes took to burrowing
A single ancestor lost all four at once, and no snake lineage ever varied again
Only the hindlimbs were ever reduced; snake forelimbs were lost far earlier
context: The Sonic hedgehog gene (SHH) drives limb growth in vertebrates, switched on in the limb bud by a regulatory enhancer called the ZRS. In snakes the ZRS is degraded — studies point to a snake-specific deletion (~17 base pairs) that knocks out essential transcription-factor binding sites — so python embryos still START a hindlimb, even a transient partial leg skeleton, before SHH fizzles and the limb aborts, leaving only vestigial pelvic spurs. Because the developmental program is only switched off, never erased, Leal and Cohn argued legs were lost and RE-ACQUIRED at least once across snake evolution. Fossils like four-limbed Tetrapodophis and hindlimb-only Najash (roughly 95–120 million years old) trace the reduction. This 're-emergence' reading is a genuine and still-debated claim, not settled textbook fact. Source: Leal & Cohn 2016, Current Biology, 'Loss and Re-emergence of Legs in Snakes by Modular Evolution of Sonic hedgehog and HOXD Enhancers' — pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27773569 ; corroborated via nature.com/articles/nrg.2016.149 and pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5484524.

question: Along the tidal mudflats and mangrove swamps of the tropics lives a fish that spends most of its life NOT swimming, but crawling and hopping across the open mud. What is this creature that seems to have left the water behind?
answer: A mudskipper
choices: A mudskipper
A jellyfish
A sea urchin
A giant clam
context: The mudskipper is a fish, but it spends most of its life out of water, hauling itself across tidal mudflats and mangrove swamps instead of swimming. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudskipper  (Legend.)

question: A mudskipper is stranded on open mud with no water to swim through, yet it crosses the flat steadily instead of just flopping in place. How does this fish get around on dry land?
answer: It plants its two pectoral fins like little arms and hauls itself forward
choices: It plants its two pectoral fins like little arms and hauls itself forward
It wriggles from side to side like a snake
It inches along by bunching up like a caterpillar
It rolls its whole body sideways down the slope
context: A mudskipper 'walks' by planting its two muscular pectoral fins like little arms or crutches and hauling its body forward across the mud. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/articles/this-fish-walks-on-land-and-breathes-through-its-skin/

question: A mudskipper crossing the mud does not just crawl. To cover ground fast, it suddenly flexes and pushes hard with its tail, flinging its whole body into a single leap. Roughly how far can one of these skips carry it?
answer: About 61 centimeters, some two feet
choices: About 61 centimeters, some two feet
About one centimeter, a fingertip
About 5 meters, most of a bus
About 20 meters, a swimming pool
context: By suddenly flexing and pushing with its tail, the mudskipper flings itself into a leap that can cover up to about 61 centimeters (2 feet) across the mud. This tail-flick skip is what gives the fish its name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudskipper  (Legend.)

question: Out on the mud in open air, a mudskipper still needs oxygen, but it is not gulping it through gills alone. Like a frog, it takes in air a second way. Through what does the mudskipper breathe while it is out of water?
answer: Through its moist skin and the wet lining of its mouth
choices: Through its moist skin and the wet lining of its mouth
Through two blowholes on its back
Through hollow spines along its spine
Through a snorkel-tube on its head
context: A mudskipper breathes air through its moist skin and through the wet lining of its mouth and throat, the way a frog does, rather than only through gills. This is called cutaneous and buccal respiration. Source: https://science.psu.edu/news/blinking-fish-reveals-clues-how-our-ancestors-evolved-water-land

question: Before a mudskipper leaves the water for a long trek across dry mud, it takes a big mouthful and packs its enlarged gill chambers full. It is carrying something with it like a built-in scuba tank. What has it stored in those puffed-out cheeks?
answer: A supply of water and air
choices: A supply of water and air
A clutch of its own eggs
A wad of sticky mud for building
A store of crushed shellfish
context: The mudskipper carries a mouthful of water and air in its enlarged gill chambers on land, like a built-in scuba tank. If those gills ever dry out, it can no longer take in oxygen. Source: https://oceanconservancy.org/blog/2022/05/12/5-facts-mudskippers/

question: On the open mud a male mudskipper suddenly rears up and drops down again and again, flares his back fin, drums his tail, and hurls himself high into the air. This looks like a threat to warn off a rival male nearby. What SECOND audience is this leaping show also aimed at?
answer: A female he is trying to impress
choices: A female he is trying to impress
A flock of seabirds he is scaring off
A cloud of biting insects overhead
A change in the weather he is answering
context: Male mudskippers defend their mud territory with dramatic push-up displays, flaring the dorsal fin, beating the tail, and leaping high into the air to warn off rivals AND impress females. The same show does double duty as courtship. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Mudskipper

question: A male mudskipper digs a burrow with a domed ceiling that traps a pocket of air, then rises to the surface again and again, gulping mouthfuls to fill the chamber for his eggs. Researcher Karen Martin counted the mouthfuls for the first bubble. Roughly how many trips did that take?
answer: About 100 mouthfuls
choices: About 100 mouthfuls
About 3 mouthfuls
About 10,000 mouthfuls
About one big gulp
context: A male digs a burrow with a domed, air-trapping ceiling and gulps mouthful after mouthful of air at the surface to stock the chamber with oxygen for his eggs; Karen Martin found a male may take roughly 100 mouthfuls to build that first air bubble. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/magazine/article/mudskipper-builds-ideal-nest-for-his-offspring  (Legend.)

question: For days the father mudskipper has kept his burrow stocked with air for the developing eggs, gulping mouthful after mouthful to hold the pocket full. Then, watching the tide, he does one deliberate thing at just the right moment that lets the eggs hatch and the young escape. What does he do?
answer: Gulps the air back out and lets water flood the burrow
choices: Gulps the air back out and lets water flood the burrow
Carries each egg to the sea in his mouth
Seals the burrow shut and abandons it
Fans fresh air across the eggs until they dry
context: After stocking the burrow with air, the father tracks the tide, then deliberately gulps the air OUT of the burrow and lets water flood in at just the right moment so the eggs hatch and the larvae can swim away. Scientist Karen Martin called the male 'really a very good papa.' Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/magazine/article/mudskipper-builds-ideal-nest-for-his-offspring  (Legend.)

question: A wolf pack closes in on a herd of musk oxen on the open Arctic tundra. These big, shaggy beasts overheat fast and can't outrun wolves, so instead of scattering they do something wolves can't crack. What do the adults do?
answer: Wheel into a tight ring, horns facing outward, calves hidden inside
choices: Wheel into a tight ring, horns facing outward, calves hidden inside
Split up and sprint in every direction to confuse the pack
Climb the nearest rocky slope to a ledge out of reach
Dive into a river and swim to the far bank together
context: Musk oxen (Ovibos moschatus) form a defensive ring: adults face outward in a phalanx of heads and horns while the calves are pressed against their mothers in the center. Against a single wolf they form a line instead of a ring. Standing their ground works because they can neither outrun nor out-endure their predators. Source: NPS, Gates of the Arctic — Circle Defense (nps.gov/gaar/learn/nature/muskox-circle-defense.htm).  (Legend.)

question: Beneath the musk ox's shaggy outer coat is a soft undercoat called qiviut, which the animal sheds in one spring moult. It's what lets the musk ox shrug off forty-below Arctic winters. How does qiviut compare to ordinary sheep's wool?
answer: About eight times warmer, and it won't shrink in water at any temperature
choices: About eight times warmer, and it won't shrink in water at any temperature
About the same warmth, but far more waterproof against snow
Slightly cooler, but it dries almost instantly after a soaking
Half as warm, but four times as strong and stiff
context: Qiviut (an Inuit word) is about eight times warmer than sheep's wool and finer than cashmere — roughly 18 micrometres versus cashmere's ~19 — and unlike wool it does not shrink in water at any temperature. The musk ox sheds it in one synchronized spring moult. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qiviut; Textile School qiviut article.

question: In the rut, two musk ox bulls back off up to 50 yards, then charge at 35 mph and smash foreheads square-on, again and again — a crash roughly equal to a 35 mph car wreck. Directly above the brain, what takes that repeated blow?
answer: About 4 inches of solid horn boss over 3 inches of skull bone
choices: About 4 inches of solid horn boss over 3 inches of skull bone
A thick pad of muscle that flexes to absorb the shock
A hollow air-filled sinus that collapses and springs back
A ridge of cartilage running between the two horns
context: A bull's forehead is armored for the collisions: about 4 inches of solid horn boss lies over 3 inches of skull bone, directly above the brain at the point of impact. Bulls repeat the head-on smash up to 20 times — the crack can be heard a mile away on a calm day — until one bull flees. Source: Alaska Dept. of Fish and Game, Muskox Species Profile (adfg.alaska.gov/index.cfm?adfg=muskox.main).

question: The musk ox once roamed across Europe, Asia, and North America, grazing the same ice-age tundra as woolly mammoths and sabre-toothed cats. When the great ice-age extinctions swept the mammoth away, what became of the musk ox?
answer: It endured, hanging on today as scattered herds in Greenland and Arctic Canada
choices: It endured, hanging on today as scattered herds in Greenland and Arctic Canada
It vanished from the wild and survives only in zoos and parks
It shrank to a dwarf form found only on remote Arctic islands
It moved south and now lives in the forests below the tundra
context: The musk ox lived alongside mammoths and sabre-toothed cats and endured the ice-age extinctions that killed the mammoth, surviving today only as scattered relict herds in Greenland and the Canadian Arctic Archipelago. Sources: oneearth.org/species-of-the-week-muskox; pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0907189107.  (Legend.)

question: A nearly hairless, wrinkled, near-blind rodent the size of a sausage spends its whole life digging through packed African earth. Its most jaw-dropping trait, unheard of in any other mammal, is that it lives:
answer: like an ant or termite colony, ruled by one breeding queen
choices: like an ant or termite colony, ruled by one breeding queen
in mated pairs that share a burrow for life
alone, meeting others only to mate
in loose herds that graze the surface at night
context: The naked mole-rat (Heterocephalus glaber) is eusocial: a single breeding queen rules while the rest are sterile workers who dig, gather food, and raise her pups for life. It is the most extreme case of eusociality known in any mammal. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, Naked mole-rat (nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/naked-mole-rat).  (Legend.)

question: Every naked mole-rat in a colony smells exactly alike, and a stranger with the wrong smell is attacked. To build that shared family scent, each colony member does one thing on purpose in the burrow's dirtiest room. What?
answer: it rolls around in the communal toilet chamber
choices: it rolls around in the communal toilet chamber
it licks the queen's fur clean each morning
it rubs noses with every rat it passes
it eats a pinch of soil from every tunnel
context: Naked mole-rats roll and wallow in their colony's communal latrine so every member picks up the same shared scent; a rat carrying the wrong colony smell is treated as an intruder and attacked. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo; O'Riain & Jarvis, colony odour studies.

question: A naked mole-rat queen is not born a queen; she becomes one. As she takes over and breeds, her body physically changes in a startling way to hold more and more pups. What actually happens to her body?
answer: her lower-back vertebrae stretch and lengthen, so she grows longer
choices: her lower-back vertebrae stretch and lengthen, so she grows longer
she grows a thick protective layer of fur
her legs shorten so she can wedge into the nursery
her teeth fuse into a single digging blade
context: The queen's lumbar vertebrae stretch and lengthen with each pregnancy, so her whole body grows longer over time. A large queen can carry as many as 30 pups in a single litter. Source: 'Growing out of a caste', Journal of Experimental Biology (journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/210/2/261); San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance.  (Legend.)

question: A naked mole-rat chisels through soil so hard-packed it would break a shovel, yet it never gets a mouthful of dirt. The trick is in how its mouth is built. Where are its front teeth?
answer: outside its lips, which close behind the teeth
choices: outside its lips, which close behind the teeth
hidden deep inside a bony beak
folded flat against the roof of its mouth
set far back near its throat
context: Naked mole-rats dig with their incisors sticking out in front of their lips, which close behind the teeth so the animal can tunnel without swallowing dirt. Each front tooth can even move on its own, like a pair of chopsticks. Source: Britannica, naked mole-rat; Smithsonian National Zoo '10 Things You Didn't Know'.

question: A naked mole-rat is a hairless rodent no bigger than a sausage, yet it tunnels through baked, concrete-hard African earth all day. Its body is specially loaded for the job: roughly a quarter of its total muscle is concentrated in one place. Where?
answer: the muscles that clamp its jaws shut
choices: the muscles that clamp its jaws shut
its shoulders and forelimbs
its neck and spine
its hind legs and tail
context: About a quarter of a naked mole-rat's entire muscle mass powers its jaw-closing muscles, which is how a hairless rodent chisels through hard-baked earth using its teeth. Source: Wikipedia, Naked mole-rat; Smithsonian National Zoo.

question: Splash acid or hot chili-pepper juice on a naked mole-rat's skin and it simply does not care. Its pain nerves work differently from every other mammal's. What single thing are they missing?
answer: a pain-signaling chemical called Substance P
choices: a pain-signaling chemical called Substance P
a fast-firing pain receptor called TRPV1
a nerve wrapping called the myelin sheath
a touch-sensing organ called the Merkel cell
context: Naked mole-rat nerves lack Substance P, a chemical that carries certain pain signals, so acid or capsaicin that would sting other animals does nothing to them. Source: Park et al., 'Selective Inflammatory Pain Insensitivity in the African Naked Mole-Rat', PLOS Biology (PMC2214810); Max Delbrück Center.  (Legend.)

question: To prove the missing chemical really was the reason naked mole-rats can't feel chili-pepper burn, scientists used a modified cold-sore virus to slip the pain-signal gene back into just ONE hind foot of a single animal. What happened to that one foot?
answer: it alone could suddenly feel the chili-pepper burn
choices: it alone could suddenly feel the chili-pepper burn
it went completely numb to every sensation
it swelled and had to be treated
it stopped growing hair around the toes
context: After the Substance P gene was delivered to one hind foot, that foot could feel capsaicin burn while the rest of the animal still could not, proving the missing chemical was the cause. Source: Park et al., PLOS Biology 2008 (PMC2214810); National Geographic.  (Legend.)

question: Scientists gave a naked mole-rat back the pain gene it was missing, expecting to make it feel everything a normal rodent feels. But one thing STILL did nothing to it, making it the only known animal that shows no pain response at all to this. To what?
answer: acid
choices: acid
cold
pressure
sound
context: Even after getting the pain gene back, naked mole-rats felt nothing from acid, making them the only known animal with no pain response to acid at all; their nerves are wired differently at a deeper level. Source: Science News, 'Spice It Up'; Park et al., PLOS Biology.

question: Seal a naked mole-rat in air with no oxygen and it does something no other mammal can do to keep its brain alive: it stops running its cells on their normal glucose fuel and switches to a backup fuel that a human brain cannot use. Which fuel does it switch to?
answer: fructose
choices: fructose
lactate
ketones
glutamate
context: When oxygen runs out, the naked mole-rat switches its cells to burn fructose, a plant-and-fruit sugar, instead of glucose, powering its body the way a plant does so its brain keeps running when a human would die. Source: Park et al., 'Fructose-driven glycolysis supports anoxia resistance in the naked mole-rat', Science 2017 (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aab3896); UIC Today.  (Legend.)

question: At oxygen levels low enough to kill a person in minutes, a naked mole-rat can survive at least five hours. Put it in air with NO oxygen at all, and after a stretch it simply gets up unharmed, as if nothing had happened. How long can it last with zero oxygen?
answer: about 18 minutes
choices: about 18 minutes
about 10 seconds
about 3 days
about a full week
context: With no oxygen at all, a naked mole-rat can last about 18 minutes and then recover unharmed. Source: UIC Today / phys.org coverage of Park et al., Science 2017; ScienceDaily.  (Legend.)

question: To feed fructose to its starving brain during oxygen loss, the naked mole-rat uses special molecular 'fructose pumps.' In every other mammal, including us, those pumps exist in only one organ. It borrowed the tool from that organ and installed it somewhere new. From which organ?
answer: the gut
choices: the gut
the liver
the kidneys
the lungs
context: The naked mole-rat's fructose pumps normally exist only in the gut in other mammals; it borrowed the intestinal tool and put it to work in the brain. Source: UIC Today; Park et al., Science 2017 (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aab3896).

question: A mouse is old at two years and rarely sees four. A naked mole-rat is barely middle-aged at the same age. How long can this rodent actually live?
answer: past 30 years
choices: past 30 years
about 6 years
about 12 years
about 20 years
context: Naked mole-rats can live past 30 years, the longest lifespan of any rodent and roughly ten times longer than a same-sized mouse. Source: AnAge / genomics.senescence.info (Heterocephalus glaber); University of Rochester news.  (Legend.)

question: For almost every animal, the older it gets the more likely it is to die that year. Naked mole-rats break that rule for at least 18 years: their yearly risk of death stays flat, so they barely seem to age. Scientists gave this near-ageless quality a name:
answer: negligible senescence
choices: negligible senescence
suspended animation
perpetual dormancy
reverse maturation
context: A naked mole-rat's risk of dying does not climb with age; its mortality stays flat for at least 18 years, a trait called negligible senescence. Longevity mechanisms are still active research. Source: PNAS / Rochester research (rochester.edu/newscenter/naked-mole-rats-cancer-aging-longevity); ScienceDirect.  (Legend.)

question: Naked mole-rat cells pump out a super-sized sugar-molecule, over five times bigger than the human version, and it makes their cells stop crowding together. Because of that one crowd-control signal, these rodents almost never fall to a deadly process that kills most other animals. Which process does it shut down?
answer: tumors forming
choices: tumors forming
blood clotting shut
wounds going septic
organs scarring stiff
context: Naked mole-rat cells pump out high-molecular-weight hyaluronan, over five times larger than the human version, which tells cells to stop crowding and forming tumors. Source: Tian et al., 'High-molecular-mass hyaluronan mediates the cancer resistance of the naked mole rat', Nature 2013 (nature.com/articles/nature12234).  (Legend.)

question: Warm-blooded mammals hold a steady inner temperature no matter the weather. The naked mole-rat is the strange exception: its body temperature drifts up and down instead, tracking its surroundings. Which animal does it behave like in this one respect?
answer: a lizard
choices: a lizard
a bird
a bat
a shark
context: The naked mole-rat is essentially the only mammal that behaves like a cold-blooded animal; its temperature drifts to match its tunnel, more like a lizard than a rodent. Source: Wikipedia, Naked mole-rat (thermoconformer), citing Buffenstein & Yahav.  (Legend.)

question: A naked mole-rat can barely warm itself, so on a cold day the colony has no inner furnace to rely on. When the burrow turns cold, what do they do to warm back up?
answer: they pile together into a tight warm huddle
choices: they pile together into a tight warm huddle
each one burrows off to trap its own heat
they eat extra food to burn for warmth
they seal the tunnels against the cold air
context: Because it cannot warm itself well, a cold naked mole-rat colony piles into a huddle and climbs to shallow, sun-warmed parts of the burrow, using teamwork instead of a furnace to stay warm. Source: 'Huddling Behavior Facilitates Homeothermy in the Naked Mole Rat', Physiological Zoology; Wikipedia.

question: A single naked mole-rat colony hollows out a tunnel network up to about 2.5 miles long. Far from being a random maze, it is organized like a tiny underground house, with separate rooms set aside for different jobs, including one whose job is:
answer: a designated toilet chamber
choices: a designated toilet chamber
a lookout tower to the surface
a graveyard for the dead
a hall for the queen to parade
context: A naked mole-rat colony can dig up to about 2.5 miles of tunnels, with separate chambers for the nursery, the food store, and even a designated toilet room. Newborn pups weigh less than a penny. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, '10 Things You Didn't Know About Naked Mole-rats'.

question: For decades the naked mole-rat was called the one mammal that CANNOT get cancer, because pathologists had never found a single tumor in one. Then in 2016 that absolute claim finally cracked. What overturned it?
answer: two aging captive males were confirmed with tumors
choices: two aging captive males were confirmed with tumors
a wild colony was wiped out by a viral outbreak
their famous super-sugar was found in mouse cells too
a queen was shown to reabsorb her own unborn pups
context: The two cases were a 22-year-old male at Chicago's Brookfield Zoo, with an adenocarcinoma in his armpit, and a 20-year-old male at the National Zoo in Washington, D.C., with a stomach tumor. Cancer in these rodents is still astonishingly rare, only two confirmed cases out of hundreds of animals examined, so 'almost never' still holds. But 'never' does not: the naked mole-rat can get cancer, just far less often than any other mammal. It is a good lesson that even a favorite textbook 'fact' gets corrected when the evidence finally shows up. Source: Delaney, Ward, Walsh, Treuting et al., 'Initial Case Reports of Cancer in Naked Mole-rats (Heterocephalus glaber),' Veterinary Pathology 53(3):691-696 (2016); PubMed 26846576; Smithsonian Insider summary (2016).

question: Researchers recorded thousands of the soft greeting chirps that naked mole-rats trade in the dark of their tunnels, then compared the calls of many separate colonies. What did the recordings reveal about these chirps?
answer: each colony speaks its own learned, queen-enforced dialect
choices: each colony speaks its own learned, queen-enforced dialect
the chirp doubles as a warning that a predator is near
a chirp's pitch reliably reveals the caller's exact age
only the reigning queen's body can produce the chirp
context: Researchers recorded thousands of the soft 'chirp' greeting calls and found every colony has its own distinct dialect. Cross-fostering proved it is learned, not inherited: pups adopted into another colony grew up chirping in their adoptive colony's accent, not their birth colony's. And the queen enforces it, when a colony loses its queen the shared accent breaks down, and a coherent dialect only re-forms once a new queen takes power. It is one of the clearest cases of a learned vocal culture in any rodent. Source: Barker, Veitl, Brecht et al., 'Cultural transmission of vocal dialect in the naked mole-rat,' Science 371(6528):503-507 (2021); DOI 10.1126/science.abc6588; PubMed 33510012.

question: An Arctic whale swims beneath the sea ice with a single long, straight, spiraling shaft jutting forward from its head — earning it a nickname borrowed from a mythical horned horse. Which whale is this?
answer: The narwhal, the 'unicorn of the sea'
choices: The narwhal, the 'unicorn of the sea'
The beluga, the 'canary of the sea'
The orca, the 'wolf of the sea'
The manatee, the 'cow of the sea'
context: The narwhal (Monodon monoceros) is a mid-sized Arctic whale famous for the long spiraling shaft that projects forward from its head, giving it the nickname 'unicorn of the sea.' Source: NOAA Ocean Exploration — 'What is a narwhal?' https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/ocean-fact/narwhal/

question: A narwhal's forward-jutting 'unicorn horn' looks like a horn, but it is nothing of the kind. Break open the mystery: what is that spiraling shaft actually made of?
answer: A single overgrown tooth — a left canine that erupts through the lip
choices: A single overgrown tooth — a left canine that erupts through the lip
A rod of solid keratin, like a rhino's horn
A fused extension of the skull's frontal bone
A stiffened cartilage spike rooted in the blowhole
context: The narwhal's 'horn' is really a tooth: a single overgrown left canine that grows straight out through the whale's upper lip, reaching up to about 10 feet (3 m) long. Source: Narwhal.org — Dr. Nweeia research page https://www.narwhal.org/about-dr-nweeia  (Legend.)

question: Every other toothed whale has a mouth lined with teeth for gripping prey. Open a narwhal's mouth and you find almost nothing — no rows of teeth at all. So how does a narwhal deal with a fish it has caught?
answer: It swallows the fish whole
choices: It swallows the fish whole
It shreds the fish against ridged plates in its throat
It grinds the fish with bony gum pads
It saws the fish apart with its tusk
context: Unlike every other toothed whale, the narwhal has essentially no teeth in its mouth — just two teeth in the upper jaw (in males, the left one becomes the tusk). With nothing to chew with, it swallows its prey whole. Source: Polar Science Center, Univ. of Washington — Narwhal FAQ https://psc.apl.uw.edu/rp/laidre/narwhal-faq/

question: A narwhal tusk is not a smooth straight spike — it twists in a spiral along its whole length. Here is the strange part scientists noticed: across every narwhal ever measured, and even in the rare two-tusked male, that spiral runs the very same direction. Which way does a narwhal's tusk always twist?
answer: Counterclockwise, to the left
choices: Counterclockwise, to the left
Clockwise, to the right
Alternating left and right by age
Randomly, differing whale to whale
context: The narwhal tusk always spirals counterclockwise (to the left). Even in the rare narwhal that grows two tusks, both spiral left — and one is always longer than the other. Source: Natural History Museum — 'Narwhals: mysterious unicorns of the sea' https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/narwhals-mysterious-unicorns-of-the-sea.html

question: For years no one knew what narwhals actually DID with their long tusks. In 2017, drones flying over Tremblay Sound in Nunavut finally filmed it: a narwhal approaches a fish and lands quick, precise taps with the tip of its tusk. What is the tap FOR?
answer: It stuns the fish, so the narwhal can suck up the dazed prey
choices: It stuns the fish, so the narwhal can suck up the dazed prey
It cracks the ice above to open a breathing hole
It signals rank to rival males nearby
It scrapes food loose from the seabed
context: In 2017, drone footage over Tremblay Sound, Nunavut, captured narwhals whacking Arctic cod with quick, precise taps of the tusk to stun the fish, then sucking up the dazed prey — the first time the behavior was ever filmed. Source: National Geographic — 'Video Solves Mystery of How Narwhals Use Their Tusks' https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/drone-footage-narwhal-tusk-mystery  (Legend.)

question: Harvard dental researcher Dr. Martin Nweeia said a narwhal tusk defies every rule he learned in dental school: it has no protective enamel and is riddled with about 10 million microscopic channels open to the ocean. Researchers think that lets the whale FEEL what about the water around it?
answer: Changes in its temperature and saltiness
choices: Changes in its temperature and saltiness
The direction of the nearest ice crack
The heartbeat of prey hiding in the dark
The pull of the Earth's magnetic field
context: Dr. Martin Nweeia found the tusk has no enamel, is permeable to seawater, and is packed with up to about 10 million nerve tubules running to its surface — leading researchers to propose it works as a sensory organ that can detect changes in the water's temperature and saltiness. The exact function is still active research, not settled fact. Source: PBS NOVA — 'Narwhal Tusks Might Be Nerve-Rich Ocean Sensors' https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/narwhal-tusks-are-actually-nerve-rich-teeth/  (Legend.)

question: Narwhals hunt Greenland halibut in the black, freezing water far below the Arctic surface, then hold their breath 25 minutes or more on one lungful to make the trip. To survive the crushing pressure down there, what does a narwhal's body physically do?
answer: Its rib cage folds and compresses
choices: Its rib cage folds and compresses
Its blood is rerouted to warm the fins
Its blowhole seals with a bony plug
Its eyes retract into protective sockets
context: Narwhals are among the deepest-diving whales, reaching about 1,800 meters (over a mile). To survive that pressure the rib cage folds and compresses, while muscles loaded with myoglobin let the whale hold its breath 25 minutes or more. Source: NOAA Climate.gov — 'The Narwhal's Tale'; UT Marine Science Institute — 'Deep-Diving Unicorns of the Sea'

question: We call it the 'unicorn of the sea,' but the Old Norse sailors who first named the narwhal chose a word far grimmer than any unicorn. Their name 'nár-hvalr' passed straight down into our word 'narwhal.' What did that Old Norse name actually mean?
answer: 'Corpse-whale'
choices: 'Corpse-whale'
'Spear-whale'
'Ghost-whale'
'Ice-whale'
context: The name 'narwhal' comes from Old Norse 'nár-hvalr' — 'corpse-whale' — thought to describe the animal's grey, mottled skin and its habit of floating motionless at the surface (a behavior called 'logging'), like a drifting body. Source: Etymonline https://www.etymonline.com/word/narwhal

question: Cephalopods like the octopus and squid ditched their outer shells long ago, but one coiled cousin still carries the same spiral shell it wore before the first dinosaur ever hatched, roughly half a billion years back. Biologists have a special two-word label for a creature that has drifted through the ages almost unchanged. Which coined term do they pin on the chambered nautilus?
answer: a living fossil
choices: a living fossil
a living relic
an ancient survivor
a time capsule
context: The chambered nautilus (Nautilus pompilius) has kept its coiled outer shell for roughly 500 million years, swimming the oceans long before the dinosaurs -- so biologists call it a 'living fossil.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chambered_nautilus  (Legend.)

question: A crab is bearing down on a chambered nautilus, whose eyes and grasping tentacles all face forward toward the threat. The nautilus fills a muscular funnel with seawater and blasts it out to escape. When that jet fires, which way does the nautilus actually shoot off through the water?
answer: backward
choices: backward
straight up
in tight circles
sideways
context: The nautilus swims by jet propulsion, squeezing water out through a forward-pointing funnel -- so the recoil shoots it backward through the sea, the same mechanism its squid and octopus relatives use. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautilus

question: An octopus reaches out with eight muscular, sucker-lined arms. Its shelled cousin the chambered nautilus goes about grabbing prey in a completely different way: it fans out around ninety slender appendages called cirri to snag a passing crab. What lets those cirri hold their catch, since not one of them carries a single sucker?
answer: they are extremely sticky
choices: they are extremely sticky
tiny hooked claws
a coating of venom
rings of sharp teeth
context: A nautilus has about 90 tentacles (cirri) -- far more than an octopus's eight -- and none have suckers; they grip prey simply by being extremely sticky. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chambered_nautilus  (Legend.)

question: The chambered nautilus lives inside only the outermost, largest room of its spiral shell -- but that shell is walled off into more than thirty sealed compartments. Instead of constantly swimming to hold its place in the water, the animal pumps gas and liquid in and out of those compartments to change how heavy it is, rising or sinking at will. What piece of human technology does this make the nautilus a living version of?
answer: a submarine
choices: a submarine
a hot-air balloon
a periscope
a diving bell
context: By pumping gas and liquid in and out of its sealed shell chambers to change its density, the nautilus rises and sinks at will instead of swimming constantly -- exactly the buoyancy trick a submarine uses. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chambered_nautilus  (Legend.)

question: An octopus eye is a self-contained ball, its inner fluid sealed away behind a lens and cornea just like our own. The chambered nautilus never grew that lens, and biologists were startled by what fills its eye instead. What is actually sitting right up against the nautilus's retina, bathing the very surface that senses light?
answer: raw ocean seawater
choices: raw ocean seawater
a drop of oil
a layer of gel
trapped air
context: Because the nautilus eye has no lens sealing it shut, the inside is open to the sea -- raw seawater flows right up against the retina, unlike every other cephalopod whose eye is a sealed fluid ball. Source: https://biologyinsights.com/nautilus-eyes-inside-the-pinhole-vision-marvel/  (Legend.)

question: The chambered nautilus drains its shell rooms to rise, and for a long time people pictured a tiny pump physically sucking the water out. The real trick is subtler: a living tube threading through the chambers, the siphuncle, actively pumps only ONE dissolved substance out of the trapped liquid into the animal’s blood. The water then leaves on its own, chasing that substance osmotically. What does the siphuncle pump out to make the water follow?
answer: salt
choices: salt
oxygen
calcium
ink
context: The siphuncle's columnar epithelial cells actively pump salt (NaCl) out of the trapped cameral liquid into the nautilus's blood; water then follows the salt osmotically and drains the chamber, and nitrogen gas (at slightly below atmospheric pressure) simply diffuses in to fill the empty space — no mechanical suction at all. This osmotic pump has a hard ceiling: below roughly 240 m the outside seawater pressure driving water back INTO the shell exceeds what the siphuncle's salt gradient can overcome, a genuine puzzle since living nautiluses routinely forage far deeper than 240 m. Source: Greenwald & Ward, 'Cameral liquid transport and buoyancy control in chambered nautilus,' Nature 286:55 (1980), nature.com/articles/286055a0; Grokipedia 'Siphuncle' (grokipedia.com/page/Siphuncle); corroborated by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautilus.

question: Look closely at the wall of one nautilus chamber and it is ruled with dozens of fine parallel lines, like tree rings squeezed into a single room. Kahn and Pompea found a modern shell lays down close to thirty of these lines between one chamber wall and the next — and that this rhythm let them read the shell as a clock. Each single fine line marks the growth the animal added in exactly one span of time. What span does one line record?
answer: one day
choices: one day
one hour
one meal
one dive
context: Modern Nautilus pompilius lays down about 30 fine daily growth lines per chamber — one line per solar day — so a full chamber records roughly 30 days, close to the 29.53-day lunar month, and the animal appears to seal off and start a new chamber about once a lunar month. Kahn and Pompea used this daily-line count as a fossil clock: the earliest nautiloids, 420 million years ago, show only about 9 lines between septa, implying a 'month' of only ~9 days back then, when the Moon orbited far closer and Earth's day was only ~21 hours. Tidal friction has since slowed Earth's spin and pushed the Moon outward, lengthening both. Source: Kahn & Pompea, 'Nautiloid growth rhythms and dynamical evolution of the Earth-Moon system,' Nature 275:606 (1978), nature.com/articles/275606a0; summarized at the University of Alaska Geophysical Institute, 'When the Days were Shorter' (gi.alaska.edu).  (Legend.)

question: Migrating European robins often set off on cloudy, moonless nights with no sun and no stars in sight, yet they still fly the correct direction. Wolfgang and Roswitha Wiltschko caged robins, altered the invisible force surrounding them, and the birds turned to match. What sense are the robins steering by?
answer: An internal magnetic compass
choices: An internal magnetic compass
A memorized map of landmarks
A pull they feel from the tides
Faint sounds carried on the wind
context: On starless nights there is nothing overhead to steer by, so the robins must carry the reference inside them. When the Wiltschkos changed the field around caged robins, the birds shifted their heading to match — the classic demonstration of an internal magnetic compass. Source: Wiltschko & Wiltschko, 'Magnetic Compass of European Robins', JSTOR https://www.jstor.org/stable/1733331 ; NWF https://www.nwf.org/Magazines/National-Wildlife/1999/Navigating-With-A-Built-In-Compass

question: A hiker's compass needle swings to point out which way is north. The caged European robin does something different: it can tell 'toward the equator' from 'toward the pole' in total darkness, without ever knowing which pole is which. Which feature of Earth's field is the robin actually reading?
answer: The angle the field lines dip into the ground
choices: The angle the field lines dip into the ground
Which way along the ground the field points
The strength of the field's steady pull
How fast the field shifts as the bird moves
context: The robin reads inclination — how steeply the field lines tilt down. That dip is shallow near the equator and steep near the poles, so 'equatorward' and 'poleward' feel different even in the dark, which is why the bird never needs to identify north or south. Source: Wikipedia Magnetoreception https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception ; Wiltschko & Wiltschko https://www.internationalornithology.org/PROCEEDINGS_Durban/Symposium/S17/S17.4.htm

question: Loggerhead sea turtle hatchlings scramble off the beach into open ocean with no parent and no map, yet each finds its way along a migratory route that curves thousands of miles across the open Atlantic. Every stretch of coast carries its own magnetic signature. When Kenneth Lohmann dropped hatchlings into the exact field of three far-apart points on that route, each one turned and swam a different, specific heading. What must a hatchling be reading from the field to pick a heading that only makes sense at that spot?
answer: Its own position on the globe
choices: Its own position on the globe
The single compass direction toward home
How far it has already swum from shore
Which way the ocean current is flowing
context: Each stretch of coast has a unique magnetic signature — a pairing of the field's angle and its strength — and the hatchling treats those like the latitude and longitude lines of a grid. Reproduce the field of a distant point on the route and the turtle swims the heading that would be correct there, proof it is reading its position, not merely a direction. Source: Lohmann Lab, 'Geomagnetic Imprinting in Sea Turtles and Salmon' https://lohmannlab.web.unc.edu/geomagnetic-imprinting/ ; Brothers & Lohmann, Current Biology 2015

question: A female loggerhead sea turtle may not be old enough to breed until she is around 35, so decades pass between the night she hatches and the night she first hauls ashore to lay eggs. When she finally returns, she picks a beach with one very particular magnetic address. Which beach is it?
answer: The very beach where she herself hatched
choices: The very beach where she herself hatched
Whichever beach is nearest at nightfall
The beach with the fewest other turtles
A different beach each year of her life
context: This is 'natal homing' — she comes back to nest within a few kilometres of where she hatched, finding it decades later by the magnetic signature she learned as a hatchling. Lohmann's team even matched 19 years of Florida nesting to it: where neighbouring beaches' signatures drifted together, turtles crowded in. Source: Brothers & Lohmann, Current Biology 2014 https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(14)01638-8 ; NWF https://www.nwf.org/Educational-Resources/Wildlife-Guide/Reptiles/Sea-Turtles/Loggerhead-Sea-Turtle  (Legend.)

question: A monarch butterfly flying up to 2,000 miles to a few fir groves in central Mexico can hold a southerly heading even under thick overcast, reading the tilt of Earth's magnetic field. In a tethered-flight simulator its compass stopped working the moment researchers painted over one body part. Where does the monarch carry its magnetic compass?
answer: In its antennae
choices: In its antennae
In its wing scales
In its curled feeding tube
In its six walking legs
context: The monarch's compass is light-dependent and lives in the antennae; blacking them out with paint knocked out the sense while the butterfly could still fly. It uses the field's inclination angle to keep its bearing on cloudy days when it cannot see the sun. Source: Guerra, Gegear & Reppert, 'A magnetic compass aids monarch butterfly migration', Nature Communications 2014 https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms5164

question: Nobody has proven how a bird's magnetic compass actually works, but the leading idea is astonishing. Scientists think a protein called cryptochrome forms a pair of molecules whose electron spins are quantum-linked, and Earth's weak field nudges those spins. If that idea is right, what might the robin experience?
answer: It may see the field as a pattern over its vision
choices: It may see the field as a pattern over its vision
It may taste the field on the back of its tongue
It may feel the field as heat along its wings
It may hear the field as a low tone in its ears
context: The reaction starts with light hitting cryptochrome (likely Cry4) in the retina, so the 'radical-pair hypothesis' suggests the bird sees the field as shading laid over what it looks at. In 2021 researchers found robin Cry4 more magnetically sensitive in a test tube than chicken or pigeon Cry4 — a good fit, but still a hypothesis, not proof the bird navigates by it. Source: Xu et al., Nature 2021 https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03618-9  (Legend.)

question: Kenneth Lohmann's team fed young loggerhead turtles for two months only inside one artificial magnetic 'location' and never inside another. Later they set each turtle into the fed spot's field with no food anywhere in the tank. The turtles instantly gave themselves away, proving they had memorized that magnetic address. What did a turtle do?
answer: Tilted upright and dogpaddled with its mouth open
choices: Tilted upright and dogpaddled with its mouth open
Buried itself in the sand at the bottom of the tank
Swam a tight circle and then floated completely still
Snapped repeatedly at its own reflection in the glass
context: Researchers nicknamed it the 'turtle dance': the loggerhead tilts vertical, pokes its head above the surface, opens its mouth, and paddles with its front flippers — the excited feeding display, performed at a spot it had learned by magnetic field alone with no food present. The same 2025 study went further and showed the turtle carries TWO separate magnetic senses: this learned MAP (which location am I at?) kept working under a radio-frequency field, while its directional COMPASS (which way is which?) was scrambled by it — so the map appears to run on iron/magnetite and the compass on quantum radical-pair chemistry, two different mechanisms in one animal. Source: Goforth, Lohmann et al. 2025, Nature, 'Learned magnetic map cues and two mechanisms of magnetoreception in turtles' (nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08554-y); dance behavior and two-month conditioning from the UNC College of Arts & Sciences release and Scientific American coverage.

question: To probe how a robin knows north, Thorsten Ritz and the Wiltschkos bathed caged birds in a radio field far too weak to move a needle — under a thousandth of Earth's own field. It wrecked their sense of direction, but only when tuned to one narrow frequency near 1.3 megahertz. What must the bird's compass sensor be, for so faint and precise a signal to disrupt it?
answer: A single unpaired electron whose spin flips in step with that frequency
choices: A single unpaired electron whose spin flips in step with that frequency
A grain of iron pulled into a shudder that matches that same frequency
A beak nerve firing rhythmic bursts that lock onto that same frequency
A cluster of pressure cells that hum and ring at that same frequency
context: The magic pitch was about 1.3 MHz (measured at 1.315 MHz in Frankfurt) — and a field only ~15 nanotesla strong, weaker than a city's electrical hum, was enough to wreck the compass when tuned there. That exact frequency is the 'Larmor' rate at which a single unpaired electron spin precesses in Earth's ~50-microtesla field, so a radio field matching it disturbs the singlet/triplet spin flips at the heart of the proposed radical pair. Iron magnets don't respond to a signal that faint and precise; a lone electron spin does — which is why this remains the single strongest evidence for the radical-pair compass. Frame honestly: it SUPPORTS the leading hypothesis, which is still not proven inside a living bird. Source: Ritz et al. 2004, Nature, 'Resonance effects indicate a radical-pair mechanism for avian magnetic compass' (PubMed 15141211); 15 nT figure, Larmor formula, and 1.315 MHz value from review PMC5627152.

question: On the Pacific islands of New Caledonia lives a glossy black crow with no woodpecker to compete with. It has taken over the woodpecker's job entirely — winkling fat grubs out of holes in dead wood. What does it use to do it?
answer: Tools it makes and wields
choices: Tools it makes and wields
Its extra-long barbed tongue
A drumming beak that splits bark
Sticky saliva on its feathers
context: The New Caledonian crow (Corvus moneduloides) fills the ecological niche of a woodpecker on islands that have none, and it is one of the only animals besides apes known to make its own tools. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Caledonian crow' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Caledonian_crow).

question: A New Caledonian crow doesn't just grab a handy twig — it manufactures a proper tool. It snips a twig from a fork in a branch, then trims the wood away until one specific feature is left at the tip. What has it shaped, that no other wild animal is known to make?
answer: A hook
choices: A hook
A flattened spade
A hollow straw
A forked splinter
context: The crow trims a fork down to a hook at the tip, then hooks grubs out of crevices — the only non-human animal known to manufacture hooked tools in the wild. Source: Nature, Hunt 1996, 'Manufacture and use of hook-tools by New Caledonian crows' (nature.com/articles/379249a0).

question: New Caledonian crows also work with pandanus leaves, whose edges carry rows of tiny backward-pointing barbs. A crow cuts a precise stepped strip so those barbs line up as a row of snags. Researchers compared the strip designs made by crow populations across the island, old shapes against new. What was true of how the designs changed over time?
answer: Newer strips were more refined than older ones
choices: Newer strips were more refined than older ones
Newer strips were cruder than older ones
Populations copied one identical strip
Only lone crows ever tweaked a strip
context: Different crow populations make slightly different pandanus tool designs that grew more refined generation after generation — a bird version of cumulative culture, and the only non-primate case known where each generation builds on the last. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Caledonian crow'; Hunt & Gray pandanus tool diversification research.

question: In a famous 2002 Oxford experiment, a captive crow named Betty faced a food bucket sunk deep in a tube. She was given a straight wire and a hooked wire — but her mate Abel snatched the hooked one and flew off. Left with only the straight wire, what did Betty do?
answer: Bent it into a hook herself
choices: Bent it into a hook herself
Called Abel back with the food
Dropped it and gave up
Threaded it through the tube wall
context: Betty bent the straight wire into a hook and lifted the food bucket out — a landmark moment in animal-cognition research. Source: Weir & Kacelnik 2002/2006, Oxford; Science, 'Was Betty the crow a genius—or a robot?' (science.org). (legend)

question: Betty's wire-bending was hailed as a flash of pure invention — she went on to hook the wire in nine out of ten later trials. Years later, new evidence forced scientists to revise that story of her feat. What did it show?
answer: Bending tools is a natural crow move
choices: Bending tools is a natural crow move
Crows can bend wire but never twigs
Only Betty ever managed the trick
Her wire had been pre-bent by staff
context: Wild crows were found to bend their tools the same way, so Betty's trick may be part of the species' natural repertoire rather than pure on-the-spot invention. Source: Science, AAAS; Royal Society Open Science, Rutz et al. 2016. (legend)

question: A New Caledonian crow is handed a short stick and a scrap of meat it cannot reach. A second, longer stick lies inside a nearby box. With no coaching and only one shot, how did the crows crack it on their very first try?
answer: Used the short stick to fish out the long one, then reached the meat
choices: Used the short stick to fish out the long one, then reached the meat
Flung the short stick at the meat to knock it closer to the bars
Wedged the short stick into the box to pry the whole lid open
Tapped the short stick until a keeper handed over the long one
context: Six of seven crows solved this 'tool to get a tool' metatool problem on the first attempt — using the short stick to retrieve the long stick, then the long stick on the meat, a hallmark of planning. Source: Wikipedia citing metatool experiments; PubMed, 'New Caledonian Crows Use Mental Representations to Solve Metatool Problems'.

question: New Caledonian crows pass the challenge from Aesop's fable 'The Crow and the Pitcher': a treat floats out of reach in a water tube, and the crow must raise the water to reach it. Offered a mix of objects, the crows picked heavy sinking stones over floaters and solid over hollow. That grasp of cause and effect roughly matched what?
answer: A five-to-seven-year-old child
choices: A five-to-seven-year-old child
A trained laboratory rat
A newly hatched chick
An adult chimpanzee's ceiling
context: By dropping sinking stones to raise the water level, the crows displayed causal understanding roughly on par with a 5-to-7-year-old child. Source: Jelbert et al. 2014, PLOS ONE; ScienceDaily. (legend)

question: In the caves of New Zealand, a creature called the glowworm dangles glowing sticky lines from the ceiling to snag flying insects. Despite its name, it is not a worm at all. What kind of animal is it?
answer: the larva of a fly
choices: the larva of a fly
a young spider
a kind of caterpillar
a small cave slug
context: The New Zealand glowworm (Arachnocampa luminosa) is really a maggot -- the larva of a fungus gnat, a fly in the order Diptera, family Keroplatidae. It glows blue-green at the tail end of its body to lure flying insects into its sticky lines. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arachnocampa_luminosa  (Legend.)

question: Tourists drift by boat through the pitch-black Waitomo Caves in New Zealand and look up at thousands of tiny blue-green glowworm lights scattered across the ceiling overhead. What does the ceiling look like?
answer: a starry night sky
choices: a starry night sky
a field of glowing mushrooms
rows of hanging lanterns
streaks of lightning
context: In the famous Waitomo Glowworm Caves, thousands of Arachnocampa luminosa larvae cover the ceiling, and their blue-green lights look exactly like a starry night sky or a galaxy overhead -- a world-famous natural spectacle visitors float beneath in the dark. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitomo_Glowworm_Cave  (Legend.)

question: A New Zealand glowworm lures flying insects toward the blue-green light glowing at the end of its body. When one larva grows hungry and needs to trap more prey, what does it do with that light?
answer: turns it brighter
choices: turns it brighter
switches it off
flashes it on and off
changes it to red
context: A hungrier Arachnocampa luminosa larva turns UP the intensity of its blue-green glow to lure more prey, then dims once it is well-fed. Its light is true bioluminescence -- a chemical light made at the end of its abdomen. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/glow-worm-new-zealand-caves

question: The New Zealand glowworm spends 6 to 12 months as a hungry, hunting larva. Then it finally transforms into an adult fly that survives only a few days before it dies. Why can the adult not live any longer?
answer: it has no mouth and cannot eat
choices: it has no mouth and cannot eat
its wings are too weak to fly
the cave cold quickly freezes it
it burns out its last light
context: The adult fly that hatches from Arachnocampa luminosa has no functional mouth -- it cannot eat at all. It lives only days (females up to about 76 hours, males up to about 96 hours) with the sole purpose of mating and laying eggs before it dies. The long larval stage exists to fund that brief adult life. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arachnocampa_luminosa  (Legend.)

question: Off the coast of Italy, a jellyfish barely wider than a pinky fingernail carries a nickname no other animal can claim: the 'immortal jellyfish.' What has scientists watching Turritopsis dohrnii so closely?
answer: When stressed, an adult can rewind into its own younger stage and start over
choices: When stressed, an adult can rewind into its own younger stage and start over
It grows to the size of a dinner plate within a single week
It glows bright enough to read a book by on the sea floor
Its sting is the most powerful of any creature in the ocean
context: Turritopsis dohrnii's bell reaches only about 4.5 millimetres across, roughly the size of a pinky fingernail - yet a stressed adult can run its life cycle backwards, earning it the 'immortal jellyfish' name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turritopsis_dohrnii  (Legend.)

question: A Turritopsis dohrnii medusa - the free-swimming adult jellyfish stage - is starved and injured. Instead of dying, it sinks to the sea floor and balls up into a featureless blob. What does that blob become?
answer: A young polyp, the stalked seabed stage
choices: A young polyp, the stalked seabed stage
A clutch of fertilized eggs anchored to the rock
A drifting swarm of newly hatched larvae
A cloud of a hundred identical adult jellyfish
context: A polyp is the stalk-like seabed stage that jellyfish grow from before budding off as free-swimming medusae. When stressed by starvation, injury, or a sudden change in temperature or saltiness, the adult Turritopsis reverts all the way back to this young polyp - running its life cycle backwards. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turritopsis_dohrnii  (Legend.)

question: To rewind into a younger polyp, Turritopsis dohrnii doesn't just shrink - its already-finished cells rebuild themselves into different kinds. A muscle cell, for instance, can turn straight into a nerve cell. What is this cell-to-cell switch called?
answer: Transdifferentiation
choices: Transdifferentiation
Photosynthesis
Metamorphosis
Hibernation
context: Transdifferentiation is a fully specialized cell switching into a different cell type - like a muscle cell becoming a nerve cell - as the jellyfish recycles its own body into a younger form. It is the mechanism behind the reversal. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6893190/

question: Popular headlines call Turritopsis dohrnii the animal that 'cannot die.' In the wild, though, most of them never live long enough to rewind at all. Why does the 'immortal jellyfish' still keep dying?
answer: Predators eat it or disease kills it while it's still an adult
choices: Predators eat it or disease kills it while it's still an adult
Its rewind only works three times before it stops
It freezes solid the first cold night of winter
It forgets how to revert once it becomes an adult
context: Myth-correction: 'immortal' only means Turritopsis dohrnii can rewind to a younger stage - it is NOT unkillable. In the wild most still die, eaten by predators or killed by disease in the medusa stage, before ever reverting. The trick is transformation, not invincibility. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turritopsis_dohrnii  (Legend.)

question: The freshwater Hydra is a tiny tentacled relative of the jellyfish. Researchers tracked thousands of them for years to answer one question: as a Hydra gets older, what does its chance of dying each year do?
answer: Stays flat - it doesn't rise as the animal ages
choices: Stays flat - it doesn't rise as the animal ages
Doubles every single month it survives
Drops to exactly zero after its first year
Climbs steeply, the way it does in most animals
context: This is called 'negligible senescence': the Hydra doesn't grow measurably more likely to die as it ages, because stem cells constantly rebuild its whole body. Source: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1521002112

question: Because a Hydra's yearly chance of dying never climbs with age, one team ran the numbers on a whole population - assuming nothing ate them. How long did they calculate a few percent would still be alive?
answer: More than 1,400 years
choices: More than 1,400 years
About 40 years
Around 200 years
Roughly 60,000 years
context: With a death rate that stays flat with age, the study calculated that even after 1,400 years, a few percent of a Hydra population would still be alive - if nothing ate them first. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4697432/  (Legend.)

question: The naked mole-rat is a wrinkled, nearly hairless rodent that digs tunnels under East Africa. Compared with a mouse of similar size - which lives about three years - how long can a naked mole-rat live?
answer: More than 30 years
choices: More than 30 years
About 5 years
Around 12 years
Roughly 100 years
context: The naked mole-rat is the longest-lived rodent, with some living more than 30 years - about ten times longer than a similar-sized mouse. Source: https://elifesciences.org/articles/31157  (Legend.)

question: Naked mole-rats almost never get cancer. Vera Gorbunova and Andrei Seluanov traced it to a thick, sugary molecule packed between the animal's cells. How does that molecule keep cancer away?
answer: It stops cells from crowding together and overgrowing
choices: It stops cells from crowding together and overgrowing
It poisons any tumor the moment it forms
It scrubs damaged DNA clean every single night
It starves fast-growing cells of all oxygen
context: The molecule is high-molecular-weight hyaluronan; it keeps naked mole-rat cells from crowding and overgrowing, which almost never lets cancer take hold. Discovered by Vera Gorbunova and Andrei Seluanov. Source: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/02/180206115143.htm

question: A lobster doesn't slow down with age the way most animals do - the oldest, biggest females can actually lay MORE eggs than young ones. They keep making telomerase, an enzyme that repairs part of every chromosome. Which part does telomerase rebuild?
answer: The tips, which normally fray shorter each time a cell divides
choices: The tips, which normally fray shorter each time a cell divides
The centromere, the pinched waist that guides the split
The histone spools the strand winds around for storage
The replication fork where the two strands unzip
context: Lobsters keep making telomerase, an enzyme that protects the ends (tips) of their chromosomes - which is partly why they keep growing and stay fertile their whole lives. Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/are-lobsters-immortal.html

question: People love to say lobsters are 'immortal' because they never stop growing. But the very act of getting bigger is what finally kills many of them. What deadly ordeal do old, giant lobsters face over and over?
answer: Molting - shedding a huge shell exhausts them and leaves them defenseless
choices: Molting - shedding a huge shell exhausts them and leaves them defenseless
Starving because their claws grow too heavy to lift food
Sinking too deep to ever return to warm water
Freezing when their blood can no longer flow
context: Lobsters are NOT truly immortal: the older and bigger they get, the harder it is to molt their shell, and many die of exhaustion or predation during that dangerous molt. Source: https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/student-contributors-did-you-know/lobsters-are-not-immortal-myth-they-are-seems-be

question: The immortal jellyfish has a cousin, Turritopsis rubra, that lives an ordinary mortal life and never rewinds. When a 2022 genome study set the two side by side, what did Turritopsis dohrnii carry that its mortal cousin lacked?
answer: Extra copies of genes that repair and protect its DNA
choices: Extra copies of genes that repair and protect its DNA
A second nervous system that overrides its first
Venom strong enough to paralyze its own predators
A shell it can retreat into whenever it is injured
context: In 2022, Maria Pascual-Torner, Carlos Lopez-Otin, and colleagues sequenced Turritopsis dohrnii alongside its close cousin Turritopsis rubra, which cannot rewind. The immortal one carried duplicated copies of DNA-repair genes and DNA polymerases, plus protective variants for telomere upkeep, stem-cell maintenance, and clearing damaged proteins - roughly twice as many gene-protection/repair genes as its mortal cousin. So the trick isn't magic: it's an expanded genetic toolkit for keeping its DNA clean. Source: Pascual-Torner, Lopez-Otin et al., 'Comparative genomics of mortal and immortal cnidarians unveils novel keys behind rejuvenation,' PNAS 2022, 119(36) (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2118763119); corroborated by The Scientist.

question: A naked mole-rat cell stops dividing while its neighbors are still far apart - long before a mouse cell would quit. Researchers digested away the giant sugar molecule packed around it, and the cell promptly formed a tumor. What had that molecule been doing?
answer: Tripping the p16 brake that halts growth early
choices: Tripping the p16 brake that halts growth early
Feeding the cell so it never needed to spread
Cloaking the cell from the animal's immune patrols
Cooling the tissue below the temperature tumors need
context: In 2013, Xiao Tian, Vera Gorbunova, Andrei Seluanov, and colleagues found naked mole-rats make a giant form of hyaluronan (HMW-HA) about five times larger than a mouse's or human's (roughly 6-12 million daltons vs 0.5-3 million). It makes cells arrest at much lower densities - 'early contact inhibition' - by triggering the p16 (p16INK4a) tumor-suppressor switch, slamming the brakes before a tumor can form. When researchers digested the molecule away or knocked out the HAS2 gene that builds it, the cells could then form tumors - proving the molecule is what protects them. Source: Tian et al., 'High-molecular-mass hyaluronan mediates the cancer resistance of the naked mole rat,' Nature 2013, 499:346-349 (nature.com/articles/nature12234).

question: A numbat is a tiny striped marsupial of Western Australia that eats almost nothing but termites, digging into their shallow underground galleries and slurping up around 20,000 of them in a single day. What tool lets it clear so many termites out of those narrow tunnels?
answer: A long tongue coated in sticky saliva
choices: A long tongue coated in sticky saliva
A set of powerful crushing jaws
A hollow snout it sucks air through
A mouthful of sharp shearing teeth
context: The numbat's tongue flicks out about 10 cm — nearly a third of its whole body length — and the sticky coating traps termites deep in their tunnels. It needs the reach because a small numbat can only work galleries close to the surface. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbat

question: Nearly every marsupial — kangaroos, possums, quolls, wombats — sleeps through the day and moves at night. The numbat is the single exception: it is fully active in broad daylight. What forces this little termite-eater onto a daytime schedule?
answer: Termites climb near the surface only in daylight
choices: Termites climb near the surface only in daylight
Its eyes are useless in total darkness
Daytime warmth keeps its small body from chilling
Night predators would easily catch it
context: The numbat is the only marsupial that is fully diurnal. A small numbat can only reach termites when they rise close to the top of their galleries, and that happens by day — so its whole schedule is set by its prey's, not by avoiding the dark. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbat

question: A female numbat gives birth to four bean-sized young, who must spend their first months of life attached to her four teats. For a marsupial, the way she carries them is very strange. Where do these newborns actually ride?
answer: Dangling in the open from exposed teats, with no pouch
choices: Dangling in the open from exposed teats, with no pouch
Sealed inside a deep fur-lined belly pouch
Tucked into stretchy pouches in her cheeks
Gripped in the curl of her bushy tail
context: Unusually for a marsupial, the female numbat has no pouch at all. Her four teats sit on a bare patch of belly protected only by crimped golden hair, and the clinging newborns dangle in the open air for months. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbat

question: A numbat shelters in a hollow log or a burrow, and when a predator comes hunting it backs all the way inside. But the entrance is still open behind it. How does the numbat stop the attacker from squeezing in after it?
answer: It jams the opening shut with its thick, tough-hided rump
choices: It jams the opening shut with its thick, tough-hided rump
It sprays a foul-smelling fluid at the entrance
It curls into a tight ball of sharp spines
It rakes the attacker back with its front claws
context: The skin over a numbat's rump is thick and tough, and it uses that hindquarter like a living door — backing in and plugging the entrance so nothing can get past it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbat
