question: For centuries sailors swore they had seen sea serpents — long silver monsters writhing at the surface. Marine scientists now think most of those reports were really one dying deep-sea creature rolling in the waves. Which animal?
answer: The oarfish
choices: The oarfish
The giant squid
The basking shark
The leatherback turtle
context: The giant oarfish is a scaleless ribbon of silver with a flaming red crest and fin running its whole length. A sick or dying one drifts up and rolls at the surface — a near-perfect match for the classic 'sea serpent' report. A 2016 River Monsters investigation concluded it is the most likely real-world origin of the myth. LEGEND (science-of-legend). Source: Florida Museum — Discover Fishes; Wikipedia 'Giant oarfish'.

question: A silvery ribbon of a fish drifts up onto a beach, stretched out roughly 8 metres (26 feet). No other bony fish alive grows this long. What is this record-holder?
answer: The oarfish
choices: The oarfish
The moray eel
The barracuda
The sturgeon
context: The giant oarfish (Regalecus glesne) is the longest bony fish alive, reliably reaching about 8 metres, with some reports up to 11. Sharks and rays grow longer, but their skeletons are cartilage, not bone. Old claims of 17-metre oarfish are considered exaggerations. Source: Florida Museum; Wikipedia 'Giant oarfish'.

question: A tall plume of long red rays rises from the head of the oarfish, spreading like a crown above its silver body. That regal look earned the fish an old folk name. What were people calling it?
answer: King of herrings
choices: King of herrings
Sea unicorn
Silver duke
Crown eel
context: A dorsal fin runs the entire length of the oarfish, tipped at the head with a tall red crest of long rays. The crownlike look earned it the folk name 'king of herrings' — giving it the appearance of a maned sea dragon. Source: Wikipedia 'Giant oarfish'; Florida Museum.

question: On the coast of Japan the oarfish has a special name — 'ryugu no tsukai,' the messenger from the sea dragon god's palace. When one washes ashore, crowds gather, because many people believe its arrival is a warning of what?
answer: A coming earthquake
choices: A coming earthquake
A rich fishing season
A royal death
A great storm at sea
context: Because the oarfish lives deep and rarely surfaces, folklore holds that it swims up to warn of an earthquake, so a stranding draws crowds. A 2019 study of 336 sightings found no real link between oarfish and quakes — so it remains a belief, not a fact. LEGEND (folk belief, framed as belief). Source: Atlas Obscura 'The Legend of Japan's Earthquake Fish'; Logically Facts (2019 study).

question: For a fish up to 8 metres long, the oarfish is a shockingly gentle giant — it has no real teeth at all. Instead it feeds by straining tiny krill and plankton from the water. What lets it filter out that swarm of tiny prey?
answer: Fine gill rakers in its mouth
choices: Fine gill rakers in its mouth
A sticky mucus net it casts out
Rows of grinding throat plates
A sucking, tube-shaped snout
context: The oarfish filters tiny krill and plankton through fine gill rakers — comblike structures in the mouth. One specimen was found with about 10,000 krill inside it. Despite its terrifying size, it is harmless. Source: Florida Museum — Discover Fishes.

question: A stranded oarfish looks as if it were forged from polished metal, flashing silver in the sun — yet unlike most fish it wears no scales at all. What coats its bare skin to give it that mirror shine?
answer: A soft layer of guanine crystals
choices: A soft layer of guanine crystals
A film of swallowed sea salt
A sheath of overlapping bony plates
A slick of reflective body oil
context: The oarfish has no scales; its body is coated in a soft, silvery layer of guanine — the same shimmering crystal that makes ordinary fish scales and mirrors flash. That is why a stranded one looks made of polished metal. Source: Florida Museum — Discover Fishes; Wikipedia 'Giant oarfish'.

question: Until 2010 nobody knew how a living oarfish actually swam — they were only ever seen dead or dying. Then Mark Benfield's team filmed one alive with a deep submersible and saw a posture that shocked them. How does the oarfish hold itself in the water?
answer: Vertically, head-up and tail-down
choices: Vertically, head-up and tail-down
Coiled in a slow rolling spiral
Belly-up, drifting with the current
Flat on the seabed like a flounder
context: Benfield et al. (2013) filmed live oarfish in the Gulf of Mexico and discovered its true posture: it hangs vertically, head-up and tail-down, rippling its long red dorsal fin to hover in the water column. Scientists think this may be a hunting trick — hanging straight up, it uses faint surface light to silhouette prey drifting above it. Source: Benfield et al. 2013, Journal of Fish Biology (doi:10.1111/jfb.12144).

question: Picture a fish that looks like a giant swimming head: a body squashed flat from the side, tall fins jutting up and down, and then it just... stops, blunt at the back with nothing trailing behind. Which ocean giant is this?
answer: The ocean sunfish (mola)
choices: The ocean sunfish (mola)
The great white shark
The bluefin tuna
The manta ray
context: The ocean sunfish (Mola mola) really does look like a swimming head that ends abruptly with no real tail. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium — Ocean sunfish.

question: The ocean sunfish (Mola mola) has no true tail fin at all. Its blunt back end is a stiff, rounded rudder — a scalloped fringe of muscle. That steering fringe isn't a shrunken tail; it's built from something else entirely on the fish. What forms it?
answer: The wrapped-around ends of its top and bottom fins
choices: The wrapped-around ends of its top and bottom fins
A stub of spine sheathed in tough skin
A fan of enlarged rear scales
A flap of cartilage grown back from the gills
context: The mola's rudder, the clavus, forms where its dorsal and anal fins wrap around and meet at the blunt rear — not a tail fin at all. Source: Wikipedia — Ocean sunfish; Monterey Bay Aquarium.

question: The ocean sunfish (Mola mola) is often seen lying flat on its side at the surface, one flank turned up to the sky and the seabirds. Scientists think this odd sunbathing pose isn't only about warmth — it also invites the birds to do something useful. What are the birds doing?
answer: Picking parasites off its exposed skin
choices: Picking parasites off its exposed skin
Guiding it away from shallow water
Warning it of approaching sharks
Cracking open its skin for food
context: Seabirds land on the basking mola and pick parasites off its skin while cleaner fish work its underside — the fish is loaded with parasites, so cleaning matters. Source: Wikipedia — Ocean sunfish; U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service.

question: The ocean sunfish (Mola mola) plunges into the crushing dark near 1,000 meters to hunt jellyfish where few predators follow — as many as 40 times a day — then labors its huge body all the way back up each time. Why the repeated trip back up?
answer: To reheat its body chilled by the cold deep
choices: To reheat its body chilled by the cold deep
To gulp air for buoyancy control
To digest food only in bright light
To shed the pressure of the deep
context: The mola dives deep to feed in cold water, then reheats its chilled body at the warm surface like a big solar panel — earning it the nickname 'solar-powered fish.' Source: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service — 'The Solar-Powered Fish with Jellies in Their Bellies: Molas'; Wikipedia — Ocean sunfish.

question: An octopus is soft all over except for one small hard part. Which part of an octopus is the only hard piece of its whole body?
answer: Its beak
choices: Its beak
Its inner shell
A plate in its gut
Its innermost sucker
context: The beak is the octopus's only hard part — everything else is pure muscle and skin. Source: Oregon Coast Aquarium DYK; sharksandco.com/the-octopus-that-can-squeeze-through-any-gap-1-7369/

question: Cornered by a hungry fish, an octopus fills its baggy body with water and blasts it out in one hard push, rocketing itself backward. Which body part does it fire that water through?
answer: Its siphon, a muscular tube
choices: Its siphon, a muscular tube
Its gills, packed with feathers
Its beak, snapped wide open
Its arms, gripping the seabed
context: The octopus fills its mantle with water and blasts it out through a muscular tube called the siphon, rocketing itself backward. Source: cimi.org/blog/octopus-jet-propulsion/; ocean.si.edu invertebrates

question: An octopus fleeing a predator releases a dark cloud into the water as it rockets away. What does that cloud do for the octopus?
answer: It hides the octopus behind a smoke screen
choices: It hides the octopus behind a smoke screen
It stuns the predator with an electric jolt
It poisons the water for a mile around
It glows to blind the predator
context: The ink is squirted into the same water jet the octopus uses to escape, making a dark screen. The ink also contains tyrosinase, which irritates a predator's eyes and garbles its smell and taste. Source: cimi.org/blog/octopus-jet-propulsion/; smithsonianmag.com ten-wild-facts-about-octopuses

question: An octopus has no bones at all, so the only thing that limits where its body can go is its one hard part — its beak. A 50-pound giant octopus can therefore pour its whole body through an opening no bigger than what?
answer: A two-inch coin
choices: A two-inch coin
A wedding ring
A keyhole
A walnut shell
context: With no skeleton, an octopus can squeeze through any gap its beak fits through — so a 50-pound animal can flow through a two-inch hole. Source: facebook.com/OregonCoastAquarium DYK post; sharksandco.com/the-octopus-that-can-squeeze-through-any-gap-1-7369/  (Legend.)

question: An octopus's beak looks and works like bone, but it isn't bone at all. It's made of chitin. Where else is that same tough material found?
answer: In crab claws and insect shells
choices: In crab claws and insect shells
In fish scales and shark skin
In coral reefs and clam pearls
In turtle shells and cow horns
context: Chitin is the same tough material that builds crab claws and the exoskeletons of insects. Source: theenvironmentalblog.org/2025/07/do-octopuses-have-beaks/

question: Most animals get by with a single heart. An octopus has a surprising number of them. How many hearts does an octopus have?
answer: Three
choices: Three
One
Two
Five
context: Two hearts pump blood only through the gills to load it with oxygen; a third pumps that blood to the rest of the body. Source: smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/ten-wild-facts-about-octopuses

question: A chameleon takes seconds to shift its color, but an octopus can flash a whole new pattern in the blink of an eye. What makes the octopus so much faster at changing color?
answer: Muscles yank its color sacs open
choices: Muscles yank its color sacs open
Sunlight warms its skin
Its blood flushes into the skin
Hormones ripple across its body
context: Under the chromatophores sit even more skin cells: iridophores that flash shimmery colors and leucophores that mirror surrounding light. Source: livescience.com/how-do-octopuses-change-color; scienceabc.com colorblind-octopuses

question: Reach out and touch something, and you feel it. When an octopus touches something with the suckers on its arms, it does something we can't. What does each sucker let the octopus do?
answer: Taste whatever it touches
choices: Taste whatever it touches
See in total darkness
Hear distant sounds
Smell across the whole ocean
context: Every sucker is studded with chemoreceptors, so the octopus tastes the world with its arms. A giant Pacific octopus has about 2,000 suckers — roughly 280 per arm. Source: gizmodo.com/researchers-finally-figured-out-how-octopuses-taste; americanoceans.org giant-pacific-octopus suckers

question: An octopus has around 500 million nerve cells, but most of them aren't in its head. Where do about two-thirds of an octopus's neurons live?
answer: In its arms
choices: In its arms
In its three hearts
In its skin
In its eyes
context: Each arm has its own cluster of nerve cells acting like a mini-brain, so an arm can grab food or explore a hole without waiting for orders from the central brain. Source: maketecheasier.com octopus-neurons; biologyinsights.com octopus-brain-anatomy  (Legend.)

question: An octopus can vanish against any rock, coral, or patch of sand it settles on, blending into the background so perfectly that its eyes seem to miss nothing. Yet scientists found a surprising limit in those eyes. What can an octopus eye NOT do?
answer: Tell one color from another
choices: Tell one color from another
Focus a crisp, sharp image
Swivel around on its own
Close behind a proper lid
context: An octopus's eyes carry just one visual pigment, making it colorblind — yet it still matches the colors around it, and exactly how it does that remains an open puzzle. Source: scienceabc.com colorblind-octopuses; pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1524578113  (Legend.)

question: Deep in the cold Pacific, scientists watched one female Graneledone boreopacifica octopus stay with her eggs, guarding and cleaning them, for an astonishing length of time — the longest of any animal known. How long did she guard them?
answer: About four and a half years
choices: About four and a half years
About three weeks
About six months
About ten years
context: For 53 months she guarded her clutch of about 160 eggs and never ate once, slowly starving, and died soon after they hatched. Source: journals.plos.org PLoS ONE 10.1371/journal.pone.0103437; nationalgeographic.com octopus-cares-for-her-eggs-for-53-months  (Legend.)

question: A mother octopus stops eating the instant her eggs are laid, then starves while guarding them and dies soon after they hatch — a death her own body triggers on purpose. In the lab, scientists found one change that switched the death off and kept her alive and feeding. What did they change?
answer: They cut out two glands behind her eyes
choices: They cut out two glands behind her eyes
They fed her a steady supply of crabs
They took every egg out of her den
They chilled the water in her tank
context: After a female lays her eggs, her optic glands release self-destructive chemicals that make her stop eating; in experiments, octopuses whose optic glands were removed stopped starving and kept living. Source: smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/ten-wild-facts-about-octopuses

question: Every octopus alive today has eight arms. But the oldest known fossil on the octopus branch, Syllipsimopodi bideni, swam the seas 100 million years before the first dinosaurs and had a body plan its descendants later reduced. How many arms did that ancient ancestor have?
answer: Ten, each with a double row of suckers
choices: Ten, each with a double row of suckers
Eight, exactly like octopuses today
Six, with the front pair fused into a hood
Twelve, ringing the mouth in a single crown
context: The ~12 cm Syllipsimopodi bideni fossil comes from the Bear Gulch limestone of Montana, dated to the Mississippian (Serpukhovian), roughly 330 to 323 million years ago. That is about 100 million years before the earliest dinosaurs, and its discovery pushed the octopus lineage's fossil record back some 82 million years past the previous oldest specimen. Crucially it had ten arms, each carrying a double (biserial) row of suckers, so the familiar eight-armed body plan came LATER, by reducing one arm pair. Source: Whalen & Landman, Nature Communications 13:1107 (2022), 'Fossil coleoid cephalopod from the Mississippian Bear Gulch Lagerstatte' (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8904582/).  (Legend.)

question: A spider hangs head-down over a game trail at night, a small stretchy web pinched between its four front legs. When a beetle wanders beneath it, what does the ogre-faced spider do with that little web?
answer: Throws it down over the beetle like a fisherman casting a net
choices: Throws it down over the beetle like a fisherman casting a net
Drops a sticky line to reel the beetle upward
Wraps the beetle after it blunders into a hanging trap
Spits a glue thread to pin the beetle in place
context: The ogre-faced spider (genus Deinopis) is a net-caster: it holds a small stretchy net between its four front legs and plunges it down over passing prey, then snaps it shut. The net is not sticky but is made of woolly cribellate silk whose coiled threads tangle up anything that touches them, and it can stretch to two or three times its relaxed size the instant it is flung, so a small net can wrap a much bigger insect. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deinopis ; https://australian.museum/learn/animals/spiders/net-casting-spiders/  (Legend.)

question: By day the ogre-faced spider does not spin a shelter or dig a burrow. Instead it survives the daylight hours in the open by doing what?
answer: Stretching its thin body and legs out straight to look like a stick
choices: Stretching its thin body and legs out straight to look like a stick
Curling into a tight ball resembling a dead bud
Wrapping itself in a papery cocoon of silk
Coating its body in bits of bark and lichen
context: By day the ogre-faced spider stretches its long thin body and legs out straight along a twig, looking exactly like a stick so predators pass it by. It only unfurls to hunt after dark. Source: https://australian.museum/learn/animals/spiders/net-casting-spiders/

question: The ogre-faced spider is named for the two big eyes staring off the front of its head. Those eyes are the largest simple eyes of any spider - what do they let it do that few hunters can?
answer: Aim its throwing net in near-total darkness
choices: Aim its throwing net in near-total darkness
Spot a warm-blooded animal by its body heat
See the ultraviolet patterns painted on flowers
Snap into sharp focus on prey a meter away
context: The genus name Deinopis is Greek for 'fearful appearance' (deinos = fearful, opis = appearance), and the 'ogre face' is those two huge central eyes. They are the largest simple eyes of any spider and gather light about 2,000 times more efficiently than human eyes, giving superb night vision. Uniquely, the spider has no reflective tapetum like a cat's; instead it grows a fresh sheet of light-sensitive membrane inside each eye every night and destroys it at dawn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deinopis  (Legend.)

question: Cornell scientists blindfolded ogre-faced spiders and found they could no longer catch crawling bugs, yet still snatched flying insects from the air. In 2020 they showed the spider pulls off that midair catch by doing what?
answer: Hearing the insect's wingbeats through sensors in its legs
choices: Hearing the insect's wingbeats through sensors in its legs
Feeling the wind gusts from the wingbeats on fine body hairs
Smelling the insect through chemical pits on its feet
Tasting vibrations carried up its own silk draglines
context: In 2020 Jay Stafstrom and Ronald Hoy at Cornell discovered the ogre-faced spider can hear despite having no ears, sensing sound through metatarsal organs near the tips of its legs. When they played low tones (about 150-750 Hz, the wingbeat frequencies of moths, flies and mosquitoes), more than half the spiders lurched into a backward flip-strike, netting the imagined flying insect out of the air. The finding confirmed a hunch Cornell's Charles Walcott had proposed roughly 60 years earlier and that other scientists had dismissed. Sources: https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2020/10/buzz-kill-spiders-hear-airborne-prey-their-legs ; https://www.sciencenews.org/article/ogre-faced-spider-hearing-catch-insects-prey-air-sound-sight  (Legend.)

question: Deep in a pitch-black South American cave, a reddish-brown bird nearly a meter across finds its way not by sight but by firing off rapid clicking sounds and listening for the echoes to bounce back off the walls -- the same trick a bat uses. Which bird is this?
answer: The oilbird
choices: The oilbird
The barn owl
The kiwi
The nightjar
context: The oilbird (Steatornis caripensis) of northern South America is one of the very few birds on Earth that echolocates. Its clicks are pitched low enough (about 2 kHz) that a person standing in the cave can hear them, unlike a bat's ultrasonic clicks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oilbird

question: The oilbird is the only night-flying bird in the world that lives entirely on fruit. Each night it leaves its cave in the dark and heads for oily palm and laurel fruits ripening high in the canopy. When the oilbird reaches a fruit, how does it get that fruit off the tree?
answer: Hovers and twists in mid-air to pluck each fruit off the branch
choices: Hovers and twists in mid-air to pluck each fruit off the branch
Perches on the branch and works the fruit loose with its hooked beak
Shakes the whole branch until ripe fruits rain down to gather below
Snips through the fruit's stalk and lets it drop into the leaf litter
context: The oilbird is the only nocturnal flying fruit-eating bird known. It takes each palm and laurel fruit on the wing, hovering and contorting in the dark to snatch them one by one, then flies on -- making it a champion seed-scatterer, since it swallows fruit whole and drops the seeds far across the forest. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oilbird  (Legend.)

question: Baby oilbirds gorge on oil-rich fruit until they grow FATTER than their own parents -- up to about a third heavier. Long ago people climbed into the caves and made use of exactly this. What did they do with the fat chicks that gave the bird its name?
answer: Boiled them down into oil to burn in lamps and cook with
choices: Boiled them down into oil to burn in lamps and cook with
Sold their bright feathers to hat-makers in the cities
Kept them as caged singers for their echoing calls
Raised them on farms as a fast-growing meat bird
context: This rendering of the fat chicks for lamp oil is the reason the bird's scientific name Steatornis literally means 'fat bird.' Framed here as historical account of the practice that named the species. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oilbird  (Legend.)

question: A single oilbird cave can hold 15,000 birds, and in the dark they all click at once -- a deafening racket of echoes. Yet each bird can still find the return of its OWN click in the storm of sound. How does an oilbird tell its echo apart from its neighbors'?
answer: Each bird clicks at a slightly different pitch from those around it
choices: Each bird clicks at a slightly different pitch from those around it
Each bird clicks only when the others fall briefly silent
Each bird fires its clicks in a rhythm it alone can recognize
Each bird aims a tight beam of clicks and ignores echoes off to the side
context: The oilbird's clicks come in astonishingly fast bursts, and neighbors pitch theirs slightly differently, so a bird can pick its own echo out of the noise of thousands clicking together. Its clicks only switch on when a cave grows too dark even for its super-sensitive eyes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oilbird

question: Deep in the rainforests of the Congo lives a shy, solitary browser with a rich dark-chocolate coat, big radar ears, and legs banded boldly in black-and-white like a zebra's. What is this forest animal?
answer: The okapi
choices: The okapi
The bongo
The tapir
The forest buffalo
context: The okapi (Okapia johnstoni) lives only in the dense rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. So shy and solitary that it stayed hidden from Western science until 1901, it was one of the last large land mammals on the planet to be described. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi

question: The okapi's boldly striped legs fool everyone into guessing zebra, but genetics says its stripes are a total red herring: it is not related to zebras at all. Its one and only living relative on Earth is a very different-looking animal. Which one?
answer: The giraffe
choices: The giraffe
The wild horse
The greater kudu
The bush pig
context: The okapi and the giraffe are the only two living members of the family Giraffidae, sharing a common ancestor about 11.5 million years ago. The okapi is essentially a giraffe that stayed short and hid in the forest — a short-necked forest cousin, the two the last survivors of their family. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi

question: An okapi has no paws to wipe its face and no pond to splash in, yet with its ~30 cm blue-black prehensile tongue it can groom two body parts that almost no other mammal on Earth can even reach. Which two?
answer: Its own eyes and ears
choices: Its own eyes and ears
The soles of its feet
The middle of its back
The tip of its tail
context: The okapi's tongue runs around 30 cm and has been reported up to 46 cm (18 inches) — long enough to lick clean its own eyes and even its own ears, making it one of the very few mammals on Earth able to lick its own ears. The same tongue wraps around branches to strip off leaves, just as its giraffe cousin strips an acacia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi

question: Chasing rumors of a striped 'African unicorn,' the colonial official Sir Harry Johnston expected to find some kind of forest-dwelling horse. Then he examined the tracks the creature left behind — and a single detail told him this was no horse or zebra at all. What did those tracks reveal?
answer: They were cloven — split into two toes
choices: They were cloven — split into two toes
They came in a slow spiral
They were webbed like a duck's
They were clawed like a big cat's
context: Legend: locals had long known the creature, and explorer Henry Morton Stanley heard of an 'atti' in 1887. Johnston expected a forest horse, but the tracks were CLOVEN-hoofed — two toes, not the single hoof of a horse or zebra. A striped skin and a skull sent to London let zoologist Ray Lankester declare it an unknown giraffe relative, naming it Okapia johnstoni in 1901. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi

question: When heavy rains flooded the caves beneath Postojna, Slovenia, pale, finger-length creatures came washing up out of the ground. The villagers were certain of what they had found: the offspring of a great beast that slept below. What did they think these washed-up animals were?
answer: Baby dragons
choices: Baby dragons
Drowned salamanders
River eels
Lost fish
context: For centuries locals believed the olm (Proteus anguinus) was the young of a dragon living deep beneath the earth, flushed to the surface by floods. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olm  (Legend.)

question: The olm is a slender, pale amphibian that spends its whole life in the black rivers of European caves. Slovene speakers gave this strange underground animal an affectionate folk name that no other creature wears. What do they call it?
answer: The human fish
choices: The human fish
The ghost eel
The cave worm
The pink serpent
context: The olm's pinkish, human-toned skin earned it the Slovene name cloveska ribica, the 'human fish.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olm

question: Most amphibians start as water-breathing larvae, then grow up and change body plan for life on land. The olm refuses to finish growing up: it stays in its baby form for its whole century in the water. What does the adult olm still wear that a grown frog has long since lost?
answer: Feathery external gills
choices: Feathery external gills
A slippery jelly coat
A sucker-tipped tail
Rows of armored scales
context: The olm keeps its larval external gills for life, a trait called neoteny that it shares with the axolotl. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olm

question: An adult olm hunts in pitch-black underground rivers where eyes are useless, and its own eyes are tiny and buried under skin. Yet it still finds the tiny animals it eats. Beyond smell and hearing, what faint signal does the olm sense to pinpoint hidden prey?
answer: The electric fields their bodies give off
choices: The electric fields their bodies give off
The warmth of their blood
The bubbles they release
The vibrations of their shells
context: The olm detects the weak electric fields of prey using special ampullary organs, letting it hunt in total darkness. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olm

question: Researchers tagged wild olms and returned to their cave rivers year after year to relocate them, expecting the animals to have wandered off. One olm astonished them: it was found in the exact same spot after an unbroken stretch of time. Roughly how long had that single olm stayed put?
answer: Over seven years
choices: Over seven years
About three months
Nearly forty years
A single winter
context: Most tracked olms moved less than 10 meters over years; one sat in the same spot for 2,569 days, over seven years. Lead researcher Gergely Balazs said 'they are hanging around, doing almost nothing' -- an energy-saving life for an animal that eats rarely and can live a century. Source: https://www.sciencealert.com/scientists-don-t-think-this-olm-bothered-to-move-much-in-7-years

question: Almost every animal alive wears its eyes in a tidy symmetrical set. Opabinia, a finger-sized swimmer from the Cambrian seas over 500 million years ago, crowned its head with a cluster of small eyes on short stalks plus one big eye set in the center. Count them: how many eyes did it have?
answer: Five
choices: Five
Two
Four
Six
context: A cluster of four eyes on short stalks plus one large eye set in the center gave Opabinia five eyes on top of its head, an odd number no living animal has. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale.

question: In 1975 Harry Whittington finished his careful restudy of Opabinia, a soft-bodied creature from the Burgess Shale, and presented his reconstruction to a room of fellow scientists. The animal was so unlike anything alive that the meeting reacted in a way no dignified science talk expects. What did the audience do?
answer: Burst out laughing, sure it couldn't be real
choices: Burst out laughing, sure it couldn't be real
Voted to have his drawing withdrawn
Demanded he re-examine the fossil
Accused him of inventing the specimen
context: The reconstruction looked so bizarre that the whole audience burst out laughing, thinking such an animal couldn't possibly have existed. It had. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale; corroborated by fossilguy.com. (Legendary/anecdotal.)

question: Opabinia was a five-eyed Cambrian oddball with no jaws and no arms. From the very front of its head, one long, flexible organ jutted out, about four times the length of the head itself. What did this strange organ end in?
answer: A grasping claw studded with spines
choices: A grasping claw studded with spines
A fan of feathery breathing gills
A ring of tiny grinding teeth
A soft glowing lure for luring prey
context: At the front of its head Opabinia carried a long, flexible nozzle or hose, roughly four times longer than its head, ending in a grasping claw studded with small spines that it used to gather food. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale.

question: Opabinia plucked morsels off the seafloor with the clawed hose on its head, then had to hand each scrap over to its mouth. For most animals the mouth sits up front, near where food is caught. But Opabinia's mouth sat in an unexpected spot that forced a whole extra maneuver. Where was its mouth?
answer: On the underside, opening backward
choices: On the underside, opening backward
At the very tip of the clawed hose
On the top of its head between the eyes
At the rear, flanking the tail fins
context: Opabinia's mouth sat on the underside of its body and pointed backward, so it used the claw on its hose to pluck food and pass it back and under to that rear-facing mouth. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale.

question: Sleek and black-and-white, the orca is famous as the "killer whale" — but that nickname gets its family wrong. What kind of animal is an orca, biologically?
answer: The largest dolphin
choices: The largest dolphin
A type of small whale
A cold-water shark
A giant porpoise
context: Orcinus orca is the biggest member of the dolphin family, Delphinidae — despite the "whale" in its common name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orca ; https://us.whales.org/whales-dolphins/facts-about-orcas/

question: Scientists divide the world's seas into five great oceans — the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and Southern. Of those five, in how many can you find wild orcas?
answer: All five
choices: All five
Just the Pacific
The three coldest
Only two
context: Orcas live in all five of the world's oceans — they are the most widely distributed of all whales and dolphins, and one of the most widely distributed mammals on Earth. Source: https://us.whales.org/whales-dolphins/facts-about-orcas/

question: A big male orca can stretch 8 metres and weigh over 6 tonnes, and its jaws are lined with more than 40 interlocking curved teeth. About how long is each of those teeth?
answer: About 10 cm — the length of your finger
choices: About 10 cm — the length of your finger
About 1 cm — like a house cat's
About 30 cm — like a steak knife
About 2 mm — barely a bump
context: An orca's teeth are about 10 cm (4 inches) long and curve inward, interlocking to grip slippery prey. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orca ; https://www.britannica.com/animal/killer-whale

question: Different orca populations, called ecotypes, each lock onto one kind of prey and pass down their own calls and hunting traditions. One rare, shy ecotype specializes in eating sharks — and the price shows in its mouth: the sharks' sandpaper skin does what to these orcas?
answer: Wears their teeth down to the gum line
choices: Wears their teeth down to the gum line
Leaves them completely toothless at birth
Turns their teeth bright orange
Makes their teeth grow back doubled
context: The elusive "offshore" ecotype eats sharks, whose rough, sandpaper-like skin grinds the orcas' teeth right down to the gum line. Source: https://www.seadocsociety.org/offshore-killer-whale-facts ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12315212/

question: A seal lounges safe on an Antarctic ice floe, out of reach of the water. Four orcas line up shoulder-to-shoulder and charge together at the ice. What are they making with that coordinated rush?
answer: A wave that sweeps the seal off the ice
choices: A wave that sweeps the seal off the ice
A loud noise to scare it into the sea
A ring of bubbles to trap it
A tunnel dug under the floe
context: Antarctic orcas hunt by "wave-washing" — charging four-abreast to push a wave over an ice floe and sweep the resting seal into the water. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/animals-up-close-wave-washing-killer-whales  (Legend.)

question: Wave-washing seals off the ice is so tricky that only about 100 orcas in all of Antarctica know how to do it. How does a young orca come to learn this rare skill?
answer: An older female of the pod teaches it, passed down the generations
choices: An older female of the pod teaches it, passed down the generations
Every orca is born knowing it by instinct
They copy it from watching seals
They invent it fresh each hunting season
context: Wave-washing is a learned tradition held by roughly 100 Antarctic orcas, taught down the generations from the pod's matriarch. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/marine-animals/orcas-wave-washing-seals

question: At Península Valdés in Argentina, sea lion pups splash in the shallows just off the sand, sure that no orca would follow them there. To grab a pup, the orca uses a hunting move so risky that almost no other sea animal attempts it. What does the orca do?
answer: Hurls itself right up onto the beach
choices: Hurls itself right up onto the beach
Dives to the seafloor and waits
Blows a net of bubbles around them
Lifts its head to peek above the surface
context: At Península Valdés, orcas deliberately beach themselves to grab sea lion pups, then squirm back to sea — and adults teach this risky technique to their young. Source: https://peninsulavaldes.com/wildlife/orcas  (Legend.)

question: Orcas are one of the very few animals, alongside humans, that go through menopause — females stop having calves in their 30s and 40s yet live to 80 or more. Lauren Brent's study found these old grandmother orcas do something surprising in lean salmon years. What?
answer: Swim at the front and guide the pod to food
choices: Swim at the front and guide the pod to food
Leave the pod to live alone
Stop eating so calves can feed
Sink to the seafloor to rest
context: After menopause, grandmother orcas become pod leaders; Brent's study found the oldest females lead from the front to salmon, especially when food is scarce and their memory matters most. Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/killer-whale-behaviour-shows-granny-knows-best.html ; https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/after-menopause-killer-whale-moms-become-pod-leaders-180954480/  (Legend.)

question: Every orca pod speaks its own "dialect" of calls, unique to that family and unchanged for over 25 years. In 1987 an orca in Puget Sound's K-pod started a stranger fad that swept all three pods in months, then vanished — and returned in 2024. What was the fad?
answer: Balancing a dead salmon on its head like a hat
choices: Balancing a dead salmon on its head like a hat
Whistling in a brand-new tune
Slapping tails in a synchronized line
Chasing boats in circles
context: The 1987 "salmon hat" fad spread across the resident pods, disappeared, then reappeared in 2024 — still unexplained. Pod dialects, by contrast, pass down almost unchanged across decades. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmon_hat ; https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/for-orcas-dead-salmon-hats-are-back-in-fashion/  (Legend.)

question: Off Norway, a pod of orcas circles a school of herring, blowing curtains of bubbles and flashing their white bellies to pack the fish into a tight glittering ball near the surface. Then one whale does the thing that actually kills the fish. What is it?
answer: Whips its tail into the ball, and the shockwave stuns the herring
choices: Whips its tail into the ball, and the shockwave stuns the herring
Lunges in with open jaws and swallows the whole ball at once
Bites the packed school clean in half with a snap of its teeth
Rams the ball at speed to crush the fish against the surface
context: This is carousel feeding. Norwegian orcas herd a herring school into a tight bait ball at the surface, working in shifts so it never scatters, then a whale swings its powerful flukes into the ball. The tail-slap sends out a shockwave and pressure change that stun or kill up to about 15 herring at once, and the whale picks off the stunned fish one by one. Herding and striking are traded around the pod so the ball stays packed. Source: Simon et al., acoustic behaviour of Norwegian killer whales during carousel foraging (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/240765692); National Geographic, "How Orcas Work Together to Whip Up a Meal" (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/magazine/article/orcas-feeding-cooperative-hunting-killer-whales); Wikipedia, "Carousel feeding" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carousel_feeding).

question: The mammal-hunting and the fish-eating orcas of the North Pacific never interbreed, keep entirely separate calls and diets, and split from each other hundreds of thousands of years ago. In 2024 a marine-mammal taxonomy committee finally voted on how to classify them. How did they end up officially ranked?
answer: As two subspecies of one killer-whale species
choices: As two subspecies of one killer-whale species
As two full and separate killer-whale species
As one single species with no subdivisions at all
As two distinct genera, split above species level
context: In 2024 Morin and colleagues proposed splitting these into two full species: the mammal-hunting Bigg's (transient) orca as Orcinus rectipinnus ("erect wing," for its tall pointed dorsal fin) and the fish-eating resident orca as Orcinus ater. The Society for Marine Mammalogy's Taxonomy Committee narrowly fell short of the two-thirds vote needed for full species, so it recognized them instead as subspecies -- Orcinus orca rectipinnus and Orcinus orca ater. Whether these lifelong-separate lineages are one species or several is still a live, unsettled debate. Source: Morin et al. 2024, "Revised taxonomy of eastern North Pacific killer whales," Royal Society Open Science (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10966402/); NOAA Fisheries feature (https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/feature-story/new-research-reveals-full-diversity-killer-whales-two-species-come-view-pacific-coast); Society for Marine Mammalogy 2024 annual review (https://marinemammalscience.org/smm-news/taxonomy-committee-2024-annual-review/).

question: A pink-and-white creature of Southeast Asian forests perches on a bare leaf with its legs flared into rounded petal shapes, and bees fly straight in to land on what they take for a bloom. What is it?
answer: The orchid mantis
choices: The orchid mantis
A pink crab spider
A flower-mimic katydid
A blossom-shaped treehopper
context: The orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) has upper leg segments flattened into heart- and petal-shapes, so its whole body reads as a pink-and-white blossom; insects fly straight toward it thinking it is a flower. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymenopus_coronatus

question: A newly hatched orchid mantis looks nothing like the pink flower it will become. Its very first body is bright red-orange and black, and it spends this stage disguised as which other insect?
answer: A hard-biting, foul-tasting assassin bug
choices: A hard-biting, foul-tasting assassin bug
A stinging paper wasp on patrol
A blister beetle oozing toxic oil
A soldier ant marching in column
context: First-instar orchid mantis nymphs are red-orange and black and mimic a foul-tasting, hard-biting assassin bug (family Reduviidae), so predators leave them alone until they molt into the pink flower form. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymenopus_coronatus

question: James O'Hanlon set orchid mantises alone on plain green leaves - with no flowers on them at all - near beds of real wild blossoms, then watched where the bees flew. What happened?
answer: More pollinators flew to the fake mantis than to the real flowers
choices: More pollinators flew to the fake mantis than to the real flowers
The bees split about evenly between the mantis and the flowers
The bees ignored the mantis until it grew larger petal lobes
The mantis had to copy one orchid's scent to draw any bees
context: O'Hanlon's 2014 field experiments showed isolated mantises on plain leaves lured wild pollinators at a higher rate than real flowers growing nearby - the first confirmed case of an animal using floral mimicry as a lure, not just camouflage. Source: O'Hanlon, Holwell & Herberstein 2014, 'Pollinator Deception in the Orchid Mantis', The American Naturalist 183(1); https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/673858  (Legend.)

question: James O'Hanlon assumed the orchid mantis's petal-shaped leg lobes existed to lure prey - but when he removed them, pollinators still flew in and got caught. So what does he now suspect those famous 'petals' are really for?
answer: Hiding the mantis from its own predators
choices: Hiding the mantis from its own predators
Signalling health to rival mantises
Sweeping pollen loose to eat off the leg
Cushioning the mantis when it drops off a branch
context: When O'Hanlon removed or rearranged the petal-shaped leg lobes, pollinators still approached - suggesting the famous 'petals' may not lure prey at all, but instead help hide the mantis from its own predators. Source: https://www.sciencefriday.com/articles/unraveling-the-orchid-mantis-mystery/

question: Stand on the African plains beside a flightless bird taller than a man, up to nine feet and past 300 pounds. It never leaves the ground because of one flaw deep in its chest. What keeps this giant grounded for good?
answer: A breastbone too flat to anchor flight muscles
choices: A breastbone too flat to anchor flight muscles
Wings far too small for its heavy body
Bones so hollow they snap under strain
Feathers that soak up water like a sponge
context: The ostrich is the largest and heaviest living bird: males stand up to 9 feet tall and weigh 220-287 pounds, with some sources reporting 300+ lb. It is flightless because its flattened sternum (breastbone) has no keel to anchor flight muscles. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).

question: An ostrich cannot fly, but a predator that chases one across open ground quickly falls behind. In a full sprint, about how fast can this two-legged giant run?
answer: Around 43 mph
choices: Around 43 mph
Around 15 mph
Around 25 mph
Around 60 mph
context: The ostrich is the fastest running bird in the world. It can sprint up to 43 mph (70 km/h) in short bursts and hold a steady cruising speed around 31 mph (50 km/h) over distance. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).

question: An ostrich hen settles a single pale egg into her ground nest. Crack one into a bowl to match it against the eggs from your fridge, and how many ordinary chicken eggs would it take to equal that one shell?
answer: About two dozen
choices: About two dozen
About three
About eight
About fifty
context: The ostrich lays the largest egg of any living bird: about 3 pounds (1,500 g) and 6 inches long, roughly the weight of 24 chicken eggs in one shell. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).

question: An ostrich eggshell is only about 3.5 mm thick, thinner than a stack of a few coins. Yet it holds a startling amount of downward force before it cracks. About how much weight can it bear pressing straight down?
answer: Enough for a grown adult to stand on it
choices: Enough for a grown adult to stand on it
Barely the weight of a sparrow
No more than a stack of paper
Only the chick's own body weight
context: An ostrich eggshell is only about 3.5 mm thick but strong enough that a grown adult can stand on it without breaking it. It can bear roughly 220 kg pressing straight down. Source: Birdfact (birdfact.com/articles/largest-bird-eggs).  (Legend.)

question: Everyone repeats that a frightened ostrich buries its head in the sand. When danger nears, what does it actually do to conceal itself on open ground?
answer: Flattens to the ground so it looks like a low mound
choices: Flattens to the ground so it looks like a low mound
Crouches low and sprints in a zigzag for cover
Sidles behind the nearest bush and holds still
Presses flat against a termite mound and freezes
context: The head-in-sand story is a myth; an ostrich cannot breathe underground. What it really does is flop flat and press its long neck and head to the ground so its body blends into the dirt and looks like a low mound from a distance. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).  (Legend.)

question: Nearly every bird alive grips the ground with three or four toes on each foot. The ostrich is the one exception, its foot pared down for sprinting. How many toes does each ostrich foot carry?
answer: Just two
choices: Just two
Only one
Four spread wide
Three, like most birds
context: The ostrich is the ONLY bird on Earth with just two toes per foot; every other bird has three or more. One toe is huge and the smaller second toe acts as an 'outrigger' to keep balance. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants; scienceinschool.org/article/2011/ostrich.

question: The ostrich carries the largest eye of any land animal, almost two inches across and rimmed in dark lashes -- startlingly big for its head. That eye actually outsizes what?
answer: Its own brain
choices: Its own brain
Its entire foot
A grown man's fist
One of its own eggs
context: The ostrich has the largest eye of any land animal, almost 2 inches (5 cm) across. Each eyeball is actually bigger than its own brain. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).  (Legend.)

question: Cornered on the plains by a big predator, an ostrich does not flee -- it strikes forward with a single clawed foot. Keepers warn by reputation that one such kick is strong enough to do what to even a lion?
answer: Kill it outright
choices: Kill it outright
Merely bruise it
Trip it long enough to escape
Frighten it with the noise
context: When cornered, an ostrich defends itself with a forward kick from its clawed foot said to be powerful enough to kill a lion. The claw can act like a knife; the kick is its main weapon against big predators. This lion-killing reputation is often repeated but is difficult to verify, so it is framed here as reputation rather than established fact. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).  (Legend.)

question: During the last ice age, our own ancestors were not the only kind of human walking the Earth. Which of these was a real, separate kind of human that shared the planet with them?
answer: The Neanderthals of Europe and western Asia
choices: The Neanderthals of Europe and western Asia
The last surviving Australopithecus troops
A tailed forest-dwelling ape-man of the Congo
The sea-dwelling merfolk of the northern coasts
context: During the last ice age at least two close cousins shared the planet with our ancestors: the Neanderthals of Europe and western Asia, and the mysterious Denisovans of Asia. Modern humans were not always the only kind of human on Earth. Source: Smithsonian Human Origins Program, humanorigins.si.edu; Max Planck Institute, mpg.de/5018269/denisovan-genome.

question: Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis) were short and powerfully built for the deep cold of the ice age. One feature of their face was strikingly broad and wide compared to ours. Which was it?
answer: The nose
choices: The nose
The ears
The chin
The forehead
context: A Neanderthal's big wide nose is thought to have warmed and moistened the frigid ice-age air they breathed, part of a body built for the cold. Source: Natural History Museum, 'Who were the Neanderthals?', nhm.ac.uk/discover/who-were-the-neanderthals.html.

question: The old cartoons pictured Neanderthals as dim, slouching 'ape-men.' But when scientists compared a Neanderthal braincase to a modern human's, what did they find?
answer: It was just as large as ours, and often a bit larger
choices: It was just as large as ours, and often a bit larger
It was roughly half the size of ours
It had no room for a frontal lobe at all
It was identical to a chimpanzee's in size
context: A Neanderthal's brain was just as large as ours, and often a bit larger, held in a long, low skull with a heavy brow ridge above the eyes. Source: Smithsonian Human Origins Program, humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/human-fossils/species/homo-neanderthalensis.  (Legend.)

question: Neanderthals hunted big ice-age game by thrusting spears into huge animals at close range, again and again. Their fossil skeletons carry a strange signature of this dangerous work. What do the bones show?
answer: Broken bones like the injuries of modern rodeo riders
choices: Broken bones like the injuries of modern rodeo riders
Teeth worn perfectly smooth from eating only grass
Fingers fused together into flipper-like paddles
Skulls thickened into a solid bony helmet
context: Neanderthals were skilled toolmakers and big-game hunters who thrust spears into large animals at close range, so often that their skeletons show broken bones like the injuries of modern rodeo riders. Source: Smithsonian Human Origins Program, humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/human-fossils/species/homo-neanderthalensis.  (Legend.)

question: The Denisovans are the other ice-age cousin, but for years scientists could barely picture their bodies. In 2008, in Denisova Cave in Siberia, what tiny scrap first revealed their existence, its genome read in 2010 by Svante Paabo's team?
answer: A single tiny finger bone
choices: A single tiny finger bone
A complete lower jaw
A footprint pressed in mud
A painted handprint on the wall
context: The Denisovans were discovered not from a skeleton but from a single tiny finger bone found in Denisova Cave in Siberia in 2008, whose genome was read in 2010 by Svante Paabo's team at the Max Planck Institute. Source: Max Planck Institute, mpg.de/5018269/denisovan-genome; Nobel Prize 2022 press release.  (Legend.)

question: Our own ancestors did not just live near these cousins, they met and interbred with them. When scientists sequenced the DNA of a living person whose roots lie outside Africa and searched their genome for the mark of that ancient mixing, what did they find?
answer: Roughly 1 to 4 percent Neanderthal DNA
choices: Roughly 1 to 4 percent Neanderthal DNA
Roughly 20 to 25 percent Neanderthal DNA
DNA from Homo erectus, but none from Neanderthals
No archaic trace at all, only in ancient fossils
context: Our ancestors met and interbred with both cousins, so most people alive today outside Africa carry a small slice of Neanderthal DNA, roughly 1 to 4 percent of their genome. Source: Max Planck Institute, mpg.de/5018269/denisovan-genome; Science, science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aad9416.

question: High on the Tibetan Plateau, the thin air holds far less oxygen than lowlands, yet Tibetans thrive there. Scientists traced part of their edge to a version of the EPAS1 gene inherited long ago from an extinct cousin. From which cousin did that high-altitude gene come?
answer: The Denisovans
choices: The Denisovans
The Neanderthals
Homo erectus
The Australopithecines
context: A version of the EPAS1 gene inherited from Denisovans helps Tibetans thrive in the thin high-altitude air, a gift from an extinct cousin found today only in Denisovans and Tibetans. Source: Nature, nature.com/articles/nature13408; PNAS, pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2020803118.  (Legend.)

question: Denisova Cave in Siberia has yielded another astonishing genome. In a girl who died about 90,000 years ago, geneticists read a mother and a father from two different kinds of human: her mitochondrial DNA was Neanderthal, but her nuclear genome was almost exactly half Neanderthal and half Denisovan. What did that make her?
answer: A first-generation child of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father
choices: A first-generation child of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father
A late Neanderthal whose people had drifted north into Denisovan land
An early Denisovan carrying leftover Neanderthal genes from long ago
A modern human ancestor caught midway between the two older cousins
context: Nicknamed 'Denny,' this ~13-year-old girl was identified in 2018 from a single ~2 cm bone fragment (Denisova 11). Her mitochondrial DNA (inherited only from the mother) was Neanderthal, while her nuclear genome was almost exactly half Neanderthal and half Denisovan, meaning one parent was a Neanderthal and the other a Denisovan. She remains the only confirmed first-generation hybrid of two distinct human groups ever found, showing that when these cousins met, they could interbreed directly, not just with our own ancestors. Source: Slon, Mafessoni, Paabo et al., 'The genome of the offspring of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father,' Nature 561:113-116 (2018), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-018-0455-x ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denny_(hybrid_hominin)  (Legend.)

question: Most non-African people carry a small, similar slice of Neanderthal DNA. But Denisovan ancestry is spread very unevenly across the world, piling up in one region and near-absent in most others. In whose genomes does Denisovan DNA reach its highest known levels?
answer: Papuans, Aboriginal Australians and other Melanesians
choices: Papuans, Aboriginal Australians and other Melanesians
Northern Europeans descended from the first cave painters
Peoples of the Siberian plains around Denisova Cave itself
East African groups nearest our species early homeland
context: Melanesians, Papuans/New Guineans and Aboriginal Australians carry roughly 4-6% Denisovan ancestry, by far the most of any human population, and a 2021 study found the Aeta Magbukon of the Philippines carry the highest known proportion of all. Most other populations carry little or none. This is a sharp contrast to the ~1-4% Neanderthal DNA shared by most non-Africans, and it maps onto where Denisovans and our ancestors actually met in Ice Age Asia, far from the Siberian cave where the first Denisovan bones were found. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denisovan ; Larena et al. 2021 (Aeta Magbukon highest Denisovan ancestry), Current Biology; https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2405889121

question: On a moonless night a mouse rustles through the leaves, and a round-faced night hunter with big forward-facing eyes drops on it out of the dark. What bird is this famous nocturnal raptor?
answer: An owl
choices: An owl
A hummingbird
A pelican
A flamingo
context: Owls are the classic round-faced, forward-eyed nocturnal raptors, built to hunt in darkness. Source: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, All About Birds.

question: A mouse in a dark field has good ears and usually hears a hunting bird coming by the swoosh of its wings. When an owl attacks, the mouse hears nothing at all. What is uncanny about how an owl flies?
answer: It flies almost completely silently
choices: It flies almost completely silently
It flies faster than any other bird
It glows faintly in the dark
It flies backward toward prey
context: An owl's wingbeats make so little noise that a mouse never hears it coming. Source: Audubon Magazine, 'The Silent Flight of Owls, Explained.'

question: An owl flies in near-total silence while a duck's wings whistle audibly. Look closely at the front edge of an owl's wing feathers and you see the trick. What runs along those leading edges that a duck's lack?
answer: Tiny comb-like serrations
choices: Tiny comb-like serrations
A stiff bony ridge
A coat of waterproof oil
A row of hooked claws
context: Comb-like serrations on the leading edge break up the turbulent air that would otherwise make a swooshing sound. Source: Audubon Magazine, 'The Silent Flight of Owls, Explained.'

question: Silent flight does more for an owl than just sneaking up on a mouse. Because its own wings barely make a sound, the owl gains a second hunting advantage in the dark. What else does the silence buy it?
answer: Its ears stay free to track the prey's rustling
choices: Its ears stay free to track the prey's rustling
Its wings never tire on long flights
It stays invisible to other owls
It can fly through heavy rain unbothered
context: With almost no wing noise of its own, the owl's ears keep tracking the prey's faint rustling in the dark. Krista Le Piane's analysis of 70 owl species. Source: Audubon Magazine.

question: A barn owl hunts in the dark almost entirely by sound, and it can place a rustle not just left or right but high or low, pinning the prey in three dimensions. What strange feature of its head makes this possible?
answer: Its two ear openings are offset, one higher than the other
choices: Its two ear openings are offset, one higher than the other
Its ears are hidden inside its beak
Its ears can be folded shut in the cold
Its ears glow to attract prey
context: The left ear opening sits higher and points down, the right sits lower and points up. This lopsided arrangement helps it place a sound in three dimensions. Source: Cornell Lab, All About Birds; Wikipedia, 'Sound localization in owls.'

question: A barn owl hunts by sound, and judging whether a rustle came from above or below is the hard part, far trickier than telling simple left from right. What cue does a barn owl rely on to place a sound as high or low?
answer: How much louder the sound is in one ear than the other
choices: How much louder the sound is in one ear than the other
The pitch of the sound
The delay of its echo
The gap in arrival timing
context: Left-vs-right comes from which ear a sound reaches first, by millionths of a second; up-vs-down comes from which ear it's louder in. Sounds from below are louder in the lower-pointing left ear, from above louder in the right. Two different cues, timing and loudness, working together. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sound localization in owls.'

question: An owl's flat, round face is a stiff dish of specialized feathers, not just a wise look. Given how heavily an owl hunts by sound, what job does that facial disc actually do?
answer: It funnels sound waves toward the ear openings
choices: It funnels sound waves toward the ear openings
It dampens the noise of the owl's own wingbeats
It shields the eyes from bright sun
It keeps rain off the beak
context: The concave facial disc collects sound waves and funnels them to the ear openings, like a satellite dish. Source: Wikipedia, 'Facial disc'; 'Sound localization in owls.'

question: A mouse tunnels along beneath a foot of fresh snow, completely out of sight. A barn owl overhead suddenly drops and strikes the exact spot. What single sense did it use to pin down a target it could not see?
answer: By hearing alone
choices: By hearing alone
By its keen sense of smell
By sensing the mouse's body heat
By feeling ground vibrations
context: A barn owl can pinpoint the exact 3-D spot of a mouse under a foot of snow guided by hearing alone, with no view of its target. Legendary but documented. Source: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, All About Birds.

question: An owl can't glance sideways the way you can; to look off to one side it has to swing its entire head around. Why can't an owl simply roll its eyes to look beside it?
answer: A ring of bone locks its huge eyes in place
choices: A ring of bone locks its huge eyes in place
Its eyes are too small to aim
It sees only straight ahead by instinct
Bright light freezes its eyes open
context: An owl's eyes are so huge and tube-shaped that they're locked by a ring of bone (the sclerotic ring) and can't roll in their sockets at all, so it must turn its whole head to look around. Source: California Academy of Sciences, 'The (Bird) Eyes Have It.'

question: Because an owl's eyes are frozen in their sockets, it has to swing its head around to see beside or behind itself, and it can crank that head astonishingly far. About how far around can an owl rotate its head?
answer: About 270 degrees, three-quarters of a full circle
choices: About 270 degrees, three-quarters of a full circle
A full 360 degrees, all the way around
About 90 degrees, a quarter turn
About 45 degrees, barely to the shoulder
context: An owl rotates its head up to about 270 degrees to either side. Legendary but true; the 'full circle' myth is false. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Solving the Mystery of Owls' Head-Turning Abilities' (Johns Hopkins study).

question: Twisting a head three-quarters of the way around would pinch shut the neck arteries and starve the brain in most animals. An owl gets away with it thanks to a bit of bony engineering around those arteries. What lets the vessels survive the twist?
answer: The bone channels around them are about ten times wider than the arteries
choices: The bone channels around them are about ten times wider than the arteries
The arteries pump blood in short bursts
A second heart sits in the neck
The blood carries built-in antifreeze
context: An owl has 14 neck vertebrae (humans have 7), and the bony holes around its neck arteries are about ten times wider than the arteries themselves, giving the vessels room to twist. Source: Smithsonian Magazine (Johns Hopkins CT/angiography study, 2013).

question: To keep an owl's brain fed with oxygen while its neck cranks around, evolution added a clever plumbing trick that a Johns Hopkins CT scan finally revealed. Where does the blood go during the big twist?
answer: Into reservoirs at the base of the skull
choices: Into reservoirs at the base of the skull
Straight back down into the heart
Out to the wingtips for storage
Into the hollow bones of the legs
context: Scientists injected dye into owls' arteries and CT-scanned them as the necks turned, finding blood pools in reservoirs at the skull base that keep the brain supplied during the twist. Source: Smithsonian Magazine; phys.org (2013).

question: When an owl seizes a struggling animal, it doesn't have to keep straining its muscles to hold on. A special mechanism in the foot snaps the grip shut and keeps it clamped. What clicks the talons closed and holds them there?
answer: A locking tendon that ratchets the grip shut
choices: A locking tendon that ratchets the grip shut
A sticky pad on each talon
A set of tiny hooks along the toes
A suction cup in the sole
context: When an owl grabs prey, its outer toe swings back so two talons point forward and two back, then a locking tendon ratchets the grip shut, clamping without any muscle effort. Source: The Owl Pages, 'Owl Feet & Talons.'

question: Everyone agrees an owl flies in near silence, but scientists still argue over what its velvety feather surface is actually FOR. One camp says it smooths the airflow over the wing. What does the rival camp, studying exactly where that velvet is densest, say it really does?
answer: It muffles the noise of feathers scraping against each other
choices: It muffles the noise of feathers scraping against each other
It smooths the airflow rushing over the wing surface
It traps warm air to keep the flight muscles from stiffening
It scatters the moonlight so the owl casts no moving shadow
context: How an owl's feathers actually kill the sound is still a live scientific debate. The long-dominant view (Kroeger, Lilley) holds that the leading-edge comb and downy velvet reduce AERODYNAMIC noise by smoothing airflow and keeping the boundary layer attached over the wing. A competing hypothesis (Christopher Clark, reviving Graham's 1934 idea) points out that the velvety 'pennulae' and vane fringes are best developed exactly where one feather rubs against the next, arguing they mainly muffle STRUCTURAL, frictional noise from feather-on-feather contact during flapping rather than airflow noise. The two camps disagree over what the velvet is even for. Source: PMC 'Evolution and Ecology of Silent Flight in Owls' (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7671161/) - Clark vs. Kroeger/Lilley; Graham (1934).

question: Every other mammal on Earth wears fur or bare skin. One alone is armored head to tail in overlapping plates made of keratin, the very same protein as your fingernails and hair. Which animal is it?
answer: The pangolin
choices: The pangolin
The armadillo
The porcupine
The hedgehog
context: The pangolin is the only mammal covered in scales. Armadillos wear bony plates under their skin; porcupines and hedgehogs bristle with modified hairs. Only the pangolin's coat is true keratin scales. Source: https://www.savepangolins.org/what-is-a-pangolin/  (Legend.)

question: When a hungry leopard closes in on a pangolin, the little animal doesn't run or fight. Instead it does the single thing that earned it the Malay name 'penggulung.' What does it do?
answer: Curls into a tight armored ball, tucking its soft belly inside
choices: Curls into a tight armored ball, tucking its soft belly inside
Freezes flat and plays dead until the danger passes
Sprays a jet of stinging venom from its snout
Puffs itself up huge with swallowed air
context: 'Penggulung' means 'one who rolls up.' The scaled back and tail wrap around the vulnerable belly and face, leaving nothing soft exposed. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/facts-about-pangolins

question: A whole pride of lions surrounds a rolled-up pangolin the size of a house cat. They paw it, bat it back and forth, and try again and again to sink their teeth in. How does the standoff end?
answer: The lions give up and walk away, leaving the pangolin unharmed
choices: The lions give up and walk away, leaving the pangolin unharmed
One lion finally cracks the shell and the pride feeds
The pangolin bolts free the moment the lions tire
The pangolin is crushed under the pride's combined weight
context: A rolled pangolin's overlapping keratin scales are tough enough that even a full pride cannot bite through. Frustrated, the lions simply move on. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/facts-about-pangolins  (Legend.)

question: A pangolin's front claws are so long and curved they're wonderful for ripping open termite mounds but clumsy for walking. To keep those claws off the ground, how does the pangolin often get around?
answer: It walks upright on its two hind legs, holding its arms and tail up for balance
choices: It walks upright on its two hind legs, holding its arms and tail up for balance
It drags itself forward on its belly like a seal
It knuckle-walks on the backs of its curled front paws
It hops with both hind feet together like a kangaroo
context: The three big digging claws on each front paw are useless for walking, so a pangolin often rears up and strides on its hind legs, tail and forelimbs raised as a counterweight. Source: https://africageographic.com/stories/fascinating-pangolin-facts/  (Legend.)

question: A pangolin has no teeth and cannot chew a single ant. To reach the insects deep inside a tunnel, it uncoils a tongue coated in sticky saliva. In a big pangolin, how far can that tongue stretch?
answer: Up to about 40 cm (16 in), longer than its own head and body
choices: Up to about 40 cm (16 in), longer than its own head and body
Up to about 10 cm (4 in), like a house cat's
Up to about 1 m (3 ft), trailing on the ground
Just past its own lips, a few centimeters
context: A big pangolin's tongue can reach 40 cm, sometimes longer than its head and body combined, gluing ants and termites to it inside their tunnels. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangolin  (Legend.)

question: To rip into an ant nest is to invite thousands of biting, stinging insects to swarm your face. Before a pangolin tears one open, it protects itself in a way most mammals can't. What does it do?
answer: It clamps its ears and nostrils shut with strong muscles
choices: It clamps its ears and nostrils shut with strong muscles
It coats its face in a thick layer of mud first
It attacks only at night when the insects are asleep
It smears itself with the nest's own scent to hide
context: Muscles let a pangolin seal its ears and nostrils closed, keeping swarming ants out while it laps up as many as 20,000 in a single day. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/facts-about-pangolins

question: A pangolin swallows its ants whole and toothless, yet somehow grinds up their crunchy shells. It manages this with a trick a chicken would recognize. How does a pangolin's stomach break down its food?
answer: Swallowed stones churn in a muscular gizzard-like stomach lined with keratin spines
choices: Swallowed stones churn in a muscular gizzard-like stomach lined with keratin spines
Powerful acid dissolves the shells completely within minutes
A second set of throat teeth crushes the ants on the way down
It regurgitates and re-swallows each meal to soften it
context: With no teeth, a pangolin swallows small stones (gastroliths) that collect in a muscular, keratin-spined stomach and grind the insects up, exactly the way a bird's gizzard works. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangolin

question: The tiny Australian peacock spider got its name from what the male does to court a female: he raises the back of his body and unfurls something normally tucked around his abdomen, then waves it at her. What does he unfurl?
answer: A fan of brilliantly colored flaps
choices: A fan of brilliantly colored flaps
A sticky net of silk threads
A pair of transparent gliding wings
A cluster of glowing light organs
context: The male raises his abdomen and spreads a fan of vividly colored flaps, waving it like a peacock fanning its tail — which is exactly how the peacock spider got its name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratus_volans  (Legend.)

question: A peacock spider carries one of the most colorful displays in the whole animal kingdom, yet finding one in the wild is famously hard. How big is a peacock spider?
answer: About the size of a grain of rice
choices: About the size of a grain of rice
About the size of a jellybean
About the size of a housefly
About the size of a ladybug
context: Both males and females are only about 5 mm long — roughly a grain of rice — yet the male packs a dazzling courtship display onto that tiny frame. Their size hid them from science for years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratus_volans

question: For a male peacock spider, the courtship dance is life-or-death, not just showing off. If his fan-waving performance fails to impress the watching female, what may she do to him?
answer: Attack, kill, and eat him
choices: Attack, kill, and eat him
Trap him in her web for days
Sting him with venom to paralyze him
Chase him off her patch of ground
context: An unimpressed female may attack, kill, and eat the male — and she may even do it after mating. That deadly stakes-raising is why the dance has to be so spectacular. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratus_volans  (Legend.)

question: A male peacock spider throws his whole body into a courtship performance for a watching female. Beyond the colors of his waving fan, he adds a second, private channel of communication. What is the other signal he sends her?
answer: Vibrations she feels through her legs
choices: Vibrations she feels through her legs
Puffs of scent drifting on the breeze
High-pitched chirps only she can hear
Quick flashes of light bounced off the soil
context: As he dances, the male drums the ground with his abdomen, sending vibrations through the surface that the female picks up through her legs. Scientists named the three vibration types rumble-rumps, crunch-rolls, and grind-revs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratus_volans

question: Part of a male peacock spider's fan is an 'ultra-black' patch that reflects less than half a percent of light. Surprisingly, it isn't made by any dark pigment. What actually swallows the light on that patch?
answer: Tiny lens-like bumps on the cuticle that trap it
choices: Tiny lens-like bumps on the cuticle that trap it
A thin layer of black oil that soaks it up
Charcoal-like grains built into the scales
A living film of dark bacteria on the surface
context: The ultra-black comes from microscopic dome-shaped bumps on the cuticle, about 6 micrometers tall, that act like tiny lenses and trap incoming light — reflecting as little as 0.35% in Maratus karrie. No black pigment is involved. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6532503/  (Legend.)

question: The shimmering blues on a peacock spider's fan can flash and shift as he moves, the same way a soap bubble or a peacock feather changes color with the angle. How does the spider produce that blue?
answer: Nanostructures on its scales that bend light
choices: Nanostructures on its scales that bend light
A dye it absorbs from the insects it eats
Blue pigment cells packed under its skin
Trapped air bubbles beneath its shell
context: The blue is structural color: microscopic nanostructures on the scales bend and reflect just the right wavelength of light — the same physics behind a soap bubble's shimmer — rather than any pigment. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6532503/

question: Folding its wings tight and plunging out of the sky, one crow-sized raptor moves faster than any other creature on Earth — quicker than a cheetah at full sprint or a racecar. Which bird is it?
answer: The peregrine falcon
choices: The peregrine falcon
The golden eagle
The great horned owl
The common raven
context: In its diving plunge the peregrine falcon is the fastest animal alive — faster than any cheetah or racecar. Source: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, All About Birds; Wikipedia 'Peregrine falcon'.  (Legend.)

question: The peregrine falcon lives on nearly every landmass on the planet — a crow-sized raptor equally at home on a sea cliff or a downtown skyscraper. Only one continent has none. Which land does the peregrine skip?
answer: Antarctica
choices: Antarctica
Australia
South America
Africa
context: Found on every continent except Antarctica, the peregrine is the world's most widespread bird of prey. Source: Wikipedia 'Peregrine falcon'.

question: A peregrine falcon on the hunt goes after pigeons, ducks, gulls, and songbirds — living prey that can fly. When a peregrine actually catches one of these birds, where does the strike happen?
answer: In mid-air, out of the sky
choices: In mid-air, out of the sky
In shallow water
In tree branches
On open ground
context: The peregrine hunts other birds on the wing, striking them out of the sky rather than catching prey on the ground. Source: Science.org; All About Birds.

question: Peregrine falcons have spread into the hearts of big cities, raising young on cathedrals, bridges, and high window ledges. What draws these cliff-hunters downtown in the first place?
answer: Flocks of city pigeons to hunt
choices: Flocks of city pigeons to hunt
Warmth rising off the pavement
Fewer eagles competing there
Bright lights that lure insects
context: Peregrines nest on skyscraper ledges and bridges where flocks of city pigeons give them an endless food supply. Source: Wikipedia 'Peregrine falcon'; All About Birds.

question: When a peregrine falcon lays eggs on a high cliff ledge, it makes no twig cup and weaves nothing. So what exactly is a peregrine's 'nest'?
answer: A shallow scrape it scratches into gravel
choices: A shallow scrape it scratches into gravel
A borrowed old eagle nest
A burrow dug in a sandbank
A bare fork in a treetop
context: A peregrine scrapes a shallow depression in gravel or soil on a high ledge and lays its eggs right there — the whole 'nest' is just a scratched-out dip. Source: All About Birds Life History; Wikipedia.

question: A peregrine falcon cruising along in ordinary flight moves at a modest 25 to 34 mph, and even flat-out chasing prey it hits only about 69 mph. So what does the falcon actually do to become the fastest animal on Earth?
answer: Fold its wings and dive in a steep plunge
choices: Fold its wings and dive in a steep plunge
Beat its wings faster than a hummingbird
Ride a jet of air from its lungs
Glide on a rising column of warm air
context: The dive, called the stoop, is what makes the peregrine a rocket — in level flight it's only ordinarily fast. Source: Buffalo Bill Center of the West.

question: The pesticide DDT nearly erased the peregrine falcon from North America. It built up inside the birds and attacked their eggs in a cruel way, so that by the 1960s not one peregrine was left breeding in the entire eastern United States. What did DDT do to the eggs?
answer: Thinned the shells until they cracked under the parents
choices: Thinned the shells until they cracked under the parents
Turned the yolks toxic to the chicks
Made the parents abandon them cold
Kept them from ever being fertilized
context: DDT thinned peregrine eggshells until eggs cracked under the parents' weight; by the 1960s the peregrine had vanished from the whole eastern U.S. Source: Wikipedia; Audubon 'Remembering Tom Cade'.

question: At over 200 mph a peregrine falcon still breathes easily through a tiny bony cone inside each nostril, even as the wind screams past. What does that little cone do to the rushing air?
answer: Spins it into a slowed spiral
choices: Spins it into a slowed spiral
Warms it before the lungs
Filters the dust from it
Splits it into two streams
