context: The bony tubercle (a baffle) in each nostril spins the rushing air into a spiral and slows it down, so the falcon can breathe at dive speed. Some jet-engine designers study it. Source: ResearchGate; Curious Sengi summaries.  (Legend.)

question: Hurtling downward at over 200 mph with a target locked in its sight, a peregrine falcon still needs to keep its eyes wet, clean, and in sharp focus. What sweeps across each eye during the plunge to protect it?
answer: A see-through third eyelid
choices: A see-through third eyelid
A clear sheet of skin from below
A slick of clear tear-fluid
A clear inner lens that slides up
context: The nictitating membrane, a transparent third eyelid, sweeps across each eye during the dive, wiping it clear while the falcon keeps its target in focus. Source: Wikipedia 'Peregrine falcon'.

question: Chasing prey flat-out in level flight, a peregrine falcon reaches only about 69 mph. But in 1999 a trained falcon named Frightful was dropped from a Cessna at 17,000 feet to chase her skydiving falconer as a lure, a chip on her back clocking the fastest bird dive ever measured. How fast did that plunge go?
answer: 242 mph
choices: 242 mph
210 mph
186 mph
273 mph
context: Frightful's 242 mph (389 km/h) dive is the fastest ever measured for a bird — more than triple her flat-out level-flight chase. Source: Guinness World Records; Smithsonian Magazine 'Falling with the Falcon'.  (Legend.)

question: Cornell professor Tom Cade set out in 1970 to bring the peregrine falcon back from near-extinction, raising captive-bred chicks in towers, fed by hidden humans so they never tamed to people, until they flew and hunted free. What proved his rescue had worked?
answer: Released falcons bred in the wild by 1980
choices: Released falcons bred in the wild by 1980
City-nesting numbers doubled by 1985
The last wild pair returned east by 1982
Wild pairs fledged three chicks by 1979
context: Cade's 'hacking' method worked: released peregrines bred in the wild by 1980, and in 1999 the bird was taken off the U.S. endangered list. Source: Audubon 'Remembering Tom Cade'; Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: In a wind tunnel, a diving peregrine falcon is one of the most streamlined shapes in all of nature — yet at the exact spots on its body where fast air would normally tear away and turn to turbulent drag, something surprising happens. What does the falcon do to keep the air smooth?
answer: Tiny back feathers pop up to keep the air clinging on
choices: Tiny back feathers pop up to keep the air clinging on
It seals every feather flat into a single glassy skin
It sheds a thin film of oil that lets the air slide by
It vents warm air through its nostrils to fill the gap
context: A wind-tunnel and computer-flow study of a life-sized diving-falcon model measured a drag coefficient as low as CD around 0.094 in the full stoop — among the most streamlined shapes in nature. But the low drag is not just the teardrop body: right where the airflow would separate, small body feathers pop up during the dive and act as passive flow-control devices — the same trick as the vortex generators (turbulators) on an aircraft wing — keeping the airflow attached and drag low at extreme speed. Source: Ponitz, Schmitz, Fischer, Bleckmann & Brucker, "Diving-Flight Aerodynamics of a Peregrine Falcon (Falco peregrinus)," PLOS ONE 9(2):e86506, 2014.

question: A stooping peregrine falcon does not aim where a dodging starling IS — it curves so it turns harder the faster the line between hunter and prey swings. Physics simulations found this is the very same steering rule engineers built into one famous machine. What guides the falcon the way it guides that machine?
answer: The homing law that steers a heat-seeking missile
choices: The homing law that steers a heat-seeking missile
The autopilot loop that holds an airliner on course
The spinning gyroscope inside a ship’s compass
The braking rhythm of a train easing into a curve
context: Physics-based flight simulations (Oxford; Mills, Hildenbrandt, Taylor & Hemelrijk, PLOS Computational Biology 2018) found the peregrine steers by proportional navigation — the same guidance law used by heat-seeking, homing missiles — turning at a rate proportional to how fast the line of sight to the target rotates. The simulated navigation constant N of about 2.6 to 3.0 matched the median N of 2.6 measured in real peregrines. The study also showed why the ultra-fast stoop matters: only at high speed can the falcon out-turn an erratically dodging bird like a starling; against straight-flying prey a slow, low attack actually worked better. Source: Mills, Hildenbrandt, Taylor & Hemelrijk, PLOS Comp. Biol. 2018.  (Legend.)

question: A pale, palm-sized creature of the sandy Argentine desert has huge claws on its front legs and spends nearly its whole life below ground. Legend gave the pink fairy armadillo a nickname for the way it moves through loose sand:
answer: the 'sand-swimmer'
choices: the 'sand-swimmer'
the 'dune-jumper'
the 'sand-diver'
the 'desert-mole'
context: The pink fairy armadillo (Chlamyphorus truncatus) was long believed to burrow through loose ground almost as fast as a fish swims through water, earning the nickname 'sand-swimmer.' It is the smallest armadillo in the world, about 3.5-4.5 inches long. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_fairy_armadillo  (Legend.)

question: The pink fairy armadillo's thin shell can flush a deeper pink and then fade paler again, because a dense web of blood vessels sits just beneath it. That color change is a clue to what the shell really does. Its main job is to:
answer: dump or hold body heat like a radiator
choices: dump or hold body heat like a radiator
shield the animal from predators' teeth
store water for the dry desert
warn rivals away with a bright signal
context: By pushing more blood into the shell the armadillo flushes pink and sheds heat; by draining blood out, the shell pales and it keeps its warmth. The shell is a thermoregulating organ, not armor. Source: https://factanimal.com/pink-fairy-armadillo/

question: Most armadillos have a shell that wraps and protects the body, but the pink fairy armadillo's rear ends in a flat, vertical armored plate facing straight backward. As the animal digs forward through loose sand, that back plate lets it:
answer: press and pack the soil behind it, corking its tunnel
choices: press and pack the soil behind it, corking its tunnel
flip upside down to roll away downhill
scoop food up toward its mouth
reflect sunlight to stay cool underground
context: The flattened rear 'butt plate' tamps and compacts the loose soil behind the digging armadillo, shoring the tunnel against collapse and sealing (corking) the burrow entrance behind it. This flattened rear plate appears unique to this species. Source: https://www.sciencenews.org/article/pink-armadillos-aint-your-texas-critters

question: A pistol shrimp hunts a small fish without ever chasing it down. Its oversized claw slams shut with a violent snap — and the prey is stunned before the shrimp has moved an inch. So what actually reached across the water and hit the fish?
answer: A jet of water fired by the snap
choices: A jet of water fired by the snap
A sticky thread it lassoed the fish with
A cloud of ink squirted to blind it
A venom spine flicked from its tail
context: The claw itself never touches the prey — the snap shoots out a jet of water that stuns the victim from a distance. Source: Versluis et al., 'How Snapping Shrimp Snap: Through Cavitating Bubbles', Science 2000; https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2000/09/000922072104.htm

question: You might picture a creature that fires shockwaves loud enough to stun fish as something big. But the pistol shrimp that does all this measures only about how long, tip to tail?
answer: 3 to 5 cm (an adult's thumb)
choices: 3 to 5 cm (an adult's thumb)
30 to 40 cm (a forearm)
1 to 2 mm (a grain of rice)
70 to 90 cm (an arm's length)
context: Only about 3 to 5 cm (1.2 to 2 inches) long, yet it produces one of the most powerful sounds, by body size, of any animal. Source: Wikipedia 'Alpheidae'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpheidae

question: During World War II, sonar operators kept hearing a constant crackling static over vast stretches of coastal seafloor, and submarines learned to park inside those noisy patches to vanish from detection. What was making the racket?
answer: Colonies of snapping shrimp
choices: Colonies of snapping shrimp
Beds of grinding sea urchins
Schools of drumming croaker fish
Currents rattling loose gravel
context: Colonies snap in such a constant din that in WWII they jammed sonar and confused submarine-detection operators — and subs hid inside shrimp beds to avoid being heard. Source: ScienceDaily, 'Snapping Shrimp Drown Out Sonar' (Science 2000); https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2000/09/000922072104.htm  (Legend.)

question: A near-blind pistol shrimp shares a burrow it dug and maintains with a sharp-eyed goby fish standing guard at the entrance. Out on the open sand, how does the shrimp know the instant the goby spots danger and bolts?
answer: It keeps one long antenna touching the goby
choices: It keeps one long antenna touching the goby
It watches the goby's shadow on the sand
It listens for the goby's alarm clicks
It tastes stress chemicals the goby releases
context: The shrimp keeps an antenna on the goby's body; if the goby flicks its tail and darts in, the shrimp instantly feels the signal and dives too. Source: Divers Alert Network, 'Symbiosis on the Sand'; https://dan.org/alert-diver/article/symbiosis-on-the-sand/

question: Scientists found the pistol shrimp's fired water jet alone doesn't quite explain the killing blow. The jet moves so fast it drops the water pressure and creates something behind it — and THAT is the real weapon. What forms and then destroys the prey?
answer: A collapsing bubble that unleashes a shockwave
choices: A collapsing bubble that unleashes a shockwave
A whirlpool that drags prey into the claw
A spark that electrocutes the water
A spray of jagged ice crystals
context: The low pressure forms a vapor-filled cavitation bubble; when it collapses it slams out a shockwave that stuns or kills. Source: Versluis et al., Science 2000; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7525291/  (Legend.)

question: A pistol shrimp loses its big snapping claw to an attacker. Rather than simply regrowing the same weapon in the same spot, what does its body do over the following molts?
answer: Its small claw becomes the new weapon; the stump regrows small
choices: Its small claw becomes the new weapon; the stump regrows small
It regrows the snapper twice as large as before
It grows a matching snapper on the other side, giving it two
It stays disarmed and switches to scavenging for life
context: The claws swap roles: the lost limb grows back as a small claw while the original small claw enlarges into a new snapping weapon. Source: Wikipedia 'Alpheidae'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpheidae

question: When a pistol shrimp's cavitation bubble collapses, it does more than make a shockwave — for an instant it emits a faint flash of light, too dim for the naked eye. Researchers named this glow with a playful term. What is it called?
answer: Shrimpoluminescence
choices: Shrimpoluminescence
Bioflash cavitation
Crustaceoglow
Snapfire radiance
context: Named because it resembles sonoluminescence — light from a collapsing bubble. Source: Lohse, Schmitz & Versluis, 'Snapping shrimp make flashing bubbles', Nature 2001; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11586346/  (Legend.)

question: Inside a pistol shrimp's collapsing bubble, for a sliver of a second, the temperature spikes to at least about 5,000 K. To grasp how extreme that is, what everyday hot thing does it very nearly match?
answer: The surface of the Sun
choices: The surface of the Sun
The core of a lightning bolt
Molten lava from a volcano
A blacksmith's forge fire
context: About 5,000 K (roughly 4,700 °C) — nearly the Sun's surface at about 5,772 K. Source: Wikipedia 'Alpheidae' (citing Lohse et al. 2001); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpheidae  (Legend.)

question: An Australian river animal has thick brown fur and a flat beaver-like tail like a mammal, but a rubbery duck-like bill, webbed feet, and it lays eggs. The males even carry venom. Name this creature:
answer: Platypus
choices: Platypus
Muskrat
Otter
Capybara
context: The platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus) of eastern Australia is one of the strangest animals alive: fur and milk like a mammal, a bill and eggs like a bird, and venom to boot. Source: Australian Museum, australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/

question: The platypus and four kinds of spiny echidna belong to a tiny club of just five living mammal species. Deep in her riverbank burrow, a mother platypus curls her body around her young-to-be, doing something the other 6,000-odd mammal species never do. What sets these five apart?
answer: Lay eggs
choices: Lay eggs
Change sex
Have no bones
Breathe through skin
context: These five are the monotremes. The platypus curls around one or two leathery eggs and incubates them for about ten days before they hatch. Source: Australian Museum, australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/

question: A newly hatched platypus is the size of a jellybean and needs milk, but its mother has no nipples at all. So how does the baby actually get its meal? (legend-tier oddity)
answer: Milk seeps through skin pores onto furry belly patches
choices: Milk seeps through skin pores onto furry belly patches
The mother regurgitates food into its mouth
It drinks river water rich in nutrients
It suckles milk from a slit in the mother's belly
context: The platypus's mammary glands are modified sweat glands, so milk seeps out through skin pores onto two furry patches where the young lap it up. Source: BBC Science Focus, sciencefocus.com/nature/do-platypuses-really-sweat-milk; Australian Museum  (Legend.)

question: A platypus glides along a muddy riverbed where a shrimp is buried out of sight, giving off no smell it can catch. Yet the platypus swims straight to it. Its rubbery bill is picking up something the shrimp cannot hide. What is the bill actually detecting?
answer: The faint electric currents from the prey's twitching muscles
choices: The faint electric currents from the prey's twitching muscles
The warmth of the prey's body
The vibration of the prey's heartbeat
The color of the prey against the mud
context: About 40,000 electroreceptors pack the platypus's bill, sensing the tiny electric fields thrown off by a hidden animal's moving muscles. Source: American Museum of Natural History, amnh.org/explore/news-blogs/platypus-electroreception-hunting

question: A platypus plunges into murky, silt-clouded water where a shrimp lies buried and nothing at all can be seen. Its bill still locks straight onto the hidden prey. What is doing the finding down there in the dark?
answer: An electric sense and touch-sensitive push rods in its bill
choices: An electric sense and touch-sensitive push rods in its bill
A heat sense reading the prey's body warmth
A magnetic sense pointing toward the prey
Sensing the silt the prey stirs up as it moves
context: Hunting effectively blind, the platypus seals its eyes, ears, and nose and relies entirely on electroreception plus touch-sensitive 'push rods' in the bill. Source: American Museum of Natural History; Australian Platypus Conservancy, platypus.asn.au/the-platypus-bill-push-rods-and-electroreception/  (Legend.)

question: In 1986 Henning Scheich built a fake 'shrimp' to test how a platypus finds prey it cannot see or smell. The platypus struck at his lifeless little lure anyway. What was Scheich secretly feeding into that fake shrimp to make it strike?
answer: A tiny electric current
choices: A tiny electric current
A faint trace of warmth
A hidden wriggling motor
A low buzzing vibration
context: Scheich's platypus struck at a lure carrying only a faint electric signal, proving electroreception. The receptors respond to signals as weak as ~20 microvolts per square centimeter. Source: American Museum of Natural History  (Legend.)

question: A platypus's bill senses prey two ways at once: an electric sense and a touch sense. Underwater, electricity races ahead while the physical pressure wave lags a hair behind. Jack Pettigrew argued in 1998 the platypus USES that tiny gap between the two signals. What does timing the gap let it work out?
answer: How far away the prey is
choices: How far away the prey is
How large the prey is
Which direction the current flows
How fast the water moves
context: Because electricity travels through water faster than the mechanical wave, the delay between the two senses encodes distance, letting the platypus range its target like a stopwatch. Source: Pettigrew et al. 1998, via Australian Platypus Conservancy

question: Handle a platypus the wrong way and only HALF of them can hurt you: the males alone carry the weapon. Sharpest during mating season, where on a male platypus's body is this weapon mounted?
answer: A hollow venom spur on each hind ankle
choices: A hollow venom spur on each hind ankle
A stinger at the tip of the tail
Fangs hidden inside the bill
Barbed claws on the front webbed feet
context: Each male carries a sharp hollow spur (about 12-18 mm) on each hind ankle, fed by a venom gland whose output spikes in the mating season. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platypus_venom; Australian Museum  (Legend.)

question: A man jabbed by a male platypus's spur is rushed to hospital. Among the people this venom has struck, it has earned a grim reputation. What makes platypus venom so notorious? (legend-tier)
answer: The pain shrugs off morphine and can last weeks or months
choices: The pain shrugs off morphine and can last weeks or months
It causes the wounded limb to swell to twice its size
It leaves the victim unable to grip for months
It triggers violent, days-long fever
context: The venom is not lethal to humans but causes excruciating pain that morphine cannot relieve, persisting for weeks or months and able to incapacitate a grown adult. Source: Slate, 2015; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platypus_venom  (Legend.)

question: In 2020 scientists shone ultraviolet light on old museum platypus pelts, expecting nothing unusual. What did the fur do under UV? (legend-tier discovery)
answer: Glows an eerie blue-green
choices: Glows an eerie blue-green
Glows a deep blood-red
Glows bright orange
Shows no reaction at all
context: Anich and colleagues reported this biofluorescence in the journal Mammalia in 2020, the first ever found in a monotreme. Source: Live Science, livescience.com/platypuses-glow-uv-light.html; ScienceDaily (Anich et al., 2020)  (Legend.)

question: An adult platypus has no teeth in its jaws, yet it happily crushes hard-shelled prey. Along with each mouthful of food it also scoops up gravel into its cheek pouches. Why gather the grit?
answer: It grinds food against horny pads, using the swallowed grit like millstones
choices: It grinds food against horny pads, using the swallowed grit like millstones
It uses the stones as ballast to sink while diving
It spits the grit to stun approaching prey
It stores the stones to build its riverbank burrow
context: With no teeth, the platypus mashes prey between horny keratin pads, the swallowed grit acting as millstones to crack hard shells. Source: AskNature, asknature.org/strategy/mouth-sorts-and-grinds-food/; Australian Museum

question: When the platypus genome was sequenced in 2008, its sex chromosomes stunned biologists. Most mammals settle sex with a single pair, but the platypus uses a whole chain of them, and part of that chain looks bird-like, resembling a chicken's. How many sex chromosomes does a platypus carry?
answer: Ten
choices: Ten
Two
Four
Twenty-three
context: The 2008 genome revealed 5 X and 5 Y chromosomes, and DNA blending mammal, bird, and reptile genes, with bird-like sex chromosomes echoing a chicken's. Source: WashU, source.washu.edu/2008/05/; ScienceAlert

question: The 2008 platypus genome caught the animal red-handed straddling two worlds. When placental and marsupial mammals adopted the placenta and switched to nursing, they junked one ancient gene their egg-laying ancestors had all carried. The platypus, alone among mammals, never threw its copy away — and it still switches the gene on. What does that surviving gene let the platypus do?
answer: Make egg yolk, even as it also makes milk
choices: Make egg yolk, even as it also makes milk
Grow a second, spare set of milk glands
Digest the shells of the eggs it lays
Regrow a lost venom spur within one season
context: The ancestral vertebrate had a cluster of three vitellogenin (egg-yolk protein) genes — chickens still carry all three. Placental and marsupial mammals lost every one when they swapped yolk for the placenta and milk. The platypus kept one working copy, an ortholog of the chicken's VtgI, sitting right beside its milk-casein genes. Low nonsynonymous-to-synonymous substitution ratios and almost no pseudogene decay confirm the gene is still functional, not a fossil — so the platypus is genetically half-reptile, half-mammal, making egg yolk and milk at once. Source: Warren et al. 2008 genome analysis (Nature nature06936); Wagner et al. 2008, 'Conservation of a vitellogenin gene cluster in oviparous vertebrates and identification of its traces in the platypus genome' (PubMed 18343608).  (Legend.)

question: A slow, cat-sized North American animal has a last-ditch trick when a predator is too close to run from: it flops onto its side, mouth hanging open and tongue lolling out, looking utterly dead. Which animal is famous for this convincing collapse?
answer: The Virginia opossum
choices: The Virginia opossum
The nine-banded armadillo
The striped skunk
The North American porcupine
context: The Virginia opossum (Didelphis virginiana) is the classic death-feigner, and its cornered collapse -- eyes glazed open, tongue out -- is literally where the phrase 'playing possum' comes from. Source: https://scienceinsights.org/do-possums-actually-play-dead-the-science-explained/

question: Faking death to survive a predator -- scientists call it thanatosis or tonic immobility -- turns out to be surprisingly common in the animal kingdom. Which of these groups of animals actually includes documented death-feigners?
answer: Beetles, ducks, frogs, and sharks
choices: Beetles, ducks, frogs, and sharks
Octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish
Bats, dolphins, and shrews
Corals, jellyfish, and sea anemones
context: Death-feigning shows up across an enormous range of animals -- beetles, spiders, crickets, ants, ducks, frogs, lizards, snakes, opossums, and even sharks and seahorses. It is one of nature's most widespread defenses. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5769822/

question: A limp opossum lying with its tongue out isn't relying on looks alone. As it faints, its anal glands leak fluid while it drools, urinates, and empties its bowels. What impression does all this create for a predator?
answer: It smells like a corpse dead for days
choices: It smells like a corpse dead for days
It masks its own scent so predators lose the trail
It gives off a musk that mimics the predator's own kind
It seems to be a healthy, easy catch
context: The musky fluid reeks of rotting flesh, so the opossum doesn't just look dead -- it smells and looks DAYS-dead. Many predators avoid spoiled meat, which can be poisonous, and drop it in disgust. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/many-animals-play-dead-not-just-to-avoid-predators

question: To a sniffing predator, a fainted opossum doesn't just look dead -- it feels and even sounds dead, thanks to real, measurable changes in its body during the faint. About how far does its heart rate drop while it lies there?
answer: By nearly half (about 46%)
choices: By nearly half (about 46%)
By about a tenth (roughly 10%)
It actually races faster than normal
It stops completely for minutes
context: Researchers measured the opossum's heart rate falling roughly 46%, its breathing dropping about 31%, and its body cooling slightly -- genuine physiology, not pretend, which is why the illusion is so convincing. Source: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/19169341_Physiological_responses_associated_with_feigned_death_in_the_American_opossum

question: Flip a shark upside down and it seizes up into a limp, helpless trance -- tonic immobility. Off Mexico, a pod of orcas called Moctezuma's pod learned to weaponize this against young great white sharks. Once a shark is paralyzed upside down, what do the orcas do?
answer: Rip out and eat its calorie-rich liver
choices: Rip out and eat its calorie-rich liver
Carry it to shore to eat later
Teach the trick to rival pods
Release it once it stops struggling
context: The orcas push young great whites to the surface and flip them upside down, locking them in tonic immobility, then tear out and devour the shark's huge, oil-rich liver -- a learned hunting move passed within the pod. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/orcas-in-mexico-have-learned-to-attack-young-great-white-sharks-by-flipping-them-upside-down-and-eating-their-livers-180987620/  (Legend.)

question: Divers still swap stories about a long-necked, small-headed creature slipping through Loch Ness. That classic silhouette actually comes from a real Mesozoic sea reptile with a long neck and a paddle at each corner of its body. What was this animal?
answer: A plesiosaur
choices: A plesiosaur
A pterosaur
An ichthyosaur
A mosasaur
context: The plesiosaur was a genuine marine reptile of the Mesozoic seas, not a dinosaur and not a living lake monster; its four-flipper, long-necked shape is where the 'Loch Ness Monster' picture comes from. Ichthyosaurs were dolphin-shaped, mosasaurs were giant sea lizards, and pterosaurs flew. Source: Natural History Museum London, 'What is a plesiosaur?' (nhm.ac.uk).

question: A plesiosaur was built like almost nothing alive in the water today. When it needed to cross the open sea, how did this reptile drive itself forward?
answer: It flapped all four flippers like underwater wings
choices: It flapped all four flippers like underwater wings
It sculled with a broad paddle-shaped tail
It swallowed water and jetted backward
It walked along the seafloor on its flippers
context: Almost no living animal does this. Computer simulations and a swimming robot showed the plesiosaur 'flew' through the water like a penguin, driving mostly with its two front flippers and adding a timed extra push with the back pair. Source: Muscutt et al. 2017, Royal Society Proceedings B; PBS NewsHour 'odd swimming style decoded by a robot'.

question: A plesiosaur spent its entire life in the open sea and never crawled onto land. Yet like a whale, it had to keep coming up to the surface again and again. What forced it to keep surfacing?
answer: It breathed air with lungs
choices: It breathed air with lungs
It needed sunlight to warm its blood
It hunted seabirds resting on the waves
It came up to shed its old skin
context: Plesiosaurs were air-breathing reptiles, so despite living their whole lives at sea they had to surface to breathe like whales do. Because they also gave live birth in the water, they never needed to come ashore at all. Source: Natural History Museum London, 'What is a plesiosaur?'.

question: A human neck and a giraffe neck both hold exactly seven bones, however long they stretch. The long-necked elasmosaurs threw that rule out entirely. About how many bones stacked up in an Elasmosaurus neck?
answer: About 72, more than almost any animal ever
choices: About 72, more than almost any animal ever
About 14, just double a giraffe's seven
About 25, like a very long-necked bird
The same 7, only each bone far longer
context: A giraffe stretches seven neck bones to enormous length; elasmosaurs instead stacked up 70-plus short vertebrae, and their cousin Albertonectes had at least 75. Source: Sachs et al. 2013, PLOS ONE, 'Revised Vertebral Count in the Longest-Necked Vertebrate Elasmosaurus platyurus'; National Geographic on Albertonectes.

question: Elasmosaurus stretched about 34 feet from nose to tail, yet its head was a tiny triangle that gulped small fish and squid whole. Of that whole 34-foot body, how much was taken up by the neck alone?
answer: Around 23 feet, about two-thirds of the animal
choices: Around 23 feet, about two-thirds of the animal
A few feet, roughly the length of the head
Around half, evenly split with the tail
Almost the whole body, leaving a stub tail
context: About 23 of Elasmosaurus's 34 feet was pure neck, nearly two-thirds of its length, tipped with that small triangular head. Source: Wikipedia 'Elasmosaurus', citing Sachs 2005 and Everhart (~10.3 m long, neck ~7.1 m, about 69%).

question: An elasmosaur carried a neck two-thirds the length of its whole body. One leading idea says this strange shape solved a specific problem it faced whenever it closed on a school of fish. What was that problem?
answer: Its bulky body would scare the whole school off before it could strike
choices: Its bulky body would scare the whole school off before it could strike
Its own long shadow fell across the water and spooked the fish
It swam too slowly to chase a darting school down
Its tiny mouth could not open wide enough to engulf them
context: This is a leading hypothesis, not proven fact: the long reach may have let the plesiosaur ease its tiny head into a fish school and snatch one before its huge body spooked them. Source: Earth Archives, 'Plesiosaurs and their absurdly long necks' (eartharchives.org), flagged as a feeding hypothesis.

question: Not every plesiosaur had that spindly neck. Their cousins the pliosaurs went the other way: short neck, enormous head. The giant Pliosaurus funkei, nicknamed 'Predator X', reached 40 to 50 feet with foot-long teeth. When researchers estimated its bite force, how did it compare with the famous land king, T. rex?
answer: Even more powerful than a T. rex's bite
choices: Even more powerful than a T. rex's bite
Roughly a tenth of a T. rex's bite
About equal, but only when biting soft prey
Weaker, since its teeth were built for gripping not crushing
context: Pliosaurs were apex predators of their seas. Researchers estimated Predator X's bite as even stronger than T. rex's, though the exact figure is debated because the skull is incomplete. Source: National Geographic, 'Paleontologists Reveal the Identity of Predator X'; Britannica; Discover Wildlife on pliosaurs (~30 cm teeth).

question: For 200 years scientists argued over how plesiosaurs reproduced, since they clearly never came ashore. A single 78-million-year-old Polycotylus fossil settled it: inside the mother's body lay one large baby. What did that fossil reveal about how plesiosaurs had their young?
answer: They gave live birth at sea rather than laying eggs on land
choices: They gave live birth at sea rather than laying eggs on land
They laid a single leathery egg that hatched inside the mother
They released clouds of tiny eggs like most fish
They carried eggs in the mouth until the young hatched
context: The one large baby, rather than a litter, hints that plesiosaurs may have cared for their young like whales or dolphins do. Source: O'Keefe & Chiappe 2011, Science 333:870-873, 'Viviparity and K-selected life history in a Mesozoic marine reptile'; Natural History Museum of LA County.

question: In December 1823 a fossil hunter prised the first complete plesiosaur skeleton from the cliffs at Lyme Regis. Its neck was so absurdly long that the great French anatomist Georges Cuvier flatly declared the specimen a forgery. How was the dispute finally resolved?
answer: A special Geological Society meeting proved it real and Cuvier admitted his error
choices: A special Geological Society meeting proved it real and Cuvier admitted his error
The skeleton was quietly reburied to end the argument
Later digs found longer-necked fossils that made it look ordinary
Cuvier's own students showed the neck bones were glued together
context: The fossil hunter was Mary Anning, whose complete plesiosaur was so long-necked that Cuvier assumed a fake, until the Geological Society examined it and he conceded he was wrong. Source: Natural History Museum London, 'Mary Anning: the unsung hero'; Geological Society online exhibition, Plesiosaurus dolichodeirus. (legend)

question: Plesiosaurs are filed under reptiles, so you would expect a body that simply runs at whatever temperature the surrounding sea happens to be. Yet oxygen isotopes locked in their fossil tooth enamel, and the growth pattern recorded in their bone, are two entirely independent readings that point the same direction. What did both lines agree these reptiles could do?
answer: Generate their own body heat, at a bird's metabolic rate, instead of borrowing it from the water
choices: Generate their own body heat, at a bird's metabolic rate, instead of borrowing it from the water
Simply match the cold ocean around them, exactly like a modern crocodile does
Warm up only after basking flipper-first at the sunlit surface between dives
Stay sluggish and slow-burning, coasting on sheer bulk to hold warmth in
context: Two separate lines of evidence converge on active, self-generated heat in plesiosaurs. Bernard et al. (2010, Science 328:1379-1382) measured oxygen isotopes in fossil tooth enamel and estimated elevated, regulated body temperatures well above the cold seas the animals swam in. Independently, Fleischle, Wintrich & Sander (2018, PeerJ 6:e4955; PMC5994164) modeled plesiosaur bone microstructure and recovered resting metabolic rates (~12-13 mL O2/h/g^0.67) and bone growth rates (~93-100 um/day) squarely in the BIRD range, far above any cold-blooded reptile, concluding plesiosaurs were 'truly endothermic' -- generating heat actively rather than coasting on body size. A 2024 reassessment (Reassessment of body temperature and thermoregulation strategies in Mesozoic marine reptiles, Paleobiology, biorxiv 2024.07.26.605303) refines the picture: plesiosaurs read as poikilothermic endotherms, body temperature ~27-34 C that still ran an advantage over the sea rather than holding a fixed value, while ichthyosaurs were the homeothermic ones. Across all three studies the shared, robust finding is self-produced, bird-level metabolic heat, not passive matching of the water. Sources: Bernard et al. 2010, Science (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1187443); Fleischle, Wintrich & Sander 2018, PeerJ (peerj.com/articles/4955/; PMC5994164); 2024 Paleobiology reassessment (biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.07.26.605303v1).

question: Plesiosaurs swallowed smooth stones by the hundred, and one Styxosaurus was found with 253 in its gut. For years the tidy explanation was ballast, weight to help the reptile sink and trim. Then someone actually weighed the stones against the animal, and the ballast idea collapsed. What did the numbers force researchers toward instead?
answer: The stones ground up tough, shelled prey in the gut like a bird's gizzard
choices: The stones ground up tough, shelled prey in the gut like a bird's gizzard
The stones anchored the reptile to the seabed while it rested
The stones were swallowed by accident while snapping at fish
The stones stored minerals the reptile drew on to grow its bones
context: These swallowed stones are gastroliths; one Styxosaurus held 253, and some elasmosaurs preserve over 100. The old 'ballast for buoyancy control' idea runs into a hard quantitative wall: recovered gastrolith mass never exceeds about 0.2 percent of the animal's body mass in any plesiosaur, far too little to sink or trim a multi-ton reptile. That shortfall has shifted the leading view toward a digestive role, grinding tough prey such as shelled cephalopods in the gut the way birds use gizzard stones, though the debate is not fully closed. Sources: Everhart, 'Gastroliths Associated with Plesiosaur Remains ... Pierre Shale'; Wings & Sander on gastrolith function; corroborated by Open University 'Solving the Riddle of the Gastroliths' and PeerJ 2024 (PMC11373562), which report gastrolith mass consistently under ~0.2 percent of body mass, insufficient as ballast.

question: Scattered across the leaf litter of Central and South American rainforests live tiny frogs painted in electric red, blue, yellow, and green -- about 200 species in shades no drab pond frog can match. What are these jewel-bright amphibians called?
answer: Poison dart frogs
choices: Poison dart frogs
Marsh peepers
Cave newts
River toads
context: The poison dart frog family holds roughly 200 species across 16 genera, many in dazzling electric colors, on the rainforest floor of Central and South America. Source: Wikipedia, 'Poison dart frog'.

question: A poison dart frog no bigger than a thumbnail hatches its eggs on the forest floor, then faces a problem: the babies need water. One parent lets the wriggling tadpoles stick to the mucus on its back and climbs a tree trunk. Where does it carry each tadpole to grow up?
answer: A pool of rainwater trapped in a bromeliad plant
choices: A pool of rainwater trapped in a bromeliad plant
A hollow log floating in a stream
A wet burrow dug at the roots
A nest woven from leaves
context: The newly hatched tadpoles cling to the mucus on a parent's back, and the adult climbs into the canopy to deposit each one, one at a time, in a tiny pool of rainwater trapped in a bromeliad plant. Source: Wikipedia, 'Poison dart frog'; World Frog Day, 'Strawberry Poison Dart Frogs And Their Parental Care'.

question: A poison dart frog doesn't hide. It sits in the open in blazing red or blue, easy for any bird to spot. Biologists call this bold display 'aposematic coloration.' What is the frog broadcasting with it?
answer: 'I am deadly -- don't eat me'
choices: 'I am deadly -- don't eat me'
'This patch of forest is mine'
'I am ready to find a mate'
'Look how big and strong I am'
context: Aposematic color is an honest warning signal -- a billboard telling predators the frog is toxic. Studies show the more toxic the frog, the more conspicuous its coloring, especially to bird predators that see color well. Source: The American Naturalist, 'Poison Frog Colors Are Honest Signals of Toxicity, Particularly for Bird Predators'.  (Legend.)

question: Deep in Colombia's Chocó rainforest lives the golden poison frog (Phyllobates terribilis) -- one of the most poisonous animals alive. A single wild frog carries about one milligram of toxin on its skin. Roughly how much damage could that one frog's poison do?
answer: Kill 10 to 20 people
choices: Kill 10 to 20 people
Kill a single small bird
Sting like a bee
Cause a mild rash
context: One wild golden poison frog carries about a milligram of batrachotoxin on its skin -- enough to kill 10 to 20 people, or roughly 20,000 mice. Source: Wikipedia, 'Golden poison frog'; National Geographic, 'Golden Poison Frog'.  (Legend.)

question: Here is the strange secret of the poison dart frog: it is not born venomous. In the wild it eats toxic ants, mites, and tiny beetles and concentrates their poisons in its skin glands. So what happens to a poison dart frog raised in a terrarium on ordinary fruit flies?
answer: It never becomes poisonous at all
choices: It never becomes poisonous at all
It grows a weaker but still deadly poison
It makes poison faster than in the wild
It loses its bright colors within weeks
context: Because the poison comes entirely from the diet, captive-bred dart frogs fed harmless insects never accumulate the alkaloids -- no captive-bred dendrobatid frog carries them, so they are completely safe to handle. Source: Understory Enterprises, 'Toxicity of Dart Frogs'; Wikipedia, 'Poison dart frog'.

question: The 'dart' in 'poison dart frog' comes from indigenous hunters who wiped their blowgun darts along a living frog's back. But the frogs most people picture -- the brilliant, jewel-colored Dendrobates -- were never the ones used. Which frogs actually armed the darts?
answer: A few species of the genus Phyllobates
choices: A few species of the genus Phyllobates
The tree frogs of the genus Hyla
Toads of the genus Rhinella
The glass frogs of family Centrolenidae
context: Only about four species, all in the genus Phyllobates, were actually used to poison darts -- not the more famous brilliant Dendrobates most people imagine. Source: Wikipedia, 'Poison dart frog'; AMNH, 'Dart Poison'.

question: A strawberry poison frog (Oophaga pumilio) mother leaves each tadpole alone in its own tiny bromeliad pool -- then keeps coming back to it, week after week, until it grows up. What does she bring each tadpole to eat?
answer: Her own unfertilized eggs
choices: Her own unfertilized eggs
Insects she has chewed soft
Algae she scrapes from the leaves
Ants she has drowned in the pool
context: The strawberry poison frog mother returns to each lonely tadpole in its private pool and feeds it unfertilized eggs; the tadpoles accept no other food and would starve without her. Source: World Frog Day, 'Strawberry Poison Dart Frogs And Their Parental Care'; NCBI PMC5702076, 'Induced parental care in a poison frog'.

question: The golden poison frog's weapon, batrachotoxin, kills in a dose the size of two grains of table salt. It jams the tiny sodium gates in nerve and muscle wide open so they can never reset. With those gates locked open, what happens to the victim?
answer: The muscles freeze and the heart stops
choices: The muscles freeze and the heart stops
The blood slowly thins and clots fail
The nerves go numb and pain fades
The lungs fill with fluid over days
context: Batrachotoxin jams open the sodium channels in nerve and muscle so they can never close, freezing the muscles and stopping the heart. A dose of roughly 2 to 7.5 micrograms -- about two grains of salt -- can kill an adult human. Source: McGill Office for Science and Society, 'Toxin on the Backs of Some Frogs Is Lethal to Humans'; Wikipedia, 'Batrachotoxin'.

question: The dyeing poison frog (Dendrobates tinctorius) pulls off a defense that seems to contradict itself. Up close its bold pattern screams danger to a nearby predator. But researchers found that from a distance those same markings do something unexpected. What?
answer: They blur together and blend into the background
choices: They blur together and blend into the background
They flash brighter to mimic a bigger animal
They shift color to match the leaf litter
They vanish as the frog stops moving
context: From up close the bold pattern warns predators, but from a distance the same colors blur together and merge with the background -- giving the frog warning coloration and camouflage at once. Source: PNAS, 'Distance-dependent defensive coloration in the poison frog Dendrobates tinctorius'.

question: On the frozen Arctic sea ice prowls the heaviest meat-eater that walks the land anywhere on Earth, a big male tipping the scale near 1,760 pounds. Which animal holds that title?
answer: The polar bear
choices: The polar bear
The Siberian tiger
The saltwater crocodile
The gray wolf
context: The polar bear (Ursus maritimus, Latin for 'sea bear') is the largest extant bear and the largest land carnivore by body mass, with adult males weighing 300-800 kg (660-1,760 lb) and standing nearly 10 feet tall on their hind legs. Source: Wikipedia, Polar bear; SeaWorld, All About Polar Bears - Characteristics.  (Legend.)

question: A polar bear settles onto the ice and holds perfectly still for long minutes, not stalking or chasing anything, just fixed on one small spot. What is it waiting for?
answer: A seal to surface for a breath, so it can strike the moment one does
choices: A seal to surface for a breath, so it can strike the moment one does
A crack of open water where it can warm its cold paws
The wind to shift so its own scent will not carry ahead of it
Its cubs to finish nursing in a den somewhere below the ice
context: This patient technique is called 'still-hunting': the bear finds a seal's breathing hole in the ice and simply waits, frozen and patient, for a seal to surface for air, then strikes. Source: Wikipedia, Polar bear; Britannica, polar bear.

question: A polar bear crosses deep, soft snow that would swallow a smaller animal, yet it barely sinks and pads along the surface. What about its build keeps it from breaking through?
answer: Front paws up to a foot across that spread its weight like snowshoes
choices: Front paws up to a foot across that spread its weight like snowshoes
Extra-long claws that hook the crust and pull it forward
Lightweight hollow leg bones that reduce how hard it presses down
A low belly that slides it along the snow like a sled
context: A polar bear's front paws reach up to 12 inches (30 cm) across, spreading its weight so it won't sink through snow, and doubling as paddles for swimming. Source: SeaWorld characteristics; ThePrimalX polar bear paws article.

question: A polar bear looks snowy white all over, but if you could part the thick fur and peek at the skin beneath, you'd get a surprise. What color is a polar bear's skin?
answer: Jet black
choices: Jet black
Pale pink
Bluish gray
Snowy white, like the fur
context: A polar bear's skin is black, visible only on the nose and footpads; the dark skin soaks up the sun's warmth like a solar panel. Source: SeaWorld, All About Polar Bears - Characteristics ('A polar bear's skin, visible only on the nose and footpads, is black.').

question: Out on the open ice a polar bear lifts its head into the wind and locks onto prey a person could never sense from that far off. Roughly how far away can it smell a seal's breathing hole?
answer: About a mile away
choices: About a mile away
About a hundred yards away
About ten miles away
Only when nearly on top of it
context: A polar bear's nose can detect a seal's breathing hole from about a mile away, and sniff out a seal hidden under three feet of packed snow. Source: Biology Insights, 'How Far Away Can a Polar Bear Smell?'; Polar Bears International seal-detection facts.

question: A polar bear's fur looks brilliant white, but a scientist examining a single strand under magnification is surprised by what the hair actually looks like up close. What is each hair actually like?
answer: Clear and hollow, scattering light so it only looks white
choices: Clear and hollow, scattering light so it only looks white
Coated in a fine layer of reflective white pigment
Bright white all the way through the shaft
Silver-tipped over a darker brown base
context: Each hair is translucent with an air-filled core; the fur only LOOKS white because the rough hollow hairs scatter sunlight, the same way snow looks white. Source: Britannica, Why Are Polar Bears White; SeaWorld characteristics.

question: Point an infrared heat camera at a polar bear standing on the snow and the animal almost disappears from the image, reading nearly as cold as the ice. Why does so little of the bear show up?
answer: Its insulation is so complete that almost no body heat escapes its surface
choices: Its insulation is so complete that almost no body heat escapes its surface
Its fur reflects the camera's infrared beam straight back
It lowers its body temperature to match the surrounding snow
The white fur blends into the white background on any camera
context: Hollow fur, dense underfur, and blubber insulate the bear so well that almost no body heat reaches its surface, which reads as cold as the surrounding snow. Source: AskNature, 'See-Through Fur Traps Light and Heat'; Harvard SITN, polar-bear-inspired invisibility cloak (2018).

question: Scientists tracking one female polar bear by GPS watched her leave the ice and swim across the open Beaufort Sea without ever stopping to rest, until she finally reached solid ice again. How long was that single nonstop swim?
answer: Nine days
choices: Nine days
Three days
Five days
Fourteen days
context: The tracked female swam about 426 miles (687 km) nonstop over nine days across the Beaufort Sea, losing 22% of her body weight before reaching ice. Reported from a USGS polar bear tracking study (2011). Source: USGS tracking study via Wikipedia, Polar bear, and PBS Nature Polar Bear Fact Sheet.  (Legend.)

question: The Portuguese man o' war drifts at the surface looking like a pale blue jellyfish. But scientists insist you should call it 'they,' not 'it.' Why do they say 'they'?
answer: It is a colony of many bodies
choices: It is a colony of many bodies
It changes sex through its life
It always swims in mated pairs
It splits in two when threatened
context: A Portuguese man o' war (Physalia physalis) is not a jellyfish and not even a single animal. It is a siphonophore: a floating colony of many specialized bodies called zooids, all genetically identical clones, so tightly fused that no one zooid could survive alone. That is why scientists say it is a 'they,' not an 'it.' Source: NOAA Ocean Service, oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/portuguese-man-o-war.html.  (Legend.)

question: A Portuguese man o' war has a gas-filled blue-purple bag standing above the water. With no fins and no tail to drive it forward, how does this creature cross the open sea?
answer: The wind blows its bag like a sail
choices: The wind blows its bag like a sail
It jets water to shoot forward
It hitches rides on passing fish
It slowly rolls with the tide alone
context: The blue-violet-to-pink gas bag on top (the pneumatophore, or float) rises up to about six inches above the water and acts as a sail to catch the wind. The man o' war has no way to swim or steer itself; it drifts wherever wind and current carry it. Source: NOAA Ocean Service; Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war.

question: A Portuguese man o' war's float sits only inches wide at the surface, yet its stinging tentacles trail down into the water below. Stretched to their limit, how far do those hidden threads reach?
answer: Longer than a blue whale
choices: Longer than a blue whale
Farther than a football field
About the height of a house
Roughly the length of a car
context: The stinging tentacles trail an average of about 10 meters (30 feet) below the float and can stretch as far as 30 meters (roughly 100 feet), longer than a blue whale, all hanging invisibly beneath a float only inches wide. Source: NOAA Ocean Service; Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war.

question: A Portuguese man o' war is a floating colony whose separate bodies each specialize in one task, like forming the float, doing the stinging, or handling digestion. What is the strange catch about any single one of those bodies?
answer: On its own it would die
choices: On its own it would die
It can regrow the whole colony
It swims off to hunt alone
It hardens into a protective shell
context: The colony is divided into jobs: one zooid type forms the gas float, dactylozooids form the stinging tentacles, gastrozooids digest, and gonozooids handle reproduction. Each body can do only its one job, and they are so dependent on one another that no single zooid could survive on its own. Source: Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war (zooid types); NOAA Ocean Service.

question: A Portuguese man o' war makes the gas that fills its float rather than gulping ordinary air. Startlingly, that homemade gas can be rich in the very same poison that pours from a car's exhaust pipe. What poison?
answer: Carbon monoxide
choices: Carbon monoxide
Chlorine
Ammonia
Methane
context: The float doesn't just hold ordinary air; the animal actively makes its own gas inside the bag, and it can be as much as 13% carbon monoxide, the same poisonous gas that comes out of a car exhaust. Source: Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war (pneumatophore gas composition).  (Legend.)

question: A sea slug called the blue dragon, smaller than a grape and floating upside-down at the surface, eats the venomous Portuguese man o' war without being harmed. Even stranger is what it does with the strongest stingers it swallows.
answer: It stores them to fire as its own weapon
choices: It stores them to fire as its own weapon
It grinds them into harmless paste
It spits them back at the colony
It uses them to build a shell
context: The blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) sorts out the strongest stingers, does not fire them, and stores them in the tips of its own feathery arms to reuse as a stolen weapon, a trick called kleptocnidy. Source: Wikipedia, Glaucus atlanticus; HowStuffWorks, The Blue Dragon Sea Slug Eats Venomous Prey and Saves the Stingers for Later.  (Legend.)

question: Portuguese men o' war sail with the wind, but their sails come in two mirror-image builds, so different individuals veer off to the left or the right rather than all running straight downwind. Biologists think this split helps the species in one specific way. Which?
answer: A whole fleet never all strands on one beach
choices: A whole fleet never all strands on one beach
The colonies can steer toward richer feeding grounds
Left and right builds can mate only with each other
Rivals are pushed apart to reduce competition
context: The sail comes in two mirror-image forms: some men o' war are 'left-handed' and some 'right-handed,' so they tack off at about 45 degrees to either side of the wind. This split means a whole fleet never all blows onto the same beach at once, sparing part of the population from stranding and dying together. Source: Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war (dimorphism and drift); ScienceDirect, Relationship between dimorphism and drift in the Portuguese man-of-war.  (Legend.)

question: The potoo is a big-eyed night bird of Central and South American forests. By day it does something bizarre: it perches bolt upright, stretches its head and bill straight at the sky, and freezes for hours. What does a motionless potoo look like?
answer: A broken-off, dead stub of the branch itself
choices: A broken-off, dead stub of the branch itself
A coiled snake draped over the wood
A clump of bright red berries
A patch of green moss on the bark
context: The potoo's daytime disguise is total: it aligns its body with a broken snag, points its bill upward, and stays motionless for hours, so it reads as a dead stub of the very tree it sits on. Its own nestlings can even resemble clumps of fungus on the wood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_potoo ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potoo

question: A potoo sits frozen on its snag, pretending to be dead wood, its huge eyes shut against the daylight. Yet if a hawk creeps closer, the 'sleeping' bird reacts before the hawk can strike. What lets a potoo track that movement without opening its eyes?
answer: Notched slits set into its own eyelids
choices: Notched slits set into its own eyelids
A transparent inner eyelid it peers through
Oversized eyes that shine through thin skin
A reflective backing that glows when shut
context: The potoo has two or three notches, or slits, in its eyelids that stay open even when the eyes are shut, letting it sense light and movement — so it can detect an approaching predator while sitting frozen with its eyes 'closed.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_potoo ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potoo  (Legend.)

question: A female potoo, a night bird of the American forests, produces a single precious egg each season. When the moment comes to lay it, where does that lone egg end up?
answer: Straight onto a bare dip on a branch or rotten stump
choices: Straight onto a bare dip on a branch or rotten stump
Inside a hole she chisels in a tree trunk
In a floating raft of reeds on the water
In a deep scrape she digs in the forest floor
context: The potoo builds nothing at all — the female lays her single egg directly into a shallow depression on a bare branch or the top of a rotten stump, and a parent hides it by perching over it like part of the wood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potoo ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_potoo

question: After dark the common potoo lifts a strange voice across the forest — a haunting run of up to eight whistled notes that forest people once took as an omen. Track those eight whistles from the first note to the last. What does the phrase do as it goes?
answer: Steadily drop in pitch and fade to silence
choices: Steadily drop in pitch and fade to silence
Rise steadily to a piercing shriek
Hold one long flat unbroken tone
Speed up into a rattling drum-roll
context: The common potoo's song is a series of up to eight whistled notes that steadily drop in pitch and fade in volume — a sound like a distant, sorrowful human cry drifting through the dark. That eerie, sinking wail earned folk names like 'ghost bird' and 'poor-me-one,' and a Peruvian tale calls it a lost child crying for its mother. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_potoo ; https://www.iflscience.com/meet-the-great-potoo-south-americas-loud-but-elusive-ghost-bird-76689  (Legend.)

question: A red kangaroo (Osphranter rufus) is born after a pregnancy of only about 33 days, so the newborn is astonishingly tiny and undeveloped. About how big is a just-born red kangaroo?
answer: The size of a jellybean, under a gram
choices: The size of a jellybean, under a gram
The size of a house cat
The size of a rabbit
The size of a human baby
context: A newborn red kangaroo is roughly 2 cm long and weighs under a gram — about the size of a jellybean or grape — and is born blind and hairless after just ~33 days. It finishes developing outside the womb. Source: a-z-animals.com/articles/a-newborn-kangaroo-is-no-bigger-than-a-jellybean/

question: Kangaroos, koalas, wombats and opossums all sit on the same branch of the mammal family tree, set apart from mice, monkeys and every other mammal. What is this group of mammals called?
answer: Marsupials
choices: Marsupials
Rodents
Primates
Amphibians
context: Marsupials give birth to tiny, barely-formed young that complete their development in (or attached to) the mother's pouch, latched to a teat. Kangaroos, koalas, wombats and opossums are all marsupials. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marsupial

question: A blind, hairless newborn red kangaroo, no bigger than a jellybean, is born at the birth canal but must somehow reach the pouch high up on its mother's belly. How does this barely-formed newborn get there?
answer: It hauls itself up through the fur on tiny clawed forelimbs
choices: It hauls itself up through the fur on tiny clawed forelimbs
Its mother lifts it in with her paws
Its mother carries it in her mouth
It is born already inside the pouch
context: The mother does not help. The newborn hauls itself up through her fur using its one well-developed feature — strong forelimbs tipped with tiny claws — while the rest of its body is still unformed. Source: a-z-animals.com/articles/a-newborn-kangaroo-is-no-bigger-than-a-jellybean/

question: The newborn red kangaroo, blind and nearly bodiless, has no eyes to steer by as it hauls itself up the fur toward the pouch — a climb it finishes in about three minutes. What guides it to the pouch?
answer: An excellent sense of smell and direction
choices: An excellent sense of smell and direction
The mother's heartbeat
Faint warmth from the pouch
The sound of the mother's voice
context: The whole climb takes about three minutes, guided by a strong sense of smell and direction — remarkable for an animal whose body is almost entirely unformed except its grasping front limbs. Source: scienceinsights.org/how-do-kangaroos-give-birth-from-embryo-to-pouch/

question: When the newborn kangaroo finally reaches a teat inside the pouch and takes it into its mouth, something happens that locks the pair together so firmly the joey can't be shaken loose even while the mother bounds at full speed. What happens?
answer: The tip of the teat swells into a bulb inside its mouth
choices: The tip of the teat swells into a bulb inside its mouth
The joey's jaws fuse shut around the teat
The pouch fills with a sticky fluid
The joey grips the teat with its claws
context: The teat tip swells into a bulb inside the joey's mouth, fusing the two together for months — it cannot be dislodged even at full speed. Newborn marsupials also have 'oral shields' narrowing the mouth to a round hole just wide enough for the teat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marsupial

question: A red kangaroo's pouch opens forward — toward her head — yet a joey never tumbles out when she leaps. She controls the opening like the neck of a drawstring bag. What lets her do that?
answer: A strong sphincter muscle that tightens the pouch opening
choices: A strong sphincter muscle that tightens the pouch opening
A flap of skin she folds over by hand
Sticky glands lining the pouch rim
The joey hooking its claws over the edge
context: A ring of sphincter muscle at the pouch opening lets the mother cinch it shut like a drawstring, so a joey in a forward-opening pouch can't fall out mid-leap. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pouch_(marsupial)

question: A wombat mother digs burrows by throwing dirt backward with powerful claws — which should mean packing soil straight onto a baby riding in her pouch. Yet the baby stays clean. Why?
answer: Her pouch opens backward, toward her hind legs
choices: Her pouch opens backward, toward her hind legs
She seals the pouch shut while digging
She digs only with her front paws held high
She carries the baby in her mouth while digging
context: A wombat's pouch opens backward, toward the hind legs, so a digging mother doesn't shovel dirt onto the baby inside — the opposite orientation to a forward-opening kangaroo pouch. Source: environment.sa.gov.au/goodliving/posts/2018/10/wombat-facts

question: The Virginia opossum (Didelphis virginiana) is the only marsupial that lives wild in North America. A single mother may give birth to more than 20 jellybean-sized young at once — far more than she can raise. What decides which survive?
answer: Only those that reach one of her ~13 teats live
choices: Only those that reach one of her ~13 teats live
The mother eats the weakest herself
The first-born pushes the rest out of the pouch
She raises whichever ones are largest at birth
context: A Virginia opossum mother has about 13 teats, so of her 20-plus newborns only those that reach and latch onto a teat survive. Her pregnancy lasts just 12–13 days, one of the shortest of any mammal. Source: sdzwildlifeexplorers.org/animals/virginia-opossum

question: A female red kangaroo can mate, then simply hold the resulting embryo — a tiny ball of about 100 cells — in suspended animation, paused and ready to resume the instant her pouch is free again. What keeps that embryo on hold?
answer: Nursing the joey already in her pouch
choices: Nursing the joey already in her pouch
A drop in the season's rainfall
The mother's body temperature falling
A hormone released only after a long fast
context: This is embryonic diapause: a fertilized egg is held as a ~100-cell blastocyst, frozen and ready to develop the moment the pouch empties. Nursing the current joey is what keeps it paused. Source: ielc.libguides.com/sdzg/factsheets/westerngraykangaroo/reproduction  (Legend.)

question: A mother kangaroo can nurse a big joey hopping alongside her AND a newborn latched in her pouch at the very same time — and each gets exactly the milk it needs. How does she manage that?
answer: She makes two different milks from two teats at once
choices: She makes two different milks from two teats at once
She alternates one milk between the two by the hour
She feeds the newborn milk and the older one solid food
Both drink the same milk but at different times
context: From two teats simultaneously she produces fat-rich milk for the older joey 'at foot' and low-fat, immune-rich milk for the tiny newborn in the pouch — different recipes at the same time. Source: a-z-animals.com/articles/kangaroos-have-one-of-the-strangest-reproductive-systems-in-the-animal-world/  (Legend.)

question: A koala (Phascolarctos cinereus) lives on eucalyptus leaves so loaded with tannins and toxins that most animals couldn't stomach them. Around 5–6 months old, a koala joey eats a special soft dropping its mother makes, called 'pap' — not for the calories. What is it really swallowing?
answer: Live gut bacteria that let it digest eucalyptus
choices: Live gut bacteria that let it digest eucalyptus
Extra minerals stripped from the leaves
A dose of the toxins to build up tolerance
Half-digested leaves ready to eat
context: Pap comes from the caecum and is packed with live tannin-protein-degrading bacteria — far richer in microbes than ordinary droppings. The joey eats it to seed its gut before its first eucalyptus leaves. Sources: australiangeographic.com.au/news/2022/07/pap-not-poop-the-gift-a-mother-koala-gives-her-joey/ ; enviromicro-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1462-2920.15858  (Legend.)

question: A female kangaroo has TWO uteruses and a central birth canal that in many kangaroos only fully tunnels open at her first birth. This doubled plumbing was locked in by an accident of how the marsupial embryo is built: a pair of tubes ends up running right between the two developing reproductive tracts, physically blocking them from ever merging into the single system placental mammals have. Which tubes wedge in there?
answer: The ureters, draining the kidneys down to the bladder
choices: The ureters, draining the kidneys down to the bladder
The Wolffian ducts, the embryonic precursors of male plumbing
The lymphatic vessels, draining fluid back toward the heart
The urethra, draining the bladder to the outside
context: In the marsupial embryo the ureters run between the two developing reproductive tracts, so the tracts can never fuse the way they do in placental mammals — which is why marsupials keep three vaginal canals and two uteruses. The two side (lateral) canals carry sperm up to the two uteruses; a separate central 'median' canal is the road the tiny joey travels down at birth. Males match the paired lateral tracts with a two-pronged, bifurcated penis. Sources: 'Why do kangaroos have 3 vaginas?' Live Science — https://www.livescience.com/animals/land-mammals/why-do-kangaroos-have-3-vaginas ; 'Kangaroos Have Three Vaginas,' National Geographic — https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/kangaroos-have-three-vaginas ; Australian Geographic — https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/nature-wildlife/2022/12/did-you-know-kangaroos-have-three-vaginas/  (Legend.)

question: A slender green insect sits stone-still on a stem, its spiky front legs folded up and held out before it, waiting for a fly to wander close. What is this ambush hunter?
answer: A praying mantis
choices: A praying mantis
A walking stick
A leaf katydid
A green lacewing
context: The praying mantis gets its name from that folded-leg posture, which looks like praying but is really a cocked spring ready to snap. Source: Live Science, high-speed video of mantis strike; My Pet Mantis hunting overview.

question: When a fly finally drifts within reach, a praying mantis snaps its folded, spike-lined front legs shut around it. From the moment it launches, how long does the grab take?
answer: About 50 to 70 milliseconds, faster than a blink
choices: About 50 to 70 milliseconds, faster than a blink
About half a second, quicker than a hand
Two to three seconds, a slow squeeze
A tenth of a minute, deliberate and steady
context: Those raptorial forelegs snap shut like a spring-loaded trap in as little as 50 to 70 milliseconds — faster than a human can blink. Source: Live Science, high-speed video of mantis strike.

question: A mantis strikes only when prey drifts into a narrow window its forelegs can reach. It pulls this off with a visual ability found in no other insect. What ability?
answer: True 3D depth perception
choices: True 3D depth perception
Heat-sensing infrared sight
A 360-degree panoramic scan
X-ray sight through leaves
context: The praying mantis is the only insect known to see in true 3D depth perception (stereo vision), letting it gauge precisely when prey is in striking range. Source: Newcastle University Press Office, 'New form of 3D vision discovered in praying mantis' (2018).

question: Big mantises grab and eat small vertebrates alive, and researchers have logged a startling range of victims. One entry stands out as the strangest catch ever recorded, seen just once. What was it?
answer: A small bat
choices: A small bat
A small snake
A newt
A hummingbird
context: Mantises have been recorded killing and eating small frogs, lizards, salamanders, snakes, mice — and, on one remarkable occasion, a small bat. Source: phys.org, 'Praying mantises hunt down birds worldwide' (2017); Nyffeler, Maxwell & Van Remsen study.

question: One tropical mantis is pink and white with wide, petal-shaped legs, and it perches on a plant to ambush the pollinators that come to feed. A field study found something startling about how well its disguise works.
answer: It draws in more insects than the real flowers nearby
choices: It draws in more insects than the real flowers nearby
It only fools insects that are already dying
It must hide among matching blossoms to work
It works only at night when flowers are closed
context: The orchid mantis is a living flower disguise, and O'Hanlon's field study found it attracts pollinating insects even better than the real flowers around it. Source: O'Hanlon, Holwell & Herberstein, 'Pollinator Deception in the Orchid Mantis,' The American Naturalist (2014). (Legendary-sounding but real.)

question: The old story says a female praying mantis always bites the head off her mate. Careful experiments show the truth is more specific: cannibalism happens mainly under one condition. Which?
answer: When the female is hungry
choices: When the female is hungry
When the male is older than the female
When the pair mate in daylight
When the female has already mated once
context: Most matings end with the male alive; the head-biting legend is overstated. In one experiment no well-fed female ate her mate, while starved females did. Source: Snopes, 'Does a Female Praying Mantis Always Eat Her Mate's Head?'; phys.org, 'Praying mantis cannibalism explained.' (A real but overstated legend.)

question: To test whether mantises really see in 3D, scientist Vivek Nityananda fitted each one with a tiny pair of blue-and-green glasses and played them a 3D movie of prey. How did the mantises react?
answer: They lunged to grab prey that was not really there
choices: They lunged to grab prey that was not really there
They ignored the screen entirely
They fled from the flickering images
They froze until the movie ended
context: Nityananda glued tiny 3D glasses onto the mantises with a drop of beeswax; when shown a 3D illusion of prey, they tried to grab it right out of the air — proving they see in 3D. Source: Live Science, 'Praying Mantises Wear Tiny 3D Glasses, for Science'; Newcastle University. (Sounds like a tall tale, but it really happened.)  (Legend.)

question: Many mantises carry a single 'cyclopean' ear in the middle of the chest, tuned to ultrasound. When it picks up the hunting calls of a bat closing in at night, the flying mantis reacts instantly. What does it do?
answer: Throws itself into a spiraling power dive
choices: Throws itself into a spiraling power dive
Freezes in midair and drops straight down
Flashes bright wing spots to startle the bat
Emits its own ultrasonic clicks to jam the bat
context: On detecting a bat's ultrasonic calls, a flying mantis spirals into a steep power dive toward the ground, escaping about 80 percent of the time. Source: National Geographic, 'Praying Mantis Uses Ultrasonic Hearing to Dodge Bats'; Yager, 'The Cyclopean Ear,' Science (1986).

question: A wolf, an owl, a cat, and a person all have both eyes pointed the same direction on the head. Where do a hunter's eyes sit — the setup that lets its two views overlap and judge exactly how far away the prey is before it pounces?
answer: on the front of the head
choices: on the front of the head
on the sides of the head
on top of the head
one on each end of a long stalk
context: Forward-facing eyes give overlapping fields of view, and that overlap is what lets a predator measure the distance to its target before it leaps. The old rhyme sums it up: 'Eyes in front, the animal hunts.' Sources: University of California / Berkeley News 'Hunter or prey? The eyes are the key' (2015-08-07); veterinaryvision.co.uk 'How animals see the World.'

question: A rabbit, a horse, and a deer are grazing with their heads down, and none of them can see far in front of its own nose — yet each can catch an ambush sneaking up from almost any direction. Where are a grazer's eyes placed to buy that near-panoramic watch?
answer: on the sides of the head
choices: on the sides of the head
on the front of the head
tucked under the ears
behind a bony hood
context: Side-set eyes give up the overlap that measures distance and trade it for a nearly all-around field of view, so a hunted animal can spot danger coming from behind or the flank. The rhyme is 'Eyes on the side, the animal hides.' Sources: New Hampshire State Parks 'Reading a Skull: Predator and Prey Differences' (nhstateparks.org); Nearby Nature 'Predators and Prey Background.'

question: A horse's side-set eyes sweep almost the whole circle around it — close to 340 degrees of watch. Yet there is one spot the horse cannot see that surprises people: not just directly behind it, but a triangle a few feet long in one other place. Where is that second blind spot?
answer: right in front of its own nose
choices: right in front of its own nose
straight up above its mane
along its left flank only
under its own belly
context: The horse's panoramic side vision leaves two gaps: one directly behind the tail, and one triangle of blindness reaching a few feet straight out from the nose. A horse briefly raising or turning its head fills the front gap, which is why a grazing horse keeps bobbing its head up. Sources: Utah State University Extension 'Equine Vision and Its Effect on Behavior' (digitalcommons.usu.edu); equinehelper.com 'How Horses See.'

question: A grazing goat drops its head to the grass, and something remarkable happens inside each eye: the long horizontal pupil rolls — the two eyes turning up to 50 degrees in opposite directions — to do WHAT as the head tilts down?
answer: keep the pupil level with the ground
choices: keep the pupil level with the ground
seal shut against flying grit
let in far more light
point both pupils at the same blade of grass
context: This eye-roll is called cyclovergence: as the goat or sheep lowers its head to eat, each eye rotates so the wide horizontal pupil stays parallel to the horizon, keeping the whole sweep of ground in sharp focus for spotting a predator even while the animal is head-down grazing. Sources: Banks et al. 2015 'Why do animal eyes have pupils of different shapes?' (Science Advances); Berkeley News 2015-08-07; The Conversation 'Revealed: why animals' pupils come in different shapes.' (Legend-tier wonder.)

question: Martin Banks's team measured 214 land animals and found the vertical slit pupil isn't a mark of big cats at all — lions and tigers have round pupils. The slit shows up almost only in predators shorter than about knee height, like house cats and geckos. What hunting style does that low, close-to-the-ground slit belong to?
answer: an ambusher lying in wait for the pounce
choices: an ambusher lying in wait for the pounce
a runner chasing prey across open ground
a night-flying glider
a filter-feeder sifting the water
context: Banks's team found the vertical slit almost always in predators under about 42 cm at the shoulder. Down near the ground, the slit sharpens the blur and disparity cues a lying-in-wait hunter uses to time the exact moment of the strike — while tall chasers like lions keep round pupils. Sources: Banks et al. 2015 (Science Advances); Berkeley News 2015-08-07; sci.news 'New Study Reveals Why Some Animals Have Vertical Pupils.'

question: A shaggy orange monkey of the Borneo rainforest is instantly known by one thing on the adult male's face. What does he sport?
answer: A drooping nose over four inches long
choices: A drooping nose over four inches long
A fan of bright blue cheek ridges
A bony crest like a rooster's comb
A mane of stiff white whiskers
context: The male proboscis monkey (Nasalis larvatus) grows the largest nose of any primate — a pendulous flap that can pass four inches (about 10 cm). Females and juveniles keep small, neat, upturned noses. Source: https://www.oneearth.org/species-of-the-week-proboscis-monkey/  (Legend.)

question: Male proboscis monkeys live in dense Borneo forest where they often can't see each other, yet a male's honking call carries far through the trees. His oversized nose does something to that call to help it travel. What?
answer: It acts as a resonating chamber that deepens and amplifies the honk
choices: It acts as a resonating chamber that deepens and amplifies the honk
It squeezes shut to force the honk out in sharp bursts
It funnels the honk straight up above the canopy
It filters out low tones so only the sharp notes carry
context: The nasal cavity works like a built-in loudspeaker: it resonates, deepening and amplifying the honk so it reaches monkeys the male cannot see. A bigger nose makes a deeper, louder call — so a female choosing a big-nosed male is reading his fitness off the sound, part visual banner and part megaphone. Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aaq0250

question: The proboscis monkey has a huge potbelly that can be a quarter of its whole body weight. That swollen belly holds a special kind of stomach. What is inside it doing the work?
answer: A chambered stomach packed with bacteria that ferment tough leaves
choices: A chambered stomach packed with bacteria that ferment tough leaves
A crop of grit and gravel that grinds the leaves to paste
A pouch of stored fat that carries it through the dry season
A tangle of extra-long coiled intestine to soak up water
context: Like a cow, the proboscis monkey has a multi-chambered stomach full of cellulose-busting bacteria that ferment tough leaves — even detoxifying poisons in near-inedible mangrove leaves. It also regurgitates and re-chews its food, the first documented rumination-like remastication in a primate. Sweet ripe fruit is dangerous: its sugars ferment inside and can bloat the monkey badly, so it eats mostly young leaves and unripe fruit. Sources: https://hakaimagazine.com/features/the-wonderful-transcendent-life-of-an-odd-nosed-monkey/ ; https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/full/10.1098/rsbl.2011.0197

question: To reach a feeding tree across a crocodile-filled river, a troop of proboscis monkeys belly-flops from the treetops and paddles across at the narrowest point. What lets them out-swim most other monkeys?
answer: Webbed hands and feet for paddling underwater
choices: Webbed hands and feet for paddling underwater
A hollow-boned tail that floats them like a cork
Oily fur that keeps water from soaking them down
Air-filled cheek pouches they gulp to stay buoyant
context: Proboscis monkeys are among the best swimmers of any monkey. Their webbed hands and feet let them dog-paddle and even swim underwater up to 20 meters (about 66 feet) to cross rivers. They slip in as silently as they can so the crocodiles don't notice them. Sources: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/proboscis-monkey ; https://www.discoverwildlife.com/tv/proboscis-monkeys-leap-into-crocodile-infested-river-bbc  (Legend.)

question: Pterosaurs ruled the skies for over 150 million years, and people often call them 'flying dinosaurs.' But that label is wrong. What kind of animal was a pterosaur?
answer: A flying reptile, its own separate branch
