question: For a century, a sharp stone flake with a shell-like fracture was read as a fingerprint of early humans -- proof someone had knapped a cutting edge. Then wild capuchins in Brazil's Serra da Capivara were filmed hammering cobbles and flinging off nearly identical flakes, yet never cutting a thing with them. What are the monkeys actually after?
answer: The quartz dust they lick off the shattered stone
choices: The quartz dust they lick off the shattered stone
Insects the hammering flushes out of the rocks
Nuts they have wedged against the anvil to crack
A hammer stone they will carry off and reuse
context: At Serra da Capivara, Brazil, bearded capuchins (Sapajus libidinosus) pound rounded quartzite cobbles against embedded anvil stones. Proffitt and colleagues (Nature, 2016) analysed 111 of the resulting artefacts and found sharp-edged flakes bearing conchoidal (shell-like) fractures nearly indistinguishable from the Oldowan cutting flakes long treated as a hallmark of early hominins. The twist: the capuchins ignore the cutting edges entirely -- they pound to lick the quartz dust and grit off the smashed cobble (likely for minerals, or to scrape away lichen). Because a wild monkey mass-produces 'stone tools' with no interest in a blade, the find complicates how archaeologists read the earliest human stone record -- as the Oxford team put it, humans may be 'not unique after all.' Source: Proffitt et al., 'Wild monkeys flake stone tools,' Nature 2016 (nature.com/articles/nature20112).

question: A big rainforest bird perches on a branch, and roughly a third of its whole length is one enormous, brightly colored beak. Which bird is it?
answer: Toucan
choices: Toucan
Flamingo
Pelican
Ostrich
context: The toucan is famous for a bill that can run up to four times the size of its own head and nearly as long as the rest of its body. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants — Toucan (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/toucan).

question: A toucan pinches a berry at the very tip of that long bill — far out past its mouth, with no way to just swallow it from there. How does it get the fruit down its throat?
answer: It jerks its head back and tosses the berry up, then catches it dropping straight down its throat
choices: It jerks its head back and tosses the berry up, then catches it dropping straight down its throat
It works the berry inward along the bill, then rolls it back to the mouth with its tongue
It clamps down to crush the berry open, then laps the sweet juice off the bill
It grips the berry against a branch, then shears off bites small enough to swallow
context: A toucan grabs fruit at the tip of its bill, then jerks its head back and flicks the food into the air so it drops straight down the throat — it eats by throwing its food and catching it. Source: HowStuffWorks — The Toucan (animals.howstuffworks.com/birds/toucan.htm); San Diego Zoo — Toucan.

question: A toucan's beak is nearly as long as the rest of its body, yet the bird flies with ease and barely feels the weight. What keeps that huge bill so astonishingly light?
answer: A crisscross scaffold of thin bony struts wrapped in keratin, mostly hollow inside
choices: A crisscross scaffold of thin bony struts wrapped in keratin, mostly hollow inside
Solid bone that grows lighter as the bird ages
A core of soft cartilage like a shark's skeleton
Air sacs the bird inflates before takeoff
context: The bill is a natural foam sandwich — an outer sheath of keratin (the stuff of hair and fingernails) over an airy inner core of bony struts and closed air-filled cells, so it weighs only a tiny fraction of the bird's body. Source: SeaWorld — Toco Toucan Facts (seaworld.org/animals/facts/birds/toco-toucan/); San Diego Zoo — Toucan.

question: A toucan roasts on a sweltering afternoon, then shivers through a chilly night — all with the same giant bill attached. Scientists found the bird uses that bill to manage its body temperature both ways. What's the trick?
answer: It ramps blood flow into the bill to dump warmth on hot days, then throttles the flow back to trap it on cold nights
choices: It ramps blood flow into the bill to dump warmth on hot days, then throttles the flow back to trap it on cold nights
It faces the bill into the breeze when hot and tucks it under a wing when cold
It grows a thicker keratin layer for winter and molts it thinner for summer
It pants with the bill wide open to cool, then clamps it shut to stay warm
context: The bill is a controllable radiator: the toucan adjusts blood flow to dump 30–60% of its total heat loss through the beak, one of the largest heat-exchange 'thermal windows' relative to body size of any animal, rivaling an elephant's ears. Source: Tattersall, Andrade & Abe (2009), 'Heat Exchange from the Toucan Bill Reveals a Controllable Vascular Thermal Radiator,' Science 325:468–470.  (Legend.)

question: A tiny hunter of the leaf litter holds its two straight mouthparts locked wide open, then releases them to slam shut faster than almost any movement in the animal kingdom -- clocked closing at over 60 meters per second. Which creature is it?
answer: The trap-jaw ant
choices: The trap-jaw ant
The bombardier beetle
The tiger beetle
The whip spider
context: The trap-jaw ant (genus Odontomachus) cocks its huge straight mandibles wide open at a full 180 degrees, then snaps them shut in about 0.13 milliseconds -- roughly 35 to 64 m/s, over 60 m/s at the top end, one of the fastest movements known in any animal. Source: Patek, Baio, Fisher & Suarez 2006, PNAS 'Ballistic jaw propulsion in trap-jaw ants'; Patek Lab, Duke.  (Legend.)

question: Cornered by a predator, a trap-jaw ant does something startling with the very same jaws it hunts with: it aims them straight down and fires. What does this do for the ant?
answer: The recoil catapults its whole body backflipping into the air
choices: The recoil catapults its whole body backflipping into the air
It burrows into the soil to hide
It sprays a jet of stinging acid
It clamps onto the predator and holds on
context: The trap-jaw ant uses one structure two ways: a lethal snap-trap on prey and an ejector seat for itself. Firing the jaws against the ground, the recoil flings the ant about 8.3 cm (3.3 inches) up and backward -- over 20 times its body length, like a five-foot-six adult leaping 44 feet with a snap of the jaw. Source: Patek et al. 2006, PNAS; Larabee & Suarez, PLOS ONE 2015; National Geographic Kids 'Fastest jaw on the draw'.  (Legend.)

question: A trap-jaw ant hunts with its jaws cocked wide open, and the instant prey wanders between them the latch fires on its own -- the ant never has to aim. What on the inside of each open jaw tells the ant that prey has arrived?
answer: Rows of sensitive trigger hairs
choices: Rows of sensitive trigger hairs
A ring of tiny suction cups
A patch of light-sensing cells
A coating of sticky glue
context: Fine sensory hairs line the inside face of each open mandible and wire directly to the nerves that release the catch -- so the jaws fire the moment prey brushes them, no aiming required. Source: Wikipedia 'Odontomachus'; Patek Lab, Duke.

question: A trap-jaw ant snaps its jaws far faster than any muscle could ever pull them -- muscle alone is simply too slow. How does the ant move them at such impossible speed?
answer: It pre-loads spring energy behind a latch, then releases it all at once
choices: It pre-loads spring energy behind a latch, then releases it all at once
It grows the jaws lighter so they fall shut on their own
It uses jets of pressurized fluid to fling them
It relies on a whip-like flick of its antennae
context: The trap-jaw ant works like a loaded crossbow: it locks the open jaws with an internal latch, builds up spring energy in advance, and releases it in an instant. That stored-and-released spring energy lets the strike accelerate at roughly 100,000 times gravity -- a snap no muscle could ever match. Source: Patek Lab, Duke; Sheila Patek in NBC News 'Trap-jaw ant has world's fastest bite'.

question: A treehopper is a tiny sap-sucking insect, but what makes it look like a spiky alien is one body part blown up huge and sculpted into thorns, antlers, or a horned helmet arching over its back. What is that overgrown part called?
answer: the pronotum
choices: the pronotum
the mandible
the ovipositor
the abdomen
context: In treehoppers (family Membracidae), the pronotum -- normally a small plate on the top of the thorax -- balloons into an ornate helmet sculpted into thorns, antlers, horns, or spiky shapes, giving each species its own alien-looking headgear. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treehopper

question: A hungry bird hunts a plant stem for soft, juicy insects, but a whole cluster of treehoppers sitting right there in the open never catches its eye. What is it about these treehoppers that lets a bird's gaze slide past them?
answer: they line up in a row so they resemble the plant's own thorns
choices: they line up in a row so they resemble the plant's own thorns
their bodies are transparent, letting the green stem show through
they flatten against the bark and match its mottled brown color
they hang motionless underneath leaves like tiny curled buds
context: Many treehoppers are thorn mimics: lined up along a stem, a row of them looks exactly like the plant's own spines, hiding the insects in plain sight from birds. Source: https://biologyinsights.com/membracidae-a-look-at-bizarre-thorn-mimicking-insects/

question: Ants will swarm and defend a cluster of treehoppers like paid bodyguards, driving off ladybird beetles and other predators. What do the treehoppers hand over as payment for this protection?
answer: honeydew, a sweet liquid waste they dribble out
choices: honeydew, a sweet liquid waste they dribble out
tiny eggs the ants carry back to feed their grubs
shed skins the ants use to line their nest
a scent trail that guides the ants to new plants
context: Treehoppers suck sugary sap and excrete a sweet waste called honeydew. Ants farm them for it -- guarding the treehoppers from predators in exchange for the sugar, a classic mutualism. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2627810/ and https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982208007409

question: A treehopper's spiky helmet is part of its thorax, so biologist Cera Fisher expected thorax-building genes to switch on as it grows. Instead hundreds of genes lit up that build a structure found nowhere near the helmet. Which structure's genes turned out to grow it?
answer: the wings
choices: the wings
the legs
the eyes
the antennae
context: The treehopper's helmet is part of the thorax, but researcher Cera Fisher found hundreds of genes giving off a wing-like pattern as it grows, prompting her reaction: 'Oh my god, how did something like that evolve?' Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/treehoppers-bizarre-wondrous-helmets-use-wing-genes-grow-180973713/

question: A rhino-sized, four-legged plant-eater roamed the plains of Late Cretaceous North America, its face carrying a short horn on the nose and two long horns above the eyes, all set on a huge bony neck frill. What dinosaur was it?
answer: Triceratops
choices: Triceratops
Stegosaurus
Ankylosaurus
Iguanodon
context: Triceratops means 'three-horned face' -- a short nose horn plus two long brow horns on a big bony frill. Source: AMNH (amnh.org/exhibitions/permanent/ornithischian-dinosaurs/triceratops).

question: Triceratops was a hulking four-legged plant-eater about 26 to 30 feet long, built low and broad on stout legs. Roughly how heavy did the biggest ones get?
answer: 6 to 10 tons
choices: 6 to 10 tons
1 to 2 tons
20 to 30 tons
40 to 50 tons
context: Triceratops was rhino-shaped and built low and heavy, weighing 6-10 tons in Late Cretaceous North America. Source: National Geographic (nationalgeographic.com/animals/facts/triceratops-horridus).

question: Triceratops bones are famous for turning up in the very last layer of rock before the worldwide dinosaur die-off begins, right at the top of its range 66 million years ago. Scientists point to a single catastrophe that ended the world Triceratops lived in. What was it?
answer: A city-sized asteroid slammed into what is now Mexico
choices: A city-sized asteroid slammed into what is now Mexico
A slow ice age froze the plains over ten thousand years
Rising seas drowned the continents in one vast flood
A supernova exploded a few light-years from Earth
context: Triceratops lived right up to 66 million years ago, one of the very last dinosaurs, wiped out in the extinction after the Chicxulub asteroid struck what is now Mexico. Source: Wikipedia Triceratops; NatGeo.

question: Behind its sharp parrot-like beak, Triceratops ground down tough Cretaceous plants with columns of teeth stacked one behind another, so a worn tooth was always replaced from below. How many teeth did this grinding system hold at once?
answer: Up to 800
choices: Up to 800
About 60
Exactly 32
About a dozen
context: These stacked columns are called 'dental batteries' -- roughly 36-40 columns of 3-5 teeth each, up to 800 total, for grinding tough plants. Source: Wikipedia Triceratops; Animalia.bio.

question: Triceratops carried the largest skull known from any land animal that has ever lived -- so big it made up nearly one-third of the whole animal from beak-tip to tail. About how long was that skull?
answer: About 8 feet
choices: About 8 feet
About 8 inches
About 30 feet
About 2 feet
context: The Triceratops skull reached about 8 feet, the largest of any land animal ever, nearly a third of its body length. Source: Wikipedia Triceratops; AMNH.  (Legend.)

question: When paleontologists surveyed healed scars on ceratopsian skulls, they found the frill's squamosal bone carried far more old wounds in Triceratops than in the single-horned Centrosaurus. What best explains why the two-horned species racked up so many more frill scars?
answer: Triceratops regularly fought each other with their horns
choices: Triceratops regularly fought each other with their horns
The scars were T. rex bites, not horn wounds
The frill marks were birth deformities, not injuries
Triceratops horns were too soft to wound anything
context: Two-horned Triceratops racked up far more squamosal wounds than one-horned Centrosaurus -- the tell-tale sign of Triceratops jousting rivals of their own kind. Source: Farke, Wolff & Tanke 2009, PLoS ONE (PMC2617760).

question: A microprobe crawling across a fossil Triceratops tooth mapped five different tissues -- one of them a soft, blood-vessel-riddled dentine you would not expect in a grinding tooth. That soft strip turned out to be the whole trick. What did it do as the tooth wore down?
answer: It wore down faster than the rest, carving a groove that kept the tooth self-sharpening
choices: It wore down faster than the rest, carving a groove that kept the tooth self-sharpening
It flexed under the load, cushioning the tooth against gritty sand and stone
It funneled fresh blood to the crown to sense which plants were the toughest
It swelled with fluid to shove the next replacement tooth up into place
context: Erickson and colleagues (2015, Science Advances) dragged a diamond-tipped microprobe across Triceratops teeth and found FIVE distinct tissues -- enamel, hard mantle dentine, orthodentine, soft vasodentine, and coronal cementum -- one more than the four-tissue teeth of horses and bison, until then thought the most complex teeth evolution had ever produced. The blood-vessel-filled vasodentine wore about 1.6 times faster than the orthodentine beside it, so grinding gritty Cretaceous plants hollowed a recessed central channel -- a 'fuller,' the very same blood-groove ground into a sword or knife blade -- that kept a sharp slicing edge instead of grinding to a blunt nub. It is an actual mechanism for how the tooth batteries stayed sharp. Source: Erickson et al. 2015, Science Advances (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4640618/); Live Science summary (https://www.livescience.com/51108-triceratops-teeth.html).

question: The classic adult Triceratops carries two long brow horns that sweep forward over its beak. But when paleontologists lined up a growth series from a 38-centimeter hatchling skull to two-meter adults, they found the brow horns rebuilt themselves as the animal aged. On a young juvenile, which way did those brow horns point?
answer: Backward toward the frill, only recurving forward once it reached adulthood
choices: Backward toward the frill, only recurving forward once it reached adulthood
Straight upward at first, then folding flat against the skull with age
Forward already, just shorter and blunter than the adult pair
Downward past the beak, then lifting and lengthening as it grew
context: Horner and Goodwin (2006, Proceedings of the Royal Society B) assembled a growth series of ten skulls, from a 38-cm baby to roughly 2-m adults, and traced how the head remodeled through life. The postorbital (brow) horns began as straight little stubs, curved BACKWARD in juveniles, straightened out in subadults, then recurved FORWARD in adults. Meanwhile the frill margin, deeply scalloped in babies, sprouted 17-19 delta-shaped triangular bones (epoccipitals) that later flattened, elongated, and fused smoothly into its edge -- so a juvenile Triceratops looked strikingly unlike the forward-horned adult everyone pictures. Source: Horner & Goodwin 2006, Proc. R. Soc. B (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1635501/).

question: A hard-shelled creature crawls and burrows across the ancient Cambrian seafloor, its body a train of jointed armored segments over soft flesh and many legs. When scientists sort the trilobites into the tree of life, which great group of animals do they turn out to be?
answer: Arthropods
choices: Arthropods
Mollusks
Corals
Sponges
context: Trilobites were arthropods — the same great group as today's insects, crabs, and spiders. Hard-shelled, jointed-limbed sea creatures, they crawled, burrowed, and swam across the ancient ocean floor for hundreds of millions of years. Source: Natural History Museum, London — 'How trilobites conquered prehistoric oceans' (nhm.ac.uk).

question: Many Ordovician trilobites weren't smooth armored ovals at all. Their shells grew elaborate features that may have fended off predators — or kept the animal from sinking into the soft seafloor mud. What did these trilobites grow all over their shells?
answer: Long, sharp spines
choices: Long, sharp spines
A thick coat of fur
Rows of suction cups
A pair of grasping claws
context: Many trilobites, especially in the Ordovician, grew elaborate spines all over their shells — long spikes for defense, or possibly to keep from sinking into soft mud — turning the armored crawler into a walking pincushion. Source: Wikipedia 'Trilobite' (Lichida and spinose forms, Ordovician–Devonian).

question: A predator looms over a trilobite on the seafloor. The little animal's back is all hard shell, but its belly and legs are soft and exposed underneath. With no way to outrun the attacker, what did many trilobites do when threatened?
answer: Curled into a tight armored ball
choices: Curled into a tight armored ball
Buried straight down into the sand
Squirted a cloud of ink
Shed its legs to escape
context: When threatened, many trilobites rolled up into a tight ball — bending the thorax and tucking the tail beneath the head — exactly like a modern pillbug or woodlouse, hiding the soft underside behind the armored shell. Source: Natural History Museum, London (nhm.ac.uk); Oxford UMNH.

question: Trilobites came in wild sizes. The biggest, Isotelus rex, stretched over two feet from head to tail. The tiniest ever found, Acanthopleurella stipulae, sat at the far opposite end of that scale. About how big was that smallest trilobite?
answer: About 1.5 millimeters, smaller than a grain of rice
choices: About 1.5 millimeters, smaller than a grain of rice
About 2 centimeters, like a coin
About 10 centimeters, like a hand
About 30 centimeters, like a ruler
context: Trilobites ranged from giant to tiny: the largest known, Isotelus rex, reached about 72 cm (over 2 feet), while the smallest, Acanthopleurella stipulae, was just 1.5 mm — smaller than a grain of rice. Source: Wikipedia 'Trilobite' (Isotelus rex; Acanthopleurella stipulae).

question: Trilobites were fantastically successful — over 22,000 kinds are known — but paleontologists warn that trilobite 'fossils' badly overcount the animals. Why do so many trilobite fossils exist for every trilobite that ever lived?
answer: Each one shed many empty shells while alive
choices: Each one shed many empty shells while alive
They laid thousands of hard-shelled eggs
Their shells split into pieces after death
They lived crowded together in vast reefs
context: Like all arthropods, a trilobite grew by molting — splitting its old shell open along built-in weak lines (facial sutures) and crawling out. Because one animal shed many times in a lifetime, a huge number of trilobite 'fossils' are actually just empty cast-off shells, not dead animals. Source: NHM London; Oxford UMNH; PMC review on trilobite moulting.

question: Trilobites carried some of the first true complex eyes in the whole fossil record — the same mosaic, many-lensed design a bee or dragonfly uses today. But one thing those trilobite lenses were made of has no match in any animal alive. What were the lenses made of?
answer: Calcite — clear crystal, actual stone
choices: Calcite — clear crystal, actual stone
A soft transparent jelly
Thin sheets of chitin shell
A ring of tiny water droplets
context: Astonishingly, trilobite eye lenses were made of the mineral calcite — actual clear crystal, a stone lens set right in the head. They are the only animals known to have made their eyes out of rock. Their compound eyes stitched many separate lens units, called ommatidia, into a mosaic picture. Source: Beaty Biodiversity Museum, UBC — 'Trilobite Eyes Are Hard'; ScienceAlert.  (Legend.)

question: Trilobites first appear deep in the Cambrian and vanish at the end of the Permian. Their run was so long that, set beside it, our own genus Homo — barely 2 million years old — is little more than a blink. Roughly how long did trilobites rule the seas?
answer: Almost 270 million years
choices: Almost 270 million years
About 40 million years
About 90 million years
About 900 million years
context: Trilobites ruled the seas for almost 270 million years — from about 521 million years ago in the Cambrian until roughly 251 million years ago. For comparison, our own genus Homo is only about 2 million years old. Source: Wikipedia 'Trilobite'; Oxford University Museum of Natural History.

question: One Devonian trilobite, Erbenochile, carried a towering eye packed with hundreds of stone lenses in dozens of vertical rows, giving it a near-360-degree view around itself. Perched right on top of that eye-tower sat one more small structure. What was it?
answer: A shell rim shading the eye from above
choices: A shell rim shading the eye from above
A second eye facing backward
A pair of long feeler-antennae
A hollow snorkel-like tube
context: Erbenochile's tall eye held roughly 560 calcite lenses in 33-36 vertical rows, giving it a nearly 360-degree view at eye level — and a rim of shell projected over the top to block glare from light overhead. It was a fossil animal wearing its own visor. Source: Fortey & Chatterton, 'A Devonian Trilobite with an Eyeshade,' Science (2003).  (Legend.)

question: After ruling the oceans for 270 million years, every last trilobite disappeared about 251 million years ago in the end-Permian catastrophe, the 'Great Dying.' It was no ordinary die-off: of every kind of living thing in the sea and on land, how much did this single event erase?
answer: More than 90% of all species
choices: More than 90% of all species
About 10% of all species
About one-third of all species
About half of all species
context: After 270 million years, trilobites vanished completely in the end-Permian 'Great Dying' — the largest mass extinction in Earth's history, which killed more than 90% of all species on the planet. Not a single trilobite survived it. Source: Oxford University Museum of Natural History; Wikipedia 'Trilobite' (end-Permian extinction).  (Legend.)

question: A phacopid trilobite's calcite eye lens looks like one plain crystal blob, but 3-D modeling revealed it as two stacked units meeting at a precisely curved inner surface. That surface matched, in its exact geometry, a lens design Descartes and Huygens would each work out on paper only 400 million years later. What optical feat did the trilobite's built-in surface pull off?
answer: Focused every ray to one crisp point
choices: Focused every ray to one crisp point
Split white light into rainbow bands
Filtered out the sea's dim blue glow
Polarized the light to cut the glare
context: Those two designs are the only aberration-correcting lens shapes humans ever derived on paper — René Descartes in 1637 and Christiaan Huygens in 1690 — yet a phacopid grew the same aspherical calcite interface some 400 million years earlier, cancelling the blur (spherical aberration) that plagues a simple lens and driving light to a single sharp focus. Clarkson & Levi-Setti first matched the geometry (Nature 261:130, 1975, 'Trilobite eyes and the optics of Des Cartes and Huygens'); Lee, Torney & Owen later measured a real magnesium-concentration contrast between the two calcite units, chemical proof the doublet was genuine (Palaeontology 50:1031, 2007).  (Legend.)

question: Millions of trilobite shells sit in collections, yet no one had ever seen what a trilobite actually ate — the soft gut never survives. Then in 2023 a synchrotron scan looked inside a 465-million-year-old Bohemolichas and found its gut packed solid. What was crammed in there?
answer: Crushed shells of clams, ostracods, and shelled seafloor prey
choices: Crushed shells of clams, ostracods, and shelled seafloor prey
A soupy mush of filtered plankton and free-drifting algae
Soft marine worms tugged live from their muddy burrows
Films of bacteria scraped off the muddy seafloor bottom
context: It was the first trilobite ever found with its gut contents preserved — 3-D imaged by high-resolution synchrotron microtomography at the ESRF — despite the millions of trilobite fossils already known. The crushed shells mark Bohemolichas incola as an opportunistic durophage: a shell-crusher and scavenger that bolted small seafloor animals whole or in fragments. Tellingly, the swallowed shells were not etched by acid, so the team inferred a neutral-to-alkaline gut like a modern horseshoe crab or crustacean, not the acidic stomach of a vertebrate. Kraft, Vaškaninová, Mergl, Budil, Fatka & Ahlberg, Nature 622:545 (2023), 'Uniquely preserved gut contents illuminate trilobite palaeophysiology'.  (Legend.)

question: Back in the Jurassic, the tuatara's relatives — the rhynchocephalians — scurried underfoot among the dinosaurs across nearly every continent. Then the whole order vanished but for this one New Zealand holdout. What earned it its famous nickname?
answer: A living fossil, its lineage older than lizards
choices: A living fossil, its lineage older than lizards
A missing link, caught mid-change to a snake
A living rainbow, for its shifting colors
A living compass, for its unerring homing
context: The tuatara is the sole surviving member of an order that flourished 200 million years ago. Its lineage split off before lizards and snakes even existed. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); NZ Geographic, 'Tuatara — A survivor from the dinosaur age'.  (Legend.)

question: A ridge of tall, pointed spines runs down a tuatara's back, standing tallest on the males. When a male squares off against a rival on his patch of rock, what does he do with that crest?
answer: Flares it and inflates his body dark
choices: Flares it and inflates his body dark
Sheds it in a startling spray of spines
Snaps it flat and plays dead
Lights it up with glowing tips
context: The Māori name 'tuatara' means 'peaks on the back', describing the spiny crest down its spine — largest in males, who erect the crest and darken as they inflate the body during territorial display. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara).

question: On the crown of a tuatara hatchling's head sits a small pale patch, ringed by scales that slowly grow over it as the animal matures. Almost no other living reptile carries anything like the organ beneath it. What is this patch?
answer: A working third eye, with its own lens and retina
choices: A working third eye, with its own lens and retina
A heat-sensing pit that maps warm prey
A pressure gland that reads coming storms
A scent organ that tastes the air
context: The tuatara's parietal eye is a genuine third eye, complete with lens and light-sensitive retina, visible in hatchlings before scales cover it. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); Animal Diversity Web (Sphenodon punctatus).  (Legend.)

question: The tuatara's third eye, perched on the crown of its head, cannot form a picture of the world. Yet it earns its keep. Researchers think this organ works as a kind of natural compass the animal uses to set its inner clock and body temperature through the changing seasons. What kind of compass is it?
answer: A sun-compass, reading daylight
choices: A sun-compass, reading daylight
A magnetic compass, reading Earth's field
A star-compass, reading the night sky
A wind-compass, reading the breeze
context: The parietal eye is thought to act as a light sensor and sun-compass, tracking daylight to regulate the tuatara's circadian rhythms and temperature rather than forming images. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); 'The lonely eye', PMC/NIH.

question: Nearly every reptile basks in the sun to warm its body, and most thrive in real heat. The tuatara is the strange exception: it stays active in near-freezing cold and can barely tolerate a warm afternoon. Its preferred body temperature — the lowest of any reptile — sits at just what?
context: The tuatara prefers a body temperature of about 16–21°C — the lowest of any reptile — and stays active down to 5°C, overheating and dying above about 28°C. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); Animal Diversity Web (Sphenodon punctatus).  (Legend.)

question: A tuatara grows slowly for its first 35 years, then keeps going for decade after decade. At the Southland Museum, a captive male named Henry stunned his keepers not merely by surviving to a great age, but by doing something no one expects of so ancient an animal. What was Henry still doing past the age of 100?
answer: Fathering new offspring
choices: Fathering new offspring
Growing a fresh set of teeth
Regrowing a lost tail
Shedding his skin whole
context: Tuatara can live past 100. Henry, a captive male at the Southland Museum, was reported still breeding — fathering offspring — at age 111. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); Animal Diversity Web (Sphenodon punctatus).  (Legend.)

question: A two-legged meat-eater about 40 feet long, standing roughly 13 feet tall at the hip and weighing up to 8 tons, stalked western North America at the very end of the age of dinosaurs, 66 million years ago. Which dinosaur was it?
answer: Tyrannosaurus rex
choices: Tyrannosaurus rex
Triceratops horridus
Stegosaurus ungulatus
Brachiosaurus altithorax
context: Tyrannosaurus rex means 'tyrant lizard king.' It stood roughly 13 feet tall at the hip and could weigh up to about 8 tons, living at the very end of the age of dinosaurs, 68 to 66 million years ago. Source: Australian Museum fact sheet, https://australian.museum/learn/dinosaurs/fact-sheets/tyrannosaurus-rex/

question: The skull of Tyrannosaurus rex housed roughly 60 teeth and the heavy jaw muscles for a bone-crushing bite. Roughly how long was that skull, from the snout tip to the back of the head?
answer: About 5 feet (1.5 m)
choices: About 5 feet (1.5 m)
About 1 foot (0.3 m)
About 15 feet (4.5 m)
About 2 inches (5 cm)
context: A T. rex skull was about 1.5 meters (5 feet) long, roughly as long as a grown person is tall, and carried around 60 teeth. A head that size gave the animal room for the bone-crushing jaw muscles that made it such a fearsome predator. Source: Australian Museum fact sheet, https://australian.museum/learn/dinosaurs/fact-sheets/tyrannosaurus-rex/

question: People picture a meat-eater's teeth as thin, knife-like blades, but the back teeth of Tyrannosaurus rex broke that expectation completely. What were those teeth shaped like?
answer: Thick and banana-shaped
choices: Thick and banana-shaped
Flat and shovel-shaped
Long and needle-thin
Curved like a comb
context: The back teeth of T. rex were thick and banana-shaped, not thin blades. The largest reached about 20 to 30 cm (8 to 12 inches) long including the root, and were built to withstand struggling prey and crush bone. Source: Extinct Atlas T. rex skull guide, https://extinctatlas.org/species-guide/tyrannosaurus-rex-skull-and-teeth/

question: When a Tyrannosaurus rex bit down hard on a struggling animal, one of its 60 teeth might snap off in the fight. What happened to the gap left behind in the jaw?
answer: A fresh tooth grew in to replace it
choices: A fresh tooth grew in to replace it
The jaw sealed the socket shut for good
A neighboring tooth slid over to fill it
The gum hardened into a bony ridge
context: T. rex replaced its teeth throughout its life. If a tooth broke off while feeding, a new tooth grew in to take its place, so the animal never ran short of weapons. Source: Australian Museum / Extinct Atlas, https://extinctatlas.org/species-guide/tyrannosaurus-rex-skull-and-teeth/

question: When Tyrannosaurus rex clamped down on a struggling Triceratops, its jaws drove down with a force paleontologists later reconstructed from tooth marks and jaw-muscle anatomy. Roughly how hard was that bite?
answer: About 8,000 pounds
choices: About 8,000 pounds
About 3,000 pounds
About 5,500 pounds
About 12,000 pounds
context: T. rex bit with a force of about 8,000 pounds, nearly 3.6 tonnes, the strongest bite of any known land animal. The pointed tips of its teeth could focus pressures up to about 431,000 pounds per square inch, enough to pulverize bone. Source: Gignac & Erickson, Scientific Reports 2017, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-017-02161-w

question: In 1998 Karen Chin described a record-breaking 15-pound fossil from Saskatchewan, the largest specimen of its kind ever found, left behind by a Tyrannosaurus rex. What was this famous find?
answer: Fossilized dung packed with crushed bone
choices: Fossilized dung packed with crushed bone
A jawbone with a tooth still lodged in it
A footprint pressed deep into old mud
A nest of eggs with unhatched young
context: The 15-pound (7 kg) T. rex coprolite, or fossilized dung, from Saskatchewan was packed with crushed fragments of a young plant-eating dinosaur's bones, proving T. rex swallowed bone. It is the largest meat-eater dropping ever found. Source: Karen Chin et al., Nature 1998, 'A king-sized theropod coprolite', https://www.nature.com/articles/31461

question: Casts of the Tyrannosaurus rex braincase reveal that one region devoted to a single sense was proportionally among the largest of any known dinosaur. Which sense was T. rex especially built for?
answer: Smell
choices: Smell
Hearing
Touch
Taste
context: The olfactory bulbs, the part of the brain handling smell, were proportionally enormous in T. rex, among the largest of any known dinosaur. It likely could detect carcasses or blood from far away. Source: AMNH, 'How Superior Senses Helped T. rex Hunt', https://www.amnh.org/explore/news-blogs/t-rex-super-senses

question: Tyrannosaurus rex is famous for the mismatch between its huge body and its stubby forelimbs, which ended in an unusual number of fingers. How many fingers did each tiny arm have?
answer: Two
choices: Two
Three
Five
Four
context: Each T. rex arm ended in just two fingers, while most of its relatives had three. The arm bones show the limbs were thick and muscular, but what T. rex actually used them for, pushing up off the ground, gripping prey, or mating, is still debated. Source: Natural History Museum, https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/how-did-tyrannosaurus-use-its-arms.html

question: Growth rings in the bones of Tyrannosaurus rex act like tree rings, marking each year of life. They reveal that between about ages 14 and 18 the animal did something dramatic. What did the rings record?
answer: A teenage growth spurt packing on pounds daily
choices: A teenage growth spurt packing on pounds daily
A long stretch of near-starvation and shrinking
A slow, steady gain across its whole lifespan
A sudden stop in growth in its earliest years
context: Growth rings show T. rex bulked up in a teenage growth spurt from about age 14 to 18, packing on roughly 4.6 pounds (about 2 kg) a day at its peak and adding most of its adult weight in just a few years. Source: Erickson et al.; Science News 'Growth Spurt', https://www.sciencenews.org/article/growth-spurt-teenage-tyrannosaurs-packed-pounds

question: Tyrannosaurus rex had a 30-foot tyrant cousin named Yutyrannus, announced in 2012, whose fossils preserved a soft-tissue feature that hints parts of T. rex may have looked different from the bare-scaled giant people usually picture. What did Yutyrannus preserve?
answer: Down-like feathery filaments
choices: Down-like feathery filaments
A fleshy throat pouch
A brightly color-banded skin patch
A dangling skin wattle
context: Yutyrannus, a roughly 30-foot feathered tyrannosaur, was found with down-like filaments, which is why scientists suspect parts of T. rex may have had a sparse feathery covering. Direct T. rex skin impressions found so far show scales, so full feathering is not settled. Source: AMNH Yutyrannus, https://www.amnh.org/explore/news-blogs/yutyrannus-huali-feathered-tyrannosaur  (Legend.)

question: In 1990 a fossil hunter spotted bones weathering out of a cliff near Faith, South Dakota, and uncovered a Tyrannosaurus rex nicknamed SUE. What makes SUE so prized by scientists?
answer: It is about 90 percent complete
choices: It is about 90 percent complete
It is the smallest T. rex on record
It was the first ever dug up
It still had skin covering the bones
context: SUE, nicknamed after fossil hunter Sue Hendrickson, is about 90 percent complete and over 40 feet long, one of the most complete T. rex skeletons ever found. SUE sold at auction in 1997 for $8.3 million and is now displayed at the Field Museum in Chicago. Source: Field Museum, https://www.fieldmuseum.org/blog/sue-t-rex  (Legend.)

question: In 2005 Mary Schweitzer found soft, still-flexible tissue inside a 68-million-year-old Tyrannosaurus rex thigh bone. Two years later she and John Asara sequenced surviving collagen protein from it and compared its amino-acid chain to living animals. Which creature's protein turned out to be the closest match?
answer: A chicken
choices: A chicken
A crocodile
An ostrich
An iguana
context: That 2007 result, published in Science, was the first time anyone had read a dinosaur's actual protein rather than just its bone shape -- and the recovered amino-acid sequence lined up with birds, matching chicken most closely of all. It was molecular confirmation of what the skeletons already suggested: birds are living theropod dinosaurs, so T. rex is far nearer kin to a barnyard hen than to any crocodile or lizard. The femur was specimen MOR 1125, nicknamed 'B-rex.' Sources: Schweitzer, Asara et al., Science 316:277-280 (2007), https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1138709 ; summary https://phys.org/news/2007-04-soft-tissue-million-year-old-tyrannosaurus-rex.html  (Legend.)

question: A small bat of Latin America is one of only three mammals on Earth that eats nothing but one food for its entire life. What is the only thing on this bat's menu?
answer: Blood
choices: Blood
Fruit
Insects
Nectar
context: The common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus) is one of just three mammal species that live entirely on blood. It doesn't suck it like the movies show -- it presses its grooved lower lip and tongue to a small cut and laps, like a cat at a bowl of milk. Source: Wikipedia, Vampire bat; HowStuffWorks 'Meet the Real Vampires of the Animal Kingdom'.

question: A vampire bat lands near a sleeping cow in total darkness and needs the one spot where blood runs closest under the skin. Three pit organs around its nose let it find that spot by sensing what?
answer: The heat radiating off the animal
choices: The heat radiating off the animal
The animal's heartbeat vibrations
The smell of the blood vessels
The faint sound of blood flowing
context: Three pit organs around the nose, called leaf pits, sense warmth radiating off a warm-blooded animal from as far as 20 centimeters away, letting the bat aim for the exact spot where blood runs closest to the surface. Source: Nature news 2011; National Geographic 'Vampire Bats Have Vein Sensors'; Wikipedia, Infrared sensing in vampire bats.

question: A vampire bat bites a sleeping tapir and the animal never stirs. Its upper incisors slice a clean nick because those teeth have an unusual trait -- what makes them so keen?
answer: They lack enamel and stay razor-sharp
choices: They lack enamel and stay razor-sharp
They inject a numbing venom first
They are coated in a slick oil
They vibrate rapidly like a saw
context: The upper incisors are so sharp and lack enamel that they slice a tiny cut without waking the animal, and they're self-sharpening. Museum workers have cut themselves just handling vampire-bat skulls. Source: Wikipedia, Vampire bat; DentisX 'The Specialized Teeth of Vampire Bats for Blood Feeding'.

question: A vampire bat laps at a tiny nick on a sleeping cow for a full 20 minutes, and the little wound never seals the way an ordinary scratch would. What in the bat lets a meal last that long?
answer: A chemical in its saliva that blocks the blood from clotting
choices: A chemical in its saliva that blocks the blood from clotting
A grip that keeps the two teeth wedged in the skin
A tongue that scrapes away each new clot
A body heat that keeps the blood warm and thin
context: The bat's saliva holds an anticoagulant nicknamed 'draculin' that blocks clotting, so the little cut keeps bleeding while the bat laps for up to 20 minutes. Source: Wikipedia, Draculin; MDPI Toxins 'Vampire Venom' (PMC6356263).  (Legend.)

question: Most of the world's 1,300-plus kinds of bat can only crawl clumsily on the ground. The common vampire bat does something no other bat can. On the ground, what can it uniquely do?
answer: Run, galloping along the ground
choices: Run, galloping along the ground
Swim across small streams
Dig burrows to hide in
Leap straight up ten times its height
context: Out of more than 1,300 bat species, only the common vampire bat can run. It gallops with a bounding gait that uses its powerful wings, not its legs, to push off the ground -- one scientist called it 'kind of like running push-ups.' Source: Riskin & Hermanson, Nature (2005); Science 'Vampires Run'.  (Legend.)

question: Cornell researchers put vampire bats on a treadmill and sped the belt up to settle whether the bat truly runs or only shuffles fast. On the high-speed film, what did the bat do that no other bat does?
answer: Leave the ground completely between strides
choices: Leave the ground completely between strides
Fold its wings and sprint on its hind legs
Grip the moving belt with hooked thumbs
Somersault forward to keep up the pace
context: On a treadmill vampire bats walk on all fours at slow speeds, but at about 1.8 km/h they break into a true run, leaving the ground completely between strides. Cornell researchers filmed them in a plexiglass cage to prove it. Source: Riskin & Hermanson, Nature (2005); Cornell Daily Sun (2005).

question: A 40-gram vampire bat can gulp over 20 grams of blood in one meal -- a third of its own weight -- so much it would be too heavy to fly home. Within two minutes of feeding, how does it lighten its load?
answer: It pees out the watery part right at the wound
choices: It pees out the watery part right at the wound
It coughs up the extra to a waiting roost-mate
It rests until the meal digests down
It clings to the prey and waits till dawn
context: A gorged bat would be too heavy to fly, so it starts peeing out the watery part of the blood within two minutes of feeding, right there at the wound. Source: Wikipedia, Vampire bat; Bohn et al., kidney physiology (PMC/PubMed 12010738).

question: A vampire bat that misses just three nights of feeding will die of starvation. When one bat comes home hungry and empty, a well-fed roost-mate keeps it alive by doing what?
answer: Throwing up part of its own blood meal into the hungry bat's mouth
choices: Throwing up part of its own blood meal into the hungry bat's mouth
Leading the hungry bat back to a fresh wound
Wrapping its wings around it to keep it warm
Sharing the warmest sleeping spot in the roost
context: A vampire bat dies after about 70 hours without a meal -- roughly three missed nights. A bat that fed well will regurgitate part of its meal into the mouth of a hungry roost-mate, giving up a little to save a friend's life. Source: Wilkinson (1984); Scientific American 'Blood Sisters'; Carter & Wilkinson (PMC3574350).  (Legend.)

question: Vampire bats share life-saving blood, and scientists watched 950 sharing bouts to learn what decides who a hungry bat will feed. One factor stood out far above the rest -- which one?
answer: Whether that bat had fed IT before
choices: Whether that bat had fed IT before
How closely the two bats were related
Which bat was physically largest
How loudly the hungry bat begged
context: Across 950 sharing bouts, the best predictor of which bat a hungry bat fed was who had fed it before -- 8.5 times more important than relatedness. Vampire bats keep score, remembering who shared and paying it back. Source: Carter & Wilkinson (PMC3574350).  (Legend.)

question: A small, dark, gelatinous animal drifts in the deep ocean, its eight arms joined by a webbed cloak and its skin a deep blood-red. Despite this cape and its fearsome scientific name meaning 'from hell,' what does this creature actually eat?
answer: Drifting flakes of dead matter it collects while floating
choices: Drifting flakes of dead matter it collects while floating
Live fish it chases down and drains of blood
Warm mammal blood, like the bat it is named for
Coral polyps it scrapes off the reef with its beak
context: The vampire squid (Vampyroteuthis infernalis) is the only cephalopod that does not chase living prey. It drifts in the deep and collects 'marine snow' — drifting flakes of dead matter. The scary name comes from its blood-red skin and cloak-like webbing, not its gentle habits. Source: Hoving & Robison 2012, MBARI news release (mbari.org).

question: The vampire squid is only about 15 centimeters long — roughly the length of your hand. Yet one of its features is famous for being, in proportion to body size, the largest of any animal on Earth. Which feature?
answer: Its globe-shaped eyes, each about 2.5 cm across
choices: Its globe-shaped eyes, each about 2.5 cm across
Its beak, sharp enough to crack open shellfish
Its brain, unusually large for a sea creature
Its webbed cloak, which can span a full meter
context: In a squid only about 6 inches long, the globe-shaped eyes are roughly 2.5 cm (1 inch) across — proportionately the largest eyes in the animal kingdom. They are huge to catch the faintest glimmer of deep-sea light. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid.  (Legend.)

question: When a predator closes in on a vampire squid, the squid flips its webbed arms up and back over its own head, turning itself almost inside out into a spiny ball that hides its soft body and points fleshy spines outward at the attacker. What do scientists call this defensive shape?
answer: The 'pineapple posture'
choices: The 'pineapple posture'
The 'artichoke fold'
The 'acorn ball'
The 'walnut curl'
context: Turning inside out into this spiny defensive shape — also called the 'pumpkin posture' — hides the vampire squid's vulnerable body and points its fleshy spines (cirri) outward at the attacker. It is the animal's signature move. Source: MBARI Animals of the Deep; Wikipedia: Vampire squid.  (Legend.)

question: Most squids escape danger by firing a black cloud of ink to hide behind. The vampire squid lives in permanent darkness where a black cloud would do nothing. So when a predator attacks, what does it release instead?
answer: A glowing cloud of bioluminescent mucus
choices: A glowing cloud of bioluminescent mucus
A jet of icy water to numb the attacker
A spray of stinging venom from its arm tips
A burst of bubbles that blinds the hunter
context: The vampire squid has no ink sac at all — ink is useless in its lightless world. Instead it squirts a glowing cloud of bioluminescent mucus full of blue light orbs to dazzle predators, a dazzling display that can last nearly 10 minutes. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid; MBARI.  (Legend.)

question: The vampire squid never swims after food. It hangs motionless and pays out two thin, sticky fishing threads to catch drifting scraps. A diver might expect these threads to reach an arm's length or so — but each one unspools far past that. How far can a single feeding thread stretch?
answer: Up to eight times the length of its own body
choices: Up to eight times the length of its own body
About half the length of its own body
Roughly the same length as its own body
Up to twice the length of its own body
context: It catches food on two long, sticky, retractable filaments that can stretch up to eight times its body length, then wipes the loaded thread back through its arms to eat. Source: MBARI news release on Hoving & Robison 2012 (mbari.org).

question: 'Marine snow' sounds pretty, but the vampire squid's meal is really made of the ocean's leftovers. Scientists bluntly describe this drifting food as a mixture of three things. Which three?
answer: Dead bodies, poop, and snot
choices: Dead bodies, poop, and snot
Salt crystals, sand, and foam
Live plankton, eggs, and larvae
Seaweed, shells, and pebbles
context: Marine snow is remains of tiny algae and animals, fecal pellets from copepods and krill, and mucus debris from gelatinous larvaceans — dead bodies, poop, and snot. Source: MBARI / Hoving & Robison 2012 (mbari.org).

question: In 1903 the German scientist Carl Chun hauled a strange deep-sea creature up in his nets and gave it the Latin name Vampyroteuthis infernalis. What did he base that dramatic name on?
answer: Its blood-red skin and cloak-like webbing
choices: Its blood-red skin and cloak-like webbing
Its habit of draining blood from fish
The bat-shaped fins on its head
The way it shrieks when pulled from the water
context: Vampyroteuthis infernalis literally means 'vampire squid from hell.' The teuthologist Carl Chun named it in 1903 for its dark blood-red skin and cloak-like webbing — not for its habits, which are gentle. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid.

question: The vampire squid makes its permanent home in a deep band of ocean, between roughly 600 and 900 meters down, that almost every other animal avoids and cannot survive in. What one deadly condition of this band does the vampire squid tolerate that its would-be predators cannot?
answer: Oxygen drops as low as 3 percent saturation
choices: Oxygen drops as low as 3 percent saturation
The water pressure crushes bone instantly
Freezing temperatures turn the water to slush
Toxic gas bubbles up from vents on the seafloor
context: This band is called the 'oxygen minimum zone.' The vampire squid lives there permanently, surviving where oxygen saturation drops as low as 3 percent — an environment so hostile that few predators can follow it there. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid; MBARI (Hoving).

question: A hungry predator bites off the glowing tip of a vampire squid's arm and swims off with its prize — yet the squid loses almost nothing. Why is the bitten-off arm tip such a clever loss?
answer: It keeps flashing as a decoy while the tip regrows
choices: It keeps flashing as a decoy while the tip regrows
It releases venom into the predator's mouth
It was already dead tissue the squid was shedding
It signals nearby squid to swarm the attacker
context: The vampire squid's body is dotted with light organs (photophores). If a predator bites off a glowing arm tip, the tip keeps flashing as a decoy while the squid escapes — and the arm tip grows back. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid; Animal Diversity Web.

question: The vampire squid is the sole survivor of an ancient order, Vampyromorphida, and biologists call it a 'living fossil.' What makes its place on the family tree so strange?
answer: It shares traits with octopuses and squids but is neither
choices: It shares traits with octopuses and squids but is neither
It is the direct ancestor of the modern octopus
It is the only cephalopod without a beak or arms
It evolved from a fish that lost its bones
context: The vampire squid is the only surviving member of the order Vampyromorphida, an ancient cephalopod lineage. It shares traits with both octopuses and squids while being neither — a true living fossil. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid; marine-biology sources.  (Legend.)

question: The modern vampire squid chases nothing — it drifts and dabs up marine snow. But its 164-million-year-old Jurassic ancestor, scanned in 3D by a synchrotron X-ray, left behind two elongated arms whose fine detail revealed a very different way of life. What did those arms carry?
answer: Rows of muscular suckers for gripping live prey
choices: Rows of muscular suckers for gripping live prey
Sticky threads for gathering drifting flakes of food
Rows of glowing organs to lure prey closer
Curved hooks for snagging small passing fish
context: The fossil is Vampyronassa rhodanica, a roughly 10-cm cephalopod from the 164-million-year-old La Voulte-sur-Rhône deposit in France. Rowe and colleagues (Scientific Reports, 2022) used synchrotron X-ray microtomography on its exceptionally 3D-preserved soft tissue, revealing robust muscular suckers on two elongated dorsal arms — forming a watertight suction seal — plus sensory appendages for detecting prey. That marks it as an active hunter, in sharp contrast to the modern vampire squid's low-energy life scavenging marine snow. Source: Rowe et al., Scientific Reports (2022), nature.com/articles/s41598-022-12269-3; via Sci.News (sci.news/paleontology/vampyronassa-rhodanica-10934.html) and ScienceDaily.

question: Early naturalists once catalogued the vampire squid as several separate species — a hatchling and an adult barely resemble each other. The oddest transformation involves its fins. As the mantle grows past about two centimeters, how do its fins change?
answer: A new pair sprouts up front and the old pair is absorbed
choices: A new pair sprouts up front and the old pair is absorbed
The single pair splits lengthwise, leaving it with four
The fins fuse into one broad fin ringing the mantle
The fins are pulled inside and it jets like a young squid
context: Juvenile vampire squid have a single pair of fins and swim by jet propulsion. When the mantle reaches about 15–25 mm long, a second pair of fins develops farther forward (anterior); once the new pair matures, the original pair is reabsorbed, and the animal switches to swimming by flapping its fins. Because it looks so different at each stage, early naturalists mistakenly described the life stages as separate species. Source: Animal Diversity Web (animaldiversity.org/accounts/Vampyroteuthis_infernalis); corroborated by Wikipedia, 'Vampire squid'.

question: A stick insect (order Phasmatodea) is long, thin, and brown, and vanishes among the branches of a bush. But it does one extra thing with its BODY that a real twig would do in the wind. What is it?
answer: It rocks and sways gently from side to side
choices: It rocks and sways gently from side to side
It curls up tightly into a hard ball
It buries itself in the loose soil below
It spins a sticky web between two leaves
context: Many stick insects sway as they walk or rest, mimicking a real twig or leaf trembling in the breeze — so even their MOVEMENT doesn't give them away. Source: Wikipedia, Phasmatodea ('swaying' behavioural crypsis).

question: A ptarmigan is a plump mountain grouse that lives where deep snow buries the ground for half the year. In winter its feathers are pure snowy white; in summer they turn mottled brown. What flips the switch between the two coats each year, right on schedule?
answer: The number of daylight hours
choices: The number of daylight hours
The temperature of the air
The first snowfall of the season
The food it finds to eat
context: The change is triggered by DAY LENGTH, not temperature — so the timing is the same every year even when snow comes early or late, which can leave a half-turned bird briefly mismatched. Source: Audubon Field Guide, Rock Ptarmigan; Alaska Dept. Fish & Game.

question: A leaf insect (order Phasmatodea) copies a leaf so exactly it has fake veins running through its flat green body and ragged brown edges. It even wears one detail that makes it look USED rather than a fresh perfect leaf. What is that finishing touch?
answer: Fake chewed-out bite marks and blemishes
choices: Fake chewed-out bite marks and blemishes
A row of bright warning eyespots
A dusting of glittering silver scales
A pair of long trailing feelers
context: The insect mimics a leaf a caterpillar already chewed on — a perfect, unblemished leaf would actually look MORE suspicious than a battered one. Source: Australian Museum, Leaf and Stick Insects (Phasmatodea).

question: An octopus resting on a reef can make its normally smooth skin erupt into a bumpy, ragged, three-dimensional surface — looking just like the seaweed and coral around it — then flatten out again to swim off. Roughly how FAST can it throw up those muscly bumps?
answer: In about a fifth of a second
choices: In about a fifth of a second
In about ten minutes
Over the course of a full day
Only once, permanently, as it grows up
context: The bumps are muscle-driven skin projections called papillae; the octopus pushes them up in about 0.2 seconds and can hold them or drop them at will. Source: Scientific American, octopus 3-D camouflage; PMC6059360, Neural Control of Dynamic 3-D Skin Papillae.

question: A decorator crab (family Majidae) doesn't just match the reef — it BUILDS its disguise onto its own shell. Its back is covered in tiny hooked bristles that grab like Velcro. What does the crab stick onto those hooks?
answer: Living sponges, algae, and stinging anemones
choices: Living sponges, algae, and stinging anemones
Flat pebbles it glues down with mucus
Shed scales borrowed from passing fish
A hard crust of dried salt and sand
context: The crab plucks bits of the reef and presses them onto its hooked bristles — anemones even add stinging defense — and can swap the decorations out as it moves to new ground. Source: Smithsonian Ocean, Decorator Crab; Wikipedia, Decorator crab.

question: A stonefish (genus Synanceia) lies so still on the reef, looking exactly like an algae-covered rock, that it can get overgrown and disappear entirely. That stillness hides a nasty surprise. What happens the instant something steps on it?
answer: Thirteen back spines fire venom automatically
choices: Thirteen back spines fire venom automatically
It inflates into a spiky ball of armor
It bites down with rows of curved fangs
It squirts a cloud of blinding black ink
context: The stonefish is the world's most venomous fish: 13 hollow dorsal spines inject venom driven purely by the pressure of the foot pressing down — no decision needed. Source: Wikipedia, Synanceia; HowStuffWorks, Stonefish.

question: In a cuttlefish's skin, every tiny pigment sac is a whole machine: its own ring of muscles yanks it open, and its own private nerve line runs straight back to the brain. Given that each sac needs all that gear, how many are crammed into a single patch of skin just one millimeter square?
answer: Around 200 of them
choices: Around 200 of them
Around 5 of them
Around 20 of them
Just a single large one
context: These pigment sacs are called chromatophores, and they're packed up to about 200 per square millimeter — each with its own muscles and its own nerve line — which is how a cuttlefish can 'paint' finely detailed patterns across its skin. Source: Roger Hanlon, National Geographic; PMC3403426, chromatophore density.

question: A flounder is a flatfish that settles flat on the seabed. In one famous lab test, scientists dropped a flounder onto a black-and-white CHECKERBOARD floor and watched its skin. What happened within about a minute?
answer: It broke into dark and light blotches copying the squares
choices: It broke into dark and light blotches copying the squares
It settled on a single grey average of the whole board
It flashed rippling stripes across its back
It darkened uniformly to a flat solid tone
context: The flounder's skin broke into dark and light blotches roughly matching the checkerboard — a striking demonstration of background-matching against an unnatural pattern, rather than just averaging or flashing. Source: American Museum of Natural History; Royal Society Open Science, flounder background-matching study.

question: Look at a shark, a deer, or a penguin: dark on the back, pale on the belly. Sunlight pours down from ABOVE, so a rounded animal casts a dark shadow across its own underside that betrays its solid 3-D shape. How does painting the belly paler defeat that shadow?
answer: The paler belly reflects light back to fill the shadow to an even tone
choices: The paler belly reflects light back to fill the shadow to an even tone
The dark back soaks up the sunlight before it can cast a shadow
The dark-pale boundary sits where a predator's eye locks, pulling the gaze off
The pale belly matches the bright surface above, erasing it from below
context: This is countershading: the naturally-shaded belly is painted paler so it reflects light back and fills in its own shadow, leaving the body one even tone that reads as flat and un-solid instead of a spottable 3-D shape. The other options are real tricks other animals use — heat-absorbing dark backs, disruptive edge patterns, mirror-belly matching the surface from below — but none is how countershading works. Source: Wikipedia, Countershading ('Thayer's law'); The Conversation, dark backs and pale bellies.

question: The satanic leaf-tailed gecko (Uroplatus phantasticus) of Madagascar looks like a dead leaf come to life. Its flat tail is notched, fake-veined, and ragged like something half-rotted. But one more feature erases the tell-tale line where a body meets the ground. What does the gecko have that blurs its outline?
answer: Fringes of skin along its edges
choices: Fringes of skin along its edges
A coat of loose downy fur
A shell of overlapping hard plates
A trailing cloud of fine bubbles
context: Skin fringes break up the gecko's silhouette against the forest floor, so predators can't find the crisp edge that would betray an animal. Source: Wikipedia, Uroplatus phantasticus; Smithsonian National Zoo, Phantastic Leaf-tailed Gecko.

question: The mimic octopus (Thaumoctopus mimicus) of the Indo-Pacific goes beyond blending in — it IMPERSONATES venomous animals to scare off predators. When it tucks six arms into its burrow and waves the other two, which deadly reef creature is it copying?
answer: A banded sea snake
choices: A banded sea snake
A stinging box jellyfish
A bristling stonefish
A venomous cone snail
context: By tucking six arms and trailing two, the octopus mimics a banded sea snake — all four choices name genuinely venomous reef animals, but the two-armed, striped display copies the snake. It also splays its arms to imitate a spiny lionfish and flattens all eight to glide like a flatfish, swapping impersonations to match whatever predator is near. Source: Wikipedia, Mimic octopus; ScienceDaily, flatfish mimicry study.

question: A cuttlefish's pigment sacs can only make a limited palette — there are shades they simply can't mix. Yet the animal still matches those colors, using a hidden second layer of skin beneath the pigment. What trick does that under-layer use to fill in a shade the pigments can't make?
answer: Mirror-like cells bounce back whatever light is around
choices: Mirror-like cells bounce back whatever light is around
It slowly grows fresh pigment to order over minutes
It borrows dye absorbed from the food it eats
It bends its whole body to catch a different angle
context: By pulling the top pigment sacs aside, the cuttlefish lets reflective under-layer cells — iridophores and white leucophores — throw back the surrounding light, filling in colors the pigments alone can't produce, and matching a shade it may not even be able to see. Source: Nature Scitable, Cephalopod Camouflage.

question: Here is the deep puzzle of the cuttlefish: with just ONE kind of light-sensor in its eye it should be colorblind, yet it matches the colors around it in about a second. Scientists haven't settled how — so what is one leading explanation they are actively testing?
answer: It reads color from how its oddly-shaped pupil blurs the light
choices: It reads color from how its oddly-shaped pupil blurs the light
It memorizes a fixed color from one bright dawn each day
It was found to grow a second light-sensor as an adult
It simply copies the nearest cuttlefish's color guess
context: Genuinely unsettled research: with one sensor the cuttlefish should be colorblind, so scientists debate whether it matches BRIGHTNESS instead of hue, or 'reads' color from the way its oddly-shaped pupil blurs different wavelengths (chromatic aberration) — the question is still open. Source: PNAS 2016, Spectral discrimination in color blind animals via chromatic aberration and pupil shape; PNAS 2011, hyperspectral imaging of cuttlefish camouflage.  (Legend.)

question: Everyone assumes a chameleon changes color by shuffling pigment through its skin. But a panther chameleon (Furcifer pardalis) gets its calm green from a deep layer of cells holding tiny guanine crystals in a tidy lattice. When an excited male flushes yellow-orange in seconds, no new pigment appears at all. What did 2015 imaging catch it doing to that crystal lattice?
answer: It stretches the lattice so its crystals sit farther apart
choices: It stretches the lattice so its crystals sit farther apart
It grinds the crystals down into a much finer, denser powder
It swivels each crystal to face straight into the bright sun
It dissolves the crystals and regrows them in a fresh new shape
context: The 2015 study (Teyssier, Saenko, van der Marel & Milinkovitch, 'Photonic crystals cause active colour change in chameleons,' Nature Communications 6:6368) overturned the old 'pigment disperses' story. In a calm chameleon the guanine nanocrystals sit packed close together, and the lattice reflects short blue-green wavelengths, so the skin looks green. When the animal gets excited it actively spreads that lattice apart -- crystal-to-crystal spacing widens by about 30% -- which shifts the reflected light to long yellow/orange/red wavelengths and turns the skin orange in seconds. So the color change is a living photonic crystal being tuned, not a pigment shuffle. Corroborated by the University of Geneva press release (unige.ch) and Science news; open-access via PMC4366488. (Grokipedia checked first, returned HTTP 403.)  (Legend.)

question: A glass frog (Hyalinobatrachium fleischmanni) has see-through skin -- superb camouflage, except its blood is bright red and ought to glow through like a warning light. Yet when the frog settles onto a leaf to sleep by day, it turns two to three times MORE transparent than when awake. How does it hide its telltale red blood?
answer: It packs most of its red blood cells into its mirror-lined liver
choices: It packs most of its red blood cells into its mirror-lined liver
It swaps the red pigment in its blood for a clear, colorless kind
It drains its blood down into its dark and opaque hind legs
It floods its body with clear fluid to dilute the red away
context: The 2022 study (Taboada et al., 'Glassfrogs conceal blood in their liver to maintain transparency,' Science 378:1315-1320) found that a sleeping glass frog pulls roughly 89% of its red blood cells out of circulation and packs them into its liver, whose mirror-like reflective coating keeps the stashed blood from showing. Emptying the red out of its see-through parts makes the frog two to three times more transparent; when it wakes and needs to move, it sends the red cells back into the bloodstream. Researchers mapped where the hidden blood went using photoacoustic imaging -- a green laser makes the packed red cells emit ultrasound. Corroborated by the NIH/NIBIB newsroom and Duke Pratt School of Engineering news. (Grokipedia checked first, returned HTTP 403.)  (Legend.)

question: Jurassic Park showed Velociraptor as a man-sized monster taller than a person. The real Velociraptor of Mongolia was actually about the size of what farmyard bird?
answer: A turkey
choices: A turkey
An ostrich
A chicken
A goose
context: The real Velociraptor stood only about 0.5 m (1.6 ft) at the hip and ran 1.5–2 m long — turkey-sized, far smaller than the man-sized monsters of the films. Source: Natural History Museum, nhm.ac.uk/discover/velociraptor-facts.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor.

question: Everyone pictures Velociraptor as a bare, scaly, lizard-skinned killer. Fossil evidence shows its arms and body were actually covered in what?
answer: Feathers
choices: Feathers
Fur
Bony scales
Slimy skin
context: Velociraptor was a feathered dinosaur — it just couldn't fly. Feathers on non-flying dinosaurs likely helped with warmth and display before flight ever evolved. Source: Turner et al. 2007, Science; nationalgeographic.com/science/article/evidence-that-velociraptor-had-feathers.

question: In 1924 Henry Fairfield Osborn gave this small, fast, meat-eating dinosaur a fitting Latin name. What does the name Velociraptor mean?
answer: Swift robber
choices: Swift robber
Terrible claw
Feathered thief
Desert hunter
context: From Latin velox ('swift') and raptor ('robber' or 'plunderer'). Osborn named it in 1924 for a small, fast, meat-eating dinosaur. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor.

question: Fossil braincases show the real Velociraptor was a sharp-sensed hunter of small prey, not the dim brute of the films. Which of these did its skull actually give it?
answer: A relatively large brain for its size
choices: A relatively large brain for its size
Heat-sensing pits like a pit viper
A second jaw joint for a wider gape
A bony crest for booming calls
context: For its size Velociraptor was smart and sharp-sensed, with a relatively large brain, keen eyes and a good sense of smell — a small, clever hunter that chased small prey, not the giant creatures of the films. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor; ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7542195/ (endocranium and trophic ecology of Velociraptor).

question: The big raptors that terrified the kitchen scene in Jurassic Park were sized after a larger American cousin of Velociraptor, not the real turkey-sized animal. Which relative did the filmmakers actually scale them to?
answer: Deinonychus
choices: Deinonychus
Tyrannosaurus
Spinosaurus
Allosaurus
context: The film's 'Velociraptors' were sized after Deinonychus, a larger raptor cousin — which is why the movie monsters dwarf the real turkey-sized, feathered Velociraptor of Mongolia. Source: nhm.ac.uk/discover/velociraptor-facts.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor.

question: Raptor footprints show no drag mark from the big curved claw on each second toe. Why did Velociraptor keep that one claw raised off the ground?
answer: To keep it sharp like a switchblade
choices: To keep it sharp like a switchblade
To grip slippery rocks
To signal to other raptors
Because it was broken
context: The sickle claw curved over 6.5 cm (2.6 in) around its arc. Held up off the ground, it stayed unworn and razor-sharp — raised and ready like a switchblade. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor; nhm.ac.uk/discover/velociraptor-facts.html.

question: In 2007 scientists examined a Velociraptor forearm bone and found a neat row of six evenly spaced bumps along it. What did those bumps turn out to be?
answer: Quill knobs where feathers anchored
choices: Quill knobs where feathers anchored
Scars from an old bite wound
Growth rings marking its age
Attachment points for venom glands
context: The six 'quill knobs' on specimen IGM 100/981 are the same anchor points where wing feathers attach in living birds — direct proof of feathered arms, even though Velociraptor could not fly. Source: Turner et al. 2007, Science, science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1145076.

question: Velociraptor's long tail was stiffened by bundles of bony rods (ossified tendons) instead of being loose and flexible. What did that rigid tail let the animal do?
answer: Turn on a dime while chasing prey
choices: Turn on a dime while chasing prey
Whip it like a club in defense
Prop itself upright to rest
Rattle it to warn rivals
context: Ossified tendons — bundles of bony rods — stiffened the long tail into a counterbalance, helping Velociraptor turn and change direction quickly at a run. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor.

question: New research says Velociraptor hunted much like a modern eagle: it leapt onto smaller prey and pinned it under its body weight, hooking the big sickle claw in to hold it fast. In this 'raptor prey restraint' model, what actually dispatched the pinned prey?
answer: Its jaws
choices: Its jaws
The sickle claw
Its stiff tail
Its front arms
context: This is the 'raptor prey restraint' model: the sickle claw gripped and pinned rather than slashed, while the jaws did the killing — just as a hawk or eagle holds prey with its talons and dispatches it with the beak. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor; livescience.com/deinonychus-dinosaur-claw-pin-grasp.

question: A famous fossil found in Mongolia in 1971 preserves a Velociraptor and a plant-eating Protoceratops frozen mid-battle, sickle claw at the throat while the plant-eater bit down. Scientists think both were suddenly buried alive together by what?
answer: A collapsing sand dune
choices: A collapsing sand dune
A rising flood
A lava flow
A tar pit
context: The 'Fighting Dinosaurs' specimen froze a real dinosaur fight in stone — the raptor's claw at the Protoceratops's throat, the plant-eater's bite snapping the raptor's right arm — when a sudden sandstorm or collapsing dune buried them mid-struggle. It is now a national treasure of Mongolia. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Dinosaurs; amnh.org/explore/ology/ology-cards/038-fighting-dinosaurs.  (Legend.)

question: When David Hone's team examined the body cavity of a Velociraptor fossil in 2012, they found a long limb bone left from one of its meals. That bone belonged to what kind of creature?
answer: A large flying reptile.
choices: A large flying reptile.
A young horned dinosaur.
A small burrowing mammal.
A slow shelled turtle.
context: The bone came from an azhdarchid pterosaur, a flying reptile with a wingspan near two metres, an animal far too large and formidable for a turkey-sized raptor to have pulled from the air alive. David Hone's team read it instead as a scavenged meal: the raptor fed on the carcass after the pterosaur was already dead. A second clue points the same way. In 2010 Hone described shed Velociraptor teeth scattered beside a tooth-marked Protoceratops jaw, read as late-stage carcass consumption, the raptor gnawing bony scraps from a head after the good meat was gone. Together they show an opportunistic carnivore that took carrion as readily as it took live prey. (Hone et al. 2012, azhdarchid gut content; Hone et al. 2010, Protoceratops jaw. https://www.ucd.ie/news/2012/03MAR12/080312-Preserved-bone-of-Pterosaur-in--stomach-of-Velociraptor.html ; https://archosaurmusings.wordpress.com/2012/03/04/velociraptor-scavenging-azhdarchid/ )  (Legend.)

question: To learn whether a fossil predator was active by day or by night, scientists measure a bony ring inside its eye socket, whose size tracks that habit in living animals. When Schmitz and Motani measured this ring in Velociraptor in 2011, what did it imply about the animal's active hours?
answer: It prowled through the dark of night.
choices: It prowled through the dark of night.
It hunted under the bright midday sun.
It stirred only at dawn and dusk.
It stayed active around the clock.
context: Schmitz and Motani measured the scleral ring, a bony circlet inside the eye socket, across 164 living species and found its shape tracks activity: a wide opening gathers faint light in night-active animals, while a thick narrow ring suits daylight hunters. Applied to fossils, Velociraptor came out nocturnal, while the plant-eater Protoceratops looked cathemeral (active by day or night), hinting the famous 'Fighting Dinosaurs' clash may have happened at twilight. It remains a genuine debate: later work questioned whether eye shape alone can cleanly separate day-active from night-active animals. (Schmitz & Motani 2011, 'Nocturnality in Dinosaurs Inferred from Scleral Ring and Orbit Morphology.' https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21493820/ ; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/dinosaurs-around-the-clock-or-how-we-know-velociraptor-hunted-by-night )  (Legend.)

question: A gardener in Georgia spots a fuzzy, bright orange-and-black bug scurrying across bare soil and calls it a 'velvet ant.' But it is not an ant at all. What is this creature actually?
answer: A wingless female wasp
choices: A wingless female wasp
A furry moth caterpillar
A flightless beetle
A ground-dwelling spider
context: The velvet ant belongs to the wasp family Mutillidae. Every female is flightless and fuzzy, while the males have dark translucent wings — they look so unlike each other that the two sexes are easily mistaken for different species. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant

question: The velvet ant is nicknamed the 'cow killer' for a sting so ferocious that a grown person will scream. If you actually measured the venom in a lab and set it beside a honeybee's, how would the velvet ant's chemistry compare?
answer: Far less toxic than a honeybee's
choices: Far less toxic than a honeybee's
More toxic than any other insect
Roughly ten times as toxic
About the same as a honeybee's
context: The screaming pain comes from overwhelming the nerves, not from poisoning the body: the venom is actually far less toxic than a honeybee's. No cow — and no human — has ever died from the sting; the 'cow killer' name is pure pain-reputation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant  (Legend.)

question: Pinch a velvet ant between your fingers and it does something startling: it rubs rough patches on its abdomen together to fire off a rapid, high-pitched chirp. What is this squeak for?
answer: To warn a predator to let go
choices: To warn a predator to let go
To call a mate over
To echolocate in the dark
To cool its body by vibrating
context: This chirping is called stridulation, made by scraping ridged patches on the abdominal segments together. Both males and females do it — a sound warning to back up the insect's other defenses when it is grabbed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant

question: An insect collector tries to mount a velvet ant on a display board and hits a wall the honeybee never presents: the steel pin simply will not go in. Sometimes the collector must first drill a hole. Why?
