answer: Its exoskeleton is armored many times harder to crush
choices: Its exoskeleton is armored many times harder to crush
Its body is coated in a slippery wax
It curls into a spiny defensive ball
Its shell is hollow and shatters the pin
context: A velvet ant's exoskeleton takes roughly eleven times more crushing force to break than a honeybee's. This tank-like armor is also what lets a female raid another wasp's nest and stay 'impervious to the stings' of the furious owners. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant

question: A female velvet ant does not build a nest of her own. Instead she creeps into the underground burrow of a ground-nesting bee, hunting for the owner's helpless young. Once she finds a bee larva, what does she do to it?
answer: Lays an egg on it so her own young can devour it
choices: Lays an egg on it so her own young can devour it
Carries it back to her own burrow
Stings it to store as paralyzed food
Eats it whole on the spot
context: The velvet ant is an ectoparasitoid: her larva feeds on the host from the OUTSIDE. Eastern cow killers (Dasymutilla occidentalis) target big diggers like cicada killers, laying an egg in the pupal case of the host's young. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant

question: In the dark leaf litter of the forest floor, a velvet worm creeps up on a cricket far too fast to catch by chasing. From a few centimetres away it launches a surprise attack that pins the cricket to the ground before it can hop. What does the velvet worm fire at its prey?
answer: Two jets of sticky glue from nozzles beside its mouth
choices: Two jets of sticky glue from nozzles beside its mouth
A cloud of choking gas from vents along its back
A cluster of barbed harpoons from its clawed feet
A jolt of electricity through the damp soil
context: The velvet worm has a pair of nozzles (oral papillae) on either side of its mouth. It sprays two jets of slime that fling a net of glue over prey from a short distance, sticking the animal to the ground before the velvet worm moves in to eat it. Source: eartharchives.org/articles/velvet-worms-the-voracious-snipers-of-the-undergrowth/  (Legend.)

question: A velvet worm's two slime nozzles are tiny, yet a single squirt lays down a wide zig-zag net of glue that blankets far more ground than a straight shot could. As the slime fires, the nozzles blur back and forth 30 to 60 times a second. Astonishingly, the animal has no muscle anywhere near fast enough to wave them. So what makes the nozzles whip that fast?
answer: The force of the fluid firing through the floppy nozzle whips it on its own
choices: The force of the fluid firing through the floppy nozzle whips it on its own
A ring of super-fast muscle unique to the mouth region
A spinning valve that flicks the stream side to side
Rapid puffs of air that buffet the jet mid-flight
context: This is an elastohydrodynamic instability: the fast fluid passing through the flexible nozzle makes it flail on its own, with no fast muscle involved. The worm's quickest real muscle is about 25 times too slow to move the nozzle that fast. Source: Concha et al., Nature Communications 2015, PMC4382676.

question: The velvet worm looks like a soft, stubby-legged worm oozing through the leaf litter, but that soft body plan is over 500 million years old, tracing back to the Cambrian seas. It is not a true worm, not an insect, and not an arthropod. Where does biology actually place it?
answer: In its own phylum, Onychophora, the 'claw-bearers'
choices: In its own phylum, Onychophora, the 'claw-bearers'
Among the segmented annelid worms, like earthworms
Among the myriapods, alongside centipedes
Among the soft-bodied molluscs, like slugs
context: The velvet worm is its own phylum, Onychophora ('claw-bearers') - a soft-bodied survivor of a Cambrian-era body plan over 500 million years old. Its closest living relatives are the tiny tardigrades (water bears). Source: Burgess Shale (Royal Ontario Museum); bmcecolevol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12862-014-0222-z.  (Legend.)

question: An Australian velvet worm, Euperipatoides rowelli, lives in a family group of up to fifteen that hunts together to bring down prey too big for one alone. When the catch is glued down, though, the group does not share it evenly - one member feeds for up to an hour and bites any who try to sneak in early. Who gets to eat first?
answer: The dominant female, usually the largest and most aggressive
choices: The dominant female, usually the largest and most aggressive
The oldest male, who leads the group on the hunt
Whichever animal landed the first slime shot
The smallest youngsters, fed before the adults
context: These velvet worm families are ruled by a single dominant 'alpha female,' usually the biggest and most aggressive, who keeps order by biting and shoving. She feeds first and alone for up to an hour before the other females, then the males and young, take their turn. Source: Reinhard & Rowell, Journal of Zoology 2005; eartharchives.org.  (Legend.)

question: A poison-dart frog and a rattlesnake both carry deadly toxins, yet you could safely swallow the rattlesnake's toxin while a single lick of the frog could kill you. Which of the two delivers its toxin as a VENOM — injected through a wound — rather than as a poison?
answer: The rattlesnake
choices: The rattlesnake
The poison-dart frog
Both of them
Neither of them
context: Venom must be INJECTED through a bite, sting, or spine; poison harms on eating, touching, or inhaling. The rattlesnake injects venom through its bite, which is why swallowing that venom is harmless — it is made of proteins too large to cross the gut wall into your blood. The poison-dart frog's toxin sits on its skin and harms on contact or if eaten. Source: Natural History Museum, 'Bite or be bitten' (nhm.ac.uk/discover/bite-or-be-bitten.html).

question: A four-legged, egg-laying Australian mammal with a duck-like bill hides a rare weapon: only the MALES grow a sharp spur on each hind ankle, wired to a venom gland in the thigh. Which animal is this?
answer: The platypus
choices: The platypus
The echidna
The wombat
The quokka
context: The platypus is one of the very few venomous mammals. Only the male carries the spur (a calcar) on each hind ankle, and it produces venom mainly during the breeding season — the weapon is for fighting rival males, not hunting. Source: Platypus venom, Wikipedia; Australian Platypus Conservancy (platypus.asn.au). LEGEND.

question: Of all the snakes on Earth, one African viper grows the longest fangs — daggers up to about 5 cm (2 inches) that fold flat against the roof of its mouth and swing forward to strike. Which snake carries these record fangs?
answer: The Gaboon viper
choices: The Gaboon viper
The king cobra
The black mamba
The reticulated python
context: The Gaboon viper (Bitis gabonica) holds the record for the longest fangs of any snake, and also the highest venom yield of any snake. The folding fangs let a short-faced viper carry blades far longer than its own mouth. Source: Guinness World Records; Smithsonian's National Zoo (nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/gaboon-viper).

question: A cobra and a viper deliver opposite kinds of death: after a viper bite the flesh swells, bruises, and bleeds, but a cobra's nerve-blocking venom can kill a victim faster by silently shutting down which part of the body?
answer: The breathing muscles
choices: The breathing muscles
The blood-clotting system
The heart's valves
The digestive tract
context: Neurotoxic venom (typical of cobras) blocks the nerve signals that command the muscles, so the breathing muscles fail and the victim cannot draw breath. Hemotoxic venom (typical of vipers) instead destroys blood cells, prevents clotting, and rots tissue — hence the swelling and bruising. Real venoms usually mix both; the clean cobra-vs-viper split is a teaching simplification. Source: Zoo Atlanta, 'Snake venoms and myths'; Snake venom, Wikipedia.

question: A spitting cobra doesn't wait to be cornered — it sprays venom up to 3 metres at a threat, and studies show it hits one particular body part with about 90% accuracy, tracking the threat's movements to place the shot. Which part is it aiming for?
answer: The eyes
choices: The eyes
The mouth
The nose
The hands
context: A 'spitting' cobra sprays venom out of forward-facing holes in its fangs, aiming for the eyes of a threat up to about 3 metres away; roughly 90% of spits hit the eyes, and the snake predicts where the threat's head will move. This is defense, not hunting. Source: Live Science, 'Secret to Spitting Cobra's Deadly Accurate Aim Revealed'; Britannica, 'Spitting cobra.'

question: A thumb-sized octopus on a reef, cornered by a diver, suddenly lights up with roughly 60 iridescent warning flashes across its body an instant before it bites with a beak loaded with tetrodotoxin. Which animal is this?
answer: The blue-ringed octopus
choices: The blue-ringed octopus
The mimic octopus
The vampire squid
The reef cuttlefish
context: The blue-ringed octopus flashes roughly 60 iridescent blue rings as an aposematic (warning) display before biting. Its tetrodotoxin is one of the deadliest nerve toxins known — far more potent than cyanide — and there is no antivenom. Source: Britannica, 'Blue-ringed octopus'; Natural History Museum (nhm.ac.uk). LEGEND.

question: A slow sea snail on a coral reef somehow hunts fast fish. It extends a fleshy tube and fires a single hollow, harpoon-like structure on a tether, stabs the fish, injects venom, and reels it in. What is that harpoon actually made from?
answer: A modified tooth
choices: A modified tooth
A sharpened claw
A hardened tentacle
A stinging hair
context: The geography cone snail (Conus geographus) fires a single hollow, barbed radular TOOTH — a modified tooth on a tether — from an extendable proboscis, then reels the speared fish back to swallow it. Source: Conus geographus, Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conus_geographus).

question: A jellyfish nematocyst goes from first touch to fully driven into the skin in about 3 milliseconds, injecting venom before the victim can react. Among all of biology, that firing ranks as which of these?
answer: One of the fastest movements known
choices: One of the fastest movements known
About as fast as a human blink
A typical nerve-reflex speed
The fastest a muscle can contract
context: On contact a nematocyst fires in roughly 3 milliseconds, driving a spined tube into the skin to inject venom — one of the fastest movements known in all of biology, far quicker than a reflex, a blink, or a muscle twitch. Each is a pre-loaded microscopic harpoon. Source: University of Melbourne AVRU, 'Venomous marine animals — jellyfish'; Firing the Sting, PMC4379534.

question: Some fish-hunting cone snails don't bother harpooning a fish — they release a cloud of a chemical the fish's OWN body already makes, and through the gills it sedates the fish into a stupor the slow snail can swallow whole. Which of the fish's own hormones have they turned into a weapon?
answer: Insulin
choices: Insulin
Adrenaline
Melatonin
Testosterone
context: Certain cone snails release a specialized INSULIN into the water; through the gills it drives the fish into hypoglycemic shock, sedating it — chemistry out-drugging a faster animal. Researchers nicknamed this sedating blend the 'nirvana cabal.' Source: PNAS 2015, 'Specialized insulin is used for chemical warfare by fish-hunting cone snails.' LEGEND.

question: The blue-ringed octopus is deadly, yet its genes contain no recipe for its tetrodotoxin. Where does the toxin actually come from?
answer: Bacteria living in its salivary glands
choices: Bacteria living in its salivary glands
A gland behind each blue ring
The venom of prey it eats
Sunlight stored in its skin
context: The octopus does not make its own toxin — symbiotic bacteria in its salivary glands produce the tetrodotoxin. That also makes it BOTH venomous (its bite injects the toxin) and poisonous (harmful if eaten). Source: Britannica, 'Blue-ringed octopus'; Natural History Museum, 'Bite or be bitten' (nhm.ac.uk).

question: The box jellyfish Chironex fleckeri carries one of the deadliest venoms in the sea, yet for decades no one knew exactly how it wrecked a cell. In 2019 a genome-wide CRISPR screen finally cracked it: the venom cannot harm a cell unless that cell hands it one particular molecule, and a common drug that strips that molecule away works as an antidote. What does the venom depend on?
answer: Cholesterol built into the cell membrane
choices: Cholesterol built into the cell membrane
Iron carried in the red blood cells
Calcium stored inside the muscle fibers
Sugar coating the cell's outer surface
context: Chironex fleckeri is often called the most venomous animal in the sea: a single individual carries roughly enough venom to kill about 60 adults, and a severe sting can stop the heart in 2-5 minutes. The venom works through pore-forming proteins (porins) that punch holes in cell membranes; potassium floods out, and the resulting spike in blood potassium (hyperkalemia) drives cardiovascular collapse. In 2019 a University of Sydney team (Greg Neely and Raymond Lau) ran a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen and found the venom requires membrane cholesterol to act. Common cholesterol-stripping drugs called cyclodextrins block the damage and, in mice, still worked as an antidote up to about 15 minutes after the sting. Sources: Nature Communications 2019, 'Molecular dissection of box jellyfish venom cytotoxicity highlights an effective venom antidote' (s41467-019-09681-1); University of Sydney news, 1 May 2019; Wikipedia, 'Chironex fleckeri'.

question: Long before any snake existed, a Late Triassic reptile on the crocodile-and-dinosaur branch was already delivering venom, and today it survives only as fossilized teeth in the rock. Laid out in sequence, those teeth are prized by scientists because they preserve which rare record?
answer: A step-by-step shift from an open surface groove to a fully enclosed internal tube
choices: A step-by-step shift from an open surface groove to a fully enclosed internal tube
A step-by-step shift from a crushing molar into a sharp slicing blade
The earliest known bite marks left by one predator upon another
A single fang regrown and resharpened dozens of times in one lifetime
context: The animal is Uatchitodon, a Late Triassic archosauriform (a reptile on the crocodile-and-dinosaur branch, roughly 220-237 million years ago), known only from its teeth. Those teeth are extraordinary because, across different specimens, they capture a complete transition series: from a shallow open groove on the tooth surface to a fully enclosed, tube-like internal canal for conducting venom, with some teeth carrying two canals apiece. This 'grooves to tubes' sequence shows the very pathway by which a venom-delivery system evolves, it predates venomous snakes by well over 100 million years, and it happened on a completely separate reptile lineage. Sources: Mitchell, Heckert & Sues 2010, Naturwissenschaften (The Science of Nature), 'Grooves to tubes: evolution of the venom delivery system in a Late Triassic reptile' (doi 10.1007/s00114-010-0729-0); Wikipedia, 'Uatchitodon'.

question: Deep in the Pacific, a delicate white vase-shaped cage sits on the muddy seafloor, its whole skeleton woven from a lattice of thin spikes. What material are those spikes made of?
answer: Silica — the same stuff as glass
choices: Silica — the same stuff as glass
Coral limestone
Woven seaweed fiber
Hardened tree resin
context: The Venus's flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is a deep-sea glass sponge whose entire skeleton is woven from silica, the same material as glass, built into a delicate white latticework cage shaped like a vase or basket, roughly 10 to 30 cm (4 to 12 inches) tall. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus'_flower_basket

question: A pair of tiny shrimp swim into a Venus flower basket as babies, feeding and cleaning inside its glass cage. As they keep growing, something happens that they never planned for. What is it?
answer: They grow too big to ever get back out
choices: They grow too big to ever get back out
They eat their way through the glass
They turn transparent like the sponge
They stop growing to stay small
context: A breeding pair of tiny shrimp (Spongicola venusta) swims into the sponge as babies, then grows too big to ever get back out through the glass lattice — so the pair spends its whole life imprisoned together inside the glass cage, cleaning it in exchange for food and shelter. Their own babies are born small enough to slip out through the lattice and find a sponge of their own. Source: https://schmidtocean.org/cruise-log-post/a-deep-sea-love-story/  (Legend.)

question: A Venus flower basket holds a single pair of grown shrimp locked inside its glass cage for life, yet the species keeps colonizing fresh sponges all across the seafloor. At which point in a shrimp's life can it move into a brand-new sponge home?
answer: Only as a newborn, small enough to slip the lattice
choices: Only as a newborn, small enough to slip the lattice
Only after molting its shell to shrink down
Only once the parent sponge dies and opens up
Only by burrowing through the sponge's soft base
context: The shrimp pair's babies are born small enough to slip out through the glass lattice and swim off to find their own sponge home — so only the parents stay imprisoned, and each new sponge gets its own captive couple. Source: https://schmidtocean.org/cruise-log-post/a-deep-sea-love-story/

question: A Venus flower basket must stand upright in the slow deep-sea current, but it grows on soft mud with nothing solid to grip. How does it hold itself up?
answer: A tuft of hair-thin glass threads driven into the mud
choices: A tuft of hair-thin glass threads driven into the mud
Suckers that clamp onto passing fish
A heavy stone it swallows for ballast
Long muscular roots that dig downward
context: The sponge anchors to the muddy deep seafloor with a tuft of glass threads — spun-glass fibers about 5 to 20 cm long and as thin as a human hair — that hold it upright in the current like a base of spun glass. Source: https://www.pnas.org/content/101/10/3358.full

question: The hair-thin glass threads that anchor a Venus flower basket in the deep-sea mud stunned materials researchers: grown in cold seawater with no furnace, they already pull off a high-tech trick the researchers' own factories struggle to match. What do these threads do?
answer: Pipe light along their length like fiber-optic cables
choices: Pipe light along their length like fiber-optic cables
Spin a trickle of electricity from the passing current
Flex toward drifting food and grip it like tiny fingers
Ring with sound to scare off circling deep-sea hunters
context: Each thread is a natural fibre-optic cable: a core of pure silica about two micrometres across, wrapped around a central organic filament and sheathed in a finely layered shell that works just like the optical cladding of a telecom cable -- and it carries light just as well. Because the sponge grows the thread in cold seawater instead of a furnace, it can lace the glass with impurities such as sodium that IMPROVE light transmission but get destroyed in high-temperature factory glass. And unlike brittle manufactured fibre, you can tie the sponge's thread in a knot without snapping it. Source: Sundar, Yablon, Grazul, Ilan & Aizenberg, 'Fibre-optical features of a glass sponge,' Nature vol. 424, pp. 899-900 (2003), https://www.nature.com/articles/424899a ; Scientific American, 'Sea Sponge Inspires Better Fiber-Optic Cables.'

question: A Venus flower basket's glass skeleton was 3D-printed beside the criss-cross lattice that human engineers have braced bridges and towers with since the 1820s, then both were loaded until they buckled -- same material, same amount. How did the sponge's design do?
answer: It carried over 20% more load before buckling
choices: It carried over 20% more load before buckling
It matched the human grid almost exactly
It gave way first but sprang back unharmed
It held less, though it bent much further
context: The sponge's cage is no plain grid: a square lattice is overlaid with a DOUBLE set of parallel diagonal struts fused across it in a checkerboard pattern. Harvard engineers Matheus Fernandes, James Weaver and Katia Bertoldi 3D-printed rival lattice shapes and ran finite-element buckling tests, and found the paired-diagonal design is over 20% stronger -- higher buckling resistance for the same amount of material -- than the criss-cross lattice humans have braced bridges and towers with since Ithiel Town patented it in the 1820s. The sponge quietly solved a load-bearing problem better than 200 years of human engineering. Source: Fernandes, Weaver, Bertoldi et al., 'Mechanically robust lattices inspired by deep-sea glass sponges,' Nature Materials vol. 20 (2021), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41563-020-0798-1 ; Harvard SEAS news, https://seas.harvard.edu/news/marine-sponges-inspire-next-generation-skyscrapers-and-bridges.

question: A small desert arachnid called a whip scorpion has no stinger and no venom anywhere in its body. When a predator lunges, it swivels its rear end toward the attacker's face and fires a fine spray. What does that spray smell strongly of?
answer: Vinegar
choices: Vinegar
Rotten eggs
Bitter almonds
Ammonia
context: That sharp vinegar smell is how the animal earned its common name: the vinegaroon. The spray is mostly acetic acid, the very acid that makes vinegar sour, and the vinegaroon can aim it from a few inches out to about a foot away. Source: Oakland Zoo, Giant Vinegaroon (oaklandzoo.org/animals/giant-vinegaroon).

question: The vinegaroon drags a long, thin, whip-like tail behind it, and it looks exactly like a scorpion's stinger. But a vinegaroon cannot sting anything: that tail holds no venom and no point at all. So what is the whip actually for?
answer: Feeling its way through the dark
choices: Feeling its way through the dark
Storing fat for the winter
Signaling to a mate
Anchoring it in its burrow
context: The whip is called the flagellum, and it works like a rear antenna. The vinegaroon waves it around to sense its surroundings in the pitch dark. True scorpions sting with their tails, but the vinegaroon's tail can only feel. Source: UF/IFAS EENY493, Giant Whip Scorpion (ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN890).

question: A cricket blunders past a hunting vinegaroon in the dark. In a blink the arachnid grabs it and the cricket is dead almost at once, without a bite, a sting, or a drop of venom. How did the vinegaroon dispatch its prey so fast?
answer: Crushes it whole in its pincers
choices: Crushes it whole in its pincers
Drains its blood through a fang
Suffocates it in a burrow
Dissolves it with acid spray
context: Those front arms are pincers called pedipalps, lined with spiny teeth. Lacking any venom, the vinegaroon simply seizes prey and crushes it, then chews it up. The same pincers can deliver a hard pinch to a careless human hand. Source: UF/IFAS EENY493 (ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN890); Oakland Zoo.

question: On its own, the vinegaroon's vinegar-acid does almost nothing to a cockroach: the roach walks away unharmed. But the vinegaroon blends a second, oily acid into its spray, and now the same mix turns lethal. Researchers propose the oily acid breaks through one particular barrier the vinegar alone could not. What does it break through?
answer: The waxy coating on the roach's shell
choices: The waxy coating on the roach's shell
The tough plates over the roach's back
The breathing holes along the roach's sides
The nerve cord running down the roach
context: The oily ingredient is caprylic acid. A roach's shell is coated in wax that repels the watery vinegar-acid, so even 85% acetic acid beads up and rolls off. Researchers propose the caprylic acid dissolves that waxy cuticle, letting the acid soak in and become lethal to insects like fly larvae. This penetration mechanism is a proposed finding, not fully settled. Source: The Transient Biologist, citing Eisner/Meinwald defensive-secretion research (thetransientbiologist.wordpress.com).  (Legend.)

question: Deep in the black midwater lurks the viperfish, a hand-sized hunter whose fangs are so absurdly long they cannot fit inside its closed mouth. So where do those needle teeth end up, forcing its jaws to hang permanently open around them?
answer: Curving back until the tips reach almost to its own eyes
choices: Curving back until the tips reach almost to its own eyes
Folding flat into grooves along the roof of its mouth
Sliding sideways into pouches inside its cheeks
Retracting into the base of its throat between bites
context: The viperfish's fangs are so long they don't fit inside its mouth; the needle teeth curve back very close to the fish's own eyes, so its jaws hang permanently agape around them. This is the animal's signature image. (Source: seasky.org/deep-sea/viperfish.html)  (Legend.)

question: Two long front fangs jut straight up from the viperfish's lower jaw, past its own eyes. In the dark it lunges at a smaller fish drifting by. As its jaws snap shut, what do those upthrust fangs form around the prey?
answer: A cage of teeth the prey cannot escape from
choices: A cage of teeth the prey cannot escape from
A funnel that flushes the prey deeper down its throat
A pair of pincers that crush the prey before swallowing
A saw that slices the prey into bite-sized pieces
context: Two prominent front fangs jut up from the viperfish's bottom jaw past its own eyes, and when it strikes, the teeth close into a cage that keeps prey from escaping. (Source: mbari.org/animal/pacific-viperfish)

question: The viperfish carries a tiny bead of living light at the very tip of one greatly elongated dorsal spine. In the black midwater, how does it turn that one dangling glow into a full belly?
answer: It waves the spine like a fishing pole and flashes the light to lure prey onto its fangs
choices: It waves the spine like a fishing pole and flashes the light to lure prey onto its fangs
It sweeps the spine across the seafloor to flush hidden prey out of the mud
It beams the light into prey eyes to blind them while it charges
It holds the light steady as a warning that keeps rival hunters away
context: The viperfish dangles a glowing photophore on the tip of a long dorsal spine and waves it over its own head like a fishing pole, flashing the light on and off to lure smaller fish right onto its fangs. (Source: seasky.org/deep-sea/viperfish.html)  (Legend.)

question: Two rows of tiny light organs run the whole length of the viperfish belly. But glowing in the pitch dark seems suicidal -- it should turn the fish into a beacon for every hunter around. Yet these belly lights are a survival trick. How do they keep the viperfish hidden?
answer: They match the dim glow drifting down from the surface so the fish casts no dark silhouette
choices: They match the dim glow drifting down from the surface so the fish casts no dark silhouette
They flash a sudden burst that startles the attacker into fleeing
They paint fake glowing eyes to make the fish look far larger
They leave a cloud of glowing particles for the fish to escape behind
context: Photophores line the viperfish's belly, glowing to mask its silhouette from predators looking up from below; this is called counter-illumination. So the fish uses light two ways at once: a lure above to attract prey, belly-lights below to hide. (Source: whoi.edu/ocean-learning-hub/ocean-facts/sloanes-viperfish)

question: Food is scarce in the deep, so the viperfish must gulp whatever it can catch, sometimes prey 20% to over 50% bigger than the viperfish itself. What trick of its own body lets a small fish swallow a meal larger than it is?
answer: It unhinges its skull and jaw and expands its whole stomach
choices: It unhinges its skull and jaw and expands its whole stomach
It slowly dissolves the prey with acid before pulling it inward
It drags the prey in whole, working it down tail-first
It stores the prey in an inflatable pouch beneath its chin
context: The viperfish unhinges its skull and opens its jaw up to 90 degrees, expanding its stomach to swallow prey 20% to over 50% larger than itself. (Source: whoi.edu/ocean-learning-hub/ocean-facts/sloanes-viperfish)

question: A viperfish's fangs are its greatest weapon, but in the darkness it sometimes strikes at prey that turns out to be too large. Those same giant teeth then become its doom. What happens to a viperfish that bites off more than it can handle?
answer: The trapped meal jams on its teeth and it slowly starves to death
choices: The trapped meal jams on its teeth and it slowly starves to death
It coughs the prey back up and swims off unharmed
Its fangs snap off and slowly regrow over several weeks
It swells up and floats helplessly to the surface
context: If a viperfish miscalculates and catches prey too big, its giant teeth trap the meal so it can neither swallow it nor spit it out, and it starves. (Source: usa.oceana.org/blog/freaky-fish-2-pacific-viperfish)

question: A fatherless clutch stunned keepers at Chester Zoo in England in 2006: a female reptile who had never been housed with a male still laid eggs that hatched into healthy babies. Virgin birth like this is so rare in backboned animals -- only about one vertebrate species in a thousand -- that it made world news. Which giant lizard was the mother?
answer: The Komodo dragon
choices: The Komodo dragon
The green iguana
The gila monster
The frilled lizard
context: The mother was Flora, a Komodo dragon (Varanus komodoensis). Virgin birth (parthenogenesis) is documented in only about 0.1 percent of vertebrate species, which is why her fatherless clutch became a headline. Source: Nature News, 'Dragon virgin births startle zoo keepers' (2006) (https://www.nature.com/news/2006/061218/full/news061218-7.html); Scientific American, 'Strange but True: Komodo Dragons Show that Virgin Births Are Possible' (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/strange-but-true-komodo-d/).

question: In an ordinary healthy colony, the egg-laying mother produces one whole caste of offspring with no father at all -- she lays some eggs without ever fertilizing them, and those still hatch. It is an everyday virgin birth hiding inside a familiar backyard insect's nest. Which insect is this?
answer: The honeybee
choices: The honeybee
The paper wasp
The bumblebee
The carpenter ant
context: In a honeybee colony the queen lays some eggs unfertilized, and those hatch into male drones -- so a drone has a mother but literally no father. It is natural parthenogenesis running inside a normal hive. Source: Britannica, 'Parthenogenesis' (arrhenotoky) (https://www.britannica.com/science/parthenogenesis).

question: At Chester Zoo in England in 2006, keepers confirmed that a female Komodo dragon (Varanus komodoensis) named Flora had produced a fatherless clutch -- she had never once been housed with a male. Of the eggs she laid, how many hatched into healthy baby dragons?
answer: Seven
choices: Seven
One
Twenty-three
Four
context: Seven of Flora's eggs hatched into healthy baby dragons, all with no father at all -- a true virgin birth. LEGEND. Source: Nature News, 'Dragon virgin births startle zoo keepers' (2006) (https://www.nature.com/news/2006/061218/full/news061218-7.html); Watts et al. 2006, Nature 444:1021-1022.

question: At London Zoo, a female Komodo dragon named Sungai laid a clutch of fertile eggs -- and the timing was the shock, because it had been more than two years since she had shared space with any male. When keepers ran DNA tests on the eggs, what did the results show?
answer: Sungai was the only parent
choices: Sungai was the only parent
A distant male had somehow fathered them
The eggs were another female's
Two dragons had shared the clutch
context: Over two years past her last contact with a male, Sungai still produced fertile eggs -- and the DNA proved she alone was the parent. A second confirmed Komodo virgin birth. Source: Nature News (2006) (https://www.nature.com/news/2006/061218/full/news061218-7.html); Watts et al. 2006, Nature 444:1021-1022.

question: At an Omaha zoo in December 2001, keepers found a newborn pup swimming in a tank that had held only female bonnethead sharks for about three years. DNA testing of the pup made scientific history. What did the results reveal?
answer: The pup carried only its mother's genes, no father at all
choices: The pup carried only its mother's genes, no father at all
The pup was fathered by a stored packet of old sperm
The pup was a cross with a nearby nurse shark
The pup had been born to a different tank's female
context: Three female bonnetheads had shared the tank for about three years with no male, and the DNA showed the pup carried only its mother's genes -- the first virgin birth ever confirmed in any shark. LEGEND. Source: Science News, 'Virgin Birth: Shark has daughter without a dad' (https://www.sciencenews.org/article/virgin-birth-shark-has-daughter-without-dad); Chapman et al. 2007, Biology Letters.

question: In the deserts of the American Southwest lives a lizard, the desert grassland whiptail (Aspidoscelis uniparens), that keepers have never once been able to breed the ordinary way -- no pairing of two kinds ever works. What is so unusual about this species?
answer: The species has no males -- every one is female
choices: The species has no males -- every one is female
The lizards change sex when they need to
Each lizard splits in half like a worm
Each must pair with a related species
context: These are entire species with no males at all -- every individual is female and reproduces only by parthenogenesis, essentially cloning herself. LEGEND. Source: Wikipedia, 'Desert grassland whiptail lizard' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert_grassland_whiptail_lizard).

question: The all-female whiptail lizards (genus Aspidoscelis) have no males in their species, yet in the desert you can still catch two of them going through the full motions of mating -- one climbs onto another, wraps her tail around her, and wriggles. Far from pointless, what does this 'pseudocopulation' actually do?
answer: Triggers the other female to make eggs
choices: Triggers the other female to make eggs
Marks which lizard owns the burrow
Cools the pair down in the heat
Warns off a circling hawk
context: The mating-like behavior helps stimulate the mounted female's body to produce eggs -- a courtship ritual kept alive in a species that abandoned males entirely. LEGEND. Source: Desert Museum, 'Whiptails (Aspidoscelis spp.)' (https://www.desertmuseum.org/books/nhsd_whiptails.php).

question: A honeybee drone hatches from an egg his mother never let a father touch -- he has a mother but, uniquely among the hive, no father anywhere in his making. That fatherless origin leaves him with a body genetically unlike every worker and queen around him. What is strange about his genetics?
answer: Haploid -- half the usual chromosome set
choices: Haploid -- half the usual chromosome set
Diploid, but every gene is a perfect copy
He carries an extra chromosome the workers lack
His genes are an even blend of two grandfathers
context: Because a drone grows from an unfertilized egg, he inherits only his mother's single chromosome set -- he is haploid, carrying half the chromosomes of the diploid workers and queens. Every cell in his body runs on that one set. Source: Britannica, 'Parthenogenesis' (arrhenotoky) (https://www.britannica.com/science/parthenogenesis).

question: Aphids -- the tiny greenfly on garden plants -- and water fleas (Daphnia) in a pond run all-female lines through the warm good times, each mother giving virgin birth to more daughters generation after generation. Then the weather turns cold and harsh. What change do they suddenly make?
answer: They start producing males
choices: They start producing males
They stop breeding entirely
They shrink to survive
They abandon the plant
context: When conditions sour, these insects and crustaceans finally make males and switch to fertilized eggs -- tougher eggs that can ride out the bad season. This on-off strategy is called cyclical parthenogenesis. Source: Britannica, 'Parthenogenesis' (cyclical parthenogenesis) (https://www.britannica.com/science/parthenogenesis).

question: A female Komodo dragon (Varanus komodoensis) housed for years with no male can still lay a clutch that hatches. Because her unfertilized eggs rebuild a full chromosome set purely from her own genes, the whole brood ends up sharing one startling trait. What are these fatherless hatchlings?
answer: Every one is a healthy son
choices: Every one is a healthy son
Every one is a healthy daughter
Every one is a sterile runt
Every one is a perfect clone
context: The trick is called terminal fusion automixis: after the egg divides, it fuses back with a leftover 'polar body,' doubling its lone set of chromosomes. Reptiles run a ZW sex system, the mirror image of mammals -- females are ZW, males are ZZ -- so a doubled egg can only come out ZZ or WW. WW embryos have no working chromosome and die, leaving nothing but ZZ, and every ZZ is male. Each is also fully homozygous, carrying two identical copies of every gene. So a fatherless Komodo clutch is always a clutch of sons -- which is why the covered virgin-birth clutches of Flora and Sungai were all boys. Source: Watts et al. 2006, 'Parthenogenesis in Komodo dragons,' Nature (PMC2391206).  (Legend.)

question: Combing the studbook DNA of 911 California condors (Gymnogyps californianus), San Diego Zoo scientists found two males whose genes held no trace of a father. What stunned the team was not the virgin births themselves, but the circumstances of the two mothers who produced them. What was surprising about these mothers?
answer: Each was penned with a fertile mate she had bred with
choices: Each was penned with a fertile mate she had bred with
Each had been hand-raised by human keepers since hatching
Each was among the very last females left alive
Each had been dosed with drugs to boost fertility
context: This broke a rule biologists had trusted for decades -- that vertebrate parthenogenesis only kicks in when a female has no mate available. Both condor mothers had fertile partners on hand and had bred with them normally before. The two fatherless chicks were ZZ males, fully homozygous (inbreeding coefficient 1.0), and they were the first parthenogenesis ever confirmed in the species. Source: Ryder et al. 2021, 'Facultative Parthenogenesis in California Condors,' Journal of Heredity 112(7):569.  (Legend.)

question: Look up on a hot afternoon and you might spot a big dark bird riding high without a single wingbeat, its wings held up in a shallow V, rocking gently side to side as it circles a rising column of warm air. Which bird is this?
answer: Turkey vulture
choices: Turkey vulture
Great blue heron
Snowy owl
Mallard duck
context: The turkey vulture soars on rising columns of warm air called thermals, wings held in a shallow V and spanning up to about 6 feet (1.8 m). Riding thermals lets it circle for hours without flapping, saving energy while it searches the ground below. Source: Wikipedia, 'Turkey vulture' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey_vulture).

question: A turkey vulture is covered in feathers over most of its body, just like other birds. But there is ONE part where it keeps only bare skin while other birds stay fully covered. Which part of the turkey vulture is naked skin?
answer: Its head and neck
choices: Its head and neck
Its legs and feet
Its wingtips
Its tail
context: The vulture's bald head is an adaptation, not ugliness. To reach meat it plunges its head deep inside a carcass, and a feathery head would trap rotting scraps and bacteria; bare skin stays clean and washes off, and it can bake sterile in the sun. Source: Cornell Lab Bird Academy / Natural Connections, 'Spring cleaning with turkey vultures'.

question: Almost every bird hunts by eyesight; a hidden carcass rotting under a thick forest canopy should be invisible from the air. Yet a turkey vulture will drop straight down onto it. How does it find a meal it cannot see?
answer: It smells it — homing in on the faint gas of early decay
choices: It smells it — homing in on the faint gas of early decay
It hears the buzz of the flies already swarming the body
It feels the warmth the decaying body gives off from far above
It follows the crows and ravens that spotted the body first
context: The turkey vulture is one of the very few birds that hunt by SMELL, a rare skill in the bird world. It homes in on ethyl mercaptan, the sulfurous gas of early decay, at just a few parts per trillion, and its olfactory brain lobe is enormous compared to other birds'. Legend-tier wonder. Source: Wikipedia, 'Turkey vulture'; Cornell Lab Bird Academy.

question: A vulture will tear into flesh that has been rotting for days — a meal crawling with germs that would poison almost any other animal — and simply digest it, unharmed. The secret is what sits in its gizzard. What is that stomach fluid like?
answer: Roughly as corrosive as battery acid, near the very bottom of the acid scale
choices: Roughly as corrosive as battery acid, near the very bottom of the acid scale
A thick alkaline slime that coats and neutralizes the meat
No sharper than a house cat's stomach, just paired with a fast gut
A cocktail of antibiotics the bird's own body brews up
context: A vulture's gizzard has a pH of slightly above 0 — about as corrosive as battery acid — while a human stomach sits around pH 2. This acid bath is the vulture's headline superpower, letting it eat rotten flesh that would sicken almost anything else. Legend-tier wonder. Source: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, 'Vultures: The Gastronic Marvel'.

question: A cow dies of anthrax, its carcass loaded with hardy spores that can survive in soil for decades and sicken almost anything that touches them. A turkey vulture arrives and eats its fill, then flies off to roost miles away, perfectly healthy. Where do the anthrax spores end up?
answer: Broken apart inside the vulture, never leaving its body alive
choices: Broken apart inside the vulture, never leaving its body alive
Riding in its gut to the roost, seeded across fresh ground in its droppings
Wiped harmlessly onto its bare legs, then dried in the sun
Coughed back up in a pellet the vulture leaves at the carcass
context: The vulture's stomach acid is so corrosive it dissolves and destroys the microbes that cause anthrax, botulism, cholera, rabies and tuberculosis — diseases that would kill other scavengers. By eating diseased carcasses and destroying the germs inside its own gut, the vulture works as a walking disease-disposal unit that stops outbreaks from spreading. Legend-tier wonder. Source: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, 'Vultures: The Gastronic Marvel'; Cornell Lab Bird Academy.

question: On a scorching day a vulture can't sweat, and panting only does so much. Then it does something that looks revolting but is brilliant: it deliberately soaks its own bare legs with its liquid waste. Streaked white, its legs now do two jobs at once. What are they?
answer: The waste evaporates to chill its blood, and its acidity kills the bacteria on its feet
choices: The waste evaporates to chill its blood, and its acidity kills the bacteria on its feet
It signals other vultures to a carcass, and warns off rival birds
It waterproofs the skin, and masks the bird's scent from predators
It hardens into a protective crust, and stores water for later
context: This behavior is called urohidrosis. A vulture urinates and defecates on its own legs; the evaporating liquid chills the blood in its bare legs and feet, and the acidic waste also kills bacteria picked up from walking on carcasses, streaking the legs white. Legend-tier wonder. Source: Wikipedia, 'Turkey vulture'.

question: A big green tree frog of Borneo leaps from a high branch and sails to a tree 50 feet away instead of dropping like a stone. What lets Wallace's flying frog ride the air across such a gap?
answer: Its toes are fully webbed to the tips, so the four outspread feet open like parachutes
choices: Its toes are fully webbed to the tips, so the four outspread feet open like parachutes
It beats its front legs like stubby wings to stay aloft
It puffs its lungs full of air and floats like a balloon
It flicks a long tail to steer and catch an updraft
context: Wallace's flying frog (Rhacophorus nigropalmatus) of Borneo, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula glides tree to tree by spreading all four feet, whose toes are fully webbed right to the tips so the outspread feet act like parachutes. Catching air with its feet and loose skin flaps along its limbs, it can glide 50 feet (15 m) or more. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace's_flying_frog ; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/amphibians/facts/wallaces-flying-frog

question: Wallace's flying frog finishes a long glide and has to stop dead on a smooth, slick leaf or trunk without bouncing off. What on its body lets it grab hold and land softly?
answer: Oversized sticky pads on its toe tips that cling to smooth surfaces
choices: Oversized sticky pads on its toe tips that cling to smooth surfaces
Tiny hooked claws that dig into the bark
A ring of suction cups around its belly
Sticky mucus it sprays ahead of itself before touchdown
context: Oversized, sticky toe pads (adhesive discs) let the frog grip and land softly, sticking to smooth leaves and tree trunks at the end of a glide. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace's_flying_frog

question: Wallace's flying frog lives almost its whole life up in the treetops and descends only to breed over a pool below. Rather than laying its eggs down in the water, what does the female build on a branch overhanging it?
answer: A whipped-up foam nest, so the hatched tadpoles drop straight into the water below
choices: A whipped-up foam nest, so the hatched tadpoles drop straight into the water below
A cup of chewed leaves glued to the branch with tree sap
A cluster of eggs stuck under a broad leaf so rain drips them down
A ball of leaves she folds shut around the eggs on the twig
context: It is a canopy frog that lives almost exclusively in the trees, descending only to breed at pools and wallows below, where the female whips up a foam bubble-nest on a branch overhanging water so the hatched tadpoles drop in. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace's_flying_frog

question: A walrus's two great tusks curve down as long as a grown man's arm. Look inside its mouth and you find these tusks are actually a very familiar kind of body part, hugely overgrown. What are they?
answer: Enormously overgrown canine teeth
choices: Enormously overgrown canine teeth
Twin horns of solid keratin
A pair of fused nose bones
Stiffened cartilage antlers
context: A walrus's tusks are two hugely elongated canine teeth, growing up to about 3 feet long, and BOTH males and females grow them. Source: https://www.pbs.org/wnet/nature/blog/walrus-fact-sheet/

question: On Arctic beaches and ice floes, walruses haul out of the sea to rest together. How many animals pile into a single one of these resting herds?
answer: Thousands, packed shoulder to shoulder
choices: A dozen or so
A hundred at most
A family of four or five
Thousands, packed shoulder to shoulder
context: Walruses haul out onto beaches and ice in enormous crowds packed shoulder to shoulder that can number in the thousands, and some Arctic haulouts reach tens of thousands of animals. Source: https://www.worldwildlife.org/resources/explainers/what-is-a-walrus-haulout-and-what-does-it-mean-for-the-planet/

question: A walrus hunts clams buried in pitch-dark seafloor mud, where its eyes are useless. What does it use to feel out each hidden shell and tell it from the sand?
answer: Hundreds of stiff, super-sensitive whiskers
choices: Hundreds of stiff, super-sensitive whiskers
Faint electric pulses from its tusks
A glowing lure dangled from its chin
Sonar clicks bounced off the mud
context: A walrus's snout carries roughly 400 to 700 stiff vibrissae that it sweeps across the dark seafloor mud to feel out buried clams, telling shell from sand by touch alone. Source: https://marinesanctuary.org/blog/sea-wonder-walrus/

question: The walrus's scientific name Odobenus means 'tooth-walker.' What does a walrus do that earned it such a strange name?
answer: Hooks its tusks over ice and hauls itself up
choices: Hooks its tusks over ice and hauls itself up
Chatters its teeth to echo-locate prey
Walks the seabed on its two long tusks
Grinds its molars to grip slick rocks
context: Odobenus means 'tooth-walker' — a walrus hooks its tusks over the edge of an ice floe and hauls its huge body up out of the water, in effect walking on its teeth. Source: https://www.pbs.org/wnet/nature/blog/walrus-fact-sheet/  (Legend.)

question: A walrus finds a clam on the seafloor and seals its lips over the shell. Seconds later the soft meat slides out whole. How does it empty the shell?
answer: A piston-like pull of the tongue vacuums it out
choices: A piston-like pull of the tongue vacuums it out
A crushing bite that shatters the shell
Grinding molars mash the shell to bits
A jet of water blasted in to flush the meat
context: A walrus clamps its lips over the shell and pulls its tongue back like a piston, creating powerful suction that sucks the soft clam meat straight out. Source: https://www.pbs.org/wnet/nature/the-weird-way-walruses-eat-with-their-tongue/33419/  (Legend.)

question: A walrus's skin is threaded with tiny blood-vessel shortcuts that can snap wide open in an instant. When they do, where does the blood suddenly rush?
answer: Straight to the skin's surface
choices: Straight to the skin's surface
Pooled deep around the heart
Rerouted to the swimming muscles
Shunted into the blubber layer
context: The pink flush works through blood-vessel shortcuts called arterio-venous anastomoses (AVAs); when they open, blood floods the skin's surface to dump body heat like a radiator, turning the walrus pink. Source: https://www.gi.alaska.edu/alaska-science-forum/why-does-walrus-blush

question: A tiny rainforest frog the size of a paperclip does the opposite of hiding: it blazes bright gold-yellow right out in the open where every predator can see it. What is that dazzling color telling anything that might take a bite?
answer: I am poisonous — don't eat me
choices: I am poisonous — don't eat me
I am looking for a mate
I am too fast to catch
I am guarding my eggs
context: The golden poison frog (Phyllobates terribilis) blazes bright gold-yellow as a warning. A small, toxic rainforest animal WANTS to be seen — camouflage would be the wrong strategy. Advertising 'I am dangerous' with bold color is called aposematism. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_poison_frog; animaldiversity.org/accounts/Dendrobatidae/

question: Curare is the classic Amazon dart poison — jungle hunters have tipped blowgun darts with it for centuries. The golden poison frog (Phyllobates terribilis) carries a skin toxin called batrachotoxin. Put head to head against curare, how does the frog toxin measure up?
answer: Chemically stronger
choices: Chemically stronger
About the same strength
Weaker but faster-acting
Only dangerous when eaten
context: Batrachotoxin from the golden poison frog is chemically stronger than curare, the classic dart poison — and terribilis carries roughly twenty times more toxin than any other poison-dart frog, which is why it alone can arm a dart with a single living touch. Source: American Museum of Natural History Bulletin v.161 art.2 (Myers, Daly & Malkin, 1978), digitallibrary.amnh.org/items/d82fffd4-13a8-4bc0-97df-40e96e7e6f14

question: The golden poison frog (Phyllobates terribilis) carries so much batrachotoxin on its bright skin that biologists measured a single frog's dose against a startling yardstick. Enough poison to kill roughly how many is on one frog?
answer: About 10 adult humans
choices: About 10 adult humans
About 2 adult humans
A single small bird
A dozen insects
context: A single golden poison frog carries enough batrachotoxin on its skin to kill around 10 adult humans (or about 20,000 mice). The Latin name terribilis means 'terrible'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_poison_frog; blog.fundtheplanet.net/rainforest-biodiversity/golden-poison-frog-phyllobates-terribilis/

question: Here is the twist about poison dart frogs that surprises everyone: a golden poison frog (Phyllobates terribilis) raised in a captive tank slowly turns HARMLESS. Why would the deadliest frog on Earth lose its poison?
answer: It steals its poison from the toxic bugs it eats
choices: It steals its poison from the toxic bugs it eats
Its skin only turns toxic in cold water
It makes poison only during breeding season
It loses toxicity as it grows older
context: Poison dart frogs don't make their own poison — they sequester it from the toxic ants, mites and beetles they eat in the wild. Off that diet, the frog gradually becomes harmless. The prime suspect for terribilis' batrachotoxin is a tiny beetle in the family Melyridae, which makes the very same toxin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_poison_frog; enviroliteracy.org/animals/what-makes-the-golden-frog-poisonous/  (Legend.)

question: The Emberá Chocó people of western Colombia arm blowgun darts using a living golden poison frog (Phyllobates terribilis) — they don't even need to kill it. So little poison arms so many darts. One frog supplies enough to tip roughly how many?
answer: 30 to 50 darts
choices: 30 to 50 darts
2 or 3 darts
A single dart
Several hundred darts
context: The frog is so toxic the darts are simply rubbed across its back while it lives; one frog tips 30 to 50 darts, which stay lethal for about a year. Only terribilis carries enough — roughly twenty times more toxin than other dart frogs — to arm a dart with a single living touch. Source: American Museum of Natural History Bulletin v.161 art.2 (Myers, Daly & Malkin, 1978), digitallibrary.amnh.org/items/d82fffd4-13a8-4bc0-97df-40e96e7e6f14  (Legend.)

question: Batrachotoxin from the golden poison frog causes runaway, unstoppable signaling — nerves and muscles fire endlessly until the victim is locked in irreversible paralysis. It does this by attacking one specific piece of cellular machinery. Which one?
answer: Voltage-gated sodium channels
choices: Voltage-gated sodium channels
Potassium channels
Acetylcholine receptors
Calcium pumps
context: Batrachotoxin jams voltage-gated sodium channels permanently open, so nerves and muscles fire endlessly — irreversible paralysis. The frog survives its own poison because a single amino-acid swap (asparagine to threonine) in its own sodium channels stops the toxin from binding. Source: pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1707873114 (Wang & Wang, PNAS 2017)

question: An orange-and-black monarch butterfly (Danaus plexippus) is dangerous to eat — but the butterfly never brewed its own poison. It got dosed as a hungry caterpillar. Which plant loaded it with bitter toxins?
answer: Milkweed
choices: Milkweed
Clover
Oak leaves
Wild rose
context: The monarch caterpillar eats milkweed and stores its bitter cardiac-glycoside toxins, so the adult butterfly is poisonous to eat — the same steal-your-poison trick the dart frogs pull, one rung over. The toxin ends up concentrated most in the wings and abdomen. Source: monarchwatch.org/blog/2020/11/05/monarch-coloration-milkweed-toxins-and-predation-by-birds/

question: A bird snaps up a bright red-and-black ladybug (family Coccinellidae) and instantly drops it, disgusted. The beetle didn't bite or run — it oozed a yellow fluid straight from its own knee joints. What is that fluid loaded with?
answer: Alkaloids like coccinelline
choices: Alkaloids like coccinelline
Sticky tree sap
A cloud of stinging acid
Sugary nectar to distract
context: Ladybugs 'reflex-bleed' — when grabbed they squeeze bitter yellow fluid from the knee-like joints of their legs. The fluid carries alkaloids like coccinelline, so the beetle tastes foul and a bird spits it out. The bright red-and-black is the honest warning label. Source: colorado.edu/asmagazine/2020/07/21/ladybugs-bright-colors-advertise-toxic-chemical-defenses

question: A striped skunk's bold black-and-white pattern isn't just for show — it works like an arrow. When a predator sees the stripes, where are they pointing?
answer: Back toward the glands that fire its spray
choices: Back toward the glands that fire its spray
Toward its face and sharp teeth
Down at its digging claws
Up at a raised, bushy tail alone
context: The skunk's stripe is an honest warning that points, arrow-like, back toward the glands that fire its spray. Predators mostly aren't born fearing it — they learn by trial and error to avoid the pattern after one bad encounter. Source: nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/skunks-stripes-warning-colors-predators

question: A 2023 study compared striped skunks across regions with very different numbers of predators, expecting one fixed coat. Instead the black-and-white pattern shifted from place to place. Where mammal predators were plentiful, the stripes turned out…
answer: Bolder and more symmetrical
choices: Bolder and more symmetrical
Fainter and messier
Wider but grayer
Exactly the same everywhere
context: The 2023 study found skunks have bolder, more symmetrical stripes where mammal predators are many, and fainter, messier stripes where predators are sparse. A warning only pays off if there's an audience to teach: no predators, no reason to pay for a loud advertisement — proof that warning color is only worth its cost where predators exist. Source: phys.org/news/2023-11-skunks-stripes-prominent-predators-sparse.html

question: The harmless hoverfly wears a wasp's yellow-and-black stripes and pinched waist — some even jab their stingless abdomen into a bird's grip to fake a jab — yet they cannot sting at all. Biologists have a name for what this stingless copycat is pulling on the wasp. What is it?
answer: Free-riding on the wasp's honest warning
choices: Free-riding on the wasp's honest warning
Two dangerous species sharing one warning
Startling the bird with a sudden bluff
Hiding by blending into the wasp swarm
context: This is Batesian mimicry: a harmless free-rider copying a dangerous animal's honest warning at no cost of its own. Birds that avoid real wasps avoid the fraud too. Contrast Müllerian mimicry, where two GENUINELY toxic species share one pattern and both back it up — as with the monarch and the viceroy, long mislabeled a Batesian cheat until Ritland and Brower (Nature, 1991) fed birds wingless abdomens and found the viceroy just as bitter. Source: rcannon992.com/2024/09/25/a-see-through-hoverfly-and-other-imperfect-wasp-mimics/; nature.com/articles/350497a0

question: Warning color only works in daylight, for a predator that can see you. So how does a dogbane tiger moth (Cycnia tenera), fluttering through the pitch-black night, warn off a big brown bat closing in by echolocation — and actually teach that bat to leave its kind alone?
answer: It clicks back at the bat with bursts of ultrasound
choices: It clicks back at the bat with bursts of ultrasound
It puffs out a bitter, throat-catching scent
It coats itself in an oil the bat tastes on contact
It hums a low buzz the bat feels in the air
context: This is acoustic aposematism — a warning broadcast as sound, not color. Naive big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus) quickly learn that clicking moths are noxious and stop hunting them (Hristov & Conner 2005, Naturwissenschaften 92:164-169). The moth makes the clicks with paired thoracic organs called tymbals. A close relative, Bertholdia trigona, pushes the same trick from warning into active defense, firing up to roughly 4,500 ultrasonic clicks per second to JAM the bat's sonar outright (Corcoran, Barber & Conner 2009, Science 325:325-327). Grokipedia; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19608920.  (Legend.)

question: Batrachotoxin kills by jamming sodium channels open, yet the golden poison frog (Phyllobates terribilis) carries a lethal dose on its own skin and shrugs it off. The textbook said its channels must carry a resistance mutation — until a 2021 study found those channels are still fully sensitive to the toxin. So what do researchers now suspect protects the frog?
answer: A protein that soaks up the toxin before it hits the channels
choices: A protein that soaks up the toxin before it hits the channels
A skin layer too dense for the toxin to pass inward
An enzyme that splits the toxin into harmless pieces
Gut microbes that neutralize the poison as it forms
context: The old story — that toxic frogs and birds evolved batrachotoxin-resistant channels — collapsed when Abderemane-Ali et al. found the sodium channels of poison frogs AND toxic pitohui birds are still sensitive to the toxin (2021, J. Gen. Physiol. 153(9):e202112872). Their proposed 'toxin sponge' — a protein that binds and sequesters batrachotoxin before it reaches the channels — is a hypothesis, not a settled answer; how these animals resist their own poison is still an open question. rupress.org/jgp/article/153/9/e202112872; UCSF news 2021.

question: A whale surfaces and, without lifting its face from the water, breathes through a hole on top of its head. That blowhole is not a brand-new organ invented for swimming. Over millions of years, which body part slowly migrated up the skull to become it?
answer: The nose
choices: The nose
The throat
The ear
The eye
context: A whale's blowhole is its nose. Over millions of years the nostrils migrated backward and up the skull until they sat on top of the head, so the animal could breathe just by breaking the surface. Source: UC Berkeley Evolution 101, 'The Evolution of Whales'.

question: Pakicetus, from about 50 million years ago, was a wolf-sized creature with long jaws and sharp meat-eating teeth that ran around the edges of ancient rivers on four legs. What single hidden clue in its skull revealed that this land-running beast belongs on the whale family tree?
answer: A whale-only structure in its ear
choices: A whale-only structure in its ear
Blubber preserved under its skin
A blowhole opening on its head
Fins where its front legs should be
context: Pakicetus was a wolf-sized, four-legged land animal (1 to 2 m long) that lived in and around water, yet its ear already carried the whale involucrum, the clue linking this running land beast to modern whales. Source: UC Berkeley Evolution 101; Thewissen et al. 2001, Pakicetus attocki.

question: Basilosaurus was a fully aquatic whale stretching 15 to 18 meters, shaped like a sea serpent, cruising the oceans about 40 million years ago. Dangling far down its long body, scientists found something startling for a creature that never left the water. What?
answer: A pair of tiny back legs with knees and toes
choices: A pair of tiny back legs with knees and toes
A set of gills tucked behind its ribs
A row of bony plates along its spine
A second smaller mouth near its tail
context: Basilosaurus still had tiny back legs, complete with a working knee joint and little three-toed feet, far too small to walk or help it swim, a leftover from its land-walking past. LEGEND-level fossil. Source: Gingerich et al. 1990, 'Hind Limbs of Eocene Basilosaurus'; Wikipedia: Basilosaurus.

question: In July 1919, a female humpback caught off Vancouver Island stunned whalers with something no whale is supposed to have: a pair of real limbs sticking four feet out of its body. Explorer Roy Chapman Andrews examined the bones and identified them as belonging to what?
answer: A leg, with shin and foot bones
choices: A leg, with shin and foot bones
An extra flipper, with fin rays
A twin calf, partly formed
A giant tumor, full of teeth
context: Very rarely a whale's genetic 'off switch' fails and it is born with real hind legs. Andrews identified a shin bone and foot bone, a throwback to the whale's land-walking ancestors. LEGEND-level. Source: Andrews 1921, AMNH, 'A Remarkable Case of External Hind Limbs in a Humpback Whale'.

question: About a month into a whale embryo's development, tiny buds appear that in most mammals would grow into back legs, then they mysteriously shrink and vanish, leaving the whale legless. What halts them is the disappearance of a single developmental signal. Which one goes missing?
answer: The Sonic hedgehog signal
choices: The Sonic hedgehog signal
The insulin growth signal
The melanin color signal
The keratin scale signal
context: A whale embryo sprouts hind-limb buds about a month in, then a genetic 'off switch' — the Sonic hedgehog signal going missing — halts them and the buds shrink away. Source: Thewissen et al. 2006, PNAS, 'Developmental basis for hind-limb loss in dolphins'.

question: Buried deep inside a living whale's body float a pair of small hip bones, left over from its walking ancestors, with no leg attached. A 2014 study found these bones are far from useless. What job do they still perform?
answer: Anchoring the muscles that control the penis
choices: Anchoring the muscles that control the penis
Storing extra oxygen for long dives
Filtering salt out of the bloodstream
Balancing the whale as it rolls and turns
context: The 2014 study showed these vestigial pelvic bones anchor the muscles controlling the penis, and grow larger in species where males compete hardest to mate. Source: Dines et al. 2014, 'Sexual selection targets cetacean pelvic bones', Evolution.

question: For years, one question nagged at whale researchers: which land animals are a whale's closest living cousins? A distinctive double-pulley ankle bone, preserved in early whale fossils like Rodhocetus and found only in even-toed hoofed mammals, finally settled it. Which living animal is the whale's nearest relative on land?
answer: The hippopotamus
choices: The hippopotamus
The camel
The pig
The deer
context: The double-pulley ankle bone (astragalus) is found only in even-toed hoofed mammals; its presence in early whales revealed the hippopotamus as the whale's nearest living land relative. Source: UC Berkeley Evolution 101; Wikipedia: Evolution of cetaceans.

question: At the very root of the whale line sits an unlikely creature: Indohyus, a raccoon-sized, deer-like plant-eater from about 48 million years ago. Its ear carried the whale involucrum, and its bones were strangely dense and heavy. What did those heavy bones let this little animal do?
answer: Wade and hide underwater from predators
choices: Wade and hide underwater from predators
Burrow deep tunnels through hard clay
Butt heads in fierce mating contests
Glide between trees on stretched skin
context: Indohyus had unusually dense, heavy bones that let it wade and hide underwater from predators, much as a hippo does today, plus the whale ear bone that gave away its place at the root of the whale line. LEGEND-level fossil. Source: Thewissen et al. 2007, Nature; ScienceDaily.

question: Maiacetus, a 47.5-million-year-old whale from Pakistan, was fossilized as a female with a smaller skeleton curled inside her pelvis. Modern whales are born tail-first, a safeguard that keeps the calf from drowning during the slow underwater delivery. This little skeleton lay the opposite way, head-first, and Philip Gingerich's team drew a bold, still-debated conclusion from it. Which one?
answer: The mother had hauled out onto land to give birth
choices: The mother had hauled out onto land to give birth
The birth happened in shallows, head held clear
The tiny skeleton is swallowed prey, not a calf
The head-first pose is a fluke of decay, not birth
context: Philip Gingerich's team described Maiacetus inuus in 2009 (PLoS ONE) from a fossil pregnant female whose calf lay head-first, the way land mammals are delivered. Because a head-down birth underwater would drown the calf, they read this as a sign that these early whales still came ashore to give birth, a halfway stage in the move from land to sea. The find is genuinely contested: Hans Thewissen argued the small skeleton might be scattered or swallowed bones rather than a true fetus, and Gingerich's team countered that the tiny skull bears no tooth marks, so it was never eaten. Sources: Wikipedia 'Maiacetus'; ScienceDaily / University of Michigan 2009 release on Gingerich et al., PLoS ONE 2009; grokipedia.com/page/Maiacetus.  (Legend.)

question: Divers who drift beside a whale shark love to point out that, for all its size and its name, it is not actually a whale at all. What is it?
answer: The largest fish alive on Earth today
choices: The largest fish alive on Earth today
The largest ray gliding in the open sea
A basking-shark cousin the size of a truck
A giant grouper of the deep coral reefs
context: The whale shark (Rhincodon typus) is a shark — specifically a carpet shark — and the biggest fish alive. It breathes through gills and never surfaces for air the way a whale, a mammal, must. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whale_shark

question: A swimmer can drift right alongside a cruising whale shark in perfect safety — unlike a great white, this giant swims with its mouth hanging wide open not to bite but to do what?
answer: Strain tiny plankton, krill, and fish eggs from the water
choices: Strain tiny plankton, krill, and fish eggs from the water
Gulp seals and large fish whole
Suck in air to fill a swim bladder
Wash sand and grit out over its gills
context: The whale shark is a gentle filter-feeder. It glides with its mouth open and sieves out plankton, krill, and fish eggs, harmless to the swimmers drifting beside it. Source: https://www.floridamuseum.ufl.edu/discover-fish/species-profiles/whale-shark/

question: A whale shark pushes more than 6,000 liters of seawater through its mouth every hour, and any ordinary sieve would clog solid within minutes under that flood of food. The trick that keeps its filter clear even has a name. What is that trick called?
answer: Cross-flow filtration
choices: Cross-flow filtration
Reverse osmosis
Capillary action
Peristaltic pumping
context: The whale shark's mouth uses cross-flow filtration: the water flows along the filter surface rather than straight through it, sweeping particles past the pads toward the throat instead of packing them into the mesh — so the sieve never clogs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whale_shark

question: A whale shark has no eyelids to shut, leaving its eyes exposed to a sea full of scrapes and stinging drifters. When something threatens an eye, how does the shark shield it?
answer: It pulls the whole eyeball partway back into the socket
choices: It pulls the whole eyeball partway back into the socket
It clouds the eye with a burst of dark ink
It rolls belly-up so the eye faces the seafloor
It seals the eye behind a bony sliding plate
context: Lacking eyelids, the whale shark can retract the eyeball into its head — drawing it back like a snail pulling into its shell — to protect the exposed eye. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/whale-sharks-have-tiny-teeth-their-eyeballs-180975240/

question: In 2020 scientists put a whale shark's eye under a microscope and found something no one expected: clustered around the iris were more than 3,000 tiny structures, each shaped like an oak leaf. What are they?
answer: Tooth-like scales — the shark has teeth on its eyes
choices: Tooth-like scales — the shark has teeth on its eyes
Light-sensing dimples that glow in the dark
Salt glands that squeeze seawater out of the eye
Suckers that grip prey drifting too close
context: The whale shark's eyeball is armored with over 3,000 dermal denticles — the same tooth-like scales that cover a shark's skin — clustered around the iris. Each looks like an oak leaf under magnification. The whale shark literally has teeth on its eyes. Source: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0235342  (Legend.)

question: A researcher meets a whale shark, snaps a clear photo of the patch of white spots just behind its gills, and drops the shot into a database of thousands. What can that one photo do that a photo of the shark's fin or tail cannot?
answer: Match it to a specific individual seen years earlier and oceans away
choices: Match it to a specific individual seen years earlier and oceans away
Estimate the shark's total body length
Reveal whether the shark is male or female
Show which regional population it belongs to
context: No two whale sharks share the same spot pattern, so the spots behind the gills serve as a natural fingerprint. A single clear photo of that patch lets scientists re-identify one specific individual against databases of thousands, even years later and oceans apart. Source: https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/whale-shark-identification-catalog-telescope-algorithm  (Legend.)

question: To match one whale shark's spots against a database of thousands, researchers needed to compare patterns fast and reliably. Instead of writing new software, they borrowed an algorithm first invented to do what?
answer: Map the positions of stars for the Hubble Space Telescope
choices: Map the positions of stars for the Hubble Space Telescope
Guide missiles toward heat given off by engines
Read the barcodes on grocery-store packages
Predict tomorrow's weather from cloud photos
context: The photo-ID system uses star-mapping math built for Hubble: the same algorithm that finds patterns of stars in the night sky now finds the right shark by its pattern of spots. Source: https://spinoff.nasa.gov/Spinoff2009/er_1.html  (Legend.)

question: In 2011 researchers tagged a female whale shark named Anne off Panama and tracked the longest whale-shark journey ever recorded — more than 20,000 kilometers. Where did that epic swim finally take her?
answer: To the Mariana Trench near Guam
choices: To the Mariana Trench near Guam
To the Galapagos Islands off Ecuador
To the reefs of the Maldives
To Australia's Ningaloo Reef
context: Anne, tagged off Panama's Coiba Island, swam 20,142 km clear across the Pacific to the Mariana Trench near Guam — the longest whale-shark migration ever documented. The Galapagos, Maldives, and Ningaloo are all real whale-shark hotspots, but Anne's track ended at Guam. Source: https://stri.si.edu/story/mystery-migration  (Legend.)

question: A whale shark's dim-light eye pigment carries a single mutation — the very change that, in a human, causes congenital night blindness. Yet in the shark it sharpens vision in the black water nearly two kilometers down. The mutation also leaves the pigment fragile, and that fragility is the whole trick. What switches this deep-sea vision on?
answer: The cold of the deep, where the fragile pigment holds together only when chilled and dissolves in warmth
choices: The cold of the deep, where the fragile pigment holds together only when chilled and dissolves in warmth
The crushing pressure of the deep, which forces the loose pigment down into its working form
The utter darkness of the deep, which shields the delicate pigment from light that would bleach it
The thin oxygen of the deep, which keeps the fragile pigment from slowly oxidizing itself away
context: Osaka Metropolitan University researchers Koyanagi and Terakita reported this in PNAS in March 2023. The whale shark's rhodopsin — the pigment that lets any vertebrate see in dim light — carries an amino-acid swap at a known spectral-tuning site (position 94) that shifts its peak sensitivity toward blue, the one color of light that still reaches the deep sea. The very same substitution in humans causes congenital stationary night blindness. What makes it work for the shark is that the altered pigment is thermally unstable: it degrades in warm surface water but functions perfectly in the cold of the deep, so the animal's own body temperature acts as an on/off switch for deep vision — blue-tuned sight that literally would not survive at the surface. Source: Koyanagi & Terakita et al., PNAS, 2023 (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2220728120); Science/AAAS coverage ('Mutation behind night blindness in humans helps whale sharks see in the dark') and Osaka Metropolitan University via EurekAlert.

question: A whale shark grows no bones, so for decades its true age was pure guesswork. Then researchers sectioned the vertebrae of long-dead sharks and matched a signal in the stacked growth bands to a dated moment in human history — proving one band forms per year. What global event gave them that calibration?
answer: The Cold War atomic-bomb tests, which stamped a burst of radioactive carbon into the bands year by year
choices: The Cold War atomic-bomb tests, which stamped a burst of radioactive carbon into the bands year by year
The Industrial Revolution, whose coal smoke shifted the ocean's carbon chemistry into the bands
The Chernobyl meltdown, which spread a pulse of radioactive cesium through the world's warming seas
The spread of leaded gasoline, whose lead settled year by year into the shark's growing cartilage
context: Because whale sharks have no bones, their age was long a matter of guesswork. Ong, Campana, Meekan and colleagues (2020, Frontiers in Marine Science) sectioned the cartilage vertebrae of long-dead sharks and matched the carbon-14 in successive growth bands against the global radiocarbon spike left by atmospheric atomic-bomb tests of the 1950s–60s — proving that one band is laid down per year. One Taiwan specimen was thereby confirmed at exactly 50 years old at death, the first unambiguous age ever pinned to the species. Crucially, band formation never stopped even in the oldest sharks, implying a true lifespan of a century or more. Source: Ong, Campana & Meekan et al., Frontiers in Marine Science, 2020 (frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fmars.2020.00188/full); phys.org / ScienceDaily, 'Cold War nuclear bomb tests reveal true age of whale sharks,' 2020-04-06.

question: An ostrich cannot fly, a penguin swims instead of soars, and an emu just runs — yet all three wear one body covering that instantly marks them as birds. What is it?
answer: Feathers
choices: Feathers
Scales
Fur
Slime
context: Feathers are the single feature unique to birds — NO other living animal grows them. Not flight, not eggs, not nests — plenty of other animals do those. But feathers belong to birds alone, so a flightless ostrich or penguin is still unmistakably a bird. Penguins even use their feathers for waterproofing and warmth in freezing water. Source: Audubon Magazine, 'The Multiple Miracles of Bird Feathers'; Cornell Lab of Ornithology.

question: Open a chicken's mouth and you'll find something a dog, a snake, or a shark all have but this bird completely lacks — a jaw full of teeth. Instead of chewing, a bird's mouth is capped with what?
answer: A toothless keratin beak
choices: A toothless keratin beak
A leathery grinding gizzard plate
A forked flicking tongue
A pouch of stinging spines
context: Birds have no teeth at all. A beak (bill) of keratin — the same stuff as your fingernails — replaces the toothy jaws their dinosaur ancestors carried. Source: Britannica, 'Why Don't Birds Have Teeth?'; Forbes/GrrlScientist.

question: To fly, a bird must be light — so its skeleton pulls a trick a running mammal's dense bones never do. Snap a bird's leg bone and it's startlingly light for its size. What's inside instead?
answer: Hollow air spaces linked to the lungs
choices: Hollow air spaces linked to the lungs
Solid heavy marrow like ours
A core of stored body fat
A rod of springy cartilage
