context: A bird's bones are 'pneumatic' — hollow and air-filled, laced with extensions of the lungs' air sacs. This lightens the skeleton so the bird weighs less in the air. Source: UCMP Berkeley, 'Morphology of the Aves'; Biology LibreTexts 29.5 Birds.

question: Not every bird carries the same number of feathers. Four birds that all live cold, wet lives on frozen northern water were counted — and one turned up wearing over 25,000 feathers, while a tiny ruby-throated hummingbird got by with just 940. Which of these cold-water birds wore the most?
answer: The tundra swan
choices: The tundra swan
The common loon
The Canada goose
The mallard
context: The tundra (whistling) swan holds the record at over 25,000 feathers — a cold, watery life demands dense insulation. A robin sits in the middle around 2,500, and the ruby-throated hummingbird has the fewest counted, just 940. Source: Audubon, 'The Multiple Miracles of Bird Feathers'; Bird Watcher's General Store.

question: The wishbone kids snap for luck after Thanksgiving dinner isn't just a carving-table game — in a live bird it's a springy brace that flexes and rebounds with every wingbeat, storing and releasing energy on the downstroke. Anatomically, which bones is it?
answer: The fused collarbones
choices: The fused collarbones
The fused shoulder blades
The fused breast plates
The fused tail bones
context: The wishbone is the furcula — a pair of fused collarbones. It acts as a spring and brace during the wing's downstroke, storing and releasing energy with each beat. Source: UCMP Berkeley, 'Morphology of the Aves'.

question: Feathers are so tied to flight that we assume they evolved FOR it — but the fossil record flips that story. When feathers first appeared on small ground-running theropod dinosaurs, those animals couldn't fly at all. So what were the first feathers most likely for?
answer: Keeping warm or showing off
choices: Keeping warm or showing off
Gripping prey while hunting
Filtering food from water
Digging burrows in sand
context: Feathers first appeared as simple filaments on ground-running theropods, probably for insulation or display, and were only later re-purposed ('exapted') for flight. Feathers came before flight, not the other way around. Source: Scientific American, 'Dinosaur Feathers Came before Birds and Flight'; Smithsonian Magazine. LEGEND.

question: Birds descend from small feathered theropod dinosaurs — which leads to a startling family fact. When scientists recovered protein (collagen) from a T. rex bone and matched it against living animals, one common barnyard bird came out as a closer relative of T. rex than a crocodile is. Which?
answer: The chicken
choices: The chicken
The pigeon
The duck
The turkey
context: The collagen recovered from T. rex bone matched the chicken more closely than any other living animal tested. Because birds ARE theropod dinosaurs, a chicken really is a closer relative of T. rex than of a crocodile. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'T. Rex Linked to Chickens, Ostriches'; Science (Asara et al. 2008). LEGEND.

question: A biologist wants the one feature that no other kind of animal on Earth shares — the single trait that defines every mammal from a mouse to a blue whale. Which does every mammal mother, and only a mammal mother, do?
answer: Feed her babies milk from her own body
choices: Feed her babies milk from her own body
Lay eggs in a warm nest
Carry her young inside a pouch
Breathe air through her skin
context: Milk from mammary glands is THE defining mammal trait — no other animal group makes milk. Carl Linnaeus named the whole class 'Mammalia' in 1758 after these milk-making glands. Source: Britannica 'Mammal'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal.

question: Run your hand over a wolf, a bat, a mouse, and a house cat and they all share one covering you can feel with your fingers. Every mammal has this at some point in its life. What is it?
answer: Hair or fur
choices: Hair or fur
Feathers
Scales
Slime
context: All mammals grow hair or fur at some point in life — it helps trap body heat. Linnaeus could have named the class 'Pilosa,' meaning 'the hairy ones,' but chose milk instead. Source: ScienceInsights 'What Makes a Mammal'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal.

question: A humpback whale looks completely bald as it glides through the ocean, yet biologists find one small thing still growing on its chin and snout for its whole life. What is it?
answer: A sparse row of whiskers
choices: A sparse row of whiskers
A cluster of barnacles
A patch of thick calluses
A fringe of baleen bristles
context: Baleen whales like the humpback and bowhead keep a thin row of whiskers on the chin and snout. Each hair sits in a nerve-packed follicle that senses water pressure and currents — an underwater feeler. Source: Drake et al. 2015, The Anatomical Record; whalescientists.com.

question: The duck-billed platypus of Australia stuns people twice over: it makes milk like any mammal, yet it lays leathery eggs. Only one other kind of living mammal pulls off that same egg-laying trick. Which is it?
answer: The echidnas
choices: The echidnas
The kangaroos
The koalas
The wombats
context: The platypus and the echidnas — together called monotremes — are the only mammals that lay eggs. Like all mammals, the mothers still make milk. Kangaroos, koalas, and wombats are Australian mammals but give live birth. Source: Australian Museum; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monotreme.

question: The platypus is a mammal, so its babies live on their mother's milk. But the way a baby platypus feeds surprises everyone who expects it to nurse like a puppy. How does it actually get its milk?
answer: It laps milk that seeps through skin on the mother's belly
choices: It laps milk that seeps through skin on the mother's belly
It drinks from a nipple like other mammals
It swallows milk the mother spits up
It absorbs milk through the eggshell
context: A platypus has no nipples — it 'sweats' milk through patches of belly skin, and the babies lap it off the fur. This is thought to be close to how the very first mammals nursed, before nipples existed. Source: milkgenomics.org 'A Time Before Nipples'; PMC4224336.

question: Every mammal hides a signature deep inside the ear that no reptile or bird can match. Reptiles and birds carry just one bone in the middle ear — how many does a mammal pack into that same space?
answer: Three
choices: Three
One
Six
Zero
context: A mammal's middle ear holds three tiny bones — the malleus, incus, and stapes (hammer, anvil, and stirrup). No other animal has all three; reptiles and birds have only one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ossicles; evolution.berkeley.edu 'Jaws to ears'.

question: Deep in the human ear sits the stirrup bone, the stapes — one of the three bones that mark us as mammals. It holds a record no other bone in your body can claim. What is remarkable about the stapes?
answer: It is the smallest bone in the whole body
choices: It is the smallest bone in the whole body
It is the hardest bone in the whole body
It is the only bone that keeps growing forever
It is the only bone with no blood supply
context: The stapes is the smallest bone in the human body — only 2 to 3 millimeters long, about the size of a grain of rice. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stapes; my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/ossicles.

question: Two of the three tiny bones in every mammal's ear — the hammer and the anvil — did not start out as ear bones at all. Trace them back through evolution and where do they come from?
answer: Bones at the back of a reptile's jaw
choices: Bones at the back of a reptile's jaw
A fish's throat gills
A bird's wishbone
A dinosaur's tail spine
context: The malleus and incus began as the articular and quadrate — bones at the back of a reptile's jaw. Over evolution they shrank and migrated into the ear, one of the clearest transitions in the whole fossil record. Source: evolution.berkeley.edu 'Jaws to ears'; PMC3552421.

question: Morganucodon, a shrew-sized creature from about 200 million years ago, was found with two separate jaw hinges working side by side in the same skull. That strange double hinge stunned paleontologists. What did it reveal?
answer: One hinge's bones were turning into ear bones
choices: One hinge's bones were turning into ear bones
Mammals and reptiles once interbred
The jaw evolved only after the ear was finished
The double hinge let it chew and swallow at once
context: Morganucodon had a double jaw joint — the new mammal joint and the old reptile joint together, one still working the jaw while the other was becoming ear bones. It is one of the most iconic transitional fossils known. Source: AMNH; Britannica 'Morganucodon'. (Legend-tier wonder.)

question: On a riverbank you spot two creatures that look almost like twins: a little lizard and a salamander, the same size and color. A naturalist tells you the surest way to tell them apart isn't the eyes or the toes - it's to touch them. What does your hand feel that gives it away instantly?
answer: The lizard is dry and scaly; the salamander is smooth and moist
choices: The lizard is dry and scaly; the salamander is smooth and moist
The lizard is warm; the salamander is icy cold
The lizard is soft; the salamander is hard and bony
The lizard is sticky; the salamander is dry and dusty
context: A reptile's skin is dry and scaly (that's the lizard); an amphibian's is smooth, moist, and slimy (that's the salamander). Even when a dry lizard and a wet salamander look almost alike, the feel gives it away at once. Source: Forest Preserve District of Will County / National Aquarium  -  'A lizard's skin is dry and scaly, while a salamander's is usually smooth and moist.'

question: The word 'amphibian' comes from Greek and means 'double life.' A frog earns that name not by living in two places at once, but by living two different lives in sequence  -  one body, then a completely rebuilt second body. What is the 'double life' actually describing?
answer: A water-breathing tadpole that transforms into an air-breathing adult
choices: A water-breathing tadpole that transforms into an air-breathing adult
A creature that can survive equally in salt water and fresh water
An animal that is awake by night and asleep by day
A body that switches between male and female as it ages
context: 'Amphibian' loosely translates from the Greek as 'dual life,' a nod to the two-stage cycle: it begins as a gilled, water-breathing larva (a tadpole), then transforms through metamorphosis into an air-breathing adult with lungs and legs. Source: Wikipedia, Amphibian.

question: A pond-side guide warns you about a classic mix-up: people see a small, four-legged, tail-dragging creature and call it a lizard, when it's really a newt  -  an amphibian. Besides the wet, slimy feel, what two things does a real lizard have that a newt never does?
answer: Clawed toes and external ear holes
choices: Clawed toes and external ear holes
A forked tongue and a rattling tail
Webbed feet and a fin along its back
A hard shell and a beak
context: Lizards are reptiles with dry, tough scales, clawed toes, and external ear openings; newts and salamanders are amphibians with no scales, no claws, and moist slimy skin. Wet and clawless means amphibian. Source: Discover Wildlife / Forest Preserve.

question: A frog can hop far from the pond to hunt bugs, but come breeding season it is chained straight back to the water's edge and cannot lay anywhere else. A desert lizard is under no such rule. What is it about the frog's EGGS that ties its whole life to water?
answer: The eggs have no shell, so in dry air they would shrivel up
choices: The eggs have no shell, so in dry air they would shrivel up
The eggs must be kept warm by the parent's body heat
The eggs are too heavy for the frog to carry overland
The eggs will only hatch in complete darkness
context: An amphibian's egg has no shell, so it dries out in air  -  which is why frogs and salamanders must lay their jelly-covered eggs in water. That single fact chains their whole life to ponds and streams. Source: Encyclopedia.com / Biology LibreTexts.

question: A snake lies stretched across a warm rock at dawn, unmoving, and won't strike at prey until the sun has climbed higher. It isn't lazy  -  it physically cannot hunt yet. Why does the snake need the rock and the sunlight before it can act?
answer: It makes almost no body heat of its own and must warm up from outside
choices: It makes almost no body heat of its own and must warm up from outside
It is blind until bright daylight sharpens its eyes
It must dry the morning dew off its scales before it can grip
It digests its last meal only while lying perfectly still
context: Reptiles are ectotherms  -  'cold-blooded'  -  producing almost no body heat of their own, so a snake or lizard must bask in the sun to warm up before it can hunt, then retreat to shade to cool down. The sun is its furnace. Source: Britannica-consensus.

question: Here's the puzzle at the heart of the reptile-amphibian split: a lizard can bake all day on a sun-blasted desert rock and cross open sand, while a salamander left in the same spot would be dead within the hour. Both are small four-legged animals  -  so what does the lizard's skin do that the salamander's cannot?
answer: Seals water inside the body with a thick, waxy, keratin-packed layer
choices: Seals water inside the body with a thick, waxy, keratin-packed layer
Reflects the sun's heat with a mirror-like silvery sheen
Stores a hidden reservoir of water in pockets under the scales
Sweats to cool the body down like a running animal
context: A reptile's main problem is preventing water loss through the skin, solved by a thick stratum corneum with waxes layered between keratinized cells. That waterproof seal is exactly why a reptile can bake on a rock or cross a desert while an amphibian, whose skin must stay wet, cannot. Source: Britannica, Integument  -  Reptiles.

question: Let a frog's skin dry out and it dies within hours, even sitting in clean, open air with its lungs working normally. The wetness isn't for comfort or camouflage, and it isn't just to keep from overheating. What job is the moist skin secretly doing that makes drying out fatal?
answer: Acting as a working lung, pulling oxygen straight through into the blood
choices: Acting as a working lung, pulling oxygen straight through into the blood
Cooling the body by constant evaporation off the wet surface
Storing venom that leaks out only while the skin is wet
Sensing the tiny vibrations of insects walking nearby
context: An amphibian's moist skin is a major organ of respiration: oxygen passes straight through the thin, wet skin into blood vessels just beneath  -  cutaneous respiration. That's the real reason the skin must stay damp, and why an amphibian can't survive in the salty sea. Source: Wikipedia, Cutaneous respiration & Amphibian.

question: The largest salamander family on Earth, the plethodontids, thrive in cool wet forests with a body plan that would kill almost any other four-legged land animal. These salamanders have no lungs at all. So where does their oxygen actually come from?
answer: Through the skin and the moist lining of the mouth
choices: Through the skin and the moist lining of the mouth
Through a pair of gills kept hidden under the throat
Through tiny air tubes running along the spine
Through swallowed air stored in a balloon-like gut
context: The Plethodontidae are the largest group of salamanders despite having no lungs whatsoever  -  they breathe entirely through their skin and the lining of their mouths, a stunning proof of how well skin-breathing works. Source: Wikipedia, Cutaneous respiration.

question: Air reaches the cells deep inside a grasshopper's body without any lungs doing the work. How does the fresh air get all the way in?
answer: Air seeps in through tiny holes along its sides and runs through branching tubes to the cells
choices: Air seeps in through tiny holes along its sides and runs through branching tubes to the cells
Its heart pumps oxygen-rich blood to the tissues like a mammal's
It absorbs oxygen through its wings while gliding
It swallows air and digests the oxygen in its gut
context: Those side-holes are called spiracles, and the branching tubes are the tracheae; together they pipe outside air directly to nearly every cell, skipping blood entirely. Source: Duke University Library Exhibit, Insect Sizes & Oxygen; Wikipedia, Respiratory system of insects.

question: The tiniest insects don't have to work at breathing at all: fresh air reaches every inner cell on its own, no pumping required. What is it about being so small that lets them get away with this?
answer: The air only has to travel a hair-short distance, so it arrives fast enough
choices: The air only has to travel a hair-short distance, so it arrives fast enough
Their extra-wide breathing holes let far more air rush in at once
Their thin outer shell soaks up oxygen straight from the surrounding air
Their cells burn so little oxygen that a trickle is plenty
context: Oxygen moves through the air tubes on its own, drifting from where it is plentiful to where it is scarce. That drift is fast over the hair-thin distances inside a small insect, so no pump is needed at all; the catch is that it only stays fast over short distances. Source: Duke University Library Exhibit, Insect Sizes & Oxygen.

question: Diffusion feeds a tiny insect's cells effortlessly. But blow that same bug up to the size of a dog and it would quickly die. Why?
answer: The oxygen drifts too slowly to reach the core, so the innermost cells suffocate
choices: The oxygen drifts too slowly to reach the core, so the innermost cells suffocate
The air tubes grow so long the bug can't push the stale air back out
The extra weight crushes the soft breathing holes shut
The blood grows too thick to carry the oxygen inward
context: Diffusion is fast over short distances but painfully slow over long ones. In a huge insect, core cells would starve for oxygen before it ever arrived. Source: Duke University Library Exhibit; eLife, insect respiratory literature.

question: Raise young insects in a sealed chamber where the air is kept low in oxygen, then compare them to normal ones. What happens to how big they grow?
answer: They grow up markedly smaller than normal
choices: They grow up markedly smaller than normal
They grow up markedly larger to grab more air
They grow at exactly the normal size
They stop growing wings but keep their body size
context: Insects reared in low-oxygen air end up much smaller than usual, direct evidence that the oxygen a body can supply, not appetite or genes alone, sets the ceiling on insect size. Source: Duke University Library Exhibit, Insect Sizes & Oxygen; PNAS related work on oxygen and insect body size.

question: A dragonfly you see today spans about a hand-width. Its Carboniferous relative Meganeura, a predator that snatched other insects out of the air, spread wings to a startling breadth. How wide?
answer: About 70 centimeters, wider than a hawk
choices: About 70 centimeters, wider than a hawk
About 40 centimeters, like a small gull
About 25 centimeters, like a large moth
About 15 centimeters, like a big dragonfly
context: Meganeura, a dragonfly-relative, was one of the largest flying insects that ever lived, with a wingspan around 65 to 75 cm, over two feet across. Source: Wikipedia, Meganeura.  (Legend.)

question: The Carboniferous also had the largest land invertebrate that ever lived: Arthropleura, a millipede-relative over 2.5 meters long and around 50 kilograms. Given that monstrous size, what did this creature actually eat?
answer: Dead and rotting plant matter
choices: Dead and rotting plant matter
Other giant insects it hunted
Small reptiles and amphibians
Fish it caught in rivers
context: Despite being a two-and-a-half-meter bug, Arthropleura was a peaceful detritivore, feeding on the dead plant litter of the ancient forest floor. Source: Wikipedia, Arthropleura.  (Legend.)

question: A big beetle can't just wait for air to drift in on its own. Watch one closely and you'll see it doing something active to force oxygen deeper through its tubes. What does it do?
answer: Squeezes its air tubes flat and lets them spring back, working them like bellows
choices: Squeezes its air tubes flat and lets them spring back, working them like bellows
Flexes its outer shell to press air along the tubes
Reverses the flow so air is pulled out through its mouth
Floods the tubes with fluid to carry oxygen inward
context: Synchrotron X-ray imaging caught insects actively collapsing and reopening their tracheae and pumping their abdomens, working the tubes like tiny bellows to push air along. Source: Science 2003, Westneat et al., synchrotron X-ray imaging of tracheal compression.

question: Scientists X-rayed the biggest beetles and traced a scaling trap: to supply a larger body, the air tubes must swell and take up ever more internal room. In the largest living beetle, how much of the leg is already given over to air tube?
answer: About 90 percent
choices: About 90 percent
About 10 percent
About 40 percent
About 5 percent
context: Extrapolate the trend and the leg fills with trachea, so there's physically no space left to build a larger beetle. Source: PNAS 2007, Kaiser et al.

question: The tidy story that Carboniferous oxygen alone made the insect giants runs into an awkward fossil record. Which stubborn fact keeps that story from being the whole answer?
answer: Giant griffenflies lived on into the Late Permian, long after oxygen had fallen
choices: Giant griffenflies lived on into the Late Permian, long after oxygen had fallen
The very largest griffenflies come from the lowest-oxygen Permian rock beds
Some later times with air just as oxygen-rich produced no insect giants at all
Giant griffenflies shrank steadily even while oxygen was still climbing toward its peak
context: The giant griffenflies (Meganisoptera) persisted into the Late Permian, after oxygen had already dropped well below its Carboniferous peak, so rich air can't be the sole cause of insect gigantism; other factors likely mattered too. Source: Wikipedia, Meganeura, oxygen hypothesis caveat; Wikipedia, Meganisoptera.

question: An insect's air-holes can open and shut, and different species work them in strikingly different ways. One of these patterns has fueled a scientific argument for decades, with no settled winner yet. What does a resting insect using that pattern do with its air-holes?
answer: Keeps them clamped shut for long stretches, then cracks them open in one quick burst
choices: Keeps them clamped shut for long stretches, then cracks them open in one quick burst
Holds them all wide open so fresh air streams steadily to every inner cell
Opens the holes along one side while sealing the other, sweeping air across the body
Squeezes and releases its whole body nonstop, driving a constant current through the tubes
context: Many resting insects don't breathe steadily at all -- they run a 'discontinuous gas exchange cycle': spiracles clamped shut for long stretches, then a brief flutter phase, then one open burst that dumps the built-up CO2. WHY they do it is a genuine, decades-old unsettled debate with three rival explanations, and no consensus has been reached. The hygric hypothesis says sealed air-holes save precious body water from evaporating out. The chthonic hypothesis says the pattern aids gas exchange in low-oxygen, high-CO2 spots like burrows and soil. The oxidative-damage hypothesis says keeping internal oxygen low shields tissues from being 'rusted' by the raw O2 the tracheae deliver straight to the cells. Tests keep partly supporting and partly undercutting each. It sharpens this ladder's core idea: direct tracheal oxygen delivery is a double-edged tool, so insects must actively throttle their air-holes rather than drink air freely. Sources: 'Discontinuous gas exchange' overview (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discontinuous_gas_exchange); Chown et al., PNAS 2007 (pnas.org/content/104/20/8357); review, Physiological & Biochemical Zoology 79(2), 2006.

question: Researchers measured more than 10,500 fossil insect wings spanning the whole history of insects. For most of that history, the largest insects grew and shrank right alongside the oxygen in the air. Then, around 150 million years ago, insect size stopped tracking oxygen -- even though oxygen stayed high. What had taken over as the new ceiling on how big an insect could get?
answer: Nimble birds became airborne hunters, and a bigger insect is a clumsier, easier-to-catch flier
choices: Nimble birds became airborne hunters, and a bigger insect is a clumsier, easier-to-catch flier
Flowering plants spread and reshaped insect diets, favoring smaller, quicker-feeding bodies
A warming climate raised their energy needs, so smaller bodies that shed heat faster won out
Crowded skies full of early flying reptiles squeezed insects into smaller, hidden lives
context: In 2012, paleobiologists Matthew Clapham and Jered Karr compiled the wing lengths of more than 10,500 fossil insects across the entire fossil record. For most of insect history, maximum body size closely tracked atmospheric oxygen -- strong support for the oxygen-limitation idea. But around 150 million years ago, in the Late Jurassic, size stopped following oxygen even though oxygen remained high. That decoupling coincides with the radiation of birds: agile, size-selective aerial predators. Because a flying insect's maneuverability drops as it grows, larger insects became easier to catch -- so predation, not air chemistry, set the new limit. This is the concrete 'what else besides oxygen' behind the older observation that giant griffenflies outlived peak Carboniferous oxygen. (Exact ancient oxygen levels are themselves estimated from geological proxies.) Source: Clapham & Karr, 'Environmental and biotic controls on the evolutionary history of insect body size,' PNAS 2012 (doi:10.1073/pnas.1204026109; PubMed 22665762).

question: About 13,000 years ago, sabre-tooth cats and one big pack-hunting predator prowled the swampy ground where downtown Los Angeles now stands, and their bones piled up in the La Brea Tar Pits by the thousands. More than 4,000 individuals of one hunter were pulled from that sticky trap - the single most common animal found there. Which ice-age predator was it?
answer: The dire wolf
choices: The dire wolf
The gray wolf
The coyote
The American cheetah
context: Aenocyon dirus (renamed from Canis dirus in 2021) is the most common mammal recovered from La Brea - over 4,000 individuals. Dire wolves and sabre-tooth cats vanished from the site roughly 13,000 years ago. Source: tarpits.org (La Brea Tar Pits official); Scientific American, 'Fossils Buried in LA Tar Pit Show Why Saber-Toothed Cats Blinked Out of Existence'.  (Legend.)

question: One kind of ice-age deer grew antlers that spanned over 4.2 metres - nearly 14 feet - wider than any deer's rack before or since. It ranged widely across Europe and its last survivors held on in western Russia until about 7,700 years ago. Which deer wore the widest antlers ever known?
answer: The Irish elk
choices: The Irish elk
The moose
The red deer
The reindeer
context: Megaloceros giganteus bore the largest antlers of any known deer, over 4.2 m across. It vanished from Ireland and most of Europe around 12,000 years ago; the last populations survived in western Russia to about 7,700 years ago. Source: Natural History Museum (London), 'The Irish elk'; Wikipedia, 'Irish elk'.  (Legend.)

question: One giant plant-eater of ice-age South America was a ground sloth that stood as tall as a modern elephant - up to 20 feet long and weighing as much as four tonnes - shuffling on huge claws before it vanished around 10,000 years ago. Which of these ground sloths was that elephant-sized giant?
answer: Megatherium
choices: Megatherium
Mylodon
Eremotherium
Nothrotheriops
context: The giant ground sloth Megatherium stood as tall as a modern elephant - up to 6 m (20 ft) long and about 4 tonnes - and went extinct in South America around 10,000-11,000 years ago. Some Megatherium bones carry cut marks, showing humans butchered them. Source: Natural History Museum (London), 'What was Megatherium?'; Britannica, 'Megatherium'.  (Legend.)

question: In 1952 archaeologist Emil Haury dug into the Naco site in Arizona and uncovered the skeleton of a Columbian mammoth with Clovis stone spear points still lodged in its bones. A single lucky throw might have felled a lesser beast - but this mammoth was so big it took a barrage. How many Clovis points did Haury find buried in it?
answer: Eight points
choices: Eight points
One point
Two points
Twenty-six points
context: At Naco (1952), Haury found a Columbian mammoth with eight Clovis fluted points in it; at the nearby Lehner site he later found mammoth bones with 13 points beside ancient fire hearths. These kill sites are cornerstone evidence for the overkill case. Source: Wikipedia, 'Naco Mammoth Kill Site' and 'Lehner Mammoth-Kill Site'.  (Legend.)

question: New Zealand's moa - giant flightless birds - were hunted to extinction within under 150 years of Polynesian settlement, most between about 1380 and 1440. You might picture a teeming multitude of hunters to erase every species that fast. Just how thin on the ground was the human population that did it?
answer: Never more than about one person per 100 square km
choices: Never more than about one person per 100 square km
About one person per 10 square km
About one person per square km
A few thousand people total across both islands
context: Moa were not in decline before Polynesian arrival, yet all species were hunted out within ~150 years by an extremely sparse human population - never exceeding about one person per 100 sq km. That tiny population still exterminated them, the clearest overkill case. Source: Nature Communications, 'An extremely low-density human population exterminated New Zealand moa'; PNAS, 'Extinct New Zealand megafauna were not in decline before human colonization'.  (Legend.)

question: The climate side argues the giants starved as their world melted. Around 14,500 years ago rapid warming began breaking apart the vast, dry grassland called the 'mammoth steppe.' Ancient DNA locked in Yukon soil records exactly what replaced those rich grasses between about 13,500 and 10,000 years ago. What took over the mammoths' feeding grounds?
answer: Mosses, shrubs and tundra
choices: Mosses, shrubs and tundra
Dense evergreen conifer forest
Bare gravel and permanent ice
Flower-rich meadows even lusher than before
context: Rising moisture turned the nutritious mammoth-steppe grasses into mosses, shrubs and tundra as the ice sheets retreated; ancient environmental DNA from Yukon soil records the turnover directly. This habitat-collapse evidence anchors the climate case. Source: Nature Communications, 'Collapse of the mammoth-steppe in central Yukon as revealed by ancient environmental DNA' (2021); Wikipedia, 'Mammoth steppe'.

question: Woolly mammoths clung on in isolated island refuges long after the last mainland herds were gone. On Russia's Wrangel Island, how late did the very last woolly mammoths survive - measured against Egypt's pyramids?
answer: Still alive well after the Great Pyramid was built
choices: Still alive well after the Great Pyramid was built
Died out a thousand years before the first pyramid
Vanished at the same time as the last mainland herds
Gone long before farming or any city existed
context: Woolly mammoths survived to about 5,600 years ago on St. Paul Island (Alaska), where fresh water dried up, and to roughly 4,000 years ago on Wrangel Island - later than the Great Pyramid of Giza, built about 4,500 years ago. Refuge survivors are a key climate-side point. Source: PNAS, 'Timing and causes of mid-Holocene mammoth extinction on St. Paul Island, Alaska' (2016); Wikipedia, 'Woolly mammoth'.  (Legend.)

question: Many researchers now suspect neither side alone killed the giants but a one-two punch of both. At the La Brea Tar Pits, one proposed mechanism links the two: as humans thinned out the big plant-eaters just when the climate was drying, something dangerous built up across the landscape. According to that La Brea idea, what built up once the grazers were gone?
answer: Unbrowsed brush that fed raging wildfires
choices: Unbrowsed brush that fed raging wildfires
A boom in small burrowing rodents
Erosion as grass roots died back
Weedy plants crowding out the last grasses
context: Many scientists now favor a synergy: climate change shrank and shifted habitats while human hunting pushed already-strained populations over the edge. At La Brea, researchers propose that killing off plant-eaters let wildfire-fuel vegetation build up just as the climate was drying - a one-two punch. Which factor mattered more is genuinely still debated. Source: Scientific American, La Brea study; History.com, 'What Killed Off Giant Animals of the Ice Age?'; PNAS, 'Explaining the Pleistocene megafaunal extinctions'.

question: Genyornis newtoni was a two-metre, 230-kilo flightless 'thunder bird' that stalked Australia until about 47,000 years ago - just as the first people arrived. Its fossil eggshell turns up charred at more than 200 sites, but a wildfire could blacken shell too. Gifford Miller's team found the one clue that fingered human cooks over a natural blaze. What gave them away?
answer: Each shard is seared at one end and raw at the other, the pinpoint burn of an egg on campfire embers
choices: Each shard is seared at one end and raw at the other, the pinpoint burn of an egg on campfire embers
Each shard is scored on the inside with stone-tool cut-marks where a blade cracked the shell apart
The shards lie heaped in rings around fire-cracked hearth-stones dragged into the camp
The shards were crammed into ash-lined roasting pits packed with charred animal bone
context: A wildfire racing across the land would bake a buried shell fairly evenly, but embers heaped under a single egg scorch one side toward 1,000 F while the far side stays raw - the pattern Gifford Miller's team read as human cooking. The charred shell shows up at more than 200 sites dating to about 47,000 years ago, right as people spread across Australia - the same window the rhino-sized Diprotodon, the marsupial lion Thylacoleo, and the giant short-faced kangaroo Procoptodon disappeared. Miller called it the first secure evidence that humans preyed directly on Australia's giant animals, by raiding Genyornis nests. That is overkill-side evidence; how much of the killing was people versus a shifting climate stays an open question. Source: Miller et al. 2016, 'Human predation contributed to the extinction of the Australian megafaunal bird Genyornis newtoni ~47 ka,' Nature Communications 7:10496; University of Colorado Boulder news, 29 Jan 2016.

question: No human set foot on St. Paul Island, in the Bering Sea, until 1787 - yet its woolly mammoths had already died out around 5,600 years ago. Five separate lines of evidence, from dung-fungus spores to lake chemistry, pin that date so tightly it is called one of the best-dated extinctions ever. With no hunter anywhere near, what finished the last mammoths?
answer: Their one freshwater lake silted up until there was nothing left to drink
choices: Their one freshwater lake silted up until there was nothing left to drink
A string of savage winters buried the last of their grazing under deep snow
The rising sea drowned the low-lying island out from under their feet
A creeping epidemic ran through the small, inbred herd until none were left
context: As the ice age ended, St. Paul shrank from part of the Bering land bridge to a scrap of about 110 square kilometres holding a single freshwater lake. Radiocarbon on 14 mammoth bones, three species of dung-fungus spore, sediment DNA, pollen, and lake-core chemistry all land on roughly 5,600 years ago (sediment DNA: 5,650 +/- 80 years), making it one of the most precisely dated prehistoric extinctions known. Russell Graham's team argued the mammoths hastened their own end: penned on shrinking ground, they stripped the plants and trampled the shoreline, speeding the erosion that choked the lake with silt until the drinking water gave out. Because no person reached the island until 1787 CE, it is a rare clean test - environment alone, with no hunter in sight, erasing a mammoth population. It pulls against the mainland kill-sites, and the overkill-versus-climate debate stays unresolved. Source: Graham et al. 2016, PNAS 113(33):9310-9314; Penn State University news.

question: A shark that spends its days lying flat and motionless on a coral reef, its blotchy patterned body melting into the seabed so prey drifts right up to it. This whole family of bottom-dwelling sharks goes by what fitting nickname?
answer: Carpet sharks
choices: Carpet sharks
Hammerhead sharks
Whale sharks
Reef tiger sharks
context: Wobbegongs make up the family Orectolobidae, the 'carpet sharks' — named for the bold, symmetrical patterns that let their whole outline vanish into the reef floor, so unwary fish swim within reach. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wobbegong

question: The wobbegong is a shark that lies flat and vanishes into a coral reef. Its very name comes from an Australian Aboriginal word — what does that word mean?
answer: Shaggy beard
choices: Shaggy beard
Silent hunter
Reef ghost
Sleeping stone
context: The name 'wobbegong' is thought to derive from an Australian Aboriginal word for 'shaggy beard,' after the branching dermal lobes that fringe the mouth. On the tasselled wobbegong these 'whisker' lobes both hide its silhouette and feel the water around its jaws. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wobbegong; https://saveourseas.com/worldofsharks/species/tasselled-wobbegong

question: A tasselled wobbegong lies dead still except for one small movement: it slowly waves its tail back and forth for hours. Why would a hidden ambush predator bother moving its tail at all?
answer: Its tail fin mimics a small fish, drawing prey close
choices: Its tail fin mimics a small fish, drawing prey close
It fans oxygen-rich water over its gills to breathe
It sweeps loose sand off its back to stay hidden
It signals to rival wobbegongs to keep their distance
context: The tasselled wobbegong's caudal (tail) fin resembles a small fish, complete with a dark eyespot near its base. By waving it slowly, the motionless shark lures curious fish straight into striking range — its beard hides it while its tail baits the trap. Source: https://saveourseas.com/worldofsharks/species/tasselled-wobbegong

question: A fish drifts within inches of a resting wobbegong. The shark can't chase — it has barely moved in hours. How does it seize the fish in a single instant?
answer: It gapes its jaws and vacuums the fish straight in
choices: It gapes its jaws and vacuums the fish straight in
It flares its gill flaps to trap the fish in a rush of water
It stuns the fish with a sharp electric pulse
It pins the fish against the reef with its broad fins
context: When prey comes close the wobbegong flings its jaws open at lightning speed; the sudden drop in pressure creates powerful suction that vacuums the fish in and swallows it whole. It doesn't chase — it waits, then inhales. Source: https://oceana.org/marine-life/tasselled-wobbegong/; https://www.floridamuseum.ufl.edu/discover-fish/species-profiles/tasselled-wobbegong/

question: Scientists watching a 1.3-metre tasselled wobbegong saw it spend a whole evening slowly gulping down a meal nearly 80% of its own length. What did this 'sleepy' shark swallow whole?
answer: A brownbanded bamboo shark
choices: A brownbanded bamboo shark
A basking sea turtle
A giant reef octopus
A giant moray eel
context: A 2010 paper in the journal Coral Reefs documented a 1.3-metre tasselled wobbegong swallowing a 1.0-metre brownbanded bamboo shark — another shark nearly its own length — gulping it down over the course of an evening. Source: https://saveourseas.com/worldofsharks/species/tasselled-wobbegong; https://www.livescience.com/animals/sharks/tasselled-wobbegong-the-master-of-disguise-that-can-eat-a-shark-almost-as-big-as-itself  (Legend.)

question: A buried wobbegong lies motionless for hours, so it cannot swim water through its mouth the way cruising sharks do -- and drawing water in through its mouth would only suck in a cloud of sand. How does it keep breathing without giving its hiding spot away?
answer: It snorkels clean water down through spiracles set behind its eyes
choices: It snorkels clean water down through spiracles set behind its eyes
It absorbs dissolved oxygen straight through its thin, patterned skin
It reverses the current, pulling water in through its five gill slits
It rises for a quick gulp of air, then sinks back into the sand
context: A resting shark cannot ram-ventilate by swimming, and inhaling through its mouth on the seabed would pack its gills with sediment. Wobbegongs breathe instead through a pair of large crescent-shaped spiracles -- openings just behind each eye. The spiracle draws clean water from above like a snorkel, and the shark buccal-pumps it back over the gills, so it can lie buried and motionless for hours without stirring up the cover that hides it. Source: Catalina Island Marine Institute, 'Spiracles: The Secret of the Benthic Shark,' and the Georgia Aquarium spotted-wobbegong profile -- https://cimi.org/blog/spiracles-the-secret-of-the-benthic-shark/

question: Wobbegongs look like shaggy relics that could have crept across reefs since the age of the dinosaurs. When Corrigan and Beheregaray sequenced the family's DNA and dated the branches, what did the tree reveal about the carpet sharks?
answer: The living species radiated only recently, within the last 20 million years
choices: The living species radiated only recently, within the last 20 million years
They are unchanged living fossils dating back to the age of the dinosaurs
They descend from a deep-water ancestor that only later colonised the reefs
Their carpet camouflage arose separately in several unrelated shark lineages
context: Despite the living-fossil look, the DNA says the opposite. Corrigan and Beheregaray's molecular phylogeny ('A recent shark radiation,' Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution, 2009) found the whole family Orectolobidae only began splitting into today's species in the Miocene, within roughly the last 20 million years, inside the Indo-Australian region. The burst was driven by the Miocene collision of the Indo-Australian and Eurasian tectonic plates, which reshaped the shallow reefs these ambush sharks depend on -- so the 'ancient carpet' is really a recent evolutionary flowering. Source: Corrigan & Beheregaray 2009, Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution 52 -- https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1055790309000736  (Legend.)

question: A stocky, short-legged predator prowls the far northern forests: shaped like a small bear, dark brown with pale side-stripes, and about the size of a medium dog. Despite that bear-like build, it is actually the largest land-dwelling member of one particular animal family. Which family?
answer: The weasel family (mustelids)
choices: The weasel family (mustelids)
The bear family (ursids)
The dog family (canids)
The raccoon family (procyonids)
context: The wolverine (Gulo gulo) is the largest terrestrial mustelid — the same family as weasels, otters, and badgers. Males run about 25–40 lb, roughly medium-dog sized, but the low-slung, muscular, bear-like shape fools people into guessing a small bear. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolverine

question: A wolverine — only 20 to 40 pounds — pads up to a fresh caribou carcass that a much larger wolf is standing over. For its size, what the wolverine does next is startling. What does it do?
answer: Drives the wolf off the kill and takes the carcass
choices: Drives the wolf off the kill and takes the carcass
Rolls onto its back to beg the wolf for a share
Waits at a distance until the wolf leaves
Buries itself in the snow to hide from the wolf
context: Lone wolverines have been documented driving wolves, bears, and cougars off their kills and claiming the carcass — ferocity out of all proportion to a 20–40 lb body. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolverine

question: Deep, soft snow blankets the north. A wolverine glides across the top of it, barely sinking, while a deer or elk many times its weight breaks through the crust and flounders belly-deep. What lets the wolverine stay up on powder that swallows heavier animals?
answer: Huge, fur-soled paws that spread its weight like snowshoes
choices: Huge, fur-soled paws that spread its weight like snowshoes
Hollow, air-filled bones that make it float
A layer of trapped body gas that buoys it up
Long claws that hook onto an icy under-layer
context: The wolverine's oversized, five-toed, fur-soled paws spread its weight so it skims over deep powder while heavier prey post-hole through. Using the snow itself as a weapon, it can run down and kill animals more than ten times its size. Source: https://www.vitalground.org/winters-warrior-wolverine-fragile-fierce/

question: A wolverine tears into a carcass frozen rock-solid in the Arctic winter — food most predators simply can't get their teeth into. Its secret is in the back of its jaw: the upper molars aren't aimed straight back like most mammals'. How are they set instead?
answer: Rotated roughly 90 degrees sideways, turned inward
choices: Rotated roughly 90 degrees sideways, turned inward
Fused into a single flat grinding plate
Curved forward into small tusks
Replaced by a hard toothless ridge of bone
context: A weasel-family trait taken to an extreme: the wolverine's upper molars are rotated about 90 degrees inward, turning the back teeth into a shearing-and-crushing tool that rips meat and bone off carcasses frozen solid. Source: https://wolverinefoundation.org/dentition-of-the-wolverine

question: A small brown forest creature of North America wears a dark band running from its snout back across each eye, like a mask pulled over a bandit's face — and it can freeze solid all winter and thaw back to life in spring. Which animal is this?
answer: the wood frog
choices: the wood frog
the spotted salamander
the pine marten
the ringtail cat
context: The wood frog (Lithobates sylvaticus) is a small brown frog of North American forests, marked by a dark 'robber's mask' band running from the snout back over each eye; it survives winter by freezing solid. Source: Discover Wildlife (discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/amphibians/wood-frog).

question: Most amphibians keep to warmer country, and biologists long assumed none could endure the true far north. Then one small brown frog broke the record for the northernmost amphibian on Earth. How far north does the wood frog actually range?
answer: north of the Arctic Circle
choices: north of the Arctic Circle
just short of the tree line
only to the Great Lakes
no farther than the northern Rockies
context: The wood frog ranges farther north than any other frog or amphibian on Earth — it is the only amphibian living north of the Arctic Circle, up past Alaska's Brooks Range. Source: University of Alaska Fairbanks (uaf.edu/news/wood-frogs-farthest-north-amphibian-cannibals.php).  (Legend.)

question: An Arctic winter would kill almost any frog. The wood frog survives it by doing something that looks, to any observer, exactly like dying — for weeks or even months at a stretch. What does the wood frog do to get through winter?
answer: it freezes solid, heart stopped
choices: it freezes solid, heart stopped
it burrows below the frost line
it slows its heart to one beat an hour
it drains its blood into its bladder
context: To survive winter the wood frog lets itself freeze solid: its heart stops, it stops breathing, its kidneys shut down, and it lies stiff and frozen — appearing completely dead — for weeks or months. Wood frogs have been recorded staying frozen as long as eight months. Source: Discover Wildlife; National Geographic 'Antifreeze-Like Blood Lets Frogs Freeze'.  (Legend.)

question: When a frozen wood frog is examined mid-winter, you'd expect maybe a skin of frost. Instead, a startling share of the water inside its whole body has turned to solid ice while it lies there stiff. About how much?
answer: around two-thirds of it
choices: around two-thirds of it
around a tenth of it
only the skin and toes
just the fluid in its gut
context: When the wood frog freezes, as much as roughly 65% — about two-thirds — of the water in its body turns to solid ice, yet it revives when it thaws. Source: National Wildlife Federation / Discover Wildlife roundup, search-verified across multiple wood-frog freeze sources.  (Legend.)

question: As the freeze begins, a wood frog's cells are in danger of losing all their water to the growing ice outside and collapsing. In response its liver suddenly floods the body with one substance that acts as a natural antifreeze. What does the liver dump in?
answer: a flood of glucose
choices: a flood of glucose
a rush of adrenaline
a wash of salt brine
a surge of alcohol
context: As freezing starts, the wood frog's liver dumps a flood of glucose (sugar) into its cells as natural antifreeze; the syrupy sugar keeps the cells from losing all their water and collapsing. Far-north Alaskan frogs add a second cryoprotectant, urea. Source: National Geographic; PMC PMC4331536.

question: When spring warms a frozen wood frog, it does not thaw evenly like a block of ice on a counter. It thaws in a particular order that gives it the best chance of coming back. Which parts revive first?
answer: the heart and brain
choices: the heart and brain
the legs and feet
the outer skin
the eyes alone
context: The wood frog thaws from the inside out — heart and brain come back first. The ice melts in about 20 minutes; the heart takes another 20-30 minutes to restart before the frog gulps, breathes, and hops away. Source: National Geographic 'Antifreeze-Like Blood Lets Frogs Freeze'.  (Legend.)

question: Unlike forest frogs that must trek to distant open water each spring, the wood frog spends the whole winter frozen right beside the shallow woodland pool where it will breed. Among the frogs of its forest, what does staying put win the wood frog?
answer: wake and mate earliest
choices: wake and mate earliest
skip the risky overland trek
claim the best pool spots
avoid the migration die-off
context: Because it overwinters right beside its breeding site and thaws as the vernal pools fill with snowmelt, the wood frog wakes and mates earlier than rival frogs that must wait for open water to thaw. Source: Discover Wildlife; Vermont Center for Ecostudies vernal-pool page.

question: A woodpecker clings upright on a tree trunk and hammers its beak into the bark in a fast, machine-gun blur. In one busy day of chiseling for insects, roughly how many times does it strike the tree?
answer: 8,000 to 12,000 strikes
choices: 8,000 to 12,000 strikes
about 200 strikes
about 800 strikes
about 40 strikes
context: A woodpecker can hammer up to about 20 times every second and lands 8,000 to 12,000 strikes in a single day. Source: ScienceABC / BirdWatchingDaily, https://www.scienceabc.com/nature/animals/how-woodpeckers-dont-get-concussions

question: A woodpecker needs a rock-solid grip to hammer bark straight-on without sliding off a vertical trunk. How are its four toes on each foot arranged to clamp the wood?
answer: Two toes forward and two toes backward
choices: Two toes forward and two toes backward
All four toes pointing forward
Three forward and one tiny backward
Two fused into a hoof-like pad
context: This two-forward, two-backward arrangement is called a zygodactyl foot, and it gives the bird a firm four-point clamp on the bark. Source: Avian Report 'Woodpecker Feet', https://avianreport.com/woodpecker-feet/

question: Feet alone can't hold a woodpecker steady against a smooth vertical trunk. It turns itself into a living tripod by pressing what third point against the bark?
answer: Its stiff, spiny tail feathers
choices: Its stiff, spiny tail feathers
Its folded wingtips
Its long hooked claws
The underside of its beak
context: The stiff, spiny tail feathers push against the trunk and, together with the two feet, form a stable three-point brace. Source: Avian Report / Animal Kingdom, https://avianreport.com/woodpecker-feet/

question: A long, loud drumroll rolls out of a dead tree, and most people assume the woodpecker is digging out insects. But that kind of hammering usually isn't feeding at all. What is the bird really doing?
answer: Claiming territory and calling a mate
choices: Claiming territory and calling a mate
Sharpening its worn-down beak
Warning the flock of a hawk overhead
Loosening sap to drink from the wood
context: A long, loud burst of hammering is a drummed message that stakes out territory and calls for a mate, the way a songbird sings. Source: All About Birds (Cornell Lab), https://www.allaboutbirds.org/news/how-to-recognize-woodpeckers-by-their-drumming-sounds/

question: A woodpecker will sometimes drum hard and fast on a surface that holds no insects at all, just to send its message. Which surface does it seek out for this?
answer: A metal gutter or street sign
choices: A metal gutter or street sign
A hollow dead snag
A wooden fence rail
A house's plastic downspout
context: Because a drum's job is to carry, woodpeckers pound loud man-made things like metal gutters, chimney caps, and street signs to broadcast as far as possible. Source: Cornell Lab / Sialis.org drumming, https://www.sialis.org/drumming/

question: A Northern Flicker jabs its short bill at an anthill, but the ants are deep down twisting tunnels its beak can't reach. How does the flicker still empty the nest?
answer: It shoots its tongue inches out past the beak tip
choices: It shoots its tongue inches out past the beak tip
It floods the tunnels with sticky spit
It cracks the mound open with its feet
It waits for the ants to march up on their own
context: The Northern Flicker's tongue extends about two inches beyond its beak to snake deep into anthills; woodpecker tongues in general can reach several inches past the bill. Source: American Bird Conservancy, https://abcbirds.org/news/woodpecker-tongues/

question: Deep in a tunnel, a woodpecker's tongue has to grab slippery grubs it can barely feel. Beyond just being long, what makes the tongue TIP able to snag and hold slippery prey?
answer: Backward-facing barbs and sticky saliva
choices: Backward-facing barbs and sticky saliva
A hard bony hook
A ring of tiny suction cups
A mild numbing venom
context: The tongue tip carries tiny backward-facing barbs and glue-like saliva that snag and hold insects probed from deep inside a tunnel. Source: Avian Report, https://avianreport.com/woodpecker-tongue/

question: The acorn woodpecker drills a single special 'granary' tree and jams one acorn into each hole it makes. The largest known of these storehouse trees held about how many acorns?
answer: Around 50,000 acorns
choices: Around 50,000 acorns
Around 50 acorns
Around 500 acorns
Around 5,000 acorns
context: The acorn woodpecker builds a 'granary' tree drilled with thousands of holes; the largest known granary held around 50,000 acorns. As the acorns dry and shrink, the birds move each one to a snugger hole. Source: Atlas Obscura / Cornell Bird Academy, https://academy.allaboutbirds.org/storing-food-the-granaries-of-acorn-woodpeckers/  (Legend.)

question: A woodpecker's tongue is so long it can't just sit in the mouth. Where does its bony support run when the tongue is drawn back inside the head?
answer: Up over the top and around the back of the skull
choices: Up over the top and around the back of the skull
Coiled inside the throat like a spring
Folded flat under the lower beak
Stored in a pouch below the eye
context: The tongue's bony support starts near the nostril, splits into a V between the eyes, loops over the top and around the back of the skull, then meets again at the base of the lower beak. Source: American Bird Conservancy, https://abcbirds.org/news/woodpecker-tongues/  (Legend.)

question: A woodpecker's beak slams into a tree and its head snaps to a dead stop from a hard blow. People long assumed a spongy skull cushions the brain like a helmet. What did 2022 research find the skull actually does?
answer: Acts as a stiff hammer for a harder hit
choices: Acts as a stiff hammer for a harder hit
Bends like rubber to absorb shock
Redirects the shock down the neck and out the tail
Splits the impact between the two jaws
context: 2022 research found the skull is no cushion; it works as a stiff hammer that makes pecking more powerful, and the brain stays safe for other reasons. Source: Current Biology 2022 'Woodpeckers minimize cranial absorption of shocks', https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(22)00855-7  (Legend.)

question: If the skull isn't a cushion, why doesn't all that hammering bruise the woodpecker's brain the way a hard knock rattles ours? The 2022 answer is surprisingly plain. What keeps its brain safe?
answer: It's small and packed too snugly to slosh
choices: It's small and packed too snugly to slosh
A cushion of fluid floats it in place
It shuts down blood flow on impact
It's wrapped in a thick fatty pad
context: The brain is small and held so snugly inside the skull that it barely moves, so it can't slosh and bruise the way a loose brain would, even at decelerations near 1,000 g. Source: ScienceABC, https://www.scienceabc.com/nature/animals/how-woodpeckers-dont-get-concussions

question: A woodpecker's head whips to a dead stop 20 times a second - hard enough that an eyeball could jolt forward out of its socket or shake the retina loose. About a millisecond before each blow, what comes to the eye's rescue?
answer: A see-through third eyelid snaps shut and pins the eye
choices: A see-through third eyelid snaps shut and pins the eye
A shelf of bone slides up from the cheek to cap the eye
A ring of muscle behind it hauls the eyeball deeper in
A pad of dense fat swells forward to wedge it firmly still
context: This is the nictitating membrane, a tough translucent 'third eyelid' many birds have but which the woodpecker puts to extreme use. Firing about one millisecond before each hammer blow, it does double duty: it shields the eyeball from flying wood chips AND physically clamps the eye in its socket, so the ~1,000+ g deceleration can't shake the retina loose or pop the eye forward. None of the bird's famous headgear helps here - the eye needs its own seatbelt. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nictitating_membrane; corroborated by ophthalmologist Ivan Schwab's award-winning work and The Naturalist's Notebook (thenaturalistsnotebook.com) pileated-woodpecker anatomy.

question: For decades, textbooks flatly declared woodpeckers immune to head injury - all that hammering, no harm done. In 2018, Boston University scientists stained the preserved brains of ten woodpeckers and compared them to blackbirds that don't drum. What turned up in the woodpeckers?
answer: Clumps of tau protein, the marker seen in concussed athletes
choices: Clumps of tau protein, the marker seen in concussed athletes
Torn axon fibers, the damage seen in whiplash victims
Rusty microbleeds, the staining seen in blast survivors
Shrunken dead neurons, the loss seen in stroke patients
context: The study, led by George Farah (PLOS ONE, Feb 2018), used Gallyas silver staining and anti-phospho-tau immunohistochemistry on museum brains of 10 woodpeckers versus 5 red-winged blackbird controls. Most woodpeckers showed build-ups of tau - the very protein tied to CTE in concussed football players - while the controls had none. It punctured the tidy 'immune to injury' story, but the debate is genuinely unsettled: whether that tau is a protective adaptation or a sign of real damage remains unresolved. Source: journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0191526 (PubMed 29394252); coverage: CBC News, 'woodpecker-brain-damage-protein.'

question: A shaggy, cold-adapted cousin of today's elephants once roamed a frozen grassland called the mammoth steppe during the last ice age. Which ice-age giant was it?
answer: The woolly mammoth
choices: The woolly mammoth
The woolly rhinoceros
The giant ground sloth
The Irish elk
context: The woolly mammoth (Mammuthus primigenius) grazed the vast, dry 'mammoth steppe' that stretched across ice-age Eurasia and North America, browsing on grasses, sedges, and forbs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth

question: A modern elephant flaps huge ears to shed heat, but a woolly mammoth living in the frozen north needed the opposite. Compared with an elephant's, its ears were:
answer: Tiny, only about a foot long
choices: Tiny, only about a foot long
Even bigger and floppier
Feathered for extra warmth
Folded flat and hairless
context: A woolly mammoth's ears were only about 38 cm long and its tail just 36 cm, so it lost far less body heat and avoided frostbite in the deep cold. Small extremities are a classic cold adaptation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth

question: A mammoth's coat had two jobs. Long coarse guard hairs draped over its flanks like a skirt to shed snow; underneath sat something soft doing the real work of trapping warmth. What was it?
answer: A dense underfur of fine hair
choices: A dense underfur of fine hair
A layer of loose feathers
A coat of oily scales
Bare wrinkled skin
context: The outer guard hairs ran up to about 90 cm long, while the soft underwool beneath, up to about 8 cm long, trapped a warm layer of air against the skin. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth

question: Even under a thick coat, a woolly mammoth needed more against ice-age cold. Beneath its skin lay a layer nearly four inches thick, plus a shoulder hump storing the same stuff as fuel for lean winters. What was it?
answer: Insulating fat
choices: Insulating fat
Extra muscle
Stored water
Hollow air pockets
context: The fat layer reached about 10 cm thick, and the fatty shoulder hump acted as a fuel and water reserve to carry the animal through hungry winters. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth

question: A woolly mammoth's tusks curved and spiraled toward each other in front of its face. Worn flat patches on preserved tusks reveal a daily chore they did with them. What was it?
answer: Sweeping snow off buried grass
choices: Sweeping snow off buried grass
Digging burrows to sleep in
Cracking open frozen rivers
Stripping bark from tall trees
context: Preserved tusks show flat polished wear patches up to 30 cm long from sweeping snow off the grass the mammoth wanted to eat, and from fighting. The biggest male tusk ever measured ran 4.05 m along the curve. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth

question: In the Siberian permafrost, whole woolly mammoths turn up after tens of thousands of years so complete that scientists can study something no bone could ever preserve. What survives inside them?
answer: Skin, hair, and stomach contents
choices: Skin, hair, and stomach contents
Only the outline in the ice
Just the tusks and teeth
A hollow shell of dried hide
context: Frozen mammoths have been recovered from Siberian permafrost with skin, hair, and even stomach contents intact after tens of thousands of years; named specimens include Berezovka, Yukagir, Dima, and Lyuba. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth  (Legend.)

question: In 2007 a Nenets reindeer herder, Yuri Khudi, and his sons found a nearly complete baby mammoth on Russia's Yamal Peninsula. Khudi named her after his wife, a name meaning 'Love.' What did they call her?
answer: Lyuba
choices: Lyuba
Dima
Berezovka
Yukagir
context: Yuri Khudi and his sons found the calf in May 2007; 'Lyuba' comes from the Russian for 'love.' She is about the size of a large dog and weighed roughly 50 kg. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyuba_(mammoth)  (Legend.)

question: Baby mammoth Lyuba was only about a month old when she died some 42,000 years ago, yet her body is the best-preserved mammoth ever found. Scientists were long puzzled by how such a healthy calf died; close study of her body finally revealed the cause. What killed her?
answer: She inhaled mud and choked
choices: She inhaled mud and choked
A cave lion ambushed her
She froze in a blizzard
She starved after losing her herd
context: Bogged down in a muddy river, Lyuba inhaled fine mud that suffocated her; afterward lactic-acid bacteria 'pickled' her body, sealing it against decay for 42,000 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyuba_(mammoth)  (Legend.)

question: Inside baby Lyuba's gut, scientists found her mother's milk and, stranger still, her mother's dung. Why would a calf mammoth swallow dung, just as baby elephants do today?
answer: To seed her gut with plant-digesting bacteria
choices: To seed her gut with plant-digesting bacteria
To ease the pain of a sore belly
To mark herself with the herd's scent
To fill up when milk ran short
context: Calf mammoths, like baby elephants, ate some of their mother's dung to stock their bellies with the gut bacteria needed to digest tough plants. Source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S104061821100173X  (Legend.)

question: Most woolly mammoths vanished from the mainland around 10,000 years ago, but a marooned population clung on far longer at one remote Arctic outpost, still alive after the Giza pyramids were built. Where?
answer: Wrangel Island
choices: Wrangel Island
Iceland
Svalbard
The Faroe Islands
context: A small, isolated population survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean until only about 4,000 years ago. This last line was inbred and descended from a single maternal lineage, and studies point to defects such as a weakened sense of smell and a coat that no longer insulated well. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth  (Legend.)

question: A woolly mammoth saved precious body heat by letting its legs, ears, and trunk run bitterly cold, yet tissue that cold normally cannot wring enough oxygen from passing blood to survive. To crack the trick, scientists rebuilt the mammoth's real blood protein from 43,000-year-old DNA and tested it. What set it apart?
answer: Its hemoglobin released oxygen even in near-freezing blood
choices: Its hemoglobin released oxygen even in near-freezing blood
It flushed the cold limbs with warm blood in bursts
Its chilled muscles ran on fuel that needs no oxygen
Its blood stockpiled spare oxygen in extra red cells
context: In a 2010 study led by Kevin Campbell, scientists spliced a ~43,000-year-old mammoth hemoglobin gene into E. coli and brewed the actual protein, 'like taking a blood sample from a living mammoth.' Normally hemoglobin grips oxygen more tightly as it cools, so chilled blood struggles to hand it off; three unusual amino-acid changes lowered that energy cost, letting mammoth blood keep unloading oxygen to near-freezing legs, ears, and trunk, something a modern elephant's blood cannot do. That let the mammoth run its extremities cold to save heat without starving them. The 'built for cold' story reached all the way down into the blood chemistry itself. Source: Campbell et al. 2010, Nature Genetics, 'Substitutions in woolly mammoth hemoglobin confer biochemical properties adaptive for cold tolerance' (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20436470; nature.com/articles/ng.574).

question: On the frozen mammoth steppe of the ice age, the woolly mammoth was not the only heavyweight grazing that cold grassland. One horn-bearing neighbor plodded the same ground beside it, crowned with a single great horn instead of tusks. Which ice-age beast?
answer: The woolly rhinoceros
choices: The woolly rhinoceros
The steppe bison
The saiga antelope
The reindeer
context: The woolly rhinoceros shared the cold, grassy mammoth steppe with woolly mammoths, reindeer, bison, and saiga antelope -- an ice-age crew scientists call the Mammuthus-Coelodonta Faunal Complex. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_rhinoceros

question: Living rhinos have a rounded front horn. The woolly rhinoceros's front horn was different: flattened side-to-side, almost blade-like, and worn smooth near the tip. That flat, scuffed horn reveals what it did with its head all winter to keep feeding.
answer: Swept it across the ground to brush snow off the frozen grass
choices: Swept it across the ground to brush snow off the frozen grass
Locked it against rivals in shoving matches over territory
Levered it under frozen trees to strip away edible bark
Drove it into hardened soil to hook up buried roots
context: The flattened blade-like horn and the sideways wear pattern together show the woolly rhino swept its head to-and-fro to clear snow off the frozen steppe grass it grazed -- the horn's shape revealing the habit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_rhinoceros

question: In 2014 a whole baby woolly rhinoceros -- nicknamed 'Sasha,' the only intact calf of its kind ever found -- thawed out of Siberian permafrost with its wool coat still on. Once the gray, muddy remains were cleaned, one detail startled the scientists.
answer: Its original fur was a light strawberry-blond
choices: Its original fur was a light strawberry-blond
Its horn had already grown longer than its legs
It still had its mother's milk in its stomach
Its skin was patterned with dark stripes
context: Sasha (Yakutia, 2014) is the only intact woolly rhino baby ever found; cleaning the remains revealed the calf's fur had been a light strawberry-blond, not the dull gray it looked at first. Legend-flagged for the celebrated find. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/sasha-woolly-rhino-mummy-siberia-ice-age-spd

question: Over 31,000 years ago, ice-age artists painted woolly rhinos on the walls of Chauvet Cave in France. Because frozen woolly rhino bodies later turned up in the permafrost, scientists could finally check those ancient paintings against the real animal -- and found what?
answer: The cave painters had drawn the rhino strikingly accurately
choices: The cave painters had drawn the rhino strikingly accurately
The painted horns were far longer than any real horn
The artists had invented a second horn that never existed
The paintings showed a coat the frozen bodies lacked
context: With BOTH frozen woolly rhino bodies AND the Chauvet Cave portraits of the same species, scientists confirmed the ice-age painters got it right, drawing the animal accurately from life tens of thousands of years ago. Legend-flagged for the famous Chauvet scene of two rhinos butting horns. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_rhinoceros

question: The easy story was that ice-age hunters slowly picked off the woolly rhinoceros until none were left. In 2020 a team led by Love Dalen read the DNA of rhinos frozen in Siberian permafrost to test that story, tracking the population across thousands of years. The genomes told a surprising tale about the rhinos' last stretch of time. What did the DNA reveal?
answer: They stayed numerous and genetically healthy, with no long decline
choices: They stayed numerous and genetically healthy, with no long decline
They had been inbreeding and dwindling for tens of thousands of years
They had boomed to record numbers in the centuries before vanishing
Their numbers had already collapsed long before people reached Siberia
context: In Lord et al. (Current Biology, 13 Aug 2020), Dalen's group sequenced one complete nuclear genome and 14 mitochondrial genomes from frozen woolly rhinos. The DNA showed the population stayed large, diverse, and not inbred from about 29,000 years ago until at least ~18,500 years ago -- meaning the rhinos thrived in northeast Siberia alongside humans for over 13,000 years without declining. The rapid crash to extinction around 14,000 years ago instead lines up with the sudden Bolling-Allerod warming. This remains a genuine, still-open scientific debate: the 'overkill' hypothesis (Paul Martin, 1967) blames human hunting, while studies like this one point to abrupt climate change -- the evidence does not yet settle it either way. Source: Wikipedia, 'Woolly rhinoceros'; Lord et al. 2020, Current Biology (via sci.news and sciencedirect.com). Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403).

question: A deep-sea crab hauled up from the sunless Pacific in 2005 was ghost-white all over, with pale legs so thickly coated in silky hair that scientists reached for a legendary monster to nickname it. Which creature lent the crab its common name?
answer: The Yeti of the Himalayas
choices: The Yeti of the Himalayas
The Kraken of the North Sea
The Loch Ness Monster
The Minotaur of Crete
context: The 'yeti crab' (Kiwa hirsuta) takes its nickname from the fabled Yeti, the abominable snowman of the Himalayas, because of its pale, hair-covered legs living in the sunless deep. Source: MBARI, 'Discovery of the Yeti Crab' (mbari.org/news/discovery-of-the-yeti-crab).

question: The furry arms of the yeti crab are not really fur but dense rows of bristles, and the crab does something with them no animal was ever caught doing before: it deliberately grows, tends, and then eats a living crop right on its own body. What is that crop?
answer: Bacteria it farms on its bristles
choices: Bacteria it farms on its bristles
Tiny shrimp it snares in the hairs
Algae that photosynthesizes there
Coral polyps that bud on it
context: The bristles (setae) carry a living crop of bacteria that the crab grows and later eats, using comb-like mouthparts to scrape it off. It is the first animal ever shown to deliberately farm bacteria on its own body for food. Source: National Geographic, 'Yeti Crabs Farm Food on Own Claws—A First'.  (Legend.)

question: A yeti crab crouched at a deep-sea vent was seen swaying its bristly claws slowly back and forth over the warm chemical-rich water seeping out, the same motion over and over. It was not swimming or fighting. Why the rhythmic waving?
answer: To wash nutrients over its crop
choices: To wash nutrients over its crop
To fan itself cool near the vent
To signal a mate in the dark
To sift the mud for buried worms
context: The slow 'dance' washes nutrient-rich vent fluid over the bacteria growing on the crab's bristles, helping them grow, like fanning a garden. Biologist Andrew Thurber, who filmed a dancing Kiwa puravida off Costa Rica, said 'baffled would be a good word for how I felt.' Source: National Geographic; Nature 2011 (Thurber et al.).  (Legend.)

question: In 2010, British scientists aboard the RRS James Cook pulled up an Antarctic yeti crab with such a thick mat of bristles across its chest that they nicknamed it after a famously hairy-chested celebrity. What did they call the Kiwa tyleri?
answer: The Hoff crab
choices: The Hoff crab
The Rambo crab
The Tarzan crab
The Elvis crab
context: The dense chest bristles reminded the scientists of actor David Hasselhoff, so Kiwa tyleri became the 'Hoff crab.' Unlike its cousins that farm bacteria on their arms, this species grows its bacterial garden mostly on that hairy chest. Source: Wikipedia 'Kiwa tyleri'; Thatje et al. 2015.  (Legend.)

question: The Antarctic Hoff crab spends its whole life jammed into a band of seafloor only a few meters wide around a deep-sea vent, never straying. Wander a little past that narrow strip, and what finishes the crab off?
answer: The near-freezing Antarctic seawater
choices: The near-freezing Antarctic seawater
The vent chemicals its gut bacteria need vanish
Its shell cannot harden in the mineral-poor water
The falling pressure ruptures its gills
context: The diffuse vent fluid the crab huddles in is only about 3.5-20 C, while the surrounding Antarctic seawater is near freezing (about 0 to -1.3 C). Too close to the vent and the crab cooks; too far and it freezes, so its entire world is just a few meters wide. Source: PLOS ONE / Thatje et al. 2015.  (Legend.)

question: A yeti crab grows its dinner as a living fuzz of bacteria matted along its bristly claws — but bristles are not a mouth, and the crop still has to travel from its arms into its stomach. Filmed feeding at the vent, the crab keeps drawing one mouth-appendage back across those claws. How does the crop get from claw to mouth?
answer: The appendage is a fine comb that rakes the bacteria loose.
choices: The appendage is a fine comb that rakes the bacteria loose.
The appendage is a hollow straw that sucks the bacteria up.
The appendage is a sticky pad that traps the bacteria fast.
The appendage is a sharp blade that shaves the bristles off.
context: The comb is a row of highly modified, comb-like setae on the crab's third maxilliped — a mouthpart. In Kiwa puravida, the crab draws it across the bacteria-coated bristles on its claws to scrape the crop free and into its mouth, in effect eating from a fork it grew on its own face. Source: Thurber, Jones & Schnabel 2011, PLOS ONE, 'Dancing for Food in the Deep Sea' — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3227565/

question: Adult Hoff crabs pack against the vent's warmth, and drifting a few centimeters into the cold starves or chills them. Yet a female heavy with eggs turns and crawls the opposite way — out onto bare, near-freezing rock — and squats there fasting for months. The eggs leave her no choice. What forces a brooding mother off the warm vent?
answer: Vent warmth would cook her developing eggs before they hatch.
choices: Vent warmth would cook her developing eggs before they hatch.
Only the cold water carries the oxygen her eggs must have.
Rival crabs raid the crowded vent and devour exposed eggs.
The packed vent leaves no bare surface to anchor her clutch.
context: In Kiwa tyleri, the Hoff crab, egg-carrying females migrate off the warm diffuse flow (about 3.5-20 C, where adults feed) out into 0 to -1.3 C Southern Ocean water, because the embryos cannot survive the vent's heat. Cut off from their bacterial crop, the mothers stop feeding entirely and burn stored fat while their yolk-fueled (lecithotrophic) larvae slowly develop — a stark tradeoff between reproducing and eating. Source: Thatje, Marsh, Roterman, Mavrogordato & Linse 2015, PLOS ONE, 'Adaptations to Hydrothermal Vent Life in Kiwa tyleri' — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4480985/  (Legend.)

question: A healthy carpenter ant picks up a few tiny spores in the rainforest, and days later those spores have grown through its whole body and are steering it to its death. People call the ant a 'zombie,' but no supernatural force is involved — a living thing has grown inside it and taken the controls. What is the real hijacker?
answer: A fungus
choices: A fungus
A virus
A worm
A bacterium
context: The carpenter ant (genus Camponotus) is taken over by the fungus Ophiocordyceps unilateralis. It is a fungus, not a virus or a 'zombie disease' — the fungus itself grows through the ant's body and drives its final acts. Source: Britannica, 'Zombie-ant fungus'; Penn State News, 'Getting to the bottom of the zombie ant phenomenon.'  (Legend.)

question: In its final act, the infected carpenter ant leaves its trail and climbs down into the understory. Then, controlled by the fungus inside it, the dying ant does one last thing that fixes its body in place for good. What does it do?
answer: Bites down and locks its jaws onto a leaf
choices: Bites down and locks its jaws onto a leaf
Digs a burrow into the soil
Wraps itself in a silk cocoon
Curls up under a fallen log
context: The fungus drives the ant into a 'death grip' — it clamps its mandibles onto a leaf and dies there. This locked bite holds the corpse in exactly the spot the fungus needs. Source: Britannica, 'Zombie-ant fungus'; Penn State News, 'Getting to the bottom of the zombie ant phenomenon.'  (Legend.)

question: A dying carpenter ant doesn't just bite anywhere on a leaf — 98% of infected ants in one Thai study clamped onto the exact same part of the underside of the leaf. Where does the death grip land?
answer: On the main vein
choices: On the main vein
On the flat middle of the blade
On the pointed leaf tip
On the leaf's stem
context: The ants bite onto a major primary or secondary vein on the underside (abaxial surface) of the leaf, not the flat blade. The tough vein is thick and sturdy enough to anchor the corpse for weeks while the fungus finishes growing. Source: Hughes et al. 2011, 'Behavioral mechanisms and morphological symptoms of zombie ants,' BMC Ecology (PMC3118224).

question: Infected carpenter ants don't clamp down just anywhere in the forest — over and over, they bite at almost exactly 25 cm above the ground, not higher and not lower. Why does the fungus drive its host to that one narrow band of the rainforest?
answer: It has the temperature and humidity the fungus needs to grow
choices: It has the temperature and humidity the fungus needs to grow
It is the exact height the fungus can no longer climb
It keeps the corpse away from ants on the ground trail
It is where leaves are widest for a strong bite
context: The bites cluster at about 25 cm (roughly 10 inches) up — measured at 25 ± 3 cm. That low, cool, humid understory has the precise temperature and moisture the fungus requires to grow and make spores. Source: Hughes et al. 2011, BMC Ecology (PMC3118224); Penn State News, 'Getting to the bottom of the zombie ant phenomenon.'

question: Researchers watching a whole population of infected carpenter ants found the final death-grip bites weren't scattered through the day — the ants all switched from erratic wandering to clamping down at almost the same moment. What sets the timing of the synchronized bite?
answer: Solar noon, with the sun overhead
choices: Solar noon, with the sun overhead
The first light of dawn
Nightfall, in full darkness
A sudden drop in temperature
context: Across the population the bites happened abruptly at midday — the sun was measured about 80 degrees up when the ants clamped down. The trigger is tied to the daily solar cycle. Source: Hughes et al. 2011, BMC Ecology (PMC3118224).  (Legend.)

question: A few days after the carpenter ant dies clamped to its leaf, the fungus pushes a long stalk out of the corpse and rains fresh spores onto the trail below, ready to infect the next ants passing under it. Which part of the dead ant does the stalk erupt from?
answer: The head
choices: The head
The abdomen
A leg joint
The jaws
context: The spore-bearing stalk grows out through a hole in the dead ant's head, then showers spores down onto the foraging trail below to catch the next ants. Source: Penn State News, 'Getting to the bottom of the zombie ant phenomenon'; Britannica, 'Zombie-ant fungus.'  (Legend.)

question: People call it 'mind control,' so in 2017 Maridel Fredericksen and David Hughes rebuilt an infected carpenter ant in 3-D expecting to find the fungus packed into one command center. Instead they found it threaded through tissue all over the body — yet one organ, the one you'd bet on for mind control, held almost no fungus at all. Which organ was it?
answer: The brain
choices: The brain
The gut
The antennae
The compound eyes
context: The fungus surrounded and invaded the ant's muscle fibers throughout the body, forming an interconnected network — but no fungal cells were found inside the brain. It is a body-hijack working the muscles directly, not a puppeteer reading the mind from inside the skull. Source: Fredericksen et al. 2017, PNAS (doi:10.1073/pnas.1711673114); Penn State News, "'Zombie ant' brains left intact by fungal parasite."  (Legend.)
